definitions.definition: 180 kriyāvādins, 84 akriyāvādins, 67 ajñānikas, 32 vainayikas, derived combinatorially from the Jain categories and the candidate causes.

name: The 4,448 diseases

definitions.definition: The Siddha tradition counts 4,448 diseases, classified by humour and organ; the classification is usually credited to Agastya.

notes: The count is the tradition's standard figure; which text first gives it is not recalled (low).

definitions.definition: The jīva is a mere semblance of consciousness in the intellect, neither real nor the original; knowing it as semblance, only consciousness remains (Sureśvara; cf. BS 2.3.50).
Everything is a manifestation (ābhāsa) of consciousness within itself, appearing as if external; the world is real as manifestation and unfolded on consciousness's own screen by its will.

relations.note: Advaita's apparent transformation; the Kashmir Śaivas hold manifestation to be real and free

name: The analytical methods of the Abhidhamma books

definitions.definition: Matrix classification (Dhammasaṅgaṇī), analysis by sutta and Abhidhamma methods with a question section (Vibhaṅga), inclusion/association (Dhātukathā), designation of persons (Puggalapaññatti), formal debate (Kathāvatthu), converse pairs (Yamaka) and conditional relations (Paṭṭhāna).

name: How the Abhidhamma was taught and handed down

definitions.definition: The Buddha taught it in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, gave the method to Sāriputta daily, and Sāriputta taught it; it was recited at the First Council and preserved by reciters; the Kathāvatthu was expanded by Moggaliputta Tissa at the Third Council from the Buddha's outline.

name: The Abhidharma as the word of the Buddha

definitions.definition: The Buddha taught the Abhidharma in scattered form; Kātyāyanīputra and others gathered it, as Dharmatrāta gathered the Udāna verses.
Not the Buddha's word; the Abhidharma basket consists of sūtras that teach dharma characteristics.
The Pali tradition holds the seven Abhidhamma books to be buddhavacana (the Kathāvatthu being set out by Moggaliputta Tissa on the Buddha's outline).

Three realms; five destinies; the receptacle world on circles of wind, water and gold, with Meru, seven golden ranges, four continents and the iron ring; eight hot and eight cold hells; heavens up to the form realm; world systems grouped in thousands up to the trichiliocosm.

relations.note: The Kośa's realms and places (twenty desire-realm places, seventeen form places) vs the Pali thirty-one planes; counts differ.

definitions.definition: Letters/words convey word-meanings as an intermediate step, like the flame in cooking; the word-meanings then convey the sentence meaning.

name: The superknowledges as necessary for benefiting beings

definitions.definition: Like a bird without grown wings, one without superknowledges cannot work for beings; they depend on calm abiding and should be sought with effort for the sake of others.
Pliancy and workability of mind lead to the higher knowledges and travel to other realms to honour buddhas; yet even knowledge of others' minds does not accord with its object except in a buddha.
The devotee's affectionate complaint that the Mother keeps her child turning like the blindfolded oil-press ox (Rāmprasād).

Vase, secret, wisdom-gnosis and fourth consecrations, ripening body, speech, mind and gnosis and authorizing the corresponding practices; the higher ones involve restricted yoga; Atiśa forbids them to celibates.
Without the precious consecration one is like an outcaste hoping to be king (Queen Dohā v16).
Seven consecrations 'of the child' (water, crown, ribbon, vajra and bell, great vow, name, permission) and the higher consecrations; three conventional, the fourth ultimate.
The dependent nature as the minds and mental factors of the three realms: it exists, while the duality of grasped and grasper it projects does not; emptiness exists within it.

relations.note: it is the dependent nature

definitions.definition: By practice and dispassion the activities of the mind are stilled (YS 1.12); Vyāsa: the mind is a river flowing both ways; dispassion dries the stream toward objects, the practice of seeing discernment opens the stream of discernment (YBh 1.12).

The two means of stilling (1.12): practice is effort toward stability, grounded by long, uninterrupted, devoted cultivation (1.13–14); dispassion dams the stream toward objects while practice opens the stream of discrimination (YBh 1.12).

Sense checked by J only through the teachings listed in evidence, all of which J read against the Sanskrit; the entity text itself was not read line by line unless stated.

definitions.definition: The two goods of the Ratnāvalī: first the dharma of higher status (good rebirth through ethics and giving), then definite goodness (liberation through the insight that 'I' and 'mine' are false); faith leads to the first, wisdom to the second (RĀ 1.3–5).

The truthful, non-angry, non-violent, calm, pure, generous, devout, compassionate, balanced and self-controlled person 'enjoys constant rasāyana' and alone gains its full benefits (Ca Ci 1.4.30-35); 'conduct according to the śāstra … is complete rasāyana' (AHS Utt 39.179-181).

name: The saving regard of the teacher (ācārya-abhimāna)

definitions.definition: For one who can do nothing, being held as his own by a true teacher is itself enough for salvation; the teacher's embrace is the final means.
The teacher is indispensable as the one who imparts the mantras and may perform surrender on the disciple's behalf.

name: Devotion to the teacher as sufficient (ācārya-niṣṭhā)

definitions.definition: Madhurakavi found his teacher by following a light and tested him with a riddle; thereafter saying his teacher's name was sweeter to him than approaching Kṛṣṇa, and he knew no other god; the teacher became mother and father to him. The recitation of this devotion to the teacher is what recovered the Prabandham for Nāthamuni.
Devotion comes chiefly by the grace of great souls, who are not different from the Lord.

relations.note: the disciple's sole reliance on the teacher (niṣṭhā) and the teacher's saving regard (abhimāna) are two sides of the Śrīvaiṣṇava teaching that Madhurakavi's devotion founds

definitions.definition: The Lord and his powers (internal, marginal, external) are simultaneously one and different, in a way reason cannot resolve and revelation affirms; the soul is his marginal power, a 'difference-and-non-difference manifestation'.

name: The taking and releasing halves of the year

definitions.definition: In the northern course the sun and wind take away moisture and strength; in the southern course the moon gives it back (Ca Sū 6.4-8; AHS Sū 3.2-7).
Self and world arose without cause, held by one who recalls only the arising of perception after life among the non-percipient gods, or by reasoning.

name: The three planes: divine, bodily, sacrificial

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.29–8.4 gives a set of six things to be known with the Lord and defines each: Brahman is the supreme imperishable; adhyātma is own being (svabhāva); karma is the sending-forth (visarga) that brings about beings' states of existence; adhibhūta is the perishable state; adhidaivata is puruṣa ('person'); adhiyajña is the Lord himself here in the body. Those who know him so know him even at the time of departure.

Correspondences are drawn in parallel series: in the realm of the gods the sun is the eater and the moon the food; in the realm of the self the breath is the eater and food is its food (ŚB 10.6.2.1–4).
The Āraṇyaka saṃhitā-teachings extend the planes to speech: stops, sibilants and vowels = earth, atmosphere, sky = eye, ear, mind (AA 3.2.5).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.

The planes are named as such in ŚB 10–11 (adhidevatam / adhyātmam) and in Nirukta 11.4 (adhiyajñam / adhidaivatam). Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:satapatha-brahmana:10.6.2.1-4, tea:aitareya-aranyaka:3.2.5.

members: adhiyajña = the Lord in the body

definitions.definition: Who may perform a rite and receive its fruit: humans, not animals or gods (MS 6.1.4–5); women as well as men, husband and wife jointly (MS 6.1.8, 6.1.17); for Vedic rites, those with Vedic learning, excluding śūdras (MS 6.1.25–38); the eligibility injunction states ownership of the fruit.

relations.note: Vedānta distinguishes the eligible for ritual from the eligible for Brahman-inquiry (P4-stage)

definitions.definition: The Śrauta rites are for human beings able to undertake them, excluding the maimed, the unlearned, eunuchs and śūdras; for the three higher classes, and for women too (KŚS 1.1.1–8).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:katyayana-srautasutra:1.1.1-8 (confirmed).

name: All schools valid for their qualified followers

definitions.definition: Bhāskararāya: the many schools are valid for their respective qualified followers; censuring them unsettles those followers, who then fall from both their own school and the Kaula, for which they are not qualified (on the Kaula Upaniṣad); hence Paraśurāma's rule of no censure (PKS 1.14).

Seekers are low, middle or highest by birth and by qualities; the highest is the dispassionate renunciant with sole refuge in Viṣṇu; eligibility for the Veda, the Tantra and the Name differs by class and gender, and the Mahābhārata was composed for those not entitled to the Veda.
The sūtras are commented on in topic-sections, each with subject, doubt, prima facie view, conclusion and connection; commentators group and count them differently.

name: The adhikaraṇa method of interpretation

definitions.definition: Each topic is set out in five members — subject, doubt, connection, prima facie view, conclusion — and the conclusion becomes a maxim (nyāya) applied elsewhere.

notes: Some later manuals give 'nirṇaya' or 'prayojana' in place of saṅgati; the Nyāyamālā's own list is followed.

relations.note: both treat teachings as means relative to the student

definitions.definition: The teaching method of scripture: provisionally superimpose (creation, sheaths, attributes) and then retract, leaving the substratum; creation-teachings are means (GK 3.15).

relations.note: Śaṅkara: 'the learned call this superimposition avidyā'

definitions.definition: The appearance, like memory, of something previously seen in something else; the mutual superimposition of self and not-self, natural and beginningless, called avidyā, the root of all empirical dealings.

Ānandaghana sings the Jina as the soul's only beloved and husband, a love without beginning or end (Covīsī 1), and the path as hidden to reason and quarrel but open to experience (Covīsī 2); devotion to the Jina is devotion to the soul's own perfected nature.
Banārsīdās and later Hindi Adhyātma poets (Dyānatrāy, Bhūdhardās) write devotional padas addressed to the self and the Jina.

name: The injunction of Vedic study and the transmission of the Veda

definitions.definition: The Veda is learned from a teacher by the injunction 'one's own Veda is to be studied'; after study one stays at the teacher's house to inquire into its sentences; every study presupposes an earlier teacher's study, without beginning.
The buddha without beginning or end, gnosis as its only eye (Nāmasaṃgīti 100).
The non-dual gnosis of immutable bliss and empty form that teaches the Kālacakra; explicitly not a creator.

Merit and demerit (qualities of selves) that cause motions without visible cause — needle and magnet, ascent of sap, upward flame, the first motion of atoms and minds — and the mind's departure at death and entry at birth; its absence is liberation (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.8, 5.2.14, 5.2.19–20 C); acts done for the unseen (VS 6.2.2).
A supersensible cause of experience must be admitted (NK stabaka 1); the Lord sets the stores of merit and demerit in motion (NBh 4.1.21).

relations.note: Mīmāṃsā's apūrva

definitions.definition: The lineage recited in the tradition: Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā (Padmabhava), Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śuka, Gauḍapāda, Govinda, Śaṅkara, and his disciples Padmapāda, Hastāmalaka, Toṭaka and the Vārttikakāra (Sureśvara).

One ever joined in non-duality succeeds; abandoning the attitude of duality one lives by non-dual conduct; the yogī takes fragrance and stench alike and is unstained by merit and sin; forms of conduct (as child, madman, king...) are whatever vow he wills; no one may be made to take the caru by force (KJN 11–12).

name: Beings are buddhas obscured by adventitious stains

definitions.definition: Beings are buddhas but covered by adventitious stains; removing them, they are buddhas (Hevajra II.4).
The stain is neither adventitious nor long-lasting, neither born without mind nor abiding in it; it is destroyed by union with emptiness while mind's gnosis-nature remains (Sekoddeśa 129–133).

relations.note: The Hevajra statement echoes the buddha-nature teaching of the Tathāgatagarbha sūtras; the Sekoddeśa's analysis refines the 'adventitious' language.

name: Āgama as rooted in or continuous with the Veda
notes: Bhāskararāya's statement read in the local Setubandha e-text; no teaching id created (U23).

definitions.definition: The Pāñcarātra is the Lord's own word and of Vedic root; its followers are brahmins.
Vaikhānasa worship follows the path of the śruti in every rite and is performed with Vedic mantras.
Tantras that teach the worship of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Rudra, Paraśiva or Sundarī are rooted in Upaniṣads such as the Rāmatāpanī and are beyond doubt (Bhāskararāya, Setubandha introduction).

name: The Āgamas as the body of Sadāśiva

relations.note: both treat a sacred whole as the Lord's body

definitions.definition: The 28 tantras are the limbs of Sadāśiva's body made of tantras and mantras, from the Kāmika as his feet to the Vātula as his garment; one scripture, manifold through the hearers.

name: The ages, the Manu-periods and the day of Brahmā

definitions.definition: The siddhāntas compute the caturyuga as 4,320,000 solar years divided 4:3:2:1, 71 caturyugas to a manvantara and 1,000 to a kalpa (SS 1.15–21; BSS 1.7–9); Āryabhaṭa alone makes the four quarters equal (Āryabhaṭīya 1.5, 3.9).

Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000, 1,000 divine years with twilights; 12,000 make a divine age; a thousand divine ages a day of Brahmā; seventy-one a Manu-period; creations and dissolutions without number (MDh 1.68–80).
The age-names appear in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa as states of a man — lying, rising, standing, moving (AB 7.15).

evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)
checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:manusmrti:1.68-72 (confirmed); tea:manusmrti:1.79-80 (confirmed); tea:manusmrti:1.5-6 (confirmed); tea:aitareya-brahmana:7.15 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Nothing is to be shunned as impure; the practitioner overcomes disgust, fear, shame and the other fetters, since one freed from the fetters is Maheśvara (Kulārṇava 13.90–91, cited in Aghora teaching).
Non-dual conduct: fragrance and stench alike; unstained by merit and sin (KJN 11.26–29).

relations.standpoint: the conduct of one freed from fetters
relations.note: both teach non-difference of pure and impure as the conduct of the free; Aghora's own texts not yet extracted

definitions.definition: Dattātreya (ādiguru) → Bābā Kālūrām → Bābā Kīnārām → the heads of Krīm Kuṇḍ (Bījārām and successors to the present Siddhārth Gautam Rām); a parallel line through Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām's Sarveśvarī Samūh.
In Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām's teaching Aghora is expressed as service of the sick (leprosy) and the outcaste and as rejection of caste and social evils, open to householders.

name: The cremation ground and the skull in Aghora

definitions.definition: The Aghora ascetic dwells and practises in the cremation ground, eats from a skull bowl and smears ash, so as to see Śiva in what is feared; details are secret and restricted.
The skull is the best of vessels for the Kaula rite (KJN 12.13).

name: Agni, the fire in the rite and in all

definitions.definition: Agni is the household priest, messenger and mouth of the gods who carries the oblation (RV 1.1), churned by Atharvan (6.16.13), guardian of ṛta, present as the flesh-eating and the oblation-bearing fire (10.16.9), as Vaiśvānara the light set in the heart (6.9).

The great brick altar built over a year in five layers, typically falcon-shaped, sevenfold to a hundred-and-one-fold (ŚB 10.2.3.18); the builder rebuilds Prajāpati, gains immortality after death and escapes re-death (ŚB 10.4.3); its 'secret' (rahasya) in ŚB 10 interiorizes it as fires built of mind, speech, breath, eye, ear and knowledge (ŚB 10.5.3).
Its layout by cord and peg, and the transformation of its shapes with equal area, are the subject of the Śulbasūtras.

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:satapatha-brahmana:10.2.3.18 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:10.4.3.1-10 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:10.5.3.1-12 (confirmed).

name: The digestive fires (agni)

definitions.definition: Pitta is the body's only fire (Su Sū 21.9); the belly-fire, the five element-fires and the seven tissue-fires (Ca Ci 15.13-15; counted as thirteen by later authors); four states — balanced, irregular, sharp, weak (AHS Sū 1.8); ojas, tejas and the prāṇas depend on agni, 'agni is the root' (Ca Ci 15.3-4).

notes: Ca Ci 15 checked in the local Devanāgarī e-text only.

definitions.definition: The referent of 'I' is the soul itself, not the ego-evolute of prakṛti; the 'I' persists in deep sleep and in release.

relations.note: the self known as 'I'; rejects the Advaita view that the 'I' is a superimposition

definitions.definition: The principle of self-assertion (SK 24), from which the organs and subtle elements proceed in its vaikṛta, bhūtādi and taijasa aspects (SK 25); it, not puruṣa, is the agent (SS 6.54).

name: Struck and unstruck sound (āhata and anāhata nāda)

definitions.definition: Nāda is twofold (ŚR 1.2.3). The unstruck is worshipped by sages by the guru's path as an easy means to liberation but has no charm for people; the struck, made into music through śrutis and notes, delights the world and breaks worldly existence (ŚR 1.2.163–167).

name: Non-injury and ritual action (Mīmāṃsā view)

definitions.definition: Violence is prohibited; a rite stated as a means for one who wishes to harm (the Śyena) is harmful, and the Veda does not enjoin the harming itself.

notes: The Bhāṭṭa position that killing enjoined as part of a rite (e.g. the Agnīṣomīya animal) is not sin is general knowledge, not checked here; see dsp:sacrificial-killing.

name: Non-violence in Jainism

definitions.definition: Violence is the severing of vitalities through careless, passion-driven activity (TS 7.13); life pervades earth, water, fire, air and plants (2.13); souls support one another (5.21). Inwardly, non-violence is the non-arising of passion and violence its arising; the other sins are forms of violence (Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 42, 44). Non-violence is called the supreme Brahman (Svayambhūstotra).
Material and psychic violence (dravya- and bhāva-hiṃsā) are distinguished; psychic violence is the root.

The pure, eternal law proclaimed by all Arhats: no being is to be killed, ruled, enslaved, tormented or driven away; all beings love life; 'you are the one you intend to kill'; the essence of wisdom is not to kill anything.

members: saṅkalpī / ārambhī / udyogī / virodhī hiṃsā (lay classification)

name: The unity of Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā (aikaśāstrya)

definitions.definition: Ritual inquiry and inquiry into Brahman are one science; the first prepares for the second, and rightly read presupposes the Lord.
To protect the health of the healthy and to allay the disorders of the sick (Ca Sū 30.26; Su Sū 1.14); the whole tantra aims at the equilibrium of the dhātus (Ca Sū 1.53).

name: The Lord's lordly yoga (yogam aiśvaram): beings in him, he not in them

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord's own power, paired with his manifestation: 'this vibhūti and yoga of mine' known in truth (10.7); Arjuna asks to hear it (10.18) and to see it; with the divine eye Arjuna is to 'behold my sovereign yoga' (11.8); the supreme form was shown 'by my own yoga' (11.47). The Lord is accordingly addressed as yogin (10.17) and great lord of yoga (11.4, 11.9).

Bhagavad Gītā 9.4–6 with 7.12: all this is pervaded by the Lord in unmanifest form; all beings abide in him, but he is not established in them; and yet beings do not abide in him — 'behold my lordly yoga'; sustaining beings and bringing them into being, his self does not abide in them; as the great wind moving everywhere abides in space, so all beings abide in him. States of the guṇas are from him, he not in them, they in him.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Chs. 10–12 contribution (extractor B; extractor A links the verses by trm:yoga). Repeats 9.5 'paśya me yogam aiśvaram' (11.8). Kept distinct from the practitioner's yoga, which the same chapters also name (10.7 avikampa yoga, 12.6 ananya yoga, 12.9 abhyāsa-yoga).
alt_notes: New concept for the Gītā's own phrase (9.5). Extractor A's cpt:aisvara-yoga and extractor B's cpt:yogam-aisvaram are merged under A's id (the stem form of the phrase). The text leaves the paradox of 9.4–5 (beings in him, and yet not in him) unresolved; the commentators' resolutions are recorded in the notes of the teaching 9.5.

definitions.definition: Power is a sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) giving non-obstruction (SK 45); the commentators list becoming minute, great, light, reaching, irresistible will, lordship, control and going where one wishes (Gauḍapāda on SK 23). Warnings: attachment to the powers is the error 'delusion', through which gods like Indra fall back (Gauḍapāda on SK 48); gaining the powers is not liberation, since they end (SS 5.82; 4.32). Yogic powers are nonetheless not to be denied (SS 5.128).
The breath's natural sound — ha going out, sa coming in — repeated 21,600 times a day without effort; knowing it gives liberation (Dhyānabindu 61–65; Yogacūḍāmaṇi 31–35; Haṃsa).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 5 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text. Some rest on teachings whose ref was corrected or only partly confirmed; the content is located, only the numbering changes: tea:hamsa-upanisad:3-hamsa-mantra (corrected); tea:hamsa-upanisad:3-hamsa-pervades-bodies (corrected).

definitions.definition: No existent arises from itself, from another, from both or without cause (MMK 1.1); non-arising (anutpāda) is the emptiness of own-nature, not the unborn self.
From the highest standpoint nothing is ever born — not from itself, another, both or neither; creation-teachings are means to lead the mind (GK 3.15).

relations.note: Gauḍapāda's non-origination is of the non-dual self; the Madhyamaka's is of all dharmas without a remaining self — the Advaita tradition insists on the difference (GK 4.99)

name: Life and four kinds of atom (Tamil Ājīvaka)

definitions.definition: (Tamil report) Five principles: life (uyir) and four kinds of beginningless, indestructible, unchanging atoms (earth, water, fire, air) that combine into bodies and separate; a single atom is seen only by the divine eye.

(As reported) Nakedness, licking the hands, refusing food brought or prepared, eating at long intervals; fourfold 'fierce, severe' austerity, abstention from tasty food, restraint of the tongue; yet (Jain report) a rule allowing cold water, seeds, food made for the ascetic and women.

name: Makkhali's enumerations of births, karmas and worlds

definitions.definition: (As reported) 1,400,000 kinds of birth, 500 kinds of karma, 62 paths, 62 intermediate aeons, six classes, eight stages of a person, 4,900 kinds of Ājīvaka, 3,000 hells, 36 dust-realms, sevenfold wombs, gods, humans, goblins, lakes, knots, precipices and dreams — all within 8,400,000 great aeons.

name: The six disācaras

definitions.definition: (Jain report) Six 'wanderers of the directions' who drew the eightfold Mahānimitta from the Pūrvas and shared it with Gosāla.

notes: Names recalled with low confidence; verify against Bhagavatī 15.

definitions.definition: (As reported) Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca and Makkhali Gosāla — the supremely white class, the only three the Ājīvikas recognize as having made an end, models of bodily austerity.
(Jain report) The assembly of the 'ignorant': 67 kinds; nothing about the soul can be known and knowing is useless — ignorance is better.
The ignorant cannot settle their inquiry or teach others; they are blind leading the blind.

name: Tamil love-poetry (akam) and praise-poetry (puṟam) as the language of devotion

definitions.definition: The Āḻvārs cast the soul's love for the Lord in the conventions of Tamil akam poetry — the heroine, her mother and friend, messengers, landscapes, the maṭal — and turn puṟam praise to the Lord's deeds and temples.

name: Death against one's will and death with one's will

definitions.definition: The ignorant die unwillingly, clinging and afraid; the wise and restrained die willingly and composed — the root of the later classification of deaths.

name: The letters a and u (akāram, ukāram)

definitions.definition: The letter 'a' is the root, foot and crown of all and the Supreme itself (taṟparam); 'u' is supreme consciousness (ciṟparam); together they are He and She. Kaṭuveḷi's 'knowing the eight and the two' is read as a and u in Tamil numerals (code language).

relations.note: a and u are the first two elements of Om

name: The mode in the form of the partless (akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti)

definitions.definition: The mental mode arising from the mahāvākya that destroys ignorance and then itself subsides; Brahman is pervaded by the mode but not illumined by the reflected consciousness in it.
'This is silver' is two cognitions, a perception and a memory lacking its 'that', whose difference is not grasped; no cognition as such is false.
(As reported) The doer does no evil and the giver gains no merit (Pūraṇa).
One of the four assemblies (84 kinds): deniers of action, for whom the world is barren and fixed.

name: The imperishable (akṣara)

definitions.definition: That on which space is woven, described only by negations, by whose command sun and moon stand apart; unknown, all rites are finite; the unseen seer (BAU 3.8.8-11); the object of the higher knowledge and source of beings (MuU 1.1.5-7); also the syllable Om.

Bhagavad Gītā 8.3, 8.11, 8.13, 8.20–21: brahman is the supreme imperishable; it is the akṣara of which the knowers of the Veda speak, which passionless ascetics enter and for which people practise brahmacarya; Oṃ is the one-syllable brahman; the eternal unmanifest beyond the unmanifest is called the akṣara, the highest goal, from which there is no return, the Lord's supreme abode.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The imperishable person (akṣara puruṣa), called kūṭastha, set beside the perishable, which is all beings; the highest person, the Lord, is higher even than it (15.16-15.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: In praise Arjuna calls the Lord the imperishable, the supreme to be known (11.18), and 'the imperishable — being and non-being, and what is beyond' (11.37). In ch. 12 'the imperishable, the unmanifest' is the object of a second kind of worship, described as indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, unchanging, immovable and constant; its worshippers also reach the Lord, but their hardship is greater, for the unmanifest goal is hard for the embodied (12.1–5).

notes: Chs. 10–12 contribution (extractor A). In 10.25 and 10.33 akṣara means 'syllable, letter' and is not this concept.

definitions.definition: The unchanging bliss that, joined with empty form, is the goal; bliss that falls away brings dispassion, suffering and death (restricted context).

name: The Akulavīra — the one beyond Kula

definitions.definition: The single reality, the 'hero beyond the Kula', in which all dharmas dissolve like rivers in the ocean; beyond all supports, aims, channels, breath-practices and rituals; neither near nor far; beyond 'is' and 'is not'; the one abiding in it is every god and every teacher (Akulavīra A.3–41, B.52–54).

relations.note: the Akula as realised

definitions.definition: The object-condition must both cause and appear in cognition; atoms cause but do not appear, aggregates appear but do not cause; so the object is the knowable form within cognition.
Contact through the universal (grasping all instances), through a cognition (the presented content of a prior cognition), and born of yoga.
The Laṅkāvatāra identifies the tathāgatagarbha with the ālayavijñāna: it evolves with the seven consciousnesses yet is pure by nature; without it there would be neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.

relations.note: one base seen as defiled (ālaya) and as pure (garbha)

definitions.definition: The eighth consciousness: maturation of karma, receptacle of all seeds, appropriator of the body; unperceived, neutral, flowing like a torrent; proved by the need to explain rebirth, the mindless attainments, the continuity of seeds and the simultaneity of cognitions; it ceases as ālaya at arhatship and is transformed at buddhahood into mirror-like wisdom.

relations.note: Faxiang keeps the ālaya distinct from suchness; the Laṅkāvatāra (ch. 6) identifies the tathāgatagarbha with it

name: Balance of alertness and calm (xingxing jiji)

definitions.definition: Calm without alertness is dullness; alertness without calm is scattered thought (Yongjia).
If illumination loses silence there is aggression; if silence loses illumination, murkiness (Hongzhi).
Jinul's seongjeok deungji; sequential counteraction is the gradual method.

The Āḻvārs approach the Lord as servant (aṭimai, Nammāḻvār), as mother of the child (Periyāḻvār as Yaśodā; Kulaśekhara as Devakī and Kausalyā), as grieving father (Kulaśekhara as Daśaratha), as cowherd companion (the Tiruppāvai girls), as bride and lover (Āṇṭāḷ; Parāṅkuśa- and Parakāla-nāyakī), and as the one who prays for the Lord's own safety (Periyāḻvār's pallāṇṭu).

relations.note: the Āḻvārs' stances answer to the Gauḍīya dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya and madhura rasas, but are not framed as rasas and include the benedictory stance, which the rasa list lacks

name: The Āḻvārs' origin: descents of the Lord's attendants, or souls raised by grace

definitions.definition: The hagiographies present the Āḻvārs as descents (aṃśa) of the Lord's weapons, ornaments and attendants — Nammāḻvār of Viṣvaksena, Periyāḻvār of Garuḍa, Kulaśekhara of the Kaustubha, Tirumaḻicai of the discus, Tirumaṅkai of the bow, Āṇṭāḷ of Bhūdevī — and yet also as bound souls to whom the Lord gave knowledge-and-love by grace (TVM 1.1.1).

notes: Aṃśa assignments recalled with low-to-moderate confidence and vary between lists; which Śrīvaiṣṇava teachers stress which reading is not recorded here (see REPORT gaps).

definitions.definition: Rasa left uncooked through weak fire, vitiated and lodged in the stomach (AHS Sū 13.25); it obstructs the channels and underlies disease; fever arises chiefly in the seat of āma and is treated by digestives (Ca Vi 3.40).

relations.note: āma blocks the channels

definitions.definition: Maitrīpa's mahāmudrā: not engaging the mind in concepts — read as the union of clear light and self-consecration, not as mere absence of thought.
(As reported) Refusing every alternative on the other world, spontaneous beings, fruit of deeds and the Tathāgata after death.
Four grounds: fear of false speech, of grasping, of cross-examination; and dullness.

relations.note: Pali and Jain names for the refusal to affirm

name: Ambubachi: the Goddess's annual menstruation

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: during the three days of ambuvācī in Āṣāḍha the Earth menstruates; at Kāmākhyā the Goddess herself is in her courses, the temple is closed, and on the fourth day it reopens and pieces of red cloth are given as prasāda (the Ambubachi Melā). A Bengali ritual calendar in the Prāṇatoṣiṇī names 'ambuvācī, three days'.

notes: Living temple practice; no scriptural verse anchoring the Kāmākhyā menstruation was checked in Phase B.

name: The āmnāyas (Kaula transmissions)

definitions.definition: Five āmnāyas from Śiva's five faces — Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern, Upper — the Upper supreme (Kulārṇava 3.7; 3.15-19). In the Kashmir–Nepal scheme reported by scholarship (moderate confidence): the Eastern is the Kula/Trika worship, the Southern Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā), the Western Kubjikā, the Northern Kālī (Krama, Guhyakālī); Nepal adds the Upper and speaks of six (ṣaḍāmnāya).
The Paścimāmnāya is 'the western of all paths' (Kubjikāmata 2.21).

notes: The assignment of goddesses to directions differs between texts; only the Kulārṇava's fivefold list is verse-checked here.

definitions.definition: Paramaśiva set forth five transmissions through his five faces (PKS 1.2); the four doors of the Goddess's palace are the eastern, southern, western and northern transmissions (PKS 3.10).

Nectar rains from the moon at the palate and is consumed by the sun; the locks and the reversed practice save it; the body filled with it does not decay (GŚ 36, 55–66); in the sky-circle is an upside-down well of nectar that only the guru-ful drink (Gorakh Bānī).
Contemplated as white, cool, fragrant nectar pouring from the sky, it conquers death and old age (KJN 5.6–11); without nectar no immortality (14.94).

In the haṭha texts the nectar dripping from the moon in the head is saved from the sun's fire by jālandhara, viparītakaraṇī and khecarī (HYP 3.70–79; DYŚ 126–128) and drunk by the yogin with the tongue turned back; the body filled with it is not abandoned by the soul (HYP 3.46; GŚ 66); its 'liquor' (amaravāruṇī) is the true meaning of transgressive drinking (HYP 3.47–49).

Immortality is prayed for as full life and freedom from death (RV 7.59.12), won by soma ('we have become immortal', 8.48.3), by gifts (10.107.2), and as a place in the immortal world of light and bliss (9.113.7–11); 'knowing the Person one goes beyond death; there is no other path' (VS 31.18); 'knowing the ageless self one does not fear death' (AVŚ 10.8.44).

relations.note: Two strands: immortality as a heavenly world reached by rite and merit, and going beyond death by knowledge (VS 31.18; AVŚ 10.8.44).

name: The Mahāmudrā of the amulet box

definitions.definition: Niguma's Mahāmudrā: ground, path and fruit enclosed like the two halves of an amulet box; the three self-liberations; the four faults self-liberated; the four kāyas.
Worship of Viṣṇu is through the fire without form, or in a consecrated image; image worship is praised as best.
Śaṅkaradeva's account of creation and the cosmic cycle, following the Bhāgavata: from the Lord the principles and Brahmā arise, and the worlds unfold and dissolve in cycles.

At the heart the bull bound threefold roars (GŚ 60); purified channels manifest nāda (GŚ-Briggs 101); in Hindi Nāth songs the unstruck sound resounds in the sky-circle; the nād horn is its outer sign.

Two modes of meditation, both necessary: analytical (dpyad sgom) investigates with discernment and is required for faith, renunciation, bodhicitta and emptiness; placement ('jog sgom) holds the mind one-pointedly; in insight analysis itself induces pliancy.

relations.note: Tsongkhapa rejects the claim that all analysis obstructs meditation

definitions.definition: Brahman is bliss (TU 3.6); the self made of bliss is the innermost of the five selves (TU 2.5); 'the essence' (raso vai saḥ) — who could live if this bliss were not in space? (TU 2.7); the highest bliss of the brahma-world on a fraction of which beings live (BAU 4.3.32); the knower of brahman's bliss fears nothing (TU 2.4, 2.9).

name: The scale of bliss (ānanda-mīmāṃsā, Taittirīya 2.8)

definitions.definition: Human bliss at its best, then a hundredfold ascent through gandharvas, fathers, gods, Indra, Bṛhaspati and Prajāpati to the bliss of brahman; each step is also the bliss of a learned man untouched by desire.

A graded measure of bliss: the fullest human bliss multiplied a hundredfold at each step through classes of beings up to the bliss of brahman (TU 2.8; BAU 4.3.33 with a different list), with the refrain that the learned one untouched by desire has each of these.

definitions.definition: Even in liberation bliss is graded: each class of the liberated enjoys a hundredfold more than the one below, up to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Śrī far above and Viṣṇu infinitely above.

relations.note: gradation continues in liberation as graded bliss

definitions.definition: Infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy — the soul's own nature, fully manifest when the four destructive karmas are destroyed (cf. TS 2.4, 10.4).

name: The fulfilment chain of mindfulness of breathing (MN 118)

definitions.definition: MN 118:15 announces and MN 118:16-43 explains a chain: mindfulness of breathing, developed and cultivated, fulfils the four establishments of mindfulness (via the four tetrads, 23-28); these fulfil the seven awakening factors (29-40); these fulfil knowledge and liberation (41-43).

relations.note: mindfulness of breathing fulfils the four establishments (tetrad 1 = body, 2 = feelings, 3 = mind, 4 = dhammas)
the four establishments fulfil the seven awakening factors

definitions.definition: The five aggregates are not-self since they lead to affliction and cannot be commanded (SN 22.59), impermanent and so not fit to be regarded as self (SN 22.59; MN 148); neither self nor what belongs to self is found (MN 22); 'a being' is a convention for the aggregates (SN 5.10; Mil 3.1.1); the Buddha declined 'there is a self' and 'there is no self' before Vacchagotta (SN 44.10).

relations.note: the Upaniṣadic and Nyāya self is what the suttas examine and do not find
the Pudgalavāda 'person' neither identical with nor different from the aggregates (U38)

definitions.definition: The ancestors eat monthly, drink svadhā and have the moon as light (ŚB 2.4.2.2); the paths of the fathers lead to cremation grounds for those who desired offspring (ĀpDh 2.9.23).
Primeval deities of several classes, satisfied by śrāddha offerings for months or forever (MDh 3.192–199; 3.267–272).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, the ancestors (pitaraḥ) depend on the rites of rice-ball and water offerings; when varṇa-mixture follows the destruction of a family, these rites lapse and the ancestors fall (1.42).
Dependent origination and the eightfold path as an ancient path travelled by the Buddhas of old, rediscovered like an overgrown road to a ruined city (SN 12.65).

What is in the cosmos is in the body and the reverse; the Lord fills both (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam invocation). This is the ground on which the Siddhars read the body's supports, circles and channels as a cosmos.

The eternal state of sorrow, without return, reached by the souls fit for darkness; the texts connect it with hatred of Viṣṇu and his devotees and with the conceit 'I am ever the Lord and the world is unreal'.
Jīvas are many, each with its own ignorance; one is liberated while others remain bound.

Reality is many-sided: a thing is permanent and impermanent, one and many, existent and non-existent, each in a definite respect (TS 5.30–32); every absolute (ekānta) assertion grasps only one side and is refuted (Āptamīmāṃsā). The Jina's word is the union of the partial views (Sanmati 3.69).
The Jain doctrine accepts all standpoints without partisanship (Anyayogavyavacchedikā 30); Haribhadra and Yaśovijaya apply it irenically to other darśanas.

name: The self (jīva, aṅga, ātman) in the Vīraśaiva view

definitions.definition: The jīva is a part of the formless Śiva through beginningless ignorance, with Śiva abiding in it as fire in the sunstone; the self is eternal and distinct from body, senses and intellect (against Cārvāka and Bauddha), atomic through contact with impurity, yet in truth shining like a lamp in the heart.

Following the six-fold verse of the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā: resolve to do what pleases, avoidance of what displeases, great faith, choosing the Lord as protector, helplessness, and self-offering; Deśika makes the first five limbs and self-offering the principal.
The same qualities are the natural adjuncts of one who knows his dependence, not limbs of a means.

name: The person the size of a thumb

definitions.definition: The inner person dwelling in the heart or the middle of the body, lord of past and future, like a smokeless flame, to be drawn out from the body like the stalk from muñja grass (KU 2.1.12-13, 2.3.17; ŚU 3.13, 5.8).

definitions.definition: Aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, prāpti, prākāmya, vaśitva, īśitṛtva, kāmāvasāyitva (bhāṣya 3.45), listed with the perfection of the body and the non-obstruction by its properties.

Minuteness, lightness, greatness, reach, irresistible will, control, lordship and settling things at will — arising from mastery of the elements, with perfection and invulnerability of the body; though able, the yogin does not overturn the order set by the earlier-perfected Lord (3.45, YBh 3.45).

Tamil aṭṭamā citti — aṇimā, makimā, lakimā, karimā, pirātti, pirākāmiyam, īcattuvam, vacittuvam — taught in the Tirumantiram's third tantra and claimed by the Siddhars; Tāyumāṉavar ranks them below stilling the mind and Kaṭuveḷi says they come only by Śiva's action.

name: Error as appearance of the indescribable (anirvacanīya-khyāti)

definitions.definition: In error an indescribable object (neither real nor unreal) is produced by ignorance for the duration of the error; the Advaita alternative to the rival theories of error.
In Sāṃkhya threefold: buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas, each with its own function, sharing the five vital winds as their common function (SK 29, 33).
One inner organ functioning as mind (doubt), intellect (decision), citta (memory) and ego (I-sense); the adjunct of the jīva, not the self.
Bhāskara: the intellect and mind are real limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the soul, part of what makes it distinct from Brahman until death.

Vallabha addresses his own mind in the Antaḥkaraṇaprabodha; the mind's flowing toward the Lord is itself service (mānasī sevā), the highest form; identification with the inner organ is one of the five joints of ignorance.
The mind is to be engaged in remembrance while the tongue sings (Upadeśāmṛta 8) and instructed (Raghunātha Dāsa's Manaḥśikṣā); bhāva 'softens' the heart (citta-māsṛṇya).

name: Mind and its parts in Dvaita

definitions.definition: Mahat, ahaṃkāra, buddhi and manas are non-eternal, uncompounded products of prakṛti; manas is the sixth sense; memory arises from mental perception; above all these stands the witness, the soul's own awareness.

name: Mind and its parts in Viśiṣṭādvaita

definitions.definition: Mind (manas), intellect (mahat/buddhi) and ahaṃkāra are evolutes of prakṛti and instruments of the soul; the actual knowing is the soul's attributive consciousness working through them; ahaṃkāra as evolute is distinct from the true 'I', the self.
The world is finite, infinite, both or neither, from meditative perception or reasoning.
Between death and birth a being with the form of its coming existence travels to its place of birth, drawn by desire; it feeds on smells.
Accepted (Kv 8.2 commentary).
Denied (Vasumitra).
Denied (Vasumitra).
Denied (Kathāvatthu 8.2).
U44 contribution: the intermediate state is 'blocked' by deity yoga or resting in reality when turning toward rebirth (Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa, from Sukhasiddhi).

bar do: counted as three in the Nāropa texts (birth-death, dream, becoming); the being of the bardo of becoming, seeing its future parents, should regard them as the guru and block rebirth or choose it (Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa).

relations.note: The Tibetan bar do teachings build on the Abhidharma intermediate existence (historical relation).

definitions.definition: The last three limbs are inner compared with the first five (3.7), but outer compared with seedless samādhi (3.8).

The self who dwells in each element, faculty and being, other than it, unknown to it, having it as body and controlling it from within — the unseen seer, the immortal (BAU 3.7.3-23); 'the inner controller, the source of all' (MāU 6).

relations.note: the inner controller is the Lord seen as controlling from within

checks.note: All 2 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 3.7.3-23; MāU 6). It rests on 2 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: The bhakti-yogin must remember the Lord at death; for the surrendered the Lord himself remembers and leads them, so no last remembrance is needed (the fourth of Varadarāja's six sayings).

Because at death the throat will be choked and remembrance may fail, the devotee hands himself to the Lord now: 'I tell you now, for that hour' (Periyāḻvār); 'let my mind enter your feet this very day' (Mukundamālā).
Qualified student, subject, relation and purpose of a teaching.

name: The Anubhava Maṇṭapa

definitions.definition: In the tradition's account, the hall of experience at Kalyāṇa where śaraṇas of every birth, women included, shared and tested their experience under Allama on the throne of the void.

notes: Scholarly account (labeled): known chiefly from the 15th-c. Śūnyasampādane and later hagiography; its form as a formal institution is debated.

name: Substitutes (anukalpa) for the Kaula substances and offerings

definitions.definition: For householders in the Kali age the sweet triad (milk, sugar, honey) replaces wine (Mahānirvāṇa 8.170-171); the last tattva is limited to one's own wife (6.14).
Pumpkin, sugarcane and spirits are 'equal to' an animal victim; coconut water or honey replace wine for the twice-born (Kālikā Purāṇa 67.23; 67.114-115).

name: Non-apprehension as a means of knowledge

definitions.definition: Where no positive means of knowledge arises, non-apprehension makes known absence; absence is real and fourfold.
Not a separate means; the five suffice.
For the most intensely graced, one hearing of the teacher's word reveals one's ever-present nature; nothing is to be done (TĀ 2; Śivadṛṣṭi 7.5-6; Anuttarāṣṭikā).

name: After-cognition (anuvyavasāya): cognition is known by a further cognition

definitions.definition: A cognition does not cognize itself; it is known by a subsequent inner perception 'I know this pot'.
Words are learned from elders' usage in which they occur in action-guiding sentences; hence they express meanings already connected, principally with the 'to-be-done'.
The mind that is sought cannot be found — and so is pacified (Bodhidharma and Huike).
Error apprehends a property where it is absent (Tarkasaṅgraha; Gaṅgeśa).
False cognition is destroyed by knowledge of truth, as dream-notions on waking; it has a real substrate (NS 4.2.33–37).
In extremity the rules may be set aside to preserve life, with later expiation, as in Viśvāmitra's taking the dog's haunch (MBh 12.139).
When livelihood by one's own duty fails, one may live by the next class's means (with limits), as set out in MDh 10.81ff. — though living permanently by another's dharma causes a fall (MDh 10.97).

checks.note: MDh 10.97 was found ('varaṃ svadharmo viguṇo na pārakyaḥ svanuṣṭhitaḥ …') in the āpaddharma section (10.81ff). Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:manusmrti:10.97.

definitions.definition: Whether or not there is another world, one who holds that there is and lives well wins in either case; the denier loses in either case.
The Vedas and the Vedāṅgas are 'lower knowledge'; the higher is that by which the imperishable is attained (MuU 1.1.4–5) — the Vedāṅga tradition's own placement of itself below realization.
Correspondingly, self-knowledge is 'the foremost of all sciences' (MDh 12.85).

definitions.definition: Seven conditions for the Vajjī republic and several sets for the monks — meeting in concord, keeping the rules, honouring elders, forest dwelling, mindfulness (DN 16).

Direct realization of God, which wins his highest grace; the gods are liberated when Hari becomes directly perceived to them; its scope is limited by fitness — few may see him as all-pervading, most see him within their own body.

relations.note: without knowledge there is no abundant grace

definitions.definition: Dvaita: the Veda has no author, not even God; it is eternal and intrinsically valid.
The Veda has no author: names of recensions come from expounders; apparent persons mentioned are sound-similarities; the unbroken chain of study has no beginning; creator-authorship is unprovable.

relations.note: a creator-author of the Veda is rejected

name: Liberation (apavarga) as the end of pain

definitions.definition: Absolute release from pain (NS 1.1.22), reached by removing false knowledge (NS 1.1.2). Mainstream view: the liberated self has neither pleasure nor cognition — there is no proof of an eternal pleasure, and seeking it would bind (NBh 1.1.22); liberation is peace in which all pain is cut off (NBh 1.1.2). Minority view (Bhāsarvajña): the cessation of pain is qualified by the experience of eternal bliss.
A destruction of pain not contemporaneous with any prior absence of pain in the same self (Muktivāda).

relations.note: the same state described through adṛṣṭa and the body

name: Exclusion (apoha) as the meaning of words

definitions.definition: Words and concepts do not reach real universals or the particulars; they apply by excluding what is other; Dharmakīrti grounds this in the similar effects of particulars, Ratnakīrti defines the word-meaning as a positive thing qualified by exclusion.

relations.note: denies the reality of the universal (sāmānya) category; see dsp:reality-of-universals

definitions.definition: Because of great compassion the Buddhas do not abide in nirvāṇa but remain acting for the whole world (Bhāvanākrama I).
The buddhas' nirvāṇa, abiding neither in saṃsāra nor in quiescence, by wisdom and compassion.

The relation between substance and mode, Brahman and its body, substance and attribute: the second can neither exist nor be known without the first, though distinct from it; it replaces both identity and the Nyāya inherence (samavāya).

Only a soul in its last cycle (caramāvarta), no longer binding karma of maximum intensity (apunarbandhaka), who performs the preliminaries (pūrvasevā) — worship of teachers and gods, good conduct, austerity, non-aversion to liberation — is fit for yoga (Yogabindu; Yogaviṃśikā).

name: Apūrva (the unseen potency of ritual action)

definitions.definition: The perishable act produces an unseen potency that yields the enjoined fruit at a later time; its existence is known from the injunction itself (MS 2.1.5, Śabara).
Identified with the injunction's 'what is to be done' (kārya), known only from the Veda.

relations.note: the apūrva brings about heaven for one who desires it
Jaimini: dharma itself gives the fruit, not a lord (as reported in BS 3.2.40)

name: Injunction proper, restriction and exclusive specification

definitions.definition: An injunction enjoins what is otherwise not obtained at all (apūrva-vidhi), restricts to one of optional means (niyama) or, where something is obtained in several ways, excludes the others (parisaṅkhyā).

name: The unprecedented physician

definitions.definition: Vāgbhaṭa's opening homage to the one who destroyed the diseases of passion and the rest that cling to all beings (AHS Sū 1.1), turning the physician's art into an image of the liberator.

notes: The identity of the physician is not stated; readings differ (Buddha, Śiva, the self).

name: Aṟam, poruḷ, iṉpam — the Kuṟaḷ's three aims

definitions.definition: The Kuṟaḷ is 'Muppāl', in three books on virtue, wealth and love; release (vīṭu) is taught within virtue (renunciation, truth, desire's end).

relations.note: dharma, artha, kāma (and mokṣa)

name: New beginning (ārambha): the effect does not pre-exist

definitions.definition: The effect is not existent, non-existent-and-existent etc. before production, but is known to have been non-existent (NS 4.1.48–50); existence does not arise from non-existence (NS 4.1.14–18); an effect is the counterpositive of a prior absence (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's pre-existent effect.

name: The path of light (arcirādi-gati)

definitions.definition: All who reach Brahman travel after death by the path of light — flame, day, bright fortnight, northern course, year, wind, sun, moon, lightning, then Varuṇa, Indra and Prajāpati as escorts — cross the Virajā and enter Vaikuṇṭha.
The ascent of the liberated devotee on the shining path, welcomed by the gods at each stage and received by the eternal ones into the Lord's world (TVM 10.9).

notes: Order and list of stations recalled; check against Śrībhāṣya 4.3 and the Arcirādi.

name: The arhat's nirvāṇa is not final

definitions.definition: The nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is a conjured resting place; śrāvakas are predicted to buddhahood; one who has entered the disciples' certainty cannot produce bodhicitta (Vimalakīrti).
Arhats still have fear, remaining birth and the ground of ignorance (Śrīmālā).

relations.note: the Pali account treats arahatta as final

definitions.definition: Deviations appearing without cause that show the measure of life and approaching death — in complexion, voice, smell, senses, mind, conduct, dreams — the subject of the Indriyasthāna (Ca In 1.3-7; 5).

name: The five things to be known (artha-pañcaka)

definitions.definition: The self to attain, the Lord to be attained, the means, the goal and the obstacle, each in five kinds.

name: The five things to be known (arthapañcaka, Nimbārka)

definitions.definition: The worshipped, the worshipper, the fruit of grace, the rasa of devotion, the obstacles.
Supposing an unseen fact without which a seen or heard fact would be impossible — a separate means of knowledge for both Mīmāṃsā schools.

name: Arthavāda (explanatory praise and blame)

definitions.definition: Non-injunctive Vedic passages; without independent purpose, they serve injunctions by praise, forming one sentence with them (MS 1.2.1, 1.2.7); fruits stated for subsidiaries are arthavāda (MS 4.3.1).
Praise or blame; supplementing injunction or prohibition; figurative, restating, or fact-stating; praise, blame, another's deed, ancient narrative.

relations.note: arthavāda is one of the six marks of purport in Vedānta manuals, where it signals the passage's purport

notes: The reconciliation principle P7-arthavada in config/principles.md derives from this concept.

name: The method of pointing out Arundhatī (arundhatī-nyāya)

definitions.definition: Leading from the gross to the subtle step by step, as one points to a faint star by first showing a bright neighbouring one; used for the progressive teaching of the sheaths.

The 'other' samādhi, preceded by practice of the cognition of cessation, with only impressions remaining (1.18); its means is higher dispassion; the mind becomes supportless, as if non-existent (YBh 1.18); nothing is cognized in it (YBh 1.2). Bhoja: reached by rejecting every arising activity 'not this, not this' (RM 1.18).
Eight forms of the view that the self survives death without perception.
Relatives within the sapiṇḍa circle are impure for ten days after a death (MDh 5.59) or for periods graded by class (5.83); infants under two are buried without water-offerings (MDh 5.68; YS 3.1).

name: From mastered senses to serenity and peace (BhG 2.64–66)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Moving among objects with senses free of passion and aversion and under the self's control, the disciplined one attains serenity (prasāda); in serenity all sorrows cease and understanding quickly becomes steady (2.64–65); without discipline there is no understanding and no cultivation (bhāvanā), without cultivation no peace, without peace no happiness (2.66).

The affliction of I-am-ness is the seeming identity of the power of seeing (buddhi) with the seer (2.6); in samprajñāta samādhi, asmitā is awareness of a single self (YBh 1.17); 'asmitā-mātra' is the sixth unparticularized principle (YBh 2.19) and the source of created minds (4.4); in the gaps of discernment the thoughts 'I am', 'mine' arise (YBh 4.27). Bhoja distinguishes asmitā (mere being shining in the inward-turned mind) from ahaṃkāra (apprehending objects as 'I') (RM 1.17).
The awakening mind is twofold, as aspiration and as engagement, like the wish to go and actually going (BCA 1.15–16).
Aspiring bodhicitta does not grow without the vow of the engaging mind, which requires prātimokṣa as its basis.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): ChU 2.23.1 names three 'branches of dharma' (sacrifice/study/gift; austerity; the student living in the teacher's house) and says the one established in brahman attains immortality; MaiU 4.3 speaks of proceeding through one's own āśramas; ŚU 6.21 of those beyond the āśramas; the fourfold scheme is formulated in the Jābāla Upaniṣad (U04) and the Dharmasūtras (U02).

definitions.definition: Activity of body, speech and mind is inflow; auspicious activity brings merit, inauspicious demerit; with passions it is sāmparāyika, without passions īryāpatha (the commentators: lasting and transient); the sāmparāyika kind has the divisions of senses (5), passions (4), non-vows (5) and actions (25); the causes of the inflow of each karma type are given at 6.10-6.27.
The activity of body, speech and mind is the channel of inflow; auspicious activity brings merit, inauspicious demerit; with passions it binds lastingly, without passions only transiently (TS 6.1–6).

checks.note: Corrected by J: Definition: "lasting/transient" replaced by sāmparāyika/īryāpatha, glosses labelled as the commentators'.

definitions.definition: Liberation and buddhahood as the turning of the basis — the ālaya or the dependent nature — from defiled to purified through the abandonment of the twofold badness; begun at the first ground, completed after the diamond-like concentration; it is the undefiled element, the dharma-body.
The threefold examination of sensual pleasures, forms and feelings (MN 13).
Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's pastimes through the eight periods of the day, the object of meditative remembrance.
Mirrored in the eight daily periods of temple service (aṣṭayāma sevā), from maṅgalā to śayana.

Brahman is defined as the source of the world's creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release; Tattvasaṅkhyāna adds happiness, sorrow, covering and light. God is the efficient cause and controller, not the material cause.
Disgust, doubt, fear, shame, loathing, family, conduct and caste (Kulārṇava 13.90).

name: The eightfold matching for marriage (aṣṭakūṭa)

definitions.definition: Bride's and groom's asterisms and signs are compared under eight heads of increasing weight — varṇa (1 point), vaśya (2), tārā (3), yoni (4), grahamaitra (5), gaṇa (6), bhakūṭa (7) and nāḍī (8), 36 in all (MC 6.21).

notes: The point values follow the rule 'each carries more than the one before' (MC 6.21); the numbers 1–8 are the standard reading.

definitions.definition: Restraints (yama), observances (niyama), posture (āsana), breath-regulation (prāṇāyāma), sense-withdrawal (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), samādhi (YS 2.29). By practising them impurity is destroyed and the light of knowledge rises to discernment (YS 2.28, YBh 2.28). Pāda 2 (this chunk) gives yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma and pratyāhāra (2.30–2.55); the last three follow in pāda 3.

Restraints, observances, posture, breath-regulation, sense-withdrawal, concentration, meditation and samādhi (2.29); their practice destroys impurity until discriminative discernment (2.28); the last three are inner limbs (3.7). Nārāyaṇatīrtha subsumes many named yogas under the eight limbs.

definitions.definition: Eight protections enclosing the devotee's life: guru, liṅga, jaṅgama, pādōdaka, prasāda, vibhūti, rudrākṣa and mantra.
The SSM's bhakta-sthala includes initiation, liṅga-wearing, ash, rudrākṣa, the five-syllable mantra and the worship and prasāda of guru, liṅga and jaṅgama among its fifteen sub-sthalas.

name: The Aṣṭottarī period system

definitions.definition: A 108-year asterism-based system of eight planets (without Ketu): Sun 6, Moon 15, Mars 8, Mercury 17, Saturn 10, Jupiter 19, Rāhu 12, Venus 21 years; applied under particular conditions (BPHS 46–47).

notes: Years and order from memory.

name: The inverted aśvattha tree of saṃsāra

definitions.definition: The world-tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns, nourished by the guṇas, binding through action, to be cut with the axe of non-attachment (BhG 15.1–4); the Anugītā's tree of Brahman (14.47).

Bhagavad Gītā 15.1–5: 'they speak of' an imperishable aśvattha with roots above and branches below, its leaves the metres; knowing it one knows the Veda; its branches spread below and above, swollen by the guṇas, with sense-objects as shoots, and its roots below are bound up with action in the human world; its form, end, beginning and foundation are not perceived here; having cut it with the strong weapon of non-attachment one is to seek the place of no return, taking refuge in the primal person from whom the ancient activity flowed; the undeluded, free of pride, delusion, attachment and desire, reach that imperishable place. (The verses do not themselves name the tree saṃsāra.)

name: 'Atat tvam asi' — Dvaita's reading of Chāndogya 6.8.7

definitions.definition: The Chāndogya teaching repeated nine times with examples is read as 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), or 'aitadātmya' as being under the Lord's control; it teaches difference, and the conceit of identity is condemned.

relations.note: the reading of 6.8.7 is one plank of the critique of Advaita

definitions.definition: Rites that lack their own procedure take it from an archetype (MS 7.4.1); transferred details are modified (ūha) or cancelled (bādha) where they serve no purpose (MS 10.1.1–2).

Pāśupatas ('beyond the āśramas') and Lākulas ('beyond the world', skull observance) in the Niśvāsamukha; the Svacchanda names skull-observers and Pāśupatas, and levels for Mausulas, Kārukas, Vaimalas and 'Pramāṇa'; the Kūrma lists Pāśupata, Soma and Lākula; some sources and scholars add the Kāpālikas (Somasiddhānta) as a third division.

name: Levels assigned to Atimārga goals by the Mantramārga

definitions.definition: Pāśupatas reach the Aiśvara level; Mausulas and Kārukas the Māyā principle; Vaimalas the level of Tejeśa; the 'Pramāṇa' the Dhruva; skull-observers and Pāśupatas are not re-created.

name: Rival accounts of liberation: transfer, possession, production, manifestation

definitions.definition: Liberation is the manifestation of the soul's own Śiva-nature, not transfer, possession or production of the Lord's qualities.
The Pāśupatas speak of the attainment of the Lord's qualities and powers in liberation.

notes: Which Atimārga school held which of the rejected views is a scholarly attribution, not stated in the passage.

name: Śaivism's two great divisions: Atimārga and Mantramārga

definitions.definition: The Śaiva scriptures distinguish the Atimārga - knowledge 'beyond the world', whose followers are not re-created - from the Mantra path, in whose Śiva-knowledge all Atimārga goals are attained with ease.

Immediately after death the being takes an airy conveyance-body (ātivāhika); over the first ten days the piṇḍas offered by the sons build, limb by limb, a hand-sized body for the preta, which joins the airy body; the preta feels hunger from the tenth day.

definitions.definition: The knower who has transcended caste and stage and abides in the Self (Avadhūta 2; Kaivalya 2; Maitreya 1.13).

definitions.definition: Oneself is guru, siddha, disciple and Śiva (KJN 11.26); the self is the first guru, binding and releasing itself (17.35); himself goddess, god, disciple and guru (Akulavīra A.26).
'You are guru and disciple' (Yogaviṣaya 6).

The innermost self: the seer of seeing, not an object of seeing (BAU 3.4.2); the light of a person when all other lights are gone (BAU 4.3.6); the person made of understanding in the heart (BAU 4.3.7); the inner controller (BAU 3.7); dearer than all (BAU 1.4.8); unborn and undying (KU 1.2.18); free from evil, old age, death, sorrow, hunger and thirst (ChU 8.7.1). It is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated upon (BAU 2.4.5).

relations.note: identity is declared in the mahāvākyas; the later schools read the identity as strict (Advaita), as body-soul relation (Viśiṣṭādvaita) or deny it (Dvaita)

name: The identity of the self and brahman

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads declare that the self is brahman: 'I am brahman' (BAU 1.4.10), 'this self is brahman' (MāU 2; BAU 2.5.19), 'that you are' (ChU 6.8.7 and refrain), 'intelligence is brahman' (AU 3.1.3); 'this self of mine within the heart is brahman' (ChU 3.14.4); 'the person yonder, I am he' (Īśa 16). How this identity is to be understood is disputed by the later schools (dsp:tat-tvam-asi, dsp:souls-one-or-distinct); this entry records only the statements.
The inner self of every being is Brahman; difference is due only to adjuncts produced by ignorance (Kāśakṛtsna's view, accepted by Śaṅkara).

relations.note: the four later-named mahāvākyas are its classic formulations

name: Delight in the self (ātmarati): the one for whom nothing remains to be done

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The person who delights in the self alone, is satisfied and content in the self, has nothing that must be done, no purpose in doing or not doing, and depends on no being for any purpose (3.17–18). Commentators divide on whether this exempts such a person from action; the next verse (3.19) still enjoins unattached action.

name: Worship for oneself and worship for others

definitions.definition: Worship is twofold: for oneself, in the liṅga received at initiation or on a ground-altar, for one's own fruit; for others, in temples with installed liṅgas, for the king and realm.

name: The atomic size of the self (aṇu-jīva)

definitions.definition: The soul is atomic, a knower, one per body, infinite in number.
The soul is atomic, a spark of Brahman.
The soul is an infinitesimal particle of consciousness.

notes: Nyāya, Sāṃkhya and Advaita hold the self all-pervading (see dsp:atomic-or-pervasive-self).

definitions.definition: Earth, water, fire and air consist of eternal, partless, imperceptible atoms of spherical size (VS 4.1.1, 4.1.6–7, 7.1.26 C); at creation, atoms set in motion by adṛṣṭa combine into dyads and so on up to the gross elements (Praśastapāda); the triad (trasareṇu) is the smallest visible thing (later manuals).
Division of wholes ends in atoms, beyond the truṭi; atoms are partless, since ākāśa's 'penetration' does not apply to non-products and the alternative is an infinite regress (NS 4.2.16–25).

name: Oneself as island, the Dhamma as island

definitions.definition: 'Live as islands to yourselves, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as island' — by the four establishments of mindfulness (DN 16; SN 47.13; DN 26); 'oneself is one's own protector' (Dhp 160).

Renunciation by one in mortal danger (ātura), by mind and speech alone, versus renunciation in due order (krama); ritual renunciation is 'occasioned' or 'unoccasioned' (Jābāla 5; Nāradaparivrājaka 3, 5).

definitions.definition: The Pāśupata initiate leaves the rules of his former āśrama for the restraints of a state beyond the four āśramas; open to brahmins of any āśrama.
Yāmuna objects that Śaivas devise āśramas outside the Vedic order.
Non-difference of soul and Brahman is natural; difference is due to real limiting adjuncts (body, senses, intellect), removed at liberation after death.

name: The authority of smṛti, custom and other scriptures

definitions.definition: Smṛti is authoritative as implying a Vedic source, but is set aside when it conflicts with the Veda or shows a worldly motive; customs of the good done without visible motive are authoritative (MS 1.3.1–7).
Texts of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata and the Buddhists have no authority for dharma, even where they agree with the Veda, because the sources of dharma are fixed in number (Tantravārttika).

name: The original relation of word and meaning

definitions.definition: The relation of word and meaning is not established by any person; it is known from the beginningless usage of elders (MS 1.1.5; Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7).
The jīva is Brahman delimited by the inner organ, as space by a pot; nothing is added or lost.

The property or relation that fixes the scope of another property — e.g. the counterpositiveness of 'absence of pot' is delimited by potness and by the relation (conjunction) through which the pot is denied; central to exact definitions such as that of pervasion.

The highest renouncer, 'who has shaken off' saṃsāra, beyond castes and stages, living without marks or rules, appearing child-like, mad or ghost-like (Avadhūta 1–2; Turīyātīta; Jābāla 6; Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 5).
The liberated wanderer who has shaken off all ties, behaves like a child, madman or dullard, is untouched by desire and learns from all beings.
The one beyond hope, vāsanā, meditation and ego, defined syllable by syllable in the Avadhūta Gītā.
The Nāth ideal of the free yogī who has shaken off all conventions and stands above all schools (SSP 6).

name: The two powers of ignorance: veiling and projecting

definitions.definition: Ignorance veils the self (āvaraṇa, tamas) and projects the world and the bodies (vikṣepa, rajas).

name: The Lord's descent (avatāra / prādurbhāva)

definitions.definition: Though unborn, the Lord comes into being by his own māyā whenever dharma declines, to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (BhG 4.6–8); knowing his divine birth frees one (4.9).
Nārāyaṇa's successive manifestations: Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi, the appearance at Mathurā; earlier the Swan and Hayaśiras (MBh 12.326.72–94).

Dvaita: the avatāras are Viṣṇu himself manifesting his eternal body of consciousness and bliss, flawless and without internal difference; apparent human weakness is displayed to delude the unfit. One must also know which beings are merely indwelt (āveśa).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Though unborn, of imperishable self and lord of beings, Kṛṣṇa comes into being (saṃbhavāmi) through his own māyā, presiding over his own prakṛti (4.6); whenever dharma declines and adharma rises he sends himself forth (4.7), age after age, to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (4.8); he has had many births, all of which he knows (4.5); whoever knows his birth and action as divine is not reborn but comes to him (4.9). The word avatāra itself does not occur.

The Lord's descents are real, taken by his will in bodies of pure sattva, not from karma, for protecting the good, destroying evil and above all for being accessible; knowing their divinity liberates. Principal (mukhya) descents are the Lord himself; secondary (gauṇa) are empowered souls.
Whenever dharma declines the compassionate Lord takes bodies to relieve the good.
Parameśvara incarnates as the five Kṛṣṇas; the incarnations, not the devatās, are to be worshipped.
Nārāyaṇa is the cause of all the avatāras, whom the Kīrtana-ghoṣā praises.

Bhagavad Gītā 9.11 with 7.24–25 (the word avatāra is not used): the deluded disregard the Lord who has taken on a human body, not knowing his supreme state as great lord of beings; he is unborn and imperishable, veiled by his yoga-māyā and not manifest to all.

names.name: divyaṃ janma karma ca (divine birth and action)

definitions.definition: The Lord (or his Puruṣa form) descends age after age in innumerable forms to protect the world; all are portions and parts except Kṛṣṇa, Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3); in the Śaiva and Śākta Purāṇas Śiva and the Goddess likewise appear repeatedly ('whenever trouble arises I will descend', DM 11).
Rūpa's classification: svayaṃ-rūpa, tad-ekātma-rūpa (vilāsa, svāṃśa), āveśa; puruṣa, guṇa, līlā, manvantara, yuga and śaktyāveśa avatāras; Kṛṣṇa is their source.

name: The lists of avatāras

definitions.definition: BhP 1.3 lists twenty-two by ordinal; BhP 2.7 adds others (Hayagrīva, Haṃsa, Hari who saved Gajendra, the Manvantara-avatāras); the Agni (2-16, 49) and Garuḍa (1.142) teach ten (Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma, Buddha, Kalki); a count of twenty-four is common in later tradition (its membership varies and no single Bhāgavata verse gives it).

members: ten: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa/Balarāma, Buddha, Kalki

name: The whole (avayavin) as a real new substance

definitions.definition: The whole is a substance over and above its parts, perceived as one, inhering in its parts (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17); the notion of the whole is also named as the cause of passion, countered by the notion of parts (NS 4.2.3; NBh).

notes: The same tradition affirms the whole's reality and prescribes attending to parts against lust — different contexts (ontology vs. practice) within Nyāya.

name: Avidyā (ignorance) in Advaita

relations.note: in the later view avidyā is the material cause of superimposition
the second covering hides the knowledge of the Supreme

definitions.definition: For Śaṅkara, the superimposition of self and not-self, removed by discrimination; for later Advaita a positive, beginningless, indescribable power with veiling and projecting powers, the cause of saṃsāra, removed by knowledge alone.
One ignorance located in and directed to pure consciousness.
Ignorances located in the jīvas, directed to Brahman.

Dvaita: a real, beginningless covering in each soul, twofold — one hiding the soul's own nature and qualities, one hiding (its knowledge of) the Supreme; only the Lord removes them and grants liberation. It does not affect God or the self-luminous in the Advaita sense; Madhva's refutations deny ignorance of a self-luminous, attributeless Brahman.
Karma, which contracts the soul's knowledge and makes it take the body for the self; not an indescribable cosmic ignorance.

members: covering of the soul's own qualities

definitions.definition: A good or bad material continuum produced by action or concentration, carrying vows and non-vows.
Unreal; the continuity of karma is the transformed series.
Brahman becomes the world while remaining wholly unchanged, as gold in ornaments; creation is manifestation, not change.

Avimukta (Kāśī) is where Rudra gives the dying the tāraka — the mantra that carries across — so that they are freed; it is also located in the body between brows and nose (Jābāla 1–2; Muktikā 1.19–21; Rāmottaratāpanī; Tārasāra). The tāraka is identified variously as Oṃ, the Rāma mantra or the Nārāyaṇa mantra.
Śiva frees those dying at Kāśī by the power of Rāma's name.

name: The imperishable (avipraṇāśa) of action

definitions.definition: A realist theory stated in MMK 17.13–20: an imperishable factor, like a debt-note, connects action to its fruit, morally indeterminate and abandoned only by cultivation (17.14–15); Nāgārjuna answers from the emptiness of action (17.21ff).

notes: Commentators ascribe the theory to the Sāṃmitīyas.

name: Manifestation and concealment of sat, cit and ānanda

definitions.definition: In matter only being is manifest; in souls being and consciousness (bliss concealed); in the Lord all three; creation and dissolution are manifestation and concealment.

Under the Bodhi tree at Uruvelā the Buddha attended to dependent origination in the three watches of the night and uttered the verses on phenomena becoming manifest to the ardent brahmin (Ud 1.1–3; Vin Mv 1.1); the house-builder verses (Dhp 153–154).

name: Sidereal and tropical reckoning

definitions.definition: Indian astronomy and horoscopy reckon longitudes sidereally (nirayana) from a fixed star-point, treating the shifting solstices as an oscillation (SS: libration of 27°); the seasons and the sun's northern and southern courses follow the equinoxes (sāyana); the difference, the ayanāṃśa, is valued differently by different schools.

notes: SS 3.9–12 on the libration from memory; not spot-checked.

name: Testing the span of life (āyuḷ parīṭcai) and the wheel of time

definitions.definition: The Tirumantiram's third tantra has sections on the wheel of time (kāla cakkaram) and the testing of the remaining life-span (āyuḷ parīṭcai), by which the yogin reads the approach of death; Siddha lore uses them.

relations.note: yogic signs of approaching death

notes: Section titles checked in the local TM e-text; contents not summarized.

definitions.definition: The span of life is computed from the planets — by the methods of Maya, the Yavanas, Maṇittha and Parāśara (exaltation-years halved in fall), of Jīvaśarman, and of Satya (by navāṃśas traversed), whom Varāhamihira prefers (BJ 7); the lords of the 2nd and 7th are the killers (māraka) whose periods bring death when life is spent (BPHS 44).

name: Āyurveda as a limb of the Atharvaveda

definitions.definition: Suśruta calls Āyurveda an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6); Caraka has the physician declare devotion to the Atharvaveda, which teaches healing by rites and mantras (Ca Sū 30.21).

Life is the union of body, senses, mind and self (Ca Sū 1.42), the continuance of consciousness (Sū 30.22); it is happy or unhappy, wholesome or unwholesome (Sū 1.41; 30.24), the wholesome life being defined by ethical and spiritual qualities.

relations.note: life is the conjunction the tripod describes

definitions.definition: A cognition is sublated when a later valid cognition shows its object was never as it appeared; degrees of sublatability define the levels of reality.

name: 'In the seen only the seen' (the Bāhiya teaching)

definitions.definition: In the seen there will be only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the sensed only the sensed, in the cognised only the cognised; then 'you' will not be 'by that' or 'in that', neither here nor beyond nor between: the end of suffering (Ud 1.10; SN 35.95).

Energy must be neither too tight nor too slack, like lute strings; one should penetrate the evenness of the faculties (AN 6.55; Vin Mv 5.1); the bases of power are developed without slackness or tension (SN 51.20).

The Kālikā Purāṇa teaches offering animals to the Goddess, says it brings heaven, liberation and victory, allows substitutes and forbids brāhmaṇas certain offerings and wine (67.1-12; 67.19-23; 67.46-52; 67.113-117). Restricted: summary only. Practised at Kāmākhyā and in Bengal; opposed by Vaiṣṇava and many Śākta dakṣiṇa worshippers.

name: The simile of the ball of string

definitions.definition: (As reported) As a ball of string thrown runs out unwinding to its end, so fool and wise run through saṃsāra to the end of suffering.
Because of the passions the soul takes in material particles fit to become karma; that is bondage. Causes: wrong view, non-abstinence, carelessness, passions, activity.
Because of its passions the soul takes in matter fit for karma: that is bondage (TS 8.2).
