name: Bandhu — the correspondences between rite, cosmos and person

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas explain every element of a rite by a hidden connection (bandhu) to a cosmic and a bodily counterpart — bricks and days, metres and classes and gods, the breaths and the seers — organized on three planes: of the gods (adhidaivata), of the self (adhyātma) and of the sacrifice (adhiyajña); knowing the connection is what makes the rite work.
Carried into the Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads as upāsanā — meditations on correspondences (e.g. breath-oblations satisfying senses, gods and regions, ChU 5.19–23; the saṃhitā-upaniṣad, TU 1.3).

name: The bardo of becoming (srid pa'i bar do)

definitions.definition: A mental body driven by karma wanders, sees the judgement of the Lord of Death and is drawn to a womb; the instructions teach closing the womb door or choosing a birth.
Precise mental labelling of each object as it arises — rising, falling, thinking, hearing — which keeps mindfulness continuous and reveals arising and passing.
Bare attention: registering what happens without reaction or comment (Nyanaponika).

name: The Bārhaspatya view of the sciences

definitions.definition: (As reported) Only economics and government are sciences; the triple Veda is a cover for one who knows the course of the world.

name: The present and the inferred (bartamān and anumān)

definitions.definition: Knowledge is of the present, verifiable in the living body (bartamān); scripture, heaven and the gods of the books are inference and hearsay (anumān).
Kabīr's parallel stance: 'I speak of what I have seen with my eyes, you of what is written on paper'.

relations.note: Opposes reliance on scripture as a means of knowledge.

name: The Bāul–Fakir exchange (context)

definitions.definition: Hindu Bāuls and Muslim Fakirs share gurus, songs and practice: Lalon, a fakir with a Muslim guru, sings of Caitanya and of the Mecca in the body; the Fakirs use Sufi terms (murśid, mārephat, nūr) for the same path. Recorded as context only (Sufism is outside scope).

notes: Context only; U49 owns the Sant–Bāul–Sufi exchange.

name: The guru in the Bāul path

definitions.definition: The Man is found only through the living guru (murśid, sāṃi); Bāuls take a dīkṣā-guru (initiation) and a śikṣā-guru (instruction in practice), and later the bhek (garb); the song itself is the guru's word, signed in his name; the teaching is secret and given only to the qualified.

name: The bazaar of the soul (Kartābhajā imagery)

definitions.definition: The world is a bazaar where a new company has come; the soul is a trader, and the true merchandise is the Master's secret.
The liberated city of Ravidās: no grief, tax, fear, decline or ranks; citizens move freely; it is at once the state of the liberated and the ideal of a just order.
The vāsanās are beginningless because the wish 'may I not cease, may I be' is universal and cannot be natural to a creature that has not experienced dying (bhāṣya 4.10).

definitions.definition: Time is being and being is time; each thing abides in its dharma-position; firewood does not become ash.

Eleven benefits of the liberation of mind by love — sleeping and waking well, no bad dreams, dear to humans and non-humans, protected by deities, unharmed by fire, poison and weapons, quick concentration, serene complexion, unconfused death, rebirth in the Brahmā world (AN 11.15); it outshines all merit (Iti 27).

name: The Kaula beyond injunction and prohibition

definitions.definition: For the (realized) Kaula there is no injunction or prohibition, merit or sin, heaven or hell (Kulārṇava 9.55-58; 9.62) — yet those who abandon ritual out of false learning go to hell (9.130) and the wilful are condemned (5.96-105).
Not reviving the past nor longing for the future, seeing with insight each present state; making the effort today, for death may come tomorrow (MN 131).

Eight principal powers of the Lord (aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitā, vaśitā, kāmāvasāyitā), ten from the guṇas and five lesser ones, each gained by a dhāraṇā on the Lord - and all obstacles for one seeking him.

definitions.definition: Two lists: (1) BhP 2.10.1 - sarga, visarga, sthāna, poṣaṇa, ūti, manvantara, īśānukathā, nirodha, mukti, āśraya, the first nine told for understanding the tenth; (2) BhP 12.7.9 - sarga, visarga, vṛtti, rakṣā, antara (manvantara), vaṃśa, vaṃśānucarita, saṃsthā, hetu, apāśraya.

name: Bhairava's severing of Brahmā's head and the skull-penance

definitions.definition: Śiva as Bhairava cuts off Brahmā's fifth head, wanders as the skull-bearer to expiate brahmin-murder, and is freed at the holy tīrtha; remembering his skull-bearer's guise destroys sin.
Within the circle all castes are twice-born and equal to Śiva — woman, man, eunuch, caṇḍāla or brāhmaṇa; when it ends they are separate again (Kulārṇava 8.96-97). Restricted: summary only.

No caste distinction in giving and drinking within the circle; the Bhairavī circle may be held when occasion arises; the Tattva circle is for those who realise 'all is Brahman' (Mahānirvāṇa 8.151-154; 8.208).

name: The Lord's subjection to his devotees (bhakta-parādhīnatā)

definitions.definition: The Lord did as his devotee told him, rolling up his serpent-bed; he takes the form his devotees love; the Āḻvār who holds the Lord in his heart asks who is greater.
'I am subject to my devotees, as if not free' (BhP 9.4.63).
Kṛṣṇa pleads to place Rādhā's foot on his head; after union he adorns her at her bidding.

name: Devotion (bhakti)

definitions.definition: Dvaita: firm love for Viṣṇu, greater than love for anything else, preceded by knowledge of his greatness; the sole means of liberation to which gifts, pilgrimage, austerity and sacrifice are subsidiary; it continues in liberation as eternal bliss.

Devotion to the Lord: accepting a leaf or flower offered with love (BhG 9.26), bearing the devotee's welfare (9.22), making even the wicked righteous (9.30), the means by which he is seen and entered (11.54), preferred over worship of the unmanifest as easier (12.2–5), attained in its supreme form by one who has become Brahman (18.54).
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa, the highest dharma, by which the ekāntins enter Vāsudeva directly (MBh 12.336.3–4, 12.332.18).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'to one who has the highest devotion to God and to his teacher as to God, these matters shine forth' (ŚU 6.23), the earliest Upaniṣadic use of the word in this sense; prayers and refuge in ŚU 3-6.
Love, longing and a melting heart for Tirumāl, given by his grace, lived as service, refuge and praise at his temples; Tamil pattu/aṉpu.
Supreme love of the nature of nectar, higher than action, knowledge and yoga, being the fruit itself; primary (one, though elevenfold) and secondary (by guṇas or motive).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The noun bhakti does not occur, but Arjuna is taught as the Lord's devotee (bhakta) and friend (4.3); the Lord responds to people in the way they resort to him (4.11); many absorbed in him and taking refuge in him reached his state (4.10); the meditator sits with thought on him and intent on him (6.14); the yogin established in oneness worships him as abiding in all beings (6.31); and of all yogins the one who worships him with faith, inner self gone to him, is the most yoked (6.47).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Knowing the Lord as the origin of all, the wise worship him, their thought on him, awakening one another and speaking of him, content and delighting (10.8–9); by undivided devotion alone he can be known, seen and entered in truth (11.54); whoever does his work, holds him supreme, is devoted, unattached and without enmity toward any being comes to him (11.55); those who fix their mind on him and worship him with supreme faith are 'the most yoked' (12.2); the devotee dear to him bears the marks of 12.13–19, and those who follow the teaching with faith are exceedingly dear (12.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: unswerving devotion to Kṛṣṇa by a yoga with no other is counted among the dispositions called knowledge (13.11); his devotee, knowing field, knowledge and knowable, becomes fit for his state (13.19); one who serves him with the unswerving yoga of devotion goes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for becoming brahman (14.26); one who knows him as puruṣottama worships him with his whole being (15.19).

relations.note: by bhakti is liberation, not otherwise

definitions.definition: Knowledge does not end devotion: the knower's 'fourth' devotion and the natural devotion of the realised continue without a sense of two.
Devotion is the self-luminous gem that remains when the lamp of knowledge may be blown out; knowledge and devotion both end suffering but devotion is the surer.

definitions.definition: Before God birth counts for nothing: saints of every caste are equally revered; outward 'crookedness' of birth does not touch inner devotion; knowing the Veda's meaning belongs to the devotee, not to birth. The saints also record the exclusion they suffered.
Rāmānanda's disciples include a weaver, a cobbler, a barber, a Jāṭ farmer and women (Bhaktamāl); Tulsī scorns caste-talk for himself as Rāma's slave.
Refuge is given to every caste and people, including tribes and Muslims; in the name there is no caste.
Caste does not count among seekers of Parameśvara; women and all castes may renounce.
For high and low the Lord is one (Annamācārya).

parallel critique; the Siddhars argue from the body and yoga, the bhakti saints from devotion
the saints deny that birth decides access to God; not all of them reject varṇa as a social order

definitions.definition: Devotion is higher than action, knowledge and yoga because it is the fruit; knowledge of a king or of food neither pleases the king nor appeases hunger; gaining devotion one becomes perfected, immortal, satisfied.

The Āḻvārs ask for nothing but service and devotion: not the drum but kinship and service through seven times seven births (TP 29); not dharma, wealth or pleasure but unwavering devotion in every birth (Mukundamālā); the name's sweetness above Indra's kingdom (Tirumālai 2).

relations.note: Advaita makes devotion a means to or a form of self-knowledge
Gauḍīya prema as the fifth aim beyond liberation states the same claim within a rasa theology

definitions.definition: The 'knowledge' that liberates is meditation — repeated, unbroken, loving remembrance of the Lord, vivid as seeing — practised daily till death and supported by the seven aids; it is bhakti, and the Lord, pleased, grants himself.

Pure devotion is nirguṇa — beyond the three guṇas — unmotivated and uninterrupted like the Gaṅgā flowing to the sea (BhP 3.29.11–12); devotion in the modes is mixed.

NBS 83 names the teachers who with one voice declare devotion supreme: Kumāra, Vyāsa, Śuka, Śāṇḍilya, Garga, Viṣṇu, Kauṇḍinya, Śeṣa, Uddhava, Āruṇi, Bali, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa and others; NBS 16–19 cites the definitions of Vyāsa, Garga, Śāṇḍilya and Nārada; the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra cites Kāśyapa and Bādarāyaṇa.
What is in the vessel is in the universe: the cosmos with its gods, rivers and pilgrimages is present in the body, which is therefore the field of search.
The eternal Vṛndāvana with its lakes and lotuses is within the body.

name: Bhārata as the land of action

definitions.definition: Only in Bhārata are deeds done that bear fruit and lead to heaven or liberation; the gods envy those born there (VP 2.3.22-25).

definitions.definition: From about the 13th c., clothed clerics (bhaṭṭārakas) presided over Digambara seats, temples, libraries and rites, filling the gap left by the near-absence of naked monks; the Bīsapantha accepts them, the Terāpantha rejected them; seats survive in the south (Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, Mūḍabidri, Humcha).
The intention to harm is itself violence and bears its fruit even if no being is actually killed — as King Yaśodhara and his mother suffered many animal births for sacrificing a cock of flour.

Forty-nine bhāvas: eight stable emotions (sthāyibhāva), thirty-three transient states (vyabhicāribhāva) and eight involuntary states (sāttvika); they 'bring into being' the poem's meaning; determinants (vibhāva) cause and consequents (anubhāva) express them (NŚ 6.17–22; 7.1–3).

relations.note: Rūpa Gosvāmī re-applies the same apparatus to love for Kṛṣṇa

definitions.definition: The verbal suffix conveys bhāvanā: the injunction's prompting force (śābdī) and the agent's activity (ārthī), each with three expectancies — what, by what, how.
The passive resultant consciousness that flows whenever no active process occurs (as in dreamless sleep), identical in type with the rebirth-linking and death consciousness of that life.

relations.note: Yoga treats deep sleep as a mental modification (nidrā-vṛtti); the Abhidhamma as the uninterrupted life-continuum

definitions.definition: Ignorance is a positive though indescribable entity, known by perception ('I am ignorant'), inference and presumption.
By inherent nature some souls are capable of liberation and some never will be (TS 2.7); even among the capable, not all will attain it.

name: Difference in practice, non-duality in union (SSM)

definitions.definition: The SSM assigns difference and non-difference to stages: at the māheśvara stage the worshipper rejects total non-duality because worship rests on the difference of Lord and servant, and non-duality comes only with realization (10.37–43); at aikya, difference and even lordship and boundness are seen to be imagined by māyā, and one who no longer thinks 'I am servant, Śiva master' stands in non-duality (14.8–9; 14.37). The text grounds this in its own principle that its teaching differs by sthala and by qualified aspirant (5.22–23).

name: Difference as the nature of things (bheda = svarūpa)

definitions.definition: Difference is not a separate property or negation but the very nature of each thing, apprehended together with the thing itself; hence the Advaita charge of mutual dependence in grasping difference fails.

relations.note: each of the five differences is the nature of its relata

definitions.definition: Knowing the self as other than body, karma and passion: 'the soul is other, matter is other' (Iṣṭopadeśa 50); all who are liberated are liberated by it, all who are bound are bound by its absence (Samayasāra-kalaśa 131).
The central practice of the Adhyātma path, rendered in the Samayasāra Nāṭaka.

relations.note: Parallel discrimination of seer and seen in Yoga, but the Jain knower is an agent with changing modes.

name: Difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda) of Brahman, souls and world

definitions.definition: Brahman is one as cause and many as effect; the souls and world are both different and non-different from it (Bhartṛprapañca: like ocean and waves; Bhāskara: difference through real adjuncts).
The relation is natural (svābhāvika), like snake and coils, sun and rays.
The relation is inconceivable (acintya).

relations.note: Advaita's unreal appearance
Viśiṣṭādvaita's inseparable body–soul relation; Rāmānuja criticised both forms of bhedābheda

definitions.definition: The order of nuns founded when Mahāpajāpatī accepted the eight principles of respect (Cv 10.1; AN 8.51); the Buddha affirms women can realise the four fruits (Cv 10.1.3); its nuns' verses (Thig) and the foremost nuns (AN 1).
The Dharmaguptaka bhikṣuṇī lineage survives in China, Korea, Vietnam and Taiwan.
Requires dual ordination by bhikṣuṇīs and bhikṣus; the bhikṣuṇī lineage was not transmitted to Tibet.
The bhikkhunī order died out; its revival is disputed (recent).

name: The two purposes: experience and release

definitions.definition: Prakṛti acts for puruṣa's sake — for another as if for itself (SK 56, 60) — for experience and release; the conjunction is for seeing and for isolation (SK 21); like milk flowing for the calf (SK 57) or people acting to satisfy a longing (SK 58); once both purposes are fulfilled there is no motive for creation (SK 66; Gauḍapāda).
The Kaula is both enjoyment and yoga; in it enjoyment becomes yoga, sin merit and saṃsāra liberation (Kulārṇava 2.23-24).

Bhṛgu, told to seek that from which beings are born, by which they live and into which they enter, knows brahman as food, then breath, then mind, then understanding, then bliss; after each he is told to seek by tapas; the sequence ends with the vidyā established in the highest space.

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

name: Bhū-maṇḍala: Meru, seven island-continents and seven oceans

definitions.definition: The earth-disc: Jambudvīpa with Meru at its centre, surrounded by the salt ocean; then Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka and Puṣkara dvīpas, each ringed by an ocean (of sugar-cane juice, wine, ghee, curd, milk and sweet water respectively), then a golden land, the Lokāloka range and darkness; Jambudvīpa has nine varṣas, of which Bhārata is the land of action.

notes: Order of the oceans from memory (VP 2.2-4; BhP 5.16-20); Phase D to check.

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: Least-sure order of the oceans resolved: it matches VP 2.4 exactly (Plakṣa/sugar-cane juice ... Krauñca/curd 2.4.57, Śāka/milk, Puṣkara/sweet water 2.4.86, golden land 2.4.93). The Bhāgavata swaps two: Krauñca/milk (5.20.18) and Śāka/curd (5.20.24). All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

name: Enjoyment and liberation as the twofold goal (bhukti-mukti)

definitions.definition: The Goddess's tantra alone accomplishes all the aims of life (SL 31); her worshipper enjoys Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī and, freed of bonds, tastes the supreme Brahman (SL 99); saubhāgya names this double blessing.

The Mantramārga distinguishes the initiate who seeks powers and enjoyments in higher worlds (bubhukṣu, the sādhaka) from the one who seeks liberation only (mumukṣu); both are legitimate and receive different initiations.
In the Kula way enjoyment itself becomes yoga: the yogin is not an enjoyer and the enjoyer does not know yoga, but the Kaula is both.
Common attainments (the eight great siddhis, the six rites) and the supreme attainment (mahāmudrā, buddhahood) are both fruits of mantra practice; the common are to be sought for the sake of beings.
Mantra rites for protection and worldly ends are practised under devotion to the Jina, while liberation comes only from the three jewels and the destruction of karma.
Śiva's scriptures in all four pādas are means to enjoyment (powers, higher worlds) and to liberation; initiates are bubhukṣu or mumukṣu accordingly.

relations.note: same distinction of common and supreme attainment

definitions.definition: The culmination of Sanatkumāra's teaching: plenitude is happiness, there is none in the small; where one sees, hears, understands nothing else, that is plenitude; it is immortal and rests on its own greatness; it is all, and it is the self (ChU 7.23-25).

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 7.23-25). It rests on 3 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: The qualities of the bodhisattva grounds

definitions.definition: On attaining the first ground the bodhisattva gains twelve sets of a hundred qualities — seeing a hundred Buddhas, receiving their blessing, living a hundred aeons, entering a hundred concentrations, shaking a hundred worlds and so on — multiplying on the higher grounds (MA ch.11).

notes: List from memory of MA's chapter on the qualities of the grounds; to check.

name: Consciousness from the elements (bhūta-caitanya)

definitions.definition: (As reported) Consciousness, absent in each element, arises in them when combined as a body — like intoxicating power — and perishes with them, like a drum's sound dying away.
(Jain report) From five elements a self arises and perishes with them.
Refuted: cognition arises only from prior cognition; mind is a beginningless continuum.
Refuted: consciousness is absent in the dead body; what experiences the elements is not one of them.

relations.note: no conscious survivor, so no other world

notes: See also dsp:consciousness-from-elements (U09).

definitions.definition: The scriptures' non-recollection and non-attention must be preceded by correct analysis of reality; mere stopping of thought is like fainting and cannot remove the obscurations (Bhāvanākrama III).

name: Seizing beings and the science of spirits

definitions.definition: Seizure by gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, ancestors, serpents, rākṣasas and piśācas, shown by superhuman knowledge and action (Su Utt 60.4-7; Su Sū 1.8); for Caraka the seizers strike only one already self-struck by prajñāparādha, and one should hold oneself the agent of one's pleasure and pain (Ca Ni 7.10-22). Summary only.
Kālī's mantra is built of seed-syllables (the Karpūrādistotra conceals them in riddles, vv. 1-5); the Mahāvidyā mantras are 'siddha' (Muṇḍamālā). Mantra syllables not reproduced.

name: Seed-syllables of the centres and elements

definitions.definition: The elements have the seeds laṃ (earth), vaṃ (water), raṃ (fire), yaṃ (air), haṃ (space) — placed in the root, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata and viśuddhi centres, with oṃ at the ājñā; the petals of the six centres carry the fifty letters (4+6+10+12+16+2); the seeds are used in the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and in meditation on the centres.
The Saṅgītaratnākara's throat centre carries on its petals the praṇava, udgītha, huṃ-phaṭ, vaṣaṭ, svadhā, svāhā, namaḥ, amṛta, the seven notes and poison (ŚR 1.2.129–130).

Experience and action perfume the store-consciousness, leaving seeds that ripen as future consciousness and its objects; the imprints of karma together with those of the twofold grasping produce rebirth; for Dharmapāla seeds are both innate and newly perfumed.
Beginningless imprints of conceptualization make cognition appear as grasped and grasper and make universals seem real.

relations.note: Sautrāntika seeds lie in the mental series itself, without an ālaya

name: The soul as God's reflection (bimba–pratibimba, Dvaita sense)

definitions.definition: The soul is a reflection (pratibimba) of God, its original (bimba): dependent on him, resembling him, and eternally different; the reflecting 'adjunct' is the soul's own nature, so the relation is eternal. The worshipper contemplates: 'You are the original, I am the reflection, though there is a difference between us.' (Not the Advaita reflection theory, in which the reflection is Brahman appearing in an adjunct.)
The central point of the Śrīcakra (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8) and the great point of the Kāmakalāvilāsa in which Śiva's light is reflected; the pair of white and red points (KKV 4-7).

In the haṭha texts bindu is the vital essence (semen; with rajas in women), identified with the moon and the nectar in the head; life depends on it and its fall is death (Amṛtasiddhi; HYP 3.88); cosmologically bindu is Śiva and rajas Śakti (SS 1.92); Śiva's nature is nāda, bindu and kalā (HYP 4.1).

In the Yoga Upaniṣads: (1) the seed-essence of the body, white (Śiva) and red (Śakti), whose retention and union are sought (Dhyānabindu, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā — summary-only); (2) the point of Oṃ; (3) identified with mind (Yogakuṇḍalī 3.5; Yogaśikhā 6.73).

name: The two material causes: bindu (pure māyā) and māyā

definitions.definition: Bindu (mahāmāyā, śuddhamāyā) produces the pure universe, the bodies of pure beings and sound; māyā (aśuddhamāyā) produces the impure universe; prakṛti with the three guṇas arises within the māyic range.

Death comes by the fall of bindu, life by holding it (HYP 3.88); semen moved by udāna is the poison-line of death (AmŚ 38); in the nectar-filled body the seed flows upward (GŚ 65); bindu arises from mind (Candrāvalokana).

The haṭha texts make the preservation of bindu central: 'death by the fall of bindu, life by holding bindu' (HYP 3.88; DYŚ 143); bindu depends on mind, life on bindu (HYP 3.90); steadiness of mind makes breath and bindu steady (4.28); loss of bindu through women is the great danger of the ghaṭa stage (DYŚ 77–80); khecarī and vajrolī (restricted) are taught to retain or draw it up.

name: The bird's path and the ant's path

definitions.definition: Śuka's path (vihaṅgama): immediate liberation through inquiry; Vāmadeva's path (pipīlikā): gradual liberation through yoga over births (Varāha 4.34–42).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: Birth in the Pure Land (wangsheng / ōjō) as the condition for awakening

definitions.definition: At death the practitioner is born by transformation in a lotus in Sukhāvatī, where he is non-retrogressive, sees the Buddha, hears the Dharma and completes the path — then returns to save beings.
Birth at death through the nenbutsu, with the Buddha's welcome; awakening is attained there.
Birth in the true land is at once the attainment of great nirvāṇa; it is settled in this life at the moment of shinjin.

names.name: wusheng zhi sheng 無生之生

definitions.definition: Birth in the Pure Land arises from the pure vow and is not the deluded birth of the three existences; dharma-nature is unborn and 'birth' is said from the side of those born; the wise seek birth ardently while knowing birth has no own-being (Tanluan, Daochuo, Jingtu shiyi lun, Chuandeng).

relations.note: reconciled by the tradition itself through the two truths: birth conventionally, non-arising ultimately

name: The Black and the White Yajurveda

definitions.definition: The Black (kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda mixes formulas and explanatory prose (Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka, Kapiṣṭhala); the White (śukla) keeps the formulas (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā) apart from the Brāhmaṇa. The tradition tells that Yājñavalkya disgorged the Yajus learned from Vaiśampāyana, which his fellows took up as partridges (Taittirīya), and received new Yajus from the Sun as a horse (Vājasaneyi).

name: The black crown of the Karmapa

definitions.definition: A crown said to be woven by ḍākinīs from their hair and offered to Düsum Khyenpa, visible only to the pure; a material replica given by the Yongle emperor to the 5th Karmapa is worn in the black-crown ceremony (the tradition's account).

name: Blending and transference (bsre 'pho)

definitions.definition: A Marpa-lineage name for the six-yoga system: blending (bsre ba) states — day and night, sleep and death, dream and illusory body — and transference ('pho ba); 'the five blendings' are carried onto the path in the bardo.

notes: The designation bsre 'pho for the Ngok tradition is from memory.

name: The blind men and the elephant

definitions.definition: Sectarians holding one-sided views quarrel like blind men each touching part of an elephant (Ud 6.4).
Bliss is Brahman's nature; the bliss of deep sleep and the joys of objects are its reflections or fragments (Pañcadaśī 11–15).

name: Bliss, clarity and non-thought (the three experiences)

definitions.definition: The typical meditative experiences (nyams) of one-pointedness; clinging to them leads to rebirth in the desire, form and formless realms respectively.

relations.note: if clung to

name: The awakening mind (bodhicitta) in the Madhyamaka manuals

definitions.definition: The resolve for awakening for all beings, born with compassion and non-dual understanding (MA 1.1); an elixir transforming the body (BCA 1.10); aspiring and engaging (BCA 1.15–16); relative and ultimate.
The second of the three points after compassion (Bhāvanākrama I).
Generated after refuge and love on seeing beings' suffering; the aspiring mind must be held by the engaging vow.
The only door to the Mahāyāna.

relations.note: the treatises systematize the sūtras' teaching

name: The aspiration for awakening in Pure Land teaching

definitions.definition: The aspiration to become a buddha is the aspiration to save beings; one who seeks birth only for pleasure is not born (Tanluan); beginners seek birth first because they cannot yet save beings in the evil world.
Not a separate requirement of birth in Hōnen's reading (disputed by Myōe).
Other-power bodhicitta is shinjin.

name: The thought of awakening (bodhicitta) in the sūtras

definitions.definition: The resolve for buddhahood for all beings; its nature is luminous, a 'no-thought'; at its first arising perfect awakening is already attained (Avataṃsaka); even the lowest aspirants to Sukhāvatī must arouse it.

notes: Relative and ultimate bodhicitta as a pair is systematized in the śāstras (U40).

definitions.definition: Ultimate bodhicitta: free of all entities, aggregates and grasper-grasped, one's own mind unborn (GST 2); conventional bodhicitta the aspiration; in the completion stage also the white drop.

An aspiration made before a living Buddha under eight conditions (Bv 2.59), a prediction, and the fulfilment of the ten perfections over countless aeons (Bv 2; Cp; Jā); in the Nikāyas 'bodhisatta' designates Gotama before his awakening (MN 4, 19, 26, 36).

relations.note: the Mahāyāna makes the bodhisattva path a universal ideal; Theravāda reserves it for aspirants to Buddhahood

name: The bodhisattva career in the Sarvāstivāda

definitions.definition: Three incalculable aeons (ending under Ratnaśikhin, Dīpaṅkara, Vipaśyin) and a hundred aeons of karma producing the thirty-two marks; perfections fulfilled as examples show; awakening in thirty-four moments.
Four conducts and ten grounds (Mahāvastu).

name: The three bodhisattva commentaries (sems 'grel skor gsum)

definitions.definition: Three Indian commentaries held to be by tenth-level bodhisattvas — the Vimalaprabhā on the Kālacakra, Vajragarbha's commentary on the Hevajra, and Vajrapāṇi's commentary on the Cakrasaṃvara — which read the tantras in the definitive sense and are central authorities for the Jonang.
The bodhisattva is ill because beings are ill, as parents are ill with their only son; the sick bodhisattva sees his illness, and beings', as unreal, and so has compassion free of sentimental views.

From the arising of the thought of awakening, through the perfections, the grounds and irreversibility, to buddhahood — undertaken for all beings, with the armor of vowing to liberate countless beings who are not found; neither destroying the conditioned nor abiding in the unconditioned.

relations.note: the arhat's path; Mahāyāna sūtras call its nirvāṇa not final

name: Bodhisattva precepts (sūtra layer)

definitions.definition: The Brahmajāla's ten major and forty-eight minor precepts; the Ākāśagarbha's root downfalls; the Upāsakaśīla's lay precepts.

notes: The Yogācāra vow ritual (Bodhisattvabhūmi) is U41.

name: The root downfalls of the bodhisattva vow

definitions.definition: The eighteen root downfalls (from the Ākāśagarbha-sūtra as compiled by Śāntideva) and forty-six secondary faults (after Asaṅga), taught in Tsongkhapa's commentary on the ethics chapter of the Bodhisattvabhūmi.

notes: Counts recalled; the source commentary (byang chub gzhung lam) is not entered as a source here.

name: The bodhisattva's training: give, protect, purify, increase

definitions.definition: The training is to give away one's body, enjoyments and merit of the three times to all beings, and to protect, purify and increase them (ŚSK 4), rooted in faith and the resolve for awakening (ŚSK 2).
Jñāneśvar's living samādhi, Muktābāī's vanishing in lightning, Tukārām's bodily ascent to Vaikuṇṭha, and Tukārām's farewell 'we go to our own village'.
Mīrā merged into Kṛṣṇa's image at Dvārakā.
Cakradhar, beheaded yet living by his followers' account, departed to the north.

name: Bodily places named for saṃyama and concentration

names.name: Bodily places named for saṃyama and concentration

definitions.definition: Places named in this part of the text: the navel wheel, the heart lotus and the light in the head (bhāṣya 3.1); the pit of the throat (3.30), the tortoise channel (3.31), the light in the head (3.32), the heart (3.34), the navel wheel (3.29). The text records what saṃyama on each is said to give; no instruction is given here.

Places for binding the mind: the navel wheel, the heart-lotus, the light in the head, the tips of nose and tongue (YBh 3.1); the throat-well, the tortoise channel in the chest (3.30–31); the heart, 'the small lotus-house in the city of Brahman' (3.34); on the navel wheel one knows the three humours and seven constituents (YBh 3.29).

name: The body and constitution in the chart

definitions.definition: The twelve signs are the limbs of Kālapuruṣa from head to feet (BJ 1.4); each planet has a constitution — the Sun pitta, the Moon vāta and kapha, Mercury all three — a colour, a caste and an element (BJ 2.4–9); the five great men are known by bodily marks and measures (BS 68); the Vāstu-man is a body laid over every site (BS 52.2–3).

name: The body as the city of the gods

definitions.definition: The body is the eight-wheeled, nine-gated unconquerable stronghold of the gods with a golden sheath covered in light, in which dwells the self-possessed wonder (yakṣa) that the knowers of Brahman know; Brahman entered it; the person (puruṣa) is so called from this stronghold (pur) of Brahman (AVŚ 10.2.28–33); the nine-gated lotus covered with three strands holds the same yakṣa (10.8.43); all the gods dwell in the person as cows in a stall (11.8.32).

relations.note: The 'three strands' (guṇa) of AVŚ 10.8.43 are later read as the Sāṃkhya qualities; the verse itself does not define them — contested.

notes: Readings of 'eight wheels' as the body's centres (cakras) are later and interpretive; not asserted.

name: The body as the sacred sites

definitions.definition: The twenty-four sites of the Heruka maṇḍala are located inwardly in the body's channels (body maṇḍala); the Hevajra lists the classes of sites.
Saraha: no holy place equals the body (People Dohā v57–59).

relations.note: Inner and outer maṇḍala.

name: The body as the Śrīcakra

definitions.definition: The guru is Śakti; the body with nine openings is the Śrīcakra; each enclosure and its deities are constituents of body and mind — the fourteen channels, ten vital airs, ten fires, the qualities, the subtle elements, the inner organ — and the fifteen Nityās are the lunar days (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
The Samayin worships the cakra only within, in the heart and the crown (Lakṣmīdhara).

members: eight (cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire, sattva, rajas, tamas) = Vaśinī etc.
unmanifest, mahat, ahaṃkāra = Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī

definitions.definition: 'The body is a temple and the jīva in it is Śiva' (Maitreya 2.1; Skanda 10); the Yogaśikhā calls it Śiva's or Viṣṇu's temple; the Bhāvanā makes the body the Śrīcakra.

For the Siddhars the Lord has made the body his temple (TM 725); the heart is the sanctum and the flesh the shrine (TM 1823); temple and sacred tank are within the mind (Sivavākkiyar) — hence both the care of the body and the scorn for stone temples.
The body is the true mosque and temple; service and worship are within (Dādū); the offering is body and mind (Ravidās).
The original Mecca is in this human body.
The body is the temple of the God (Kulārṇava 9.41); the guru knows the unity of the body and the cosmos (13.88).

Some rest on teachings whose ref was corrected or only partly confirmed; the content is located, only the numbering changes: tea:bhavana-upanisad:1-5 (partially-confirmed).

name: The body as the eternal Vṛndāvana

definitions.definition: The eternal Vṛndāvana, with its lakes and lotuses where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa sport, is within the human body; the innate Man dwells there.

name: The body in the Āḻvār hymns

definitions.definition: The world and elements are the Lord's body, he their life (TVM 1.1.7); the human body is 'impure' and joined to false knowledge (Tiruviruttam 1), yet may be marked as the Lord's (PAT 5.4.1) and, in love, weeps, sleeps not and melts (TVM 7.2.1). The Āḻvār hymns give no teaching on subtle anatomy, channels or centres.

The body is analysed into its parts and elements and not found as a self (BCA 9.58–60; RĀ 2.1); it is to be protected as an instrument for beings' benefit and given to them (ŚSK 4–5); bodies arise from action and afflictions, which are empty (MMK 17.27). No subtle-body anatomy of channels and centres is taught in these sūtra-path texts (that belongs to the Vajrayāna).

name: The bodies of those born in Sukhāvatī

definitions.definition: Beings born there appear by transformation in lotuses, all golden in colour, with the thirty-two marks, no difference between gods and humans, superknowledges and life without limit (vows; Nāgārjuna's verses); none of them is a woman or lacks faculties.

name: The body in Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: The substrate of movement, senses and experience (NS 1.1.11), earthy (NS 3.1.27), produced by past karma (NS 3.2.60).

Bodies of earth (ours), water (Varuṇa's world), fire (Āditya's world) and air (Vāyu's world); some beings are not womb-born (VS 4.2.9 C; Tarkasaṅgraha); breath is air moving in the body, one but named prāṇa, apāna etc. by adjuncts.

notes: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika has no subtle-body (liṅga-śarīra) or cakra anatomy in its root texts; the transmigrating mind is atomic.

name: The four portals and the fifth, the treasury (sgo bzhi mdzod lnga)

definitions.definition: An alternative ordering of Bön: the White Waters (wrathful mantra), Black Waters (magic, rituals, funerals), the Land of Phan (monastic and sūtra teaching), the Master's Guidance (Dzogchen), and the fifth, the treasury comprising all.

notes: Optional (Bön). From memory.

name: The base of all and awareness in Bön Dzogchen

definitions.definition: The base (kun gzhi) is empty and clear; awareness (rig pa) is its knowing; their inseparability (dbyer med) is the natural state; not recognizing it the moving mind arises.

relations.note: functionally the ground of Nyingma Dzogchen

notes: Optional (Bön).

name: The nine ways of Bön (theg pa rim dgu)

definitions.definition: Four causal ways (phywa gshen: prediction and diagnosis; snang gshen: rites for the gods of the visible world; 'phrul gshen: magical rites against harm; srid gshen: funerary rites) and five fruitional ways (dge bsnyen: lay virtue; drang srong: monastic ascetics; a dkar: tantra of the white A; ye gshen: higher tantra; bla med: the Great Perfection).

notes: Optional (Bön). The list follows the Southern Treasure scheme of the Zijid.

name: Buddhist historians' three phases of Bön

definitions.definition: Some Buddhist historians (e.g. Thuken's Crystal Mirror) describe Bön in three phases: 'revealed' (brdol bon), 'deviant' ('khyar bon) and 'transformed' (bsgyur bon, borrowing Buddhist texts).
The Bön tradition rejects this schema as a polemical account.

notes: Recorded as the opponents' account (reported by Buddhist historians); see dsp:bon-and-buddhism.

definitions.definition: One who thinks himself free is free, one who thinks himself bound is bound (Aṣṭāvakra); bondage and liberation are said of the Lord only through the guṇas (Uddhava Gītā); bondage is bondage to vāsanā (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha).

name: Bondage of action (karma-bandha)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action binds: the world is bound by action except action done for sacrifice (3.9); one yoked with the understanding of yoga casts off this bondage (2.39), leaves behind good and evil deeds (2.50) and, abandoning the fruit, is freed from the bondage of birth (2.51); those who follow the teaching with faith are released from actions (3.31).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the Lord's acts of sending forth beings do not bind (nibadhnanti) him, seated as one indifferent and unattached to them (9.9); whatever one does, eats, offers, gives or practises as austerity, done as an offering to the Lord, frees one from the bonds of action (karma-bandhana) with their good and bad fruits, and, yoked in the yoga of renunciation, freed, one comes to him (9.27–28).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: whoever knows the Lord as unstained by actions is not bound by actions (4.14); the one content with what comes unsought, beyond the pairs of opposites, the same in success and failure, is not bound even when acting (4.22); actions do not bind the self-possessed one who has renounced actions by yoga and cut doubt by knowledge (4.41); the constant renouncer, free of the pairs, is easily released from bondage (5.3); the unyoked one, attached to the fruit through desire, is bound (5.12).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The roots of the aśvattha stretch below in the human world, binding through action (karma-anubandhin) (15.2); rajas binds the embodied one by attachment to action (14.7).

relations.note: action done as yoga, without attachment and for sacrifice, does not bind

name: The book in place of the image

definitions.definition: In the nāmghar and sattra the sacred book (Bhāgavata or Kīrtana-ghoṣā) is enthroned on the guru-āsana and worshipped instead of an image.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What one attains who abides in the brahmic state (brāhmī sthiti) of steady wisdom even at the time of death (2.72).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The goal named in 5.24–26: the yogin whose happiness, delight and light are within, having become Brahman, attains brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24); seers with impurities destroyed, dualities cut, self-restrained and devoted to the welfare of all beings attain it (5.25); for self-knowing ascetics free of desire and anger it is near on every side (5.26). Related expressions in ch. 6: peace culminating in nirvāṇa that abides in the Lord (6.15), becoming Brahman and the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman (6.27–28).

name: Brahman's real transformation into the world (pariṇāma)

definitions.definition: The world is a real transformation of Brahman through its power; effect is both different and non-different from cause.
The world is a real transformation of the Lord's power.
Transformation without change (avikṛta).
Transformation of the external power only (śakti-pariṇāma).

In dissolution Brahman has souls and matter as a subtle body without name and form; in creation, as a gross body with name and form; Brahman is thus the material and efficient cause, and the transformation is real, yet belongs to the body, leaving Brahman untouched.

relations.note: Advaita's apparent transformation
the effect is a real state of the existent cause

definitions.definition: The realms of Brahmā reached by the brahmavihāras (DN 13) and the jhānas; Brahmās mistake their realm for permanent (MN 49; DN 1).

After the awakening the Buddha inclined not to teach, the Dhamma being deep and against the stream; Brahmā Sahampati implored him, and seeing beings like lotuses at different depths he opened the doors to the deathless (SN 6.1; MN 26; DN 14; Vin Mv 1.5).

The student, initiated by the teacher who bears him as an embryo, fills the worlds with fuel, girdle, toil and tapas; by brahmacarya and tapas the king guards the realm, a maiden wins a husband and the gods struck down death (AVŚ 11.5).

In the Upaniṣads brahman is that from which beings arise, by which they live and into which they return (TU 3.1.1); being, one without a second (ChU 6.2.1); truth, knowledge, infinite (TU 2.1.1); understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); plenitude (ChU 7.23-24); the imperishable (BAU 3.8.8; MuU 1.1.5). It has two forms, formed and formless (BAU 2.3.1), and is also given only by negation — 'not so, not so' (BAU 2.3.6).
The cause of the world's origin, sustenance and dissolution, known from scripture, the purport of all the Upaniṣads.
The one non-dual reality, existence–consciousness–bliss, identical with the inner self; nirguṇa in itself, saguṇa (Īśvara) through māyā.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Brahman is every factor of the sacrifice and is what is to be reached (4.24); it is the fire into which sacrifice is offered (4.25); the eternal Brahman is reached by those who eat the remainder of sacrifice (4.31); the yoked sage soon reaches it (5.6); actions are placed in it (5.10); it is flawless and the same, so that those whose mind rests in sameness are established in it (5.19–20); the yogin becomes Brahman (brahma-bhūta) and attains brahma-nirvāṇa and contact with Brahman (5.24, 6.27–28).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna acknowledges Kṛṣṇa as the supreme brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier, the eternal divine Person, as all the seers declare (10.12–13).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the knowable is brahman, beginningless and supreme, neither sat nor asat (13.13); it has hands, feet, eyes and ears everywhere and stands enveloping all (13.14); appears through the sense-qualities yet is without senses, is unattached yet supports all, without guṇas yet their experiencer (13.15); is inside and outside beings, moving and unmoving, not to be known through subtlety, far and near (13.16); undivided yet as if divided, sustainer, devourer and generator of beings (13.17); light of lights beyond darkness, knowledge, knowable and reached by knowledge, set in the heart of all (13.18); seeing the many as resting in the one one attains brahman (13.31); by unswerving devotion one becomes fit for becoming brahman (14.26); Kṛṣṇa is the foundation of brahman (14.27).

relations.note: the texts first speak of each separately and then declare them one

definitions.definition: In the Ṛgveda brahman is the potent formulation and prayer (its lord is Bṛhaspati); in the Atharvaveda and White Yajurveda it becomes the name of the highest: 'homage to the highest Brahman' (AVŚ 10.8.1), 'those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme' (10.7.17), Brahman entered the golden city of the body (10.2.33), 'that is brahman' (VS 32.1), 'Oṃ, the void is brahman' (VS 40.17).

Brahman is the sacred formulation and Veda, and also the first principle: 'in the beginning this was Brahman', which descended into the worlds by name and form (ŚB 11.2.3); 'Brahman the self-existent' heads the teacher-lineages (ŚB 10.6.5.9), offers itself into all beings (ŚB 13.7.1.1), and as a 'great wonder' creates a second god from itself (GB 1.1.1).

relations.note: The Skambha hymn identifies the frame of the world with the highest Brahman.

definitions.definition: The one non-dual reality called Brahman, Paramātman and Bhagavān (BhP 1.2.11); Bhagavān possesses the six excellences and is properly Vāsudeva (VP 6.5.74-79); Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3.28).
One non-dual reality realised in three ways: as Brahman (effulgence, incomplete), Paramātman (indwelling partial expansion) and Bhagavān (full, with all powers); Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself.

relations.note: the one Lord seen by function

name: Worship of Brahman in the Mahānirvāṇa

definitions.definition: Brahman is pure being beyond speech and mind, known in samādhi by those who see equally (Mahānirvāṇa 3.7-8), worshipped with the mantra 'oṃ saccidekaṃ brahma'; 'all is Brahman' is the attitude of the Tattva circle (8.208).

name: Creation accounts of the Brāhmaṇas

definitions.definition: Several coexisting accounts: the waters and the golden egg with Prajāpati's first words (ŚB 11.1.6); non-being as the breath-seers (ŚB 6.1.1); neither being nor non-being but mind (ŚB 10.5.3); Prajāpati as boar raising the earth (TB 1.1.3), as tortoise (ŚB 7.5.1.5); the dwarf Viṣṇu (ŚB 1.2.5); the fish and the flood (ŚB 1.8.1); worlds, lights, Vedas, utterances and Oṃ (AB 5.32).

notes: The boar, tortoise, fish and dwarf appear here before their later Purāṇic form as avatāras (U07).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:satapatha-brahmana:11.1.6.1-3 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:6.1.1.1-5 (confirmed); tea:taittiriya-brahmana:1.1.3.5-6 (partially-confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:7.5.1.5 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:1.8.1.1-10 (confirmed); tea:aitareya-brahmana:5.32 (confirmed). The boar cosmogony is confirmed at the anuvāka level only (TB 1.1.3; the kaṇḍikā 5–6 could not be fixed, see tea:taittiriya-brahmana:1.1.3.5-6). The other accounts are text-located.

definitions.definition: The Lord's command to Vallabha at Gokul: by dedicating oneself to Kṛṣṇa in initiation, the five kinds of faults of body and soul are removed, and one becomes fit for service.

Women are recorded as seers of Ṛgveda hymns and verses — Lopāmudrā, Ghoṣā, Apālā, Viśvavārā, Vāc Āmbhṛṇī, Śraddhā, Sūryā, Yamī, Indrāṇī, Śacī, Romaśā, Śaśvatī, Sārparājñī, Godhā, Agastya's sister and others — and listed together by the Bṛhaddevatā; the Atharvaveda says a maiden wins a husband by brahmacarya (AVŚ 11.5.18).
Formal question-and-answer contests on the hidden meaning of rite and cosmos, with a wager and sometimes deadly stakes (ŚB 11.6.3; 11.4.1).

checks.note: ŚB 11.6.3 is Janaka's brahmodya at which Yājñavalkya answers Śākalya. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:satapatha-brahmana:11.6.3.1-11.

name: The devotee as bride of the Lord (the bridal mood)

names.name: nihakarmī pativratā (the faithful wife without works) — an aṅga of the anthologies

definitions.definition: Kabīr sings as the bride whose husband, King Rām, has come home, with body as altar and mind as priest; the pain of separation (birah) is the bride's longing; the devotee as faithful wife (pativratā) of the one Lord.
The madhura mood realized in the human pair, each seeing the other's svarūpa as Rādhā or Kṛṣṇa (restricted context; doctrine only).
The lover longing for the Man of the Heart as for a beloved.

relations.note: Corresponds to the madhura (amorous) mood of the Gauḍīya rasa scheme; the Sants do not systematize moods.

definitions.definition: One awakened by himself to the Dhamma, not a god, gandhabba, yakkha or human, having abandoned the effluents (AN 4.36); endowed with ten powers and four confidences (MN 12); the rediscoverer of an ancient path (SN 12.65); one of a line of Buddhas (DN 14).

relations.note: the Buddha of the suttas is not an incarnation of a god; the Purāṇic avatāra reading is an external interpretation

name: The Buddha as a person of valid cognition

definitions.definition: The Buddha has become (bhūta) a means of valid cognition: he knows what is to be abandoned and adopted with its means, through compassion cultivated over many lives and the seeing of selflessness; he is the teacher, the Sugata and the protector; his authority is proved, not assumed.

name: The three (four, five) bodies of a buddha in the tantras

definitions.definition: Dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya and nirmāṇakāya with the svābhāvikakāya; the two form bodies arise through aspiration and compassion (Queen Dohā v64–68).
The generation and completion stages yield the three bodies (Tōh 2292 no. 25); some systems add the body of great bliss.

relations.note: The tantric count includes the Mahāyāna three bodies and adds the essence (and great-bliss) body.

name: The Buddha's body and qualities in the Sarvāstivāda

definitions.definition: Refuge in the Buddha is refuge in the non-learner's dharmas that make a Buddha, not in his body; all Buddhas are equal in accumulation, dharma-body and benefit to the world, not in lifespan, caste or stature; the eighteen exclusive qualities.

relations.note: The Lokottaravāda holds the Buddha's bodily life itself to be supramundane.

definitions.definition: Countless world-systems in all directions, each with its buddha; buddhas from them gather and testify; the Lotus-Treasury world-ocean holds them on a lotus.

Scholars do not realize that the buddha is in the body (People Dohā v82); the bodiless hidden in the body (v110); no pilgrimage place equals the body (v57–59); the body is the abode of all buddhas (Advayasiddhi).

relations.note: The siddha motif of the body as the true holy place is shared with Nāth, Tamil Siddha and Sant poetry.

definitions.definition: All beings have the Tathāgata within, covered by adventitious defilements — the dharmakāya not yet freed; the realm of beings neither increases nor decreases; it is empty of stains and not empty of qualities; all beings, even icchantikas, have it.
The Laṅkāvatāra: taught to remove the fear of no-self, meaning emptiness; the Avataṃsaka: the Tathāgata's wisdom present in all beings.
Buddha-nature is the ultimate itself, permanent, present in all beings complete with the buddha-qualities, empty only of adventitious stains.
Kongtrul reads it as the other-empty ground of the Great Madhyamaka; Mipham as the union of luminosity and emptiness, neither mere absence nor permanent entity.

For the Nyingma (Mipham), the sugata-essence is the union of luminosity and emptiness with the qualities spontaneously present, neither a mere absence nor a self; the Guhyagarbha makes it the source from which beings' conceptual karma emanates the realms.

The 'cause' of awakening present in all beings, for three reasons (the dharmakāya pervades, suchness is undifferentiated, the potential is present) — Jewel Ornament ch.1; identified by Nāropa with the luminous mind obscured by adventitious stains, and by the 3rd Karmapa with mind's clarity-emptiness.
Within the Karma Kagyu read both as empty of own-nature (the 8th Karmapa) and as empty only of what is other (the shentong reading of the 8th Situ and Jamgön Kongtrul): not yet reconciled.

relations.note: the sūtras call it 'self'; the Laṅkāvatāra says it is not a self
buddha-nature = the emptiness of the highest meaning (Mahāparinirvāṇa); = emptiness (Laṅkāvatāra)

name: Buddha-nature as the emptiness of the highest meaning and the middle way

definitions.definition: Buddha-nature is paramārtha-śūnyatā, which is wisdom and the middle way (Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 27).

name: Buddha-nature in Chan, Seon and Zen

definitions.definition: The nature of awakening in every being, identical with the self-nature; 'if the self-nature is awakened, beings are buddhas; if deluded, buddhas are beings'.
'Whole being is buddha-nature'; impermanence is buddha-nature (Dōgen).
'All beings are originally buddhas' like ice and water (Hakuin).
One's own numinous knowing is the true buddha (Jinul).

relations.note: Chan inherits the Nirvāṇa-sūtra and Awakening of Faith teaching; the embryo image is rare in Chan.

name: Buddhahood in one life and one body

definitions.definition: The diligent can awaken in this very life (bka' dpe phyi ma: 'the instruction for the diligent to awaken in this life'; Karṇatantravajrapada: 'no doubt it gives buddhahood in this life'); Milarepa is the exemplar.

The first evolute (= mahat), whose nature is determination; bearer of the eight dispositions (SK 23); it accomplishes all experience for puruṣa and discriminates puruṣa from pradhāna (SK 37); unconscious, it appears conscious by taking on the shade of consciousness (Vācaspati on SK 5).

name: Not unsettling the understanding of the ignorant

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The knower should not create a split in the understanding (buddhibheda) of the ignorant attached to action, but, acting with discipline, lead them to all actions (3.26); the one who knows the whole should not unsettle the slow who do not (3.29).
The re-evolution of the world, the loss of the beings' radiance through craving for the savoury earth, the arising of sexes, property, the elected king and the four classes from occupations (DN 27).

relations.note: the Vedic origin of the classes from the cosmic Person's body (RV 10.90), rejected in DN 27

name: The Buddhist subtle body (channels, winds, drops)

definitions.definition: Thirty-two (or 72,000) channels with three principal — lalanā (left, moon), rasanā (right, sun), avadhūtī (centre) — and four (Hevajra) or six (Kālacakra) cakras; winds as the mount of mind; white and red drops; the yoga of drawing the winds into the central channel.
The dohās speak of wind and mind ceasing where sun and moon do not enter (People Dohā v26–27) and of the three channels as bellows and forge (Kamparipa).

relations.note: The Hindu haṭha six-cakra body and the Buddhist four-cakra body share the three channels (the Sekoddeśa itself equates lalanā/iḍā and rasanā/piṅgalā) but differ in the number and meaning of the centres.

name: Caitanya as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa combined

definitions.definition: Caitanya is Kṛṣṇa who took Rādhā's mood and complexion to taste her love; also the yuga-avatāra of Kali inaugurating the chanting of the name.
Caitanya is the union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body, and so the model of the sahaja union of the two principles in the human; the Gosvāmīs knew this esoteric meaning.
Caitanya returned as Āulcānd to reveal the sahaja religion.

In early medieval western India many monks lived permanently in temples, handling their property; Haribhadra condemned this, and Jineśvara's debate at Aṇahilapāṭaka (1024) won recognition for monks living in lodgings (vasati), the origin of the Kharatara reform.

The Siddhar ideal of dying to death while living: 'this root makes one die without dying' (Rāmatēvar 2); leaving the fatal fruit to 'die without dying' (Aḻukaṇṇi 9); crossing over without dying (Kuṭampai 13); knowers have no Yama (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 10).

relations.note: liberation while living, in the idiom of conquering death

definitions.definition: Six centres (mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddhi, ājñā) in most Yoga Upaniṣads, with the thousand-petalled lotus above; the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa (4.1) counts nine cakras and six ādhāras, while the Yogacūḍāmaṇi (3) speaks of six cakras and sixteen ādhāras; the Yogaśikhā adds four pīṭhas (Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Uḍyāna); counts and attributes differ between texts.

The haṭha texts give different body-maps: six centres (ādhāra/mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddha, ājñā) with the thousand-petalled lotus above (GŚ 10–15, 60–62, 78–85; ṢCN); the Nāth scheme of six (or nine) centres, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids (Vivekamārtaṇḍa; Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati); the Śiva Saṃhitā's centres with Kailāsa, the sahasrāra, 'outside the body called brahmāṇḍa' (5.151); the GS's twelve-petalled lotus within the thousand-petalled where the guru is meditated on. Numbers, petals, letters and deities differ between texts.

In Pūrṇānanda's Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa (1577) the six centres are strung on the brahmanāḍī within citriṇī, vajrā and suṣumnā: mūlādhāra (4 petals, earth, LAṂ, Brahmā, Ḍākinī), svādhiṣṭhāna (6, water, VAṂ, Viṣṇu), maṇipūra (10, fire, RAṂ, Rudra), anāhata (12, air, YAṂ, Īśa), viśuddha (16, space, HAṂ, Sadāśiva), ājñā (2, mind, praṇava, Śambhu), and the thousand-petalled lotus with Paramaśiva above.

Six centres below the thousand-petalled lotus; the Saundaryalaharī places earth in the mūlādhāra, water in the maṇipūra, fire in the svādhiṣṭhāna, air in the heart, space in the throat and mind between the brows (SL 9), and worships a Śiva-Śakti pair in each (SL 36-41).

The six supports (āṟu ātāram) — mūlātāram, cuvātiṭṭāṉam, maṇipūrakam, anākatam, vicutti, ākkiñai — with the crown-space above; the goddess and the fire at the root; the guru's grace burns them away with the fifty-one letters (Aḻukaṇṇi 35).

relations.note: six-centre maps vs the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati's nine; not reconciled in the texts themselves

name: The three Indian lineages of Cakrasaṃvara

definitions.definition: Lūipa's, Ghaṇṭāpa's and Kāṇha's (Kṛṣṇācārya's) traditions of Cakrasaṃvara practice.

Years are counted from the start of the Kali age, the Śaka era (78 CE, used by the siddhāntas and Varāhamihira's rules, BS 8.20–21), the Vikrama era (57 BCE), and regional eras such as the Kollam era of Kerala (825 CE); the national calendar of India (1957) adopted the Śaka era.
The fierce goddess blazing at the navel who burns the tathāgatas and melts the moon at the crown (Hevajra I.1); first of Tilopa's six dharmas, from Caryāpa.

relations.note: Both are a feminine inner fire/power awakened in the lower body and rising through the central channel; the Buddhist texts frame it as bliss joined with emptiness, not as Śakti uniting with Śiva.

name: The candidate causes of the Śvetāśvatara

definitions.definition: ŚU 1.2 lists time, inherent nature, fixed order (niyati), chance, the elements, the womb and the person as causes to be considered, and rejects them singly and in combination; ŚU 1.3 and 6.1 answer that the cause is God's own power and greatness.

checks.note: All 3 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ŚU 1.2; ŚU 1.3; ŚU 6.1). It rests on 3 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: Lunar combinations

definitions.definition: Planets (other than the Sun) in the 2nd from the Moon give sunaphā, in the 12th anaphā, in both durudharā; none on either side gives the ill kemadruma (BJ 13); Jupiter in an angle from the Moon gives gajakesarī (later texts); benefics in the 6th, 7th and 8th from the Moon give adhi yoga.

notes: BJ 13 content from memory; not spot-checked. Scholarly account: sunaphā, anaphā, durudharā and kemadruma are Greek-derived terms.

definitions.definition: Where the Kubjikā transmission first descended (Kubjikāmata 1; 2.21).
Where the Kaula scripture came down (Kaulajñānanirṇaya colophons; 22.12).

name: The Cara (sign) period system

definitions.definition: In the Jaimini system the periods belong to signs, counted forward or backward from the ascendant according to the sign's nature, each lasting as many years as its lord is distant from it (Jaimini 2; BPHS 50).

notes: Rules summarized from memory; chapter references not checked.

definitions.definition: Seven (or eight, with Rāhu) planets ranked by their degrees in their signs become the significators of self, minister, brother, mother, son, kin and wife; the highest is the ātmakāraka (Jaimini 1.1.11; BPHS 32.1–4).

name: Caraka as a portion of Śeṣa, identified with Patañjali

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: Caraka is a partial incarnation of the serpent Śeṣa (Bhāvaprakāśa Pūrva 1.57-65); Cakrapāṇi salutes the lord of serpents who removed the faults of mind, speech and body by the Yoga Sūtra, the Mahābhāṣya and Caraka's redaction — one author of all three.

notes: Scholarly account keeps the three authors distinct (labelled in tch:caraka).

definitions.definition: 'Whoever would attend on me should attend on the sick' (Vin Mv 8.26); the qualities of a good nurse.
The name, God, the guru and the devotees are the four real things of the dharma.

name: The materialists' experiments on the condemned

definitions.definition: (As reported) Sealing a criminal in a jar, weighing him alive and dead, cutting him open — no soul seen; answered with similes of dream, the hot iron ball, the conch and the fire-sticks.

name: The four elements as the only principles

definitions.definition: (As reported) Earth, water, fire and air are the principles; body, senses and objects are their aggregates; space is not counted.
(Jayarāśi) Stated only to reflect worldly belief; they too do not stand examination.

name: Heaven, hell, lord and release in this world

definitions.definition: (As reported) Heaven is pleasure, hell is pain, the lord is the king, release is the death of the body.

name: Pleasure as the aim of life

definitions.definition: (As reported) Live happily while life lasts; take pleasure as one takes the fish with its bones; what is past does not return.

name: The siddha-poets of the Caryāgīti

definitions.definition: About fifty songs by some two dozen siddhas, each song signed by its poet: Kāṇha (the largest number, about thirteen), Bhusuku (about eight), Saraha (four), Kukkuripa (three), Lūipa, Śānti and Śabara (two each), and Virūpa, Guṇḍarī, Cāṭila, Kambalāmbara, Ḍombī, Mahīdhara, Vīṇā, Āryadeva, Ḍheṇḍhaṇa, Dārika, Bhāde, Tāḍaka, Kaṅkaṇa, Jayanandī, Dhāma and Tantrī (one each).

notes: Song counts are recalled from the standard edition; the presence of Lūipa, Kukkuripa, Virūpa, Bhusuku, Kāṇha, Ḍombi, Śānti, Saraha, Śabari, Bhadra, Tāḍaka, Dārika and Kaṅkaṇa was confirmed by name searches in the local Tibetan of Munidatta's commentary (Tōh 2293). Identification of Caryāgīti poets with the siddhas of the lives (e.g. Śānti = Ratnākaraśānti, Kambalāmbara = Kambala, Dhāma = Dhamupa) is traditional and uncertain.

name: Categories (padārtha) in Mīmāṃsā

definitions.definition: Substance, quality, action, universal and absence (the later Bhāṭṭa manuals), with darkness and sound among substances.
Eight: substance, quality, action, universal, dependence (paratantratā), power (śakti), similarity (sādṛśya) and number (saṅkhyā).

notes: From memory (Mānameyodaya; Prakaraṇapañcikā's Tattvāloka); not checked here.

name: The fourfold scheme of the śāstra (heya, heya-hetu, hāna, hānopāya)

definitions.definition: Saṃsāra full of suffering (what is to be abandoned), the conjunction of pradhāna and puruṣa (its cause), the absolute ceasing of the conjunction (the abandonment) and right seeing (the means): the śāstra is fourfold as the science of healing is fourfold (disease, cause, health, medicine) (YBh 2.15). Also named as heya (YS 2.16), heya-hetu (YS 2.17), hāna (YS 2.25) and hānopāya (YS 2.26).

As medicine has four parts — disease, its cause, health, remedy — so the śāstra has four: saṃsāra (what is to be avoided, future suffering), its cause (the conjunction of seer and seen), liberation (avoidance, the absence of conjunction) and its means (right seeing, unwavering discernment) (YBh 2.15; YS 2.16–26).

definitions.definition: Four alternatives — is, is not, both, neither — none of which is asserted of the ultimate (MMK 22.11; 25.17–18); in 18.8 the four statements form the Buddhas' (graded) instruction.

name: Pārśva's fourfold restraint and Mahāvīra's five vows

definitions.definition: Pārśva taught restraint from violence, falsehood, theft and possessions (chastity being implied in non-possession) and allowed garments; Mahāvīra taught five great vows and nakedness; the Keśin–Gautama dialogue explains the difference by the dispositions of the people of each era, and Pārśva's followers joined Mahāvīra's order.

relations.note: the fourfold restraint was expanded into the five great vows

definitions.definition: The soul wanders through 8.4 million species; the human birth is the rare chance to remember the Name before Kāl grinds it between the mill-stones again.
The wheel of eighty-four under Kāl's law of karma, from which the initiate is freed.
Destruction needs no cause; everything arisen perishes of itself at once; apparent destruction by fire is the non-arising of a similar series.
Things are momentary, but impermanence is a real characteristic acting on each dharma.
Some formations endure for a time (Vasumitra).
Wrong view, non-abstinence, carelessness, passion and activity (TS 8.1); they are removed in order through the guṇasthānas.

relations.note: Wrong view ends at stage 4, non-abstinence at 5–6, carelessness at 7, passion at 11/12, activity at 14 (commentaries).

definitions.definition: Invisible forms of time — the swift and slow apogees and the node — bind the planets with cords of air and draw them, while the wind Pravaha drives them; so arise their varied motions and latitudes (SS 2.1–8).

name: The fourth state (cauthā pad) in Sant usage

definitions.definition: Beyond waking, dream and sleep and beyond the three qualities lies the 'fourth state' (cauthā pad, turīya), in which the Lord is known; Kabīr uses the Nāth-Vedāntic term.

relations.note: Same name as the Upaniṣadic fourth, used devotionally.

notes: Recalled usage; no verse located.

definitions.definition: Huineng forbids worldly mourning, leaves a last verse and dies seated; at death one should see the aggregates as empty and neither follow welcoming buddhas nor fear terrifying signs (Huangbo).
Birth-and-death is the life of the buddha (Dōgen, Shōji).
The formless precepts, repentance and refuges given at the Dafan temple; 'when the mind is level, what need to keep precepts?'; Huineng's refraining from meat among hunters.
Eisai: the precepts are the foundation of Zen, against the Daruma school.
Receiving the precepts (jukai) and leaving home are essential (Dōgen's twelve-fascicle essays); the sixteen bodhisattva precepts.

name: Dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land (chanjing shuangxiu)

definitions.definition: Chan and Pure Land reach the same end by different roads; 'Chan is the Chan of Pure Land, Pure Land the Pure Land of Chan'; practise one gate deeply; Yanshou's myriad good practices include recitation. The 'four alternatives' ascribed to Yanshou (with Chan and Pure Land like a tiger with horns) are a later formulation.
In Chan contexts recitation is used as a huatou ('who is reciting the Buddha's name?') or as a practice for those of lesser capacity (as reported in the Pure Land sources).

notes: The Chan side is contributed only as reported in Pure Land texts; U42 owns the Chan definitions.

definitions.definition: Supernatural power is carrying water and hauling firewood (Layman Pang).
Powers appear only through gradual cultivation, are 'uncanny matters' and should not be used (Jinul).
Freedom in the 'samādhi of sporting in supernatural powers' belongs to one who sees the nature (Platform Sūtra).

The self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins, the senses the horses and their objects the roads; with understanding and a yoked mind the senses are like good horses and one reaches Viṣṇu's highest step; without it one goes on in saṃsāra (KU 1.3.3-9).

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (KU 1.3.3-9). It rests on 2 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Six: Niśītha, Mahāniśītha, Vyavahāra, Bṛhatkalpa, Daśāśrutaskandha and Jītakalpa (Pañcakalpa in older lists).
Four: Niśītha, Vyavahāra, Bṛhatkalpa, Daśāśrutaskandha.
A mind void of 'I' and 'mine', working and living without self-grasping; the practical meaning of suññatā.

name: Chöd: cutting ego-clinging at the root

definitions.definition: What Chöd cuts is not an external enemy but self-clinging, the root of the mind's afflictions and of the four māras; the view of emptiness is applied as the blade.

name: The Chöd feasts (distributions)

definitions.definition: The body-offering is visualized in several 'feasts' — white, red, multicoloured and black — differing in what the body becomes and to whom it is given (summary only; restricted).

notes: Membership and meanings recalled with low confidence.

name: Chöd as the Dharma that went from Tibet to India (the tradition's account)

definitions.definition: Indian scholars tested Machig, accepted her teaching and carried it to India; the only Dharma said to have travelled in that direction.
The large hand-drum, the bell and the thighbone trumpet accompany the sung Chöd liturgy; the melodies are transmitted with the practice.
Chöd is traced in a 'father' strand from Padampa Sangye and a 'mother' strand from Machig Labdrön, and distinguished as sūtra-tradition and tantra-tradition Chöd (and their union).

name: The world as the play of consciousness (cidvilāsa)

definitions.definition: The one self-luminous reality sports as the world without change or second; words, ignorance and knowledge all fall away before it, and the realised live a natural devotion. Readers differ on whether this is Śaṅkara's Advaita or a distinct non-dualism that does not posit ignorance as a principle.

relations.note: the play is the union of Śiva and Śakti

name: The Cīnācāra and the Vasiṣṭha–Buddha story

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: Vasiṣṭha failed to win the Goddess by Vedic austerity and was sent to Mahācīna, where the Buddha taught him the Kula way, beginning with purity, the paśu disposition and breath-yoga (Rudrayāmala 17.105-140); Buddha and Vasiṣṭha are the two Kula-Bhairavas perfected by Ugratārā's mantra (Tārā Tantra 1.2-4).

The mind is coloured by the object (4.17), its modifications are always known to its lord puruṣa, who does not change (4.18), it is not self-luminous because it is seen (4.19), coloured by seer and seen it is all-objective (4.23), and though variegated by countless vāsanās it is for another because it acts in combination (4.24).

The mind is a product of the guṇas (YBh 1.2), seen and not self-luminous (4.19), variegated by countless latent tendencies yet existing for another (4.24); it is one, has many objects and endures (YBh 1.32); it has seen properties (cognitions) and seven unseen ones — stilling, merit, impressions, transformation, life, movement, capacity (YBh 3.15); coloured by seer and seen it apprehends all (4.23). Commentators equate it with the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

Scattered, stupefied, distracted, one-pointed and stilled (YBh 1.1); samādhi in the distracted mind is not yoga; samprajñāta occurs in the one-pointed, asamprajñāta in the stilled mind.

name: The four conditions of the mind's sattva (YBh 1.2)

definitions.definition: Vyāsa: the mind has three guṇas; its sattva, whose form is illumination, mixed with rajas and tamas is fond of lordship and sense-objects; pierced by tamas it goes toward adharma, ignorance, non-dispassion and non-lordship; when the covering of delusion is worn away and only touched by rajas it goes toward dharma, knowledge, dispassion and lordship; freed even of the trace of rajas it is established in its own form, reduced to discernment of the difference of sattva and puruṣa, and goes to the meditation of the cloud of dharma (YBh 1.2).

definitions.definition: Consciousness occurs in fixed series: the five-door process of up to seventeen mind-moments (life-continuum, adverting, sense consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, seven impulsions, two registrations), mind-door processes, absorption and path processes; each moment conditions the next by proximity, contiguity, absence and disappearance.

Real forces neither material nor mental: possession, non-possession, homogeneity, the non-perceptual state, the two attainments, life faculty, the four characteristics, and the three collections of names, phrases, syllables.
Designations for states of the series.

Mind's nature is described as inseparable clarity and emptiness (gsal stong), appearances as appearance-emptiness (snang stong, 'like a moon in water'), the experience of the method path as bliss-emptiness (bde stong), awareness as awareness-emptiness (rig stong).

Consciousness is one in its characteristic of knowing but 89 types by plane, kind and association: 54 sense-sphere (12 unwholesome, 18 rootless, 24 beautiful), 15 fine-material, 12 immaterial, 8 supramundane (121 when the supramundane are multiplied by five jhānas).

relations.note: Yoga's citta is one mind-stuff with modifications; the Abhidhamma's citta is a series of momentary consciousnesses of many types

definitions.definition: Mantras (male deity) and vidyās (female deity); male, female and neuter by their endings; fiery and lunar, awakening with the flow of breath in the right, left or both channels (ŚT 2.57–63); seed (bīja), compound (piṇḍa, kūṭa) and longer mantras.
Bound (baddha), freed (mukta) and eternal (nitya); bound souls seek enjoyment or release, and seekers of release seek kaivalya or the Lord, by bhakti or prapatti.
Five kinds: eternal, freed, bound, isolated (kevala, those in kaivalya) and seekers of release (mumukṣu).

name: Obligatory, occasional, desire-prompted and prohibited acts

definitions.definition: Nitya acts (lifelong) and naimittika acts (on occasions) are to be performed — they destroy past sin and avert the demerit of omission; kāmya acts bring their fruits and more births; niṣiddha acts bring demerit. The seeker of release does the first two and avoids the last two.
The seeker of release abstains from prohibited and desire-prompted acts, exhausts past karma by experience, and destroys it by self-knowledge with calm, restraint and celibacy.

Souls are liberated or worldly; worldly souls are with or without mind, mobile or immobile; one-sensed beings are embodied in earth, water, fire, air and plants; others have two to five senses (TS 2.10–24); the lowest are the nigoda beings sharing one body.

relations.note: The extent of non-violence follows from the extent of life (one-sensed beings included).

definitions.definition: Pots are only clay, names being a matter of speech; so the world is non-different from Brahman (ChU 6.1.4; BS 2.1.14).
The fourth empty, all-empty, the cause of the world and the ultimate truth; realized at the fourth stage (abhisambodhi).
Tilopa's clear light of mind; the Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa's clear-light yoga with its appearances.

Mind-as-such co-emergent is the dharmakāya; appearances co-emergent are the light of the dharmakāya; thoughts co-emergent are the waves of the dharmakāya: the instruction joins the disciple to what was never separate.

relations.note: the Buddhist innate (U44) as taught in the Kagyu instruction

definitions.definition: Songs speak in double meanings (sandhyā-bhāṣā) of the body, the moons, the tide and the Man, so that practice is taught only to the initiated.
The manuals and padas conceal the practice in the language of Vaiṣṇava rasa.
The Bhāber Gīt is deliberately obscure, using the imagery of the bazaar and the company; the teaching is gupta.

relations.note: The Sant upside-down song and the Bengali coded song share the device of paradox that hides and reveals.

name: Cognition as an adventitious quality of the self

definitions.definition: Cognition (buddhi = jñāna = upalabdhi) is a non-eternal quality of the self produced by the contact of self, mind, sense and object; it is not the self's nature and is absent in liberation (NS 1.1.15, 3.2.1–9; NBh 1.1.22).
The individual self's cognition, desire and effort are non-eternal; the Lord's are eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Vedānta's self-luminous consciousness as the self's nature.

definitions.definition: Non-injury, truth, not stealing, purity and sense-restraint for all four classes (MDh 10.63), with giving, self-control, compassion and patience (YS 1.122); the Arthaśāstra's list for all (1.3.13).

relations.note: both are class-independent lists of virtues (MDh 6.92; 10.63)

definitions.definition: Reciting the teaching together in numbered lists so that the holy life may last (DN 33), the model of the councils.
Five stages: vajra recitation, mind isolation (the empties), self-consecration, clear light, union.
The six-branch yoga culminating in empty form and immutable bliss.

Rebirth may follow an earlier deed, a later one, or the view at death, so those who see only part generalise wrongly (MN 136); results are graded by the doer's development (AN 3.100); kamma's results are unthinkable in detail (AN 4.77).

The ordinary person conceives each thing — earth to nibbāna — as self, in self, from self or 'mine' and delights in it; the trainee should not conceive; the Tathāgata does not, having understood that delight is the root of suffering (MN 1); 'I am' is a conceiving (MN 140).

name: The conjunction of puruṣa and prakṛti (saṃyoga)

definitions.definition: Their conjunction, like that of the lame and the blind, produces creation (SK 21), makes the unconscious seem conscious and the indifferent seem an agent (SK 20); it is due to non-discrimination (SS 1.55) and its cause is variously given as karma, non-discrimination (Pañcaśikha) or the subtle body (Sanandana) (SS 6.67–69).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: puruṣa, situated in prakṛti, experiences the guṇas born of prakṛti, and attachment to them causes its births in good and bad wombs (13.22); whatever being is born, moving or unmoving, is from the union (saṃyoga) of the field and the knower of the field (13.27).
