name: Consciousness and wisdom (rnam shes / ye shes)

definitions.definition: Consciousness is dualistic knowing under delusion; wisdom is the same knowing recognizing its nature; the path does not replace one with the other but reveals the latter in the former.

A recurring story: the vital powers (speech, sight, hearing, mind and others) dispute which is best; each leaves the body in turn and it survives; when breath begins to leave, all are uprooted, and they acknowledge breath as best (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1; PrU 2.3-4; KauU 2.14; cf. BAU 1.3 and 1.5.21).

definitions.definition: The Tathāgata uses the world's expressions without grasping them (DN 9); 'being' is a convention like 'chariot' (SN 5.10); in the ultimate sense no person is found (Mil 3.1.1) — the root of the commentarial two truths (sammuti- and paramattha-sacca).

relations.note: the commentarial two truths (sammuti- and paramattha-sacca) build on these passages

definitions.definition: Appearances that function as they appear are the correct conventional; those that do not (a mirage as water) the incorrect (Jñānagarbha); the correct conventional is the ladder to reality (MH 3.12).
Conventional things satisfy only when unexamined, arise and cease, and can function (MAL 64).
Candrakīrti distinguishes the correct and incorrect conventional only from the world's standpoint; for the noble ones all of it is merely conventional (MA 6.25–28, from memory).

name: Correspondences (bandhu) between body, ritual and cosmos

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads pair items of the body (adhyātma) with items of the cosmos (adhidaivata) and of the ritual: the horse and the cosmos (BAU 1.1), the senses and deities (AU 1.1-2), mind and space (ChU 3.18), wind and breath as 'gatherers' (ChU 4.3), the fivefold (TU 1.7), combinations (TU 1.3), the person as sacrifice (ChU 3.16-17).

name: Cycles of cosmic time across the families

definitions.definition: Four ages (kṛta, tretā, dvāpara, kali) making a mahāyuga; a day of Brahmā (kalpa) and its night of dissolution.
Endless alternation of ascending and descending half-cycles (utsarpiṇī, avasarpiṇī), each of six periods, in Bharata and Airāvata.
Aeons (kalpa) of formation, duration, destruction and emptiness; the great aeon made of eighty intermediate aeons.

notes: 'kalpa' is shared vocabulary with different measures and structures.

definitions.definition: From the self space, from space wind, then fire, water, earth, plants, food, the person; also (2.6.1) the one who desired to be many performed tapas, created all and entered it.

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

name: Cosmology in the Gelug curriculum

definitions.definition: The Abhidharmakośa's world system (Mount Meru, four continents, the desire, form and formless realms, the eon cycle) studied as the conventional cosmology, alongside the Kālacakra's different system; both are taught as conventional presentations.

notes: Sources: src:abhidharmakosa, src:kalacakra-tantra, src:sheja-rabsel (Sakya).

name: The world and its extent in Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: Saṃsāra is beginningless (MMK 11.1); the views that the world is eternal or not, finite or infinite rest on the prior and posterior ends and do not arise for one who sees all as empty (27.1–2, 27.29); the three realms and the ten virtuous and non-virtuous paths are taught conventionally (RĀ 1).

relations.note: the same set of undetermined questions

name: Cosmology: space, time and the worlds

definitions.definition: The path of space (deśādhvan): the worlds from Kālāgni to the highest, measured and ordered within the tattvas (TĀ 8); the path of time (kālādhvan): the cycles of time mirrored in the movement of the breath (TĀ 6); the world as the Lord's play and as phases of cognition.

notes: Chapter-level; no worlds enumerated here.

definitions.definition: Rājagaha (after the parinibbāna), Vesālī (a century later, on the ten points), Pāṭaliputta under Aśoka (Kathāvatthu).
A council under Kaniṣka in Kashmir compiled the Vibhāṣā (Xuanzang).

name: Courting dishonour and the exchange of merit and sin

definitions.definition: The second-stage ascetic hides his sign and provokes contempt; those who revile him receive his demerit and he receives their merit; dishonour is the highest restraint and makes his austerity complete. Kauṇḍinya: undertaken only after gaining knowledge, with impurity reduced and the teacher's leave, without breaking the restraints.

From Brahman associated with māyā arise space, air, fire, water, earth (TU 2.1) as subtle elements, then by quintuplication the gross; creation is sport, a superimposition taught to lead to the uncreated; Brahman is both material and efficient cause.

name: Creation and dissolution of the world

definitions.definition: There is no proof of a first creation or of a dissolution destroying everything; beings arise and perish continually, 'as today' (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 66–68, 113).
Things arise and perish gradually; people were always born of parents (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the Lord is the origin and dissolution of the whole world (7.6; 9.18); at the close of a kalpa beings go into his prakṛti and at its beginning he sends them forth again, taking hold of his prakṛti (9.7–8); prakṛti brings forth the moving and unmoving with him as overseer (9.10); manifest things arise from and dissolve into the unmanifest with Brahmā's day and night (8.18–19). These acts do not bind him (9.9).

notes: Kumārila's Tantravārttika (on MS 1.3.6) nevertheless speaks of fourteen Manus in every kalpa; how this sits with ŚV 113 is not discussed in the passages checked.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

name: Cosmic creation and dissolution by Maheśvara's will

definitions.definition: At the end of a Brahmā's lifespan Maheśvara wills dissolution and all products are resolved into atoms; then He wills creation for the selves' experience: through adṛṣṭa motion arises in atoms, dyads and the elements arise in order, Brahmā is born in a cosmic egg and appointed to create beings (Praśastapāda).

name: Creation, dissolution and the Lord's cosmic deeds in the Āḻvār hymns

definitions.definition: When nothing existed the Lord created Brahmā, gods, worlds and lives; Nārāyaṇa made Brahmā and Brahmā Śiva; he pervades the elements as life in a body; at dissolution he swallows the worlds and lies as a child on a banyan leaf, and restores them; he measured the worlds as Trivikrama.

notes: The banyan-leaf and world-swallowing images are pervasive in the Prabandham; specific verse refs not recorded.

name: Creation accounts of the principal Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The self alone in the beginning says 'I am', divides into man and woman and emits all pairs (BAU 1.4.1-4); death/hunger at the beginning (BAU 1.2); the self creates worlds and a cosmic person whose organs become deities (AU 1); being thinks 'may I be many' and emits heat, water and food (ChU 6.2-3); non-being becomes being and an egg (ChU 3.19); from the self space, wind, fire, water, earth (TU 2.1); Prajāpati's pair of matter and breath (PrU 1.4); like sparks from fire (BAU 2.1.20; MuU 2.1.1); by tapas (TU 2.6; MuU 1.1.8).

queries: prepared segments: BĀU 1.4.1-4, BĀU 1.2, AU 1, ChU 6.2-3, ChU 3.19, TU 2.1, PrU 1.4, BĀU 2.1.20, MuU 2.1.1, TU 2.6
checks.note: All 11 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 1.4.1-4; BĀU 1.2; AU 1; ChU 6.2-3; ChU 3.19; TU 2.1; PrU 1.4; BĀU 2.1.20; MuU 2.1.1; TU 2.6; MuU 1.1.8). It rests on 12 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Kālī dwells in the cremation ground with jackals around her (Kālī Tantra dhyāna); the vīra worships her there at night (Karpūrādistotra, restricted); corpse and skull seats (śava-sādhana, pañcamuṇḍī) belong to the same setting (restricted, summary only). In Bengali devotion the heart is made the cremation ground so that the Mother may dance there (song ascribed to Rāmprasād, low confidence).

relations.note: fierce setting vs auspicious forms

definitions.definition: What leads to dispassion, release, dismantling, few wishes, contentment, seclusion, energy and unburdensomeness is the Dhamma and the Teacher's instruction (AN 8.53).
(As reported) Pervasion cannot be established by any means; an adventitious condition cannot be excluded; inference proves either nothing new or nothing at all.
One who denies inference uses it in making his intention known.
Idols, pilgrimage, ritual bathing, touch-purity, fasting and sacrifice, sectarian garb, the Veda and the Qur'ān recited without love are rejected; the yogī dyed his clothes, not his mind.
Every outward offering is already defiled (milk by the calf, flowers by the bee); purity is of the mind.
Your path is covered by temple and mosque.

name: The siddhas' critique of ritual, caste and scholasticism

definitions.definition: Saraha and Tilopa mock Brahmin fire offerings and Vedic recitation, Śaiva ash-smearing, Jain nudity, Buddhist monastic austerity and scholastic learning, pilgrimage and bathing, and even tantric maṇḍala and mantra when taken as ends; the innate is not in them.

relations.note: Parallel critique by the Tamil Siddhars; historical connection not established.

name: The critique of sacrifice and funeral offerings

definitions.definition: (As reported) Sacrifice, śrāddha and the Veda are a livelihood of priests; the Veda was made by buffoons, knaves and demons.
Animal sacrifice, fire-worship and caste by birth are refuted; if the slain beast goes to heaven let brāhmaṇas slay brāhmaṇas.
(As reported) 'There is no gift, no sacrifice, no offering.'

relations.note: both the Lokāyata and the Buddhist Jātaka turn the sacrificed-animal argument against the brāhmaṇas

name: Vedic ritual and scripture in Vīraśaiva teaching

definitions.definition: Basava will put the Veda to the touchstone and fetter the śāstras; worship of the moving replaces sacrifice and temple.

The SSM upholds the Veda and Āgama as one in meaning but declares sacrifices, the Agnihotra and austerities not worth a fraction of liṅga-worship or the five-syllable mantra, and useless without devotion.
A clear crystal appears red near a red flower; so the self appears with the qualities of its adjuncts.

name: The sūtra as object of worship

definitions.definition: Writing, honoring, reciting and teaching a sūtra is supreme merit; where it is kept or taught is a caitya without relics, the Tathāgata's whole body.
Simply being still — the silent guru's whole teaching to Tāyumāṉavar; stilling the mind is harder than every power (taming elephants, transmuting metals, entering other bodies).

Curable disorders turn back by opposite-quality medicines rightly applied; no remedy is taught for the incurable (Ca Sū 1.62-63); a physician who treats the incurable loses wealth, learning and fame (Sū 10.8).

The four ages and dharma's decline through them (MBh 3.148; Vyāsa to Śuka 12.224); the Lord's coming age after age (BhG 4.8); Mārkaṇḍeya's vision of the dissolution (3.186); in the Rāmāyaṇa, Nārada ties austerity by each varṇa to the ages (7.74).

name: Śiva as the small space in the heart

definitions.definition: The dahara of Chāndogya 8.1 is Śiva, the supreme ether that is his cit-śakti.

Fate (daiva) is karma made in another birth; success comes from fate and human effort together, like a harvest from rain and ploughing; a single defect ruins all (Yogayātrā 1.3–4). Favourable planets alone do not bring success, or the astrologer would be king; rites alone do not, or the priest would be king (1.5–6). Yet an act begun under ill-placed planets destroys its doer, and a well-timed one succeeds with slight effort (BS 103.59–60). The smṛti says fate is human effort of a former body and a chariot does not move on one wheel (YājñSm 1.349–351).

relations.note: both the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and Varāhamihira call fate one's own former action; they differ in weight — the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha makes present effort all-powerful, Varāhamihira requires both

definitions.definition: Life depends on both: daiva is one's own former deed, puruṣakāra present effort; weak daiva is overcome by effort and weak effort by strong daiva; some karma is fixed in time, some roused by conditions (Ca Vi 3.29-36); karma-born diseases subside only with the exhaustion of karma (Śā 1.116-117).

The astrologer (sāṃvatsara, daivajña) must be of good family, pleasing, learned in all three branches, pure, skilled and eloquent (BS 2); only a seer crosses the ocean of Kālapuruṣa (BS 2.4); the king must honour him, and even forest-dwelling renunciants consult him (BS 2.6–8); one who predicts by trickery, feigned possession or eavesdropping is no knower of fate (BS 2.15); the Kerala manual requires daily worship, recitation and truthfulness of him (Praśna Mārga 1).
Female enlightened or worldly beings who reveal instructions (Nāropa's old woman, Virūpa's Nairātmyā), guard the secret and punish breaches.

Four-armed, terrible-faced, with loose hair and garland of heads, sword and severed head in the left hands, fearlessness and boon in the right, on Śiva as a corpse, united with Mahākāla, smiling (Kālī Tantra as quoted in Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra); the Karpūrādistotra gives the same hands (v. 4). Bengali legend ascribes the fixing of this form to Kṛṣṇānanda.

Giving to worthy recipients at due times and places; the sixteen great gifts (tulāpuruṣa, hiraṇyagarbha, etc.); gifts made in life or at death ease the road of the dead (Vaitaraṇī cow, umbrellas, sandals, food).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: The giver's wealth does not waste away; who eats alone has only sin (RV 10.117); givers of gifts stand high in heaven and partake of immortality (10.107.2).

name: The dance of Naṭarāja and the Chidambaram tradition

definitions.definition: Śiva dances the ānanda-tāṇḍava in the hall of Chidambaram (the 'space of consciousness'), witnessed by Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda; the dance is the five acts, the raised foot being grace; Chidambaram is also the heart within the body.
Śiva as dancer in the cremation ground (Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār) and in the golden hall of Tillai (Tēvāram, Tiruvicaippā, Tirumantiram's ninth tantra).

name: The dangers of forcing (the texts' own warnings)

definitions.definition: The breath is to be tamed gradually like a lion, elephant or tiger, otherwise it kills the practitioner (HYP 2.15); improper practice causes hiccup, asthma, cough, pains of head, ears and eyes (2.16–17); release, fill and hold it 'skilfully' (2.18); draw and release it slowly, never holding too long (GŚ 51); beginning at the wrong season or without moderate diet brings disease (GS 5.8–9, 5.16); viparītakaraṇī needs ample food or the fire burns the body (HYP 3.80–81); khecarī's preparation only under a guru (Khecarīvidyā).

name: Darkness as mere absence of light

definitions.definition: Darkness is not a substance but the absence of light (VS 5.2.21 C).

Life unfolds through periods ruled by planets or signs: Varāhamihira's periods of planets placed in angles, succedents and cadents (BJ 8); Parāśara's many systems — asterism-based (Viṃśottarī, Aṣṭottarī, Ṣoḍaśottarī …), sign-based (Cara, Sthira, Nārāyaṇa …), Kālacakra, Yoginī and others — 'not all accepted by all' (BPHS 46.3–11).

Beyond the nine openings, the tenth door: twofold as the path of nectar and the path of death, at the root of the brahma-staff; the śaṅkhinī-mouth between the royal teeth through which nectar flows (AmŚ 31–32, 69–70).

name: The ten descents (daśāvatāra) in the Gīta Govinda

definitions.definition: Fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Balarāma, the Buddha (who in compassion condemned animal sacrifice) and Kalki — all forms taken by Kṛṣṇa, to whom the hymn's closing verse bows as the bearer of the ten.
The devotee's stance 'I am your servant' rather than 'I am He', and the giving of the fruits of work to the jaṅgamas and the community; in modern maṭhas, free feeding and schooling.
'I am the servant; the Lord is the master in the form of all' — Hanumān's and Bharata's devotion.
Servant-devotion alone is cultivated; the erotic mood is not.
'Keep me as your servant' — Mīrā's plea alongside her bridal love.
Tyāgarāja prefers service near Rāma to wealth; Bhadrācala Rāmadās, Rāma's servant, reproaches his master.

relations.note: dāsya is one of the devotional relationships

name: The day and night of Brahmā

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.17–19: Brahmā's day lasts a thousand ages and his night likewise; at the coming of day all manifest things come forth from the unmanifest, at the coming of night they dissolve into it; the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly. Even Brahmā's world is a world of return (8.16).

Brahmā's day and night each last a thousand ages; at day beings emerge from the unmanifest and at night dissolve into it, again and again (BhG 8.17–19); at the end of a kalpa beings enter the Lord's prakṛti (9.7).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, combining extractor A's entry and extractor B's cpt:ages-and-day-of-brahma (the Gītā does not give the ages or the Manu-periods).

definitions.definition: At death the body burns with the sacrificial implements, but the self, its owner, goes to the heavenly world; the fruits of rites are enjoyed in another world, which is why knowing the self as distinct from the body matters for ritual.

name: Death and the attainment of cessation distinguished

definitions.definition: At death bodily, verbal and mental formations cease, vitality is exhausted, heat dissipated and the faculties broken up; in cessation the formations cease but vitality and heat remain and the faculties are clear (MN 43).

For the knower the place and manner of death do not matter - even without memory, in a holy place or an outcaste's house, he is liberated at the moment of knowledge (Paramārthasāra 83); the last moment only assists the deluded (90); funerary rites and a rite of immediate departure exist for initiates (TĀ 19, 24-25).

name: Death and impermanence in the Madhyamaka manuals

definitions.definition: Recollection that one will die and go alone, leaving relatives and possessions (BCA 2.32, 2.62), and that all born beings are subject to the lord of death (CŚ ch.1), turns the mind from craving toward the Dharma; nirvāṇa and the Tathāgata after death are not described by the four alternatives (MMK 25.17–18).

name: Death and rebirth-linking in the Abhidhamma

definitions.definition: Death comes by exhaustion of life-span, of kamma, of both, or by a destructive kamma; at death a kamma, a kamma-sign or a destiny-sign presents itself; death consciousness is followed immediately by rebirth-linking with that object — there is no intermediate existence.

name: Taking death, bardo and rebirth as the three bodies

definitions.definition: In the Highest Yoga Tantra generation stage (Guhyasamāja and others), the practitioner rehearses the dissolution of death as the dharmakāya, the intermediate state as the sambhogakāya and rebirth as the nirmāṇakāya, preparing to transform the actual processes in the completion stage and at death.

relations.note: the eight dissolutions of dying are the first phase

definitions.definition: At death the body born of mother and father perishes, while the constant subtle body, perfumed by the dispositions, transmigrates to divine, animal or human birth according to virtue and non-virtue (SK 39–40, 44, 53); suffering from old age and death lasts until the subtle body ceases (SK 55). The knower's body falls when impressions are exhausted, and isolation follows (SK 67–68). The teachers disagreed on the subtle body at death and birth (Yuktidīpikā on SK 39).

name: Death and dissolution in Śākta teaching

definitions.definition: For the steadfast knower the place of death makes no difference — an outcaste's house or Kāśī — for he is liberated while living (PKS 10.82); the Kaula Upaniṣad teaches liberation in this very body without departure on the path of the gods (with Bhāskararāya); at the great dissolution all the gods perish while the Goddess's consort sports on (SL 26).

name: Death in Yoga: clinging, omens, departure

definitions.definition: Clinging to life (abhiniveśa), a fear of death found even in the newborn worm, shows past births (2.9, YBh 2.9); karma ripening as life-span is fast or slow, and saṃyama on it or omens give knowledge of death — omens personal, from other beings and from the gods (3.22, YBh 3.22); mastery of udāna gives departure at will at death (3.39); the mass of karma manifested at death forms the next birth (YBh 2.13).
At death speech merges in mind etc.; the knower of the attributeless Brahman does not depart (his prāṇas merge here); the meditator departs by the crown channel and the path of light.
Triśikhi 119–127: the cessation of throbbing at particular points of the limbs and failure to see the tip of one's tongue foretell the time of death.

The haṭha compendia include the signs of approaching death: the Haṭhatattvakaumudī's chapter on kālavañcana; the Śiva Svarodaya's prognostication from the breath; the Śiva Saṃhitā's gazing at one's shadow-image in the sky (seeing it whole means long life).

In jyotiṣa, early death is foretold by ariṣṭa yogas at birth (BJ 6; BPHS 9) and a king's death by portents such as images weeping or sweating (BS 45.8); longevity is computed and the killing planets identified (BJ 7; BPHS 44).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: Death and dying in the Sant and Bāul traditions

definitions.definition: Death (kāl) stands over every head: do today what you would do tomorrow; the clay will knead the potter; between the mill-stones none survives; yet the death the world fears is joy to the devotee; Kabīr went to Maghar to die to refute the belief that dying in Kāśī liberates; he returned the sheet of the body unstained.
At death Kāl's messengers let pass the soul that bears the true Name and the pān-parvānā; the caukā rite is performed for the dead.
The Master himself receives the initiate at death; meditation is daily rehearsal of death.
The cage of green bamboo will break; if the neighbour touched me the torments of death would go; Bāuls and fakirs are commonly buried (samādhi) rather than cremated, as Lalon was at Cheuṛiyā.

notes: Bāul burial practice recorded from general report (moderate confidence).

name: Deathbed practice and right mindfulness at death

definitions.definition: The dying person faces west, fixes mind and voice on Amitābha; companions recite with him, record and repent visions; those who have taken wine or meat keep away; friends pledge in advance to help one another complete the ten recitations; do not move or weep over the dying.
The person of shinjin does not depend on the manner of death or deathbed rites.

relations.note: analogous emphasis on the state of mind at death (BhG 8.5-6 and the Purāṇas / the ten recitations); the Pure Land relies on the Buddha's welcome, not on the thought alone

definitions.definition: Amitābha and the holy assembly appear before the dying practitioner (19th vow; Smaller Sūtra); Huiyuan's vision before death.
The nenbutsu practitioner is welcomed at death (Senchakushū; the raigō paintings).
Belongs to those of various practices; not awaited by the person of shinjin.
The fruit of the five golden dharmas: a mind that does not die and a body that does not err, i.e. realization of the undying nature; practised through wind and deity yogas (restricted).
Debate aims at truth; only two grounds of defeat are valid; stating superfluous members or using tricks is itself a fault.

name: The method of monastic debate (rtsod pa)

definitions.definition: A standing challenger, opening with Mañjuśrī's syllable 'dhīḥ', poses consequences to a seated defender, clapping and stamping at each point; the defender may answer only 'I accept', 'the reason is not established', 'there is no pervasion' or ask 'why?'; debate is a meditation that sharpens analysis and cuts wrong views.

relations.note: a Tibetan form of Buddhist debate practice
Nyāya's classification of debate types

notes: Recalled; symbolism of the clap varies in explanation.

name: The debts (ṛṇa) and the possibility of liberation

definitions.definition: The objection that lifelong Vedic debts, afflictions and duties leave no room for liberation is answered: 'debt' is figurative; the renunciant places the fires within the self; the stages of life allow for liberation (NS 4.1.59–62; NBh).

name: Decline and renewal of human life

definitions.definition: Human lifespan falls to ten years through neglect of Dhamma and rises to eighty thousand as virtue returns (DN 26).

name: The two aspects of the true Dharma and its decline

definitions.definition: The true Dharma is scripture and realization, upheld by those who teach and practise; since the Teacher has passed, the teaching is at its last breath and seekers must not be heedless.
In the 'last five hundred years' of the true dharma's destruction, some will still have faith in and keep these sūtras; the Lotus's peaceful practices are for the latter age.

relations.note: Both describe the decline of the teaching; the Kośa's twofold āgama/adhigama frame.

name: The duration and decline of the true Dhamma

definitions.definition: The true Dhamma would have lasted a thousand years; with women's going forth it will last five hundred (Cv 10.1.6; AN 8.51); the monks' conditions of non-decline (DN 16).

relations.note: the commentarial doctrine of the decline of the Sāsana (U37)

definitions.definition: For Yoga, sleep is itself an activity of the mind, whose support is the cognition of absence (YS 1.10) — a cognition because it is recollected on waking ('I slept happily', 'I slept heavily') — and it must be stilled in samādhi like other cognitions (YBh 1.10); the knowledge of dream or sleep may serve as a support for steadying the mind (1.38).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): in deep sleep one has merged with being, 'gone to one's own' (ChU 6.8.1); one desires no desire and sees no dream, embraced by the intelligent self, beyond sorrow (BAU 4.3.19-22); one lies in the hitā channels (BAU 2.1.19); the mind overcome by light (PrU 4.6); Indra objects that there one does not know oneself (ChU 8.11).
In deep sleep the self rests in the Lord within the heart, its knowledge contracted; it persists as 'I', as the memory 'I slept happily' shows.

queries: prepared segments: ChU 6.8.1, BĀU 4.3.19-22, BĀU 2.1.19, PrU 4.6, ChU 8.11
checks.note: All 5 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 6.8.1; BĀU 4.3.19-22; BĀU 2.1.19; PrU 4.6; ChU 8.11). It rests on 7 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: In deep sleep the soul, covered by tamas, rests in Hari as Prājña, neither desiring nor seeing; yet the witness still perceives time (and the self), so deep sleep is not the absence of all awareness.

name: Deep sleep in Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: In dreamless sleep there is no affliction — the analogy for liberation's possibility (NS 4.1.63).
No cognition arises in deep sleep because the mind rests in the channel purītat and lacks contact with the skin-sense, which every cognition requires (commentarial tradition on the Muktāvalī).

notes: The purītat account is confirmed in a local commentary e-text (Subodhinī) but not traced to a root text here.

name: Bhakti defined across the schools

definitions.definition: Nārada Bhakti Sūtra: supreme love (parama-prema) for the Lord, of the nature of nectar; not desire but relinquishment; its own fruit.
Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra: supreme attachment (parānurakti) to Īśvara — a form of rāga, not knowledge, not an act.
NBS 16–19's doxography: attachment to worship (Vyāsa), to hearing his stories (Garga), love not opposed to delight in the self (Śāṇḍilya), offering all acts and anguish at forgetting him (Nārada).
The Āḻvārs: love (aṉpu), longing (ārvam) and a melting heart lit as a lamp for Nāraṇaṉ; 'knowledge-and-love' (matinalam) given by the Lord's grace.
Rāmānuja: knowledge that has become love (prīti) — steady remembrance (dhruvānusmṛti) of the Lord, vivid as perception, won by his grace.
Madhva: very firm love (sneha), greater than love for anything else, preceded by knowledge of the Lord's greatness.
Rūpa Gosvāmī: pure devotion (uttamā bhakti) is favourable cultivation of Kṛṣṇa, empty of other desires and unobscured by knowledge and works.
Madhusūdana Sarasvatī: the mind melted by the Lord's qualities flowing continuously toward him; the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi: devotion is the constant search into one's own true nature.
The Bhāgavata: devotion free of the guṇas is the mind's unbroken movement toward the Lord, like the Gaṅgā to the sea, unmotivated and uninterrupted.
The Gītā: by undivided devotion the Lord is known, seen and entered; supreme devotion is reached by one who has become Brahman.

relations.note: a comparative view of cpt:bhakti

notes: Graded equivalences between the defining terms are recorded on the terms (trm:parama-prema, trm:paranurakti, trm:matinalam, trm:kanta-bhava) with rests_on. The schools do not accept each other's definitions: Advaita reads devotion as a means to or form of self-knowledge; the Nārada Sūtra holds it is the fruit; Rāmānuja makes it a form of knowledge; the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra denies that it is knowledge.

name: Definitive and provisional teaching in the Kunjed Gyalpo

definitions.definition: The Kunjed Gyalpo calls the separate teachings of the three-kāya teachers provisional (drang ba'i lung) with respect to suchness, and the teaching that everything is one in the nature beyond effort definitive.

relations.note: a text-internal use of the neyārtha / nītārtha distinction

definitions.definition: The true liṅga is within the body — the all-pervading one above the lotuses in which all dissolves; liṅgas of stone, wood or clay are to be abandoned (KJN 3.9–31).

relations.standpoint: the liṅga as the site of dissolution
relations.note: Śaiva traditions distinguish the partless and embodied liṅga; the Kaula rejects the external liṅga altogether

definitions.definition: The body is a cage with eight rooms and nine doors and a mirror-palace above, where the unknown bird comes and goes; its currents, lotuses and 'moons' are known only through the guru; it is the only temple.
The body's inner lakes and lotuses as the abode of the divine couple.

name: The body as the self (dehātmavāda)

definitions.definition: (As reported) The person is the body qualified by consciousness, known from 'I am fat, I am thin'.

notes: The Vedāntasāra's graded list (tea:vedantasara:refutation) distinguishes Cārvākas who take the gross body, the senses, the breath or the mind as the self.

name: Transformation of body and of metal

definitions.definition: Rasa-śāstra's purpose is liberation through transforming the body (dehavedha), not gold-making; metal-transmutation (lohavedha) is to be tested first and then applied to the body (SDS 23-25).

The deity is that to which the offering is directed, as named in injunction or mantra; the sacrificial act, not the deity, is principal and produces the fruit; the deity's embodiment and eating are not established — mantra and arthavāda statements implying them are not meant that way (MS 9.1.6–9, Śabara).
The Brahma Sūtra reports Jaimini as denying gods eligibility for certain meditations.

name: Worshipping the deity by becoming the deity

definitions.definition: One who is not Śiva should not worship Śiva: the worshipper first makes himself Śiva by nyāsa and meditation ('śivo bhūtvā śivaṃ yajet').
The Pāñcarātra worshipper, purified by bhūtaśuddhi and nyāsa, contemplates himself as one with the Lord before worship (recalled; low confidence on the wording of the maxim in Vaiṣṇava manuals).
In deity yoga the practitioner generates himself as the deity with its form, maṇḍala and 'divine pride', knowing the form to be empty.
The worshipper realizes identity with the Goddess in the Śrīcakra and in the body (the body as Śrīcakra).

relations.note: shared ritual logic; the Buddhist tradition insists the deity is empty of own nature while the Śaiva holds the self to be Śiva

notes: The maxims 'nādevo devam arcayet' / 'śivo bhūtvā śivaṃ yajet' are recalled from ritual manuals, not anchored to a verse here (no rests_on).

definitions.definition: Meditating oneself as the deity — appearance inseparable from emptiness, with the deity's pride — the distinctive method of the mantra way; 'there is no meditator, no mantra, no deity: mantra and deity abide in the nature free of elaboration' (Hevajra I.5).
The feature distinguishing mantra from the perfection vehicle: the wisdom realising emptiness itself appears as the deity's body.

name: Dependent origination

definitions.definition: 'When this exists, that comes to be' (SN 12.21): suffering arises through conditions and ceases with their cessation; deep and hard to see (DN 15); whoever sees it sees the Dhamma (MN 28); the middle between existence and non-existence (SN 12.15); it stands whether Tathāgatas arise or not (SN 12.20).
Twelve limbs in three sections over three lives: defilement, karma, ground; a beginningless wheel.

Seeing dependent origination is seeing the dharma and the Buddha; outward (seed-sprout) and inward (twelve links) dependent origination is neither eternal nor annihilated (Śālistamba); what arises from conditions is unborn and empty (Anavatapta); the twelve links rest on mind (Daśabhūmika 6).

Dependent origination, free of the eight extremes, is the pacification of elaboration (dedication) and is emptiness (24.18); conventionally the twelve links, by which the ignorant forms the formations and suffering arises, and by whose knowledge it ceases (MMK 26); whoever sees it sees the four truths (24.40).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's pre-existent effect; see dsp:causation
creation by God is one of the three sectarian tenets rejected in AN 3.61

notes: U38 contribution to a shared concept (U36 owns the sutta account).

name: Dependent origination in the Abhidhamma and commentaries

definitions.definition: Expounded by the sutta method across three lives — three periods, twelve factors, twenty modes, three links, four groups, three rounds (defilement, kamma, result) — and by the Abhidhamma method within a single moment of consciousness; the wheel has no maker and no experiencer.
The whole sequence happens in daily life at each unmindful contact; 'birth' is the birth of the ego.
To be understood intellectually (with a chart) before insight practice.

relations.note: the commentarial and Abhidhamma exposition of the sutta teaching

name: From dwelling on objects to ruin (BhG 2.62–63)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: For one who dwells on sense objects attachment arises; from attachment desire; from desire anger; from anger delusion; from delusion confusion of memory; from loss of memory destruction of understanding; from that one perishes (2.62–63).

notes: The skeleton records the same sequence as the obstacle obs:chain-from-dwelling-on-objects.

name: The descent of Āyurveda (Brahmā to the sages)

definitions.definition: Brahmā → Prajāpati (Dakṣa) → the Aśvins → Indra; then (a) Bharadvāja, sent by the assembled sages, learns from Indra and teaches the sages, and Punarvasu Ātreya teaches six disciples (Ca Sū 1.3-40); (b) Indra teaches Dhanvantari, who as Divodāsa of Kāśī teaches Suśruta and others (Su Sū 1.20-21); (c) Indra teaches Ātreya and other sages (AHS Sū 1.3; Bhāvaprakāśa, where Ātreya himself goes to Indra).
The devotees to be honoured are those who do not desire even liberation; one asks only for devotion.
Tukārām asks for no liberation or wealth, only never to forget God and the saints' company.
Beside the pair's rasa, Vaikuṇṭha and liberation are nothing.

relations.note: the four liberations are not sought

name: Destiny according to the measure of Oṃ at death

definitions.definition: Nādabindu 12–16: one who dies while dwelling on each of the twelve measures attains a corresponding birth or world, the last giving the eternal Brahman.

definitions.definition: Both born of Prajāpati, they contend over the worlds; the Asuras offer into their own mouths in pride, the gods into one another's, and so win the sacrifice (ŚB 5.1.1.1–2); the Asuras lose by barbarous speech (ŚB 3.2.1.23–24) and receive darkness and illusion from Prajāpati (ŚB 2.4.2.5).

definitions.definition: A baby, an old person, a sick person, a criminal punished and a corpse, about which Yama questions the wrongdoer (MN 130; AN 3.36).
The gods can give only worldly fruit and are themselves bound; their worship is forbidden to the seeker.

name: The two paths after death: of the gods and of the fathers

definitions.definition: Those who know (the five fires) and who venerate faith and austerity in the forest go by the flame, the day, the waxing fortnight, the northern course, the year/gods' world, the sun, the moon and lightning to brahman and do not return; those who venerate sacrifice, works and gifts go by smoke, night, the waning fortnight, the southern course, the fathers' world and the moon, and return; those who know neither become small creatures (ChU 5.10; BAU 6.2.15-16; PrU 1.9-10; KauU 1.2-3; ChU 4.15.5).
The path of the gods (beginning with light) for meditators, without return; the path of the fathers (smoke, the moon) for ritualists, with return and residual karma.

definitions.definition: The Śākta Upaniṣads declare the Goddess — Devī, Tripurā, Sītā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī — to be Brahman, the primordial nature and the inner self; the great sayings are her (Bahvṛca).
Śrīvidyā identifies Lalitā with Brahman beyond qualities and with the partless supreme principle (LSN 43-45; YH 2.73-74).

name: The Goddess as Mahāmāyā and the supreme

definitions.definition: The Śākta hymns take up the Purāṇic Mahāmāyā: she makes the universe whirl as queen of the supreme Brahman (SL 98).

The Goddess is eternal, the world is her form; she deludes even the wise and, pleased, liberates; she is the cause of all worlds, the primordial Prakṛti beyond Hari and Hara; all knowledges and women are her forms; she alone exists and her powers return into her.

name: The three episodes of the Devī Māhātmya

definitions.definition: First carita (ch. 1): Yoganidrā leaves Viṣṇu to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha; middle carita (chs. 2-4): the Goddess from the gods' radiance slays Mahiṣa; last carita (chs. 5-13): Ambikā with Kālī-Cāmuṇḍā and the Mothers slays Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa-Muṇḍa, Raktabīja, Niśumbha and Śumbha.

name: The devotee's indifference to powers and liberation

definitions.definition: Those who desire enjoyment, liberation or powers are restless; the devotee is desireless and so at peace.
The 'supernatural capacity' given by grace is capacity to relish the Lord, not yogic power.

The Āḻvārs want neither Indra's kingdom nor dharma, wealth and pleasure, nor the 'drum' as a reward, but only service and devotion in every birth; the Tiruppallāṇṭu admits seekers of wealth and of self-realisation (kaivalya) only if they give those aims up.
Having gained love one desires nothing and has no zeal for other ends; devotion is higher than action, knowledge and yoga.
Terms like birth, rebirth, heaven and hell have an everyday sense and a Dhamma sense referring to present mental states.

relations.note: a hermeneutic of levels of meaning, applied by Buddhadāsa beyond the commentarial use

name: The Dhamma and discipline as teacher

definitions.definition: After the Buddha's death the Dhamma and discipline he taught are to be the teacher (DN 16); monks are to be islands to themselves (DN 16; SN 47.13).

name: Wandering for the welfare of the many

definitions.definition: 'Wander forth for the welfare and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world' (Vin Mv 1.11).
The Buddha to Vakkali: seeing the Dhamma is seeing the Buddha (SN 22.87); the Buddha is called one whose body is the Dhamma (dhammakāya) in DN 27.

name: The inner bodies of the Dhammakāya method

definitions.definition: Resting the mind at the centre of the body, the meditator sees a bright sphere and successive refined bodies (human, divine, Brahma, formless Brahma, and the Dhammakāya bodies of the paths), culminating in the Dhammakāya of the arahant.

notes: From secondary knowledge only; no primary text read.

definitions.definition: Twenty-two triads and one hundred Abhidhamma dyads (in clusters: roots, taints, fetters, ties, floods, bonds, hindrances, misapprehension, clinging, defilements) plus forty-two sutta dyads, by which every dhamma is classified; the Paṭṭhāna applies its conditions to the same matrix.
Whether or not Tathāgatas arise, the element stands — specific conditionality (SN 12.20), the three marks (AN 3.136) — which a Tathāgata discovers and makes known.

What is natural for a bodhisatta: descent from Tusita, conception and birth with earthquakes and light, a virtuous mother who dies seven days after birth, birth standing, the lion's roar 'this is my last birth', the thirty-two marks (DN 14).

name: Combinations for wealth and poverty

definitions.definition: Relations of the lords of the 2nd, 11th, 5th and 9th houses give wealth; afflictions of those houses and lords give poverty (BPHS 41–42).

notes: Chapter-level; rules summarized from memory.

name: Dhāraṇī and mantra in the sūtras

definitions.definition: Dhāraṇīs protecting the preacher (Lotus 26), the Heart's mantra of the perfection of wisdom, the Śūraṅgama mantra, the six-syllable vidyā of Avalokiteśvara.

Rash acts of mind, speech and body; greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, shamelessness, envy, excessive passion and covetousness; harsh, false and untimely speech; acts that harm others (Ca Sū 7.26-29; AHS Sū 4.24) — as against the natural urges that must not be suppressed (Sū 7.3-4).

Dharma is the beneficial object (artha) marked by injunction: the enjoined act that joins a person with the highest good; perception cannot know it, and what the Veda states only as a means for harm (the Śyena) is not dharma.
An object with a purpose made known by the Veda — the sacrifice and the like (Arthasaṅgraha).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): created by brahman as the power of the ruling power; nothing higher; dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); the three branches of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); 'practise dharma' (TU 1.11); one's own dharma lifts the elemental self (MaiU 4.3); the self is beyond dharma and adharma (KU 1.2.14).

relations.note: dharma lies outside the reach of perception and the means based on it
the declared fruit of the paradigm rites

name: Phenomena and their nature (dharma and dharmatā)

definitions.definition: All knowables are summed up as dharmas — the appearance of duality and names, saṃsāra — and dharmatā — suchness free of grasped and grasper, nirvāṇa; the transformation of the basis is the shift from the one to the other.

The property-bearer conforms to properties past, present and not yet determinable (3.14); since everything has the nature of everything, without an enduring continuant there could be no experience or memory (YBh 3.14).

Virtue is a disposition of buddhi that leads upward but not to release (SK 23, 44); Gauḍapāda defines it through compassion, giving and the Pātañjala restraints and observances. Vedic means are impure through animal killing (SK 2; Vācaspati with Pañcaśikha). The knower of the principles is liberated in any stage of life (verse quoted by Gauḍapāda); outward signs of renunciation without knowledge are a false contentment (Gauḍapāda on SK 50); gifts given with conceit bind (Kramadīpikā); one's own duty supports meditation (SS 3.35).

name: Transformation of property, time-mark and state

definitions.definition: What holds for the mind holds for the elements and senses: transformation of property (dharma), of time-mark (lakṣaṇa: future, present, past) and of state (avasthā) (3.13, YBh 3.13); difference of sequence explains difference of transformation (3.15).

name: The dharma as a raft

definitions.definition: Even dharmas are to be abandoned once crossed, still more non-dharmas.

notes: The raft simile is the Pali Alagaddūpama Sutta's (MN 22).

name: Dharma as the source of prosperity and the highest good

definitions.definition: That from which prosperity and the highest good result (VS 1.1.2); the Veda's authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3); merit produced by enjoined acts (Tarkasaṅgraha); common and particular duties (Praśastapāda).

Consciousness as an attribute of the self, distinct from the self-luminous self that has it: eternal, it contracts through karma in bondage and expands to omniscience in release; it reveals objects to its owner and is manifest only to him.

name: Interpenetration in the Avataṃsaka (sūtra layer)

definitions.definition: Worlds in each atom and pore, the Buddha's body filling the dharmadhātu, Maitreya's tower in which every tower contains all others without obstruction.

notes: Huayan's systematic doctrine (Indra's net, four dharmadhātus) is U54.

definitions.definition: The samādhi that arises for one without desire even in prasaṃkhyāna, from discrimination-vision in every way, when the seeds of saṃskāra are destroyed (4.29 with bhāṣya); from it the cessation of afflictions and karma (4.30) and the liberation of the knowing one while living (bhāṣya 4.30).

For one without self-interest even in the highest reflection, complete discernment brings the samādhi called cloud of dharma (4.29); from it afflictions and karma cease (4.30), knowledge becomes infinite (4.31) and the guṇas complete their sequence (4.32). Vyāsa also names the pure mind's meditation 'dharmamegha' (YBh 1.2).
Dharmameghā ('cloud of dharma') is the name of the tenth bodhisattva ground, on which the bodhisattva is consecrated by the buddhas' rays and rains the dharma on beings like a cloud.

definitions.definition: Dharman is what upholds: the first sacrifices were 'the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16); the dead go to heaven and earth 'according to dharman' (10.16.3); men break the gods' dharmas through thoughtlessness (7.89.5); the Earth bears peoples of various dharmas (AVŚ 12.1.45).
Pali Dhammapada (26 chapters, 423 verses).
Udānavarga (33 chapters, c. 1000 verses).
Gāndhārī Dharmapada (Khotan manuscript).
Patna Dharmapada (22 chapters, c. 414 verses; affiliation proposed).
A Sahasravarga (Dharmapada chapter of thousands) embedded in the Mahāvastu.

name: Health as balance of the dhātus

definitions.definition: Disorder is imbalance of the dhātus, balance is the normal state; health is happiness, disorder suffering (Ca Sū 9.4); balance of the dhātus is the effect the tantra seeks (Sū 1.53); health is doṣa-balance (AHS Sū 1.20).
Dhī is the visionary thought the poets 'yoke' and fashion into hymns, which Savitṛ is asked to impel (RV 3.62.10, 5.81.1); with manīṣā in the heart the seers found the bond of being (10.129.4).

Beyond denotation and indication, words and meanings suggest an implied sense — a fact, a figure or a rasa — which is the soul of poetry; rasa can only be suggested (DhĀ 1.1, 1.4, 1.13); the name comes from the grammarians' dhvani that manifests the sphoṭa.

relations.note: Ānandavardhana models dhvani on the grammarians' sounds manifesting the sphoṭa

name: The Diamond Sūtra's 'A is not A, therefore it is called A'

definitions.definition: The recurring formula of the Vajracchedikā: what the Tathāgata taught as X (merit, buddha-dharmas, the perfection of wisdom, dust, world, the marks, beings, self) is taught as not-X; therefore it is called X — affirming the conventional name while denying the ultimate referent.

relations.note: the name conventionally, its emptiness ultimately

name: The nine similes for the conditioned (Vajracchedikā 32)

definitions.definition: Conditioned things are to be seen as stars, a fault of vision, a lamp, a magical show, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning and a cloud; Kumārajīva has six: dream, illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, lightning.
The liberated soul remains different from Brahman and from other souls; the five differences and gradation 'are not lost even for the liberated'.

relations.note: the five differences hold 'even for the liberated'

name: The difficulty of faith in the easy practice

definitions.definition: The arrogant and lazy can hardly believe this teaching; to hear and entrust is the hardest of hard things.
The practice is easy but shinjin hard; 'easy to go, yet no one goes'.

Bīsapantha (older temple practice, bhaṭṭārakas, fresh offerings, attendant deities), Terāpantha (17th-c. lay reform: no bhaṭṭārakas, dry offerings, no attendant deities), Tāraṇapantha (aniconic; scriptures in shrines), Totāpantha (a mixed practice; low confidence), and in recent times the Kānjī Svāmī movement.

The Mūla Saṅgha (Kundakundānvaya, with the Nandi, Sena, Deva and Siṃha gaṇas and later the Balātkāra gaṇa), and the Kāṣṭhā, Drāviḍa and Māthura saṅghas — the latter three condemned as deviant in Devasena's Darśanasāra, later accepted as Digambara branches; the Yāpanīya was a separate order.

Gautama, Sudharman (Lohārya) and Jambū (omniscients); Viṣṇu, Nandimitra, Aparājita, Govardhana, Bhadrabāhu (śrutakevalins); eleven daśapūrvins beginning with Viśākha; five knowers of the eleven Aṅgas; four knowers of the Ācārāṅga ending with Lohārya II (names low confidence).
The consecrated sacrificer is made an embryo again, the hut his womb, his garments the membranes; he is born at the final bath (AB 1.3); by consecration he makes his future world (ŚB 6.2.2.27).
Consecration for sacrifice is the twice-born's third birth, after the mother and initiation (MDh 2.169).

relations.note: both rites are conceived as births

definitions.definition: Rising at the brāhma muhūrta, cleaning teeth, collyrium, nasal oil, gargling, oil massage, exercise to half strength, bathing, measured food, good conduct and sleep after remembering gods and teachers (AHS Sū 2; Ca Sū 5; Su Ci 24).
Verbal knowledge cannot dispel delusion, as talk of a lamp cannot dispel darkness; the truth within is missed by those bewildered in scriptures (Kulārṇava 1.96-100).

name: Claims and display of powers among the orders

definitions.definition: All six teachers claimed to be arahants with powers to win the sandalwood bowl; the Buddha forbade monks to display superhuman powers to lay people; the six teachers' contest of wonders ended in their rout.
At death the senses and elements withdraw, the moon, sun and winds gather at the heart, samādhis arise; periods of seven days follow (Tilopa, from Sukhasiddhi).
By habituation earth and the other elements dissolve into awareness and self-appearance becomes mahāmudrā (Caluki).

relations.note: The later synthesis identifies the death process with the stages of the completion stage; the Indian texts read state the parallel only implicitly.

name: The dissolution of the elements at death

definitions.definition: At death earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into wind, wind into consciousness, with outer and inner signs; then the white appearance, the red increase and the black near-attainment, after which the ground luminosity dawns.
Supreme nibbāna is enjoyment of the five sense pleasures, or one of the four absorptions.

name: The Lord's action without need

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Kṛṣṇa has nothing to do and nothing to gain in the three worlds, yet keeps acting, for if he did not, people would follow his path, the worlds would perish and he would be the maker of confusion (3.22–24).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the Lord made the fourfold class order by the division of guṇa and karma, yet is to be known as its non-doer (akartṛ), imperishable (4.13); actions do not stain him and he has no longing for their fruit, and whoever knows him thus is not bound by actions (4.14); knowing this, the ancient seekers of liberation acted (4.15).

relations.note: the Lord's own action is given as the example for acting to hold the world together

name: The divine and demonic endowments (daivī and āsurī sampad)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.15; 9.11–13: evil-doers who have resorted to a demonic disposition (āsura bhāva) do not take refuge in the Lord; those who disregard him in human form, of vain hopes, vain acts and vain knowledge, resort to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras; the great souls resort to the divine nature (daivī prakṛti) and worship him with undivided mind.

Two kinds of beings: the divine endowment (fearlessness, purity, non-harm, truth, compassion and the rest) leads to liberation; the demonic (hypocrisy, pride, anger, harshness, ignorance) to bondage; the demonic deny a Lord and live for desire (BhG ch. 16).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A sight granted by the Lord or a seer: Kṛṣṇa gives Arjuna a divine eye to see the universal form (BhG 11.8); Vyāsa gives Sañjaya sight of the whole war (MBh 6.2; BhG 18.75).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Because Arjuna cannot see the Lord with his own eye, the Lord gives him a divine eye with which to behold his sovereign yoga (11.8).

definitions.definition: By the Lord's grace the devotee attains the eternal abode even while acting (BhG 18.56, 18.62), crosses all obstacles (18.58), sees the universal form (11.47), and is lifted from the ocean of saṃsāra (12.7); the Lord dwelling in the heart destroys the darkness of ignorance (10.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: To those ever yoked who worship him with love the Lord gives the yoga of understanding (10.10) and, out of compassion, abiding in their own being or in his own (ātma-bhāva-stha), destroys the darkness born of ignorance (10.11); Arjuna's delusion is gone through the word spoken out of favour to him (11.1); the Lord gives the divine eye (11.8) and, being gracious (prasanna), shows the supreme form by his own yoga (11.47); Arjuna prays 'be gracious' (11.25, 11.31, 11.45) and seeks his grace (11.44); for those whose awareness (cetas) is set on him the Lord becomes before long the deliverer from the ocean of death and saṃsāra (12.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 7 and 9 (without the word prasāda): the Lord makes the worshipper's faith unwavering and ordains the fruits obtained (7.21–22); for the undivided devotee he himself carries acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema) (9.22); for the constant rememberer he is easy to reach (8.14).

definitions.definition: The name ('Viṭṭhala', 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari') is the easy means for all, needing no rule of time, place or caste; sung together in kīrtan it lights the lamp of knowledge.
Rāma's name is greater than both his formless and embodied forms, mediates between them, is the one support in Kali and the ferrying mantra at death in Kāśī.
Kṛṣṇa's name is the first of the four real things; it saves even when uttered unknowingly (Ajāmila) and removes offences when sung constantly.
Do not be lazy with Hari's name; death is ever at hand.
The name is the jewel-wealth that spending does not lessen and thieves cannot steal.
Rāma's name at dawn, in mind and speech, is the beginning of the day's discipline.

The name 'Nārāyaṇa' is the refuge found after long searching; it gives family, wealth, heaven, grace and strength, more good than a mother; its sweetness is worth more than Indra's kingdom; singing it, past and future faults burn like cotton in fire; by it the senses are guarded and Yama's servants trampled.
Being sung of, the Lord quickly manifests himself and makes his devotees experience him; hearing and singing his qualities are means to devotion even in worldly life.
The Lord himself whispered the eight-syllable mantra into Tirumaṅkai's ear (the tradition's account).

relations.note: the name as the dharma of the Kali age
the Gauḍīya teaching that even a semblance of the name saves extends the same claim

name: Divine pride (the self as deity)

definitions.definition: In deity yoga the practitioner affirms 'I am of vajra nature', 'as all tathāgatas are, so am I' (Tattvasaṃgraha) — an identity grounded in emptiness, not in a permanent self.

notes: The Tibetan term is standard; a single Sanskrit technical equivalent is not fixed here.

name: The Lord's reciprocity: as one approaches, so one is received (BhG 4.11)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4.11: in whatever way people approach the Lord, in that way he receives them; humans follow his path in every way.

notes: Commentators read the second line either as all paths being finally the Lord's or as people following his example (cf. 3.23).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The body born of the creation of Hara and Gaurī, permanent though the six-sheathed body is not; those who gain it without abandoning the body are the rasa-siddhas, served by mantras (SDS 7-9; Rasahṛdaya 1.7).

name: The 108 divine sites (divya-deśa)

definitions.definition: The temples where the Lord abides in his image, each 'sung' (maṅgaḷāśāsana) by one or more Āḻvārs — 106 on earth with the Milk Ocean and Paramapadam making 108; the Āḻvārs long to be born even as a step or a fish at Tiruvēṅkaṭam and see the Lord at Śrīraṅgam from feet to face.
The temples sung by the Āḻvārs, where the Lord abides as the image; visiting and praying for his welfare (maṅgaḷāśāsana) at them is a Śrīvaiṣṇava practice.

notes: Regional distribution recalled as Cōḻa 40, Pāṇḍya 18, Malai (Kerala) 13, Naṭu 2, Toṇṭai 22, Vaṭa (north) 11, plus 2 celestial — moderate confidence.

name: The divine sound of the Jina

definitions.definition: An undifferentiated sound issuing from the Jina without movement of lips, at set times of day, understood by every being in its own speech and rendered into scripture by the gaṇadharas.
The Jina speaks Ardhamāgadhī, which by a supernatural excellence becomes the speech of each listener.

name: The Lord's relish of his devotees' faults (doṣa-bhogya)

definitions.definition: Out of motherly love the Lord relishes the faults of those who come to him, as a cow licks its newborn calf.
The Lord overlooks the faults of the surrendered (does not see them), but does not relish faults.

name: Placing the other schools as lower stages of one's own

definitions.definition: All philosophies are roles of the one conscious Lord: Buddhists rest in the intellect-principle, Jains in the qualities, Vedic knowers in the Person, Pāñcarātrikas in the unmanifest; the Trika alone sees the self as both transcendent and immanent.
Mādhava's compendium arranges sixteen systems from the Cārvāka upward ending in Advaita; Madhusūdana holds that all sages intend the one Lord and their differing paths suit differing capacities.

Haribhadra sets out six darśanas without polemic; Siddhasena holds that there are as many doctrines as ways of speaking, and that the Jina's word is the aggregate of all the one-sided views; the Sūtrakṛtāṅga tradition classes rival doctrines as 363 kinds of kriyāvāda, akriyāvāda, ajñāna and vinaya.
The Brahmajāla surveys the ascetics' and brahmins' theories about past and future on sixty-two grounds, all arising from contact and feeling, which the Tathāgata knows and goes beyond.
Bhāviveka examines the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Vedānta and Mīmāṃsā and grants what is acceptable in the Vedānta only as the emptiness the Buddha taught.

notes: Each such ranking is one tradition's view (see dsp:ranking-of-other-revelations); being ranked lower is rejected by the ranked tradition.

name: Devotees of the Kali age in the Tamil land

definitions.definition: In the Kali age devotees of Nārāyaṇa arise in great numbers in the Draviḍa lands by the Tāmraparṇī, Kṛtamālā, Payasvinī, Kāverī and the western river (BhP 11.5.38–40); the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition reads this as the Āḻvārs.
With the coming of the dark Lord's singing and dancing devotees the curse on lives is gone, hell laid waste and the Kali age will perish (TVM 5.2.1).
Six substances — prakṛti, time, pure sattva, attributive consciousness, soul, Lord — and ten non-substances — sattva, rajas, tamas, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, conjunction and potency.

Sex is twofold: the bodily marks and the rise of the karma of sexual desire, which need not coincide; liberation may be reached with any psychological sex but only with the male body — the Digambara key to reading canonical passages about women among the liberated.
Śvetāmbaras accept the distinction but hold that liberation is possible with the female body.
A substance possesses qualities (co-present, inseparable, themselves without qualities) and modes (successive states); the becoming of qualities is transformation (TS 5.38, 5.41–42).
Dream objects are real while dreaming and sublated on waking; so the waking world before knowledge; the jīva sleeps in beginningless māyā.
Dream objects are created by the Lord for the dreamer's experience of the fruits of karma; they are real for their duration and for the dreamer alone.
Dreams are not false: they are produced from latent impressions (vāsanā) by the Lord as Taijasa abiding in the mind.

name: The dreams of a Tīrthaṅkara's mother

definitions.definition: Fourteen: elephant, bull, lion, the anointing of Śrī, a garland, the moon, the sun, a banner, a full vase, a lotus lake, the milk ocean, a celestial palace, a heap of jewels, a smokeless fire.
Sixteen: adding a pair of fish and a lion-throne (and substituting the palace of the nāgas for the heavenly palace in some lists; low confidence on the details).
Dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi: the world exists only while perceived, like dream (Prakāśānanda); sṛṣṭi-dṛṣṭi: Īśvara creates an empirical world that exists before and apart from individual perception (majority view).

name: The five parts of the Dṛṣṭivāda

definitions.definition: Parikarma, sūtra, pūrvagata (the fourteen Pūrvas), anuyoga and cūlikā.

name: Everything is suffering for the discerning (YS 2.15)

definitions.definition: For the discerning (vivekin) everything is suffering, because of the suffering of transformation (pariṇāma), of torment (tāpa) and of impression (saṃskāra), and because of the conflict of the functions of the guṇas (YS 2.15). Vyāsa: the yogin is the eyeball on which a strand of wool troubles, and the ordinary person is not so troubled (YBh 2.15); only suffering not yet come is to be avoided (YS 2.16, YBh 2.16).

Because of the sufferings of change, anguish and impressions, and the conflict of the guṇas, everything is suffering for the discerning (2.15); the yogin is sensitive to it like an eyeball (YBh 2.15); even the happiness of contentment is suffering compared with kaivalya (YBh 3.18).

definitions.definition: Liberation, reached by the Lord's grace: impersonal (absolute cessation of suffering) and personal (the Lord's powers of knowing and acting); it is union with and proximity to Rudra, from which there is no return.
Yāmuna reports it as mere absolute cessation of pain (opponent's report).

relations.note: Kauṇḍinya sets the Pāśupata lordship beyond others' isolation

name: Dying while a guṇa predominates (BhG 14.14–15, 14.18)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The guṇa that has increased when the embodied one dies decides what follows: dying when sattva has increased, it reaches the stainless worlds of those who know the highest (14.14); dying in rajas it is born among those attached to action, and dissolved in tamas in deluded wombs (14.15). Those abiding in sattva go upward, the rājasa stay in the middle, and the tāmasa, abiding in the workings of the lowest guṇa, go downward (14.18). The fruits of the guṇas are named in 14.16: the stainless fruit of well-done action, pain, ignorance.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Merged from extractor A's cpt:dying-in-a-predominant-guna and extractor B's cpt:gunas-and-destiny-after-death (both new). The verse's 'pralayaṃ yāti' is dying, the same word as the cosmic dissolution of 14.2. Compare cpt:last-thought-at-death (8.5-6), which concerns the last thought, not the prevailing guṇa.

definitions.definition: Sāriputta's teaching to the dying Anāthapiṇḍika not to cling to anything seen, heard, sensed or cognised, nor to this world or the next (MN 143); the ten perceptions to the sick Girimānanda (AN 10.60); the Buddha's last words (DN 16).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self gathers the particles of energy into the heart, the tip of the heart lights up, and it departs by the eye, the head or another part, followed by breath and the functions, knowledge and action holding it (BAU 4.4.1-2); speech merges into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat, heat into the highest deity (ChU 6.8.6, 6.15); the creaking cart and the fruit loosed from its stalk (BAU 4.3.35-38); the inner sound is no longer heard (BAU 5.9); the breaths do not leave the dead man; the name remains (BAU 3.2.11-12).

At the appointed time illness arises, senses and strength fail, the heat of the body stirred by wind breaks the vital points, udāna rises, speech fails and sight whirls, Yama's messengers are seen; the thumb-sized person leaves the body (through an upper or lower opening according to destiny), looking back at home; the good die easily, the wicked in terror.

Senses and elements dissolve (form into sound … earth into water … into consciousness); consciousness dissolves into appearance (sign: moonrise / smoke), appearance into increase (sunrise / lamp), increase into attainment (darkness), attainment into clear light (dawn, a cloudless sky); the eighty conceptions cease and white, red and mind meet.

name: The abode of wisdom in the body (Heart-essence anatomy)

definitions.definition: Wisdom dwells in the heart (tsitta palace) as the youthful vase body; the peaceful deities in the heart and the wrathful in the skull; the crystal kati channel connects heart and eyes, through which the lamps manifest.

relations.note: Dzogchen's anatomy of wisdom differs from the completion stage's channels, winds and drops

name: The early and later diffusions (snga dar, phyi dar)

definitions.definition: The Nyingma are the school of the early translations (snga 'gyur) of the imperial period; the later translations (gsar ma) from the late 10th c. founded the Kadam, Sakya, Kagyu and others.

name: Early (pre-classical) Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: The tradition traces Sāṃkhya to Kapila, Āsuri and Pañcaśikha and to teachers such as Janaka, Vasiṣṭha and Dvaipāyana (Yuktidīpikā on SK 72). Earlier formulations are preserved in the Mahābhārata's Mokṣadharma (Pañcaśikha's teaching to Janaka; Vasiṣṭha–Karāla and Yājñavalkya–Janaka dialogues with 24/25/26 principles), in the Bhagavad Gītā's 'sāṃkhya' (knowledge) and field-knower teaching (ch. 13–14, 18.13), in Caraka's account of twenty-four principles (Śārīrasthāna 1), and in Aśvaghoṣa's report of Arāḍa's teaching (Buddhacarita 12, a Buddhist report). Upaniṣadic hierarchies (Kaṭha 3.10–11) and the word 'sāṃkhya' (Śvetāśvatara 6.13) are claimed by Sāṃkhya as its scriptural basis.

relations.note: early enumerations precede the classical 25 (scholarly view)

notes: Refers to U05 (Mahābhārata, Gītā), U30 (Caraka), U03 (Upaniṣads); chapter refs recalled, not checked.

definitions.definition: Guarding the original true mind (Hongren) and guarding the one (Daoxin).

name: The easy path and the difficult path

definitions.definition: The bodhisattva path has a difficult way of strenuous effort (like walking overland) and an easy way of faith and calling buddhas' names (like sailing); Tanluan identifies the easy way with birth by the Buddha's vow.
Shinran's first master Nāgārjuna 'taught the easy practice'.

In the epic, the immortal head of Rāhu swallows sun and moon in enmity (MBh 1.17; cf. Svarbhānu in RV 5.40); the siddhāntas explain that the moon covers the sun and the earth's shadow covers the moon (Āryabhaṭīya 4.37); Varāhamihira rejects the rival accounts of Rāhu, states the shadow-cause as the truth of the śāstra, and explains that Rāhu is present at eclipses by Brahmā's boon to receive the offerings, so that the name is used figuratively (BS 5.1–15).

name: Observances at eclipses

definitions.definition: An eclipse is a time for bathing, gifts, oblations and recitation, whose offerings Rāhu receives by Brahmā's boon (BS 5.14); the digests prescribe a period of restriction before it (vedha/sūtaka) without cooking or eating, bathing at its start and end, and great merit for recitation and gifts during it; a child born during an eclipse needs a pacification rite (BPHS 91).

notes: Rules from the dharmaśāstra digests summarized from memory.

definitions.definition: Effort (prayatna) brings success in both worlds; laziness loses both; effort is joined to devotion to Rāma.

Buddhi's sāttvika form is virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power; its tāmasa form their opposites (SK 23). They are innate, natural or acquired (SK 43); they perfume the subtle body (SK 40). Virtue leads upward, non-virtue downward, knowledge to liberation, error to bondage; dispassion to absorption in prakṛti, passion to saṃsāra, power to non-obstruction (SK 44–45). By seven of them prakṛti binds herself, by one (knowledge) she releases herself (SK 63).
Internal medicine, śālākya, surgery, toxicology, the science of spirits, children's medicine, rejuvenation and virilization (Ca Sū 30.28; Su Sū 1.7-8; AHS Sū 1.5).
In the Four Tantras: body, children, women, spirits, wounds, poisons, old age and virility.

Existing things go unperceived through excessive distance, excessive nearness, impaired senses, inattention, subtlety, obstruction, being overpowered and mixture with the similar (SK 7); prakṛti is unperceived through subtlety (SK 8).
Grasping sign and form, similarity, contrast, attentiveness, repetition, the yoga of knowledge, hearing again, and (so) recalling the seen, heard and experienced (Ca Śā 1.148-149).

name: The eight great chariots of practice lineages

names.name: sgrub brgyud shing rta chen po brgyad

definitions.definition: Tibetan practice mapped as eight complete lineages of practice.

members: Orgyen Nyendrub (approach and accomplishment of the three vajras)

name: The eight consciousnesses

definitions.definition: The five sense-consciousnesses, mental consciousness, the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa-manas) and the store-consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna); the last is the root in which the others arise like waves; the treatises (Triṃśikā, Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Cheng weishi lun) present them as three transformations of consciousness.

The pramāṇa authors (following Dharmakīrti) generally speak only of the six consciousnesses; Tibetan doxography calls them 'Cittamātrins following reasoning' in contrast to 'followers of scripture' who accept eight.
Five sense-consciousnesses, mind-consciousness, manas and the ālayavijñāna, from which the others arise like waves; the Saṃdhinirmocana's ādāna/ālaya holds all seeds.

The 3rd Karmapa distinguishes the eight consciousnesses from the five wisdoms into which they transform when recognized (all-ground → mirror-like; afflicted mind → equality; mental → discriminating; five senses → all-accomplishing; with dharmadhātu wisdom).

relations.note: Theravāda Abhidhamma counts six consciousnesses with bhavaṅga, no ālaya

notes: U39 contributes the sūtra-layer definition under the same id. The P definition's doxographic claim is the Tibetan tenet-system (grub mtha') account, recorded as such.

name: Tsongkhapa's eight difficult points of Prāsaṅgika

definitions.definition: No ālaya distinct from the six consciousnesses; no reflexive awareness; no autonomous syllogisms; external objects accepted conventionally; śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas realise the selflessness of phenomena; grasping at the self of phenomena is an affliction; disintegration is a functioning thing; hence a unique account of the three times.

relations.note: rejects reflexive awareness
rejects a distinct store-consciousness

name: The eight factors of the rule of diet

definitions.definition: Nature, preparation, combination, quantity, place, time, rules of eating, and the eater (Ca Vi 1.21).
(Jain report) Gosāla's last drink, song, dance, salutation, the last storm-cloud, sprinkling elephant, battle of stones, and himself as last tīrthaṅkara — proclaimed around his death.
Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, Paiśāca (MDh 3.21).
