name: The eight freedoms and ten endowments

definitions.definition: The precious human life free of the eight unfree states (hells, pretas, animals, long-lived gods, barbarians, wrong views, times without a buddha, impaired faculties) and endowed with five personal and five circumstantial endowments.

relations.note: the Mahāyāna elaboration of the rarity of human birth

name: The eight gateways of spontaneous presence

definitions.definition: The eight ways in which the ground's display emerges: as compassion, as light, as wisdom, as kāyas, as non-duality, as freedom from extremes, as the gate of pure wisdom and as the gate of impure saṃsāra.

notes: Member list from memory; order uncertain.

definitions.definition: Non-harming, sense-restraint, compassion, feeling, patience, conquest of anger, meditation and knowledge are the flowers with which the body-liṅga is worshipped (KJN 3.25–26).
Knowledge-obscuring (5), perception-obscuring (9), feeling (2), deluding (28), lifespan (4), body-making (42), status (2), obstructive (5): ninety-seven subdivisions by this count.

Knowledge-obscuring (5 subtypes), perception-obscuring (9), feeling (2), deluding (28), lifespan (4), body-making (42, expanded to 93), status (2) and obstructive (5) — 97 (or 148) in all (TS 8.4–13); each has its own causes (TS 6.10–27).

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

definitions.definition: HYP 2.44: sūryabhedana, ujjāyī, sītkārī, śītalī, bhastrikā, bhrāmarī, mūrcchā, plāvinī (with sahita and kevala as the two kinds of retention, 2.71); GS 5.47: sahita, sūryabheda, ujjāyī, śītalī, bhastrikā, bhrāmarī, mūrcchā, kevalī. RESTRICTED as to method and measures.

Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, which turn around the world; the noble disciple reflects that they are impermanent and is not swept away (AN 8.6); a mind unshaken by them is the highest blessing (Snp 2.4).

name: The eight manifestations of Padmasambhava (gu ru mtshan brgyad)

definitions.definition: Tsokye Dorje (lake-born vajra), Padmasambhava, Loden Chokse, Padma Gyalpo, Nyima Özer, Shākya Senge, Senge Dradrok and Dorje Drolö — forms taken in different episodes of his life.

name: The eight basic qualities of the householder

definitions.definition: Abstaining from wine, meat and honey with the five small vows (Samantabhadra), or with the five udumbara fruits (later authors).
Dependent origination is without cessation, arising, annihilation, permanence, unity, plurality, coming and going (MMK dedication).
Those on the path to and in the fruit of stream-entry, once-return, non-return and arahantship — the Saṅgha of the four pairs (AN 6.10; Snp 2.1; Ud 5.5).

name: The nine groups: eight pentads and one triad

definitions.definition: The Gaṇakārikā sums the system as gains, impurities, means, places, stages, purifications, factors of initiation and strengths (five each) plus three livelihoods; the teacher is the knower of these nine groups.

name: The eight potencies and seventeen qualities

definitions.definition: Heavy, oily, cool, blunt, light, rough, hot and sharp potencies, with seventeen qualities of disorders and remedies and three post-digestive tastes.
Aśoka tree, rain of flowers, divine sound, pair of fly-whisks, lion-throne, halo, divine drum, triple parasol — the attendants of the omniscient Jina shown in his images.

name: The eight kinds of prātimokṣa discipline

definitions.definition: Monk, nun, probationer, male and female novice, male and female lay follower, and the fast-day keeper; four in substance; abstaining from 5, 8, 10 or all things to be avoided.

On the uposatha the lay follower abstains, like the arahants, from killing, stealing, all sexual activity, lying, intoxicants, eating after midday, entertainment and adornment, and high luxurious beds (AN 8.41).

name: The eight qualities of the Lord (eṇkuṇam)

definitions.definition: Self-dependence, pure body, natural understanding, omniscience, natural freedom from bonds, boundless grace, infinite power, boundless bliss (from the Āgamas, used to gloss Kuṟaḷ 9).

name: The eight sāttvika signs of ecstasy

definitions.definition: Stambha, sveda, romāñca, svara-bheda, vepathu, vaivarṇya, aśru, pralaya — with degrees from smouldering to blazing.
Letter-, word- and sentence-sphoṭa, each taken as individual or as universal (six), plus the partless word and partless sentence; the later grammarians hold only the sentence-sphoṭa real.

name: The eight topics and seventy points of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra

definitions.definition: Three knowledges (of all aspects, of paths, of bases), four trainings (full realization of all aspects, culmination, serial, instantaneous) and the dharmakāya.

Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, Kaulinī: composers of the Sahasranāma, deities of the eight-triangle enclosure, givers of poetry (SL 17), and in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire and the three qualities.

name: The eight vidyādharas of the Kagye transmission

definitions.definition: The eight Indian masters to whom the ḍākinī entrusted the eight heruka tantras: Mañjuśrīmitra (body), Nāgārjuna (speech), Hūṃkara (mind), Vimalamitra (qualities), Prabhahasti (activity), Dhanasaṃskṛta (Mamo), Rambuguhya-Devacandra (worldly offering) and Śāntigarbha (wrathful mantra).

notes: Assignment of masters to classes from memory.

definitions.definition: Seeing forms while having form, seeing forms externally, being intent on 'beautiful', the four formless spheres and the cessation of perception and feeling; one who enters and emerges from them and has destroyed the effluents is 'freed both ways' (DN 15; DN 16).
Entering (other bodies), knowing others' minds, acting at will, divine sight and hearing, memory, radiance and invisibility at will, all from concentration of the purified mind (Ca Śā 1.140-141).

relations.note: the more common list of aṇimā etc.

name: The eighteen exclusive qualities of a Buddha

definitions.definition: Ten powers, four confidences, three applications of mindfulness, great compassion.
The six sense faculties, six objects and six consciousnesses (MN 115; MN 148).

name: The eighteen faults absent in the Jina

definitions.definition: Hunger, thirst, fear, anger, attachment, delusion, anxiety, old age, disease, death, sweat, fatigue, pride, pleasure, wonder, sleep, birth and distress — hence the Jina does not eat.

A different list of eighteen: the five obstructions (to giving, gain, enjoyment, repeated enjoyment and energy), laughter, liking, disliking, fear, disgust, grief, desire, wrong view, ignorance, sleep, non-restraint, attachment and aversion — hunger and thirst are not among them (moderate confidence).

relations.note: the Digambara list excludes the kevalin's eating; the Śvetāmbara list does not

definitions.definition: The lists agree on eighteen but differ: VP 3.6.21-23 and BhP 12.7.23-24 name the Śiva (Śaiva); Matsya 53 and the Nārada's index name the Vāyu; KūP 1.1.13-15 names both, taking the 'Vāyavīya' as the Brahmāṇḍa. Traditional extents total four lakh verses (BhP 12.13.4-9).

name: The eighteen great Mahāyoga tantras (tantra section)

definitions.definition: The tantra section of Mahāyoga: five root tantras of body, speech, mind, qualities and activity (Sangs rgyas mnyam sbyor, Zla gsang thig le, Gsang ba 'dus pa, Dpal mchog dang po, Karma mā le), five practice tantras, five activity tantras and two supplementary tantras (the Rnam snang sgyu 'phrul drva ba and the Noose of Method), with the Guhyagarbha as their summary root.

notes: Members recalled from memory; the practice and activity tantras not listed (gap). Noose of Method and several root tantras are extant in the local Derge Kangyur (Tōh 835; 366-367; 477; 487-488).

name: The eighteen vital points (aṣṭādaśa marmasthāna) of withdrawal

definitions.definition: Eighteen points of the body, from the big toes upward to the head, with fixed distances between them, through which the breath and attention are drawn and held one after another as a form of sense-withdrawal (Yoga Yājñavalkya; Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā).
The same eighteen points in the Triśikhibrāhmaṇa, Darśana and Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣads, the fifth of their five withdrawals.

notes: The list of the eighteen points and their distances is not entered as members because the unit could not verify it; check the Yoga Yājñavalkya (ch. 7) and the Triśikhibrāhmaṇa.

name: The eighteen promulgators of jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: Later saṃhitās (e.g. those of Nārada and Kaśyapa) list eighteen originators of jyotiṣa: Sūrya, Pitāmaha, Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Parāśara, Kaśyapa, Nārada, Garga, Marīci, Manu, Aṅgiras, Lomaśa, Pauliśa, Cyavana, Yavana, Bhṛgu and Śaunaka.

notes: List recalled from memory; its source verse and exact membership vary by text. Check before use.

definitions.definition: The saṃskāras of mercury to be learned before its use (SDS 18-22; RRS 11.15-16). RESTRICTED: their names and procedures are not recorded here.

name: The eighteen schools and their lists

definitions.definition: Vasumitra: nine Mahāsāṃghika and eleven Sthavira groups arising in the second to fourth centuries after the parinirvāṇa.
Dīpavaṃsa/Mahāvaṃsa: eighteen (twelve Theravāda-derived, six Mahāsaṅgītika-derived) plus six later.
Vinītadeva/Tibetan tradition: eighteen in four groups — Sarvāstivāda, Mahāsāṃghika, Saṃmitīya, Sthavira.
Bhavya records a list according to the Saṃmitīyas (details not given here).

notes: The number eighteen is traditional; the actual lists differ in names, counts and derivations.

name: The eighteen Siddhars (patiṉeṇ cittarkaḷ) — the lists

definitions.definition: (1) The popular list (widely printed, with samādhi places): Nandi (Kāśī), Agastya (Anantaśayanam), Tirumūlar (Chidambaram), Bogar (Palani), Koṅkaṇar (Tirupati), Maccamuṉi (Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam), Kōrakkar (Poyyūr), Caṭṭaimuṉi (Srirangam), Cuntarāṉantar (Madurai), Rāmatēvar (Aḻakar malai), Kuṭampai (Māyavaram), Karuvūrār (Karūr), Iṭaikkāṭar (Tiruvaṇṇāmalai), Kamalamuṉi (Tiruvārūr), Patañjali (Rāmēśvaram), Taṉvantiri (Vaitīsvaraṉkōyil), Vālmīki (Eṭṭukkuṭi), Pāmbāṭṭi (Caṅkaraṉkōyil). Names moderate, places low confidence.

(2) The Tirumantiram's own lineage lists (checked locally): Nandi's eight — the four Nandis, Śivayoga, Patañjali, Vyāghrapāda and Tirumūlar (TM 67) — and Tirumūlar's mantra-line — Mālāṅkaṉ, Intiraṉ, Cōmaṉ, Piramaṉ, Uruttiraṉ, Kanturu, Kālāṅki, Kañcamalaiyaṉ (TM 69).

(3) The poets of the printed Siddhar anthologies, largely absent from list (1): Sivavākkiyar, Paṭṭiṉattār, Pattirakiriyār, Aḻukaṇṇi, Kaṭuveḷi, Kuṭampai, Pāmbāṭṭi, Iṭaikkāṭar, Akappēy, with works ascribed to Tirumūlar, Caṭṭaimuṉi, Rāmatēvar and Tiruvaḷḷuvar (the local Project Madurai series checked).

(4) Other lists (not reconstructed here) add or substitute names such as Kākapucuṇṭar, Urōmarisi, Pulippāṇi, Tēraiyar, Yūkimuṉi, Kālāṅki, Pulastiyar, Sivavākkiyar and Paṭṭiṉattār; the number eighteen is conventional and the membership varies from source to source.
Tāyumāṉavar praises the 'host of Siddhas' (cittarkaṇam) who attained the harmony of Vedānta and Siddhānta.

notes: The hallucination sweep should check list (1) against printed sources (e.g. the Abhidhāna Cintāmaṇi, Zvelebil's 'The Poets of the Powers') and record the variant lists it finds.

definitions.definition: Eight chief siddhis residing in the Lord (aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitā, vaśitā, fulfilment of desire) and ten from the guṇas (freedom from hunger and thirst, far hearing and seeing, speed of mind, taking any form, entering another body, dying at will, sporting with the gods, accomplishing one's resolve, unobstructed command), with lesser ones such as knowing the three times and others' minds; all are obstacles for one seeking the Lord.

names.name: the vow of sincere mind and entrusting

definitions.definition: Read by Shandao as 'beings who call my name even ten times'; the exclusion of grave offenders is a gate of restraint.
The vow that selected the nenbutsu alone as the practice for birth.
The vow of sincere mind and entrusting (shinjin), whose three minds are one mind given by Amida; the cause of birth in the true land.

Beings of the ten directions who sincerely entrust themselves, wish to be born and think of Amitābha even ten times are born there, except those who commit the five grave offences and slander the dharma.

Śiva taught eighty-four postures (HYP 1.33; GŚ 6; HR; Jogapradīpikā) — or as many as there are species, 8,400,000, of which 84 are distinguished and 32 useful for mortals (GS 2.1–2); of these the texts select four (HYP 1.34), two (GŚ 7) or thirty-two (GS 2.3–6).

name: The eighty-four siddhas

definitions.definition: The canonical list of great adepts in Abhayadatta's lives and the parallel songs of Tōh 2292: men and women of every caste and trade who realized mahāmudrā.

relations.note: The Nāth and Buddhist lists of eighty-four overlap (Mīna/Matsyendra, Gorakṣa, Cauraṅgi, Jālandhara, Kāṇha, Carpaṭi) but are distinct lists.

notes: Tōh 2292's order (read locally) follows Abhayadatta's with a few different names.

name: The eighty-four siddhas in Nāth tradition

definitions.definition: The Nāths revere eighty-four siddhas; the Haṭhapradīpikā names over thirty mahāsiddhas beginning with Ādinātha (1.5–8); the Varṇaratnākara gives a list of eighty-four mixing Nāth and Buddhist names.

relations.note: overlap with the Buddhist list of Abhayadatta (U44/U49 treat the overlap)

name: The two lists of eighty-four siddhas compared

definitions.definition: The Tibetan-transmitted list (Abhayadatta's Lives, Tōh 2292 songs) of eighty-four Buddhist siddhas — among them Lūipa, Virūpa, Saraha, Mīnapa, Gorakṣa, Cauraṅgī, Kāṇha, Jālandhara, Tilopa, Nāropa, and four women.

The Nāth tradition speaks of eighty-four siddhas and nine Nāths; its lists (e.g. the Haṭhapradīpikā's mahāsiddhas) mix Nāth names with names also found in the Buddhist list (Mīna, Cauraṅgī, Virūpākṣa, Carpaṭi, Kānerī).
A Maithili prose work's list of eighty-four (Varṇaratnākara, early 14th c.) mixes Nāth and Buddhist names.

members: shared names (in both traditions): Mīna/Matsyendra, Gorakṣa, Cauraṅgī, Jālandhara, Kāṇha, Virūpa/Virūpākṣa, Carpaṭi, Nāgārjuna
names only in the Buddhist list: Saraha, Lūipa, Tilopa, Nāropa, Maitrīpa and most others
names only in Nāth lists: Ādinātha, Gahinī, Revaṇa, Bhartṛhari, Gopīcandra and others

relations.note: the Buddhist list
the Nāth list
the Tamil count of eighteen, which also includes Korakkar (Gorakṣa)

notes: The number 84 is shared; the membership differs. The overlap is recorded as brw:natha-mahasiddha (U21) with U49 evidence.

definitions.definition: Thirty-three conceptions of the first empty (from detachment and fear to envy), forty of the second (passion, joy, pride …) and seven of the third (forgetting, confusion …): 160 subtle natures by day and night, moved by wind.
There is one jīva whose ignorance projects all others, as in dream; associated with dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda (Prakāśānanda; surveyed by Madhusūdana).
Some beings (Brahmā, gods not corrupted, the mind) are eternal, others not.

name: The dharma of the one-pointed (ekāntika / sātvata dharma)

definitions.definition: Exclusive devotion to Nārāyaṇa, practised by the ekāntins — non-violent, knowing the self, delighting in the welfare of beings — the best dharma, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga, taught to Arjuna before the battle, handed down from the beginning of the Kṛta age (MBh 12.336).
Refuge in Kṛṣṇa alone, excluding other gods, images and Vedic rites; as watering the root nourishes the whole tree, worship of Kṛṣṇa satisfies all.

relations.note: both are refuge in the Lord alone; Ekaśaraṇa adds the exclusion of other deities and centres on the name

name: The 101 sthalas of the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi

definitions.definition: The SSM's full map: 44 sub-sthalas on the side of the soul (bhakta 15, māheśvara 9, prasādi 7, prāṇaliṅgi 5, śaraṇa 4, aikya 4) followed by 57 on the side of the liṅga (9, 9, 9, 9, 12, 9), from piṇḍa to jñānaśūnya.

notes: Full ordered list in pth:siddhantasikhamani-101-sthalas.

name: The five fivefold elements in the body (Amaraughaśāsana)

definitions.definition: Earth as bone, flesh, skin, channels, hair; water as saliva, urine, blood, sweat, perspiration; fire as hunger, thirst, sleep, sloth, radiance; air as running, leaping, contracting, extending, restraining; space as passion, aversion, shame, fear, delusion (AmŚ 11–17).
Space and the other five elements are neither existent nor non-existent, neither characterized nor characteristic (MMK 5.7); the person is not the six elements, singly or together (RĀ 2.1).

The 'twelve-limbed basket of the gaṇin' composed by the gaṇadharas: Ācārāṅga, Sūtrakṛtāṅga, Sthānāṅga, Samavāyāṅga, Vyākhyāprajñapti (Bhagavatī), Jñātādharmakathā, Upāsakadaśā, Antakṛddaśā, Anuttaraupapātikadaśā, Praśnavyākaraṇa, Vipākaśruta, and the lost Dṛṣṭivāda.

name: The eleven forms of attachment (ekādaśa-āsakti)

definitions.definition: Devotion, though one, appears as eleven attachments: to the glory of the Lord's qualities, to his form, to worship, to remembrance, to service, to friendship, to parental love, to love as a beloved, to self-offering, to absorption in him, and to supreme separation.

relations.note: five items coincide with the Bhāgavata's nine (remembrance, worship, service, friendship, self-offering)
the servant, friend, parental and beloved attachments answer to the Gauḍīya dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya and madhura rasas

notes: Order of vātsalya and kāntā differs between editions.

definitions.definition: Eleven centres — genitals, navel, heart, throat, mouth, head, crown-tip, skull-junction, back, with petals of five, eight, ten, twelve, sixteen, a hundred, ten million (KJN 5.25–27); eleven places of knowledge up to the brahmarandhra and summit (17.2–4).

relations.note: different counts of the body's centres in different Nāth texts

definitions.definition: Five sense capacities (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose), five action capacities (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals) and manas, all from ahaṃkāra (SK 24–28); not made of the elements (SS 2.20, 5.84).

name: The eleven stages of the householder (pratimā)

definitions.definition: Right view, vows, equanimity, holy-day fasting, giving up living food, not eating at night, celibacy, giving up undertakings, giving up possessions, not approving household acts, not accepting food prepared for oneself (Ratnakaraṇḍa).

Śvetāmbara list (Upāsakadaśā tradition): view, vow, sāmāyika, pauṣadha, kāyotsarga, celibacy, giving up living food, giving up undertakings, not employing others, not accepting prepared food, living like a monk (recalled).
Five of knowledge, five of action and mind as the eleventh, of both natures (MDh 2.89–92).

checks.note: MDh 2.89–92 was found: 'ekādaśendriyāṇy āhuḥ … śrotraṃ tvak cakṣuṣī jihvā nāsikā caiva pañcamī | pāyūpasthaṃ hastapādaṃ vāk caiva daśamī smṛtā', the five buddhīndriyas and five karmendriyas (2.91), and 'ekādaśaṃ mano jñeyaṃ svaguṇenobhayātmakam' (2.92). All eleven members match.

definitions.definition: Kula knowledge shines only for those purified by past merit, devoted to guru and scripture, calm, discreet and obedient (Kulārṇava 2.30-35); the path is harder than walking a sword's edge (2.122).

The texts say success comes to anyone who practises — young, old, sick or weak (HYP 1.64; DYŚ 37) — whatever his sect: brāhmaṇa, śramaṇa, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist (DYŚ 38); nāda is for the dull too (HYP 4.65, 4.80); householders can succeed (SS 5.186, 5.210–212); but some practices succeed only for the virtuous and envy-free (HYP 3.95); the SS grades aspirants and assigns them yogas; the Jyotsnā holds the dispassionate alone properly eligible and lists who may receive haṭha.

relations.note: universal eligibility by practice vs graded fitness; see the interpretation log (P4-stage)

name: Embraced, never to be abandoned (shequ bu she)

definitions.definition: Each ray of Amitāyus's light shines through the ten directions and embraces the beings who recollect him.
At the moment the thought of saying the nenbutsu arises in entrusting, one shares in being embraced.

In the womb the jīva, from the seventh month conscious, remembers its past births and prays to the Lord, resolving to lift itself out; at birth it loses that knowledge. Death is the body's ceasing to function, birth the taking of 'I am this' toward a body.

name: The formation of the body in the womb

definitions.definition: The Garbha Upaniṣad's account of the body's elements and constituents, the embryo's monthly growth, and its memory and vow in the ninth month, forgotten at birth — the tradition's own account.

checks.note: The Garbha content is located. The e-text section numbers differ from the skeleton's: the embryo's growth is §3; see the teaching checks. All 5 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text. Some rest on teachings whose ref was corrected or only partly confirmed; the content is located, only the numbering changes: tea:garbha-upanisad:2 (corrected); tea:garbha-upanisad:3 (corrected).

definitions.definition: Seed, blood and karma-driven consciousness with the five elements form the embryo, which passes through fish, tortoise and pig phases and is born after thirty-eight weeks.

relations.note: both teach conception from seed, blood and a transmigrating consciousness; stages differ

name: Absorption through any emotion fixed on the Lord

definitions.definition: Desire, anger, fear, affection, oneness or friendship constantly directed at Hari bring absorption in him: the gopīs by desire, Kaṃsa by fear, Śiśupāla by hatred (BhP 7.1.30; 10.29.15; VP 4.15.2).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: BhP 7.1.30, 10.29.15 and VP 4.15.2 (Śiśupāla's sāyujya) located. All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: The world is empty of self and of what belongs to self (SN 35.85); a meditative dwelling in which what is absent is seen as empty and what remains as present, descending to the signless and liberation (MN 121); dwelling in emptiness internally (MN 122); 'look upon the world as empty' (Snp 5.16).

relations.note: Madhyamaka universalises emptiness as lack of own-nature of all dharmas; the suttas speak of emptiness of self

name: The emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects

names.name: rnam kun mchog ldan gyi stong nyid

definitions.definition: The Kālacakra's ultimate — empty form united with unchanging bliss — identified by Dolpopa with the other-empty dharmatā, as opposed to an emptiness of annihilation.

relations.note: Dolpopa's identification of the tantra's and the sūtras' ultimate
unchanging bliss is the bliss aspect of the same ultimate
relations.standpoint: Kālacakra as read by the Jonang

definitions.definition: Emptiness is the relinquishing of all views; those for whom emptiness is a view are incurable (MMK 13.8); the Buddha taught for the abandonment of all views (27.30).
Like one who asks for the 'nothing' he was offered, or a medicine that stays in the stomach, emptiness taken as a view cannot cure (PsP on 13.8).

relations.note: guards against reifying emptiness

definitions.definition: Emptiness too is empty: there is nothing non-empty for it to be the emptiness of as an entity (MMK 13.7); 'empty' is only said for designation (22.11); by habituation even the notion 'nothing exists' is abandoned (BCA 9.33).

relations.note: one of the listed emptinesses

definitions.definition: Avalokiteśvara sees the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness) as empty (of own-being in the Sanskrit-short text); form is emptiness and emptiness is form, and likewise for the other four; all dharmas have the mark of emptiness, unarisen and unceased, and in emptiness there are no aggregates, sense-bases, realms, links of dependent origination, four truths, knowledge or attainment.

In the shorter Sanskrit recension: Avalokiteśvara sees the five aggregates as empty of own-being (svabhāva-śūnya); form is emptiness and emptiness form, and likewise vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra and vijñāna; all dharmas have the mark of emptiness, unarisen, unceased; in emptiness there are no aggregates, sense-bases, realms, links, truths, knowledge or attainment.

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.
Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

name: Emptiness in the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras

definitions.definition: All dharmas — aggregates, elements, links, truths, paths, fruits, buddhahood and nirvāṇa — are empty of own-being, unborn, like illusions and dreams; the bodhisattva does not apprehend even 'bodhisattva' or 'perfection of wisdom'; emptiness is not destruction, and is not itself to be grasped.

relations.note: the sūtras of the 'third turning' re-read emptiness as emptiness of stains only
what depends on conditions is called empty

definitions.definition: Emptiness is the non-existence of duality and the existence of that non-existence; its synonyms are suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate and the dharmadhātu; it is neither defiled nor pure; the ultimate is neither existent nor non-existent.

relations.note: the Yogācāra 'other-emptiness-like' formula: X is empty of duality, and the emptiness exists
emptiness is the perfected nature

name: The garbha empty and not empty

definitions.definition: Empty of the separable defilements; not empty of the inseparable buddha-qualities (Śrīmālā 9; RGV 1.154-155); the Mahāparinirvāṇa's wise see both the empty and the non-empty.
The locus classicus of other-emptiness: the element is empty of separable stains and not empty of inseparable qualities — read as definitive.

relations.note: emptiness restricted to the stains

definitions.definition: The image arising from emptiness, seen with eyes open or closed like a dream after the ten signs; the cause sealed by immutable bliss.
Exchanges in which the teacher responds to questions with ordinary words, gestures, shouts or blows to provoke awakening (Mazu, Linji).
Testing students for the three leaks.

Pulse, touch, tongue, colour, voice, eyes, stool and urine are examined to find the disease, its cause and its remedy — after Kuṟaḷ 948–949: examine the disease, its cause, the means of allaying it, the patient, the measure of the illness and the time.
All phenomena of one taste in the innate; tastes differ for the unrealized, not for the realized.
The yogin in union sees self and enemy, jewel and chaff, heaven and hell as equal (Pañcakrama 5.30–34).
Since happiness is equally dear and suffering equally unwelcome to self and others, one protects all as oneself, as the many limbs are protected as one body (BCA 8.90–96; ŚSK 1).
The first part of the Śāntideva method: since all equally wish happiness and not suffering, there is no reason to cherish oneself more.

relations.note: cultivated first (ādau) in BCA 8.90

definitions.definition: Evenness in success and failure is yoga (BhG 2.48); the wise see the same in all (5.18) and 'even here' conquer creation (5.19); the yogin sees the self in all (6.29) and others' pleasure and pain as his own (6.32); Jaigīṣavya is unmoved by praise and blame (MBh 12.222).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Being the same in success and failure (4.22); neither hating nor craving (5.3); seeing a learned brahmin, cow, elephant, dog and dog-eater with an equal eye (5.18); the mind established in sameness, as Brahman is the same (5.19); neither rejoicing at the pleasant nor agitated by the unpleasant (5.20); composure amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour (6.7); clod, stone and gold alike (6.8); equal regard toward friend, foe, neutral, good and wicked (6.9); seeing the same everywhere (6.29), by comparison with oneself (6.32). Arjuna calls the yoga taught 'yoga as sāmya' (6.33).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Evenness (samatā) is among the states that arise from the Lord (10.5); the worshippers of the imperishable are even-minded everywhere (12.4); the devotee dear to the Lord is the same in pain and pleasure (12.13), to foe and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, and holds blame and praise equal (12.18–19).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Constant evenness of thought (sama-cittatva) when the wanted or unwanted befalls is among the dispositions called knowledge (13.10); one who sees the supreme lord standing the same (samam) in all beings sees, and seeing him equally present everywhere does not harm himself and goes to the highest goal (13.28–29); the one gone beyond the guṇas is the same in pain and pleasure, toward clod, stone and gold, the pleasant and the unpleasant, blame and praise, honour and dishonour, friend and foe (14.24–25).

name: Essence, nature and compassion — the three aspects of the ground

definitions.definition: The ground's three inseparable aspects: empty essence (ngo bo), luminous nature (rang bzhin), all-pervading compassion (thugs rje); the Kunjed Gyalpo's opening chapter already sets out the retinues as coming from 'its own nature, own essence and own compassion'.

relations.note: essence-dharmakāya, nature-sambhogakāya, compassion-nirmāṇakāya

definitions.definition: The Buddha awakened incalculable aeons ago; his lifespan is immeasurable and his parinirvāṇa a skillful display (Lotus 16; Golden Light 2).
The Tathāgata's body is the permanent vajra body (Mahāparinirvāṇa).

Āyurveda is eternal because beginningless, because its marks are established by nature (like the heat of fire), and because the nature of things is eternal; its 'origin' means only its being understood and taught (Ca Sū 30.27); Brahmā 'remembered' it (AHS Sū 1.3).

relations.note: parallel to the Mīmāṃsā claim of the Veda's authorless eternity; Caraka grounds it on the nature of things rather than on authorlessness

definitions.definition: Words, i.e. the letters, are eternal and manifested by utterance: utterance is for conveying to another; the same word is recognized everywhere; utterances are counted as repetitions; there is no cause of destruction (MS 1.1.18–23, against the view of 1.1.6–11).

relations.note: the eternal word is the letters, not a sphoṭa

definitions.definition: Rules and prohibitions are equal for the knower; purity as prescribed by the half-knowing is impurity in Śiva's view (VBT 123); rules based on difference are not direct means (TĀ 4); the Mata rejects the samaya rules (TĀ 4.262); equanimity toward friend and foe (VBT 125).

Prosperity from pure food taken with restraint and recitation; taint lies in injury (VS 6.1.8–12, 6.2.6–10 C); the life-stages yield merit according to purity of intention (6.2.3–5); ablution, fasting, celibacy, residence with the teacher, forest-dwelling, sacrifice, giving and observances for the unseen (6.2.2); common duties such as non-injury, truthfulness and non-stealing (Praśastapāda).
'Supernatural power and wondrous function: carrying water and hauling firewood' (Layman Pang).
'Wash your bowl' (Zhaozhou); 'walking too is Chan' (Yongjia).
Practice amid activity surpasses practice in stillness (Hakuin).

name: The evil person as the true object of the vow (akunin shōki)

definitions.definition: The vow was made for beings full of passions who cannot free themselves; those who rely on their own good are not its object until they turn; hence 'even the good person attains birth, how much more the evil person'. This is not licence: poison is not to be taken because there is an antidote.
Even the evil-doer of the lowest grade is born by ten recitations at death (Contemplation Sūtra, Daochuo).

name: Mutual examination of teacher and disciple

definitions.definition: Before entering the bond, teacher and disciple examine each other, since a broken pledge harms both; a merciless, angry, rigid or boastful person is to be avoided as guru (Gurupañcāśikā 6–7).
The supreme secret: giving oneself to others and taking others as oneself, since all suffering comes from desiring one's own happiness and all happiness from desiring others' (BCA 8.120–136).
The heart of mind training: reversing the objects of self-cherishing and other-cherishing, enacted by sending and taking (Seven Points 2.6; Eight Verses 7).
The second of the two methods of generating bodhicitta, from Śāntideva; the Guru Pūjā makes it the heart of practice.
Taught as the 'practice of a bodhisattva' by Tokmé Zangpo.

Exclusive practice: ten of ten are born; mixed practice: one or two in a hundred, for thirteen reasons of lost right mindfulness and non-accord with the vow (Shandao); the mixed stop in the land of sloth (Huaigan).
Right and miscellaneous differ in five pairs; cast aside the miscellaneous.

name: Existence of dharmas in the three times (sarvāstivāda)

definitions.definition: Dharmas of past, present and future all exist as real entities; proven by scripture, by consciousness arising from two, by consciousness requiring an existent object, and by the results of past karma; the times differ only by activity.
Only the present exists; the conditioned arises having not been and ceases having been; results come from the transformed series.
Only unripened past karma exists of the past (Vibhajyavāda position).
Past and future do not exist as entities (Vasumitra).
Rejected in Kathāvatthu 1.6–1.8.

relations.note: The Sautrāntika alternative rests on momentariness.

name: Past and future exist in their own form

definitions.definition: Past and future exist in their own form because properties differ in their time-paths (4.12); otherwise knowledge of them would be objectless and action for future fruit pointless (YBh 4.12); manifest or subtle, they are guṇas (4.13).

Passing meditative experiences are distinguished from stable realization; experiences are to be treated as 'neither good nor bad' (Milarepa to Gampopa); only realization marks the yogas. The ḍākinī's question to Nāropa — words or meaning? — turns on the same distinction.

Faith, vow and holding the name are the three provisions for birth: whether one is born depends on faith and vow, the grade on the depth of practice (Ouyi); faith is the source of the way (Wang Rixiu).
Believe that birth is attained with one calling, yet practise with the whole of life (Hōnen).
Practice (gyō: the name) and entrusting (shin: shinjin) are both Amida's gift and are inseparable; shinjin is the cause and the nenbutsu its expression in gratitude.

relations.note: Chinese 'faith' is the practitioner's; Shinran's shinjin is given

definitions.definition: Liberation is not: cutting off good and bad karma, Veda recitation, the supportless state, the attainment of form/bindu/nāda by meditation, the bliss of Kaula worship with wine, meat and union, the movement of kuṇḍalinī, or an even gaze; it is the mind seeing the mind in sahaja-samādhi (AmŚ 46–54).

name: Fate and human effort (daiva and puruṣakāra)

definitions.definition: Several causes are debated: nature (svabhāva, Prahlāda 12.215), time (Bali 12.217), fate (daiva), human effort (Draupadī 3.28–33) and karma (Gautamī 13.1); the Gītā counts daiva as the fifth of five causes of action (18.14), and Bhīṣma teaches that fate does not bear fruit without effort (13.6.7).

name: The fate of the one fallen from yoga

definitions.definition: One who falls from yoga is not lost: he dwells in the worlds of the meritorious, is reborn among the pure and prosperous or in a family of yogins, recovers his former understanding and, perfected through many births, reaches the highest goal (BhG 6.37–45).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Arjuna asks what becomes of one with faith who does not strive enough and whose mind falls from yoga before perfection — does he perish like a torn cloud, fallen from both (6.37–39)? Kṛṣṇa: there is no destruction for him here or hereafter, for no doer of good goes to a bad end (6.40); he dwells for endless years in the worlds of the meritorious and is reborn in a pure and prosperous house (6.41), or — rarer — in a family of wise yogins (6.42); there he regains the understanding of his former body and strives again (6.43), carried on by his former practice even against his will; even the mere enquirer into yoga passes beyond śabda-brahman (6.44); striving, cleansed, perfected through many births, he reaches the highest course (6.45).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

name: Fear of emptiness and its end

definitions.definition: 'I am not, I will not be' terrifies the childish and ends fear for the wise (RĀ 1.26); emptiness calms suffering, so if there is no 'I' whose would the fear be? (BCA 9.56–57).

name: Rules for timing festivals and vows

definitions.definition: Festivals and vows are fixed by tithi, asterism or solar ingress; when a tithi spans two days the digests rule which day holds it (the tithi at sunrise, or the one covering the prescribed part of the day), and a tithi 'pierced' (viddha) by the previous one may be rejected; Vaiṣṇava and Smārta rules differ, notably for Ekādaśī (Kālamādhava; Nirṇayasindhu; Dharmasindhu; Haribhaktivilāsa).
The nibandhas (Kālamādhava, Nirṇayasindhu, Dharmasindhu) decide the right day for each rite from the extent of the tithi at sunrise and in the relevant part of the day.

notes: Rules summarized from the digests; teachings not yet extracted.

name: The fifteen kinds of liberated beings

definitions.definition: Liberated as Tīrthaṅkara or not; during or outside a Tīrthaṅkara's ford; self-enlightened, enlightened by an outer cause (pratyekabuddha) or taught; in female, male or neuter body; in Jain garb, other garb or as householder; singly or together.
Digambaras read the categories of sex and garb retrospectively or as psychological sex, not as liberation from a female or clothed body.

name: The fifteen meanings of the Pañcadaśī (Varivasyārahasya)

definitions.definition: The Gāyatrī meaning, the six Yoginīhṛdaya meanings, and the meanings of the name, of the sound-form, of part of the name, of the Śaktas, of fusion, the collective, the qualified and the great-saying meaning (VR 57-59); knowing them is required, since recitation without meaning bears no fruit (VR 54-56).

relations.note: the six YH meanings are included among the fifteen

name: The fifteen Nityās

definitions.definition: Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, Vahnivāsinī, Mahāvajreśvarī, Śivadūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā, Jvālāmālinī and Citrā, around Tripurasundarī the sixteenth; the Vāmakeśvara and Tantrarāja give their mantras and rites; the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad makes them the fifteen lunar days.

notes: Order and some names from memory (PKS 4 lists them with mantras, not reproduced).

name: The fifteen subdivisions of the nyepa

definitions.definition: Each nyepa has five kinds with their own seats and functions.

Five universal, five particular, eleven wholesome, six root afflictions, twenty secondary afflictions and four variable factors, as listed in the Triṃśikā and counted as fifty-one in the Baifa mingmen lun and Cheng weishi lun.

relations.note: the Sarvāstivāda count

name: The fifty demonic states of the aggregates (Śūraṅgama)

definitions.definition: Ten states for each aggregate that arise in deep meditation; harmless if not taken as sagehood, disastrous if taken so.

name: The fifty-two mental factors (cetasika)

definitions.definition: Mental factors arising with consciousness: 13 ethically variable (7 universals: contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, life faculty, attention; 6 occasionals: applied thought, sustained thought, decision, energy, rapture, desire), 14 unwholesome and 25 beautiful.

members: 14 akusala (moha, ahirika, anottappa, uddhacca, lobha, diṭṭhi, māna, dosa, issā, macchariya, kukkucca, thīna, middha, vicikicchā)

relations.note: feeling, perception and the fifty formations

definitions.definition: All is burning — the senses, their objects, consciousness, contact and feeling — with the fires of lust, hatred and delusion and with birth, ageing and death (SN 35.28; Vin Mv 1.21).

At Rājagaha after the parinibbāna, five hundred arahants under Mahākassapa recited the discipline (Upāli) and the Dhamma (Ānanda), declined to abolish the minor rules, and charged Ānanda with faults including advocating women's ordination (Cv 11).

relations.note: the councils as remembered by the several schools (U38)

definitions.definition: Secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, with applied and sustained thought, rapture and bliss born of seclusion, pervading the body like bath powder kneaded with water (DN 2); remembered by the bodhisatta from childhood (MN 36); lust is abandoned through it (MN 44).

name: The first schism: Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika

definitions.definition: After the Vesālī council the defeated Vajjiputtakas formed the Mahāsaṅgītika (Dīpavaṃsa).
Mahādeva's five points split the order under Aśoka (Vasumitra; hostile Vibhāṣā account).
The elders enlarged the Vinaya; the majority kept the old text (Śāriputraparipṛcchā).
Schism proper (saṅghabheda) is a wheel- or act-schism; its lie is the gravest sin.

name: The first teaching and the first disciples

definitions.definition: At Isipatana the Buddha taught the five monks the middle way and the four truths (SN 56.11) and not-self (SN 22.59); Koṇḍañña gained the eye of Dhamma, and all five became arahants (Vin Mv 1.6).

name: Fitness of the student and the secrecy of knowledge

definitions.definition: Etymology is not to be taught to one ignorant of grammar, not a pupil, or incapable (Nirukta 2.3–4).
Knowledge asks to be guarded as a treasure, not given to the scornful or crooked; better to die with it than sow it in barren soil (MDh 2.113–115; VDh 2.8–9).

definitions.definition: Penetrating one's mind, generating bodhicitta, the vajra on the moon disc, making it firm, arising as the Buddha body — Sarvārthasiddhi's awakening in the Tattvasaṃgraha.
Emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace — performed by Śiva through his power, all for the souls' release; concealment ripens mala, withdrawal gives rest.
Aintoḻil, enacted in Naṭarāja's dance: drum, fearless hand, fire, planted foot, raised foot.

Emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment and grace; the bound individual performs them too - as manifesting, relishing, reflecting, planting the seed and dissolving (PH 10-11); bondage and liberation are Śiva's play (Paramārthasāra 33).

Creation, preservation, withdrawal, concealment and grace are done by the Goddess in the forms of Brahmā, Govinda, Rudra, Īśvara and Sadāśiva (LSN 63-64), each god acting on her command given by a flicker of her brows (SL 24).

relations.note: the same five acts, ascribed to the Goddess

name: The five acts in the Pāñcarātra

relations.note: same five functions, differently ordered; the Śaiva list is recorded by U18/U19

definitions.definition: Concealment, creation, maintenance, dissolution and grace, performed by Śrī as Nārāyaṇa's power.

name: The five aggregates

definitions.definition: Form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, whatever of each is past, future or present (SN 22.48); as aggregates of clinging they are suffering in brief (SN 56.11) and identity (MN 44); like foam, a bubble, a mirage, a plantain trunk and a magic trick (SN 22.95); the burden (SN 22.22).

The conditioned dharmas grouped as matter, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness; feeling and perception are separated from the other mental factors because they are the roots of dispute and saṃsāra.
Each aggregate is not self (Mahāvastu's version of the second sermon).
The basis on which the person is designated, neither identical with it nor different.

relations.note: both analyse the person into five, but the aggregates are not layers of a self

notes: U38 contribution to a shared concept.

name: The five kinds of performance (poison to nectar)

definitions.definition: Religious acts done for this-worldly reward (poison), for heavenly reward (venom), mechanically (non-performance), as a step toward the true (its cause) and with understanding and longing for release (nectar); only the last two count (Yogabindu).

name: The five augmenting conditions of reciting (Shandao)

definitions.definition: Extinction of sins, protection and long life, seeing the Buddha, being embraced, and the testimony of birth.

name: The five states (avasthā) in the Siddhānta

definitions.definition: Waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond-the-fourth, through which the embodied soul passes; the Tamil commentators place them at the brow, throat, heart, navel and root with decreasing numbers of instruments (35, 25, 3, 2, 1 — low confidence).

name: The five states of the soul (Tattvārtha 2.1-2.7)

definitions.definition: Subsidential (2), destructional (9), mixed (18), rising (21, including four passions) and inherent (3): the soul's own nature (svatattva).

The soul's states are subsidential, destructional, mixed, rising and inherent, with 2, 9, 18, 21 and 3 divisions (TS 2.1–7); at liberation all cease except perfect right view, knowledge, perception and siddhahood (10.3–4).

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

definitions.definition: Gross, transformable, projectable, fiery and karmic bodies, each subtler than the last; the fiery and karmic bodies are unobstructed and beginninglessly joined to every worldly soul, and carry it between births (TS 2.36–49).

relations.note: Both are layered bodies, but the Jain bodies are material vehicles of the soul, not coverings of an unchanging Self.

definitions.definition: Tathāgata (Vairocana), vajra (Akṣobhya), jewel (Ratnasambhava), lotus (Amitābha), action (Amoghasiddhi): the families of the maṇḍala into which aggregates, elements, afflictions and gnoses are ordered; the Guhyasamāja places Akṣobhya at the centre, the yoga tantras Vairocana.
Equanimity, re-initiation, purification by special austerity, subtle passion and perfect conduct (TS 9.18), rising with the guṇasthānas.

name: The five co-causes (kāla, svabhāva, niyati, pūrvakṛta, puruṣakāra)

definitions.definition: Time, own-nature, destiny, former deeds and effort: each held alone is wrong view, all together right view.

name: The five clear lights and their five times

definitions.definition: Clear light is natural, of wisdom, of samādhi, of suchness and of realization; it arises at death, in the central channel, in sleep, when equipoise and post-equipoise are one taste, and at insight (bka' dpe phyi ma).

The Goddess's couch has Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara as its legs and Sadāśiva as its plank; without her they are corpses (LSN 61; PKS 3.10); in SL 94 the four gods become the couch and Śiva its coverlet.
Śānta, dāsya (prīta), sakhya (preyas), vātsalya and madhura (ujjvala), in ascending intensity; each richer mood includes the qualities of the lower.

relations.note: the classical aesthetic rasas are worldly; Rūpa's are directed to Kṛṣṇa

name: The five concentrations of embodied meditation

definitions.definition: Earth (a lotus in an ocean of milk), fire (the syllable arhaṃ burning the lotus of the eight karmas and the body), wind (scattering the ashes), water (washing them away) and the essential (seeing oneself as the pure Siddha) (YŚ 7; Jñānārṇava).
Sign, name, discrimination, right knowledge and suchness.
Space, air, fire, water and earth, arising from the five subtle elements; specific, and calm, turbulent or dull (SK 22, 38).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): from the self arose space, from space wind, from wind fire, from fire water, from water earth (TU 2.1); earth, wind, space, water and light as the five great elements (AU 3.1.3); the fivefold quality of yoga — earth, water, fire, wind, space (ŚU 2.12); ChU 6 has a threefold scheme (heat, water, food).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): space, air, fire, water and earth with their qualities (sound, touch, form, taste, smell), each succeeding one having one more quality (Ca Śā 1.27-28); the person's six dhātus are the five elements and consciousness (Śā 1.16; 5.4); in Suśruta space is rich in sattva, air in rajas, fire in sattva and rajas, water in sattva and tamas, earth in tamas (Su Śā 1.20).

Nilam (earth), nīr (water), tī (fire), vaḷi (air), viṇ / ākāyam (ether): the body and every drug are made of them; the humours are compounded of them — vaḷi of air (and ether), aḻal of fire, aiyam of earth and water.

queries: prepared segments: TU 2.1, AU 3.1.3, ŚU 2.12, ChU 6
checks.note: All 4 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (TU 2.1; AU 3.1.3; ŚU 2.12; ChU 6). It rests on 4 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: The five elements in Sowa Rigpa

definitions.definition: Earth, water, fire, wind and space compose body, nyepa, food and medicine; tastes and potencies arise from them.
Flesh, divine, wisdom, dharma and buddha eye, all possessed by the Tathāgata.

name: Why buddha-nature was taught: the five faults (RGV 1.156-157)

definitions.definition: Discouragement, contempt for inferior beings, grasping the unreal, denying the real, and excessive self-love are removed by the teaching that all beings have buddha-nature.

name: The five forms of God (para, vyūha, vibhava, antaryāmin, arcā)

definitions.definition: The one Lord is present as the supreme (para) in Vaikuṇṭha, the four vyūhas, the descents (vibhava), the inner controller (antaryāmin) and the consecrated image (arcā), in ascending order of accessibility; the arcā is the most accessible.
Bhagavān exists as the supreme (para), the emanations (vyūha), the descents (vibhava), the inner controller (antaryāmin) and the consecrated image (arcā).

notes: The fivefold list is standard in Pāñcarātra and Śrīvaiṣṇava writing; a single verse stating all five is not anchored here. U14 records the Viśiṣṭādvaita version.

name: The five founding masters of the Sakya (sa skya gong ma lnga)

definitions.definition: Sachen Kunga Nyingpo, Sönam Tsemo, Drakpa Gyaltsen, Sakya Paṇḍita and Chögyal Phagpa — the first three called the 'three white ones' (lay), the last two the 'two red ones' (monastic), after their robes.

notes: The white/red naming recalled with moderate confidence.

name: The five gates of mindfulness (wu nianmen)

definitions.definition: Worship (body), praise and calling the name (speech), aspiration = śamatha, contemplation = vipaśyanā of the 29 adornments, and transfer of merit; they bring the five gates of merit (approach, great assembly, dwelling, chamber, garden of play), the last being the return to teach.
Read by Shinran as Amida's practice transferred to beings, not the practitioner's.
Hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, humans and gods, with the paths leading to each and to nibbāna (MN 12).
Śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha and Tathāgata lineages, the indeterminate and those without lineage (Laṅkāvatāra).
To beings (bali), men (hospitality), ancestors (svadhā), gods (svāhā) and Brahman (self-study) (ŚB 11.5.6.1–3; TA 2.10).
The householder's daily expiation of the five slaughter-places: teaching/study, water-offering, fire-offering, bali, honouring guests (MDh 3.68–70).

checks.note: ŚB 11.5.6.1–3 ('pañcaiva mahāyajñāḥ … bhūtayajño manuṣyayajñaḥ pitṛyajño devayajño brahmayajña iti'), TA 2.10 and MDh 3.68–70 were all found; the five members match. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:satapatha-brahmana:11.5.6.1-3, tea:taittiriya-aranyaka:2.10, tea:manusmrti:3.68-70.

name: The five restraints as 'great vow' across Jain, Yoga and Brahmanical renunciation

definitions.definition: Abstention from violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness is the vow; kept in part it is the small vow, in full the great vow (mahāvrata) of the mendicant.
The same five are the yamas; unlimited by birth, place, time or occasion they are the great vow (mahāvrata).
The Dharmasūtras give the renouncer a set of vows of the same kind (non-injury, truth, not stealing, celibacy, renunciation).
The five lay precepts overlap (non-killing, non-stealing, sexual restraint, truthful speech) but replace non-possession with abstention from intoxicants.

relations.note: the Terāpanth's distinction is a later Jain development

notes: The list and the term mahāvrata are identical in Jain and Yoga texts (see brw:jain-mahavratas-and-yoga-yamas). The Dharmasūtra list is recalled at chapter level.

definitions.definition: Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, doubt: the first field of dhamma-contemplation, known as present or absent, with the arising, abandoning and non-recurrence of each known (MN 10:36).

Sense checked by J against the passage(s) of the teachings listed in evidence (name and definition fit); full content not read line by line.

definitions.definition: Guiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen and Fayan — the lineages recognised by the Song, each with its teaching devices (Rentian yanmu).

name: The five faculties and five powers

definitions.definition: Faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom (SN 48.10); as powers they cannot be shaken by their opposites.
For those not born into the state, asaṃprajñāta samādhi is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi and insight, each giving rise to the next.

relations.note: YS 1.20 lists śraddhā, vīrya, smṛti, samādhi, prajñā

definitions.definition: Arrest of grey hair, attainment of the desired, taking forms at will, the imperishable portion, and the great jewel — destruction of old age and death (KJN 17.12–13).

name: The fourfold and fivefold jhāna schemes

definitions.definition: The suttas count four jhānas; the Abhidhamma also counts five by separating the removal of applied and of sustained thought; the fifth has only equanimity and one-pointedness.

relations.note: the Abhidhamma's fivefold count of the same absorptions

definitions.definition: Knowledge is sensory (mati), scriptural (śruta), clairvoyant (avadhi), mind-reading (manaḥparyaya) and omniscient (kevala); the first three can be erroneous in one of wrong view; up to four can coexist, omniscience stands alone (TS 1.9–33).
Nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, śānti and śāntyatīta, the five enclosing divisions of the principles, purified in initiation.

Conception (descent into the womb), birth, renunciation, omniscience and nirvāṇa of each Tīrthaṅkara, at each of which the gods come to celebrate — at birth Indra bathes the child on Mount Meru; the events are re-enacted in the consecration of images (pañcakalyāṇaka-pratiṣṭhā).

Kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla and niyati, which with māyā limit universal agency, knowledge, fullness, eternity and pervasion into the individual's 'only a little, only this, only now, only here' (Paramārthasāra 16-17).
Śiva clothed in body and coverings is the jīva; without coverings he is Paraśiva (PKS 1.5).

Avalambaka (chest; supporting), kledaka (stomach; moistening), bodhaka (tongue; taste), tarpaka (head; nourishing the senses), śleṣaka (joints; binding) (AHS Sū 12.15-18; functions without names in Su Sū 21.14).
Dharmakāya, sambhogakāya, nirmāṇakāya, with the unchanging vajrakāya and the fully enlightened (abhisambodhi) kāya; the Guhyagarbha says the five kāyas are spontaneously perfected.

relations.note: an expanded form of the trikāya

definitions.definition: By substitution of opposites (in insight), by suppression (in concentration), by cutting off (in the path), by tranquillization (in fruition), by escape (nibbāna).
Mādhūkara, prākpraṇīta, ayācita, tātkālika and upapanna (Sannyāsa 2.65–70).

definitions.definition: Sālokya, sārṣṭi, sāmīpya, sārūpya and oneness (ekatva), which pure devotees do not accept without service to the Lord.

checks.note: Rests on tea:kapila-gita:3.29.11-14, tea:kapila-gita:3.25.34-38; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

name: Five kinds of liberation (sārṣṭi, sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya)

definitions.definition: The knower of the Śiva-Śakti pair beyond the principles attains, according to the degree of worship, the five liberations: equal power, same world, nearness, same form and union (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 11); union is granted even to one who says 'Bhavāni tvam' (SL 22).

relations.note: adds sārṣṭi (equality of power) to the usual four

definitions.definition: Minor, momentary, showering, uplifting and pervading rapture.
Induced one after another at points in the body as the first stage of the old meditation.

Ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion and clinging to life (YS 2.3), which Vyāsa calls the five errors (viparyaya) (YBh 2.3, 1.8); ignorance is the field of the rest, each of which may be dormant, attenuated, interrupted or fully active (YS 2.4). They are the root of the karma-store (YS 2.12) and are thinned by kriyā-yoga (YS 2.2).

Ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion and clinging to life (2.3) — the five errors (YBh 2.3), called tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra and andhatāmisra (YBh 1.8); ignorance is their field (2.4); they are the root of the karmic residue (2.12); gross forms are removed by meditation, subtle ones by involution (2.10–11); they cease through the cloud of dharma (4.30).

name: The five kinds of knowables (Vātsīputrīya)

definitions.definition: Past, future, present, unconditioned, and the inexpressible (the person).

notes: Known through Vasubandhu's citation (AKBh 9) — an opponent's report.

name: The five liberations and their refusal

definitions.definition: Sālokya, sārṣṭi, sāmīpya, sārūpya and sāyujya/ekatva; pure devotees do not accept them without service (BhP 3.29.13) and desire neither powers nor freedom from rebirth (11.14.14).

name: The five lights and the five elements

definitions.definition: The ground's display arises as five-coloured lights, the radiance of the five wisdoms; not recognized, the lights solidify into the five elements (space, air, fire, water, earth) and the body; in realization the elements return to light, as in the rainbow body.
In the Kunjed Gyalpo's setting the sambhogakāya retinues are named earth, water, fire, wind and space; at death the elements dissolve one into another.

notes: Colour-element correspondences vary between texts; the list is indicative (low confidence on pairings).

relations.note: elements returning to light

definitions.definition: Aintu malam: āṇavam, kaṉmam, māyai, māyēyam (the products of māyā) and tirōtāyi (Śiva's concealing power, called a mala by figure).
Sanskrit lists give four or five bonds: mala, karma, māyā, rodha-śakti, and for souls of the pure worlds bindu (vaindava) — enumeration varies.

name: The five means (upāya) of the Nimbārka school

definitions.definition: Karma (duty), vidyā (knowledge), upāsanā or dhyāna (meditation), prapatti (surrender to the Lord) and gurūpasatti (surrender to the guru); grace for the humble crowns them.

notes: Listed in the school's manuals (e.g. Vedāntaratnamañjūṣā); exact locus to verify.

definitions.definition: Proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion (NS 1.1.32–39): e.g. 'the mountain has fire; because it has smoke; whatever has smoke has fire, like a kitchen; so is this; therefore so'. The members embody all four means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); a ten-member view is rejected (NBh 1.1.32).
Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, going (VS 1.1.6).

name: The five names and five sounds (Sant Mat)

definitions.definition: At initiation five names (of the lords of the five regions) are given for simran and kept confidential; each region has its sound — bell and conch, drum/thunder, sārangī, flute, vīṇā.

notes: The five names themselves are held confidential by the tradition and are not recorded.

name: The five kinds of unattached ascetic

definitions.definition: Pulāka, bakuśa, kuśīla, nirgrantha and snātaka, distinguished by restraint, learning, transgression, tīrtha, outer sign, leśyā, rebirth and stage (TS 9.46–47).
Events are governed by five orders — of temperature/seasons, seeds, kamma, mind, and Dhamma — so not everything experienced is due to kamma.
Expounded at length in Ledi Sayadaw's Niyāma Dīpanī as the cosmic order without a creator.

Accumulation, preparation (four aids to penetration), seeing (sixteen moments; first ground), cultivation (remaining grounds) and completion; the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Triṃśikā describe the passage from preparation to seeing as the progressive abandonment of the grasped and the grasper.

Pācaka (digesting, between stomach and intestine), rañjaka (colouring rasa; liver and spleen in Suśruta, stomach in Vāgbhaṭa), sādhaka (heart; accomplishing intellect and aims), ālocaka (eye), bhrājaka (skin) (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.10-14).
An arhat may be tempted by others, has non-knowing, has doubt, is instructed by others, and the path arises through an utterance — presented as heresy.
Refuted in Kathāvatthu 2.1–2.6 (commentary: Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas).

name: The five powers of mind training

definitions.definition: The whole practice condensed for a lifetime and for the time of death: resolve, familiarisation, the white seed, repudiation (of self-cherishing) and aspiration.

notes: Member names follow the commentaries (recalled).

definitions.definition: Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna and samāna are all breath (BAU 1.5.3); PrU 3.5-7 assigns them places: apāna in the organs of excretion and generation, prāṇa in eye, ear, mouth and nose, samāna in the middle distributing food, vyāna in the channels, udāna leading upward at death; ChU 3.13 links them with the five openings of the heart and ChU 5.19-23 with the five first offerings of food.

relations.note: the later yoga lists of vital currents include these five

name: The five vital breaths in the Kashmirian scheme

definitions.definition: Prāṇa and apāna (waking and dream), samāna (deep sleep), udāna (the fourth, fiery, rising in the centre), vyāna (beyond, all-pervading) (ĪPK 3.2.19-20); in the āṇava practice they carry the seven blisses (TĀ 5.43-52).
Abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech and intoxicants — 'five great gifts' of safety to countless beings (AN 8.39).

relations.note: four of the five overlap with the yamas of YS 2.30 and the Jain vows

definitions.definition: Before worship: purification of oneself, of the place, of the substances, of the mantras and of the liṅga.
Protection of knowledge, austerity, absence of conflict, cessation of suffering, manifestation of bliss (Jīvanmuktiviveka ch. 4).

Five relations of the real and the apparent (lord and minister): apparent within real, real within apparent, coming from within the real, arriving within both, arrived within both; also the five ranks of merit.
Studied as a late stage of Hakuin's kōan curriculum.

name: The five right practices and the rightly determined act

definitions.definition: Reading the Pure Land sūtras, contemplating, worshipping, calling the name, praising and offering — all directed to Amitābha; calling the name is the rightly determined act, the others auxiliary.
Set aside the auxiliary and choose the rightly determined act.

members: calling the name (chengming) — the rightly determined act

name: The five powers: consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, action

definitions.definition: Cit, ānanda, icchā, jñāna, kriyā - the powers of Śiva that appear as the five pure tattvas (Paramārthasāra 14).
The bodhisattva masters the inner science, the science of reasons (logic), the science of language, medicine and the crafts — logic to refute opponents and to inspire faith.

name: The five sheaths (pañca-kośa) as defined in Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1-2.5

names.name: pañca ātmānaḥ (five selves) — annamaya, prāṇamaya, manomaya, vijñānamaya, ānandamaya

definitions.definition: Five selves, each "made of" (-maya) something, each person-shaped, each within the previous and filling it, with the refrain "tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā yaḥ pūrvasya" (its embodied self is this very one, the one of the former; the construal is disputed): the self made of the essence of food (2.1.1); of breath (head prāṇa, wings vyāna and apāna, self ākāśa, support earth; 2.2.1); of mind (head yajus, wings ṛc and sāman, self ādeśa, support Atharvāṅgiras; 2.3.1); of understanding (head śraddhā, wings ṛta and satya, self yoga, support mahas; 2.4.1); of bliss (head priya, wings moda and pramoda, self ānanda, support brahman; 2.5.1). The knower, departing, approaches all five (2.8.5, 3.10.5). The word kośa does not occur in the text.

TU 2.1-5 teaches five selves, each within and filling the one before and each person-shaped: made of the essence of food, of breath, of mind, of understanding and of bliss, with brahman as the tail and foundation of the last; TU 3 reaches the same five as successive understandings of brahman. The TU calls them selves 'made of' (-maya); the name 'sheath' (kośa) for them is later Vedānta usage.
Food, vital air, mind, intellect and bliss sheaths, which seem to cover the self; taught progressively so that the self is known as distinct from each; the bliss-sheath is not Brahman (Śaṅkara).
Five kōcams among the ninety-six: aṉṉamayam, pirāṇamayam, maṉōmayam, viññāṉamayam, āṉantamayam.

relations.note: Bhṛgu's identifications of brahman (3.2-3.6) follow the same five names in the same order.

checks.note: Corrected by J: Definition: "the later being the embodied self of the earlier" replaced by the text's refrain with its construal marked as disputed (see teachings 2.3.1-2.6.1).

The note's claim is confirmed: in TU 2 the five are selves 'made of' (-maya) food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss. The word kośa does not occur anywhere in TU 2; in the whole prepared TU it occurs only at 1.4.1 ('brahmaṇaḥ kośo 'si'). All 3 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (TU 2.1-5; TU 3; TU 2). It rests on 4 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Bliss, leaping up, trembling, sleep and whirling (MVT 11.35; TĀ 5.107).
Birth, herbs, mantras, austerity and samādhi (4.1). The text does not give recipes or methods.
Powers arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (4.1, YBh 4.1); only the mind born of meditation is without residue (4.6).

definitions.definition: Worldly, Vedic, spiritual (Sāṃkhya-Yoga), Atimārga and Mantra, in ascending order.

name: The five streams (srotas) of Śaiva revelation

definitions.definition: The Mantra-tantras issue from Sadāśiva's five faces: Siddhānta from the upper (Īśāna), Gāruḍa from the east, Vāma from the north, Bhūta from the west (Sadyojāta) and Bhairava from the south.

name: The five sūtras and one treatise (Chinese Pure Land canon)

definitions.definition: Later Chinese Pure Land adds to the three sūtras the Samantabhadra conduct-and-vows chapter and the Śūraṅgama chapter on Mahāsthāmaprāpta's penetration through recollection, with Vasubandhu's treatise.

notes: Grouping attributed to Wei Yuan (four sūtras) and Yinguang (fifth) — recalled, not checked.

name: The five systems of knowledge (Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, Veda, Pāśupata)

definitions.definition: Five systems holding different views, proclaimed by Kapila, Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord himself, Apāntaratamas and Śiva respectively, in all of which Nārāyaṇa is the culmination (MBh 12.337.59–67).
The non-specific elements of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, from ahaṃkāra as bhūtādi, from which the gross elements arise (SK 22, 25, 38).

name: The five elements in the breath

definitions.definition: In each nostril-flow the five elements arise in turn, recognized by the breath's length, direction, colour and taste (Śiva Svarodaya).

name: The five temperaments (carita) and their remedies

definitions.definition: Practitioners dominated by lust, hatred, delusion, conceit or discursive thought are given the unattractive, loving-kindness, dependent origination, the analysis of elements and mindfulness of breathing respectively.

name: Jamgön Kongtrul's Five Treasuries

definitions.definition: The five great collections that preserve the Tibetan traditions.

members: Treasury of Knowledge (shes bya kun khyab mdzod)
Treasury of Kagyu Mantra (bka' brgyud sngags mdzod)
Treasury of Precious Treasures (rin chen gter mdzod)
Treasury of Extensive Teachings (rgya chen bka' mdzod)
notes: Some lists add or substitute the Uncommon Treasury (thun mong ma yin pa'i mdzod).

definitions.definition: Form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness: the second field of dhamma-contemplation, each known with its arising and passing away (MN 10:38).

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): prāṇa (head; breathing, swallowing; upholds intellect, heart, senses, mind), udāna (chest; speech, effort, memory), vyāna (heart; all movement), samāna (near the fire; digestion) and apāna (pelvis; elimination and birth) (AHS Sū 12.4-9); vāyu 'whose self is prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna and apāna' upholds the body (Ca Sū 12.8).

Prāṇa and the others are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29; SS 2.31); the Kramadīpikā places prāṇa at mouth and nose, apāna at the navel, samāna at the heart, udāna at the throat, vyāna at the joints.

relations.note: the Upaniṣadic five breaths, here as divisions of the vāta doṣa

definitions.definition: Abstention from violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness — in part (small vows) for householders, in full (great vows) for ascetics (TS 7.1–2).
Śvetāmbara ascetics add not eating at night as a sixth vow (Daśavaikālika).

relations.note: Same five names as Patañjali's yamas; Patañjali calls them the great vow when universal (YS 2.31). The Jain vows carry the Jain definitions (e.g. violence as careless severing of vitalities).

name: The five activities of the mind (pañca vṛttayaḥ)

definitions.definition: Valid cognition (pramāṇa: perception, inference, testimony), error (viparyaya), conceptual construction (vikalpa), sleep (nidrā) and memory (smṛti), each afflicted (kliṣṭa) or unafflicted (akliṣṭa) (YS 1.5–1.11). Afflicted ones are caused by the afflictions and become the field for the karma-store; unafflicted ones have discernment as object; the two arise in each other's gaps; activities and impressions produce each other in an unceasing wheel (YBh 1.5). All of them are of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion, and are to be stilled (YBh 1.11).

The mind's activities are five — valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep and memory — each afflicted or unafflicted (YS 1.5–11); activities and impressions produce one another in a ceaseless wheel (YBh 1.5); all have the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion and are to be stilled (YBh 1.11).
