name: The five grounds of monastic judgment

definitions.definition: Āgama (supernormal knowledge), śruta (scripture), ājñā (instruction), dhāraṇā (retained tradition) and jīta (established practice), used in that order of preference.
Five 'skies' or spaces of the body to be known and contemplated (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2); in the SSP named ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, tattvākāśa and sūryākāśa (recalled).
Mirror-like, equality, discriminating, accomplishing and dharmadhātu gnosis: the purified aggregates or afflictions, each of a buddha family; the Yogācāra four plus the dharmadhātu gnosis.

name: The five-year cycle of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: A cycle of five years (saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, anuvatsara, idvatsara) under Prajāpati, beginning with sun and moon together at Śraviṣṭhā in Māgha, with intercalary months to reconcile lunar and solar time.

notes: Names of the five years from memory (moderate).

checks.note: VJ Ṛk 1 ('pañcasaṃvatsaramayaṃ yugādhyakṣaṃ prajāpatim') and the start at Śraviṣṭhā in Māgha (Ṛk 6) were found. The five year names, which the entry flags as from memory, are not in the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa text. They are attested in exactly this form in Varāhamihira's Bṛhatsaṃhitā 8.24: 'saṃvatsaro 'gniḥ parivatsaro 'rka idādikaḥ … prajāpatiś cāpy anuvatsaraḥ syād idvatsaraḥ'. The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.13.115–122 has a variant list (saṃvatsara, parivatsara, iḍāvatsara, anuvatsara, vatsara). So the names are right for the tradition, but they come from later jyotiṣa and purāṇa sources, not from the cited VJ verses. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:vedanga-jyotisa:r.1, tea:vedanga-jyotisa:r.6.

name: The fivefold analysis (of self or Tathāgata)

definitions.definition: Sought as identical with the aggregates, different from them, containing them, contained in them, or possessing them, the self (or Tathāgata or person) is not found (MMK 16.2; 22.1).

name: The fivefold equality of Śiva and Śakti (pañcavidha-sāmya)

definitions.definition: Samayā (the Goddess) and Samaya (Śiva) are equal in seat (adhiṣṭhāna), in state (avasthāna), in action (anuṣṭhāna), in form (rūpa) and in name (nāma), and so of equal primacy (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).
Bhāskararāya repeats the five equalities (seat of worship, acts such as creation, dance, names such as Bhairava, form such as redness), crediting the Subhagodaya commentator (on LSN 37).

name: The fivefold hierarchy of religion (laukika, vaidika, ādhyātmika, atimārga, mantra)

definitions.definition: Religious teaching is graded as worldly, Vedic, spiritual (Sāṃkhya-Yoga), Atimārga and Mantra; in the Kāmika each is spoken by one of Sadāśiva's five faces, each fivefold, making twenty-five streams.

name: The fivefold Mahāmudrā (phyag chen lnga ldan)

definitions.definition: Mahāmudrā practised with five parts: bodhicitta, the body of the yidam, devotion to the guru, the Mahāmudrā view, and dedication/aspiration — Jigten Sumgön's and Phagmodrupa's teaching, also transmitted in the Drukpa.

name: The flower sermon

definitions.definition: On Vulture Peak the Buddha held up a flower, Mahākāśyapa smiled, and the Buddha entrusted him with the treasury of the true Dharma eye outside the teachings.

notes: Tradition's account; attested only in Chinese sources from the Song (Tiansheng guangdeng lu, 1036; the apocryphal Dafan tianwang wenfo jueyi jing).

definitions.definition: Meditation on the Goddess is of two kinds; the formless is beyond speech and mind and reachable only by yogins through great effort; a form is imagined for the formless Kālī to steady the mind and awaken subtle meditation (Mahānirvāṇa 5.137-140); the formless Goddess produces form for the sake of worship (Nirvāṇa Tantra 1.2-5).

The spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness and neither-perception-nor-non-perception, reached by passing beyond perceptions of form (MN 111; MN 121); the bodhisatta learned the third and fourth from Āḷāra and Uddaka and rejected them as not leading to nibbāna (MN 26); each is a basis for insight (AN 9.36).

name: Dharmākara's forty-eight vows

definitions.definition: The vows (T360) establishing Sukhāvatī: no evil destinies, golden bodies, superknowledges, infinite light and life, birth for all who call on him (18th), welcome at death (19th), rebirth by dedicating merit (20th).

Tanluan singles out three vows as proof of other-power — the 18th (birth by ten recitations), 11th (rightly established group), 22nd (surpassing the stages; returning to save beings); the Sanskrit recension has 47 vows.
Shinran reads five 'true' vows (11th, 12th, 13th, 17th, 18th) and the provisional 19th and 20th, and the 22nd for the returning aspect.

notes: Detailed doctrine of the vows: U43.

definitions.definition: Ten kasiṇas, ten foulnesses, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four formless states, one perception (repulsiveness of nutriment) and one defining (of the four elements); ten lead only to access, thirty to absorption.

relations.note: the Visuddhimagga's subjects of calm versus the sutta frame of mindfulness; several subjects overlap

name: Gautama's forty sacraments and eight virtues

definitions.definition: Forty sacraments (8 bodily rites, 4 Vedic vows, final bath, marriage, 5 great sacrifices, 7 cooked-food, 7 oblation and 7 Soma sacrifices) and eight virtues of the self (compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, calm, auspiciousness, generosity, freedom from greed); the virtues, not the sacraments, decide union with Brahman (GDh 8.14–25).

checks.note: GDh 8.14–25 has the forty sacraments in the stated groups, then the eight virtues of the self (dayā sarvabhūteṣu, kṣāntiḥ, anasūyā, śaucam, anāyāsaḥ, maṅgalam, akārpaṇyam, aspṛhā); the eight members match. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:gautama-dharmasutra:8.14-25.

name: The mental factors in six classes

definitions.definition: Ten universal, ten universal good, six universal defiled, two universal bad, ten restricted defiled, and (in the later count) eight undetermined (remorse, sleepiness, reasoning, investigation, passion, aversion, pride, doubt).
Prior absence, destruction, absolute absence, mutual absence (Tarkasaṅgraha), foreshadowed in VS 9.1–12.
The domain of the Buddhas, the domain of jhāna, the results of kamma, and speculation about the world (AN 4.77).

name: The four activities (las bzhi) and the siddhis

definitions.definition: Tantric practice brings ordinary accomplishments (thun mong gi dngos grub) — above all the four activities of pacifying, enriching, magnetizing and subjugating — and the supreme accomplishment (mchog gi dngos grub), buddhahood; the ordinary ones are to be used only for others and are not the goal.

notes: The Mañjuśrī sādhana tantra of the wheel of the four activities (src:jampal-lezhi-khorlo) is named for them.

definitions.definition: Uḍḍīyāna (thighs), Kāmarūpa/Kāmagiri (yoni), Jālandhara (breasts), Pūrṇagiri (shoulders and neck), with Devīkūṭa (feet) (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.41-43).
Kāmākhya, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara and Oḍra as the levels beyond form, form, word and body (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7).

name: The four Āgamas (Chinese) as parallels to the Nikāyas

definitions.definition: Dīrghāgama (T1) — 30 sūtras.
Madhyamāgama (T26) — 222 sūtras.
Saṃyuktāgama (T99) — 1362 sūtras (Taishō count); also T100 and T101.
Ekottarikāgama (T125) — 472 sūtras; school affiliation debated.

name: The four ages of the doctrine (Dolpopa)

definitions.definition: The doctrine declines through the four ages; the definitive teaching of the age of perfection (kṛtayuga) is restored by Dolpopa's 'fourth council'.
Edible food, contact, mental volition and consciousness, which sustain beings, each with its simile (SN 12.63; MN 9; MN 38).

name: Dharma and the aims of life (trivarga, puruṣārtha)

definitions.definition: Dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa, all treated in the epic (MBh 1.56.33); dharma is the source of artha and kāma (18.5.49); Rāma asks Bharata whether he pursues each at its time (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).

notes: U05's contribution; the Dharmaśāstra account is given by U02.

name: The four āmnāya maṭhas (the tradition's account)

definitions.definition: Śaṅkara founded four cardinal monasteries, each with a Veda, a mahāvākya, a first ācārya and Daśanāmī names: Śṛṅgeri (south; Yajur; ahaṃ brahmāsmi; Sureśvara; Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, Purī), Govardhana, Purī (east; Ṛg; prajñānaṃ brahma; Padmapāda; Vana, Araṇya), Śāradā, Dvārakā (west; Sāma; tat tvam asi; Hastāmalaka; Tīrtha, Āśrama), Jyotirmaṭh (north; Atharva; ayam ātmā brahma; Toṭaka; Giri, Parvata, Sāgara). The Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi pīṭha claims foundation by Śaṅkara too, which the others dispute. See lin:dasanami (U57) for the living order.

name: The four kinds of religious performance

definitions.definition: Performance from affection (prīti), from devotion (bhakti), from scripture (vacana) and without attachment (asaṅga) (Ṣoḍaśaka; YDS on asaṅga in the prabhā view).
Upakrama (introduction), nikṣepa (placement of meanings), anugama (following the text) and naya (standpoints) — the method of the Anuyogadvāra.
Digambara literature is classed as narrative (prathamānuyoga), cosmology and karma (karaṇānuyoga), conduct (caraṇānuyoga) and substances (dravyānuyoga) (Ratnakaraṇḍa 43–46).

The Digambara arrangement of all scripture: prathamānuyoga (narratives of the great persons: the purāṇas), karaṇānuyoga (cosmology and the mathematics of karma: Tiloyapaṇṇatti, Gommaṭasāra), caraṇānuyoga (conduct: Mūlācāra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra) and dravyānuyoga (substances and the self: Kundakunda, the Tattvārthasūtra).

Āryarakṣita is said to have divided the teaching into four anuyogas — caraṇakaraṇa (conduct), dharmakathā (narrative), gaṇita (calculation, cosmology) and dravya (substances) — because pupils could no longer grasp all aspects of every sūtra at once.
Of right faith, right knowledge, right conduct and austerity, brought to completion at the end of life.

relations.note: the three jewels with austerity added (as in Uttarādhyayana 28)

name: The four topics: what is to be abandoned, its cause, abandonment, the means

definitions.definition: Having understood what is to be abandoned, what produces it, its absolute abandonment and the means to that, one attains the highest good (NBh 1.1.1).

relations.note: Structural parallel with the four noble truths and with the Yoga Bhāṣya's fourfold (YBh 2.15); a parallel of form, not of doctrine.

definitions.definition: Nature (prakṛti), duration (sthiti), intensity/fruition (anubhava) and quantity (pradeśa); nature is the eight karma types (8.4), duration is given for each (8.14-8.20), fruition is experiencing and follows the name (8.21-8.22), quantity concerns the particles in all the soul's space-points (8.24).

Bondage is of nature (which karma), duration (how long), intensity (how strong its fruit) and quantity (how many particles) (TS 8.3); activity determines nature and quantity, passion determines duration and intensity (commentaries).

name: The four attachments to be parted from

definitions.definition: Attachment to this life, to saṃsāra, to one's own purpose, and grasping — whose absence is dharma practice, renunciation, bodhicitta and the view.
Tight focus (1st–2nd states), interrupted engagement (3rd–7th), uninterrupted engagement (8th) and spontaneous engagement (9th).

definitions.definition: Scripture, the teacher, personal experience and the historical account of the lineage — by which the result of the path is established.

name: The four stages of yoga (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti)

definitions.definition: Four stages 'in all yogas' (HYP 4.69), first taught in the Amṛtasiddhi: in the HYP they are marked by the piercing of the three knots and by the inner sounds (4.70–77); in the DYŚ by signs of breath-mastery, the union of prāṇa and apāna, the element-concentrations and rājayoga (81–147); in the Śiva Saṃhitā by bodily signs, the seeing of karma's 'three peaks' and liberation while living.
Beginning, the 'pot' stage in which breaths, mind and selves unite, familiarity (kuṇḍalinī in the suṣumnā), and completion (natural yoga, liberation while living) — Yogatattva 20ff.; Varāha 5.71–75.

definitions.definition: Love, compassion, rejoicing and equanimity pervading all directions without measure (DN 13; MN 62); a divine abiding here (Snp 1.8); the path to the Brahmā world (DN 13) and a basis for liberation of mind (MN 43).

relations.note: YS 1.33's maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā; see brw:buddhism-yoga-four-attitudes

definitions.definition: The four branches of Guhyasamāja practice (sevā, upasādhana, sādhana, mahāsādhana).

name: The four cakras of the Hevajra

definitions.definition: Nirmāṇacakra at the navel, dharmacakra at the heart, saṃbhogacakra at the throat, mahāsukhacakra at the head, correlated with the four bodies and the four joys.
Channels of formation, of existence, of connection and of life.

name: The four general characteristics of karma

definitions.definition: Karma is definite, grows greatly, is not met if not done, and once done is not lost.

name: The four characteristics of the conditioned

definitions.definition: Birth, duration, decay and impermanence as real forces, with secondary characteristics.
Designations of the series: arising having not been, ceasing having been, the continuity and its change.

name: The four ways of leaving as it is (cog bzhag bzhi)

definitions.definition: View like a mountain, meditation like an ocean, conduct as appearances, fruit as awareness — each 'left as it is'.

name: The Siddhānta doxography of rival schools

definitions.definition: Rival doctrines are ranked in circles — outermost (Lokāyata, Buddhists, Jains…), outer (Vedic darśanas, Māyāvāda, Pāñcarātra…), inner-outer (Pāśupata, Kāpālika and other Śaiva sects), and inner (Śaiva views close to the Siddhānta) — each refuted in turn.

notes: Four groups of six are traditionally counted; membership lists low confidence.

definitions.definition: Noun, verb, preverb and particle (Nirukta 1.1); the verb signifies becoming, the noun being.
The same four read into the 'four horns' of RV 4.58.3 (Mahābhāṣya).

name: The four clear instructions on purity (Śūraṅgama)

definitions.definition: Cutting off lust, killing, stealing and false claims as the foundation of samādhi.

name: The four conditions (baddha, mumukṣu, sādhaka, siddha)

definitions.definition: Bound, seeker, practitioner and accomplished: the Dāsbodh's account of the stages of a life.

name: The four cycles of the instruction series

definitions.definition: Śrī Siṃha divided the instruction series into the outer, inner, secret and innermost secret unsurpassed cycles; the last is the Heart-essence (snying thig).

definitions.definition: The commentaries define each dhamma by its characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause.
That the mind turn to the Dharma, the Dharma become the path, the path clarify confusion, and confusion dawn as wisdom — the whole path in four lines.

Meditation is fixing the mind on one object for up to a muhūrta (TS 9.27); it is sorrowful (four kinds), cruel (four kinds), virtuous (examining the command, harm, fruition and structure) and pure (four stages: with multiplicity, reasoning and shifting; with unity and reasoning; subtle activity; ceased activity); only the last two lead to liberation (9.28–44).
A steady mind is dhyāna, a moving one is citta (Dhyānaśataka 2).

relations.note: TS 9.41–44 use vitarka and vīcāra but define them as scriptural cognition and shifting among object, word and activity — not Patañjali's gross/subtle object-absorptions.

name: The four dhyānas of the Laṅkāvatāra

definitions.definition: The dhyāna of the foolish (no-self of persons), of examining meanings (no-self of dharmas), of taking suchness as object, and the Tathāgata's dhyāna.

The embodied (piṇḍastha, with five concentrations), the word-based (padastha, on mantras and letters), the form-based (rūpastha, on the Arhat) and the formless (rūpātīta, on the Siddha) — in Śubhacandra's Jñānārṇava and Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra 7–10.
Earth (solidity), water (cohesion), fire (heat), air (motion), internal and external, seen as 'not mine' (MN 28; MN 62); the four vipers (SN 35.238).

In the Nāropa texts the elements are known through their dissolution: earth into water, water into fire, fire into wind, wind into consciousness at death and in yoga; inner heat does not progress unless the 'equal taste of the four elements' is known.

relations.note: the Brahmanical and Sāṃkhya lists add space (ākāśa) as a fifth element; the suttas' six-element list adds space and consciousness

definitions.definition: Earth, water, fire and wind each return to their own nature; with the senses and their objects they branch from one root (Cantongqi).
At death, see that the four elements are without self (Huangbo).
The deluded take the four elements as their body (Jinul).
'When the four elements scatter, where do you go?' (Doushuai's third barrier).

relations.note: The Indian mahābhūtas (earth, water, fire, wind) as received in Chinese Buddhism.

name: The four empowerments

definitions.definition: Vase, secret, wisdom-knowledge and word (or precious) empowerments, purifying body, speech, mind and all three and planting the seeds of the four kāyas; received from the guru in guru yoga.

Mild (mṛdu) → mantrayoga, success in twelve years; middling (madhya) → layayoga; strong (adhimātra) → haṭhayoga with its limbs, six years; strongest (adhimātratama) → all the yogas, three years (SS 5.10–14; DYŚ 12 for the mild).

name: The four great and eight lesser Kagyu schools

definitions.definition: Four great schools founded by disciples of Gampopa and his nephew — Karma, Tsalpa, Barom, Phagdru — and eight lesser founded by disciples of Phagmodrupa — Drikung, Drukpa, Taklung, Trophu, Martsang, Yelpa, Yazang, Shugseb. The guardian deities of the four directions, who offer the Āṭānāṭiya protection (DN 32) and first heard the proclamation of the wheel (SN 56.11).

name: The four greatnesses of the lamrim teaching

definitions.definition: Understanding all teachings as non-contradictory; taking all scriptures as instructions; easily finding the Conqueror's intent; being saved from the great misdeed of rejecting the dharma.

name: The four guests of the Chöd offering

definitions.definition: The recipients of the visualized body-offering: the Three Jewels (devotion), the protectors (qualities), the six classes of beings (compassion), and harmful spirits and karmic creditors (repaying debts).

name: The four perfections of the dharmakāya

definitions.definition: Permanence, bliss, self and purity — the true nature of the Tathāgata's dharmakāya and nirvāṇa, reversing the inverted views about the Tathāgata; cultivated by faith, wisdom, samādhi and compassion.
Concentration through desire, energy, mind and investigation, with formations of striving, developed without slackness or tension (SN 51.20); for a monk, 'long life' (DN 26).

name: The four immeasurables / attitudes across Buddhist, Yoga and Jain teaching

definitions.definition: Love, compassion, rejoicing and equanimity pervading all directions without measure; the Buddha says other wanderers teach the same but cannot say where each culminates (the beautiful, infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness).
Friendliness, compassion, gladness and equanimity toward the happy, the suffering, the virtuous and the non-virtuous clear the mind.
Friendliness toward all beings, joy (pramoda) toward the more virtuous, compassion toward the afflicted and impartiality (mādhyasthya) toward the unruly, as supporting reflections of the vows.

name: The four inversions and their reversal

definitions.definition: The ordinary inversions take the impermanent as permanent etc.; the śrāvakas' inverted view takes the Tathāgata's permanence, bliss, self and purity as impermanent, suffering, no-self and impure.

First jhāna: secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, with applied and sustained thought, rapture and bliss born of seclusion; second: with inner confidence and unification, rapture and bliss born of concentration; third: equanimous, mindful, clearly comprehending, feeling bliss; fourth: neither pleasant nor painful, purity of mindfulness through equanimity (DN 2; SN 45.8) — each with its simile of bodily pervasion; right concentration.

relations.note: the Yoga Sūtra's samādhi with vitarka and vicāra shares vocabulary; the two traditions do not identify their states

name: The four joys (ānanda)

definitions.definition: Joy, supreme joy, joy of cessation and innate joy, arising in consecration and completion-stage yoga as the drop moves through the cakras; the innate is known between supreme joy and cessation (Tilopa) or as the fourth (Saraha).
Saraha warns against identifying the experienced moments with the innate (King Dohā v27).

relations.note: Each joy is paired with one of the four moments.

name: The four passions and their sixteen varieties (Tattvārtha 8.9)

definitions.definition: Anger, pride, deceit and greed, each with four varieties: anantānubandhī, apratyākhyāna, pratyākhyāna, saṃjvalana; sixteen in all, forming the conduct-deluding karma of the passions.

Anger, pride, deceit and greed, each in four grades — endless-binding (blocking right view), blocking partial renunciation, blocking full renunciation, and smouldering (blocking perfect conduct) — with nine quasi-passions (TS 8.9).

name: The three and four kāyas in the Kagyu

Giving, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct and consistency (acting alike), by which bodhisattvas gather beings; Śrīmālā vows to use them.
Diet, behaviour, medicine and external therapy, from gentle to strong.
Mind is tāmasa (restless, petty), rājasa (coming and going) and sāttvika (steady in dharma); the fourth is beyond the three guṇas, marked by nirvāṇa (Jñānakārikā 2.6–9).
Reverent, exclusive, uninterrupted and long-lasting practice, to be kept until the end of life (Shandao).
The 'manner of practice' (sagyō), contained in the conviction of birth.
Variety (vicitra), ripening (vipāka), dissolution (vimarda) and the signless (vilakṣaṇa), paired with the four joys.

A coded teaching on four bodily substances ('moons') whose secret handling under a guru belongs to Bāul body practice; the tradition insists it is secret and ruinous without a guru. RESTRICTED: no details recorded.

name: The four negations of the holy life (MN 76)

definitions.definition: Annihilationism, non-action, no-cause, and seven bodies with the fixed round — each makes the holy life pointless.
Yijing and the Tibetan tradition: Mahāsāṃghika, Sthavira, (Mūla)sarvāstivāda, Saṃmitīya.
A word may refer to a thing by name only, by representation (image), by potentiality (what it was or will be) or by its actual present state; distinguishing these avoids confusion (TS 1.5).

name: The four roots of good conducive to penetration

definitions.definition: Heat, summits, acceptance, highest worldly dharmas — worldly cultivation of the sixteen aspects of the four truths before the path of seeing.

relations.note: Mahāyāna places them as the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) of the five paths.

name: The four noble truths (cattāri ariyasaccāni)

definitions.definition: DN 22:17-21: as the fifth field of dhamma-contemplation the four truths are known 'as they really are', and each is expanded: suffering as birth, ageing, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, despair, the disliked, the lost, the unobtained, in brief the five aggregates of clinging; origin as threefold craving arising and settling in the dear-looking and pleasant-looking; cessation as the complete fading and ceasing of that craving, in the same places; the way as the noble eightfold path.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, the way to its cessation; the fifth field of dhamma-contemplation, each known 'as it really is' (MN 10:44).

Suffering, its origin (craving), its cessation, and the path (the noble eightfold path) (SN 56.11); to be fully understood, abandoned, realised and developed; what the Buddha declares because it is beneficial (MN 63; SN 56.31); all wholesome states are included in them as footprints in an elephant's (MN 28).
Taught in the order of realization; all that has outflows is suffering; realized in sixteen moments.
Taught at Ṛṣivadana with the two extremes and three turnings.
In emptiness there are no suffering, origin, cessation or path (Heart); of the four only cessation is permanent, the one truth and refuge (Śrīmālā).

notes: U38 contribution to a shared concept.

name: The four notions (self, being, soul, person)

definitions.definition: Ātma-, sattva-, jīva- and pudgala-saṃjñā, whose presence means one is not a bodhisattva; the buddhas are free of all notions.

Residential, peripatetic, luminous and celestial-vehicle gods (TS 4.1–42); the higher excel in lifespan and purity but have less movement, possession and pride; gods cannot take vows and must be reborn human to be liberated.
Matter originates from kamma, consciousness, temperature and nutriment.

name: The four pādas: caryā, kriyā, yoga, jñāna

definitions.definition: Every Āgama has four sections (vidyā/jñāna, kriyā, yoga, caryā); as a path, the initiate's conduct, ritual, yoga and knowledge.
Four successive stages, each containing all four in miniature (caryā-in-caryā etc.), with fruits sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya; the four paths of servant, son, friend and the true path.
Several Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (e.g. the Pādma) are likewise divided into four quarters — knowledge, yoga, ritual and conduct.

The Tirumantiram's four paths (caryai, kiriyai, yōkam, ñāṉam) are accepted by Tāyumāṉavar and underlie the Siddhars' view that outer worship belongs to the lower rungs, which the knower leaves behind.

relations.note: the textual quarters of an Āgama and the four stages share names

notes: U49 contribution: the four-quarter division is shared by Śaiva Āgamas and Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (brw:saiva-siddhanta-pancaratra).

name: The four pādas of an Āgama

relations.note: the Tamil Siddhānta reads caryā-kriyā-yoga-jñāna as ascending stages (U18/U51)

notes: Scholarly note: the neat fourfold arrangement is an ideal that many surviving texts do not follow.

definitions.definition: Knowledge (vidyā/jñāna), ritual (kriyā), yoga and conduct (caryā); all of Śiva's scriptures are said to have them and to serve enjoyment and liberation.
The Pādma Saṃhitā is arranged in the four pādas jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā.
What is real in the ultimate sense is fourfold: consciousness, mental factors, matter and nibbāna; everything else (persons, things, time, place) is concept.

Each cognition has a seen part (image), a seeing part, a self-witnessing part and a witnessing of the self-witnessing part (Dharmapāla, adopted by Xuanzang); others admitted one (Sthiramati: only self-witnessing is real), two (Nanda) or three (Dignāga) parts.

relations.note: Dignāga's three-aspect cognition is the basis

name: The four paths and four fruits

definitions.definition: Stream-entry, once-return, non-return and arahantship, each a path moment followed by fruition; the paths abandon the fetters in stages; supramundane consciousness has jhāna character.

notes: The sutta path map is pth:four-stages-of-awakening (owned by U51).

relations.note: path and fruit take nibbāna as object

definitions.definition: Physician, medicine, attendant and patient, each with four qualities; the physician is chief (Ca Sū 9.3-13; AHS Sū 1.27-29).

Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara and Oḍḍiyāna, transformations of the four fused powers, located in the subtle body at kanda, pada, rūpa and beyond form (YH 1.41-42); the Goddess dwells in Jālandhara and Oḍyāṇa (LSN 82).
Where the Tathāgata was born, awakened, first taught and attained final nibbāna (DN 16).

name: The four essential points for analysing selflessness

definitions.definition: Identifying the self to be negated; ascertaining that such a self must be either one with or different from the aggregates; ascertaining that it is not one; ascertaining that it is not different.

relations.note: a condensed form of the chariot reasoning

name: The four powers of confession

definitions.definition: Support (refuge and bodhicitta before Vajrasattva), regret, resolution not to repeat, and the antidote (practice, mantra) — the purification in Vajrasattva practice.
Purification of wrongdoing by the power of repudiation (regret), of reliance (refuge and bodhicitta), of the remedy (virtuous practice) and of restraint (resolving not to repeat).

members: gnyen po kun tu spyod pa'i stobs

definitions.definition: Constant (nitya) - the continual perishing of beings; occasional (naimittika) - of the three worlds at the end of Brahmā's day; elemental (prākṛtika) - of the whole egg into Prakṛti at the end of his life; final (ātyantika) - liberation by knowledge.
Daily (deep sleep), occasional, elemental and final (liberation).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: Authoritative testimony, perception, inference and yukti (Ca Sū 11.17-26); for diagnosis three (Vi 4.3); in the debate chapter tradition and analogy also appear among the terms (Vi 8.27).

relations.note: Nyāya counts four with analogy and without yukti

definitions.definition: Perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony (NS 1.1.3); tradition, presumption, inclusion and non-apprehension are reduced to them (NS 2.2.1–2). Bhāsarvajña accepts only three (no separate comparison).
The four means organize the Tattvacintāmaṇi's four books.

name: The preliminaries of breath-control (place, time, diet, purification)

definitions.definition: Before breath-control the Gheraṇḍa requires, in order, a suitable place (a secluded hut in a good land, not a far country, forest, capital or crowd), the right time (beginning in spring or autumn, not in the cold, hot or rainy seasons), moderate diet, and the purification of the channels (by seed-syllables or by dhauti); only then prāṇāyāma.

relations.note: Preliminaries of prāṇāyāma, the fifth of the Gheraṇḍa's seven means.

name: The aims of human life (puruṣārtha)

definitions.definition: Dharma, artha and kāma, whose combination is the good (MDh 2.224), with mokṣa sought after the debts are paid (MDh 6.35–37); dharmaśāstra prevails over arthaśāstra in conflict (YS 2.21).
Artha is foremost, dharma and kāma being rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).
The three pursued over a hundred-year life without mutual harm; dharma, artha, kāma in descending weight; mokṣa in old age (Kāmasūtra 1.2).

notes: The early texts speak of three aims (trivarga); mokṣa as a fourth aim (caturvarga) is systematized later.

evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)
checks.note: MDh 2.224, 6.35–37, YS 2.21, Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7 and Kāmasūtra 1.2 were all text-located. The entry's note that mokṣa as a fourth aim is a later systematization agrees with the texts: Manu, Kauṭilya and Vātsyāyana speak of the trivarga. definitions.definition: Speech is measured in four quarters; the wise brahmins know them; three are hidden and do not stir; men speak the fourth (RV 1.164.45). The verse does not name them; the Nirukta records several readings (Oṃ and the three vyāhṛtis; noun, verb, preposition, particle; mantra, ritual text, brāhmaṇa and ordinary speech; ṛc, yajus, sāman and ordinary speech; speech of creatures; speech in the self), and later schools read the levels of speech.

relations.note: Grammarians and Kashmir Śaivas later read the four quarters as the levels of speech (vaikharī, madhyamā, paśyantī, parā) — an interpretive correspondence.

definitions.definition: (As reported) The four topics on which Sañjaya refuses each of four alternatives: another world, spontaneously born beings, fruit of good and bad deeds, the Tathāgata after death.
Human birth, hearing the dharma, faith in it, and energy in self-restraint are hard to obtain (Uttarādhyayana 3.1); hence 'wake up — the nights do not return'.
Souls, deities, world and Parameśvara are eternal and distinct; only Parameśvara liberates.
The reality of a meditative object is established by the reasoning of dependence, of efficacy, of valid proof (through perception, inference and scripture) and of the nature of things.
Rely on the dharma not the person, the meaning not the letter, definitive not provisional sūtras, gnosis not consciousness; the finger is not the moon.
Restraining unarisen unwholesome states, abandoning arisen ones, developing unarisen wholesome states and maintaining arisen ones; identical with right effort (SN 45.8).

For a pleasant abiding here and now (the jhānas), for knowledge and vision (perception of light), for mindfulness and clear comprehension (knowing feelings, perceptions and thoughts arise and pass), and for the destruction of the effluents (rise and fall of the aggregates) (AN 4.41).

name: The four samayas of the Great Perfection

definitions.definition: Non-existence (med pa), evenness / all-pervasiveness (phyal ba), spontaneous presence (lhun grub) and singularity (gcig pu): commitments kept by realization; the Kunjed Gyalpo speaks of 'samaya with nothing to guard'.

name: The four establishments of mindfulness (cattāro satipaṭṭhānā)

definitions.definition: Contemplation of body, feelings, mind and dhammas, the one-way path for purification and realisation of nibbāna (MN 10:2-3), taught in twenty-one sections.

In MN 118 they are fulfilled by mindfulness of breathing (each tetrad of the sixteen steps is one foundation: body, feelings, mind, dhammas) and, developed, they fulfil the seven awakening factors (MN 118:23-40); a monk community 'devoted to their development' is described at mn118:13.

Contemplating body, feelings, mind and dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief for the world (MN 10); fulfilled by mindfulness of breathing and fulfilling the awakening factors (MN 118); one's own pasture (SN 47.6).

name: The four doctrines of the rivals (samavasaraṇa)

definitions.definition: All non-Jain teachers fall under kriyāvāda (action has fruit; soul exists), akriyāvāda (denial of action, of soul or of its fruit), ajñānavāda (knowledge is useless or impossible) and vinayavāda (salvation by reverence and discipline alone) — 363 views in the later count (180, 84, 67, 32).

notes: See also U33's treatment of the same scheme (trm:samavasarana-vada).

definitions.definition: Action, dharma, great and pledge seals, from the Tattvasaṃgraha's ritual seals to Advayavajra's stages of realization.

name: The four kinds of established tenet (siddhānta)

definitions.definition: Common to all systems, peculiar to one system, implied (adhikaraṇa), provisionally accepted (abhyupagama) (NS 1.1.26–31).

name: The four siddhāntas of the Pāñcarātra

definitions.definition: Mantra-siddhānta (one form predominant), Āgama-siddhānta (four forms), Tantra-siddhānta (nine forms) and Tantrāntara (a four- or three-faced deity).
An old man, a sick man, a dead man and a renunciant, whose sight moves the bodhisatta (Vipassī in DN 14) to go forth.

name: The four stages of awakening and the eight noble persons

definitions.definition: Stream-enterer (three fetters abandoned), once-returner (lust, hatred, delusion attenuated), non-returner (five lower fetters abandoned) and arahant (all ten), each with a path and a fruit — eight noble persons, four pairs (DN 16; MN 64; Ud 5.5); women and men alike can realise all four fruits (Cv 10.1.3).
Stream-enterer to arhat do not think 'I have attained', for nothing is attained (Vajracchedikā 9).

relations.note: the Abhidhamma presentation of path and fruit (U37)

name: Waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): BAU 4.3 analyses this world, the other world, the junction (dream) and the state without desire or dream; ChU 8.7-12 leads Indra through the body, the dream-self and the sleeper to the self; MāU 3-7 names four quarters of the self — vaiśvānara (waking), taijasa (dream), prājña (deep sleep) and the fourth; KU 2.1.4 and AU 1.3.12 (three dwellings, three dreams); MaiU 7.11.

Waking is cognition, dream thought-construct, deep sleep non-discrimination (Śiva Sūtra 1.8-10); the fourth is enjoyed amid them and to be poured into them like oil (1.7, 3.20); spanda never departs in any state (SK 1.3).
Correlated with the breaths: prāṇa/apāna in waking and dream, samāna in sleep, udāna in the fourth, vyāna beyond (ĪPK 3.2.19-20).

The Goddess is Viśva in waking, Taijasa in dream, Prājña in sleep, the fourth, and devoid of all states (LSN 62-63); in inner worship the union of the three states is betel and the fourth is prostration (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).

relations.note: the Māṇḍūkya's scheme; the Śaivas add turyātīta

name: Waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth as forms of Viṣṇu

definitions.definition: Dvaita reads the Māṇḍūkya's four quarters as four forms of the Supreme Self in all beings: Viśva presiding over waking, Taijasa creating dreams in the mind, Prājña lord of deep sleep, and Turīya at the dvādaśānta, attained by the liberated. The soul experiences the states; God governs them.

relations.note: Prājña is the form presiding over deep sleep

name: The states of the afflictions (dormant, attenuated, interrupted, fully active)

definitions.definition: Prasupta (dormant), tanu (attenuated), vicchinna (interrupted), udāra (fully active) (YS 2.4). Vyāsa: dormancy is the seed-state of bare potency awakened by facing a support; attenuation is by the cultivation of the opposite; interruption is acting again and again in this or that form (anger absent at a time of passion); fully active is having gained activity toward an object; he adds a fifth, the burnt-seed (dagdha-bīja) state, in the one of the last body (YBh 2.4).

The afflictions may be dormant, thinned, interrupted or active (2.4); Vyāsa adds a fifth, 'burnt-seed' state, found only in one whose afflictions are exhausted, 'skilled' and in his last body (YBh 2.4).

definitions.definition: Scattered, coming-and-going, clinging and dissolved, with increasing steadiness and bliss; stillness comes from indifference (audāsīnya), not force, culminating in the no-mind state (YŚ 12).

relations.note: Analogous graded states of mind to Vyāsa's five bhūmis (kṣipta … niruddha); the word vikṣipta is shared.

name: The four tenet systems (grub mtha' bzhi)

definitions.definition: Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Cittamātra and Madhyamaka (Svātantrika, Prāsaṅgika), studied as a ladder of increasingly subtle views, each refuting the grosser object of negation of the one below.
Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra and Mādhyamika as a graded sequence (Mokṣākaragupta; later Tibetan grub mtha').

notes: Contribution to the U41 concept; sources: src:precious-garland-of-tenets, src:drubta-chenmo.

name: The four thoughts that turn the mind (blo ldog rnam bzhi)

definitions.definition: Contemplation of the precious human birth, of impermanence and death, of the defects of saṃsāra and of karma, which turn the mind from worldly life to the Dharma; the first part of the preliminaries.
The preliminaries of mind training (Seven Points 1.1): the precious human life, death and impermanence, karma, and the faults of saṃsāra.
The topics of the small and middling scopes that turn the mind from this life and from future lives.
The topics of the impure vision.
The precious human life, death and impermanence, the cause and effect of karma, and the faults of saṃsāra; contemplated first (Jewel Ornament ch.2–6; the common preliminaries).

name: The four transcendent lords of Bön (bde gshegs gtso bo rnam bzhi)

definitions.definition: Satrig Ersang (the mother of wisdom), Shenlha Ökar (the god of compassion / body of perfection), Sangpo Bumtri (the father, creator of existence) and Tönpa Shenrab (the teacher).

notes: Optional (Bön).

name: The four transmissions of Tilopa (bka' babs bzhi)

definitions.definition: Tilopa received the six dharmas from four Indian sources: inner heat from Caryāpa, illusory body and clear light from Nāgārjuna, dream from Lavapa, and intermediate state and transference from Sukhasiddhi (Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa); other Kagyu lists assign them differently (e.g. adding Kukkuripa or the Hevajra/Guhyasamāja/Mahāmāyā/Cakrasaṃvara tantras).

notes: The attribution list is from the local Tōh 2330 (U44's source); variant lists from memory.

definitions.definition: Under a teacher who claims constant omniscience, an oral transmitter, a reasoner, or one dull and eel-wriggling.
Clinging to sensual pleasures, views, rules and observances, and a doctrine of self (SN 12.2; MN 11).

name: The four means (upāya)

definitions.definition: Anupāya (no means: realization by the teacher's word), śāmbhava (thought-free immersion), śākta (contemplation with the mind alone), āṇava (breath, seals, visualization, letters, places); graded by the intensity of grace; liberation is the same whatever the means (MVT 2.21-23; TĀ 1.165-170, chs. 2-5).

notes: The path map itself is pth:kashmir-four-upayas (owned by U51).

definitions.definition: All rival doctrines fall into four assemblies: action, non-action, ignorance, discipline.

Two valid cognitions of the ultimate (of the enumerated and the non-enumerated ultimate) and two of the conventional (of limited, impure vision and of pure vision); pure-vision valid cognition establishes the purity of appearances taught in the tantras.

name: The three Vedas (trayī) and the fourth

definitions.definition: From the Puruṣa sacrifice came the verses, chants, metres and formulas (RV 10.90.9); the ṛc is speech, the yajus mind, the sāman breath (VS 36.1); the older reckoning is the threefold Veda of the śrauta rite, to which the Atharvaveda is added as the fourth in the Purāṇic account of Vyāsa's division.

name: The four vidyādhara levels (rig 'dzin rnam bzhi)

definitions.definition: The fruits of the Mahāyoga path: the matured vidyādhara (mind matured as the deity, body not yet transformed), the vidyādhara with power over life, the mahāmudrā vidyādhara and the spontaneously present vidyādhara, equal to buddhahood.

notes: Mapped as a path in pth:mahayoga-four-vidyadharas.

definitions.definition: Taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the impure as pure and the selfless as self; the afflictions arise in dependence on the errors about pleasant and unpleasant and ignorance ceases with them (MMK 23.1–2, 23.23); Catuḥśataka chs. 1–4 overcome them in turn.

name: The four visions of direct crossing (snang ba bzhi)

definitions.definition: Direct perception of dharmatā; increase of experience; awareness reaching its full measure; exhaustion of phenomena in dharmatā — the stages of direct crossing (restricted practice; only the doctrine is recorded).

relations.note: the final vision can issue in the rainbow body

notes: The path map pth:dzogchen-four-visions is owned by U51.

definitions.definition: Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa (knowledge and strength), Pradyumna (lordship and virility) and Aniruddha (power and splendour), each nonetheless possessing all six qualities.
As reported by Śaṅkara: Vāsudeva the highest Self, Saṅkarṣaṇa the soul, Pradyumna mind, Aniruddha ego-sense — a doctrine of the soul's origination he rejects.

Vāsudeva (all six qualities), Saṅkarṣaṇa (knowledge and strength), Pradyumna (lordship and virility), Aniruddha (power and splendour), with functions in creation, maintenance, dissolution and teaching, and as objects of meditation.
Categorical, distinguishing, by counter-question, by setting aside.

At buddhahood the transformed basis is mirror-like wisdom, on which depend the wisdoms of equality, discernment and accomplishment; in the Cheng weishi lun they are the transformed eighth, seventh, sixth and five sense consciousnesses.

relations.note: consciousness-to-wisdom mapping of the Cheng weishi lun

name: The four wisdoms in the Platform Sūtra

definitions.definition: The eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms — great perfect mirror, equality, wondrous observing, accomplishing what is to be done — which are 'only names without real nature', not apart from the three bodies of one's nature.

members: wisdom accomplishing what is to be done (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna)

relations.note: Yogācāra's four wisdoms read as aspects of the self-nature.

name: The four yogas (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja)

definitions.definition: The haṭha texts' classification of yoga into mantrayoga (lowest), layayoga, haṭhayoga and rājayoga (highest) — first in the Dattātreyayogaśāstra (9), then the Amaraughaprabodha, Śiva Saṃhitā (5.9) and others; the Śiva Saṃhitā assigns them to four grades of aspirant; the Yogabīja and Haṭharatnāvalī call them one 'great yoga'. The DYŚ also says the eight-limbed yoga of Yājñavalkya and the haṭha of Kapila differ in practice, not in fruit.

One yoga divided in practice into four (Yogatattva 19); for practitioners of dull, middling and superior capacity (Varāha 5.10); in the Yogaśikhā four inner stages of one great yoga, each reinterpreted (mantra as reversed haṃsa, haṭha as union of sun and moon, laya as union of knower and supreme, rāja as union of rajas and retas).
Yoga is fourfold — mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja — with haṭha as the means to rājayoga (Amaraughaprabodha).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 7 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

relations.note: the same four yogas are the frame of the Dattātreyayogaśāstra

name: The four yogas of Mahāmudrā

definitions.definition: One-pointedness (rtse gcig), simplicity (spros bral), one taste (ro gcig) and non-meditation (sgom med), each lesser, middling and greater — twelve levels; each marked by realization rather than passing experience.

members: ro gcig (one taste) — lesser, middling, greater

relations.note: correlations with the paths and grounds differ between Kagyu masters (dsp:four-yogas-and-the-grounds)

name: The paths of the Gītā: action, knowledge, meditation and devotion

definitions.definition: The Gītā names two ancient paths, knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas and action for the yogins (3.3), holds them one in result (5.4–5), adds meditation (ch. 6) and devotion (chs. 7–12), and states that some see the self by meditation, some by Sāṃkhya, some by action, and some by worship after hearing (13.24–25). Commentators rank them differently (see dsp:gita-primary-teaching).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Some see the self in themselves by themselves through meditation, others by the yoga of sāṃkhya, others by the yoga of action (13.25); others, not knowing thus, worship after hearing from others and they too cross death (13.26); unswerving bhakti-yoga carries one beyond the guṇas (14.26). The verses set these side by side without ranking them.

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Ch. 12 offers, by capacity, fixing mind and understanding on the Lord (12.8), the yoga of practice (12.9), work for the Lord (12.10) and relinquishing the fruit of all actions (12.11); it then ranks knowledge above practice, meditation above knowledge and relinquishing the fruit of actions above meditation, peace following on relinquishment (12.12).

relations.note: devotion is one of the Gītā's paths and, for the Vaiṣṇava readers, their culmination

Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Mounting to mind-only, not imagining external objects; resting in suchness and passing beyond mind-only; passing beyond the imageless; abiding in the imageless and seeing the Mahāyāna — read by Kamalaśīla as stages of meditation.
Prāthamakalpika, madhubhūmika, prajñājyotis, atikrānta-bhāvanīya; the bhāṣya on 3.51 sets the invitation of the high-station gods before the second and the reflection that follows.

The beginner (prāthamakalpika), the honey-stage yogin (madhubhūmika) with truth-bearing insight, the one whose insight is light (prajñājyotis) who has mastered elements and senses, and the one beyond what is to be cultivated (atikrāntabhāvanīya) whose aim is the mind's dissolution (YBh 3.51).

definitions.definition: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years plus junctions (4,800, 3,600, 2,400, 1,200), dharma declining through them; the means of each age differ (meditation, sacrifice, worship, singing the name).

definitions.definition: Bhīṣma's fourfold dhyāna-yoga; in the first meditation reflection, reasoning and discrimination arise (MBh 12.188.1, 12.188.15), and the persevering sage reaches the happiness of nirvāṇa.
(Buddhist report) Nātaputta's teaching of restraint by all 'waters'.
(Jain account) Pārśva's law of four restraints, differing in form but not aim from Mahāvīra's five vows.
Monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen, together the 'ford' (tīrtha) founded by a Tīrthaṅkara; the Kalpa Sūtra counts Mahāvīra's as 14,000 monks, 36,000 nuns, 159,000 laymen and 318,000 laywomen.

name: The fourteen stages of quality (guṇasthāna)

definitions.definition: Fourteen stages of the soul's purification: wrong view, the taste [of falling], mixed, right view without vows, partial restraint, careless restraint, careful restraint, unprecedented, non-returning gross passion, subtle passion, subsided delusion, destroyed delusion, omniscient with activity, omniscient without activity (Sarvārthasiddhi 1.8; Gommaṭasāra); the Tattvārthasūtra itself gives a ten-stage series of increasing shedding (9.45).
Banārsīdās added a chapter on the guṇasthānas to the Samayasāra Nāṭaka so that the knower of the self also knows the stages of conduct.

notes: The path map itself is pth:jain-fourteen-gunasthanas (owned by U51).

definitions.definition: Destiny, sense, body-type, activity, sex, passion, knowledge, restraint, perception, leśyā, capacity for liberation, right faith, rationality, nourishment — the grid through which the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama examines souls in the fourteen guṇasthānas.

name: The fourteen Pūrvas

definitions.definition: The 'former' texts contained in the Dṛṣṭivāda: Utpāda, Agrāyaṇīya, Vīryapravāda, Astināstipravāda, Jñānapravāda, Satyapravāda, Ātmapravāda, Karmapravāda, Pratyākhyāna, Vidyānupravāda, Kalyāṇa (Avandhya), Prāṇāvāya, Kriyāviśāla and Lokabindusāra; lost after Bhadrabāhu (in meaning, the last four after him; in text, progressively).
Part of the Agrāyaṇīya survives in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and part of the Jñānapravāda in the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

notes: Names and order recalled with moderate confidence.

name: The fourteen root downfalls

definitions.definition: The fourteen breaches that destroy the tantric pledge, to be memorized after consecration (Gurupañcāśikā 49).

members: not relying on the pledge substances

definitions.definition: The four Vedas, six Vedāṅgas, Purāṇa, nyāya, mīmāṃsā and dharmaśāstra (YS 1.3).
Kauṭilya's fourfold division of sciences — investigation (Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Lokāyata), the triple Veda, economics, governance (Arthaśāstra 1.2).

checks.note: YS 1.3 has 'purāṇanyāyamīmāṃsādharmaśāstrāṅgamiśritāḥ | vedāḥ sthānāni vidyānāṃ dharmasya ca caturdaśa'. Kauṭilya's fourfold division was found at Arthaśāstra 1.2.1, 1.2.8 and 1.2.10. definitions.definition: Seven upper worlds - Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svar, Mahar, Janas, Tapas, Satya - and seven lower worlds (the pātālas) within the cosmic egg; the first three (trailokya) are dissolved every night of Brahmā; the yogin rises through them (BhP 2.2.22-31).

name: The creation of beings and the worlds by guṇa

definitions.definition: Creation of beings is fourteenfold: eight divine, five animal, one human (SK 53); the upper worlds abound in sattva, the root in tamas, the middle in rajas, from Brahmā to a blade of grass (SK 54); even there suffering from old age and death is common (SK 55; SS 3.53). The Kramadīpikā names the eight divine classes (daiva, paiśāca, rākṣasa, yākṣa, gāndharva, aindra, prājāpatya, brāhma) and five animal (domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, plants).

With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, neither painful nor pleasant, with purity of mindfulness through equanimity, the body pervaded by the pure bright mind like a man wrapped in white cloth (DN 2); the basis for the direct knowledges and the point from which the Buddha attained final nibbāna (DN 16).
The ultimate beyond the four extremes; clinging to emptiness as a negation is itself an extreme (Gorampa).
Accepted in the sense that the meditative wisdom realising emptiness is free of dualistic appearance and of the elaborations of inherent existence.

relations.note: as the MMK's pacification of elaborations

name: The eight freedoms and ten advantages (dal 'byor)

definitions.definition: A precious human life is free of the eight unfree states (hells, hungry spirits, animals, long-lived gods, barbarians, those with wrong views, where no buddha has come, those with impaired faculties) and has ten advantages, five personal and five circumstantial.

name: Taking the fruit as the path

definitions.definition: The unsurpassed path of the Mahāyāna's essence takes the fruit as the path and abides as the fruit from the beginning (Queen Dohā v69).

name: A full life of a hundred autumns

definitions.definition: The ideal of a full human life: 'may we see, live, hear and speak a hundred autumns' (RV 7.66.16; VS 36.24); the living set a boundary against death and ask for long life (RV 10.18.4); rites for long life (AVŚ 8.1).
The āhitāgni is burned with his own fires and implements (ŚB 12.5.2); a funeral mound is later built (ŚB 13.8); the funeral mantras are collected in TA 6.
Cremation with the Yama hymn, burial of infants, water-offerings, bone-collection, ten days' impurity, the first-year offerings and the uniting with the ancestors (ĀśGS 4.1–6; YS 3.1–2; MDh 5.59–68).

definitions.definition: The Sarvadurgatipariśodhana's maṇḍala rites to purify the dead from rebirth in the lower realms, basis of funerary practice in Nepal and Tibet.
The Buddha who will arise when human life has risen again to eighty thousand years (DN 26).

The medieval and modern monastic lineages — Tapā (1228), Kharatara (1024), Añcala, Pārśvacandra, Tristuti, Upakeśa and others — each with its line of ācāryas (paṭṭāvalī), ritual details and festival calendar.

name: The debates of the eleven gaṇadharas

definitions.definition: Each of the eleven brāhmaṇas who became Mahāvīra's gaṇadharas held a hidden doubt, resolved by Mahāvīra: whether there is a soul (Indrabhūti), karma (Agnibhūti), a soul other than the body (Vāyubhūti), real elements (Vyakta), rebirth in like form (Sudharman), bondage and liberation (Maṇḍika), gods (Mauryaputra), hell-beings (Akampita), merit and demerit (Acalabhrātṛ), another world (Metārya), nirvāṇa (Prabhāsa).

Birch-bark scrolls in Gāndhārī (Kharoṣṭhī) from the 1st c. BCE–3rd c. CE, the oldest Buddhist manuscripts: sūtras, verses, Abhidharma, commentaries, avadānas; the British Library scrolls were found in a pot dedicated to the Dharmaguptakas.

relations.note: the two communities disagree on whether branding is required

definitions.definition: Through the prenatal viṣṇubali the Vaikhānasa is a Vaiṣṇava before birth and does not take the branding initiation.
The five sacraments, beginning with branding, make one a Vaiṣṇava.

The eight rules accepted by Mahāpajāpatī as her ordination: a nun ordained a century bows to a monk ordained that day; no rains without monks; fortnightly asking; invitation and penance before both Saṅghas; ordination by both after two years' training; no abuse of monks; no admonishing of monks (Cv 10.1.4; AN 8.51).

name: Secondary and supreme devotion (gauṇī and parā/mukhyā bhakti)

definitions.definition: Secondary devotion is threefold, by the guṇas or by the motive (the distressed and the others), each earlier kind better; primary devotion is love itself, one though it appears in eleven forms.
Secondary devotion — singing, remembering, worship — is the cause of and leads to supreme devotion (Śāṇḍilya Sūtra, as recalled).

relations.note: gauṇī → parā compares with the Gauḍīya sādhana → bhāva → prema; the Gauḍīya scheme has an intermediate stage the sūtras do not name
the guṇa-grading of secondary devotion is the Bhāgavata's grading (BhP 3.29)

definitions.definition: Mahāmudrā in the sūtra approach (emptiness of the mind as Nāgārjuna taught) and the mantra approach (clear light of great bliss); meditation first on the conventional nature of mind, then on its emptiness; the various Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen instructions are said to converge in one intent.

name: The Gelug monastic curriculum of the five great texts

definitions.definition: After the Collected Topics, Types of Mind and Types of Reasons, monks debate for many years on five subjects: the Perfection of Wisdom (Abhisamayālaṅkāra), Madhyamaka (Madhyamakāvatāra), Pramāṇa (Pramāṇavārttika), Abhidharma (Abhidharmakośa) and Vinaya (Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra), using their college's textbooks; the course ends in the geshe examinations.

notes: Sources: src:bsdus-grwa, src:lorig, src:tarig, src:gelug-yigcha, src:abhisamayalamkara, src:madhyamakavatara, src:pramanavarttika, src:abhidharmakosa, src:vinayasutra-gunaprabha.

definitions.definition: Arising as the deity: dissolving into emptiness, generating the deity from seed syllables, the maṇḍala, the consecration and sealing, with clarity and divine pride; the Tattvasaṃgraha's five abhisaṃbodhis are its model in the yoga tantras.
Reality presencing as the fundamental case: to study the self is to forget the self and be verified by the myriad dharmas.

name: The Goddess's gentle and fierce forms

definitions.definition: One Goddess appears in gentle (saumya) forms — Lalitā, Umā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī — and fierce (ghora) forms — Durgā, Caṇḍikā, Kālī, Cāmuṇḍā; all goddesses and all women are her portions (Devī Māhātmya 11); knowers of the āgamas name her Speech, Padmā or Pārvatī, but she is 'a certain fourth' (SL 98).
Lalitā is the gentle, beautiful queen, but her war-names show fierce powers in her service — Vārāhī, Jvālāmālinī, the Nityās (LSN 25-33).

members: saumya: Lalitā, Umā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Bālā
ghora/ugra: Durgā, Caṇḍikā, Kālī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī

name: The seven means of the yoga of the pot (Gheraṇḍa)

definitions.definition: Purification (by the six acts), firmness (posture), steadiness (mudrā), calm (withdrawal), lightness (breath-control), direct perception of the self (meditation), non-attachment and liberation (samādhi) (GS 1.9–11).

The four destructive (ghātiyā) karmas — knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding, obstructive — obscure the soul's own qualities; their destruction yields omniscience (TS 10.1). The four non-destructive — feeling, lifespan, body-making, status — continue in the living omniscient until death.

name: Teacher, transmission and secrecy in the Gītā and epic

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna, his nature struck by pitiable weakness and his mind bewildered about dharma, asks what is decisively better, declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple (śiṣya) who has taken refuge (prapanna), and asks to be instructed (2.7); the teaching follows from 2.11. Duryodhana tells Droṇa that the opposing army was arrayed by Drupada's son, 'your intelligent disciple' (1.3; Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the epic).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the Lord declared the imperishable yoga to Vivasvat, Vivasvat told it to Manu and Manu to Ikṣvāku (4.1); received thus in succession (paramparā) it was known by the royal sages, and over a long time it was lost here (4.2); the Lord declares the same ancient yoga to Arjuna because he is his devotee and friend, for it is the highest secret (4.3). Knowledge is to be learned from the knowers who have seen the truth, approached with prostration, thorough questioning and service; they will teach it (4.34).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the Lord announces knowledge together with vijñāna, after which nothing further remains to be known (7.2), and declares it again as the most secret (guhyatama) knowledge to Arjuna, who does not cavil (anasūyu) (9.1); it is the royal knowledge and the royal secret, the supreme purifier, directly apprehended, in accord with dharma, very easy to practise and imperishable (9.2); those without faith in this dharma do not reach the Lord (9.3).

The yoga was handed down from Vivasvat to Manu to Ikṣvāku and the royal sages, then lost and taught again (BhG 4.1–3); Arjuna becomes a disciple (2.7); knowledge is learned from seers of truth by prostration, inquiry and service (4.34); it is not to be told to one without austerity or devotion (18.67); Sañjaya heard it by Vyāsa's grace (18.75); after instruction the disciple decides (18.63); Kṛṣṇa cannot repeat it (Anugītā 14.16.11); knowledge may be received even from a śūdra (MBh 12.306.85), yet Vidura, of śūdra birth, defers to Sanatsujāta (5.41.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the teaching on field and knower has been sung by the seers, in the metres and in the brahmasūtra words (13.5); attendance on the teacher is among the dispositions called knowledge (13.8); some worship having heard from others (13.26); the knowledge of the guṇas is announced as the highest, by which all the sages reached perfection (14.1); chapter 15 is called 'this most secret teaching' (15.20).

definitions.definition: The current positions of the planets counted from the natal Moon, 'what is generally used in practice': each planet is good in certain places (the Sun in the 3rd, 6th, 10th; Jupiter in the 2nd, 5th, 7th, 9th; Saturn and Mars in the 3rd and 6th; all in the 11th) and troublesome elsewhere (BS 103.2–4); refined by obstruction-points and by aṣṭakavarga.

name: The Lord as the real agent (hari-kartṛtva)

definitions.definition: The soul's acts are done by Hari's impulsion within it; one performs prescribed duties without desire, remembering Hari as doer and goal, so that all activity of mind, speech and body is his worship — this is 'yoga'.

name: Gods and demons as the mind's own display

definitions.definition: Gods and demons have no existence apart from the mind; as long as there is ego-clinging there are demons, and when it is cut there are none; hope of gods and fear of demons are both cut.

name: The gods as names of the One

definitions.definition: Several hymns hold that the many gods are names or forms of one: 'they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni … the One Being the inspired speak of in many ways' (RV 1.164.46); the poets shape the one bird into many with words (10.114.5); 'great is the one asura-ship of the gods' (3.55); the one name-giver of the gods (10.82.3); 'that is Agni, that the Sun … that brahman' (VS 32.1). Yāska: the one Self of the deity is praised in many ways, the other gods are its limbs (Nirukta 7.4). The liturgy nonetheless addresses each god as a distinct recipient.

relations.note: The names-of-the-One teaching is one aspect of the Saṃhitās' teaching on the One.

notes: The modern labels 'henotheism/kathenotheism' are scholarly metadata and not used here.

name: The fivefold transmission (gojū sōden)

definitions.definition: Jōdo-shū's rite of transmitting the teaching in five stages of texts and oral instruction to monks and lay people, systematised in the Chinzei line (Shōgei).

notes: Structure recalled only in outline; no text read.

definitions.definition: The succession of realized masters — Vajradhara, Tilopa, Nāropa, Marpa, Milarepa, Gampopa and the masters of each school — supplicated as a 'golden rosary' because each is held to have realized the teaching before passing it on.
Those who cannot awaken themselves need a great good friend to show them the nature; yet each must awaken himself ('when deluded the teacher ferries, when awakened one ferries oneself').
The tradition holds Gorakṣa to be deathless and to have appeared in each of the four ages at different places.
The Jain Isibhāsiyāiṃ includes Maṅkhaliputta among the arhat seers and gives him a teaching on the steadfast protector who is not moved.

relations.note: a Jain text keeps a respectful saying of the teacher whose doctrine other Jain texts reject

name: Spiritual lineage (gotra) and the five lineages

definitions.definition: Beings have a lineage for awakening either naturally present or developed; they belong to the disciples', solitary buddhas', bodhisattvas' or undetermined lineage, and some to none (agotra); the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra also says all beings have suchness as their embryo. Faxiang (Kuiji) teaches the five fixed lineages.

relations.note: Tathāgatagarbha teaching: all beings will become buddhas

definitions.definition: Dvaita: liberation comes only by Viṣṇu's grace (his 'choosing'); knowledge and devotion win it; it is graded, and it reaches lower beings through the higher (Vāyu and the gods).
The Lord's aruḷ: he graciously gave the Āḻvār knowledge-and-love free of delusion; the Lord came to Tiruppāṇ and Tirumaṅkai unasked; those who recite the Tiruppāvai receive his grace everywhere.
Devotion is gained chiefly by the grace of great souls or a drop of the Lord's grace; even the company of the great is gained by his grace alone.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self is attained by the one whom it chooses (KU 1.2.23; MuU 3.2.3); 'by the grace of the creator' one sees the Lord (ŚU 3.20; KU 1.2.20 reads 'serenity of the constituents'); favoured by him the goose gains immortality (ŚU 1.6); Śvetāśvatara knew brahman by God's grace (ŚU 6.21); refuge in God (ŚU 6.18).
The saints' company and discernment come only by Rāma's grace; he destroys the sins of ten million births the moment a being turns to him.
As Hari keeps me, so I remain; nothing is achieved by one's own effort.
The Lord raises the lowly by his own mercy; Rām gives to all (Malūkdās); the guru's grace awakens sahaj.
Take me across, O merciful one — I have no boat or fare.

relations.note: without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation
the Gītā's prasāda; same Lord's grace in epic idiom
Tamil aruḷ is also the Śaiva Siddhānta word for Śiva's grace; the Āḻvārs' aruḷ is Tirumāl's — same name, different Lord for each tradition

name: Grace (anugraha) as the Lord's fifth act
notes: U18/U19 record Śiva's five acts; this is the Pāñcarātra contribution.

definitions.definition: Grace is the last of Lakṣmī's (the Lord's) five acts — concealment, creation, maintenance, dissolution, grace.
Aruḷ is Śiva's own power, always with the soul like light with the eye, embodied as the guru; liberation is by grace alone, the soul's effort being itself grace-enabled.
The Lord's grace protects in every danger and 'took me as his own' — the devotee's whole hope.

name: Grace through the hierarchy of souls

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu gives liberation, Vāyu by his permission; liberation, knowledge and their fruits come to the lower by the grace of the higher, not otherwise.

name: Gradation of the manifest self (plant, animal, man)

definitions.definition: The self is increasingly manifest from plants (sap) to animals (thought) to man, who has the most intelligence, knows tomorrow and seeks the immortal through the mortal (AA 2.3.2).

checks.note: AA 2.3.2 has the self increasingly manifest in plants, animals and man. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:aitareya-aranyaka:2.3.2.

name: Graded standpoints: external objects and cognition-only

definitions.definition: Dharmakīrti argues at times as though objects were external (causing images in cognition) and at times from the standpoint of cognition-only, where cognition is non-dual; later commentators (and Tibetan doxographers, who call the school 'Sautrāntika' or 'Yogācāra' accordingly) treat these as successive levels.

notes: Named here with the tradition's own vocabulary (bāhyārtha-naya / vijñapti-naya as used by the commentators); the commentators' labels are recalled.

name: Graded teaching fitted to the hearer

definitions.definition: The Buddhas taught self, no-self and neither (MMK 18.6) and the four statements of 18.8 as graded instruction; like a grammarian teaching the alphabet, the Buddha taught some to avoid evil, some for merit, some based on duality and some the profound non-dual (RĀ 4.94–96); first turn from demerit, then from self, then from all views (CŚ 8.15).

relations.note: the graded teaching grounds the provisional/definitive distinction

name: Graded places of worship by eligibility

definitions.definition: God is in fire for brāhmaṇas, in the heart for the wise, in images for the unawakened, everywhere for the knowers of the self (Kulārṇava 9.44).

name: The grades of Śaiva initiates
notes: Standard in Siddhānta paddhatis (e.g. Somaśambhu); no verse-level teaching recorded in this pass.

definitions.definition: Samayin (after samaya-dīkṣā), putraka (after nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, seeking liberation), sādhaka (consecrated to master a mantra for powers) and ācārya/deśika (consecrated teacher who may initiate and install).
Samayin, putraka, sādhaka (seeker of powers, bubhukṣu) and ācārya; the mumukṣu is liberated at death.

Vyāsa: by the means, nine kinds of yogin — mild, middling, intense means, each with mild, middling or intense ardor (saṃvega) — and further distinctions; the samādhi and its fruit is nearest for the intense (YS 1.21–1.22, YBh 1.20–1.22).

Yogins are of nine kinds — mild, middling or intense in means, each with mild, middling or intense ardor; for the intensely ardent samādhi is near, and nearest for the intense in means and ardor (1.21–22, YBh 1.20–22).

definitions.definition: Persons differ: what is medicine for the gradual is poison for the simultaneous and vice versa; the simultaneous way is for those with prior training, the gradual for beginners (Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa). The Kagyu manuals likewise alternate analytical and resting meditation according to the student.
The Queen Dohā closes with the wish that beings attain mahāmudrā by the gradual and the simultaneous entry; the songs also praise instantaneous liberation (Queen Dohā v8).

The step-by-step path of the suttas: faith and going forth, virtue, sense restraint, mindfulness and clear comprehension, contentment, seclusion, abandoning the hindrances, the four jhānas, the direct knowledges and the destruction of the effluents (DN 2; MN 27; MN 39; MN 107); final knowledge comes by gradual training, not at once (MN 70); the ocean slopes gradually (Ud 5.5).

name: The planets as avatāras of Viṣṇu

definitions.definition: Janārdana takes the form of the planets to give beings the fruits of karma; to destroy the daityas, strengthen the gods and establish dharma, the avatāras were born from the planets: Rāma from the Sun, Kṛṣṇa from the Moon, Narasiṃha from Mars, the Buddha from Mercury, Vāmana from Jupiter, Paraśurāma from Venus, the Tortoise from Saturn, the Boar from Rāhu and the Fish from Ketu (BPHS 2.3–7).
Every planet aspects the seventh house fully and the 3rd/10th, 5th/9th and 4th/8th with one, two and three quarters; Saturn, Jupiter and Mars have full aspect on these respectively (BJ 2.13).

relations.note: Parāśarī planetary aspect vs Jaimini sign-aspect; both are taught side by side in BPHS

name: What the planets signify (kārakatva)

definitions.definition: Each planet signifies parts of the person and world: the Sun the self and father and kingship, the Moon mind and mother, Mars strength and siblings, Mercury speech and learning, Jupiter knowledge, children and teachers, Venus desire and spouse, Saturn sorrow, servants and longevity (BJ 2.1 and later texts).

notes: Beyond BJ 2.1 the list follows common later texts (BPHS 32; Phaladīpikā 2) from memory.

name: Grammar as a path to liberation

definitions.definition: Grammar is nearest to Brahman, the highest austerity, the door to liberation and remedy for the impurities of speech, the first rung of the ladder and the straight royal road (VP 1.11–16); the refinement of words is the attainment of the supreme self (VP 1, verse uncertain); correct usage brings merit (Mahābhāṣya on 6.1.84).

name: The grand divisions of creation (Sant Mat)

definitions.definition: Creation is in three (or four) grand divisions: piṇḍ (physical, the body), aṇḍ (astral), brahmāṇḍ (causal, to Trikuṭī/Daswān Dwār) — Kāl's domain — and above them the purely spiritual Dayāl Deś; spirit, spirit-and-mind, and mind-and-matter.
The mass of doubt raised with the whole body on the huatou; 'great doubt, great awakening'.
Hakuin's great doubt 'as if frozen in a sheet of ice' before the breakthrough.
Bankei (in the Rinzai line) rejects cultivating doubt, saying it trades the buddha-mind for a doubt.

name: The Great Madhyamaka (dbu ma chen po)

definitions.definition: The definitive Madhyamaka of the third wheel, the Maitreya texts, Nāgārjuna's hymns and the Kālacakra, beyond the extremes because conventional phenomena do not truly exist and the ultimate does not not exist.
Kongtrul's summit of the sūtra tenets: other-emptiness Madhyamaka.

notes: The Nyingma (Rongzom, Mipham) use 'Great Madhyamaka' for a Madhyamaka of the union of appearance and emptiness; that usage is not merged here.

name: The great matter of birth and death

definitions.definition: Birth and death is the great matter, impermanence swift; merit cannot save the deluded self-nature.

name: The Great Perfection (rdzogs pa chen po)

definitions.definition: Everything is already complete in the nature of mind; there is nothing to add by meditation, samaya or path; whatever appears is one in suchness and to be left unaltered.
The unsurpassed way of Bön, the same name for Bön's highest teaching.

name: Great purity and equality (dag mnyam chen po)

definitions.definition: All phenomena are primordially pure as deities and pure lands and equal as emptiness; purity and equality are inseparable (the 'superior two truths' of Mahāyoga). The Guhyagarbha shows the aggregates as the buddhas and all as unborn in being born.

relations.note: the Mahāyoga 'superior' two truths add purity of appearance to the sūtra two truths

definitions.definition: When the ground-appearances arise, recognizing them as self-display is liberation; not recognizing them, awareness takes them as other, dualistic grasping arises and the realms unfold — 'one ground, two paths'.
In the Guhyagarbha: from the sugata-essence one's own conceptual karma emanates bodies, abodes and sufferings; grasping I and mine ties knots in space.

name: The ground (gzhi) in the Great Perfection

definitions.definition: The primordial state prior to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa: essence primordially pure, nature spontaneously present, compassion all-pervading; neither buddha nor being, it becomes one or the other by recognition or non-recognition of its display.
The ground of the ground-path-fruit scheme: buddha-nature, present in all beings.

relations.note: the ground is the buddha-nature of the sūtras seen from the Atiyoga standpoint
the ground is not the saṃsāric all-base

name: Ground, path and fruition in Mahāmudrā

definitions.definition: The ground of purification is mind itself, clarity-emptiness; the purifier is the vajra yoga of Mahāmudrā; the purified are adventitious stains; the fruit is the stainless dharmakāya.
Nāropa: the one mind is 'known as ground, path and fruit' and as 'the three tantras of cause, method and fruit'.

name: The two exegetical schools of the Guhyasamāja

definitions.definition: The Ārya school (Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, Nāgabodhi, Candrakīrti; Akṣobhya maṇḍala; five stages) and the Jñānapāda school (Buddhajñānapāda; Mañjuvajra maṇḍala; the Mukhāgama).

name: The classification of Purāṇas by the guṇas

definitions.definition: Matsya 53.68-69: sāttvika Purāṇas glorify Hari, rājasa Brahmā, tāmasa Agni and Śiva, mixed ones Sarasvatī and the ancestors. The Padma (as cited) assigns six Purāṇas to each guṇa; the Garuḍa's Brahmakāṇḍa gives a different, graded list. Śaiva texts counter with lists in which most Purāṇas glorify Śiva (not checked here).

definitions.definition: Particularized (viśeṣa: five elements, ten faculties, mind), unparticularized (aviśeṣa: five tanmātras and I-am-ness alone), mere mark (liṅga-mātra: the great principle) and unmarked (aliṅga: the primal, pradhāna) (YS 2.19, YBh 2.19).

The guṇas exist at four levels: the particularized (sixteen: five elements, ten senses and mind), the unparticularized (five tanmātras and I-am-ness), the mere mark (mahat) and the unmarked (pradhāna) (2.19, YBh 2.19); subtlety of objects ends in the unmarked (1.45).
