name: The guṇa-classification of knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness

definitions.definition: Knowledge, action, agent, intellect (buddhi), steadfastness (dhṛti) and happiness are each sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (BhG 18.19–39) — sāttvic knowledge seeing one imperishable being in all, sāttvic happiness 'poison at first, nectar at the end'.
Secondary devotion is graded by the guṇas; the one who crosses māyā goes beyond the three guṇas; love itself is free of the guṇas.

name: The qualities and the elements in Sant teaching

definitions.definition: Māyā binds with the noose of the three qualities (guṇa), from which the three gods arise; the body is woven of the five elements, which return to their source at death.
The three guṇas and five tattvas originate in the region of Brahm (Trikuṭī) and belong to Kāl's creation.

name: The guṇas as the doers of action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: No one remains without acting, being made to act by the guṇas born of prakṛti (3.5); all actions are done by the guṇas, and the one deluded by ahaṃkāra thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27); the knower of the truth about guṇas and actions thinks 'the guṇas move among the guṇas' and is not attached (3.28); those deluded by the guṇas are attached to their workings (3.29); beings follow their own nature (3.33).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The seer who sees no doer other than the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains the Lord's state (14.19); the one beyond the guṇas stands firm, knowing only that 'the guṇas are operating' (14.23). Actions are done by prakṛti alone (13.30).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The Moon, Sun and Jupiter are of sattva, Mercury and Venus of rajas, Mars and Saturn of tamas (BJ 2.7); a person's predominant guṇa shows in conduct — compassion and devotion (sattva), arts, sacrifice and passion (rajas), deceit, sloth and anger (tamas) — with seven mixed kinds (BS 68.8–9); BPHS 77 gives the fruits of the guṇas.

relations.note: jyotiṣa assigns the three guṇas of the common (Sāṃkhya) teaching to the planets

name: Going beyond the guṇas (guṇātīta)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Having gone beyond these three guṇas, bound up with the body's arising (deha-samudbhava), the embodied one, freed from birth, death, old age and pain, attains immortality (14.20). Asked for the marks, the conduct and the means (14.21), Kṛṣṇa describes one who neither hates illumination, activity and delusion when present nor longs for them when gone; who sits as one indifferent, unshaken, knowing only that 'the guṇas are operating'; who is the same in pain and pleasure, toward clod, stone and gold, in blame and praise, honour and dishonour, toward friend and foe, and has given up all undertakings (14.22-14.25). The means named is serving the Lord with unswerving bhakti-yoga, by which one goes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for becoming brahman (14.26); seeing no doer but the guṇas and knowing what is beyond them leads to the Lord's state (14.19).

relations.note: immortality (14.20); fitness for becoming brahman (14.26)
the state of one no longer bound by the guṇas (14.5, 14.20)

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.

notes: New concept (extractor B) for the Gītā's portrait of the one gone beyond the guṇas, the counterpart of cpt:sthitaprajna (2.54–72) and cpt:qualities-of-the-devotee (12.13–20); extractor A records it through trm:gunatita and phn:marks-of-gunatita. The text does not call this state liberation while living; compare cpt:liberation-while-living (U05), whose Gītā definition names 'the one beyond the guṇas'.

name: The guru in the minor Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The guru removes darkness ('gu' darkness, 'ru' its remover) and is the supreme Brahman (Advayatāraka); he is Hari (Brahmavidyā), Brahmā-Viṣṇu-Sadāśiva (Yogaśikhā 5); his word breaks the pot that hides the lamp; without his grace the natural state is hard to reach (Varāha 2.76).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Knowledge is to be learnt from 'the knowers who see the truth' (jñāninas tattvadarśinaḥ), approached with prostration, thorough questioning and service; they will instruct it (4.34). The teaching itself is presented as passed down in succession from Kṛṣṇa (4.1–3). The word guru does not occur in these verses.
Without a guru even Viṭṭhala's companion Nāmdev was 'unbaked'; the guru (Nivṛtti, Visobā, Janārdana) shows God everywhere; the saint is mother (māulī).
The guru's foot-dust cleans the mirror of the mind; the true guru is the helmsman of the human boat.
The Dāsbodh sets out the marks of the true guru and disciple.
The guru is one of the four real things, with the name, God and the devotees.

definitions.definition: The teacher is the means (Śiva Sūtra 2.6); the revelation of the Śiva Sūtra and its lineage (Kṣemarāja; Bhāskara, Vārttika 1.3-9).
Secrecy and qualification: the teaching is for those devoted to the teacher, heroic and thought-free (VBT 157-160); the lineage from Śrīkaṇṭha and Durvāsas (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-122).

name: The guru as the deity present in human form

definitions.definition: No god is beyond the guru and no mantra beyond his sandals; the guru is to be tested and so is the disciple.
The innate is known only from the true guru; without a guru there is no supreme siddhi.
Only one who has a guru drinks the nectar in the upturned well of the sky.
The true guru (satguru) gives the Name and is honoured above God as the means to him.
To souls who know only human forms Śiva appears in human form as the guru (as a hunter uses a decoy deer), or teaches from within to the more advanced; the guru is to be served as Śiva.
In initiation the ācārya becomes Śiva by ritual identification; Śiva's power acts through him.

relations.note: shared idea of the guru as the divine

definitions.definition: Devotion is the head of meditation: realization of Mahāmudrā comes through the guru's blessing received with devotion; the guru is regarded as Vajradhara; the qualified guru has the three trainings and experience; Marpa's prostration to the deity rather than the guru is told as a warning; seeing mind directly is 'the guru's kindness'.

name: Teacher, lineage and initiation in Dvaita

definitions.definition: Knowledge descends from Nārāyaṇa (as Vyāsa, author of the Brahmasūtras) through Madhva and the maṭha pontiffs; the qualified disciple gains the supreme knowledge from the teacher's grace, hears the commentaries and reflects on them with companions; the ācārya initiates the prepared devotee into Hari's worship; renunciants receive the praṇava and new names; debate (vāda) between teacher and disciple serves the truth.

One initiating guru and many instructing gurus; the Lord within (caitya-guru); the guru is to be honoured as Kṛṣṇa's representative; qualification is knowledge of Kṛṣṇa, not birth; guru and disciple should examine each other.
Initiation is given by the ācārya's descendants (the Gosvāmī houses); the disciple's relation is to the Lord through the guru's family.

name: The guru in the haṭha texts

definitions.definition: Haṭha is learned 'by the path taught by the guru' (HYP 1.14, 2.1); kuṇḍalinī wakes by the guru's grace (3.2); viparītakaraṇī is known from the guru's instruction 'not from ten million śāstras' (3.78–79); the one who gives traditional instruction in the mudrās is the Lord himself (3.129); knowledge, liberation and the natural state are hard to obtain without a true guru's compassion (4.8–9); knowledge from the guru's mouth is potent, otherwise fruitless (SS 3.11); samādhi comes through the guru's grace and devotion to him (GS 7.1).

relations.note: the same teaching seen in the texts and in the living Nāth order (U21)
relations.standpoint: haṭha manuals vs the Nāth order

name: The guru in the Kaula way

definitions.definition: The guru is father, mother and Maheśvara, and protects when Śiva is angry (Kulārṇava 12.49); rare is the guru who removes suffering rather than wealth (13.104-108); the supreme guru cuts the fetters, gives initiation by piercing and takes up the paśu (13.79), removes the eight fetters and knows the body's lotuses (13.88-94); 'gu' is darkness and 'ru' its remover (17.7).
The vajra master is inseparable from Vajradhara (Gurupañcāśikā 22), greater than the Buddha in kindness (Pañcakrama 4.2); attainment follows him; to despise him is to despise all buddhas.
The innate is found only from the true guru's mouth; the guru is the boat, the physician, the sun of gnosis.
Viśvapāda, Vicitrapāda, Śvetapāda, Bhaṭṭapāda, Macchendrapāda and others are worshipped by name; Bhairava explains these names as his own (KJN 9.6–9; 16.11–21).

Three forms of the one Śiva met by the devotee: the guru who initiates (Śiva himself present, 11.19–21), the liṅga he gives, and the jaṅgama — the moving Śivayogin whose sight, touch and worship sanctify (11.37–43); the first three of the eight shields.

The guru is Brahman, not other than the Self; 'gu' darkness, 'ru' its remover; the roots of meditation, worship, mantra and liberation are the guru's form, feet, word and grace; the teaching is secret, for the devoted only.
The avadhūta's many teachers; the self as its own teacher.
The guru is the means to God and is honoured above God for that reason (guru and Govind).
The guru is truth; the Kartā is present in the Mahāśay.

name: Haṃsa — the swan / the self as breath-mantra

definitions.definition: The inner self as the 'swan' that moves with the breath (haṃ-sa), reversed as so'ham 'I am He'; meditated as a bird with fire and moon as wings; its knowledge (haṃsa-vidyā) is called the only means to liberation (Brahmavidyā) and the inner sacrifice (Pāśupatabrahma); also the name of the third kind of renouncer.

relations.note: Viewed as a mantra the haṃsa is the ajapā-gāyatrī.

definitions.definition: The haṃsa dwells in the bodies of breathing beings as the knot of prāṇa and apāna and is repeated 21,600 times a day, called so 'ham (Yogaviṣaya 28–29).
'Haṃsa haṃsa' is to be said always in the body (KJN 13.2); the jīva is the haṃsa (6.5) moving up and down and dissolving at the end of the twelve (17.18).
The sixteen names 'hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare, hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa hare hare' taught by Brahmā to Nārada as the means of crossing Kali, bound by no rule (Kalisantaraṇa).

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu is supreme over all — full of qualities, free of defects, beyond the perishable and the imperishable; this is the great purport of all scripture, and 'Brahman' and all names primarily denote him.

name: Haribhadra's eight views of yoga

definitions.definition: Mitrā, tārā, balā, dīprā, sthirā, kāntā, prabhā, parā (YDS 13), with light like straw-fire, cow-dung fire, wood fire, lamp, gem, star, sun and moon (15), correlated with the eight limbs (yama … samādhi), the removal of eight faults (fatigue, anxiety, distraction, agitation, confusion, delight in other, pain, attachment) and the rise of eight qualities (non-aversion, desire to know, desire to hear, hearing, understanding, reflection, right apprehension, right practice) (16); the first four are unstable and precede the breaking of the knot, the last four are stable.

relations.note: Haribhadra's own correlation of each view with one of Patañjali's eight limbs (YDS 16).
Sthirā (right view after the knot is broken) corresponds to the fourth guṇasthāna; the first four views precede it (commentarial).

notes: Path map: pth:haribhadra-eight-drstis (owned by U51).

name: The five yogas of the Yogabindu

definitions.definition: Adhyātma, bhāvanā, dhyāna, samatā and vṛttisaṃkṣaya, each better than the last because it joins the soul to liberation (Yogabindu 31).

relations.note: Vṛttisaṃkṣaya echoes Patañjali's cessation of vṛttis but denotes the cessation of the soul's karmically-born activities leading to omniscience.

name: Yoga by desire, by scripture and by capacity

definitions.definition: Icchā-yoga (wish with carelessness), śāstra-yoga (diligent practice according to scripture) and sāmarthya-yoga (by capacity, beyond scripture), the last twofold — renunciation of dharmas and renunciation of yoga (YDS).

name: The identity of Hari and Hara

definitions.definition: Passages that make Viṣṇu and Śiva one: the Kūrma's Īśvara Gītā, Hari as all the gods in Gajendra's rescue, Śambhu as the foremost Vaiṣṇava (BhP 12.13.16); set against sectarian passages that subordinate one to the other.
Narahari Sonār found Śiva in Viṭṭhala.

relations.note: unity vs Śiva's superiority to Brahmā and Viṣṇu

name: Haṭha and rājayoga need each other

definitions.definition: Without haṭha rājayoga does not succeed and without rājayoga haṭha does not; both are practised to completion (HYP 2.76; SS 5.181); those who practise only haṭha without knowing rājayoga labour without fruit (HYP 4.79); all haṭha and laya methods are for rājayoga (4.103); tattva is the seed, haṭha the field, detachment the water (4.104).

relations.note: the Amanaska rejects laborious haṭha methods as means to the mindless state; see dsp:amanaska-critique-of-hatha

name: Health as the root of the four aims

definitions.definition: Health is the supreme root of dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa; disease robs it and life (Ca Sū 1.15); life is the means of dharma, wealth and happiness (AHS Sū 1.2).

relations.note: Rasa Śāstra makes the undecaying body itself the condition of liberation

definitions.definition: Instructions passed orally 'from mouth to ear', originating with Vajradhara and the ḍākinīs, through Tilopa, Nāropa and Marpa; sealed for thirteen generations (Karṇatantravajrapada); later branches: the Rechung, Ngendzong and Dakpo hearing lineages.

name: The heart and the senses in the Āḻvār hymns

definitions.definition: The heart-mind (neñcu) is exhorted as a companion to worship and rise, melts with love, and holds the Lord within it; the five senses (aivar) are thieves to be put under guard; the mind of the love-sick girl knows no sleep.

name: The heart as seat of inner seeing

definitions.definition: The seers searched in the heart (RV 10.129.4); a fixed light is set in the heart (6.9.5–6); the wise see with heart and mind (10.177.1); Vena saw the highest hidden in secret (VS 32.8); the mind is heart-seated (34.6).

name: The heart-base (hadaya-vatthu)

definitions.definition: Mind-element and mind-consciousness-element occur in dependence on a material base; the canon (Paṭṭhāna) leaves it unnamed and the Dhammasaṅgaṇī does not list it; the commentaries and manuals identify it as the heart, within the blood in the heart cavity.

notes: The Theravāda's only 'seat of mind' teaching; no channel/cakra anatomy is taught in the Abhidhamma (contrast the borān and Dhammakāya bodily bases).

name: The petals of the heart lotus and the moods

definitions.definition: The mind's dispositions follow the petal of the eight-petalled heart lotus on which the jīva rests — virtue, sleep, cruelty, sin, play, movement, love, charity — with the centre as dispassion or all-knowing (Haṃsa; Dhyānabindu).

definitions.definition: Cakrasaṃvara (Heruka) in union with Vajravārāhī: the deity couple embodying bliss and emptiness, at the centre of the maṇḍala of the twenty-four sites.
Nine possible relations of a reason to similar and dissimilar cases, of which two are valid, two contrary and five inconclusive.

name: The pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa)

definitions.definition: Five in the sūtra: inconclusive, contradictory, prakaraṇasama, sādhyasama, kālātīta (NS 1.2.4–9).
Five in the Navya list: inconclusive (three kinds), contradictory, counterbalanced, unestablished (three kinds), sublated; the adjunct (upādhi) makes a reason unestablished as to pervasion.

notes: The correspondence of the old and new lists (arrows) is the usual later reading, not stated in the sūtra.

definitions.definition: Objects are higher than the senses, mind higher than objects, intellect higher than mind, the great self higher than intellect, the unmanifest higher than the great, the person higher than the unmanifest; there is nothing higher (KU 1.3.10-11; restated at 2.3.7-8 with sattva).

relations.note: the top of the ladder is the puruṣa

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (KU 1.3.10-11). It rests on 3 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Hindu and Turk fight over Rām and Rahīm and neither knows the secret; the mullā shouts as if God were deaf, the paṇḍit worships stones; the one Lord is in every body.
Hindu and Muslim are two hands, two eyes of one body; the body is mosque and temple.
Temple and mosque block the path; rosary and tasbīh make no real difference.

The Golden Germ who arose in the beginning as the one lord of what exists, giver of self and strength, whose shadow is immortality and death; born from the great waters; named Prajāpati (RV 10.121); Prajāpati moves unborn in the womb and is born in many ways (VS 31.19).

relations.note: One of the Saṃhitās' creation accounts.

definitions.definition: Love (hita) is the first principle: the divine pair are its two forms, and it is also the path and the goal; Hita Harivaṃśa embodies it.

name: The three aspects of the internal power: hlādinī, sandhinī, saṃvit

definitions.definition: Pleasure, existence and knowledge aspects of the Lord's own power (VP 1.12.69); the essence of hlādinī is love, whose summit is Rādhā.

name: The homonymous tantric authors

definitions.definition: The tradition identifies the tantric Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva and Candrakīrti with the Madhyamaka masters; the scholarly account places the tantric works c. 9th–10th c. and treats the authors as distinct.

members: the tantric Nāgārjuna and the Madhyamaka Nāgārjuna
the tantric Āryadeva (Karṇaripa) and the Madhyamaka Āryadeva
the tantric Candrakīrti and the Madhyamaka Candrakīrti
notes: Ids: tch:nagarjuna-siddha, tch:aryadeva-tantric, tch:candrakirti-tantric (tantric) vs. tch:nagarjuna, tch:aryadeva, tch:candrakirti (Madhyamaka, U40).

name: The chart reveals the ripening of past karma

definitions.definition: The horā reveals the ripening of the karma, good and bad, earned in a former birth (BJ 1.3); the science shows it as a lamp shows objects in the dark (LJ 1.3); Janārdana in the form of the planets gives beings the fruits of their karma (BPHS 2.3); sins of former births appear as childlessness and other afflictions (BPHS 83).

relations.note: the karma 'earned in a former birth' now ripening, which the chart shows, corresponds to what Vedānta calls prārabdha; the jyotiṣa texts do not use the threefold classification themselves

definitions.definition: All disorders are finally hot or cold; mkhris pa and blood disorders are hot, rlung and bad kan cold.

name: Groupings of houses

definitions.definition: Angles (kendra: 1, 4, 7, 10), succedents (paṇaphara: 2, 5, 8, 11) and cadents (āpoklima: 3, 6, 9, 12); trines (1, 5, 9); increasing houses (upacaya: 3, 6, 10, 11); bad houses (duḥsthāna: 6, 8, 12); death-dealing houses (2 and 7) (BJ 1.15–18; BPHS 44). Later practitioners also group the houses by the four aims of life (dharma 1-5-9, artha 2-6-10, kāma 3-7-11, mokṣa 4-8-12).

notes: The four-aims grouping is modern-popular; classical source not located.

definitions.definition: No renunciation is required: grinding, gardening, potting, trading and service become worship when joined to the name; the Lord comes to the house.
Worldly life (prapañca) is to be lived with vigilance and effort alongside the highest aim.

relations.note: the Mahānubhāva ideal is renunciation and wandering

name: How the one appears as many (the three theories)

definitions.definition: Three explanatory theories of the jīva and Īśvara: limitation (avaccheda, Bhāmatī), reflection (pratibimba, Vivaraṇa) and semblance (ābhāsa, Sureśvara); the tradition treats them as alternative methods (prakriyā) converging on identity.

name: The heart and the space within it

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self dwells in the heart, smaller than a grain and greater than the worlds (ChU 3.14.3); the small space in the lotus of the heart contains heaven and earth (ChU 8.1.1-3); the heart has five openings (ChU 3.13); from it spread the channels (KU 2.3.16; PrU 3.6); the person made of mind in the heart (BAU 5.6; TU 1.6).
The Heart of Bhairava, seed of the universe (Parātrīśikā 24); the heart-space of meditation (VBT 49).
Consciousness as vibrancy is 'the Heart of the Supreme' (ĪPK 1.5.14).

queries: prepared segments: ChU 3.14.3, ChU 8.1.1-3, ChU 3.13, KU 2.3.16, PrU 3.6, BĀU 5.6, TU 1.6
checks.note: All 7 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 3.14.3; ChU 8.1.1-3; ChU 3.13; KU 2.3.16; PrU 3.6; BĀU 5.6; TU 1.6). It rests on 7 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: The heart as seat of consciousness and ojas

definitions.definition: The heart ('mahat', 'artha') holds consciousness, the self with its qualities, mind and its objects and the supreme ojas, and is the root of the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.3-14); the seat of consciousness and abode of ojas (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 5.49); Bhela places citta in the heart and manas between head and palate.

HYP 1.5–8 names some thirty-three great Siddhas, beginning with Ādinātha, Matsyendra, Śābara, Ānandabhairava, Cauraṅgī, Mīna, Gorakṣa and Virūpākṣa and ending with Kāpālika, who by haṭha broke the staff of time and roam the universe (1.9). Several names recur in the Buddhist list of eighty-four Mahāsiddhas and in Nāth lists (see U21, U49).

relations.note: overlapping lists, not identical; U49 compares the Nāth and Buddhist lists

name: The icchantika and the question of universal buddhahood

definitions.definition: The Mahāparinirvāṇa moves from excluding icchantikas to affirming their buddha-nature and refusing a fixed icchantika (four alternatives).
The Laṅkāvatāra: two kinds of icchantika; five lineages including agotra.
A basis for the powers and for the destruction of the effluents (SN 51.20; DN 26).
Two related things established neither as one nor as different are not established at all: goer and going (MMK 2.18–21), fire and fuel (10.1), self and aggregates (18.1).

name: The similes of illusion, dream and mirage

definitions.definition: Arising, abiding and ceasing, and afflictions, actions, bodies, agents and fruits are like an illusion, a dream, a city of gandharvas or a mirage (MMK 7.34; 17.33; 23.8); empty words negate like one magical man stopping another (VV 23).
The self-consecration body of wind and mind, 'like a rainbow in the sky', the conventional truth, obtained only by the guru's grace; joined with clear light in union.
Seeing everything as illusion, dream, mirror-image and painted Vajrasattva (Tilopa, from Nāgārjuna).

Forms of the formless are imagined for the sake of worshippers (Rāmapūrvatāpanī 1.7); yogins see Śiva in the Self, images are for the ignorant (Darśana 4.59); for the renouncer image-worship leads to rebirth (Maitreya 2.26).

checks.note: Darśana 4.59 is located: śivam ātmani paśyanti pratimāsu na yoginaḥ | ajñānāṃ bhāvanārthāya pratimāḥ parikalpitāḥ. All 3 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: The eternal, unslayable embodied one (dehin / śarīrin)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The embodied one is eternal, indestructible, immeasurable, unborn, everlasting and primeval; it neither slays nor is slain and is not slain when the body is slain; weapons, fire, water and wind do not affect it; it is all-pervading, stable, unmoving, unmanifest, unthinkable and unchangeable; it passes into another body as through the ages of life and as one changes clothes; hence it is not to be grieved for (2.12–30).
Bhagavad Gītā 14.5: the guṇas bind the imperishable embodied one (dehinam avyayam) in the body; 14.20: the embodied one who goes beyond them attains the immortal.

relations.note: The embodied one is unchanged while it passes from body to body.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Merger: probably the same as the skeleton's broader cpt:the-self (BhG 2.11–30 etc.); both extractors used this id, so it is kept; flagged for the de-duplication pass. The text of 2.11–30 names it dehin or śarīrin, or refers to it by pronoun (ayam, enam); it does not use the word ātman there, so 'ātman' is not listed among its names (the commentators' identification is recorded as a partial equivalence on trm:dehin).

definitions.definition: The bodhisattva's liberation in which Sumeru enters a mustard seed and the four oceans a pore without change — a display that shows the non-obstruction of dharmas.
Perception begins as a bare, non-conceptual awareness like an infant's, followed by determinate cognition of the thing with its universal etc.; both are perception.
Indra, strengthened by soma, slays the serpent Vṛtra who enclosed the waters, releasing them and becoming king of what moves and rests (RV 1.32).

name: No embodied being can remain without action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: No one ever remains even for a moment without acting; all are made to act by the guṇas born of prakṛti (3.5); even the maintenance of the body needs action (3.8); even the person of knowledge acts according to his nature (3.33).
All dharmas are by nature inexpressible; words attach to designations and imagined natures, not to the thing's own nature, which is the object of non-conceptual cognition.
The particular is inexpressible; words and concepts reach only exclusions.
Awakening must be confirmed by a teacher; awakening without a teacher is 'natural heterodoxy' (Xuance to Yongjia).
Inka shōmei, the certification of completed training.

name: The inner meaning of the Kula substances

definitions.definition: The Kulārṇava gives the rationale: bliss is the form of Brahman residing in the body and the substance manifests it; wine is Śakti, meat Śiva, the enjoyer Bhairava, and the bliss of their union is liberation (5.79-80); those devoted to inner worship are dearest (5.70).
The Tattva circle is truly performed only by those in whom 'all is Brahman' arises (Mahānirvāṇa 8.208); inner worship offers the mind, breath and senses in place of outer substances (5.143-146).

notes: Later yogic readings (e.g. wine as the nectar from the crown, maithuna as the union of Kuṇḍalinī with Śiva) are widespread in Bengal and Nepal commentaries; not anchored here to a specific verse.

definitions.definition: Rites internalized: the haṃsa as fire and praṇava as thread (Pāśupatabrahma), eating as oblation to the prāṇas (Prāṇāgnihotra), the world offered into the fire of knowledge (Sannyāsa 2.100), the renouncer's five inner sacrifices (Śāṭyāyanīya 12–17).

definitions.definition: The true sacrifice is austerity burning karma: austerity the fire, the soul the altar, right exertion the ladle, the body the fuel, restraint the peace-formula (Harikeśa, Uttarādhyayana 12).

relations.note: the Vedic sacrifice re-read as inner discipline
rejects the animal sacrifice in favour of austerity

name: The inner topknot and sacred thread

definitions.definition: Knowledge is the topknot and the Self, Brahman or praṇava the sacred thread of the renouncer, replacing the outer ones (Jābāla 5; Brahma; Paramahaṃsa; Parabrahma; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.77–85).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 8 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: 'One thinks he has drunk soma when they crush the plant; the soma the brahmins know, of that no one eats' (RV 10.85.3); only the 'cooked' by tapas attain Soma's filter (9.83.1).

relations.note: An instance of the ritual substance understood beyond its outer form.

definitions.definition: Solstices, equinoxes, new moon and eclipses are the movements of breath between iḍā and piṅgalā and between the base and the head (Darśana 4.39–47; Śāṇḍilya 1.15).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 2 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: The sacred places are located within: Vārāṇasī between brows and nose, Prayāga in the heart, etc. (Darśana 4.48–59; Jābāla 2); the suṣumnā is the supreme tīrtha (Yogaśikhā 6); wandering to outer tīrthas is 'lowest of the low' (Maitreya 2.21).
The Gaṅgā is in the pure mind's bowl; the fish is thirsty in water while the Lord is in one's own house.
The original Mecca is the human body.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 4 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: Nanyang Huizhong: the insentient preach; one hears when free of the feelings of consciousness; Dongshan's inquiry into this led to his awakening.

name: The inseparability of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa ('khor 'das dbyer med)

definitions.definition: The Sakya view of the Lamdre: the causal continuum, the all-base as union of clarity and emptiness, holds saṃsāra and nirvāṇa inseparably; when obscured it appears as saṃsāra, when purified as nirvāṇa.

relations.note: MMK 25.19–20 as the sūtra counterpart

name: The insight knowledges (vipassanā-ñāṇa)

definitions.definition: The Visuddhimagga's purification by knowledge and vision of the way consists of eight knowledges and conformity; the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha lists ten insight knowledges (adding comprehension); the later tradition counts sixteen by adding the discernment of mentality-materiality, of conditions, change-of-lineage, path, fruit and reviewing.
The stages as they unfold in noting practice, described in The Progress of Insight.

notes: The numbered list of sixteen is later than the Visuddhimagga (correction to the unit brief); path map pth:sixteen-insight-knowledges is owned by U51.

name: The internalization of ritual (in its Saṃhitā beginnings)

definitions.definition: Already in the Saṃhitās the rite is referred beyond its outward form: the gods sacrificed the sacrifice (RV 10.90.16); the soma the brahmins know none eats (10.85.3); the first act of the fire-altar is the yoking of mind (VS 11.1); honouring a guest is itself the sacrifice (AVŚ 9.6); mind is the one in which the seven-hotṛ sacrifice is spread (VS 34.4).

notes: The fuller internalized rites (e.g. the prāṇāgnihotra of the Āraṇyakas) are U02's.

name: Transgressive practice and its inner reading, across families

definitions.definition: The Kula substances (wine, meat and the rest) are declared Śakti and Śiva and their union bliss; inner worship is dearer than outer; without the samaya discipline the wilful fall.
The haṭha texts quote the Kaula saying about eating cow's flesh and drinking the liquor of the immortals and read it as the tongue turned back into the skull and the nectar that flows there.
The Yoginī tantras give an intentional language of substitute words for substances, places and acts, not to be revealed to the unconsecrated; conduct in the cremation ground is for the qualified.

relations.note: the Kaula also teaches that the realized stands beyond rule; the inner reading is not the only one the texts give

notes: Summary level only; no ritual procedures are recorded (restricted material).

name: Transgressive language given a yogic sense

definitions.definition: The HYP takes Kaula-sounding injunctions — eat cow's flesh, drink the liquor of the immortals, seize the young widow between Gaṅgā and Yamunā, worship the liṅga neither by day nor by night — and explains them as yogic acts: the tongue entering the palate, the moon's nectar, kuṇḍalinī between iḍā and piṅgalā, restraint of sun and moon (3.47–49, 3.109–110, 4.42).

Already in the Brāhmaṇas the rite is carried into the person: the self-sacrificer knows each rite builds his own self (ŚB 11.2.6.13); fires are built of mind and knowledge (ŚB 10.5.3); the Agnihotra is 'truth offered in faith' (ŚB 11.3.1.4); feeding brāhmaṇas is 'offering into Brahman' (ĀśGS 1.1.2).
In the Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads: the inner Agnihotra of speech and breath (KU 2.5), the breath-oblations at meals (ChU 5.19–24), the sacrifice in the body (Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
The renouncer deposits the sacred fires in himself (MDh 6.38) and the true self-sacrificer sees the self in all beings (MDh 12.91).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.25–30 carries the language of the fire-offering over to inner disciplines: the senses offered into the fires of restraint, sense objects into the fires of the senses, the activities of senses and breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint kindled by knowledge, prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa.

relations.note: outer rite and inner rite are two poles of one doctrine

definitions.definition: All cognitions are valid of themselves; a capacity not present in a thing cannot be given by another; validity is set aside only by a cognition of the object's being otherwise or knowledge of a defect in the cause — neither of which can arise for the authorless Veda.
Validity is known by inferring the cognition from the knownness it produces.
Validity is known with the self-luminous cognition itself.
Validity is known by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) of the cognition (as reported by Gaṅgeśa).

relations.note: intrinsic validity plus the absence of an author makes the Veda unassailable

name: The balance of the two deeds (iruviṉaiyoppu)

definitions.definition: When good and bad karma come to balance and the soul regards both alike, and āṇava is ripe, grace descends and the guru appears.

name: The personal liṅga worn on the body (iṣṭaliṅga)

definitions.definition: Śiva himself, given by the guru at initiation as a small liṅga worn on the body for life and worshipped on the palm; Śiva abides in it from the moment of initiation, so it needs no invocation; the outer liṅga is to be worn 'knowing it is of that same form' as the inner.
The body bearing the liṅga is itself the temple: the moving (jaṅgama) against the fixed (sthāvara) shrine.

name: Iṣṭāpūrta, merit of sacrifice and gift

definitions.definition: The merit of what one has sacrificed and given, with which the dead are reunited in the highest heaven (RV 10.14.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 8.28, 9.20–21: the merit declared for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts wins heaven, is exhausted, and brings return to the mortal world; the yogin who knows the teaching passes beyond all such merit to the supreme primal place.

relations.note: Merit rejoins the dead in Yama's heaven.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The word iṣṭāpūrta does not occur in the Gītā; 8.28 speaks of the fruit of merit (puṇya-phala) declared for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts, and 9.20–21 of the merit that wins heaven and is spent.

definitions.definition: Classical Sāṃkhya posits no established Īśvara: the SK does not mention one; Gauḍapāda argues that the attributeless Īśvara could not produce what has guṇas (on SK 61); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds that Īśvara is not established (1.92–99), that karma, not a Lord, yields fruit (5.2–12), and that effects depend on ahaṃkāra, not Īśvara (6.64) — yet it admits emergent lords: the one absorbed in prakṛti who becomes all-knowing and all-doing (3.55–57). Vijñānabhikṣu salutes the Lord (Sāṃkhyasāra 1.1.1).

Īśvara is a special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), the teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by the praṇava (1.27). He is ever free and ever Lord, his pre-eminence resting on excellent sattva, without equal or superior; his purpose is compassion for beings (YBh 1.24–25). Devotion to him brings samādhi near (1.23, 2.45); he favours the devotee by mere intention (YBh 1.23). He is not the material of the world. Vijñānabhikṣu makes knowledge of the Supreme Lord the swift cause of liberation (YV 1.51).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord' (Īśa 1); the lord of all, controller of all (BAU 4.4.22; MāU 6); the one God, Rudra-Śiva, the māyin, lord of lords, whose power is innate, who gives grace and frees from fetters (ŚU 1.10, 3.2, 4.10, 6.7-9); Indra/prāṇa as lord of the world who makes one do good or bad (KauU 3.9).

Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati: no means of knowledge reaches him, a bodiless being cannot will creation, compassion would create only happiness, and purposeless action is unintelligible; later Bhāṭṭas dedicate dharma to Īśvara/Govinda.
No Īśvara directs dharma and adharma or moves atoms; fruits arise from dharma and adharma with their circumstances.
The Brahma Sūtra reports Jaimini's view that dharma itself gives the fruit.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Kṛṣṇa is unborn, of imperishable self and lord of beings, coming into being by his own māyā (4.6); he responds to people as they resort to him (4.11); he made the fourfold class-order yet is the imperishable non-doer (4.13); actions do not stain him and he has no longing for their fruit (4.14); he is the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, great lord of all worlds and friend of all beings (5.29); he is seen everywhere and everything in him (6.30). Whether the 'lord' (prabhu, vibhu) of 5.14–15, who creates no agency and takes on no one's merit or sin, is the supreme Lord or the embodied self is disputed by commentators.

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord is unborn, without beginning, the great lord of the world (10.3); the beginning of the gods and great seers, whose origin they do not know (10.2); from him alone arise all the states of beings (10.4–5), and the seven great seers and the Manus, sharing his being (mad-bhāva), were born of mind (10.6); he is the origin of all, from whom everything proceeds (10.8), the seed of all beings without whom nothing moving or unmoving could exist (10.39); he stands supporting the whole world with a single portion (10.42); he alone knows himself by himself (10.15); Arjuna praises him as father, object of worship and weightiest teacher of the world, with none equal (11.43), who pervades all and is therefore all (11.40).

relations.note: differs from liberated puruṣas in never having been bound

definitions.definition: Brahman associated with (or reflected in) māyā: omniscient, omnipotent creator and ruler, giver of fruits of action, object of devotion; his lordship depends on adjuncts and is real at the empirical level.
The prototype (bimba) consciousness whose reflection is the jīva.

name: Īśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha and the transmission of Yoga

definitions.definition: Īśvara is the teacher even of the ancients (1.26); the first knower out of compassion taught the doctrine to Āsuri through a created mind (YBh 1.25). Commentators read 'anuśāsana' (1.1) as Patañjali's re-teaching of yoga first taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and give the lineage Pitāmaha — Śeṣa (Patañjali) — Vyāsa — Vācaspati and Vijñānabhikṣu. In the stages of saṃyama 'yoga itself is the teacher' (YBh 3.6).
Bhagavad Gītā 9.9–10: the acts of sending forth beings do not bind the Lord, who sits as if indifferent, unattached to them; prakṛti gives birth to the moving and unmoving with him as overseer.
The Lord produces the effect as he wills, all at once or in sequence, depending neither on karma nor on the soul; karma bears fruit only when favoured by his will.
Rejected: a Lord who distributes unequal lots independently would be partial; the Lord's creation depends on beings' karma (BS 2.1.34), and a merely efficient Lord is inconsistent (BS 2.2.37).

name: The Lord's play as the ground of creation

definitions.definition: The Lord's activity is play: in play he produces, favours and conceals the effect; the teacher's activity is for grace.

A distinct self with qualities — free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness; with merit, knowledge and concentration; with eightfold lordship — who assists human effort and makes it fruitful, sets karma and the elements in motion, is like a reliable person and a father to beings (NS 4.1.19–21; NBh 4.1.21); the all-knowing maker proved by inference (NK 5.1; Gaṅgeśa); worshipped by all schools under different names (NK stabaka 1).
Maheśvara, by whose will creation and dissolution occur; saluted as the cause at the start of the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha. The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra itself does not name Īśvara.
The one omniscient supreme self with eternal cognition, desire and effort, author of the Veda, whose will fixes word-meanings (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Yoga's Īśvara is a special puruṣa who is not the maker of the world; Nyāya's Īśvara is the efficient cause.

definitions.definition: The world is real, established by perception, scripture ('viśvaṃ satyam') and above all the witness, whose deliverances are never sublated; the Advaita definitions of falsity and inferences to it fail.
Since 'that' (omniscient Lord) and 'thou' (limited self) conflict in their direct meanings, the contradictory elements are dropped and pure consciousness retained, as in 'this is that Devadatta'.

name: The Jain brāhmaṇa and householder rites

definitions.definition: Bharata made the vow-keeping laity who would not tread on sprouts into brāhmaṇas, gave them the sacred thread as a sign of their vows and the life-cycle rites (kriyā) — a Jain counterpart of the Brahmanical saṃskāras.
The true brāhmaṇa is made by conduct, not birth (Uttarādhyayana 25).

relations.note: both make varṇa depend on conduct or occupation rather than birth alone

name: The councils (vācanā) of the Jain canon

definitions.definition: Pāṭaliputra (after the twelve-year famine, c. 160 years after the nirvāṇa, with Sthūlabhadra); Mathurā under Skandila and, at the same time, Valabhī under Nāgārjuna (c. 827–840 years after); Valabhī under Devarddhigaṇi (980 or 993 years after, 453 or 466 CE), where the canon was written down and the recensions reconciled.
The Digambaras do not accept these councils as preserving the authentic Aṅgas.

name: Death, lifespan-binding and rebirth in Jainism

definitions.definition: The lifespan karma for the next life is bound once during the present life; at death the soul passes in transit to the destiny so fixed; the lifespans of the spontaneously born and those in their last body cannot be cut short (TS 2.25–30, 2.53, 8.10). The soul-colouring (leśyā) at death is said to accompany rebirth (Śvetāmbara canon, recalled).
Signs foretelling the time of death are described so that the practitioner can prepare (YŚ 5).

Niryukti (Prakrit verse, ascribed to Bhadrabāhu), bhāṣya (Prakrit verse, e.g. Jinabhadra, Saṅghadāsa), cūrṇi (Prakrit-Sanskrit prose, e.g. Jinadāsa), and ṭīkā or vṛtti (Sanskrit: Haribhadra, Śīlāṅka, Śāntisūri, Abhayadeva, Malayagiri); with the Aṅgas these form the 'five-limbed' (pañcāṅgī) scripture of the Mūrtipūjakas, which the Sthānakavāsīs reject beyond the root texts.

name: Jain mantra and its practice

definitions.definition: The Namaskāra mantra is held eternal and the essence of the scriptures; its shorter forms (16, 6, 5, 4, 2, 1 syllables — e.g. 'a-si-ā-u-sā', 'arhaṃ', 'oṃ' analysed as the five initials) are recited and meditated on by the teacher's instruction (Dravyasaṃgraha 49; YŚ 8). Word-based meditation places letters on lotuses in the body. Protective hymns (Uvasaggaharaṃ, Bhaktāmara, Kalyāṇamandira, Ṛṣimaṇḍala) are recited with associated yantras and mantras.
The Sūrimantra, given orally to ācāryas at installation, and the Vardhamāna-vidyā; worship of the Siddhacakra (nine padas).
Mantra manuals of the goddesses Padmāvatī and Jvālāmālinī (Malliṣeṇa, Indranandi) for protection and worldly ends; the Jñānārṇava condemns using mantra and meditation to harm others.

notes: Restricted material (rites for worldly ends, secret mantras): summary only.

name: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga's review of rival doctrines

definitions.definition: Book 1 ch. 1 reviews in turn the five-element view, the one-self view, soul-is-body, the non-agent self, the self-as-sixth, the Buddhist momentary aggregates, destiny, ignorance, the doctrine of intention and the creation views, answering each; Book 2 continues with the lotus parable and Ārdraka's debates.
The Arhat speaks the meaning (artha); the gaṇadharas compose it as sūtras; the scripture so formed is in meaning beginningless and eternal, re-proclaimed by every Tīrthaṅkara.
The Digambaras add that the Jina's teaching issues as the divine sound (divyadhvani), which the gaṇadharas render.

relations.note: unlike the authorless Veda of the Mīmāṃsakas, Jain scripture has a knowing speaker, the omniscient

name: The divisions of the Jain community

definitions.definition: The main division into Śvetāmbara and Digambara (with the extinct Yāpanīya between them), turning on monastic nudity, women's liberation, the omniscient's eating, the canon and details of Mahāvīra's life; within the Śvetāmbaras, the image-worshipping Mūrtipūjakas and the aniconic Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs; within the Digambaras, the Bīsapantha, Terāpantha and Tāraṇapantha.
The Digambaras arose from Śivabhūti's Boṭika schism, 609 years after the nirvāṇa.
The Śvetāmbaras arose from monks who stayed in the north during Bhadrabāhu's famine and adopted clothing.

members: Digambara (Bīsapantha, Terāpantha, Tāraṇapantha, Kānjī Svāmī movement)

definitions.definition: Sound is a mode of matter (TS 5.24), not eternal; speech is produced from the linguistic class of matter; scripture is śruta-jñāna grounded in the omniscient's teaching; the Tīrthaṅkara's divine sound (divyadhvani) is understood by all beings in their own tongues. Words refer by name, representation, potentiality and actuality (TS 1.5).

relations.note: Against the Mīmāṃsā doctrine of eternal sound and an authorless Veda.

definitions.definition: The Tattvārthasūtra's seven realities — soul, non-soul, inflow, bondage, stopping, shedding, liberation — whose right understanding is right view (TS 1.2, 1.4); the Śvetāmbara canon and Kundakunda count nine categories by adding merit and demerit.
The nine realities (nava tattva): jīva, ajīva, puṇya, pāpa, āsrava, saṃvara, nirjarā, bandha, mokṣa (Navatattvaprakaraṇa; Haribhadra's Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya).

relations.note: Belief in the realities is the content of right view (TS 1.2).

name: Teacher, lineage and transmission in Jainism

definitions.definition: The teaching descends from the omniscient Tīrthaṅkara through the gaṇadharas and the lineage of ācāryas; initiation (dīkṣā) with hair-plucking and the great vows; study under the teacher (vācanā); confession and expiation before the teacher; the teacher adapts instruction to the student; the ācārya receives the secret Sūrimantra at installation (Śvetāmbara).

Haribhadra: conventional yoga is serving the teacher and hearing scripture according to capacity (Yogaśataka 3–4); Hemacandra adds what is 'established by experience' to what was learned from scripture and teacher (YŚ 12.1).

name: The Jain wheel of time

definitions.definition: Time is beginningless; in Bharata and Airāvata a descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī) and an ascending one (utsarpiṇī) of six periods each follow one another endlessly; twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras appear in the third and fourth periods; we live in the fifth period of the descending half (TS 3.27–28). Durations are measured in pit- and ocean-measures down to the instant (samaya).

Time turns without beginning in descending (avasarpiṇī) and ascending (utsarpiṇī) halves of six ages each; at the end of the third age of the descending half the wish-fulfilling trees fail, the patriarchs (kulakara) and then Ṛṣabha teach the arts of civilization, and twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras appear in the third and fourth ages.

relations.note: A cyclic scheme of decline and ascent like the four yugas, but with six periods in each half and no creation or dissolution of the world.

notes: Contribution from the canon and purāṇas; the systematic cosmology is U35's.

name: Jain views of the other darśanas

definitions.definition: Every rival doctrine is a standpoint taken as absolute (Sanmati 3.47); the Jina's word is the union of the partial views (Sanmati 3.69); the Jain doctrine alone, accepting all standpoints, is not partisan (Anyayogavyavacchedikā 30). Polemical works refute other schools; doxographies present them without polemic (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya).

Haribhadra: no partiality for Mahāvīra, no hatred for Kapila — accept whatever is reasoned (Lokatattvanirṇaya 38); the goal is one under many names (YDS 129–130); Ānandaghana: the six darśanas are the limbs of the Jina (Covīsī 21).

notes: Relevant to principles P2 and P3; the Jain tradition does not thereby accept that the other darśanas are equally true.

definitions.definition: Concentric continents and oceans, each double the last, around round Jambūdvīpa with Meru at its navel; its seven regions (Bharata … Airāvata) divided by six ranges; humans live only within the Mānuṣottara range (2.5 continents); lands of action (Bharata, Airāvata, Videha) and lands of enjoyment (TS 3.7–39).

Many fall ill at once through vitiated air, water, land and season; the root is adharma, whose source is prajñāparādha — unrighteous rulers, war and curses; remedies are purification, rejuvenation, truth, compassion, giving, worship, good conduct and good company (Ca Vi 3.3-23).

name: What words denote: universal or substance

definitions.definition: Vājapyāyana: the universal; Vyāḍi: the individual substance; Patañjali accepts both; Bhartṛhari shows that both finally denote Being (sattā) / the Real, which is Brahman (Mahābhāṣya on P 1.2.64; VP 3.1–2).

Offspring of unions across classes form further birth-groups (jāti) — 'with the grain' (anuloma) or 'against the grain' (pratiloma) — each with its occupation; lineages may rise or fall in status over seven generations of marriage (MDh 10.5–65).

checks.note: MDh 10.5–65 (anuloma/pratiloma groups) and 10.64–65 (rise over seven generations) were found; MDh 10.24 gives the causes of saṅkara. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:manusmrti:10.64-65.

name: The six impediments to a universal (jātibādhaka)

definitions.definition: Uniqueness of the individual, equivalence of extension, cross-division, infinite regress, loss of nature, lack of relation (Udayana).

name: The six topics of the Jewel Ornament

definitions.definition: Cause (buddha-nature), basis (precious human life), condition (spiritual friend), method (instructions), result (the kāyas), activity (non-conceptual benefit of beings).

Consecrated images of the Jinas are worshipped by laity with material offerings and by all with inner worship; the image is the Jina 'placed' (sthāpanā) and a support for recalling his qualities, not a grace-giver; the canon shows gods and Draupadī worshipping Jina images.
Image worship is practised (the Bīsapantha with fresh offerings, the Terāpantha with dry, non-living offerings only).
Rejected: the thirty-two Āgamas contain no injunction to it, and worship with water, flowers and lamps harms living beings; devotion is to the Jina's qualities and to living mendicants.
Rejected likewise.
Rejected; the shrines keep scriptures instead of images.

name: The two modes of mendicant life

definitions.definition: The Jinakalpa — solitary, naked or nearly equipment-less, of extreme rigour, for those of the strongest constitution and scriptural learning — and the Sthavirakalpa — life in the community with minimal clothing and equipment; the first ended after Jambū, the second is the valid mode now.
The Digambaras recognize no such lapse: nudity remains the only mode of full renunciation.

name: Jinen hōni (naturalness by the working of the vow)

definitions.definition: Being made so of itself by the vow, without calculation; the formless supreme Buddha is jinen; Amida is the means to know it; 'no working is true working'.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): being enters the elements 'with this living self' (ChU 6.3.2); life does not die (ChU 6.11.3); the bird that eats the fruit and grieves beside the Lord (MuU 3.1.1-2; ŚU 4.6-7); the jīva as a hair-tip part, fit for infinity (ŚU 5.9); the elemental self bound by karma (MaiU 3.1-2).

Eternal, atomic, self-luminous as 'I', a knower with attributive consciousness, an agent dependent on the Lord, an enjoyer, essentially his servant (śeṣa), a mode of Brahman; countless, and remaining distinct in liberation.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The Lord's eternal portion 'having become the living being' (jīva-bhūta) in the world of the living draws the senses with the mind as sixth (15.7); as master (īśvara) of the body it takes them with it when it obtains a body and when it departs from one, as the wind carries scents from their seat (15.8); presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste, smell and the mind it partakes of objects (15.9). The deluded do not see it departing, staying or enjoying, accompanied by the guṇas; those with the eye of knowledge see it, and striving yogins see it established in themselves (15.10–11).

Dvaita: each soul is eternal, sentient, atomic, dependent, a reflection of God, different from God, from matter and from every other soul, with an innate and unalterable fitness; its identity with Brahman is denied as contrary to experience and scripture.
Bhagavad Gītā 7.5: the Lord's higher nature 'has become the living being' (jīvabhūtā) and upholds the world.

definitions.definition: The individual self is consciousness conditioned by the inner organ (and ignorance): agent, enjoyer and transmigrant through adjuncts, in truth Brahman; explained by limitation, reflection or semblance.

name: The soul as a part (aṃśa) of Brahman

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: 'A portion (aṃśa) of me indeed, eternal, having become the living being (jīva-bhūta) in the world of the living' draws to itself the senses with the mind as the sixth, which abide in prakṛti (15.7). The verse says 'of me' (the speaker, Kṛṣṇa), not 'of brahman'; the commentators divide on the sense of 'portion' (an apparent part, a real part as mode, a separated part; dsp:bhagavad-gita-jiva-as-amsa).
A part delimited by real adjuncts.
A naturally distinct part and power, dependent on the Lord.
A spark-like part of Brahman with bliss concealed.
A separated part (vibhinnāṃśa) of the marginal power.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Chs. 13–15 contribution, from extractor A's entry (cpt:jiva-as-part-of-brahman) and extractor B's new cpt:jiva-as-amsa (mapped here: reuse of the data/ id). B's account of the living being's activity in 15.8–11 is recorded under cpt:jiva.

name: The soul as the Lord's marginal power, his eternal servant

definitions.definition: The soul is Kṛṣṇa's marginal (taṭasthā) power, eternally his servant, able to turn toward the internal power (devotion) or the external (māyā).

The body is the temple and the jīva is Sadāśiva; bound by fetters or karma it is jīva, freed it is Sadāśiva — as paddy and husked rice (Kulārṇava 9.41-43); bound by the eight fetters one is a paśu, freed one is Maheśvara (13.90-91).

The jīva is supreme, partless, eternal, called the lord and the all-pervading Śiva; it is haṃsa, mind, breath and intellect; called jīva while in the body, supreme Śiva once the body is left (KJN 6.4–7); the jīva is the person, the haṃsa, Śiva (17.33).

The soul is an eternal, formless, conscious substance marked by cognitive activity (upayoga); agent and enjoyer of its karma; co-extensive with its body, contracting and expanding like a lamp's light; souls are innumerable and each distinct; worldly or liberated (TS 2.8–10, 5.3, 5.16; Dravyasaṃgraha 2).
By the ultimate standpoint the soul is the pure knower, not the doer of material karma; 'the soul is other, matter is other' is the whole of reality (Iṣṭopadeśa 50; Samayasāra 38).

The Ācārāṅga's starting point: one who knows 'my soul is reborn' believes in soul, world, karma and action; the soul is eternal as substance and non-eternal as modes; the self is the doer and undoer of its own happiness and suffering, its own friend and foe.

relations.note: Unlike the Sāṃkhya-Yoga puruṣa, the Jain soul is an agent, changes in its modes and is body-sized.

name: Samādhi as the union of the individual and supreme self

definitions.definition: The haṭha texts describe the self in samādhi as the union of jīvātman and paramātman (HYP 4.7; DYŚ 82, 114), 'separating mind from body and uniting it with the supreme self' (GS 7.3) — 'I am Brahman, being-consciousness-bliss' (GS 7.4); the Śiva Saṃhitā's one eternal knowledge (1.1). The metaphysics is borrowed from Advaita; the practice texts do not argue it.

A Siddhar enters samādhi and is enclosed alive, remaining present at the shrine; the eighteen have such shrines in the popular list (Palani, Chidambaram, Tiruvaṇṇāmalai…). Recorded as belief; no practice details.

By nature souls are of three classes: fit for liberation (gods, sages, ancestors, rulers, the best humans), ever-transmigrating (middling humans), and fit for blinding darkness (daityas, rākṣasas, piśācas, the lowest humans). The texts state this plainly; souls of the third class reach darkness especially through hatred of Hari.

relations.note: the three classes are the broadest division of the gradation

name: The jīva-portion and the supreme-Self portion

definitions.definition: Every being contains two portions, of the individual soul and of the supreme Self; in the planets, the gods' powers and the full avatāras (Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Narasiṃha, Varāha) the supreme-Self portion predominates, in men the jīva-portion; the avatāras come forth from the planets and return into them, and beings finally merge into the unmanifest (BPHS 1.21–24; 2.1–10).
The devotee who has let the self die while alive fears nothing and is served by Hari; the warrior who cuts off his own head wins the field; burn your own house and come with me.
Dying daily in meditation by withdrawing to the eye centre.
The love-practice of the one who has died while alive.
Steady wisdom apprehending identity; virtues arising without effort; no licence for misconduct; living for others' good; unbroken realization in activity and absorption.

After perfect knowledge, virtue and the rest cease to cause, but the knower remains embodied through the momentum of impressions, like a potter's wheel (SK 67); knowledge burns future karma like burnt seeds (Gauḍapāda). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra names the one liberated while living and grounds it in the need for liberated teachers — otherwise the blind would lead the blind (3.78–84).

Vyāsa: with the cloud of dharma the afflictions are uprooted and karmic residues destroyed; 'when afflictions and karma cease, the wise one is liberated while living', since error is the cause of becoming (YBh 4.30); one whose afflictions are exhausted has no karma for a future birth (YBh 2.12) and is 'in his last body' (YBh 2.4).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the word is later, but the texts say the mortal 'attains brahman here' when all desires in the heart are released (BAU 4.4.7; KU 2.3.14), that the knots are cut 'here' (KU 2.3.15; MuU 2.2.8), that the best knower of brahman delights in the self yet is active (MuU 3.1.4), and 'if one has known it here, there is truth' (Kena 2.5).

In the minor Upaniṣads: the state of one who, knowing the Self, is freed while the body continues on the momentum of prārabdha; marked by freedom from 'I' and 'mine', from vāsanā and from the mind's properties (Muktikā 2; Varāha 4; Tejobindu 4); the dissolution of mind 'with form'.

In the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha: the seventh stage; outwardly engaged, inwardly cool; mind 'dead' (manonāśa); one acts as custom requires, like one half-asleep. In the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā: the liberated is neither distracted nor absorbed, the same wherever he is. In the Rāma Gītā: living out prārabdha free of ego until merging.
The perfected one does not notice the body, which lives on while its karma lasts; though in the body he is not in it.
The destruction of ignorance, completion of human aims, is the state of liberation while living.
On knowledge, past karma is destroyed and future karma does not cling, but the body continues till prārabdha is exhausted; the knower is free while living.

Promised by knowledge of the cakra-code (YH 1.86) and of the worship-code (YH 3.1), by three muhūrtas of the Bhāvanā contemplation, and to the steadfast practitioner wherever he dies (PKS 10.82); it is release from the eight bonds (Dīpikā); the Rudrayāmala places it at the end of the ladder of births (Bhāskararāya).

In the haṭha texts a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4): the yogin in samādhi, not devoured by time nor bound by karma, knowing neither heat nor cold, 'remaining in waking as if asleep, without breath', is liberated (4.106–112); nirguṇa meditation and samādhi make one jīvanmukta, who may leave the body at will or roam with powers (DYŚ 111–118); SS 3.67 speaks of the calm jīvanmukta at niṣpatti.
Rejected: while the body remains, karma remains; the knower or surrendered is assured of release but released only at death.
Denied by Bhāskara.
Redefined as the state of one who serves Hari in all conditions.

In living liberation the mind is the seed and the spotless; the yogī standing on the path of death should know this and practise; by this path comes steadiness (AmŚ 55–59); jīvanmukti is a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); 'die the death Gorakh died' (Gorakh Bānī).
Śiva in a human body plays on earth; his touch liberates (KJN 17.37–41).
After grace and knowledge the body continues by prārabdha; the jīvanmukta acts as Śiva's servant among devotees, untouched by deeds.
The initiate liberated by nirvāṇa-dīkṣā is released at death; the body continues until prārabdha is exhausted.
The accomplished (siddha) abides in the Self, free of doubt, while acting rightly in the world.

name: Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) in Kashmir Śaivism

definitions.definition: Firm realization of oneness with consciousness while the body is experienced (PH 16); the liberated sees all as his own glory and regards the knowable as not different from himself (ĪPK 4.12-13).
The liberated acts without taint, his conduct free of rule, his worship inner (Paramārthasāra 61, 69-80).

relations.note: shared name; the Kashmir Śaivas add that the world is known as one's own real manifestation

definitions.definition: The perfected one does not notice whether the body stands or sits, as a drunk his cloth; the body lives on until its karma is spent, but he does not re-enter the dream (BhP 3.28.37-38); Keśidhvaja acts without attachment and is freed.

name: Liberation in life in a stable body (Rasa)

definitions.definition: Knowledge of identity with Śiva in an ageless, deathless body (Rasārṇava 1.8); liberation after death is unseen and 'meaningless' (1.9-13); liberation from knowledge, knowledge from practice, practice in a stable body (Rasahṛdaya 1.10); siddhas have attained it in mercurial bodies (SDS 11-12).

relations.note: Advaita's jīvanmukti depends on knowledge, not on bodily immortality

name: The lamp of knowledge and the gem of devotion

definitions.definition: Knowledge is a lamp prepared with great labour and easily blown out by māyā and the powers; devotion is a self-luminous gem needing neither oil nor wick; both end suffering, but the path of knowledge is a sword's edge and devotion melts the Lord at once.

name: Combination of knowledge and works (jñāna-karma-samuccaya)

definitions.definition: Liberation is attained by knowledge of Brahman combined with the lifelong performance of one's prescribed duties; works are not abandoned upon knowledge.

notes: Opposed by Śaṅkara and Sureśvara, for whom knowledge alone liberates (see dsp:jnana-karma-samuccaya).

name: Limbs of yoga redefined as knowledge

definitions.definition: In the Tejobindu, Triśikhi, Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa and Darśana each limb is given an inner Vedāntic meaning — e.g. prāṇāyāma as seeing all as Brahman, āsana as indifference, dhyāna as 'so'ham' — alongside or instead of the bodily practice.

name: Knownness (jñātatā) and the inference of cognition

definitions.definition: Cognition is not perceived; it produces a property of manifestness in the object, from which it is inferred.

name: Jyotiṣa as the eye of the Veda

definitions.definition: The Vedas exist for the sacrifices, which depend on times; so the science of time is the eye (cakṣus, nayana) of the Veda and stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas like a peacock's crest; Parāśara calls his horā the 'eye of the Veda heard from Brahmā's mouth', says none can know past and future without it, and warns that one who condemns it goes to hell.

relations.note: jyotiṣa is one of the six limbs

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: the science is not man-made — the Sun taught it to Maya through a portion of himself, the same śāstra told to the seers in every age with only the time-difference changing (SS 1.2–9); Āryabhaṭa raised it from the ocean of knowledge by Brahmā's grace (Āryabhaṭīya 4.49); Parāśara tells it as heard from Brahmā (BPHS 1.6); later lists name eighteen promulgators.

name: The three branches of jyotiṣa (skandha-traya)

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa rests on three branches: gaṇita or siddhānta (computation of the planets' motions), horā (nativities) and saṃhitā (omens and mundane matters); Parāśara calls the horā the best of the three; Varāhamihira composed works in all three.
Kerala authors speak of six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga): nativity (jātaka), sphere (gola), omens (nimitta), interrogation (praśna), electional timing (muhūrta) and computation (gaṇita).

notes: The six-limb list is from memory (Praśna Mārga ch. 1) and is low confidence.

name: Teacher, pupil and the handing down of jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa passes from teacher to pupil, often father to son (Varāhamihira from Ādityadāsa; Gaṇeśa from Keśava; Rāma and Nīlakaṇṭha from Ananta), and is given only to the calm, devoted, truthful believer — never to another's pupil, an unbeliever or a cheat (BPHS 1.7–8). The secret chapter is withheld from none who is very devoted (SS 12.11). Authors bow to the former promulgators and do not discard their works (BJ 28.10; BS 105.2); counterfeiting the text destroys merit and life (Āryabhaṭīya 4.50); even foreign Yavanas who master it are honoured like seers (BS 2.14).

name: The ultimate as named in jyotiṣa texts

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa texts name the ultimate in their invocations and cosmogonies rather than teach it: Brahman, unthinkable and unmanifest, without and with qualities (SS 1.1); Vāsudeva the supreme Brahman, from whom Saṅkarṣaṇa, the golden egg and Aniruddha-as-Sun arise (SS 12.12–21); Ka, one and many, the supreme Brahman (Āryabhaṭīya 1.1); Viṣṇu, one and unmanifest, with his three powers (BPHS 1.9–20); the Sun as self of all and door of liberation (Yogayātrā 1.1; BJ 1.1); for the Bṛhat Saṃhitā the ultimate cause is disputed among Kapila, Kaṇāda and those who say time, nature or karma (BS 1.7).

A yoga is a configuration giving a definite fruit; the Yavanas counted 1,800 nābhasa yogas (BJ 12.1); the main families are royal (rāja), wealth (dhana), poverty (daridra), the five great men, lunar yogas, nābhasa yogas, renunciation (pravrajyā) and misfortune (ariṣṭa).

name: Kabīr's comings in the four ages

definitions.definition: Sat Sukṛt (Satya), Munīndra (Tretā), Karuṇāmay (Dvāpara), Kabīr (Kali).

name: The Kabīr Panth cosmogony (Sat Puruṣ and Kāl Nirañjan)

definitions.definition: The Sat Puruṣ emanated sixteen sons; Nirañjan by austerity won the three worlds and Ādyā, begot Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś, and as Kāl binds souls; Kabīr comes in every age to lead souls back to Satlok.
Bījak: from light, sound and one woman came Hari, Brahmā and Tripurāri, and the world of forms.

relations.note: Inverts the Purāṇic account by making the creator a fallen power.

name: The six Kadam treatises (bka' gdams gzhung drug)

definitions.definition: Bodhisattvabhūmi, Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra, Śikṣāsamuccaya, Bodhicaryāvatāra, Jātakamālā and Udānavarga — the texts studied in Potowa's textual tradition.

The two living forms of the vidyā: Kādi, after Manmatha (Kāmarāja), taught by the Tantrarāja ('Kādimata') and encoded in SL 32; Hādi, after Lopāmudrā. The Bhāvanā Upaniṣad teaches its contemplation 'according to the Kādi and Hādi doctrines'; the Bahvṛca Upaniṣad names the Kādi, Hādi and Sādi vidyās; the twelve upāsakas each have their own form.

name: The Eight Herukas / Eight Pronouncements (bka' brgyad)

definitions.definition: The sādhana section of Mahāyoga: five transcendent (Mañjuśrī-Yamāntaka body, Hayagrīva speech, Yangdag mind, Chemchok-Amṛta qualities, Vajrakīla activity) and three mundane (Mamo, Jigten Chötö, Möpa Drakngak) heruka practices, entrusted to eight Indian vidyādharas and given by Padmasambhava to his disciples.
The soul's fulfilment is service to the Lord with Śrī, done for his pleasure alone, here and eternally in Vaikuṇṭha; its highest form is service to his devotees.
'At all times without break, staying close, we must do faultless service' (TVM 3.3.1); the drum the girls asked for is to be his kin and serve him alone for seven times seven births (TP 29).

Kaivalya, as the text states it: the isolation that follows when dispassion is reached even towards the discrimination-born powers and the seeds of defect are destroyed (3.50); when sattva and puruṣa are equal in purity (3.55); the return to source of the guṇas empty of puruṣa's purpose, or the establishment of the power of consciousness in its own form (4.34).

The goal: when discrimination arises, prakṛti — her purpose served — ceases for that puruṣa like a dancer who has shown herself (SK 59, 65–66); the knower remains embodied for a time (SK 67), and at the body's end attains isolation that is certain and final (SK 68). It is not the manifestation of bliss, nor going anywhere, nor annihilation (SS 5.74–83), but the destruction of obstacles (SS 6.20) and the complete cessation of the threefold suffering (SS 1.1, 3.85). Strictly, bondage and release belong to prakṛti (SK 62).

The absence of the conjunction of seer and seen (2.25); arising when sattva and puruṣa are equal in purity (3.55) and from dispassion even toward the highest power (3.50); the return of the guṇas, their purpose fulfilled, to their source, or the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34). Vyāsa: then the puruṣa is the light of its own form alone, stainless, alone (YBh 2.27, 3.55).
Enjoyment of one's own self apart from the Lord; a lesser goal.
Not permanent.
Permanent, with no return.
In HYP 4.62 kaivalya is what remains when the mind dissolves by abandoning the knowable.

Sāṃkhya's account of liberation

name: Kāl and Dayāl (the negative and the merciful power)

definitions.definition: Creation below Daswān Dwār is ruled by Kāl, the negative power (universal mind), who administers karma and keeps souls in the three worlds; above is Dayāl, the merciful, whose Saints free souls.
Kāl Nirañjan against the Sat Puruṣ.
Dvaita: time is eternal (as a flow) and non-eternal (in its divisions), directly perceived by the witness even in deep sleep; everything seen or remembered is set in it.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): time is one of the candidate causes rejected by the Śvetāśvatara (1.2, 6.1); God is the maker of time (6.2, 6.16); brahman has two forms, time and the timeless; 'time cooks all beings in the great self' (MaiU 6.14-16).

In jyotiṣa time is twofold — the destroyer of worlds and measurable time, gross and subtle (SS 1.10–11) — beginningless and endless, inferred from the planets (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11); the Sun is its self and maker (SS 12.18; Yogayātrā 1.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord says: 'of those that reckon I am time' (10.30), 'I alone am imperishable time' (10.33), and, answering 'who are you?', 'I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds' (11.32).
An eternal insentient substance without guṇas, part of the Lord's body, ruling change in the realm of play and present but not ruling in the eternal realm.

definitions.definition: Death at the exhaustion of life's measure is timely; death midway through wrong conduct, like an axle broken by overload, is untimely; both exist (Ca Vi 3.37-38; Śā 6.28); the life-span of this age is a hundred years (Śā 6.29).

name: Time as the power of the Word-Brahman

definitions.definition: Time is the independent power of Brahman by which sequence, birth and the other modifications appear; the 'wire-puller' of the world-machine (VP 1.3; 3.9).

Time is the seven-reined horse whose wheels are all beings; in Time are tapas, the eldest and brahman; Time is lord of all and father of Prajāpati; from Time arose the waters, brahman, tapas, the quarters and the Vedas (AVŚ 19.53–54).
Yoga is 'the cheating of time' (GŚ 2); the yogī in samādhi is not devoured by time (GŚ 98); when kuṇḍalī wakes time is cheated (HYP 3.3); by preserving bindu one conquers death (HYP 3.88).
Taught as most secret: the mind in the heart until unmanī turns back death (KJN 6.27–28); the nectar meditations (5.6–11).

The haṭha texts promise the conquest of time/death: the Siddhas 'broke the staff of time' (HYP 1.9); breath held, fear of death is gone (2.39–40); when kuṇḍalinī wakes, death is cheated (3.3); mudrās grant 'cheating of time' (3.130); suṣumnā devours time (4.17); the one established in rājayoga cheats time (4.103); the Haṭhatattvakaumudī has a chapter on it.

name: The Kālacakra calendar and the epoch 1027

definitions.definition: The Kālacakra's astronomy and calendar; its sixty-year cycle is reckoned from 1027 CE, the basis of the Tibetan rab byung cycles.

notes: The epoch year as the scholarly account gives it; the tradition reckons from Śambhala.

definitions.definition: Not accepting teachings on tradition, lineage, report, scripture, logic, inference, reasoned reflection, a view, a speaker's competence or respect for a teacher, but on knowing for oneself which states are unwholesome and lead to harm (AN 3.65).

name: Kālāmukha monasteries, assemblies and royal preceptors

definitions.definition: Temple-based maṭhas (chief among them the Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāve) grouped in the Śakti- and Siṃha-pariṣads, their pontiffs learned in many systems and serving as rājagurus; the maṭhas fed, taught and healed.

Time imagined as a person: the signs are his limbs from head to feet (BJ 1.4), the Sun his self, the Moon his mind and so on (BJ 2.1); his ocean cannot be crossed even in mind by one who is not a seer (BS 2.4). An affliction to a sign afflicts the corresponding limb of the native.

name: Kālī as the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva

definitions.definition: As trees rise from the earth and bubbles from water, Brahmā and the gods are born from Kālikā and dissolve into her (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.42-43); she gives birth, protects and dissolves, and so is Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśa (Karpūrādistotra 12-14).

name: Kālī as Time and the devourer of Time

definitions.definition: Mahākāla devours all beings; Kālī devours Mahākāla and is therefore the primordial Kālikā (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32); she is 'mother of Time' (5.140) and witnesses Time at play (13.12); in the Krama she is the power of kalana in twelve phases (U19).

relations.note: Kashmirian Krama analysis of the same power

name: The epoch of the Kali age

definitions.definition: The siddhāntas count days from the beginning of the Kali age (by their reckoning 3102 BCE); Āryabhaṭa dates himself by it — 3600 years elapsed at his 23rd year (Āryabhaṭīya 3.10) — and dates the Bhārata war to the end of the previous quarter (1.5).

Her form is imagined according to her qualities: black because all colours — all beings — vanish into her; the crescent for immortality; three eyes as moon, sun and fire; boon and fearlessness to protect; seated on a red lotus as ruling the worlds of rajas; pure consciousness watching Time play (Mahānirvāṇa 13.5-13; 5.140).
The devotional songs question and affirm her blackness: black to the world, she lights the lotus of the heart (Kamalākānta).

name: Kālī standing on Śiva as a corpse

definitions.definition: When Kālī manifests as dissolution Sadāśiva becomes a corpse: with Śakti he is Śiva, without her a corpse (śava), though he remains the Person (Toḍala 1.20-25); the Kālī Tantra's meditation places her on the heart of Mahādeva in corpse form (Tantrasāra).

name: The dharma of the Kali age

definitions.definition: Kali is full of faults, and gambling, drink, illicit women, slaughter and gold are its dwellings; yet in Kali merit comes quickly: singing the name gives what earlier ages won by meditation, sacrifice and worship, and śūdras and women gain merit easily by service.
Congregational chanting of the name is the dharma of Kali, inaugurated by Caitanya; in Kali there is no other way.
In Kali all paths are ruined; Kṛṣṇa alone is the refuge.
In Kali neither ritual, devotion nor discernment stands; the name alone supports; yet no age equals Kali for one with faith, since singing Rāma's qualities crosses existence without effort.
In Kali the name sung together suffices without sacrifice or austerity.
In Kali rites, pilgrimages and other gods do not save; Kṛṣṇa's name is the refuge.

name: Kalpa, the day of Brahmā and his lifetime

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.17, 9.7–8: the day of Brahmā extends to a thousand yugas and his night likewise (8.17); at the end of a kalpa all beings go into the Lord's prakṛti, and at the beginning of a kalpa he, taking hold of his own prakṛti, sends forth again the whole multitude of beings, helpless under prakṛti's power (9.7–8).

A thousand cycles of four ages (mahāyugas) with fourteen Manus make a day of Brahmā (kalpa), followed by a night of equal length; Brahmā lives a hundred years of such days, in two halves (parārdha); the present is the first day of his second half (Śveta-Vārāha kalpa, seventh manvantara, Kali age - tradition's reckoning).
