name: The cycle of aeons in the Abhidharmakośa

definitions.definition: A great aeon of eighty intermediate aeons in four periods (formation, duration, destruction, emptiness); human lifespan rises and falls between 80,000 and ten years; decline through craving and bad action; destruction by fire, water and wind.

relations.note: Same fourfold aeon and the destructions by fire, water, wind.

definitions.definition: Countless unsurpassed qualities: the six (knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility, splendour) and those that make him approachable — compassion, motherly love, gracious condescension, accessibility, lordship; they belong to him in every form.

relations.note: the Pāñcarātra's six are the core set

definitions.definition: The whole of the holy life (SN 45.2); the first support for the maturing of the mind's liberation (Ud 4.1); true and false friends (DN 31).

The meditation subject is received from a good friend who is lovable, respected, esteemed, able to counsel, patient, able to give deep talk and never urges to what is useless; best is the Buddha, then the great disciples, then an arahant, and so on down to one who knows the texts; a person can be a decisive-support condition.
Close personal training under an experienced forest teacher who knows the pupil's mind.
Formal request of the meditation subject from the teacher with offerings.

Kāma seeks one's own pleasure and prema the Beloved's (as the Caitanya-caritāmṛta says); the Sahajiyā holds that prema is refined out of kāma, not reached by suppressing it; the washerwoman's love had no trace of lust.

relations.note: Orthodox Gauḍīyas accept the same definitions but deny that prema can be reached by refining human kāma.

name: Desire (and anger) as the enemy (BhG 3.36–43)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What impels a person to sin against his will is desire, and anger, arising from rajas, all-devouring and greatly sinful — the enemy (3.37); it covers knowledge as smoke covers fire, dirt a mirror and the membrane an embryo (3.38–39); its seat is the senses, mind and understanding, through which it deludes the embodied one (3.40); controlling the senses first, and knowing what is beyond the understanding and steadying the self by the self, one is to slay it (3.41–43).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: desire and anger recur as a pair to be overcome: one who can withstand here, before release from the body, the surge (vega) that arises from desire and anger is yoked and a happy person (5.23); brahma-nirvāṇa is near on every side for ascetics freed from desire and anger (5.26).

relations.note: desire covers knowledge and deludes the embodied one

name: Desire as the first seed of mind

definitions.definition: Desire (kāma) arose in the beginning as the first seed of mind (RV 10.129.4; AVŚ 19.52.1).

name: The three lineages: kama, terma and pure vision

definitions.definition: The long lineage of the spoken word (ring brgyud bka' ma), the short lineage of treasures (nye brgyud gter ma) and the profound lineage of pure visions (zab mo dag snang).

From the threefold Śakti comes the seed, from the seed desire, from desire poison (death); the spotless dwells subtly within the mind; all three reside at the root of the brahma-staff (AmŚ 38–45); desire is longing for objects and poison its dissolution — abandoning both one resorts to the spotless (Candrāvalokana).

The white and red points (Śiva and Śakti) and the point of their union, the sun that is the 'I'; kāma because it is lovely and kalā as the points of fire and moon; this vidyā is the sequence of the Goddess's cakra, and one who knows it becomes Mahātripurasundarī (KKV 6-8).
The Goddess 'whose form is the kāmakalā' (LSN 73); the Saundaryalaharī's meditation on it (SL 19) is taught for attraction.

The Goddess of the yoni-pīṭha at Kāmagiri in Kāmarūpa (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42, 18.49), 'the great vidyā in the form of the yoni' who is all four aims of life (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4, 1.9-13). The temple on Nīlācala was rebuilt by the Koch king Naranārāyaṇa in 1565 (historical metadata, moderate confidence).
Seat of the Kaula scripture and yoginīs (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 22.10-12).

Kamma is intention; its source is contact, its result threefold in time, its cessation the cessation of contact, the way the eightfold path (AN 6.63); beings are owners of their deeds (MN 135); dark, bright, mixed and neither (AN 4.232); the same deed ripens differently in the developed and undeveloped (AN 3.100); not everything felt is due to past deeds (MN 101; AN 3.61).

relations.note: the shared Indian doctrine of action and result, defined here by intention
the Sarvāstivāda/Sautrāntika treatment (U38)

definitions.definition: By function (productive, supportive, obstructive, destructive); by order of ripening (weighty, death-proximate, habitual, reserve); by time (here and now, next life, later lives, defunct); by place (unwholesome, sense-sphere wholesome, fine-material, immaterial).

name: Death and the hells in the Kapila Gītā

definitions.definition: The attached householder dies in torment, is led by Yama's messengers, suffers in hells the fruit of his deeds and returns to birth.

name: The principles in the Kapila Gītā

definitions.definition: Twenty-four principles — five gross elements, five subtle elements, ten senses, and the fourfold inner instrument (mind, intellect, ego, citta) — with time as the twenty-fifth, identified with the Lord.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): first taught in secret — 'one becomes good by good action, bad by bad' (BAU 3.2.13); 'as one acts, as one behaves, so one becomes'; desire → resolve → action → result (BAU 4.4.5); rebirth 'according to action and knowledge' (KU 2.2.7; KauU 1.2); conduct determines the womb (ChU 5.10.7); action does not cling to the knower (ChU 4.14.3; Īśa 2); the knots cut, actions are exhausted (MuU 2.2.8).

In Sāṃkhya virtue and non-virtue are dispositions of buddhi, not of puruṣa (SK 23; SS 5.25); they carry the subtle body upward or downward (SK 44) and ripen as experience; the fruit of action comes from karma, not from a governing Lord (SS 5.2); with knowledge they cease to act as causes — future karma burnt like seeds, present karma exhausted (SK 67; Gauḍapāda).
Karma is primarily the enjoined act; its fruit comes through the apūrva; dharma and adharma produce bodies and experiences until exhausted.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The course of action is deep (4.17); action binds when done from desire with attachment to fruit (5.12), but not when done without attachment, for the sake of sacrifice, with actions placed in Brahman (4.20–23, 5.10); knowledge burns all actions to ashes (4.19, 4.37); all sacrifices are born of action (4.32) and all action culminates in knowledge (4.33); the Lord is not stained by actions and whoever knows this is not bound (4.14).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the fruit of well-done action (karmaṇaḥ sukṛtasya) is said to be sāttvika and stainless, the fruit of rajas pain, the fruit of tamas ignorance (14.16); rajas binds by attachment to action (14.7); actions are done in every way by prakṛti alone (13.30).
Non-virtuous, virtuous and unmoving actions and their results (Jewel Ornament ch.6); Milarepa's life shows grave evil karma purified by remorse, ordeals and practice.

name: Cause and effect for the awakened

definitions.definition: The fox kōan: 'not falling into' cause and effect brought five hundred fox-lives; 'not obscuring' cause and effect freed him.
Dōgen: deep faith in cause and effect; denial of causality is wrong view.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Even sages are bewildered about what action and inaction are (4.16); one must understand action (karma), vikarma and inaction (akarma), for the course of action is deep (4.17); the wise one sees inaction in action and action in inaction (4.18). The text does not define vikarma.
The way of action is deep: one must know action, wrong action and inaction, and see inaction in action and action in inaction (BhG 4.16–18); actions burnt in the fire of knowledge (4.19, 4.37).

name: Karma and rebirth in Kashmir Śaivism

definitions.definition: Karma bound by false knowledge perishes in the fire of knowledge like a roasted seed; the knower is untouched by merit and demerit; the one who dies midway on the path enjoys higher worlds and completes the path in another birth (Paramārthasāra 55-62, 96-102).

name: Karma as volition and what volition produces

definitions.definition: Karma is volition (mental) and the bodily and vocal action it produces, manifest and unmanifest; fourfold as black, white, black-white and neither.
Mental karma includes covetousness, malice and wrong view.
Bodily and vocal karma are volitions; their results come through the transformed series.

name: Classes of action for the seeker

definitions.definition: Desire-prompted (kāmya) and forbidden (niṣiddha) acts to be avoided; daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika) and expiatory (prāyaścitta) rites and meditations (upāsana) to be performed for purity.
Sin not yet fructifying, latent, as seed and about to fructify are destroyed in sequence by devotion; even prārabdha yields.

Karma cannot be exhausted by experiencing it, for new karma is always made; ritual works win only the lowest grace (heaven); release needs grace won by knowledge; prārabdha karma still runs its course.
Fruition is experiencing; it accords with the name of the karma; from it comes shedding (nirjarā).

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

relations.note: purified by duties the student acquires the four means

definitions.definition: Works cannot remove ignorance, being not opposed to it; performed without desire they purify the mind and generate the desire to know (or knowledge); knowledge excludes the sense of agency, so works and knowledge are not combined.

name: Karma and its uprooting in the haṭha texts

definitions.definition: The body arises from good and bad deeds and turns the soul through birth and death like a water-wheel (GS 1.6–7); when breath flows in suṣumnā and mind enters the void the yogin uproots all karma (HYP 4.12); the yogin in samādhi is not bound by karma (4.108); at niṣpatti the seeds of beginningless karma are crossed (SS 3.66); in paricaya he sees the 'three peaks' of his karma (SS 3.61).

Karma is subtle matter drawn in through the soul's activity and bound by its passions, adhering to all its space-points (TS 8.2, 8.24); the soul's passional states are 'psychic karma', the particles 'material karma'.
By the ultimate standpoint the soul is not the doer of material karma; it is the doer only of its own states.

relations.note: Karma here is a material substance, not only a latent impression.

name: Adversity as the return of one's own deeds

definitions.definition: Whatever harm befalls one is the wheel of one's own past deeds returning; the fitting response is to turn the weapon on self-grasping.

name: Karma of mind, speech and body

definitions.definition: Ten wrongs — three mental, four verbal, three bodily — with mind as instigator; bodily faults lead to plant-births, verbal to bird and beast births, mental to low human births (MDh 12.3–9); the residue of deeds shapes birth, form and fortune (ĀpDh 2.1.2.3); one's own conduct raises or lowers class in the next birth (ĀpDh 2.5.11.10–11).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:manusmrti:12.3-9 (confirmed); tea:apastamba-dharmasutra:2.1.2.2-3 (confirmed); tea:apastamba-dharmasutra:2.5.11.10-11 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Karma is bound, remains (sattā), rises in fruition (udaya), can be prematurely drawn out (udīraṇā), transferred between subtypes (saṅkramaṇa), increased or decreased in duration and intensity (utkarṣaṇa, apakarṣaṇa), subsided (upaśama), fixed (nidhatti) or made unalterable (nikācanā); it is experienced by its nature and then shed (TS 8.21–23; Gommaṭasāra).

Action is intention and intended action (MMK 17.2–3); if it lasted until ripening it would be permanent, if it perished it could bear no fruit (17.6); because it is without own-nature it is unarisen and so does not perish (17.21); agent and action are like emanations (17.31–33).
Agent and enjoyer are spoken of with reference to the unity of a continuum (BCA 9.73); the Mādhyamika does not deny action and fruit but their own-nature (PsP 17.30).

relations.note: the realist 'imperishable' is not needed if action is empty
shared doctrine of action and fruit, but denied own-nature

name: The six means of distinguishing rites

definitions.definition: A different word, repetition, number, quality, context and name (Śabara's list at MS 2.1.1; treated in adhyāya 2).

Union with a physical consort as a method of the higher consecrations and completion stage; the texts insist on consecration, qualification and non-attachment and warn against mistaking its bliss for the ultimate. Summary only.

Rooted in the afflictions, the karmic residue ripens in this or a future birth (2.12); while the root remains it ripens as birth, life-span and experience (2.13); the mass accumulated in a life, manifested at death, produces one birth (YBh 2.13); merit only removes obstruction, like a farmer opening a dyke (4.3).

name: No fruit without deed, no deed without fruit

definitions.definition: Body and experience arise from the fruits of one's own past acts (NS 3.2.60); accounts that would make one reap what one did not do (akṛtābhyāgama) are rejected (NS 3.2.38, 3.2.72 DCS); even the Lord brings about fruits without annulling what each has done (NBh 4.1.21).
The Kaula teaching is 'heard as handed down in succession', passing from ear to ear (KJN 6.8–9; 17.10).

name: The Kartā (Master) present in the human

definitions.definition: God is the one Kartā, present in Āulcānd (Caitanya returned) and in the living guru; he is worshipped alone, in the human, not in images.
'Among people, people's custom; with the true guru, oneness': the Kartābhajā keeps caste and religious custom outwardly while worshipping the Kartā alone within.

name: The ascending order beyond the senses (Kaṭha 1.3.10-11)

definitions.definition: Above the senses are the objects, above them the mind, above it the intellect, above it the great self (mahān ātmā), above it the unmanifest (avyakta), above it the person (puruṣa); nothing is higher than the person, who is the limit and the highest goal.

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

name: The chariot simile of Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3

definitions.definition: The self is the lord of the chariot, the body the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, the mind (manas) the reins, the senses (indriya) the horses and the objects (viṣaya) their roads (1.3.3-4). With an unyoked mind the senses are unruly like bad horses and one goes to saṃsāra; with a yoked mind they are obedient like good horses and one reaches the highest place of Viṣṇu, from which there is no rebirth (1.3.5-9).

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

definitions.definition: The avadhūta stage is the saṃnyāsa of the Kali age (Mahānirvāṇa 8.221); avadhūtas are of four kinds, complete (paramahaṃsa) and incomplete; the Śaiva avadhūta is consecrated by the complete consecration (14.142-149).
The vīra avadhūta holds 'I am Śiva, the bliss of Bhairava'; fruits are graded by caste (Nirvāṇa Tantra 14.1-10).

name: The descent of the Kaula in the four ages

definitions.definition: The Kaula came down as Jñānanirṇiti, Mahat, Siddhāmṛta and, in Kali, Matsyodara; stolen by Kārttikeya and swallowed by a fish, it was recovered by Bhairava as fisherman; it came from Candradvīpa and is in every house of the yoginīs in Kāmarūpa (KJN 16.27–48; 22.10–12).

name: Karma and rebirth in the Kaula view

definitions.definition: Souls covered by ignorance take birth after birth according to merit and demerit in 8.4 million kinds of bodies; the subtle body lasts until liberation; only human birth allows knowledge of reality (Kulārṇava 1.9-17); Kula dharma leads beyond return (2.30).

name: The Kula ritual as interpreted by Abhinavagupta (summary)

definitions.definition: Tantrāloka 29 treats the secret Kula worship with a consort and Kaula substances as the outward form of the union of Śiva and Śakti in consciousness, for qualified initiates; one born of such a union is 'yoginībhū', a vessel of knowledge (29.162-163). Summary only.

notes: Restricted subject: summary only.

name: The Kaula scriptures named in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya

definitions.definition: Kulapañcāśikā, Kulasāgara, Kulogha, Hṛdaya, Bhairavodyānaka, Candrakaula, Jñānanirṇaya, and from them Sṛṣṭikaula, Mahākaula, Timira, Siddhāmṛta, Mātakaula, Śaktibheda, Ūrmikaula, Siddheśvara and the Vajra-born (KJN 21.2–7).

name: Secrecy and concealment in the Kaula way

definitions.definition: The teaching comes 'from ear to ear' and must not be given to the deceitful (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 6.8-14); reveal the guru but guard the mantra (Kulārṇava 11.88); the Kaulas go 'inwardly Śākta, outwardly Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava in the assembly' (Kaulāvalīnirṇaya 10.94; Kālīvilāsa 7.12); open worship destroys perfection.

Śiva as the supreme Brahman, being–consciousness–bliss (Kulārṇava 1.7-8), whose truth is beyond both duality and non-duality (1.110), realised as the bliss of the union of Śakti and Śiva residing in the body (5.79-80).

Herbal, breath, yogic and mineral-metal regimens to make the body firm, reverse grey hair and wrinkles (TM 727) and prolong life for yoga. The tradition warns that mineral and mercurial kaṟpam without a guru is deadly; and Kuṭampai asks what need of kaṟpam the true knower has (2).
In Siddha medicine kaṟpam is the rejuvenative branch (kaṟpa maruttuvam).

relations.note: Āyurveda's rasāyana

name: Perfection of the body and immortality (kāya-siddhi, amaratva)

definitions.definition: The body filled with the moon's nectar does not leave the embodied one (GŚ 66); the great siddhas broke the staff of Time and roam the universe (HYP 1.9); 'the swallowing of the body by the body' (Jñāneśvarī 6.291).
Immortality by devotion to guru and yoginīs (KJN 5.33); the five jewels ending in the destruction of old age and death (17.12–13); the body standing like a thunderbolt with no dissolution (15.25).

Without the body life perishes and true knowledge cannot be reached; knowing the means to nourish the body, one nourishes the life (TM 724); the Lord has made the body his temple (TM 725). Kāya citti removes karma and opens higher powers (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 14); vāci yoga makes it free of obstacles (Caṭṭaimuṉi 4).

In the haṭha texts bodily perfection (dehasiddhi, HYP 3.103) and immortality (amaratva, a synonym of samādhi, 4.3) are fruits of retaining bindu and nectar; the DYŚ's perfected yogin may keep his body and roam the worlds at will (115–118); the Yogabīja's 'ripe body'.

relations.note: KJN 6.7 also teaches that the jīva is Śiva once the body is left; the two emphases stand side by side in the text
as means, in TM 724

definitions.definition: Honest labour in one's own occupation is worship — 'work is Kailāsa' — and must not be interrupted even for guru, liṅga or jaṅgama, nor gather beyond the day's need.

relations.note: the fruit of kāyaka is shared as dāsōha

definitions.definition: Seeing one's own nature at the words; examples: Huineng on the Diamond Sūtra, Xiangyan at the pebble, Lingyun at peach blossoms, Dongshan at his reflection.
The breakthrough of great doubt (Hakuin at the temple bell), to be followed by post-awakening practice.
Awakening is like the moon in water; Dōgen de-emphasises kenshō as a goal separate from practice.

relations.note: Corresponds to the path of seeing (darśanamārga) of the five paths; band B5 (first direct seeing) in the interpretation layer.

name: Knowledge-itself and the means of knowledge (kevala / anupramāṇa)

definitions.definition: Valid knowledge is what accords with its object; it is knowledge itself (of God, Lakṣmī, yogins, others) and its three means (perception, inference, authoritative word); memory is valid; presumption and comparison are inference.

Knowledge of all substances in all their modes (TS 1.29), arising when delusion and then the knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring and obstructive karmas are destroyed (10.1); the soul's own nature fully manifest. Its possibility is argued from the degree-wise diminution of faults (Āptamīmāṃsā 4–5).
In the omniscient, knowledge and perception alternate moment by moment (Jinabhadra); Siddhasena holds them identical (Sanmati kāṇḍa 2).
Omniscient knowledge and perception are simultaneous (Digambara commentators).

Mahāvīra's attainment: 'infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete and full' knowledge and perception, arising in pure meditation after the destruction of the obscuring, deluding and obstructing karmas; 'who knows one knows all'.

relations.note: Both are named 'kevala/kaivalya' final states, but the Jain state is omniscience of all modes by a soul that remains individual; Patañjali's kaivalya is the seer's isolation from prakṛti.
Omniscience precedes final liberation at the end of life (TS 10.1–5).

definitions.definition: The omniscient, while his gross body lasts, takes food; hunger and the other hardships due to feeling-karma occur in him (Tattvārthasūtra 9.11 read literally); Mahāvīra recovered from illness on food brought from Revatī.
Affirmed with arguments by Śākaṭāyana.

Denied: hunger and thirst are among the eighteen faults absent in the Jina; without deluding karma feeling-karma cannot cause hunger; the omniscient's body is sustained without morsel-food; he has no bodily pleasure or pain.

The living omniscient (13th stage) has destroyed the four destructive karmas but keeps the four others; he teaches, moves and at the end may equalise his remaining karmas by expanding his soul through the universe (kevali-samudghāta) before liberation.
The kevalin does not eat, suffer hunger or disease; the eleven hardships of TS 9.11 are figurative (Sarvārthasiddhi); his knowledge and perception are simultaneous.
The kevalin takes food, as the scriptures show of Mahāvīra; knowledge and perception alternate (Jinabhadra) or are identical (Siddhasena).
Listed by the Visuddhimagga among the three kinds of concentration; the sub-commentary makes momentary unification the concentration of the pure-insight practitioner.
Built up by uninterrupted noting; sufficient to suppress the hindrances and carry insight to the path.

name: The abbot, the master and the king (mkhan slob chos gsum)

definitions.definition: Śāntarakṣita, Padmasambhava and Trisong Detsen, the three founders of Buddhism at Samye.

name: Hereditary succession of the Khön family

definitions.definition: Leadership of the Sakya passes within the Khön family (in later centuries alternating between its two palaces, Phuntsok and Drolma), the throne-holder being the Sakya Trizin; the Ngor and Tshar abbacies follow their own lines.

name: Oneness of person and Dharma (kihō ittai)

definitions.definition: In Namu Amida Butsu the person who entrusts and the Dharma that saves are one; the Buddha's attainment and beings' birth were accomplished together (Anjin ketsujōshō; Rennyo).
Associated with the Seizan milieu of the Anjin ketsujōshō (attribution uncertain).

name: The sword that kills and the sword that gives life

definitions.definition: The teacher's double function of cutting off and restoring (Yuanwu).

name: 'If you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha'

definitions.definition: Not being bound by any object of veneration or attachment, inner or outer; figurative, as Linji says he only cures sickness and unties bonds.
Repeated as the fruit of passing the barrier of 'wu' (Wumen).
All beings are to be held dear and their kindness contemplated — as mothers in past lives and as the field in which one gains merit and patience.
Prior absence, absence by destruction, mutual absence and absolute absence; if absence were not real, curd would be in milk and consciousness in earth.

Knowledge: perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge; non-knowledge: doubt, error, indefinite cognition, dream (Praśastapāda); non-knowledge arises from defects of senses and impressions (VS 9.25–27 C).

name: Kinds of death (canonical classification)

definitions.definition: Death of the wise-among-the-wise (the omniscient), of the wise (the renunciant), of the wise-ignorant (the vowed layperson), of the ignorant (right faith without vows) and of the ignorant-among-the-ignorant (wrong faith).
The Ācārāṅga's three forms of the wise monk's death and the Prakīrṇakas on the preparation of the dying (restricted theme: the texts' conditions only).

Five kinds of death — 'wise-wise' (of the omniscient), wise (of the ascetic), wise-foolish (of the layman), foolish (of one with right view but no vows) and foolish-foolish (of the wrong-believer); the wise death by renunciation of food is praised (Bhagavatī Ārādhanā).

notes: Classification recalled; Bhagavatī Ārādhanā also lists seventeen kinds of death (not recorded here).

definitions.definition: Initiation by touch (sparśa), by sight (dṛk) and, rarest, by piercing (vedha) (Kulārṇava 14.53-66).

Initiation acts on the soul, not caste or body; it is the cause of the other means and, as nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, destroys past and future karma through mantra-power, the present body continuing like a potter's wheel. It is samaya- (or viśeṣa-) and nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, followed by consecrations (abhiṣeka) of sādhaka and ācārya; for the incapable the observances are purified away ('seedless', nirbīja), for the capable they remain ('with seed').
Initiation (dīkṣā) into Bhagavān's mantras and worship; in Śrīvaiṣṇava usage the five sacraments.
Samaya, viśeṣa and nirvāṇa dīkṣā, then consecrations (ācāryābhiṣeka, sādhakābhiṣeka); nirvāṇa-dīkṣā with or without 'seed'.
Seven modes: by look, touch, word, thought, scripture, yoga and the fire rite.

Endogenous, exogenous and mental (Ca Sū 11.45); adventitious, bodily, mental and natural — hunger, thirst, old age, death, sleep (Su Sū 1.24-25); curable (easy or difficult) and incurable (palliable or rejectable) (Ca Sū 10.9).

name: The kinds of liberation of mind

definitions.definition: Immeasurable, through nothingness, emptiness and signless liberations of mind, which differ in name but are one in meaning in that the unshakeable liberation is empty of lust, hatred and delusion, the 'makers of measure, something and signs' (MN 43).
Self-manifest (svayambhu), divine (daiva), bāṇa, sages' (ārṣa) and man-installed liṅgas are the supports of temple worship; the liṅga given by the guru is the support of one's own worship.

name: The grades of the descent of power (śaktipāta)

definitions.definition: Grace depends on the Lord's freedom alone; intense, middling and mild, each in three degrees (nine grades); its signs are devotion to Rudra, mantra-success, control of beings, completion of undertakings and poetic power with sudden knowledge of scripture (MVT 2.14-16; TĀ 13); graded by scripture (TĀ 13.300-301).

notes: Nine-grade scheme recalled from TĀ 13 / Tantrasāra 11 (chapter level).

definitions.definition: Originative (utpatti), applicatory (viniyoga), performative (prayoga) and eligibility (adhikāra) injunctions.
Deeds, action and energy are effective; all Buddhas teach it; there is an element of initiative.
The true kiriyavāda: knowing self and world, influx and stopping, bondage and wearing away of karma.

name: The Siddhas of the Kula (Kaulajñānanirṇaya lists)

definitions.definition: The Kaulajñānanirṇaya names Siddhas who brought down the Kula in the ages, with '-pāda' names (e.g. Vyāghrapāda, Pañcaśikhipāda, Lambodarapāda), and a Goddess's list (Hiḍinipāda, Samudrapāda, Lavaṇapāda, Dhīvarapāda, Siṃhalapāda and others) (9.6-9).

notes: Names read from a corrupt e-text; spellings uncertain.

name: The wearing away of the afflictions (kleśa-kṣaya)

definitions.definition: The afflictions are thinned by kriyā-yoga (YS 2.2), made like burnt seeds by discerning insight (YBh 2.2), abandoned in gross form by meditation and in subtle form by involution (YS 2.10–2.11); insight-born impressions cause their wearing away (YBh 1.50); with them worn away, karma no longer ripens (YBh 2.13).

definitions.definition: The seventh consciousness, which takes the store-consciousness as its object and thinks 'I', always accompanied by self-view, self-delusion, self-conceit and self-love; it is the source of the sense of 'I' even in unconscious states, and is transformed into the wisdom of equality.

relations.note: its self-grasping is what the knowledge of selflessness removes

definitions.definition: Old cases used for commentary, verse and contemplation; the Wumen guan, Blue Cliff Record and Book of Equanimity collect them.
Dahui's contemplation of the critical phrase of a case, with the doubt kept alive in daily life.
A graded kōan curriculum under a teacher (Hakuin's line).
Dōgen collected and commented on kōans but taught just sitting; the realized kōan (genjōkōan) is reality itself.
Meditators on the qualified Brahman go by the path of light to the Brahma-world and are liberated with its ruler at the end of the cycle.

name: Liberation together with Brahmā at the dissolution

definitions.definition: Knowers who go by the path of light to Brahmā's world reach the Supreme together with Brahmā at the great dissolution; some others are liberated without departing.

Every cognition unfolds as emission (sṛṣṭi), persistence (sthiti), withdrawal (saṃhāra) and the nameless (anākhya), in the object, the means of knowledge and the subject - twelve Kālīs in all (TĀ 4.145, 4.148-172).

name: The six means of fixing sequence

definitions.definition: Direct statement, purpose, textual order, position, the order of principals, and the order once begun.

name: For the rite or for the person

definitions.definition: An element is either for the sake of the rite or for the sake of the person; what is for the person is what gives him delight (MS 4.1.1–2). Self-knowledge is argued by Bhāṭṭas to be both (Śāstradīpikā).
Austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (YS 2.1), for cultivating samādhi and thinning the afflictions (YS 2.2); taught for the practitioner whose mind is not yet concentrated (YBh 2.1).
Austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (2.1), for cultivating samādhi and thinning the afflictions (2.2); taught for the unconcentrated mind; austerity must not disturb the mind (YBh 2.1).

definitions.definition: Giridhar Gopāl is Mīrā's only husband; for him she casts off family honour and public shame.

name: Kṛṣṇa as the Lord himself (svayaṃ bhagavān)

definitions.definition: Kṛṣṇa is the source of all avatāras, not an avatāra of Viṣṇu (BhP 1.3.28 as governing statement).
Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇa is the highest form of Brahman.
Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Brahman with Rādhā.

name: The made and the innate paths (kṛtaka and sahaja)

definitions.definition: The Kaula path is twofold: the 'made' (kṛtaka), in which kuṇḍalī is impelled by seals, mantras, oblations and ear-whispered formulas, and the 'innate' (sahaja), abiding in samarasa (Akulavīra B.43–45); conceptions, even of the centres and deities, keep one turning (Jñānakārikā 2.20–23).
The Amaraughaśāsana likewise refuses to call kuṇḍalinī's movement liberation and places liberation in sahaja-samādhi (AmŚ 52–54).

The moment is time at its utmost minuteness and alone real; sequence is the flow of moments; hours and days are constructions of the buddhi (YBh 3.52); sequence is apprehended at the end of a transformation (4.33); saṃyama on moment and sequence gives discriminative knowledge (3.52). Permanence is twofold: unchanging (puruṣa) and changing (guṇas) (YBh 4.33).

name: Perishable, imperishable and the Supreme Person

definitions.definition: Following Gītā 15.16–18: the perishable are all souls whose bodies perish (Brahmā, Śiva and the gods included); the imperishable is Lakṣmī; the Supreme Person beyond both is Hari.

Several teachings are placed in the mouths of kṣatriyas who teach brahmins: Ajātaśatru teaches Gārgya Bālāki, noting that this reverses the natural order (BAU 2.1); Pravāhaṇa Jaivali says the five-fires knowledge had never before gone to brahmins (ChU 5.3.7; BAU 6.2.8); Aśvapati teaches the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11); Citra teaches Āruṇi (KauU 1.1); Janaka is taught by and rewards Yājñavalkya (BAU 4).

name: The field and the knower of the field (kṣetra–kṣetrajña)

definitions.definition: The body and all of prakṛti with its modifications is the field; the one who knows it is its knower; the Lord is the knower in all fields; knowledge of both is true knowledge (BhG 13.1–6, 13.33–34).
Vāsudeva is the knower of the field (MBh 12.326.38).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: This body is called the field and whoever knows it the knower of the field (13.2); the Lord is also (api) to be known as the knower of the field in all fields, and knowledge of field and knower is knowledge (13.3). The field in brief: the great elements, the sense of 'I', understanding, the unmanifest, the ten faculties and the one, the five domains of the senses, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, sentience and steadiness, with their modifications (13.6-13.7). Every being arises from the union of field and knower (13.27); the possessor of the field illumines the whole field as the sun the world (13.34); those who know their difference with the eye of knowledge go to the highest (13.35).
The body-field of elements, senses, mind and passions is known by the Lord as knower of every field (Jñāneśvarī 13).

relations.note: the knower of the field corresponds to the Mokṣadharma's twenty-fifth ('the knower is the twenty-fifth', 12.294.38)

members: ekam ('the one'; manas per the commentators)

definitions.definition: Praised as the coiled power of knowledge, will, action and sound, she splits the liṅga and emerges dark and bent (Kubjikāmata 2.2-5), becoming Kubjikā out of shame when asked for the transmission (2.14); her krama-worship enters the Agni Purāṇa (143-144).

relations.note: the hymn describes her as coiled like a sleeping serpent

name: The seats in the Kubjikā tradition

definitions.definition: The Goddess's journey names Śrīśaila, Kiṣkindhā and Oḍḍiyāna (Kubjikāmata 2.23-40); the four seats are levels of the supreme yoni (11.6-7).

name: The sixfold order (ṣaṭprakāra) of the Kubjikā body

definitions.definition: Self, power, haṃsa, breath, channels and body form a sixfold order in which the world is born and which awakens the Kula path (Kubjikāmata 11.13-16); chapters 11-16 set out the six centres with their deities and yoginīs.
Kula is Śakti and akula Śiva, their relation kaula; the Goddess is Kaulinī and also akulā (Bhāskararāya on LSN 36-37).
Akula is Śiva, Kula is Śakti; the Kaulas are adept in joining them (Kulārṇava 17.27); for Kaulas 'the non-Kula becomes Kula' (9.62).
Kula is the totality of powers (Śakti), Akula Śiva beyond it; consciousness finally dissolves into the Akula abode (TĀ 4.170); the Kaula rule dwells in Bhairava's heart (Parātrīśikā 4).
Kula is the domain of Śakti — the body, its centres and the yoginīs — and Akula is Śiva beyond it, where Bhairava abides at the end of aeons; the nectar is 'beyond Akula and Kula' (KJN 14.97; 16.41).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, each family has eternal family dharmas, which perish when the family is destroyed; then adharma prevails, the family's women are corrupted, varṇa-mixture arises, the ancestors fall, and those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell (1.40–44).

relations.note: their loss leads to varṇa-mixture (Arjuna's argument)

definitions.definition: Worship of a young girl as the Goddess — in the eastern tantras and in the Bengal Durgā-pūjā; the Kulārṇava forbids insulting a maiden or girl (11.61).

The coiled power lying at the base of the suṣumnā, blocking the door to Brahman; awakened by fire, breath and mind she rises through the centres and knots to unite with Śiva in the crown; 'bondage for the ignorant, liberation for yogins'; in the Varāha the supreme power from which breath, fire, bindu, nāda and mind arise.

The coiled power at the base of the central channel, blocking its mouth; the support of all yoga (HYP 3.1); awakened by the guru's grace (3.2) and by breath, locks and mudrās (3.5, 3.66–69) she straightens like a struck snake, pierces the knots and lotuses and the mind becomes supportless; for yogins she is liberation, for fools bondage (3.107). The GŚ says she is coiled eightfold, the ṢCN three and a half times; the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa describes her ascent through six centres to union with Paramaśiva.

The coiled power closing the door of Brahman, awakened by the fire of yoga with mind and breath (GŚ 30–31) or by the guru's grace (HYP 3.2), rising through suṣumṇā; asleep in the downward four-petalled lotus (AmŚ 60–64); the world-mother, pedestal of the liṅga of the void (Jñāneśvarī 6.272–273). The Amaraughaśāsana denies that its movement is itself liberation (AmŚ 52).
One of the names of Śiva's Will (KJN 20.11); the coiled Vāmā rising from the anus to the dvādaśānta (17.23); the 'made' Kaula path as against the innate (Akulavīra B.43).

The Goddess herself, dwelling in the mūlādhāra, piercing the knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, mounting the thousand-petalled lotus, showering nectar and returning to sleep in the kula-pit in three and a half coils (LSN 38-40; SL 9-10); seen by the pure-minded as a digit slender as lightning above the six lotuses (SL 21).
Tamil kuṇṭali: the coiled power at the root, in whose seat Guha is invoked; roused by the guru, it passes the six supports through the central channel to the moon of nectar.
The coiled power at the base, waked by posture and the locks, rising through the centres to merge in the supreme at the crown (Jñāneśvarī 6; summary only).

Śākta view (Pūrṇānanda): the Goddess herself, coiled three and a half times round the Svayambhū liṅga, is led up through the centres to unite with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus, the bliss of which is liberation (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 51-53).
Kubjikā is praised as coiled like a sleeping serpent (Kubjikāmata 2.2).
Kuṇḍalinī practice working up from the lower cakras is held to be unnecessary and hazardous; the Sants begin at the eye centre and rise by the sound.
Sundardās describes rousing the serpent power as part of yoga, below devotion and knowledge.

relations.note: Rising kuṇḍalinī pierces the three knots (the knots obstruct her path).

name: The all-creating king: bodhicitta as the creator of all

definitions.definition: In the mind series the nature of mind speaks as 'the all-creating king': teacher, teaching, retinue, place and time arise from it; there is no maker apart from it; it is self-arising wisdom beyond cause and condition. It is not a creator deity separate from beings but the nature of mind itself.

relations.note: the Nyingma deny a creator god; the 'all-creator' is awareness

name: The all-base (kun gzhi) distinguished from the dharmakāya

definitions.definition: Longchenpa distinguishes the all-base — the neutral, unaware ground of karmic traces — from the dharmakāya, and all-base consciousness from wisdom; an indifferent, blank state is the all-base, not awareness.
In Bön the kun gzhi is itself the ultimate base, empty and clear, inseparable from awareness.

relations.note: the same word names different things

definitions.definition: Bhāratavarṣa is divided into a centre and eight directional regions like the parts of a tortoise, each governed by three asterisms from Kṛttikā, so that an affliction of an asterism falls on its lands (BS 14).

Through austerity and the destruction-cum-subsidence of karma ascetics may gain powers — the transformable, fiery and projectable bodies, clairvoyance and mind-reading, healing touch, sky-walking and others (TS 1.21–25, 2.47–49); outward wonders do not prove a teacher's greatness (Āptamīmāṃsā 1), and to use or seek them is carelessness.
Hemacandra describes entering another body only as a wonder useless for liberation (YŚ 6.1); Śubhacandra warns against pursuing powers through breath-control.

relations.note: Both traditions treat powers as distractions from liberation.

definitions.definition: Śrī is Nārāyaṇa's eternal, independent power whose body is the six qualities, who performs his five acts, and in whom one takes refuge.

name: Lakṣmī as eternally free and dependent

definitions.definition: Lakṣmī is the highest dependent being: eternally untouched by sorrow, never bound, 'imperishable' (akṣara) in body, superior to all souls in every quality, yet infinitely below and wholly dependent on Viṣṇu; as Śrī, Bhū and Durgā she is the higher prakṛti.

name: The incarnation of Śiva as Lakulīśa

definitions.definition: The tradition's accounts: Śiva enters an abandoned corpse in a cremation ground and becomes the brahmacārin Lakulī at Kāyāvatāra, with four disciples (Liṅga P.); the Lord in a brahmin's body descends at Kāyāvataraṇa and teaches Kuśika at Ujjayinī (Kauṇḍinya); Śiva is born to Viśvarūpa and Sudarśanā, enters the body of the dead infant, and at last merges into the Brahmeśvara liṅga at Kāyāvarohaṇa (Kāravaṇa-māhātmya).

notes: Scholarly dating (c. 2nd c. CE) is kept on tch:lakulisa as labelled metadata.

definitions.definition: The Sahasranāma recounts the war in names: Mantriṇī and Daṇḍanāthā, the fire-wall, Gaṇeśa from Kāmeśvara's glance, the destruction of Bhaṇḍa and the revival of Kāma (LSN 25-33).
Bhaṇḍāsura, born from the ashes of Kāma burnt by Śiva, conquers the worlds; Lalitā arises from the gods' sacrificial fire, weds Kāmeśvara, defeats Bhaṇḍa with her śaktis and revives Kāma.

definitions.definition: Lalitā is the qualityless, partless Brahman (LSN 43-45), consciousness and bliss seated on the five Brahmas (LSN 61), 'cit' being Brahman itself (Bhāskararāya on name 4), and at once the queen on Kāmeśvara's lap; the mahātattva meaning of the mantra is the partless supreme principle (YH 2.73-74).

The Śākta Upaniṣads have the Goddess declare herself Brahman (Devī Upaniṣad); she alone is the self, what is other is unreal, and 'the one real thing called Lalitā is the non-dual, partless supreme Brahman' (Bahvṛca 5).

relations.note: the Śrīvidyā statement of the general Śākta doctrine

name: Lalitā's four weapons as the mind's powers

definitions.definition: Her noose is attachment, her goad anger, her sugarcane bow the mind and her five flower-arrows the five subtle elements (LSN 2-3); in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the bow is the mind, the arrows the five tanmātras, the noose attachment and the goad aversion.

name: Signs of the grounds in the Vajra Verses

definitions.definition: The Vajra Verses mark each ground by an inner sign (the stopping of a measure of wind, in finger-widths) and an outer sign (the drop stabilised at a place of the body), together with powers such as shaking and visiting emanation fields.

notes: Completion-stage (restricted) content; summary only.

name: The transmission and secrecy of the Lamdre

definitions.definition: The long lineage runs Virūpa — Kāṇha — Ḍamarupa — Avadhūtipa — Gayadhara — Drokmi — (Seton Kunrig — Zhangtön Chöbar) — Sachen; the short lineage from Virūpa directly to Sachen in vision. The Vajra Verses were long kept unwritten; Sachen was told to keep the teaching secret for years; the Lobshé remained a restricted explanation for close disciples.

notes: Lineage order and the secrecy period recalled; check against Sakya histories.

definitions.definition: Bull (Ṛṣabha), elephant, horse, monkey, curlew or ruddy goose, red lotus, svastika, crescent moon, makara, śrīvatsa (or wish-tree), rhinoceros, buffalo, boar, falcon (or porcupine), vajra, deer, goat, nandyāvarta (or fish), water-jar, tortoise, blue lotus, conch, serpent (Pārśva), lion (Mahāvīra) — variants give the Śvetāmbara then the Digambara emblem.

Words are dependently arisen and empty yet function (VV 22–23); 'empty' is said only for designation (MMK 22.11); the ultimate is taught only through convention (24.10); in reality the object to be named has ceased (18.7) and no dharma was taught by the Buddha to anyone (25.24).

relations.note: the Word-brahman is refuted in the Tattvasaṅgraha

name: The languages of the early canons

definitions.definition: The Sarvāstivāda and Mūlasarvāstivāda transmitted their canon in Sanskrit (Turfan, Gilgit).
The Lokottaravāda Vinaya texts are in a Prakrit-coloured 'Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit' (Mahāvastu, Prātimokṣa, Bhikṣuṇī-Vinaya).
The earliest manuscripts, associated with the Dharmaguptaka, are in Gāndhārī written in Kharoṣṭhī.
The Theravāda transmits its canon in Pali, held to be Māgadhī, the Buddha's own language.

notes: Skeleton summary; the Vinaya permission to learn the words of the Buddha 'in one's own dialect' (Cullavagga V.33 and parallels) is interpreted differently by the schools (not detailed here).

definitions.definition: Bodhidharma gave Huike the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra; Huike's followers carried it as the essence of mind; the Lengqie shizi ji builds a lineage of its masters.

name: The last thought and resolve at death

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Abiding in the brāhmī sthiti even at the time of death (antakāle 'pi), one attains brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'as his resolve is in this world, so he becomes on departing' (ChU 3.14.1); 'with whatever thought one has, one enters breath' (PrU 3.10); 'mind, remember what was done' (Īśa 17); meditation on Om until death determines one's world (PrU 5); the refuge in three sayings at death (ChU 3.17.6).

What one remembers at death shapes what follows: Bharata dying absorbed in a fawn became a deer; Ajāmila calling 'Nārāyaṇa' was rescued; remembrance of Nārāyaṇa at the end is the highest gain of life (BhP 2.1.6); the dying should meditate on the Lord (12.3.50); the yogin whose karma remains should recall yoga at departure (MkP 42.16-17); Kāśī tradition speaks of Śiva's instruction at death.
What one thinks at death determines what one becomes (Yogaśikhā 1.31; Nāradaparivrājaka 5).
Remembering or uttering the name at death saves even a sinner (Ajāmila); Haridāsa died with the name and Caitanya's form before him.
Tradition's account: Vallabha took renunciation at the end of life, left a final instruction (Śikṣāślokī) and entered the Ganges at Kāśī.
Liberation after death: the devotee attains the Lord's nature by his grace (Daśaślokī 2, 9).
The mind at death follows the habit of a lifetime; remember the Lord always (Jñāneśvarī 8).
The name uttered at death saves even unknowingly (Ajāmila).

relations.note: absorption at death vs absorption through a lifelong emotion

name: The last thought at death

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.5–7: whoever departs remembering the Lord alone at the time of the end comes to his state; whatever state one remembers when leaving the body, to that one goes, having always been shaped by it; therefore one should remember him at all times (and, for Arjuna, fight).

Whatever state one remembers when leaving the body, to that one goes, having been absorbed in it; so one should remember the Lord at all times (BhG 8.5–7); the guṇa prevailing at death determines the next birth (14.14–15).

definitions.definition: Ācārya Bhikṣu distinguished worldly (laukika) duties — social help, saving bodily life, charity to the unrestrained — from spiritual (lokottara) dharma, which alone stops karmic inflow; the first may be socially good but is not dharma in the strict sense.
Opponents hold that compassion that saves life (jīva-rakṣā) and giving are themselves religious merit and part of dharma.

The householder's discipline: the six directions and mutual duties, the four defilements of action and four biases, the six drains on wealth, true friends (DN 31); four sources of welfare now and hereafter (AN 8.54); five wrong trades (AN 5.177); the blessings (Snp 2.4).

name: Meditation and Abhidhamma study by laypeople

definitions.definition: Ledi Sayadaw taught insight and Abhidhamma to laypeople and authorized lay teachers.
Lay teachers (Saya Thetgyi, U Ba Khin, Goenka) and courses open to all.
Retreat centres open to lay meditators under the Buddha Sāsana Nuggaha Organization.
One can practise at home as well as in a monastery (Platform Sūtra); the formless verse for laypeople.
Dahui's letters teach officials to practise the huatou amid affairs.
Suzuki Shōsan: each occupation is buddha-practice.
When breath is exhausted and mind dissolves there is samarasa (GŚ 94); when breath and mind both dissolve one is liberated, not otherwise (Candrāvalokana).

In the HYP laya is the lord of the breath, resting on nāda (4.29); 'the forgetting of objects because latent impressions do not arise' (4.34); an indescribable bliss, whether or not it is called liberation (4.30–32); Ādinātha taught a crore and a quarter kinds (4.66; DYŚ: eight crore saṅketas, 14–24).

name: The learner's and the non-learner's union

definitions.definition: Arising from clear light, the body of union is the learner's union while the clear-light fire still purifies tendencies, and the non-learner's union when nothing remains to purify — the fruit.

relations.note: non-learner's union = buddhahood

name: The levels of speech (parā, paśyantī, madhyamā, vaikharī)

definitions.definition: Speech sprouts in parā, leafs in paśyantī, buds in madhyamā and blossoms in vaikharī; reversed, sound dissolves (Yogakuṇḍalī 3.18–19); from the power at the base arise all letters, mantras, scriptures and the seven notes (Yogaśikhā 3).

Parā (supreme speech = reflexive awareness itself, ĪPK 1.5.13), paśyantī, madhyamā and vaikharī; the Kashmir Śaivas add parā above the grammarians' three and deny that paśyantī is ultimate (Śivadṛṣṭi 2.1).
The Yoginīhṛdaya's question-and-answer is Śiva himself, by his vimarśa aspect, descending through paśyantī to vaikharī (Dīpikā on YH 1.1).

Bhartṛhari names three — vaikharī (articulated), madhyamā (mental, sequential), paśyantī (undivided, sequence withdrawn) — and calls the Veda their supreme station (VP 1.142 with Vṛtti); Nāgeśa adds parā and locates the four in the root centre, navel, heart and throat.
Four levels — parā, paśyantī, madhyamā, vaikharī — as the stages by which śabda-brahman, dwelling as kuṇḍalinī, becomes the letters (ŚT 1.14).
Nāda rises from the knot of Brahmā through navel, heart, throat and head to the mouth and has five names by these places (ŚR 1.3.3–5; Bṛhaddeśī 23–25).

name: Levels of truth across the families (two truths, three levels, niścaya–vyavahāra)

definitions.definition: The Buddhas teach relying on two truths, worldly convention and the ultimate.

Gauḍapāda distinguishes what exists by imagined or dependent convention from the ultimate, and the worldly, pure-worldly and supramundane; later Advaita counts three levels (ultimate, empirical, illusory); Śrīharṣa says the Brahma-vādin differs from the Mādhyamika in exempting consciousness.
The Jains speak of the ultimate and conventional standpoints (niścaya- and vyavahāra-naya) within a many-sided view.

relations.note: the reconciling principle P1 itself; the Advaita tradition holds the ultimate to be the self-luminous Brahman, the Madhyamaka holds it to be emptiness — the tradition of each rejects the other's ultimate

name: Liberation (mokṣa) in later Mīmāṃsā

definitions.definition: Release comes by the exhaustion of karma: avoiding desire-prompted and prohibited acts, performing obligatory and occasional ones, knowing the self, and exhausting past karma by experience, so that no new body arises; release is an absence, hence permanent, not an enjoyment of pleasure (Kumārila); the absolute dissolution of the threefold bond, without bliss (Pārthasārathi); some Bhāṭṭas held that innate bliss manifests.
The absolute end of embodiment through complete exhaustion of dharma and adharma, reached by abstention, experience and self-knowledge with calm and restraint; the self remains in mere being.
The sūtra and Śabara speak of heaven as the fruit of rites; release as a goal is added by the later teachers; later Bhāṭṭas teach dharma offered to Īśvara as the cause of the highest good.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Chapters 1–3 name the goal in several ways without systematising them: fitness for immortality (amṛtatva, 2.15); freedom from the bondage of birth and going to the state free from ill (padam anāmayam, 2.51); brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72); attaining the highest (param, 3.19); perfection (saṃsiddhi, 3.20); release from actions (3.31).

In the Gītā: brahmanirvāṇa (2.72, 5.24–26), non-return (8.15–16), entering the Lord after knowing him by devotion (18.55), freedom from birth, death and old age beyond the guṇas (14.20); in the Mokṣadharma: the twenty-fifth becoming alone (kevala) on awakening and attaining the state of the twenty-sixth (12.294, 12.296).
Entry through the sun and the vyūhas into Vāsudeva, the ekāntins entering him directly (MBh 12.332.13–18).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: those who take refuge in the Lord and strive for release (mokṣa) from old age and death know Brahman, the adhyātma and action completely (7.29); the great souls who come to him, having reached the highest perfection, do not come to rebirth, whereas all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return (8.15–16); the imperishable unmanifest, the supreme goal and the Lord's supreme abode, is that from which those who reach it do not return (8.21); departing by the bright course, knowers of Brahman go to Brahman — the course of non-return (anāvṛtti) (8.23–24, 8.26); offering every act to the Lord, one is freed (vimukta) from the bonds of action and comes to him (9.28).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: chs. 4–6 name the goal in several ways: not being born again and coming to the Lord (4.9); release from the inauspicious (4.16); going to the eternal Brahman (4.31, 5.6); supreme peace (4.39, 5.12, 5.29); non-return (apunarāvṛtti, 5.17); brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24–26); being forever free (sadā mukta) while intent on mokṣa (5.28); peace culminating in nirvāṇa (6.15); the highest course (parā gati, 6.45).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The chapters name the goal as: not being born again (13.24); crossing beyond death (13.26); going to the highest goal (13.29) or to the supreme (13.35), with release from the prakṛti of beings (13.35); reaching brahman (13.31); the highest perfection (14.1) and, having come to the same nature as the Lord, not being born at creation nor troubled at dissolution (14.2); the immortal, freedom from birth, death, old age and pain (13.13, 14.20); fitness for becoming brahman (14.26); the place from which none return, the Lord's supreme abode (15.4–6). Whether 'my state' (mad-bhāva, 13.19, 14.19) names the same goal the commentators read differently.

relations.note: release, being an absence, is permanent; heaven, being produced, perishes
