definitions.definition: Not produced but eternal: the bodiless nature of the self, the attainment of bliss and cessation of sorrow, revealed by knowledge; one in all (BS 3.4.52); no return.

name: Liberation and omniscience in the Gelug

definitions.definition: Liberation (nirvāṇa) is the final cessation of the afflictive obscurations by the wisdom directly realising emptiness; buddhahood (omniscience) is the further removal of the obscurations to knowledge, which only bodhicitta-motivated practice accomplishes.
The obscurations of afflictions and of knowables are exhausted only by the perfection of wisdom joined with method.
The pot breaks and water merges with water; the one who has died while living cannot die; freedom is now, in sahaj.
The soul (haṃs) that has received the true Name passes Kāl and returns to Satlok, never to be reborn.
Begampura, the city without sorrow.
Return of the soul to Sach Khand and beyond to Anāmī, within at most four lives of initiation.

relations.note: The Sant jīvan-mṛtak and sahaj correspond to liberation while living; the Kabīr Panth and Sant Mat add a post-mortem return to Satlok/Sach Khand.

name: Liberation while living

definitions.definition: The Gītā speaks of creation conquered 'even here' by those established in sameness (5.19), of brahmanirvāṇa near on every side for self-knowers (5.26), and of the one of steady wisdom and the one beyond the guṇas; Janaka claims freedom while ruling (MBh 12.17.18) and Sulabhā tests the claim (12.308).

notes: The word 'jīvanmukta' is later; see U13 for the Advaita concept.

name: The stages of life (āśrama)

definitions.definition: Bhṛgu teaches the four āśramas (MBh 12.184); Yudhiṣṭhira's wish to renounce is answered with arguments for the householder's and king's stage (12.7–36); Janaka teaches Śuka that the āśramas are to be passed in order, though one already free may renounce (12.312–313); the son urges seeking the self without delay (12.169).

notes: U05's contribution; the Dharmaśāstra account is given by U02.

name: The world as the Mother's play

definitions.definition: The Mother dances, sings and keeps time by herself (song ascribed to Kamalākānta).

name: The limbs of yoga in the Yoga Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The Yoga Upaniṣads give six-limbed (Amṛtanāda — with tarka; Dhyānabindu; Yogacūḍāmaṇi), eight-limbed (Darśana, Śāṇḍilya, Triśikhi, Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa, Varāha, Yogatattva) and fifteen-limbed (Tejobindu) schemes, often with a second, knowledge-based definition of each limb.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: The whole path is framed as the relation of the soul (aṅga, 'limb') to Śiva (liṅga): knowledge is the aṅga and the eternal knowable the liṅga; the aṅgaliṅgī has each mounted in the other.

name: Liṅga-initiation

definitions.definition: The guru bathes the disciple with consecrated water, whispers the five-syllable mantra secretly into his right ear, installs a liṅga in the disciple's breath and places it in his hand, to be worn for life; dīkṣā gives knowledge and destroys the fetters and removes the duality of guru and disciple.
Initiation is open to all — women, children and every occupation; Allama received the liṅga from the yogi Animiṣa.

notes: Secrecy: the mantra is given 'secretly' (nigūḍham, SSM 6.21).

name: Śiva as niṣkala and sakala; the liṅga

definitions.definition: Śiva alone is both partless Brahman and with form, so he alone is worshipped both in the formless liṅga and in the image; the unmarked (aliṅga) Śiva is the root of the mark (liṅga).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: The teachings it rests on were located; tea:siva-purana:1.5.10-13 has a partial or corrected result (see its check).

definitions.definition: The subtle body, produced first, unattached, constant, made of the principles from mahat down to the subtle elements (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas, the ten capacities and the five subtle elements), transmigrates, perfumed by the dispositions, without enjoying (SK 40); it needs a support like a picture or shadow (SK 41) and plays its parts like an actor (SK 42). The subtle bodies are constant; the bodies born of mother and father perish (SK 39). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra calls it 'seventeen, one' (3.9) and admits a conveying (ātivāhika) body (5.103). Vindhyavāsin denied the subtle body (Yuktidīpikā on SK 39).

relations.note: corresponds to the subtle body of Vedānta's three bodies, though composed differently (interpretive)

name: Death as union with the liṅga

definitions.definition: The death of a devotee is liṅgaikya; the dead are buried seated, holding the liṅga, rather than cremated, and no ancestral rites or death-pollution follow; the saints' deaths are narrated as union at sacred places.
One who at death drinks water in which a rudrākṣa has been pressed, thinking of Rudra, goes to Rudra's world.

notes: Burial practice details are general knowledge of the community (moderate confidence), not from a cited text.

name: Union of liṅga and aṅga (liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya, aikya)

definitions.definition: Liberation as the soul's immersion in the ocean of Śiva's bliss, free of longing for sense-pleasure; the self contemplated as dissolved in the sky of consciousness by the nature of sāmarasya; 'like water in water' in common exposition.
Death of the devotee is itself called liṅgaikya: Basava at Kūḍalasaṅgama, Allama and Akka at Kadaḷi.
In Śrīpati's Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita the soul (aṅga) qualified by devotion and Śiva (liṅga) qualified by Śakti attain union in equal essence; the non-duality is real, not an appearance.

name: The appearance of the liṅga of fire

definitions.definition: While Brahmā and Viṣṇu disputed supremacy a boundless column of fire appeared; neither could find its ends; Śiva appeared from it.

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: The four classifications, four guest-host relations, four illumination-function relations, three mysteries and three essentials, and the four shouts.

name: The necessity of a living master

definitions.definition: Only a living Sant Satguru can initiate, give the secret of the sound and guide and protect the soul within and at death; past masters cannot.
Kabīr promised a line of forty-two ācāryas through whom souls receive the Name, and warned of false teachers.

name: Loathing this defiled world, joyfully seeking the Pure Land

names.name: enri edo, gongu jōdo 厭離穢土・欣求浄土

definitions.definition: Vaidehī's turning from this evil world; the three realms as a dark house to be loathed; two practices of loathing (impurity contemplation) and joyful aspiration; Genshin's first two chapters.

The sixth point: sixteen (in the later arrangement) rules — abiding by the three general points, not speaking of others' faults, abandoning hope of results, not letting the practice become pride, and so on.

The seventh point: twenty-one (in the later arrangement) guidelines — doing everything with one intention, resolving at the start and reviewing at the end of the day, meditating on those who provoke one, training impartially and wholeheartedly.

The universe (loka) is finite world-space within infinite empty non-world, uncreated and beginningless, shaped like a man standing with arms akimbo, fourteen rajju high: the seven hells below, the disc of the middle world at the waist, the heavens above, and the abode of the liberated at the crown; mobile beings live only in the central channel (trasa-nāḍī) (TS 3–4, 5.12, 10.5–8; Tiloyapaṇṇatti; Lokaprakāśa).

name: The person is the measure of the world

definitions.definition: Whatever is in the world is in the person and vice versa: earth is the person's form, water moisture, fire heat, wind breath, space cavities, brahman the inner self; Prajāpati is mind, Indra ego-sense, the sun intake, Rudra anger, Soma serenity; creation is conception and the four ages childhood, youth, age and disease (Ca Śā 5.3-5); seeing the world in oneself and oneself in the world gives rise to the true understanding that leads to release (Śā 5.7).
Even the knower of the highest follows the worldly path; there fool and wise are alike; practices are delightful while unexamined.
The Buddhas outwardly follow worldly conventions — washing, eating, medicine, ageing — for the sake of beings, without being subject to them.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One should act with a view to holding the world together (3.20): people do what the best person does and follow the standard he sets (3.21); Kṛṣṇa himself acts for this reason (3.22–24); the wise should act unattached as the unwise act attached, and not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant attached to action (3.25–26, 3.29).

The wise act unattached for the welfare and cohesion of the world, as Janaka did and as the Lord himself acts though he has nothing to gain, without unsettling the understanding of the ignorant (BhG 3.20–26).

name: The Lord in the heart of all beings

definitions.definition: The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, moving them by his māyā (BhG 18.61); he is the self seated in the heart of all (10.20), the source of memory and knowledge (15.15), seated in the heart of all as the light of lights (13.17), and dwelling in his devotees' hearts destroys their darkness (10.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Kṛṣṇa says he is seated in the heart of all, and that memory, knowledge and removal (apohana: their loss, as most commentators take it, or reasoning that excludes) come from him (15.15); the knowable is said to be set in the heart of all (13.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: 'I am the self seated in the resting-place (āśaya) of all beings' (10.20); abiding in their own being or in his own (ātma-bhāva-stha; the reflexive leaves open whose), the Lord destroys the darkness born of ignorance (10.11).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.
Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.

definitions.definition: The Lord is in every body as musk in the deer's navel, oil in sesame, fire in flint; he is 'in the breath of the breath', not in temple, mosque, Kaaba or Kailāsa.
Between you and me what difference? As gold and bracelet, water and wave.
The neighbour in the mirror-city, near yet a hundred thousand leagues away; the one who speaks but is not seen.

relations.note: The Sant 'Lord within' and the Bāul 'Man of the Heart' are the indwelling divine in two idioms (P3-path); the Bāuls stress the body and the living human, the Sants the Name.

name: The loss of the canon (Digambara account)

definitions.definition: The knowledge of the Aṅgas and Pūrvas declined step by step after Mahāvīra — three omniscients (62 years), five śrutakevalins (100), eleven knowers of ten Pūrvas (183), five of the eleven Aṅgas (220), four of the Ācārāṅga (118) — until 683 years after the nirvāṇa no complete Aṅga was known; only portions reached Dharasena and Guṇadhara and were written as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa. The Śvetāmbara Āgamas are therefore not the original scripture.

name: The seven parables of the Lotus

definitions.definition: Burning house (ch. 3), lost son (4), medicinal herbs (5), conjured city (7), jewel in the robe (8), king's topknot jewel (14), physician and his sons (16) — each showing skillful means leading to the one vehicle.

notes: The traditional East Asian count (Vasubandhu's commentary, Tiantai); Kumārajīva chapter numbers.

definitions.definition: Associations of monks and lay people vowing together to be born in the West, from Huiyuan's vow of 402 to Shengchang's society, Zongze's Lotus assembly and Mao Ziyuan's repentance halls.

name: Powers, wealth and self-enjoyment as lower ends

definitions.definition: Wealth, lordly power (aiśvarya) and even kaivalya are ends the Lord can grant but lesser than him; the wise devotee seeks nothing but the Lord (ananya-prayojana); seeking other ends is an obstacle.

name: The luminous mind

definitions.definition: 'This mind is luminous, defiled by adventitious defilements'; the ordinary person does not understand this, so there is no development of mind for him; the noble disciple does (AN 1.51–52). The commentary identifies the luminous mind with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) (U37).
Mind is luminous by nature and the defilements are adventitious; hence emptiness is neither defiled nor pure; only the mind that is dharmatā is called luminous by nature.
Because mind is luminous by nature and the stains adventitious, the stains can be wholly removed by cultivating their antidote (seeing selflessness).
The nature of mind is originally pure, defiled by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).
Attributed to the Vibhajyavādins in the Vibhāṣā.
Rejected: a defiled mind is not by nature pure.

Mind itself is clear light: clear because it is awareness, non-conceptual because self-awareness does not conceptualize itself (Nāropa); 'as the sun's essence cannot be obscured by aeons of darkness, so the clear-light essence of mind cannot be obscured by aeons of saṃsāra' (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v12).

relations.note: later Mahāyāna texts cite a luminous mind; the Pali passage does not posit an innate buddha-nature
the commentarial identification with the life-continuum (U37)
The Theravāda commentaries read the luminous mind as the life-continuum; the Mahāsāṃghika as the mind's original purity.

notes: Shared id (U38 contributes the early-school definition).

definitions.definition: The commentary identifies the luminous mind of AN 1.49–52 with the life-continuum, defiled by adventitious defilements.
The radiant citta known in meditation; defilements are visitors (Ajahn Mun); ignorance can reside in its radiance (Ajahn Maha Boowa).

Months are lunar (new-moon-ending in the south and west, full-moon-ending in the north) and named after the asterism of the full moon (Caitra from Citrā, Vaiśākha from Viśākhā …); a lunar month without a solar ingress is intercalary (adhika) and one with two is lost (kṣaya); solar months run from ingress to ingress (SS 1.13), and some regions (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Bengal, Odisha) keep solar calendars; the yuga, year, month and day began together at Caitra's bright first (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11).

name: The madman's conduct (smyon pa'i spyod pa)

definitions.definition: Conduct beyond convention for the realized — 'practise the conduct of a madman in the great charnel ground' (Tilopa's Acintya) — embodied in the Kagyu 'divine madmen' Tsangnyön Heruka and Drukpa Kunley; not for beginners.
(As reported) As the power to intoxicate arises from kiṇva, jaggery, dhātakī flowers and the like, none of which has it singly, so consciousness from the elements.
The central consciousness whose unfolding gives the bliss of consciousness (PH 17-18).
The gap between breaths, cognitions, pleasure and pain, where reality shines (VBT 24-26, 61-62, 103, 126).
The unmeṣa between one thought and the next (SK 3.9).
Eating one dies, not eating one dies — one crosses by restraint; laugh and play but do not break the mind (Gorakh Bānī); breathe slowly, neither holding too long nor releasing hastily (GŚ 51).

The Abhidharma's four conditions, own-natures of dharmas, conditioned characteristics (arising, abiding, ceasing), the unconditioned and the 'imperishable' of karma are examined and shown not to exist by own-nature (MMK 1, 7, 17).

name: Madhyamaka's critique of a creator God

definitions.definition: If Īśvara creates unwillingly he depends on another, if by desire he depends on desire; the elements are not Īśvara (BCA 9.119–126).
An eternal cause would produce all effects at once or never (TS, examination of Īśvara).
The authorless Veda and the denial of an omniscient being are rejected (MH 9–10).
The same in the Tattvasaṅgraha's examinations of revelation and of the seer of supersensible things.
The means of knowledge are established neither by themselves nor by others nor by their objects (VV 31–51); the sixteen categories are ground down as mutually dependent (Vaidalyaprakaraṇa).

Arising from itself (the pre-existent effect) is pointless and endless (Buddhapālita on MMK 1.1); primal matter cannot be the one eternal cause of the world (MH 6); the Sāṃkhyas are among those who do not pass beyond 'is' and 'is not' (RĀ 1.61).
Bhāviveka's chapter on the Vedānta sets out the doctrine of the one eternal self (puruṣa) and rejects a permanent agentless self as unable to act or be known (MH 8).
Śāntarakṣita rejects the Upaniṣadic single eternal consciousness because cognitions are many and momentary (TS, examination of the self).

Consciousness is no more real than its object; reflexive awareness and the storehouse are rejected; 'mind only' denies a creator other than mind and is of provisional meaning (MA 6.45–97; BCA 9.15–25).
Bhāviveka rejects the real other-dependent nature and accepts external objects conventionally (MH 5).

Later Indian and Tibetan doxographies divide Mādhyamikas: by method into Prāsaṅgika and Svātantrika; by the account of the conventional into Sautrāntika-Madhyamaka (external objects conventionally, Bhāviveka) and Yogācāra-Madhyamaka (mind-only conventionally, Śāntarakṣita); Maitrīpa's Tattvaratnāvalī into those holding non-duality illusion-like and those holding the non-foundation of all dharmas; the Jñānasārasamuccaya ranks Madhyamaka above the other tenet systems.

The tradition's line runs from the Buddha's Perfection of Wisdom through Nāgārjuna (who received the sūtras from the nāgas in the tradition's account), Āryadeva and Rāhulabhadra, to the commentators Buddhapālita, Bhāviveka and Candrakīrti, Śāntideva, and Śrīgupta–Jñānagarbha–Śāntarakṣita–Kamalaśīla, and on to Tibet (Atiśa; Patsab Nyima Drak) and China (Kumārajīva). Commentary on a root text by a lineage master is the mode of transmission; no secret initiation is required, but emptiness is to be taught only to a fit vessel.
Pali (Māgadhī) is the language of intrinsic nature and the root language of all beings; the analytical knowledge of language recognizes it.

name: Great brahman as the Lord's womb; the Lord as seed-giving father (BhG 14.3–4)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The Lord's womb is great brahman (mahad brahma); in it he places the germ, and from that the origin of all beings comes (14.3). Of whatever forms come into being in all wombs, great brahman is the womb and the Lord is the seed-giving father (14.4). The commentators take 'great brahman' here as prakṛti; the verses call it only 'great brahman' and 'my womb'.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: New concept, merged from extractor A's cpt:mahad-brahma-as-womb and extractor B's cpt:mahad-brahma-yoni. The commentators identify this 'great brahman' with prakṛti (the Lord's prakṛti of the three guṇas, or non-conscious matter in its subtle state); the verses do not use that word. Compare 9.10 (prakṛti gives birth under the Lord's oversight) and 7.10 (the Lord as the eternal seed of all beings).

definitions.definition: (As reported) The span of the fixed round of every being.
Compassion is the seed, water and ripening of buddhahood and is praised first (MA 1.2).
Compassion alone is the root of all Buddha qualities and is cultivated first (Bhāvanākrama I).

name: Mahāmudrā (the great seal) in the Kagyu

definitions.definition: The nature of one's own mind — empty, luminous, unborn, beyond speech and thought — which 'seals' all phenomena; at once the ground (mind's nature), the path (recognizing and sustaining it through the guru's pointing-out, śamatha–vipaśyanā and the four yogas) and the fruit (the dharmakāya). 'Though Mahāmudrā cannot be shown…' (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v1).
The Mahāmudrā of the amulet box: ground, path and fruit enclosed together; the three self-liberations.

relations.note: the Nāth/haṭha 'mahāmudrā' and sahaja absorption share words, not the Buddhist view of emptiness
Mahāmudrā's mind-nature is the sūtra 'luminous mind' as recognized in meditation

notes: Distinct from prc:mahamudra (the haṭha seal) and the U28/U21 senses of trm:mahamudra.

name: The union of Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen

definitions.definition: Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen are of one essence and may be practised together (3rd Karmapa's Karma Nyingthig; Karma Chagmé; Tselé Natsok Rangdröl).

notes: Nyingma masters also compare them; distinctions insisted on by either side are recorded in U45.

definitions.definition: (Jain report) Gosāla's lore of foretelling gain, loss, pleasure, pain, life and death.
A lore that sometimes fails and brings no release.
Monks and nuns wander, beg, keep no possessions, harm no creature and dwell in remembrance of the incarnations; open to women and all castes.
A teaching claimed from the Buddha, a Saṅgha, learned elders or one elder is checked against the discourses and the discipline (DN 16).

name: The grace and company of great souls

definitions.definition: Devotion comes chiefly by the grace of great souls or a drop of the Lord's grace; their company is hard to gain, unfathomable and unfailing, and is itself gained by his grace, for there is no difference between him and his people.
The Āḻvārs seek the company and service of devotees: the Tiruppāvai's girls wake one another before approaching the Lord; Kulaśekhara longs for the devotees of Śrīraṅgam.

Four Upaniṣadic sentences of identity — prajñānaṃ brahma, ahaṃ brahmāsmi, tat tvam asi, ayam ātmā brahma — understood through implication as conveying a partless meaning; the means of liberating knowledge.

name: The four great sayings (mahāvākya)

definitions.definition: A later grouping (Advaita tradition) of four Upaniṣadic sentences, one from each Veda: prajñānaṃ brahma (Ṛgveda: AU 3.1.3), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (White Yajurveda: BAU 1.4.10), tat tvam asi (Sāmaveda: ChU 6.8.7), ayam ātmā brahma (Atharvaveda: MāU 2; also BAU 2.5.19). The Upaniṣads themselves do not use the word 'mahāvākya'.

U04 contribution: the minor Upaniṣads treat the four sayings as a secret initiatory teaching (Śukarahasya), assign one to each Veda and maṭha (Maṭhāmnāya), give them to the renouncer at initiation (Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka) and read them as the Goddess (Bahvṛca).

notes: Ref correction: AU 3.1.3 is also cited as AU 3.3 (two-level numbering); both refer to the same passage.

queries: prepared segments: AU 3.1.3, BĀU 1.4.10, ChU 6.8.7, MāU 2, BĀU 2.5.19
checks.note: All four sayings are located: 'prajñānaṃ brahma' AU 3.1.3 (= AU 3.3); 'ahaṃ brahmāsmi' BĀU 1.4.10; 'tat tvam asi' ChU 6.8.7 and its refrain; 'ayam ātmā brahma' MāU 2 and BĀU 2.5.19. Their assignment to the four Vedas matches the texts' Veda affiliations checked above. That the word 'mahāvākya' is not in these Upaniṣads and the grouping is later Advaita usage is consistent with the texts searched. All 5 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (AU 3.1.3; BĀU 1.4.10; ChU 6.8.7; MāU 2; BĀU 2.5.19). It rests on 5 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages. Refs given in another numbering: AU 3.3 = AU 3.1.3 in three-level numbering.

Located: Śukarahasya (the four sayings with seer and metre), Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38, the Maṭhāmnāya (eBhāratī: tattvamasi, ahaṃ brahmāsmi, ayam ātmā …) and Bahvṛca (prajñānaṃ brahma …). All 4 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text. Some rest on teachings whose ref was corrected or only partly confirmed; the content is located, only the numbering changes: tea:bahvrca-upanisad:4-9 (partially-confirmed).

name: The ten grounds of the Mahāvastu

definitions.definition: Durārohā, Baddhamānā, Puṣpamaṇḍitā, Rucirā, Cittavistarā, Rūpavatī, Durjayā, Janmanideśa, Yauvarājya, Abhiṣeka.

relations.note: The Daśabhūmika's ten grounds (Pramuditā …) have different names and contents; any historical link is a scholarly hypothesis.

name: The Mahāvidyās as the ten avatāras

definitions.definition: Toḍala 10.9-11 identifies the Mahāvidyās with Viṣṇu's avatāras — Tārā the Fish, Bagalā the Tortoise, Dhūmāvatī the Boar, Chinnamastā Nṛsiṃha, Bhuvaneśvarī Vāmana, Mātaṅgī Rāma, Tripurā Paraśurāma, Bhairavī Balabhadra, Mahālakṣmī the Buddha, Durgā Kalki, Kālī Kṛṣṇa — and promises equality with Mahādeva to their worshipper.

relations.standpoint: Śākta (the Goddess as source of the avatāras)
relations.note: Vaiṣṇava traditions reject the subordination of the avatāras to the Goddess

name: Bagalāmukhī / Pītāmbarā (eighth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Golden-yellow, in yellow garments, seizing an enemy's tongue with her left hand and raising a club with her right, on a throne amid an ocean (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: the power of paralysing (stambhana) enemies and speech; the one-faced Mahārudra, destroyer of the world, is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.14).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Bhairavī / Tripurabhairavī (fifth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Red as a thousand rising suns, wearing a garland of heads, holding rosary and book (or noose and goad) and showing fearlessness and boon (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: the fierce power of dissolution and austerity; Dakṣiṇāmūrti is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.11); in the Bṛhaddharma Satī herself is Bhairavī within Śiva's body.

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Bhuvaneśvarī (fourth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Radiant as the rising sun, three-eyed, crowned with the crescent, holding noose and goad and showing boon and fearlessness (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: queen of the worlds and of space; Tryambaka is her Bhairava because he delights in her in heaven, earth and the underworld (Toḍala 1.9-10); in the Devī Gītā the supreme Goddess appears as Bhuvaneśvarī.

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Chinnamastā (sixth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Self-decapitated, holding her own head and a cleaver, three streams of blood rising from her neck — one into her own mouth and two into those of her attendants Ḍākinī and Varṇinī — standing on the god of love and his wife in union (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: Kabandha ('the headless') is her Bhairava, by whose worship one becomes lord of all powers (Toḍala 1.12-13). A Bengali account (Prāṇatoṣiṇī, citing earlier texts) tells that she cut off her own head to feed her hungry attendants.

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: The Bhairava consorts of the Mahāvidyās

definitions.definition: Each Mahāvidyā is worshipped with her Bhairava at her right: Mahākāla (Dakṣiṇakālī), Akṣobhya (Tārā), five-faced Śiva (Tripurasundarī), Tryambaka (Bhuvaneśvarī), Dakṣiṇāmūrti (Bhairavī), Kabandha (Chinnamastā), none for the widow Dhūmāvatī, Mahārudra (Bagalā), Mataṅga (Mātaṅgī), Sadāśiva as Viṣṇu (Kamalā) (Toḍala 1.3-19).

name: Dhūmāvatī (seventh Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: An old, smoky, dishevelled widow in a chariot bannered with a crow, holding a winnowing basket, hungry and quarrelsome (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: she has no Bhairava because she bears the form of a widow (Toḍala 1.13); worshipped to remove enemies and misfortune.

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Kālī (first Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Dark, naked, four-armed — sword and freshly severed head in the left hands, fear-dispelling and boon-giving gestures in the right — with a garland of heads, a girdle of hands, loose hair, lolling tongue and three eyes, standing on Śiva as a corpse in the cremation ground (Kālī Tantra dhyāna in the Tantrasāra). Teaching: she devours Time (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32); without her Śiva is a corpse (Toḍala 1.25); in the Toḍala she became Kṛṣṇa (10.11).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Kamalā / Kamalātmikā (tenth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Golden, seated on a lotus, bathed by four elephants pouring nectar from jars, holding lotuses and showing boon and fearlessness (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: a tantric Lakṣmī of prosperity and grace; Sadāśiva in Viṣṇu's form is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.16).

members: Bhairava: Sadāśiva in the form of Viṣṇu
avatāra (Toḍala 10): — (the Toḍala assigns Buddha to Mahālakṣmī)
notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Mātaṅgī (ninth Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Dark green, playing the vīṇā, with a parrot (standard dhyāna, recalled); as Ucchiṣṭa-Mātaṅgī she receives leftover food. Teaching: goddess of speech, music and learning, a 'tantric Sarasvatī'; Mataṅga (Dakṣiṇāmūrti, 'joy of the world') is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.15).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: The origin of the ten Mahāvidyās in the Satī–Śiva story

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: Satī wishes to attend her father Dakṣa's sacrifice, to which Śiva was not invited; when Śiva refuses, she turns dark and terrible and fills the ten directions with ten forms, the Mahāvidyās; she explains that she is the root Nature who took birth to win him, and goes (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.78-134; Mahābhāgavata 8). Her death at the sacrifice leads to the scattering of her body and the pīṭhas (Kālikā Purāṇa 18).

name: Ṣoḍaśī / Tripurasundarī (third Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Red, a sixteen-year-old, holding noose, goad, sugarcane bow and five flower arrows, seated on Sadāśiva on a couch whose legs are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: supreme beauty and bliss; with the five-faced Śiva as her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.7-8); her full cult is Śrīvidyā (U23).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: Tārā (second Mahāvidyā)

definitions.definition: Blue-black, short and pot-bellied, standing in the archer's stance on a corpse, wearing a tiger skin and a garland of heads, with a single tawny braid (ekajaṭā) bearing Akṣobhya; in her four hands sword and cleaver, skull-cup and blue lotus (standard dhyāna, recalled). Teaching: she who ferries across (tāraṇa) and goddess of speech (Nīlasarasvatī); Akṣobhya is her Bhairava because he drank the ocean's poison unagitated (Toḍala 1.4-6); linked with Mahācīna, Vasiṣṭha and the Buddha (Rudrayāmala 17; Tārā Tantra 1).

notes: Iconography marked 'standard dhyāna, recalled' is from memory of the common meditation verses, not checked against a text in Phase B.

name: The great vow of the skull (mahāvrata)

definitions.definition: Living as a Kapālin with a skull-bowl and skull-staff, in imitation of Bhairava's penance for Brahmā's head; by it a man becomes an ascetic (as reported).
The Lākula observance 'beyond the world' with skull and khaṭvāṅga.

relations.note: the vow re-enacts the myth

name: The four yogas as one great yoga

definitions.definition: The Yogabīja and the Haṭharatnāvalī teach that mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja are aspects of one 'great yoga' (mahāyoga), against a strict hierarchy of lower and higher yogas.

name: The four Māheśvara schools of the doxographers

definitions.definition: Vācaspati: Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Kāruṇika-siddhāntins, Kāpālikas.
Yāmuna and Rāmānuja: Kāpālikas, Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas, Śaivas.
Guṇaratna: Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Mahāvratadharas, Kālamukhas.

name: The transmission of the Maitreya teachings

definitions.definition: Maitreya taught Asaṅga, who taught Vasubandhu (the 'lineage of vast conduct'); in Tibet the teachings came through Sajjana to Ngok Loden Sherab (the explanatory, analytic transmission) and to Tsen Kawoche (the meditative transmission); two texts were, by tradition, rediscovered by Maitrīpa.

notes: Tibetan tradition's account.

definitions.definition: Āṇava mala, one with many powers, ripens through embodied experience and Śiva's concealing power until it is ready to be removed; then śaktipāta.
Malaparipākam, with iruviṉaiyoppu, is the condition for the descent of grace.
Urine, faeces and sweat and the wastes of each tissue (AHS Sū 1.13; Su Sū 15.5; Ca Ci 15.18-19); the body is rooted in doṣa, dhātu and mala (Su Sū 15.3).
The mind is the battlefield: restless elephant, thief, bird; defeat and victory are the mind's; the Name recited while it wanders is not remembrance; when it dies the Lord is found.
Sundardās: the mind is thief, monkey, mad elephant, tamed only by the guru's word and discrimination.
The mind is Kāl's agent, attached to the soul up to Trikuṭī; the soul must be freed from it by the sound current.
The mind addressed in every song ('o mind'), to be turned to truth and to the Man.
The eleventh organ, partaking of both sense and action capacities, whose function is construction (saṅkalpa) (SK 27).

name: The mind (manas) as one and atomic

definitions.definition: One per body, atomic; its mark is the non-simultaneity of cognitions; apparent simultaneity is like the firebrand circle, due to its swift movement (NS 1.1.16, 3.2.56–59); cognition belongs to the self, not the mind (NS 3.2.19).
An eternal atomic substance, one in each body because efforts and cognitions are not simultaneous (VS 3.2.1–3, 7.1.30 C); its first motion at creation is caused by adṛṣṭa (VS 5.2.14).

Beyond the senses; one, atomic; its presence or absence explains knowledge arising or not; it directs the senses, restrains itself, reasons and considers, and then buddhi decides (Ca Sū 8.4-7; Śā 1.18-23); unconscious though active, the self being the conscious agent (Śā 1.75-76); three kinds by guṇa (Śā 3.13; 4.36); located between head and palate, with citta in the heart (Bhela Ci 8).

relations.note: Caraka counts only manas and buddhi here; no fourfold inner organ

definitions.definition: Mind is swiftest of flying things (RV 6.9.5), it wanders far and can be called back from Yama (10.58), it is yoked by the inspired (5.81.1; VS 11.1); the Śivasaṅkalpa verses call it the divine far-goer of waking and sleep, the one light of lights, knowing, thought and steadfastness, the immortal light within, holder of past, present and future, in which the Vedas are set and all thought woven, the heart-seated charioteer (VS 34.1–6); desire was its first seed (RV 10.129.4).

name: The two doṣas of the mind (rajas and tamas)

definitions.definition: Rajas and tamas are the doṣas of the mind (Ca Sū 1.57; Śā 4.34; AHS Sū 1.21); they are allayed by knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (Ca Sū 1.58) — 'knowledge of intellect, steadiness and the self' (AHS Sū 1.26).

name: The diseases of the mind (mānas rog)

definitions.definition: Delusion is the root of all mental disease; lust, greed and anger are wind, phlegm and bile; cured by Rāma's grace with the true guru as physician, faith, restraint and devotion.

name: The Man of the Heart (maner mānuṣ)

definitions.definition: The divine person dwelling in the human body — the unknown bird, the uncatchable Man, the neighbour in the mirror-city — longed for, sought through the guru and met in the body; worship of the human leads to becoming the golden human.

relations.note: Bāul and Sahajiyā names of the same indwelling Man.

definitions.definition: The Goddess's supreme abode - the jewel island with enclosures of metals and gems and the Cintāmaṇi palace (Devī Bhāgavata), and Lalitā's city Śrīnagara with its enclosures (Lalitopākhyāna).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: DBhP 12.10-12 (local eBhārati) and Lalitopākhyāna 3.31-37 located. All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

name: Maṇidvīpa and Śrīnagara, the Goddess's world

definitions.definition: The jewel island in the ocean of nectar with its wish-tree gardens and palace of wish-gems (SL 8; Devī Bhāgavata 12.10-12).

Śrīnagara on Meru's central peak with its enclosures, the Cintāmaṇi palace whose four doors are the four āmnāyas, and the couch of five corpses, visualized in worship with forty-four mantras (LSN 21-23; PKS 3.10).

name: The maidservant's mood (mañjarī-bhāva)

definitions.definition: Summary: the aspiration to serve Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa as one of Rādhā's young maidservants, seeking no union with Kṛṣṇa, taught in Raghunātha Dāsa's Vilāpakusumāñjali and cultivated through the inner perfected identity; its specifics are transmitted by the guru.

notes: Recorded at summary level; the lineages treat detailed identity instruction (siddha-praṇālī) as confidential.

definitions.definition: The part of the Veda recited as prompting the performance; meaningful like any sentence against the objection that mantras are meaningless (MS 1.2.31–40, 2.1.32).
Mantras serve by recalling items connected with the performance.

name: The mantra as the deity's body

definitions.definition: Śiva's body is made of mantras (the five brahma-mantras as his faces); the mantra is the deity, not a name for it.
The deity arises from and dissolves into its seed syllable; the mantra is the deity's speech and essence.
The Namaskāra mantra is the embodiment of the five supreme beings and is meditated on as letters on lotuses in word-based meditation (padastha).
The mantra-manuals treat letters and seeds as the bodies of their deities.

Śiva has no body of māyā; for worship and grace he is given a body of mantras — the five brahma-mantras (Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta) as his faces and the six limb-mantras — made of the pure śakti; the mantras themselves are conscious beings in office.

relations.note: scripture as Sadāśiva's body (U08)

definitions.definition: 'Veda is the name for mantra and brāhmaṇa'; Brāhmaṇas are injunctions, the rest explanatory statement (ĀpŚS 24.1.30–33).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:apastamba-srautasutra:24.1.30-33 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: A mantra must be received from a qualified guru — pure, self-controlled, learned in the Āgamas and Veda, devoted to japa, calm, following yoga — by a qualified disciple who serves the guru and is tested one to four years according to class (ŚT 2.141–153); the mantra is kept secret (gopana is the tenth purification, ŚT 2.122); defective mantras must be purified (ŚT 2.64–123).

relations.note: the Śaiva initiation types into which mantra-dīkṣā fits

name: Testing a mantra's suitability (mantra-śodhana)

definitions.definition: Before giving a mantra the guru tests its fit with the disciple by tables of letters — the akaḍama-cakra and others dividing mantras into 'accomplished, to be accomplished, well accomplished, hostile' (siddha, sādhya, susiddha, ari) — and by the 'debt and credit' (ṛṇa-dhana) reckoning between the letters of the mantra and of the disciple's name; the Padārthādarśa on ŚT 2 gathers several such methods.

notes: Located in the Padārthādarśa on Śāradātilaka paṭala 2 (checked in the local e-text; verse anchors not fixed). Procedures not recorded.

name: The division of Śaivism into Atimārga and Mantramārga
members: Atimārga (Pāśupata, Lākula; later also Kālāmukha/Kāpālika in scholarly schemes)
Mantramārga (Siddhānta; Bhairava tantras — Mantrapīṭha and Vidyāpīṭha; Vāma; Gāruḍa; Bhūta)

relations.note: the Mantramārga's dual goal marks it off from the Atimārga

notes: U17 owns the Atimārga's own account (lin:atimarga). The 'householder vs ascetic' contrast follows scholarly synthesis (Sanderson) of the texts and is to be checked against the Niśvāsamukha in Phase D.

definitions.definition: The Mantramārga's scriptures rank the Atimārga (the ascetic Pāśupata and Lākula paths, for liberation alone) below the Mantramārga, whose initiates may seek powers and enjoyments as well as liberation, and which is open to householders.

name: Mantrapīṭha and Vidyāpīṭha
notes: The Kāmika says only that the Bhairava tantra is 'twofold'; the names Mantrapīṭha/Vidyāpīṭha are from other scriptures (e.g. Jayadrathayāmala) and scholarly synthesis.

definitions.definition: The twofold Bhairava tantra of the southern face (Kāmika: 'twofold'): the Mantrapīṭha centred on male Bhairava forms such as Svacchanda, and the Vidyāpīṭha centred on goddesses and feminine mantras, subdivided into Yāmala and Śakti tantras.

name: The manvantaras and the fourteen Manus

definitions.definition: Each day of Brahmā has fourteen Manus: Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama (Auttama), Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, Vaivasvata (the present), then the Sāvarṇis beginning with Sūrya-Sāvarṇi (the Devī Māhātmya's Suratha); each interval has its Indra, gods, seven sages and avatāra; names of the later Manus vary between Purāṇas.

notes: MkP 50-100 (chapter colophons checked) narrates the manvantaras.

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: DM 13 (MkP 93.17) located; MkP manvantara chapters confirmed by colophons (e.g. 53 'manvantarakathana'); the local e-text ends at ch. 93, so 'MkP 50-100' is only partly checkable. All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: The Evil One, lord of death and sensual desire, who tempts and threatens the Buddha and the nuns (Snp 3.2; SN 4; SN 5), has ten armies (Snp 3.2), and finds no opening in one who roams in his own pasture (SN 47.6) or develops mindfulness of the body (MN 119).
Mārga: the 'sought-out' music fixed by Brahmā and Bharata, performed before Śiva for well-being; deśī: regional music sung at will that delights people (ŚR 1.1.22–23; Bṛhaddeśī 13).

name: The marks of the saint (the true devotee)

definitions.definition: The saint calls the afflicted his own, is softer than wax yet firm as diamond, bears insult like water quenching fire, and sees the Lord in all beings.
Rāma dwells in hearts free of lust, anger, pride and greed, that see others' wives as mothers and others' wealth as poison and rejoice in others' good.
The true Vaiṣṇava knows others' pain, helps without pride and speaks ill of none (Narsinh Mehta).
The best devotee sees the Lord in all and all in the Lord.

relations.note: the regional saints' lists restate the Bhāgavata's marks of the devotee
the Gītā's steady-minded one and the saint share equanimity and freedom from passion

definitions.definition: Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, cognition (NS 1.1.10).
Inhalation and exhalation, closing and opening of the eyes, life, movement of the mind, modifications of the other senses, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort (VS 3.2.4 C).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): 107 marmas of five kinds (Su Śā 6.3-4); the three great ones — head, heart, bladder (Ca Sū 29.3). Detailed treatment: U58.

Known through the Trika: Mata scriptures reject the samaya rules and lineage-based exclusions in favour of realizing one's own unbounded awareness, and rank between Dakṣiṇa and Kula (or between Kula and Trika) in the hierarchy of revelations.

name: The letters as the fifty seats

definitions.definition: The Goddess is 'of the form of the fifty seats' (LSN 156): the fifty letters of the alphabet as sacred seats; the mātṛkā is placed on the disciple at initiation (PKS 1.38-39).

The fifty letters in natural order (mātṛkā, A to KṢA) as the emanation of the tattvas (Parātrīśikā 5-9), and in the scrambled order mālinī uniting vowels and consonants (Śiva and Śakti); the ground of limited knowledge when unrecognized (Śiva Sūtra 1.4) and of liberation when awakened by the teacher (2.7).

Śabda-brahman, dwelling as kuṇḍalinī, manifests as the letters (ŚT 1.14); the fifty letters from a to kṣa are the Goddess's body and the matrix of all mantras, installed on the body in mātṛkā-nyāsa and used as a rosary of letters.

name: Fifty letters, fifty forms of Viṣṇu

definitions.definition: The fifty letters designate fifty forms of Viṣṇu — Aja, Ānanda, Indra, Īśa, Ugra, Ūrja, Ṛtambhara and so on — used in nyāsa and worship.

The word appears as Indra's many-formed powers (BAU 2.5.19, quoting RV 6.47.18), as deceit (PrU 1.16), and in the Śvetāśvatara as the Lord's power: 'know prakṛti to be māyā and the great Lord the māyin' (4.10), from which the māyin projects the world and in which the other is confined (4.9); knowing him there is 'the cessation of all māyā' (1.10). Whether māyā here means the world's unreality is not stated by the texts (see dsp:world-real-or-appearance).

Bhagavad Gītā 7.14–15, 7.25: the Lord's divine māyā, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross; those who take refuge in him alone cross it; it carries off the knowledge of evil-doers; veiled by his yoga-māyā the Lord is not manifest to all.
The Lord's beginningless indescribable power of three guṇas, inferred from its effects, by which Brahman appears as the world; neither being nor non-being; removable by knowledge.
'I and mine, you and yours' is māyā; the world is a colourless painting on the void, neither simply true nor false; worship of Hari alone is real, the world a dream.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

Located: BĀU 2.5.19 ('indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate', = RV 6.47.18, found in DCS); PrU 1.16 ('na māyā ca'); ŚU 4.9-10 and 1.10 ('viśvamāyānivṛttiḥ'). All 2 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 2.5.19; PrU 1.16). It rests on 4 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

relations.note: One entity viewed cosmically (māyā) and individually (avidyā) in the Vivaraṇa/Saṃkṣepaśārīraka usage; distinguished by Vidyāraṇya.

definitions.definition: Māyā is not an independent illusion but the Goddess's own power: she is Mahāmāyā, queen of the supreme Brahman, who makes the universe whirl (SL 98), 'of the form of both knowledge and ignorance' (LSN 87).
She herself becomes mind, space and the elements; nothing is beyond her transformation (SL 35); yet Bhāskararāya's tradition also names her 'substratum of the illusory world' (LSN 142).
The Kaula Upaniṣad: ignorance is knowledge, the world is the Lord, the impermanent is permanent — nothing is other than Śakti (with Bhāskararāya's gloss).

relations.note: Advaita's māyā is indeterminable and sublated by knowledge; the Śākta māyā is the real power of the Goddess

definitions.definition: Māyā is the great swindler (mahāṭhaginī) who takes a different form in every house — Kamalā, Bhavānī, the idol, the pilgrim-water — and binds with the three qualities; at the origin 'one woman' from whom the gods came; often 'gold and woman'.

Māyā is the wondrous, creative or cunning power of a god: by it Varuṇa measured out the earth (RV 5.85.5), Indra goes in many forms (6.47.18); the wise see the bird anointed with the asura's māyā with heart and mind (10.177.1).

name: Māyāmoha: the Purāṇic account of Buddhist and Jain teaching

definitions.definition: The Purāṇas report that Viṣṇu emitted a deluding form (Māyāmoha), or became the Buddha, to lead the demons away from the Veda by teaching Jain and Buddhist doctrine (VP 3.17-18; Agni 16; BhP 1.3.24; cf. BhP 5.6.9 on the Arhat king) - an opponent's report.

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: Dvaita's case against Advaita: ignorance cannot belong to a self-luminous attributeless self or to the all-knower; the indeterminable is unproven; the world's falsity is unproven; 'māyā' in scripture means God's will; and an attributeless Brahman is indistinguishable from the Mādhyamika void.

The texts explain the name in two ways: as 'force' — kuṇḍalinī rises 'by force' (haṭhāt, HYP 3.111) and is to be seized 'by force' (3.109) — and as the union of 'ha', the sun, and 'ṭha', the moon (Yogabīja; quoted by the Jyotsnā as from the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati), i.e. of prāṇa and apāna in breath-control. The Śārṅgadhara Paddhati distinguishes Gorakṣa's haṭha from that of Mṛkaṇḍu's son.

In the texts 'upaniṣad' means a secret teaching or hidden name/correspondence: its upaniṣad is 'the real behind the real' (BAU 2.1.20); the upaniṣad of the asuras (ChU 8.8.4); 'we have told you the upaniṣad' (Kena 4.7); the rule 'do not beg' is the upaniṣad of the breath-brahman (KauU 2.1). The gods love the cryptic (AU 1.3.14).

queries: prepared segments: BĀU 2.1.20, ChU 8.8.4, Kena 4.7, KauU 2.1, AU 1.3.14
checks.note: All 5 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 2.1.20; ChU 8.8.4; Kena 4.7; KauU 2.1; AU 1.3.14). It rests on 6 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Against Kautsa's claim that mantras are meaningless, Yāska holds they are meaningful because their words are those of ordinary speech; the one who recites without understanding is a load-bearing post (Nirukta 1.15–18).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:nirukta:1.15 (confirmed); tea:nirukta:1.16 (confirmed); tea:nirukta:1.18 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Six: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation and non-apprehension; a means of knowledge apprehends the previously unapprehended and is free from causal defect and from any sublating cognition.
Five: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison and postulation; every experience other than memory is a means of knowledge.

relations.note: dharma is known only by verbal testimony (the Veda)

definitions.definition: Units from the prāṇa (the time of a breath) and vināḍī to the nāḍī, the sidereal and civil day, lunar and solar months, the year which is a day of the gods (SS 1.11–14), up to the yuga and kalpa; nine kinds of measure are distinguished — of Brahmā, the gods, the fathers, Prajāpati, Jupiter, the sun, the civil day, the moon and the stars (SS 14).

name: The Medicine Buddha's teaching in Tanaduk

definitions.definition: The Four Tantras are taught in the medicine city Tanaduk by the Medicine Buddha's emanation Rigpé Yeshe, at the request of Yilé Kyé, before four retinues.

name: The tree of healing (the three trees of the Root Tantra)

definitions.definition: The whole science summarized as three trees — the basis, diagnosis, treatment — with roots, nine trunks, forty-seven branches and two hundred and twenty-four leaves; flowers of health and long life; fruits of Dharma, wealth and happiness.

members: root of the basis (health and disease)

definitions.definition: Illness from excessive or unbalanced striving — rising heat, cold legs, fear, exhaustion — cured by naikan and the soft-butter method (Hakuin, Yasenkanna).
Wrong ways of sitting are called a 'sickness, not meditation' (Platform Sūtra); confused thought and dullness are sicknesses (Yongjia).

The Contemplation Sūtra's first thirteen contemplations are meditative good, the three meritorious acts and nine grades non-meditative good — Śākyamuni's 'essential gate'; the Buddha's intent, however, is the calling of the name ('universal vow').

name: Menstruation as sacred in Śākta rites

definitions.definition: The Goddess's menstruation is honoured at Kāmākhyā (Ambubachi); some late Kaula tantras treat menstrual blood ('self-born flower') as a sacred substance (restricted, named only).
Mental action is the gravest of the three kinds of action, as the sages' anger emptied the Daṇḍaka forest — which shows that minds act directly on minds without external objects.

name: The mental origin of disease: ignorance and the three poisons

definitions.definition: The distant cause of all disease is ignorance of selflessness, never parted from beings as a shadow from a bird; from it come desire, hatred and delusion, and from them rlung, mkhris pa and bad kan.

Objects are understood to arise from mental speech; knowing them as mere speech, the meditator rests in mind-only; the path of calm gathers the names of the teachings, insight investigates their meanings.

name: Mercury and mica as the seeds of Śiva and the Goddess

definitions.definition: Mercury is born of the great union of Śiva and the Goddess, 'the rasa of my body' (Rasārṇava 1.34-36); mica is Gaurī's seed, mercury Hara's; their union destroys death and poverty (SDS 9-10); Maheśvara was born as the great rasa to save the world (RRS 1.22).

name: Meditation as mere absence of thought (as criticized)

definitions.definition: The position that awakening is reached by simply not thinking or attending to anything, criticized by Kamalaśīla as leading only to dullness (Bhāvanākrama III); in the Tibetan accounts ascribed to the Chan master Moheyan at Samye.

notes: Stated from the critic's side; Moheyan's own account is in the Dunhuang sources (see dsp:sudden-or-gradual).

definitions.definition: Building temples and giving produce blessings; merit lies in the Dharma body — seeing the nature (Huineng on Emperor Wu).

name: Meru and Jambudvīpa: the shared cosmography of the families

definitions.definition: Seven ring-continents and oceans around Jambudvīpa, with Meru at its centre and Bhārata as the land of action.
Jambūdvīpa, round, a hundred thousand yojanas across, with Meru as its navel, surrounded by continents and oceans; Bharata and Airāvata as regions of the six-period cycles.
The receptacle world on circles of wind, water and gold; Meru amid seven golden ranges, with four continents, Jambudvīpa to the south.
Vyāsa's cosmology of seven worlds from Avīci to the back of Meru and above.

notes: Same names (Meru, Jambudvīpa, Bhārata) with different geometries in each family.

definitions.definition: The practice that avoids devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification — the noble eightfold path (SN 56.11); the balanced energy of the lute (AN 6.55); in doctrine the middle between 'all exists' and 'all does not exist', i.e. dependent origination (SN 12.15).
The path free of the extremes of existence and non-existence, eternalism and annihilationism, identified with emptiness and dependent origination (MMK 24.18; 15.7–10; RĀ 1.61–62).

relations.note: the self-mortification rejected in SN 56.11 and MN 36
the same middle between 'is' and 'is not'

name: The middle way as true examination of dharmas (Kāśyapaparivarta, Samādhirāja)

definitions.definition: 'Is' and 'is not', permanent and impermanent, self and no-self are extremes; the middle between them — formless, unshowable, without abode — is the middle way; the wise do not take a stand even in the middle.
Buddha-nature is the middle way (Mahāparinirvāṇa).

relations.note: the early middle way between extremes (U36) extended to all dharmas

definitions.definition: The inner sense by which the self grasps its relation to objects and by which the self is known in saṃsāra; some Bhāṭṭas held it persists in release as the organ of the self's bliss.
The conjunction of self and mind, located in the body, is the non-inherent cause of the self's qualities; hence the self's qualities appear only where the body is.

name: Mind and speech — the two tracks of the sacrifice

definitions.definition: Mind and speech are a yoked pair carrying the sacrifice, mind the greater (ŚB 1.4.4.7); the sacrifice has two tracks, mind (the silent brahman priest) and speech (the other priests) (ChU 4.16.1–2; AB 5.33); in the inner Agnihotra speech and breath are offered into each other (KU 2.5).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:satapatha-brahmana:1.4.4.7 (confirmed); tea:chandogya-upanisad:4.16.1-2 (confirmed); tea:kausitaki-upanisad:2.5 (confirmed).

name: The mind as the cause of bondage and liberation

definitions.definition: Not people, gods, the body, planets, karma or time but the mind turns the wheel of saṃsāra; all disciplines culminate in its mastery (Bhikṣu Gītā); the mind attached to the guṇas binds, devoted to the Person frees (Kapila).

relations.note: the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha extends the mind's causality to the world itself

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:mind-as-cause-of-samsara
checks.note: Rests on tea:uddhava-gita:11.23.42-45, tea:uddhava-gita:11.23.50-57, tea:kapila-gita:3.25.15-18, tea:moksopaya:1.2.5-7; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement. Caveats on tea:uddhava-gita:11.23.42-45 (see their checks) do not affect this entry.

name: Mind as clarity and knowing (gsal zhing rig pa)

definitions.definition: The definition of mind in the Types of Mind literature and the object of Gelug Mahāmudrā: mere clarity and knowing, formless, in which objects appear; its ultimate nature is emptiness.
The clarity aspect of the causal continuum's union of clarity and emptiness.
The mind alone is the seed, cause of arising and persistence; bindu arises from mind as ghee from milk (Candrāvalokana); in living liberation the mind is the seed and the spotless (AmŚ 57).

name: The bond of mind and breath

definitions.definition: Mind and breath are mixed like milk and water: when breath moves mind moves, when breath is still mind is still (HYP 2.2); who binds the one binds the other; the mind has two causes, latent impressions and breath, and when one is destroyed both are (4.21–25); the mind is lord of the senses, breath lord of the mind, laya lord of breath (4.29); knowledge cannot arise while breath lives and mind is not dead (4.15); the living soul is pulled up and down by prāṇa and apāna (GŚ 26–29).

name: Mind as the cause of bondage and liberation

definitions.definition: Mind attached to objects binds, mind free of objects liberates (Amṛtabindu 2; Śāṭyāyanīya 1–3); mind alone is saṃsāra (Maitreya 1.5).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 4 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: Mind and its parts in Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: The Abhidharma analysis of mind — consciousness arising from faculty and object (MMK 3.7), the aggregates, intention (17.2–3), the afflictions (23) — is accepted as conventional description; under analysis the mind is not found as a real entity, and the domain of mind ceases in the nature of things (18.7).
No storehouse consciousness and no reflexive awareness are needed even conventionally; the continuum of the aggregates suffices for karma (MA 6; BCA 9.73).
The seeker addresses and trains the mind: go by devotion, remember Rāma at dawn, inquire who is truly happy.
'O my mind, cling to Rāma's feet' (Śaṅkaradeva's bargīt).
'Tell me truly, O mind' (Tyāgarāja).

name: Mind only (sūtra layer)

definitions.definition: 'This triple world is mind only' (Daśabhūmika 6); 'all is made by mind' (Avataṃsaka); 'this mind makes the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha' (Contemplation Sūtra); the image in samādhi is cognition only (Saṃdhinirmocana 8); the world is what is seen of one's own mind (Laṅkāvatāra).
Kagyu masters teach that 'appearances are mind' (3rd Karmapa; Nāropa's conventional truth) but add that mind is empty; Nāropa criticizes mind-only proponents who take non-dual mind as truly real.

notes: Yogācāra's philosophical system: U41.

name: The Pure Land as mind only (weixin jingtu)

definitions.definition: Mind, Buddha and beings are one; the Western land is born within one's own mind (Zunshi); every land is the Bliss of mind-only and every buddha the Amitābha of one's nature (Tianru); yet one must be born in a buddha-land because one's power is insufficient (Yanshou), and to deny the Western land while unable to live in a latrine without disgust is self-deception (Zhuhong).
Not accepted: the Pure Land is pointed to in a direction and given form for ordinary beings.
The Western Land is near for the wise: as the mind is pure the buddha-land is pure; bodhisattvas and realms are states of mind.
'This very place is the Lotus Land' (Hakuin).

relations.note: the Pure Land application of 'this mind makes the Buddha'
held together with, not instead of, the Western land by Yanshou and Zhuhong

notes: Pure Land schools (U43) hold a different view of Amitābha's land; see also Ōbaku nenbutsu Zen.

name: Mind-to-mind transmission

definitions.definition: The Dharma is transmitted from mind to mind, each awakening himself; the robe is only a token (Hongren); the Platform Sūtra lists the line of transmission; in the Dunhuang version, possession of the text marks transmission.
The silent transmission concerned only 'knowing' (Zongmi).
Face-to-face transmission (menju) and documents of succession (shisho).

notes: The tradition's account; scholars regard the early lineage claims as constructed in the 8th century.

definitions.definition: The editorial division of the non-principal Muktikā Upaniṣads into Sāmānya-Vedānta, Yoga, Sannyāsa, Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava groups, used by the Adyar Library series and later catalogues; it is not found in the Muktikā.

checks.note: Confirmed: the groups follow the Adyar volumes (Yoga 1920, Sāmānya Vedānta 1921, Vaiṣṇava 1923, Śaiva 1925, Śākta 1925, Saṃnyāsa 1929) and match the local group lists in raw_etexts. The Muktikā itself lists by Veda only. No teaching ids cited.

name: Moderate diet (mitāhāra) in the haṭha texts

definitions.definition: Moderate diet is smooth, sweet food eaten to please Śiva, leaving a quarter of the stomach empty (HYP 1.58); the chief of the yamas (HYP 1.38; DYŚ 30); lists of wholesome and unwholesome foods (HYP 1.59–63; GS 5.17–25; DYŚ 64–66); without it yoga brings disease (GS 5.16).

The world is false (mithyā): not unreal like a hare's horn, not real like Brahman, but indescribable and sublatable; defended by the inference 'because it is seen, insentient, limited' and by five definitions.

Primordial liberation (ye grol), self-liberation (rang grol), liberation upon arising (shar grol), naked liberation (cer grol) and liberation from extremes (mtha' grol); thoughts are said to be freed like meeting an old friend, like a snake uncoiling its knot, or like a thief in an empty house.

Release from saṃsāra by Viṣṇu's grace into the unobstructed enjoyment of one's own bliss, in eternal difference from and dependence on him, in forms such as sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya and sāyujya, graded by fitness, with bhakti continuing and the liberated desiring only in accord with the Lord's will; not the mere cessation of ignorance.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the goal is named 'immortality' — the desireless knower's breaths do not depart; being brahman he goes to brahman (BAU 4.4.6); the serene one reaches the highest light and appears in his own form (ChU 8.12.3); the knower becomes brahman (MuU 3.2.9); freed from name and form like rivers in the ocean (MuU 3.2.8); knowing God one is freed from all fetters (ŚU 1.8, 6.13); ŚU 6.16 names saṃsāra and mokṣa.

After the body falls, the soul goes by the path of light to Vaikuṇṭha, manifests its own nature, keeps its individuality, experiences the whole Brahman as his mode, shares his bliss and powers except cosmic functions, never returns, and serves him eternally.
Non-difference with Brahman after death, once the adjuncts have fallen.
Attainment of the Lord's nature in non-separation, with the soul's distinctness preserved; by grace.
Maryādā souls attain union (sāyujya) or Akṣara; puṣṭi souls receive service in the Lord's play, valued above liberation.
Freedom from māyā is a by-product; the goal is prema-service in Kṛṣṇa's abode; sāyujya is rejected.
Equality with Śiva.
Liberation is given by Parameśvara alone through the incarnations; the devatās cannot give it.
The devotee does not desire liberation, only devotion.
Liberation is not asked for; remembrance and the saints' company are.
Union (sāyujya) is the only lasting liberation; the accomplished is free while living.

queries: prepared segments: BĀU 4.4.6, ChU 8.12.3, MuU 3.2.9, MuU 3.2.8, ŚU 1.8, ŚU 6.13, ŚU 6.16
checks.note: All 7 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 4.4.6; ChU 8.12.3; MuU 3.2.9; MuU 3.2.8; ŚU 1.8; ŚU 6.13; ŚU 6.16). It rests on 8 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Separation from all conjunctions through the absence of rajas and tamas and the exhaustion of strong karma — non-return (Śā 1.142); reached by the recollection of truth and the understanding 'this is not I, not mine', after which the self, become brahman, has no mark (1.143-155); disengagement, the tranquil imperishable brahman, called nirvāṇa (Śā 5.11-23).

relations.note: Rasa Śāstra requires an undecaying body for liberation in life

name: Signs of liberation in the chart

definitions.definition: Horā names configurations indicating liberation: Jupiter exalted in the 6th, an angle or the 8th, or the 12th rising in a benefic navāṃśa with the other planets weak (BJ 25.15); the kārakāṃśa exalted gives constancy in dharma and kaivalya, and Ketu in the twelfth from it gives kaivalya (Jaimini 1.2.13, 1.2.69).
Release from all karma through the absence of the causes of bondage and through shedding (TS 10.2); it follows omniscience and the stopping of all activity; the liberated do not return.
The self conquered by passions is saṃsāra; the same self conquering them is liberation (YŚ 4.5).

When adṛṣṭa is absent there is no contact with a body and no new appearance (VS 5.2.20 C); knowledge of the categories arising from dharma brings detachment, no new merit and demerit accrue, and when the old are exhausted the self, without seed, takes no body — a quiescence like fire whose fuel is burnt (Praśastapāda).
Each consciousness has three sub-moments (arising, presence, dissolution); a material phenomenon lasts seventeen mind-moments.

(1) From destruction: destruction has no cause, so a thing perishes by nature as soon as it arises (Dharmakīrti); (2) from existence: to exist is to be causally efficacious, which an enduring thing could not be either successively or at once (Dharmottara, Jñānaśrīmitra, Ratnakīrti: yat sat tat kṣaṇikam).
Complete nudity ('the form of the newborn') is required of the fully renounced; clothing, however small, is possession and bars liberation even for a Tīrthaṅkara.

Possession is attachment; clothes and bowls kept for restraint are not possessions. The Ācārāṅga allows three, two, one or no garments; Mahāvīra went naked, but the naked Jinakalpa mode lapsed after Jambū, and the Keśin–Gautama dialogue shows the outward sign is secondary to knowledge, faith and conduct.
Nudity is the normal sign, but a garment may be kept by exception, and at death may be given up; women and those with just cause are not excluded from liberation.

name: The monkey's way and the crow's way

definitions.definition: Yogaśikhā 1.140–144: gradual completion within one body (monkey), or rebirth and swift fruition through a siddha guru (crow).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: At death the ground clear light ('mother') arises; the clear light recognized in practice ('child') meets it, and for the sharpest faculties this is dharmakāya buddhahood.

The ground luminosity that dawns for every being at death (mother) meets the luminosity recognized in practice (child); for the practitioner who recognizes it the meeting is liberation in the dharmakāya.
The Bön teaching of mother and son clear light at death.

Death has its own path (RV 10.18.1) and fetters (AVŚ 8.1.4); the mind can go to Yama and be called back (RV 10.58); 'let me not go to the house of clay' (7.89.1); one prays to be freed from death 'like a cucumber from its stalk, not from immortality' (7.59.12); the immortal and mortal are of one origin (1.164.30).

Every undertaking — sacraments, marriage, journeys, building, consecration, sowing — is begun at a moment whose almanac-limbs, rising sign and planetary placements suit it (MC 1–13); an act begun under ill-placed planets destroys its doer, one begun at the right time succeeds with little effort (BS 103.59–60); yet timing alone does not guarantee success (Yogayātrā 1.5).

The list of 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān in the Muktikā, one for each surviving Vedic branch, with their Vedas and peace-chants, taught as a graded curriculum for liberation (Māṇḍūkya → 10 → 32 → 108).

checks.note: Confirmed from the e-text Muktikā: the 108 names in 1.30-39, the Veda lists with peace-chants in the prose, the graded study Māṇḍūkya → 10 → 32 → 108 in 1.26-29, and one Upaniṣad per śākhā in 1.12-15. The group counts (10+24+20+17+15+8+14 = 108) match the local group lists and Wikipedia. All 4 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: Uttarādhyayana, Daśavaikālika, Āvaśyaka, and Piṇḍaniryukti or Oghaniryukti.
Uttarādhyayana, Daśavaikālika, Nandī and Anuyogadvāra (with the Āvaśyaka counted separately).
A root consciousness underlying the six, reported by Asaṅga as the Mahāsāṃghika precursor of the storehouse consciousness.

relations.note: Asaṅga's Yogācāra identification; not attested in surviving Mahāsāṃghika texts.

name: The muni and the long-haired one

definitions.definition: The wind-girdled munis in soiled brown, entered by the gods, ecstatic with munihood, ride the winds while mortals see only their bodies; the long-haired one bears fire, poison-drink and heaven and earth, flies through the air seeing all forms, knows the minds of beings and drank with Rudra (RV 10.136).

name: Muppu, the secret salt of the alchemists

definitions.definition: The 'three salts', named as the key to fixing mercury, to transmutation and to making the body last for aeons (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 17); its composition is deliberately veiled in code language and to be learned only from a guru. Summary only.

name: Music as a path to liberation

definitions.definition: Struck nāda 'delights the world and breaks bondage' (ŚR 1.2.167); nāda-worship is worship of the three gods (ŚR 1.3.2); the knower of vīṇā, śrutis and tāla goes the way of liberation without effort, and the knower of song who fails in yoga becomes Rudra's attendant (YājS 3.115–116); for Tyāgarāja there is no liberation without devotion joined to knowledge of nāda.
Singing the pair's play in dhrupad is worship; the image of Bāṅke Bihārī appeared in answer to Svāmī Haridās's song.
Music without devotion does not lead to the good path; joined to devotion it is worship of Śiva as sound and of Rāma (Tyāgarāja).
Bargīts in classical rāgas and the sung drama are forms of worship.

name: The nābhasa ('sky') yogas

definitions.definition: Configurations formed by the pattern of all the planets: the Yavanas counted 1,800; Varāhamihira gives the three āśraya yogas (rajju, musala, nala), the two dala yogas (mālā, sarpa — taught by Parāśara), and the ākṛti and saṅkhyā yogas — thirty-two in all; they give their fruits in all periods (BJ 12).

notes: The 3+2+20+7 = 32 count is from memory.

name: Nāda — the inner sound

definitions.definition: The unstruck sound heard within when breath and mind are stilled; listened to in stages from loud to subtle it absorbs the mind 'like milk in water'; its end is the soundless Brahman and the state beyond mind; in the Yogaśikhā nāda is bindu and bindu is mind, and no mantra is higher than nāda.

The inner (unstruck) sound heard in the purified suṣumnā; the HYP makes attention to it the chief of the layas (4.66), maps its sounds onto the four stages (4.69–77) and says whatever is heard as nāda is śakti and the soundless is the supreme Brahman (4.101–102); Śiva is 'of the nature of nāda, bindu and kalā' (4.1).

Everything — song, instrument, dance, speech, the world — depends on nāda; it is named from breath (na) and fire (da), rises from the knot of Brahmā to the mouth in five forms, and is struck or unstruck (ŚR 1.2.1–3; 1.3.3–6; Bṛhaddeśī 16–25).
The second emanation from the supreme after Śakti; within the threefold bindu, the union of Śiva and Śakti (ŚT 1.7–9).
Śiva is embodied in sound; the seven notes arise from his five faces; music joined to devotion is worship (Tyāgarāja).

relations.note: Listening to nāda dissolves mind into the state beyond mind.
the unstruck nāda of the yogins is the music treatises' anāhata

name: Śakti, nāda, bindu: the emanation of sound

definitions.definition: From the supreme Lord come Śakti, nāda and bindu; bindu divides into bindu (Śiva), bīja (Śakti) and nāda (their union); from them Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā and Vāmā, Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu (will, knowledge, action); from the dividing bindu the unmanifest sound, śabda-brahman; from bindu-Śambhu Sadāśiva, Īśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu and Brahmā (ŚT 1.7–16).

The consciousness of all beings unfolded as the world, bliss without a second, worshipped by nāda-worship through which Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara are worshipped (ŚR 1.3.1–2); without nāda there is no song, note or dance and the world is made of nāda (Bṛhaddeśī 16–18).

name: The subtle phases of pronouncing the mantra (bindu to unmanā)

definitions.definition: Bindu, ardhacandra, rodhinī, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpikā, samanā and unmanā, each half the length of the one before, unmanā being timeless (Varivasyārahasya with Prakāśa).

After a, u, m the utterance of the praṇava passes through bindu, ardhacandra, nirodhikā, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpinī, samanā and unmanā, each subtler and shorter, sound dissolving into the soundless.

name: Nāḍī leaf-reading

definitions.definition: The tradition's claim: seers wrote on palm leaves the lives of those who would one day come to consult them; the reader finds the leaf through the thumb-impression and questions, and reads chapters on the life, past births, curses and remedies.

notes: Recorded as the tradition's claim; documented practice is recent (recent: true).

definitions.definition: The pulse at the root of the thumb as witness of life, with the gaits of the doṣas (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 3.1-5); a later addition to the classical examinations.

name: The channels (nāḍī)

definitions.definition: The Bhāvanā Upaniṣad names fourteen channels — Alambusā, Kuhū, Viśvodarā, Vāruṇā, Hastijihvā, Yaśasvatī, Aśvinī, Gāndhārī, Pūṣā, Śaṅkhinī, Sarasvatī, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā — as the deities of the fourteen triangles of the Śrīcakra.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 101 channels of the heart, one going to the crown by which one reaches immortality (KU 2.3.16; ChU 8.6.6); the 72,000 hitā channels in which the sleeper rests (BAU 2.1.19); 101 × 100 × 72,000 branch channels through which vyāna moves (PrU 3.6); coloured fluids and the sun's rays in the channels (ChU 8.6.1); the suṣumṇā (MaiU 6.21).

The haṭha texts count 72,000 channels arising from the bulb (GŚ 16; HYP 1.39, 4.18) — or 350,000 (SS 2.13) — with ten (GŚ 17–22) or fourteen (SS 2.13) principal and three chief: iḍā, piṅgalā and suṣumnā; they must be purified before the breath can enter the middle (HYP 2.4–5); only suṣumnā matters, the rest are 'useless' (HYP 4.18).

72,000 channels spread from the kanda near the navel; ten or fourteen are principal (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, sarasvatī, gāndhārī, hastijihvā, pūṣā, yaśasvinī, alambusā, kuhū, śaṅkhinī, vāruṇī, viśvodarī, payasvinī); the suṣumnā is the path of liberation; iḍā carries the moon, piṅgalā the sun.
Ten principal nāṭis among the ninety-six: iṭakalai, piṅkalai, cuḻumuṉai, kāntāri, atti, cikuvai, alampuṭai, puruṭaṉ, caṅkiṉi, kuku (Tamil forms; list recalled at moderate confidence).

notes: Names as in the eBhāratī text of the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad (variant: Payasvinī for Aśvinī).

definitions.definition: The heart has a hundred and one channels; the one rising to the crown (suṣumnā) is the knower's path at death; in seated worship the suṣumnā is contemplated as shining, lit above the crown by the sun's rays.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: A person does not attain actionlessness by not undertaking actions, nor perfection by renunciation alone (3.4).

relations.note: no one can in fact stay without action

definitions.definition: Beyond treating feelings of the three times, the final cure is freedom from upadhā (grasping), the supreme cause of suffering (Ca Śā 1.94-97).

name: Classes of asterisms for action

definitions.definition: For choosing times the asterisms are grouped by nature, each group paired with a weekday: fixed (dhruva), movable (cara), fierce (ugra), mixed (miśra), swift/light (kṣipra), soft (mṛdu) and sharp (tīkṣṇa); each suits particular undertakings (BS 97.6–9; MC 2.2–8).

members: cara: Svātī, Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj

definitions.definition: In sacrificial rites the sacrificer bears a name derived from his asterism (VJ r.28); later practice assigns a syllable to each asterism-quarter for choosing a child's name.
The name uttered inattentively or with another intent destroys sin and gives liberation (Ajāmila), but only pure chanting gives love; offences block its fruit.
Words in injunctions that name rites rather than enjoin qualities, recognized on four grounds.

name: Name and form (nāmarūpa)

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the unmanifest became manifest by name and form (BAU 1.4.7); being entered with the living self and differentiated name and form (ChU 6.3.2); space accomplishes name and form (ChU 8.14); at release name and form are left behind like rivers in the ocean (MuU 3.2.8; PrU 6.5).

notes: Buddhist nāmarūpa (mentality-materiality) is a different technical sense.

name: Non-difference of the name and the named

definitions.definition: The name is Kṛṣṇa himself, fully empowered, not an ordinary word; it reveals itself to a tongue turned to service.
Birth for all was settled as Namu Amida Butsu at Amida's awakening; the name itself is birth; the practitioner casts off even faith and simply says it.

The name of the Tathāgata of Unhindered Light breaks all ignorance and fulfils all aspirations when called in accord with reality (Tanluan); hearing the name with joy even for one thought gains unsurpassed merit.
The name gathers all the virtues of the Buddha's inner realization and outer activity, as 'house' contains all its timbers (Senchakushū 3).
The auspicious name embodying all virtues is the great practice.

relations.note: analogous doctrines of the saving power of a divine / buddha name; the Pure Land grounds it in a buddha's vow, the Hindu traditions in the identity of name and named

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument: varṇa-mixture leads family-destroyers and the family to hell (1.42); those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell there for an indefinite time, as tradition says (1.44).

Places of torment below the earth in the south within the three worlds, ruled by Yama, each matched to classes of sin (BhP 5.26: twenty-eight; VP 2.6 and MkP 12 other lists); release comes by exhaustion of the karma, by remembrance of the Lord, or by the transfer of a righteous person's merit (MkP 15); VP 2.6.46 teaches that heaven and hell are names for merit and sin.
