name: Before creation: the Nāsadīya account

definitions.definition: Before creation there was neither non-being nor being, death nor immortality, night nor day; That One breathed windless by its own power; darkness hidden by darkness; That One was born by tapas; desire arose as the first seed of mind; seers found the bond of being in non-being in their hearts; the gods came later; whether even the overseer in the highest heaven knows is left open (RV 10.129).

members: the overseer who knows or does not know

name: The Nāth initiation of the Vārkarī saints

definitions.definition: Ādinātha → Matsyendranātha → Gorakṣanātha → Gahinīnātha → Nivṛttinātha → Jñāneśvar: Jñāneśvar's own statement of the line through which he received knowledge, with the charge to relieve beings in the Kali age.

name: Nāth cosmogony: the origin of the body (SSP 1)

definitions.definition: From the nameless supreme its own power comes forth, and through the powers Parā, Aparā, Sūkṣmā and Kuṇḍalinī the supreme bodies and finally the human body arise (SSP 1).

name: The Nāth critique of ritual and caste

definitions.definition: For one who knows the supreme there is no caste, sacrifice, fasting, pilgrimage, image or rite (Akulavīra A.42–48, B.93–96); no lunar day or fast is prescribed — rely on knowledge alone (KJN 21.10); the yogī meditates where there is neither temple nor mosque (Gorakh Bānī); the external liṅga is rejected (KJN 3.14–18).

name: The guru in the Nāth tradition

definitions.definition: Without the true guru the nectar cannot be drunk (Gorakh Bānī); by the guru's grace alone body and supreme state become one taste (SSP 5); kuṇḍalinī wakes by the guru's grace (HYP 3.2); the realised one liberates by his touch (KJN 17.38–40); the disciple awakens the guru when he forgets (Gorakṣavijaya).
Ādinātha → Matsyendra → Gorakṣa, and from Gorakṣa the siddhas and panths (HYP 1.1–9; Yogaviṣaya 3–5); in Maharashtra Gorakṣa → Gahinī → Nivṛtti → Jñāneśvar (Jñāneśvarī 18).

Initiation in stages: first the cutting of the top-knot, the mantra and the black cord (the aughaṛ); after probation the splitting of the ear-cartilages and the wearing of the earrings (the darśanī / kānphaṭa), with a new name ending in -nāth; the Gorakṣaguṭikā tells of Gorakṣa taking 'the split ear and the cut top-knot'.

name: The insignia of the Nāth yogī

definitions.definition: Earrings (darśan/mudrā), the nād horn on the black selī cord, ash, the dhūnī fire, patched cloak, begging bowl and the greeting 'ādeś'; depicted already in the Padmāvat (1540).

Principal seats include the Gorakhnāth Maṭh (Gorakhpur), Gorakh Ṭillā / Tilla Jogian (Punjab, historically the chief seat), Kadri (Mangaluru), Dhinodhar (Kutch), Asthal Bohar (Rohtak), the Mahāmandir (Jodhpur), Tryambakeśvar and Madhi (Maharashtra), and seats in Nepal (Gorkha; Mṛgasthalī).
Nāth yogīs (like other renouncers) are not cremated but buried seated in a tomb called samādhi, over which a shrine may be raised.

name: The powers (siddhi) in Nāth and Kaula teaching

definitions.definition: Powers arise as signs of practice on the centres: trembling, speech in tongues, levitation, poetry, knowledge of past and future, change of form, the eight powers, entering other bodies (KJN 7.20–24; 8.30–45; 14.15–42).
The eight powers arise in the nectar-filled body (GŚ 65); the siddhas broke the staff of Time (HYP 1.9).

relations.note: powers are signs, but are not to be grasped (Akulavīra B.84)

definitions.definition: (As reported) No gift, sacrifice, offering, fruit of deeds, this or other world, mother, father, spontaneously born beings, or ascetics who have realized the other world.
(As reported) Pāyāsi's view and experiments; the Isibhāsiyāiṃ's materialist statement.

name: The nature of mind in the siddha songs

definitions.definition: Mind itself is the seed of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, like space, beyond colour and shape, unstained by virtue and vice, clear light unobscured by aeons.

relations.note: The siddhas' 'clear light of one's own mind' and the Ārya school's fourth empty are described in the same words (prabhāsvara); the first is pointed out directly, the second reached through the dissolution of winds.

name: Drama as the fifth Veda for all classes

definitions.definition: At the gods' request Brahmā made the Nāṭyaveda from the four Vedas — recitation, song, acting and rasa — because the Vedas may not be heard by śūdras; it is for all classes and shows the moods of the three worlds (NŚ 1.11–17, 1.107).
The SSP teaches nine centres of the body (2nd upadeśa); the list is recalled as from the root (brahma) centre to the sky centre above the crown, not checked.

Hearing, singing, remembering, serving the feet, worship, obeisance, servitude, friendship and self-offering (BhP 7.5.23-24); the Śiva Purāṇa's three means (hearing, singing, reflection) are a Śaiva counterpart.
Tulsī's own nine taught to Śabarī (saints' company first, guileless trust last); any one suffices.
The Bhāgavata's nine expounded one by one, culminating in self-offering.
Of the nine, hearing and singing are foremost.

name: The nine means of devotion (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa)

definitions.definition: Holy company; talk of the Lord's stories; singing his qualities; expounding his words; guileless service of the teacher as the Lord; virtuous conduct with steady worship; worship through his mantra; honouring devotees and seeing him in all with dispassion; inquiry into his nature — open to women, men and animals alike; the first leads to the rest in order.

relations.note: differs from the Bhāgavata's nine forms (hearing, singing, remembering, serving the feet, worship, bowing, servitude, friendship, self-offering)

name: The nine dharmas (navadharma) of Nepal

definitions.definition: Nine Mahāyāna sūtras venerated as a set by Newar Buddhists: Aṣṭasāhasrikā, Gaṇḍavyūha, Daśabhūmika, Samādhirāja, Laṅkāvatāra, Saddharmapuṇḍarīka, Tathāgataguhya, Lalitavistara, Suvarṇaprabhāsa.

notes: Newar Vajrayāna is U55.

definitions.definition: Śailaputrī, Brahmacāriṇī, Candraghaṇṭā, Kūṣmāṇḍā, Skandamātā, Kātyāyanī, Kālarātri, Mahāgaurī and Siddhidātrī, named by Brahmā in the Devī Kavaca and worshipped one on each night of Navarātri.

The seven visible planets — Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn — with the two nodes Rāhu and Ketu make the nine grahas; they are forms of Janārdana giving the fruits of karma, and from them the avatāras are born (BPHS 2.3–7); their synonyms include Greek-derived names (BJ 2.2–3); they are worshipped together in the planetary sacrifice (YājñSm 1.295–308; BPHS 84).

name: Correspondences of the nine planets

definitions.definition: Each planet has its own image-material, colour, mount and weapons (BPHS 84.4–13), its fuel-stick and gift (YājñSm 1.295–306), and in later texts its gem: ruby (Sun), pearl (Moon), coral (Mars), emerald (Mercury), yellow sapphire (Jupiter), diamond (Venus), blue sapphire (Saturn), hessonite (Rāhu) and cat's-eye (Ketu).

notes: The planet–gem table is from later texts (commonly Phaladīpikā 2); the Bṛhat Saṃhitā's gem chapters do not assign gems to planets.

name: The nine relations of Lord and soul

definitions.definition: Father–son, protector–protected, master–servant, husband–wife, knower–known, owner–owned, support–supported, self–body, enjoyer–enjoyed.

name: The Navya-Nyāya analysis of cognition and its contents

definitions.definition: Every qualified cognition has a qualificand (viśeṣya), a qualifier (prakāra) and a relation (saṃsarga), with corresponding properties (viśeṣyatā, prakāratā, saṃsargatā) that determine one another (nirūpaka / nirūpita); properties and absences are specified by their delimitors, counterpositives and relations; valid cognition is apprehending in X the property X has as qualifier.

name: The doctrine of standpoints (nayavāda)

definitions.definition: A thing is known through valid knowledge and standpoints (TS 1.6); the seven standpoints — naigama, saṃgraha, vyavahāra, ṛjusūtra, śabda, samabhirūḍha, evambhūta — each grasp one aspect (1.33); the two root standpoints are substance-oriented and mode-oriented; each taken alone is false, all together right (Sanmati). Every rival doctrine is a standpoint made absolute.
Five standpoints with subdivisions (Śv TS 1.34–35); Mallavādin's wheel of twelve views; Yaśovijaya's refuge in all standpoints.

relations.note: The standpoints are the analytic instrument of many-sidedness.

notes: Source of the ontology's reconciliation principle P2-standpoint.

name: Bridal love: the devotee as the heroine (nāyikā-bhāva)

definitions.definition: The Āḻvār becomes the girl in love — Parāṅkuśa-nāyakī, Parakāla-nāyakī — spoken of by her mother and friend, sending messengers, threatening to ride the maṭal; Āṇṭāḷ, a woman, sings her own bridal longing and dreams of her wedding.
The gopīs of Vraja are the example of devotion — but their love never lacked knowledge of his greatness and sought his happiness, unlike a paramour's.
Rādhā passes through the heroine's states — waiting, wronged, estranged by pride, going to the tryst, holding her lover in her power.

relations.note: both take the Vraja women's love as the model: the Āḻvārs as poets in Tamil akam voice, the Gauḍīyas as a method of practice following the Vraja residents

definitions.definition: The urine is examined for colour, density, smell, froth and deposit (nīrkkuṟi), and by a drop of oil placed on it (neykkuṟi): spreading like a snake shows vātam, like a ring pittam, standing like a pearl kapam.

name: Neither monk nor layman (hisō hizoku) and the married clergy

definitions.definition: After laicisation Shinran called himself neither monk nor layman; Shinshū clergy marry; in the last age only nominal monks remain and are still to be honoured; one does not worship other deities for worldly benefit.
Hōnen: live in whatever way lets you best say the nenbutsu — as a hijiri or married.
Whatever is held real lacks own-nature, being neither truly one nor truly many, like a reflection (MAL 1); a thing without real unity cannot be a real plurality of such units.
Once shinjin is settled, the nenbutsu is said in gratitude for Amida's benevolence, not as a cause of birth.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the instruction (ādeśa) about brahman — 'not so, not so', for there is nothing beyond this 'not so' (BAU 2.3.6) — and the description of the self as ungraspable, indestructible, unattached, unbound (BAU 3.9.26, 4.2.4, 4.4.22, 4.5.15); akin to the negations of the imperishable (BAU 3.8.8), of the fourth (MāU 7) and 'from which words turn back' (TU 2.4).

In the Sāṃkhya Sūtra the practice of the principles proceeds by giving up each with 'not this, not this', whence discrimination (3.76) — the renunciation of identification with each principle, as in the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64).
Brahman is taught by negating every specification; negation terminates in Brahman, the 'reality of the real', which is not negated.

name: Neither percipient nor non-percipient after death

definitions.definition: Eight forms of the view that the self survives death neither with nor without perception.

name: Provisional and definitive meaning

definitions.definition: The Buddhist hermeneutic: the Akṣayamati calls sūtras teaching emptiness definitive and those teaching self and beings provisional; the Saṃdhinirmocana calls the first two turnings provisional and the third definitive.

relations.note: the two sūtras apply the distinction differently

notes: Reconciliation principle P5-neyartha is drawn from these texts.

name: Provisional and definitive meaning in Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: Teachings of arising, self and mind-only are provisional (neyārtha), requiring interpretation, while teachings of emptiness and non-arising are definitive (nītārtha), following the Akṣayamatinirdeśa (PsP 1; MA 6.94ff).

name: The white-robed, long-haired community (gos dkar lcang lo'i sde)

definitions.definition: The lay tantric sangha of the Nyingma, householders keeping tantric vows beside the monastic sangha, with hereditary family lineages.

name: The preliminaries (ngöndro)

definitions.definition: The common preliminaries (the four thoughts) and the four special ones — refuge with prostrations and bodhicitta, Vajrasattva purification, maṇḍala offering, guru yoga — each usually accumulated a hundred thousand times before Mahāmudrā instruction.

notes: Shared with U45; this is the Kagyu definition.

name: The samādhi of recollecting the Buddha

definitions.definition: The king of samādhis, in which the Buddha and his assembly are seen clearly before one's eyes; reached through contemplation or through continuous (and loud) recitation; a seven-day hall practice.

The extinguishing of greed, hatred and delusion (SN 38.1), the unconditioned (SN 43.12; AN 3.47), the cessation of becoming (SN 12.68), described by negation as the sphere without elements, formless spheres, worlds, coming or going (Ud 8.1) and as the unborn, unmade (Ud 8.3); realised in this life (with residue) and at death (without residue) (Iti 44); not a self (MN 1; Dhp 279).
The one unconditioned ultimate reality (paramattha-dhamma), with the characteristic of peace; distinct from mere absence (commentarial).

relations.note: liberation as each tradition defines it; Theravāda denies that nibbāna is the self or Brahman
the arahant's living nibbāna versus the final passing

name: Nibbāna in the Abhidhamma and commentaries

definitions.definition: The unconditioned element, existing and apprehensible by the path, one in nature, with or without residue, void, signless and desireless; not a self and not a creator.
A realm and true self where the Dhammakāyas abide (contested).
The coolness of extinguished defilements here and now.

relations.note: the Theravāda denies any self in liberation

name: The five means of knowing disease

definitions.definition: Cause, prodrome, manifest signs, response to trial, pathogenesis (Mādhava Nidāna 1.4; AHS Sū 1.22).

name: Sleep in Āyurveda

definitions.definition: Sleep comes when the tired mind and senses withdraw from their objects; happiness, strength, knowledge and life depend on it; seven kinds — from tamas (root of sin), kapha, fatigue, adventitious, disease-following, and from night's nature (the nurse of beings) (Ca Sū 21.35-38, 21.58-59; AHS Sū 7.53-56).

notes: The text names six sources; commentators count seven by dividing fatigue of mind and body.

definitions.definition: Inner heat, illusory body, dream, clear light, transference and bardo as taught by Niguma — the root of the Shangpa's five golden dharmas.

name: The schismatics (nihnava)

definitions.definition: Seven (Sthānāṅga) or eight (with the Boṭikas, in the Āvaśyaka commentaries): Jamāli (action in progress is not yet done), Tiṣyagupta (the soul is only its last space-point), Āṣāḍha (agnosticism about who is a true monk), Aśvamitra (momentariness), Gaṅga (two cognitions at once), Rohagupta (three categories), Goṣṭhāmāhila (karma touches but does not bind the soul), and Śivabhūti (nakedness required).

notes: Doctrines of the middle five recalled with low confidence.

name: The play in the inner grove

definitions.definition: The natural pair (sahaja jorī) Kuñjabihārī and Śyāmā, never joined and never parted, play eternally in the grove; this is the whole of reality for the devotee.
The groves of Vṛndāvana as the eternal scene of the pair's love.

name: Being merely the instrument (nimitta-mātra)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: After declaring himself Time, the destroyer of worlds, the Lord tells Arjuna that the opposing warriors have already been struck down by him; Arjuna is to rise, win glory and be 'merely the instrument' (nimitta-mātra); he is to slay Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa and the others 'already slain by me', and not be distressed (11.32–34).

notes: New concept (extractor A) for the Gītā's phrase 'nimitta-mātraṃ bhava' (11.33); the term is trm:nimitta-matra (extractor B). Compare cpt:god-as-true-agent (a later school's formulation). The Gītā passage does not itself discuss the relation of this to the agent's responsibility.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

name: The nine enclosures (āvaraṇa) of the Śrīcakra

definitions.definition: From outside in: (1) bhūpura, Trailokyamohana, cakreśvarī Tripurā, Prakaṭa yoginīs (the powers Aṇimā etc., the eight Mothers, the ten mudrā-powers); (2) sixteen petals, Sarvāśāparipūraka, Tripureśī, Gupta yoginīs (the sixteen attractions); (3) eight petals, Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, Tripurasundarī, Guptatara (the eight Anaṅga goddesses); (4) fourteen triangles, Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka, Tripuravāsinī, Sampradāya yoginīs; (5) outer ten, Sarvārthasādhaka, Tripurāśrī, Kulottīrṇa; (6) inner ten, Sarvarakṣākara, Tripuramālinī, Nigarbha; (7) eight triangles, Sarvarogahara, Tripurāsiddhā, Rahasya (the eight goddesses of speech); (8) the triangle, Sarvasiddhiprada, Tripurāmbā, Atirahasya (Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī); (9) the point, Sarvānandamaya, Mahātripurasundarī, Parāparātirahasya.

notes: Names of the cakras, cakreśvarīs and yoginī classes from memory of the standard navāvaraṇa-pūjā (PKS 5, Nityotsava); not checked verse by verse.

name: The nine creations of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa

definitions.definition: Three primary (of mahat, the elements, the senses), five secondary (immobile, animals, gods, humans, anugraha) and the Kaumāra creation of the Kumāras, both primary and secondary.

definitions.definition: Earth, water, fire, air, ākāśa, time, space, self, mind (VS 1.1.4 C); substance is what has motion and qualities and is an inherent cause (VS 1.1.14 C).

name: The nine exemplars of the nine forms of devotion

definitions.definition: A verse widely quoted in Gauḍīya works names an exemplar for each form: Parīkṣit in hearing, Śuka in singing, Prahlāda in remembering, Lakṣmī in serving the feet, Pṛthu in worship, Akrūra in obeisance, Hanumān in servitude, Arjuna in friendship, Bali in total self-offering.

notes: The verse ('śrī-viṣṇoḥ śravaṇe parīkṣid abhavat ...') is recalled as cited in the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu (Eastern division) or the Padyāvalī; exact location not recalled, so no teaching id is created.

definitions.definition: Four formless (Śiva, Śakti, Nāda, Bindu), one form-formless (Sadāśiva, the liṅga), and four with form (Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā) — the one Śiva appearing for worship.

name: The body as the city of nine gates (navadvāra pura)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Having renounced all actions by the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action (5.13).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The same image occurs in Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.18 (navadvāre pure dehī).

name: The nine grades of birth in Sukhāvatī

definitions.definition: Upper, middle and lower birth, each in three grades (Contemplation Sūtra 14-16), from those with the three minds to the evil-doer saved by ten recitations at death; the Larger Sūtra's three classes of aspirants.
For Shandao all nine grades are ordinary beings differing by good or evil conditions met, not sages of the stages; the three minds are required of all.
The nine grades belong to the 'essential gate' of self-power good leading to the transformed land.

name: The nine Nāths (nava-nātha)

definitions.definition: Lists vary by region. The Marathi list (Navanātha Bhaktisāra): Macchindra, Gorakh, Jālandhar, Kānif, Carpaṭ, Nāg, Bhartarī, Revaṇ, Gahinī — as the nine Nārāyaṇas. North Indian and Nepalese lists differ (lists recorded by Briggs and others are not reproduced here).

notes: Members = the Marathi list only; variant lists are a gap to be filled from sources.

definitions.definition: Śṛṅgāra (erotic), hāsya (comic), karuṇa (compassionate), raudra (furious), vīra (heroic), bhayānaka (terrible), bībhatsa (odious), adbhuta (marvellous) — eight in drama (NŚ 6.15); śānta (peace) as ninth in the NŚ's śānta passage, Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta and Mammaṭa ('lovely with nine rasas', KP 1.1); four are sources of the other four (NŚ 6.39–41). Others add preyas (Rudraṭa), vatsala (SD 3.251) or bhakti.

relations.note: Rūpa Gosvāmī's five primary and seven secondary devotional rasas re-arrange the nine

name: The nine stages of settling the mind (Yogācāra sources)

definitions.definition: Placing, settling firmly, re-settling, settling closely, taming, calming, fully calming, one-pointing and concentrating; with six powers (hearing, reflection, mindfulness, awareness, vigour, familiarity) and four attentions (forced, interrupted, uninterrupted, spontaneous); the five faults and eight remedies of the Madhyāntavibhāga are the obstacles and antidotes along the way.

Placing, continuous placing, repeated placing, close placing, taming, pacifying, thorough pacifying, one-pointedness and equipoise; achieved through six powers and four attentions, with the five faults and eight antidotes, following the Śrāvakabhūmi and Madhyāntavibhāga.

relations.note: calm is a requisite of the path of preparation

name: The nine vehicles (theg pa rim pa dgu)

definitions.definition: Śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha and bodhisattva (the vehicles leading from the origin of suffering); kriyā, ubhaya and yoga (the vehicles of Vedic austerity, outer tantras); mahāyoga, anuyoga and atiyoga (the vehicles of overpowering means, inner tantras). Each is complete for its practitioners; the higher include the lower.
The Kunjed Gyalpo's nine passes, scriptures and paths lead to the single vehicle of the all-creator, which is reached without travelling.

relations.note: both traditions order their teaching in nine vehicles; the contents differ

name: The ninety-six principles

definitions.definition: Varāha 1's enumeration of 96 tattvas: the 24 Sāṃkhya principles plus elements, bodies, states, six modifications, six waves, six sheaths, six enemies, three jīvas, guṇas, karmas, actions, inner functions, four sublime attitudes and fourteen deities; the Pāśupatabrahma makes the 96 the haṃsa's sacred thread.

The Siddha and Siddha-medical enumeration of the embodied person (toṇṇūṟṟāṟu tattuvam), in the commonly given form: elements 5, sense-organs 5, sense-objects 5, organs of action 5, their functions 5, inner faculties 4, knowing (aṟivu) 1, channels (nāṭi) 10, winds (vāyu) 10, receptacles (ācayam) 5, sheaths (kōcam) 5, supports (ātāram) 6, circles (maṇṭalam) 3, impurities (malam) 3, humours (tōṣam) 3, desires (ēṭaṇai) 3, qualities (kuṇam) 3, deeds (viṉai) 2, passions (irākam) 8, states (avattai) 5 = 96. Aḻukaṇṇi speaks of 'the ninety and six' (19) and of all the principles burnt in realization (36).
The same count is the anatomical base of Siddha medicine: health and disease are read against the ninety-six.

checks.note: Varāha 1.6-15 is located: the four attitudes (muditā, karuṇā, maitrī, upekṣā) at v. 13 and the fourteen deities (dik … īśvara) at v. 14. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

relations.note: Śaiva Siddhānta's 36 are the cosmic principles; the 96 enumerate the embodied person
the first 24–25 of the 96 overlap the Sāṃkhya principles

notes: The overall count is certain; the membership given is the one most often printed, recalled at low confidence — some lists include the nine openings (vācal 9) and differ elsewhere. The Varāha Upaniṣad has its own 96.

name: Impartiality and the middle way (nipakh, madh)

definitions.definition: Dādū takes no side between Hindu and Turk and walks the middle between indulgence and harsh renunciation.
The realm of intense suffering in which beings experience the results of evil deeds, examined by King Yama (MN 130; MN 129).

names.name: nirguṇ bhakti / nirguṇ rām kī bhakti

definitions.definition: Love and remembrance directed to the formless Rām who is in every body, through the Name and the true guru, without images, avatāras or rites; the Lord is 'neither one nor two' and yet the Beloved.
Ravidās's devotion to the formless Lord as sandalwood to water, gold to bracelet.
Dādū's remembrance of the one stainless Rām of Hindu and Turk.

relations.note: The Sants love the nirguṇa as a person without accepting saguṇa forms as final; saguṇa bhaktas (e.g. Tulsīdās) reply that the two are not different.
saguṇa Brahman is Īśvara

definitions.definition: Brahman in itself is without attributes; the same Brahman with the adjunct of māyā is the Lord with attributes, object of worship, real at the empirical level. Texts teaching form serve meditation (BS 3.2.15).

No difference between the formless and the embodied; the formless becomes embodied by the devotee's love; the name mediates between them; yet for the devotee the embodied Rāma and devotion are to be preferred (Bhuśuṇḍi against Lomaśa).
Viṭṭhala standing on the brick is the self-known One; Jñāneśvar's non-dual teaching and the saints' love of the form are held together.
The Sants place the nirguṇa above the saguṇa: stone images, pilgrimages and the avatāra (the son of Daśaratha) do not reach the secret of the Name.
Caraṇdās joins both: nirguṇa knowledge with devotion to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
The Lord's grace needs no cause in the soul ('the kitten carried by the cat').
The Lord's grace is free, but he takes the soul's surrender as its occasion (vyāja) so as not to be partial ('the baby monkey clinging').

The falling away of karma, either after fruition (savipāka) or ahead of time through austerity (avipāka) (TS 8.23, 9.3); shedding increases innumerable-fold at each of ten stages from right view to the Jina (9.45).
The yogin makes constructed minds from I-ness alone (4.4); one mind impels the many (4.5); the one born of meditation is without residue (4.6).

Minds created from I-am-ness alone (4.4), all directed by one mind (4.5); of the five kinds (by the five sources), only the meditation-born is without residue (4.6, YBh 4.6); the first knower taught Āsuri through a created mind (YBh 1.25).

definitions.definition: The drawing of the soul's attachment from the world into Kṛṣṇa through his play, culminating in forgetfulness of the world and love in separation.

name: Relinquishment, single-mindedness and indifference (nirodha, ananyatā, udāsīnatā)

definitions.definition: Devotion is not desire, being relinquishment — the laying down of worldly and Vedic activity in the Lord; this means single-mindedness toward him (giving up other supports) and indifference to what opposes him (doing only what is favourable to him); its means include giving up sense-objects and attachment.

The cessation of perception and feeling, beyond the formless spheres: verbal, bodily and mental formations cease in that order, while vitality and heat remain, unlike a dead person (MN 43; MN 44); reached through the progressive cessation of perception (DN 9); emerged from with the contacts of empty, signless and undirected (MN 44).
The temporary cessation of consciousness and mental factors, attained by non-returners and arahants who have the eight attainments, after preparatory resolutions.
The Kulārṇava's last chapter explains terms by their syllables, e.g. guru from 'gu' (darkness) and 'ru' (restraint) (17.7-9).

Not abandoned, not attained, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither ceased nor arisen (MMK 25.3); neither existent nor non-existent (25.4–10); what, when grasping and depending, is saṃsāra, is nirvāṇa when not grasping and not depending (25.9); the ending of the conceptions of existence and non-existence (RĀ 1.42).

relations.note: a shared goal-word, but nirvāṇa is not an attained state of an existent self

definitions.definition: Read by Vācaspati into NS 1.1.4 ('non-verbalizable' and 'determinate').
Indeterminate perception ('this is something') is inferred, not perceived; determinate perception has a qualifier (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: Manner of death and the next world in the chart

definitions.definition: The eighth house and the 22nd decan show the manner of death (BJ 25.1–11); the lord of the decan occupied by the stronger luminary shows the world one came from — gods (Jupiter), fathers (Moon, Venus), animals (Sun, Mars) or hell-beings (Saturn, Mercury) (BJ 25.14) — and the lords of the 6th/8th decans or planets in the 7th the world one goes to (BJ 25.15).

relations.note: the Upaniṣadic/Gītā paths after death are by knowledge and time of death; horā reads the destination from the chart

name: The ultimate and conventional standpoints (niścaya and vyavahāra)

definitions.definition: Kundakunda's pair: the ultimate (pure) standpoint sees the soul as unbound, one and made of knowledge; the conventional describes it through its relations with karma, body and practice; the conventional is needed to teach the ultimate but is not its real meaning (Samayasāra 8, 11, 14); the wise disciple understands both and becomes impartial (Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 8).

For the Adhyātma movement the ultimate standpoint and self-experience are the heart of the path; one-sided adherence to either standpoint is a wrong view (niścayābhāsa, vyavahārābhāsa) (Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka; Ardhakathānaka).

Haribhadra: in the ultimate sense yoga is the three jewels in the soul, in the conventional sense their causes such as serving the teacher (Yogaśataka 2–4); Yaśovijaya joins knowledge-yoga and action-yoga.

The standpoint of ultimate reality (niścaya), the 'real', shows the soul as pure knower beyond all stages and distinctions; the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra), the 'unreal', speaks of knowledge, faith, conduct, bondage and stages and is indispensable for teaching those at the lower stage, as one must speak to a foreigner in his language.
Ṭoḍarmal warns against both one-sided errors — clinging to niścaya talk while neglecting conduct, and clinging to vyavahāra rites without knowing the self.

relations.note: Analogous only: both distinguish an ultimate from a conventional account, but the Jain ultimate is the soul's own pure nature, not emptiness; Jain texts would reject identification with the Buddhist ultimate.

definitions.definition: A prohibition turns one away from harmful acts; where the negation cannot attach to the injunctive, it is an exclusion forming a positive vow of not-doing.

relations.note: both link degrees of the divine form to kinds of worship; neither tradition equates the schemes

definitions.definition: The supreme Brahman Nārāyaṇa has a subtle, imperishable, partless form, stood for by the fixed image, and a gross form with parts, cause of all, stood for by the movable image that receives full worship.

name: Action without attachment to its fruit

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action performed with a right only to the act and not to its fruit, without attachment, the same in success and failure, 'established in yoga' (2.47–48); yoked with understanding it leaves behind good and evil deeds and frees from the bondage of birth (2.50–51); undertaken with the organs of action by one whose senses are controlled by the mind (3.7); done for sacrifice (3.9), for the holding together of the world (3.20, 3.25), and finally resigned to Kṛṣṇa (3.30).
Acting as duty, with evenness, abandoning attachment and the fruit, offering the act to the Lord; action so done does not bind (BhG 2.47–48, 3.19, 4.20, 9.27–28, 18.6).
Yudhiṣṭhira's dharma practised 'not for the fruit of dharma' (MBh 3.32.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: undertakings free of desire and intention (4.19); abandoning attachment to the fruit, ever content, dependent on nothing (4.20); acting for the sake of sacrifice, action dissolves (4.23); acting with actions placed in Brahman, abandoning attachment, one is unstained like a lotus leaf (5.10); yogins act for self-purification (5.11); the yoked one abandons the fruit and gains peace, the unyoked is bound by attachment to it (5.12); the true renunciant and yogin does the required action without depending on its fruit (6.1).

relations.note: the wise yoked with understanding, abandoning the fruit, go to the state free from ill; the unattached reach the highest
The practice of the karmayoga commitment.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The pair's love-play in the groves is eternal, without beginning, separation or departure; separation is only felt within union.
The natural pair play for ever in the nikuñja.

relations.note: the Rādhāvallabha eternal play admits no real separation

name: The Nityās as the lunar days and time

definitions.definition: The fifteen Nityās are the fifteen lunar days, the unfolding of time (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad); the Śrīvidyā's digits wax and wane with the moon over sixteen days, so the moon is the Śrīcakra (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10); the Tantrarāja correlates the Nityās with days and breaths.
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, devotion to Īśvara (YS 2.32).
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (2.32, YBh 2.32).

definitions.definition: (As reported) There is no cause or condition for defilement or purification, no effort; beings are transformed by destiny, circumstance and nature; all things are fixed.
A tenet that ends in inaction; the doctrine of cause (hetu) is the safe course; Makkhali's doctrine is the worst of all.
One-sided niyati is a wrong view; niyati with time, own-nature, deeds and effort is right view.

relations.note: in the Jain synthesis niyati is one of five co-causes

name: Niyoga / kārya (the command, what is to be done)

definitions.definition: The content of injunctions and the primary meaning of Vedic sentences: the act as to be done, identical with the apūrva, prompting the eligible person by itself.

relations.note: the rival Bhāṭṭa account of what the injunction conveys

name: The Jain denial of a creator

definitions.definition: The universe of eternal substances is uncreated and beginningless; a creator-God is refuted — where was he before, why would a perfect being create, an unembodied maker cannot act (Ādipurāṇa 4; Āptaparīkṣā; Anyayogavyavacchedikā 6); the omniscient Jina is worshipped but does not create or intervene.
Haribhadra reinterprets 'Īśvara' as the soul capable of perfection and each soul as the 'maker' of its own condition (Śāstravārtāsamuccaya 3).
Being without the mind of seeking and discriminating is the ultimate; 'one person of the Way without mind' surpasses offerings to all buddhas (Huangbo).
Ten ways of practising no-mind (Jinsim jikseol).

The Mādhyamika has no thesis of his own, so the faults of a thesis do not apply (VV 29); one without a position of existence, non-existence or both cannot be refuted (CŚ 16.25); the great-souled have no position (YṢ 50).

name: No-thought as tenet, no-form as substance, non-abiding as root

definitions.definition: The Platform Sūtra's three: no-thought is not being stained by objects amid thought (not blankness), no-form is being free of forms amid forms, non-abiding is the original nature that does not stop in any dharma.
No-thought as tenet (Shenhui).
No-thought alone as the whole of practice (Wuzhu).

name: The noble eightfold path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga)

definitions.definition: DN 22:21: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, each defined; right mindfulness is defined as the four establishments of mindfulness and right concentration as the four jhānas.

Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration (SN 45.8); contained in the three trainings (MN 44); right view comes first and each factor has a mundane and a supramundane form (MN 117); where it is found, the four kinds of ascetic are found (DN 16).

name: The noble persons in the Abhidharma

definitions.definition: Candidates and fruits of the four stages, distinguished by faculties (follower through faith / through dharma; resolved through faith / attained through view), with subtypes (seven-times, family-to-family, single-interval; five and more kinds of non-returner; body-witness; the six arhats).

relations.note: Same four paths and fruits; the Kośa adds the faculty-based subtypes.

definitions.definition: Seeking the unborn, unageing, deathless security from bondage rather than what is itself subject to birth and death (MN 26).

name: The self is not the agent; the guṇas act

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self neither slays nor is slain, and the one who knows it cannot be said to slay or cause to slay (2.19–21); actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti, and only one deluded by the sense of 'I' thinks 'I am the doer', while the knower of the truth sees that the guṇas move among the guṇas and is not attached (3.27–28).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: having abandoned attachment to the fruit, though fully engaged in action one does nothing at all (4.20); the yoked knower of reality thinks 'I do nothing at all' while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing, speaking, releasing, grasping and opening and closing the eyes, holding that the senses move among the objects of the senses (5.8–9); having renounced all actions with the mind, the embodied one dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action (5.13); the master (prabhu) creates neither agency nor actions nor the link of action with its fruit — inherent nature (svabhāva) is at work — and the pervading, mighty one (vibhu) takes on no one's sin or good deed (5.14–15). Whether prabhu and vibhu name the embodied self or the Lord is disputed by the commentators.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: prakṛti is the cause in agency (13.21); one who sees actions done by prakṛti alone and his self as not the doer sees (13.30); the supreme self, beginningless and without guṇas, though in the body neither acts nor is tainted (13.32), as space is not tainted (13.33); the seer who beholds no agent other than the guṇas and knows what is higher than them attains Kṛṣṇa's state (14.19).

relations.note: what the self does not do is done by the guṇas

Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.

notes: Chs. 4–6 contribution, from extractor A's cpt:akartrtva (the knower's side). In these chapters the text says the senses, or svabhāva, act (not, as in 3.27–28, the guṇas).

definitions.definition: Nothing arises from itself, from another, from both or without cause (MMK 1.1; 21.13).
Refuted one by one in MA 6.8–104, beginning with arising from self, rejected by Buddhapālita as pointless and endless.

relations.note: Gauḍapāda's non-origination uses the same fourfold negation; the grounds differ (unborn Brahman vs. emptiness)

definitions.definition: The sage of the Aṭṭhakavagga holds no formulated view, does not dispute, does not proclaim 'here alone is purity' and does not take himself as equal, superior or inferior (Snp 4.3, 4.8, 4.9); even right view is a raft (MN 22; MN 38).
A cognition that does not construct its object, first attained on the path of seeing; preparatory, fundamental and subsequently-obtained; not absence of thought, sleep or unconsciousness.
Cognition in itself is undivided; the division into grasped, grasper and awareness is seen by deluded vision.
Where there is nothing grasped there is no grasping; consciousness abides in cognition-only.
The buddha-dharma is non-dual; the supreme Way only dislikes picking and choosing; 'faith in mind is non-dual'.

name: The non-duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa

definitions.definition: 'What is saṃsāra is certainly nirvāṇa' (People Dohā v122); not conceiving them as two is the mode of the dharmadhātu (Queen Dohā v10–11).
Union is where saṃsāra and nirvāṇa become one by abandoning the two concepts (Pañcakrama 5.2).
Since each holds himself dearest, one who loves himself should not harm another (Ud 5.1); protecting others protects oneself (SN 47.19).
Hatred is appeased by non-hatred — an eternal law (Dhp 5; Vin Mv 10.2); love even under the saw (MN 21).

name: The realm of beings neither increases nor decreases

definitions.definition: Sattvadhātu = tathāgatagarbha = dharmakāya; the one dharmadhātu with three aspects.
'Whatever is meditated is my sickness': the nature is not produced by meditating; resting without fabrication is not a meditation on an object.

relations.note: the fourth yoga of Mahāmudrā is also called non-meditation

name: Non-retrogression of those born in Sukhāvatī

definitions.definition: Those born cannot fall back, for five reasons: the vow's power, the Buddha's light, the teaching of the birds and trees, the company of bodhisattvas only, and a life as long as the buddhas' (Jingtu shiyi lun); unlike Tuṣita.

Called the highest dharma (MBh 1.11.12; 13.116; 3.297.55); taught by Tulādhāra (12.253–256), Vicakhnu (12.257) and Vidura (5.33.48); the meat-seller notes that no one lives without harm (3.199); the kṣatriya's righteous war is his own dharma (BhG 2.31).
The ekāntins are non-violent; the Lord is worshipped by sacrifice without slaughter (MBh 12.336; 12.323–324).
When analysing wisdom finds no dharma arisen in the three times, the yogin enters non-conceptual wisdom pacifying all elaboration (Bhāvanākrama III).
When neither being nor non-being remains before the mind, it is pacified without object (BCA 9.34–35).
Thirty-odd bodhisattvas each name a pair and its transcendence; Mañjuśrī says non-duality is beyond expression; Vimalakīrti's silence is the entry itself.
Śākaṭāyana and the Nairuktas hold that all nouns derive from verbs; Gārgya and some grammarians deny it; Yāska defends derivation, always attending to meaning (Nirukta 1.12; 2.1).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:nirukta:1.12 (confirmed); tea:nirukta:2.1 (confirmed).

name: Number, letters and names in jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa encodes numbers in letters and words — Āryabhaṭa's alphabetic numerals, the kaṭapayādi code of the Jaimini Sūtras and Kerala, and the object-number words (bhūtasaṃkhyā) of the siddhāntas; the word horā itself is explained by dropping syllables from aho-rātra (BJ 1.3); names are drawn from the birth-asterism (VJ r.28).
The unobscured knowing of the empty, quiescent mind — the true nature; 'the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders'.
Recognised by tracing back the radiance: the one who hears, sees and asks.

relations.note: Both describe a knowing nature of mind not obscured by defilements; the Chan term derives from Zongmi/Heze, not from the Pali luminous-mind passage; Theravāda does not treat the luminous citta as an ultimate.

name: The experiences of bliss, clarity and non-thought

definitions.definition: Signs of meditation that arise naturally; attached to, bliss leads to the desire realm, clarity to the form realm and non-thought to the formless realm; released without clinging they support realization.

relations.note: when grasped

name: Installing mantras and letters on the body (nyāsa, sakalīkaraṇa)

definitions.definition: Before worship the body is made divine by placing mantras, the limbs (aṅga) of the deity's mantra and the letters of the alphabet on its parts.
Elaborate installations (e.g. the sixfold nyāsa) place the Goddess, her mantras and the letters on the body.
Syllables (oṃ āḥ hūṃ and the deity's seeds) are placed at the crown, throat and heart, and the body is seen as the deity's maṇḍala.
Jain worship begins with 'sakalīkaraṇa', protecting and consecrating the body by placing the syllables of the homage to the five supreme beings on the limbs.

relations.note: outer sites installed in the body (Buddhist)
the Jain five supreme beings as the content of the installation

notes: The Jain term sakalīkaraṇa (shared with Śaiva manuals) is recalled; flagged for checking.

name: The chain from false knowledge to liberation (NS 1.1.2)

definitions.definition: False knowledge → faults (attachment, aversion, delusion) → activity (good and bad acts of body, speech and mind, producing merit and demerit) → birth → pain; this unbroken series is saṃsāra. When knowledge of truth removes false knowledge, each successive link falls away and absolute liberation results (NS 1.1.2; NBh 1.1.2).

name: The yogic means to knowledge of truth in Nyāya

definitions.definition: Knowledge of truth arises from repeated practice of a particular samādhi (NS 4.2.38), which is possible through prior practice despite intruding objects and hunger (4.2.39–41); yoga is to be practised in forests, caves and sandbanks (4.2.42); for liberation one purifies the self by yama and niyama and by yoga and the method of the inner self — austerity, breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, fixation, and repeated contemplation of objects (4.2.46; NBh); with study, reflection and discussion (4.2.47–49).

name: Fearsome places (gnyan sa) and charnel grounds

definitions.definition: Places inhabited by powerful spirits — charnel grounds, lonely springs, trees and passes — where Chöd is practised because fear arises there and exposes self-clinging.

Perception of light and vision of forms arising in concentration and vanishing when the imperfections of concentration arise; the bodhisatta abandoned eleven imperfections to stabilise them (MN 128); the perception of light is a development of concentration leading to knowledge and vision (AN 4.41).

name: The object is independent of any one mind (4.15-4.16)

names.name: The object is independent of any one mind (4.15-4.16)

definitions.definition: With the object the same, minds differ (4.15); the object does not depend on a single mind (4.16); it is common to all puruṣas, and minds work separately in each puruṣa, from whose connection apprehension arises (bhāṣya 4.16).

A thing is common to many minds and stands on its own (4.14–16): the same thing produces pleasure, pain, delusion or indifference in different minds (YBh 4.15); if it depended on one mind, what would it be when that mind was distracted? (4.16); it is known or unknown as it colours the mind (4.17). Vyāsa rejects those who say the object is only a construction of cognition, like a dream (YBh 4.14), and those who say 'all is mind only' (YBh 4.23).

name: The object of devotion: the Lord as other, the self as one, or both (Śāṇḍilya Sūtra)

definitions.definition: Kāśyapa: devotion is directed to the Lord's majesty, because he is other; Bādarāyaṇa: to the one self; Śāṇḍilya: to both, by scripture and reasoning.

notes: Sūtra wording and numbers recalled with low confidence.

definitions.definition: What reasoning must refute is inherent existence — existence from the object's own side, not posited by conceptual designation; to negate less leaves the root of saṃsāra, to negate more destroys conventional existence and falls into nihilism.
Gorampa: in ultimate analysis the four extremes themselves are negated, without Tsongkhapa's qualifier; conventional appearances are not established even conventionally under analysis.

relations.note: Gelug and Sakya differ on whether the negandum is qualified

name: The law of the land and the Buddha's Dharma (ōbō / buppō)

definitions.definition: Keep the law of the land as fundamental and humanity and justice first, while keeping shinjin within; do not disparage other buddhas and kami (Rennyo).
Giving food and drink in the name of dead relatives, who wait outside the walls and live on what is given here (Khp 7 / Pv 1.5).

name: Ojas

definitions.definition: The supreme essence of the tissues, identical with strength (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); seated in the heart, pervading the body, whose loss is death (Ca Sū 17.74-75); the 'supreme' ojas in the heart and the ojas carried by the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.7-9); three disorders: displacement, vitiation, loss (Su Sū 15.24).

relations.note: Suśruta: ojas is bala (strength)

notes: The terms para/apara ojas are Cakrapāṇi's gloss on Ca Sū 30.7-9 (recalled).

name: Ölmo Lungring and Tagzig

definitions.definition: The land of Tönpa Shenrab's birth in Tagzig, with the nine-storeyed Yungdrung mountain at its centre, from which Bön spread to Zhang Zhung and Tibet.

notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Oṃ

definitions.definition: The one-syllabled Brahman to be uttered at death (BhG 8.13), the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8), the first word of 'oṃ tat sat' with which rites begin (17.23–24), 'among words the one syllable' (10.25).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the Lord is the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8) and the oṃkāra along with the three Vedas (9.17); Oṃ is 'the one-syllabled Brahman', uttered at departure while remembering the Lord (8.13).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: 'Of utterances I am the single syllable' (10.25), the syllable named in 8.13 as 'om, the one-syllabled brahman'.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: U05's contribution; the Upaniṣadic and mantra-śāstra accounts are given by U03 and U31.

definitions.definition: Oṃ analysed into three measures plus the half-measure (with Vedas, fires, worlds, deities, guṇas and colours), into twelve measures with destinies at death (Nādabindu), and sixteen measures ending in parā (Nāradaparivrājaka 8; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 8 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: An omniscient knower of dharma is not seen now, cannot be proved to have existed, cannot be established by his own scripture without circularity, and could not be recognized by the non-omniscient; an omniscience by all six means of knowledge would not be denied, but not a perception of dharma.
Bhagavad Gītā 7.26: the Lord knows all beings past, present and to come, but no one knows him.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: In Īśvara the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25); for one with only discernment of sattva and puruṣa there is knowledge of all (3.49); discriminative knowledge is all-embracing and without sequence (3.54); when coverings are gone knowledge is infinite and what remains to be known is little (4.31).
An omniscient being is possible: the mind, freed from the afflictions by cultivating selflessness, can know all things; this answers the Mīmāṃsā denial (Tattvasaṅgraha, last examination; MH 10).
The abode of Śiva in the crown is called Brahman by some, Viṣṇu's state by others, Haṃsa by others (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 50); the commentary: the final goal of Śaivas, Śāktas and Vaiṣṇavas alike.

name: The one great matter of the afterlife (goshō no ichidaiji)

definitions.definition: Life is fleeting — rosy cheeks in the morning, white ashes in the evening; take to heart the matter of the life to come and rely on Amida.

name: One ground, two paths, two results

definitions.definition: Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa have one ground; recognition (awareness) and non-recognition (ignorance) are the two paths; buddhahood and saṃsāra the two results.
Recited daily in the Aspiration of Samantabhadra.
Buddhas and beings are only the one mind, without beginning or end, beyond all measure (Huangbo).
The one mind as the source that mirrors the myriad dharmas (Yanshou).

relations.note: Chan's one mind draws on Laṅkāvatāra and Awakening of Faith language; not identical with Yogācāra's analysis of consciousness.

name: One mind, two aspects (Awakening of Faith)

definitions.definition: Mind as suchness and mind as arising and ceasing; the ālaya where the two combine.

name: One ultimate, many names

definitions.definition: Brahman, one without a second, is sung in many ways by the seers, so knowledge from a single teacher is not firm; the Veda's interpretations differ with natures.

The one from which words turn back is the Person of the Sāṃkhyas, the Brahman of the Vedāntins, the pure consciousness of the Vijñānavādins and the void of the Śūnyavādins; for the one established in the supreme it may be described with the terms no-self and emptiness; the external-object and consciousness doctrines are one for us.
The undivided understanding regarding Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śakti, the Sun and Gaṇeśa is right yoga; the one lord became fivefold.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:one-ultimate-many-names
checks.note: Rests on tea:uddhava-gita:11.9.31, tea:uddhava-gita:11.14.1-3, tea:moksopaya:3.5.3-7, tea:moksopaya:3.66.10-14, tea:moksopaya:6.195.1-4, tea:ganesa-gita:1.21-24; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

notes: Text-layer statements that bear directly on ult:the-one (ṚV 1.164.46). Traditions that deny such equivalence (e.g. Buddhist schools on 'śūnya' as a name of a substantial ultimate) are not represented in these verses.

definitions.definition: There is only one buddha-vehicle; the three are its skillful presentations; all who hear the Lotus become buddhas.
The two vehicles enter the great vehicle; the arhat's nirvāṇa is not final (Śrīmālā).

relations.note: the fixed-lineage view

definitions.definition: The Contemplation Sūtra was taught for ordinary beings of feeble mind like Vaidehī; all nine grades are ordinary beings; one must deeply know oneself as an ordinary being without escape.
The foolish being full of blind passions to the end, without a single true mind; the very object of the vow.
Hōnen, finding himself unable to keep precepts, meditation or wisdom, took the path for ignorant ordinary people and taught the learned to behave like those who know not a letter.
The mind without contrivance, grasping or rejecting, in walking, standing, sitting and lying (Mazu, Nanquan).
Just be ordinary with nothing to do (Linji).
Present awareness left just as it is — uncontrived, unspoiled by conceptions — which is the dharmakāya when recognized; 'the great way of the ordinary'.

relations.note: ordinary mind is the co-emergent mind recognized

definitions.definition: 'Come, monk' ordination by the Buddha, then by the three refuges (Vin Mv 1.12), then by formal act of the Saṅgha; the nuns' ordination by both Saṅghas (Cv 10).

name: How speech arises in the body

definitions.definition: The self grasps meanings with the intellect and joins the mind to the wish to speak; the mind strikes the body's fire, which drives the wind up from the chest to the head and mouth, where the phonemes are formed (PŚ 6–9).

relations.note: the Śikṣā's physiology of breath serves pronunciation, not meditation

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:paniniya-siksa:6-9 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: The mind is originally awake; non-awakening depends on it; actualized awakening returns to it (Awakening of Faith); perfect enlightenment is the original mind (Yuanjue jing).
One's face before thinking good or evil; the self-nature pointed to directly.
The empty, calm, numinous knowing mind (Jinul).
The self-nature is originally pure, unborn, complete, unmoving and productive of all dharmas; delusion only covers it like clouds cover the sky.

Dharmakīrti infers other minds from observed action and speech, valid for proponents of external objects and of cognition-only alike; Ratnakīrti holds that at the ultimate level they are not established.
Minds influence one another directly as dominant conditions (Viṃśatikā).
The power of Amitābha's original vow as the dominant condition of birth and of all that follows; the easy path rides on it (Tanluan).
Birth through the nenbutsu that accords with the Buddha's vow; the practitioner keeps calling.
Wholly Amida's working: shinjin and the nenbutsu are given; the practitioner's 'no working is true working'.

relations.note: the defining pair
analogous only: in both, liberation is effected by another's power; Pure Land posits no creator Lord and Shinshū denies that Amida is a god among gods
analogous: total reliance on the saviour's vow / surrender to the Lord as the means; the Shinshū 'no calculation' resembles the Tenkalai 'cat' view

definitions.definition: The outer wheel of cosmos and time, the inner wheel of the body's channels and breaths (21,600 a day), and the 'other' (alternative) Kālacakra of deity and maṇḍala that purifies the first two.

name: Learning the word of the Buddha in one's own language

definitions.definition: The Buddha refuses to have his word put into Vedic metre (chandas) and allows it to be learned 'in one's own language' (Vin Cv 5.33); the commentary reads this as the Buddha's own language, Māgadhī, identified by the tradition with Pali.

relations.note: the commentarial doctrine that Māgadhī is the root language of beings (U37)

definitions.definition: Kuoan's ten pictures from searching for the ox to entering the marketplace.
Puming's whitening-ox series ending in 'both vanished'.
Absence of certainty not accompanied by a desire to infer.
Kṛṣṇa as devotee in five aspects: Caitanya, Nityānanda, Advaita, Śrīvāsa, Gadādhara.
Fixed (dhruva), worship (kautuka), festival (utsava), bathing (snapana) and offering (bali) images; the dhruva receives flowers only, the kautuka full worship.

name: All substances are made of the five elements

definitions.definition: Every substance is pañcabhautika; earthy, watery, fiery, airy and spatial substances have characteristic qualities and actions; nothing is not a medicine when rightly used (Ca Sū 26.10-12).

Five real and eternal differences — God and soul, God and matter, soul and soul, soul and matter, matter and matter — holding in every state including liberation; knowing them is a condition of liberation.
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna, closing the five adhyāyas, muttered daily as the five purifiers.

Five codes of conduct: liṅgācāra (exclusive worship of the liṅga), sadācāra (honest livelihood and moral life), śivācāra (equality of all devotees), bhṛtyācāra (servant-humility) and gaṇācāra (defence of the community and faith).
The SSM's exclusivity (no other gods), its duty to protect liṅgas and devotees at the cost of life and its rule on revilers of Śiva are the textual background of liṅgācāra and gaṇācāra.

name: The Pañcācārya lineage and the transmission of the SSM

definitions.definition: Śiva taught the doctrine to the Goddess and Nandin; the gaṇa Reṇuka, emerging from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki, taught Agastya; five ācāryas appear from liṅgas in every age and found the five pīṭhas; the SSM's compiler stands in the ācārya line of Muddadeva and Siddhanātha.

name: The doctrine of the five fires

definitions.definition: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali's teaching: yonder world, the rain-god, this world, man and woman are five sacrificial fires; the offerings are faith, Soma, rain, food and semen, so that at the fifth offering water becomes 'person'; the knower of it goes by the path of the gods (ChU 5.3-10; BAU 6.2).

checks.note: All 2 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 5.3-10; BĀU 6.2). It rests on 5 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: The five periods of the day (pañcakāla)

definitions.definition: The Pāñcarātrin's day is ordered as approach, gathering, worship, study and yoga.
Emesis, purgation, decoction enema, oil enema and nasal evacuation, preceded by oleation and sudation; seasonal cleansing prevents disease (Ca Sū 7.46-49; AHS Sū 1.25; 4.25-26). Summary only.
Parameśvara's five incarnations — Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Dattātreya, Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ, Govindaprabhu, Cakradhar — through whom alone liberation is given; grace passes from one to the next.
Na-ma-śi-vā-ya, read as concealment, mala, Śiva, grace, soul; the order of the letters maps the soul's path from bondage to Śiva; meditated as the means of purification (Civañāṉa Pōtam 9).
Namaccivāya as the devotee's refuge and the essence of the Vedas (Tēvāram, Tiruvācakam).

name: Mantra: the five syllables and the praṇava

definitions.definition: 'Namaḥ śivāya' is the designation of Śiva and root of all mantras; the name 'Śiva' reveals brahman in its primary sense; the five syllables comprise all that exists in fives; with Oṃ it is six-syllabled; Oṃ arises from 'so'ham'; mental repetition is best.

name: The five marks of a Purāṇa (pañcalakṣaṇa)

definitions.definition: A Purāṇa treats creation (sarga), secondary creation (pratisarga), dynasties (vaṃśa), the Manu-intervals (manvantara) and the deeds of the dynasties (vaṃśānucarita) (VP 3.6.24; KūP 1.1.12; Matsya 53.65); the Bhāgavata calls the five-mark Purāṇas the 'small' ones (12.7.10).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: VP 3.6.24, KūP 1.1.12, Matsya 53.65, BhP 12.7.10 located. All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: When Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus or Saturn is strong in its own sign or exaltation in an angle, one of the five great men is born — Rucaka, Bhadra, Haṃsa, Mālavya, Śaśa — each with his bodily marks and measures (BS 68; BPHS 75).

Bliss is the form of Brahman residing in the body; the five 'M's (wine, meat, fish, grain or gesture, union) manifest it and are used in secret, exposure leading to hell (PKS 1.12); the daily worship continues without them when they are unavailable (PKS 1.24); the Tripurā Upaniṣad (12) speaks of such offerings. Summary only.
Rejected by the Samaya school as non-Vedic (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).

name: The five limbs of the almanac (pañcāṅga)

definitions.definition: The quality of any moment is read from its lunar day, weekday, asterism, yoga (27, from Viṣkambha to Vaidhṛti) and karaṇa (11), each with its deity and class (MC 1–2; BS 97–99).

Arhats (embodied omniscients), Siddhas (liberated), Ācāryas (heads of orders), Upādhyāyas (teachers) and Sādhus (ascetics), honoured in the Namaskāra mantra; together they have 108 qualities (12 + 8 + 36 + 25 + 27). The Jina is worshipped as the model of qualities to be attained, not as a giver of grace (Sarvārthasiddhi maṅgala).

Arhats, Siddhas, Ācāryas, Upādhyāyas and Sādhus, saluted in the Namaskāra that opens the Bhagavatī (Śvetāmbara) and the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama (Digambara); the salutation is to qualities and ranks, not to named individuals.

name: The 108 Pāñcarātra saṃhitās
notes: Scholarly metadata: F. O. Schrader (1916) combined several saṃhitās' lists into over 200 titles; many titles are lost. Members are the src entries with lineage lin:pancaratra.

definitions.definition: Tradition speaks of 108 saṃhitās spoken by the Lord; lists of titles in different saṃhitās disagree.

name: The five categories of the Pāśupatas (pañcārtha)

definitions.definition: The whole teaching is summed up as effect (kārya), cause (kāraṇa), union (yoga), rule (vidhi) and the end of suffering (duḥkhānta), all implied in the first sūtra.
Śaṅkara reports the same five as taught by Paśupati for release from the paśus' bond, and rejects the accompanying view of the Lord as merely efficient cause.
Liṅga-wearers are not subject to the pollutions of birth, death, menstruation, leftovers or caste.
The teacher who has become Śiva is not tainted by birth- and death-pollution (14.16).

name: The five tattvas / five M's (pañcatattva, pañca-makāra)

definitions.definition: Wine, meat, fish, parched grain and ritual union, used in the Kaula worship of Śakti (Mahānirvāṇa 5.22-24). Restricted: summary only. The texts bind their use to initiation, consecration and the samayas, and condemn their use for pleasure: wine alone gives no perfection (Kulārṇava 2.117); the uninitiated, wilful or addicted go to hell (5.96-105).
The Kālīvilāsa forbids them in the Kali age, allowing only the paśu disposition (4.2-3).

name: The five flows (pañcavāha) of goddesses

definitions.definition: Vyomavāmeśvarī, Khecarī, Dikcarī, Gocarī and Bhūcarī - the goddess-groups of consciousness, subject, inner organ, outer senses and objects - which delude the ignorant and liberate the knower (Kṣemarāja on PH 12, citing the Krama).

notes: The correlation of each group with a level is recalled from Kṣemarāja's commentary; low confidence.

definitions.definition: The gross elements are formed by combining half of each subtle element with an eighth of each of the other four.
Concepts are twofold — concept as meaning (what is made known) and concept as name (what makes it known); they have no intrinsic nature; the Puggalapaññatti treats persons as such designations.

Dependent on eye and form eye-consciousness arises; contact, feeling, perception, thinking, and proliferation follow, whence perceptions and notions tinged with proliferation beset a person (MN 18); rooted in 'I am' (Snp 4.14); disputes arise from it (Snp 4.11).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): MuU 1.1.4-5 is the root text — the lower knowledge is the four Vedas and six ancillary sciences, the higher that by which the imperishable is grasped; Nārada knows only mantras, not the self (ChU 7.1.3).

Knowledge is twofold by eligibility: Śiva's knowledge, revealing the Lord, is higher; the Veda and the rest, revealing the bound soul and its bonds, are lower — different as the night-vision of a man and a cat.

checks.note: All 2 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (MuU 1.1.4-5; ChU 7.1.3). It rests on 2 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

relations.note: Pāñcarātrins and Vaikhānasas claim Vedic roots instead

name: Supreme devotion, supreme knowledge, highest devotion

definitions.definition: Three ripening states of love for the Lord prayed for in the Śaraṇāgati Gadya: longing that cannot bear separation, direct vision, and love for which loss of the vision would be unbearable.

name: The parable of the two rivers and the white path

definitions.definition: A traveller between a river of fire (anger) and of water (greed) crosses a narrow white path (the aspiration for birth) urged by Śākyamuni from the east and called by Amitābha from the west (Shandao).
Shinran reads the white path as other-power shinjin and the voices as the two Honoured Ones' command and call.
Four for monks — sexual intercourse, theft, killing a human or inciting death, falsely claiming superhuman states — entailing loss of monkhood (Vin Pār 1–4); eight for nuns.
The Bījak's virtue of testing all doctrines, gods and practices as the mind's own products, as a jeweller tests gems; the discerning one (pārakhī) is not deceived by words.

The gopīs' love outside marriage is taken as the model of the practitioner's love for a partner (not the spouse), because it is selfless, risky and full of longing; recorded as doctrine only (restricted). The path is said to be hard as holding an elephant with a spider's thread.

relations.note: For the Gauḍīyas parakīyā belongs to Kṛṣṇa's līlā only and is never a human practice.

definitions.definition: Rūpa: the gopīs' paramour love is the summit of amorous rasa; Jīva: they are Kṛṣṇa's own potencies, so svakīyā in truth; Viśvanātha: parakīyā eternally. Love is defined as desire for Kṛṣṇa's pleasure, not one's own.
Rādhā as Kṛṣṇa's eternal consort; the school's view is generally described as svakīyā.
(As reported) There is no other world, because there is no one who goes there; no one returns from it.
The Lokāyatikas' denial is a wrong 'teaching of non-self'.

name: The supreme state of the Nāths (param pad; alakh nirañjan)

definitions.definition: The supreme is named the 'state' (pada), the spotless (nirañjana), the invisible (alakh), the void (śūnya) and Śiva; it is stainless, motionless, sky-like knowledge and bliss, into which the yogī enters as milk into milk (GŚ 99–100); the yogī meditates on the supreme state 'where there is neither temple nor mosque' (Gorakh Bānī).

relations.note: the Akulavīra of Matsyendra's school is described in the same apophatic terms; the Nāth texts do not themselves equate the names

name: Consideration (parāmarśa) as the instrument of inference

definitions.definition: The cognition 'this has smoke pervaded by fire' is the proximate cause of inferential cognition, not the memory of pervasion alone (Gaṅgeśa; Tarkasaṅgraha).
The validity of a cognition is produced by excellences in its causes and known extrinsically — from the success of the activity it prompts (NBh 1.1.1) or other inference (Gaṅgeśa).
Prakṛti really transforms into its products through the guṇas, by combination and transformation, like water differing in different receptacles (SK 16); the world so produced is real (SS 6.52).

relations.note: Advaita's apparent transformation (the Advaita account)

definitions.definition: The final passing of the Buddha or an arahant; the Buddha passed up through the jhānas and formless attainments to cessation, down again, and attained final nibbāna on emerging from the fourth jhāna (DN 16); what happens to the Tathāgata after it is undeclared (MN 72).

The Siddhars veil yoga, alchemy and medicine in coded names and riddles — the house of three-times-two, the horse of twelve feet, the root tamarind, the eight and the two — so that only a guru's disciple can decode them; glossaries such as the Akattiyar paripāṣai explain some. The veiling is itself a warning against misuse.

relations.note: the 'intentional/twilight language' of the Buddhist siddhas: comparable device

name: Parokṣa — the gods' love of the hidden

definitions.definition: 'The gods love the cryptic and dislike the obvious': ritual and cosmic realities are given indirect names (indha → Indra; svāpyaya → svapna), and the teaching of correspondences is itself 'secret' (ŚB 10.5.2.19; 14.6.11.2; AB 3.43).

name: Metal and mineral preparations (parpam, centūram) — names and warnings only

definitions.definition: Calcined metal and mineral medicines — parpam (white calx), centūram (red calx), cuṇṇam, kaṭṭu, meḻuku — held by the tradition to be the most potent Siddha medicines. The tradition's own warnings: raw minerals and metals are poison; they must be purified (cutti) and processed exactly as the guru teaches; wrongly made they kill; they are given only with strict regimen (pattiyam) and by a qualified physician. No processes, ingredients or doses are recorded here.

name: The parts of a sāman

definitions.definition: A sāman is a verse (from the ārcika) turned into song, with stretched vowels, repetitions and stobhas, divided among the chanters as hiṅkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, upadrava and nidhana.

notes: The fivefold and sevenfold sāman are expounded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (U03).

name: The nominal and the non-nominal ultimate

definitions.definition: The ultimate beyond all elaboration (aparyāya) and the ultimate accordant with it — the negation of arising and the wisdom of reasoning (paryāya) (Tarkajvālā on MH 3).

name: The poisonous minerals (pāṣāṇam) and the nine of Palani

definitions.definition: The tradition counts sixty-four pāṣāṇams, thirty-two natural and thirty-two prepared; Bogar is said to have made the Palani image of Murukaṉ from nine (navapāṣāṇam). Recorded as the tradition's account; no identities or processing.
'The western of all paths', given by the Goddess to the Siddhas and spread from Candradvīpa through Śrīśaila, Kiṣkindhā and the western Himalaya (Kubjikāmata 2.20-42).

name: The passions as the family of the Tathāgata

definitions.definition: The body-view, ignorance, craving, the poisons and the sixty-two views are the Tathāgata's family: as lotuses grow in mud, buddha-qualities grow in beings in the mud of passions, not in those who have entered the unconditioned.

The world is bound by passion and freed by passion (Hevajra II.2); the same deeds that bind free when joined with means (Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa 6); as the knower of poison eats poison unharmed (v. 18); 'great passion' is a name of the Buddha.
Tilopa: as one who has taken poison (knowingly) is not killed by it, the yogin is not bound by sense pleasures.
Seven Buddhas within ninety-one aeons — Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, Gotama (DN 14); twenty-four from Dīpaṅkara in the Buddhavaṃsa.

name: The paśu (bound soul) in the Pāśupata system

definitions.definition: All conscious beings but the Lord, with or without bodies, including gods and those liberated by Sāṃkhya-Yoga; bound by the kalās; their bondage is lack of lordship.

The jīva bound by ego is the paśu, the Lord is Paśupati; release from the bond (pāśa) through the pāśupata vow and ash (Atharvaśiras 5; Jābāli); 'bound by the husk it is paddy, without husk rice' (Skanda 6–7).
