name: Death and the final stage in Pāśupata practice

definitions.definition: In the fourth stage the ascetic lives in the cremation ground until the body falls, remembering Rudra; the fifth stage is without body, its place Rudra himself; the liberated brahmin does not return.
Dying at Kāyāvarohaṇa leads to Rudra's world (Kūrma P.).
Knowledge, austerity, permanence (constant union with the god), steadiness and perfection (Gaṇakārikā); Kauṇḍinya: knowledge, austerity, constant union with the god, yoga, arising of the qualities.

False knowledge, demerit, the cause of attachment, falling away and the root of the paśu-state (Gaṇakārikā); Kauṇḍinya: ignorance, demerit, habituation to objects, non-attainment of steadiness, lack of lordship.
Residence (with the teacher, i.e. the faculties of learning), observance, muttering and meditation, constant remembrance of Rudra, and grace.
Teacher, people, cave (or empty house), cremation ground and Rudra - the places of the five stages in order.
Kauṇḍinya's list: the dwelling, the world, the empty house, the cremation ground, Rudra.
The absolute removal of each of the five impurities.

name: The five stages of Pāśupata practice (avasthā)

definitions.definition: Manifest (vyakta: the sign shown, in the temple), unmanifest (avyakta: sign hidden, courting dishonour among people), conquest (jaya: of the senses, in cave or empty house), cutting (cheda: in the cremation ground), completion (niṣṭhā: all activity ceased, in Rudra).

relations.note: each stage has its place

definitions.definition: Devotion to the teacher, clarity of mind, conquest of opposites, merit and vigilance.

Material (knowledge of disciple and teacher, the ritual items, the brahmin disciple), time (forenoon), rite, image and teacher; initiation is by ash consecrated with the five mantras before the southern image.

name: The kalās: ten effects and thirteen instruments

definitions.definition: The insentient parts that bind the soul: ten effects (earth, water, fire, air, space; sound, touch, form, taste, smell) and thirteen instruments (five knowledge-senses, five action-organs, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas).
The Lord (Pati) alone is the independent cause who emits, maintains, withdraws and favours the effect; he acts by will and play, not by dependence on karma.
Everything dependent on the Lord: the knowledge-qualities of souls (vidyā), the insentient parts (kalā) and the souls (paśu); eternal but produced, favoured and concealed by the Lord in play.

name: The powers of the Pāśupata yogin

definitions.definition: Powers arise with yoga: distant seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing and omniscience (power of knowing); swiftness of mind, taking forms at will, acting without organs (power of acting); and eight marks of perfection - subject to none, not to be entered, not to be slain, fearless, imperishable, unaging, deathless, unobstructed. They arise gradually after six months of constant yoga and make the yogin a chief of Mahādeva's troops. The texts present them as signs and as part of liberation, not as dangers.
The Skanda Purāṇa tells of Pāśupata siddhas who went to Śiva's abode in the same body.
Hostile dramas attribute flight and power over gods and heavens to Kāpālikas.

name: Teacher and disciple in the Pāśupata tradition

definitions.definition: The disciple is a tested brahmin of good family, keen senses and desire to know, who seeks the end of suffering, not dharma, wealth, pleasure or isolation; the teacher acts from grace, knows the nine groups and consecrates; one with scripture but without faith or knowledge of the groups is a pseudo-teacher.
Alms (stages 1 and 3), discarded food (stage 2), whatever is obtained (stage 4); none in stage 5.
Perception, inference and scripture (the teaching from Maheśvara through the teachers); other alleged means are included in these.
The teachers from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara saluted daily (Ratnaṭīkā); eighteen are named by Jain doxographers; the Mathurā inscription counts ten generations from Kuśika to 380 CE.

name: The rule (vidhi): observance and its aids

definitions.definition: Activity producing merit: primary - the observance (vows and the six doors) - and secondary - re-bathing and the like; it begins with ash, has censure in the middle and ends with feigned folly, and has three limbs, gift, worship and austerity.
A quality of the paśu: cognitive (discriminating - called citta - or not) or non-cognitive (merit and demerit).
Yamas: non-harming, celibacy, truthfulness, non-dealing, non-stealing; niyamas: non-anger, service of the teacher, purity, light diet, vigilance - all ten counted as yamas.

relations.note: a parallel five-and-five scheme; members differ (asaṃvyavahāra, akrodha, guruśuśrūṣā, āhāralāghava, apramāda)

name: Yoga as union of self and Lord

definitions.definition: Yoga is the conjunction of the self with the Lord through the mind; in action (muttering, meditation on Oṃ in the heart) or in the cessation of action; it arises for one of unclouded mind who practises.

name: The path of method and the path of liberation

definitions.definition: The Kagyu path has two streams: the path of method (thabs lam) — the six yogas on the basis of empowerment — and the path of liberation (grol lam) — Mahāmudrā; they are practised together, inner heat being 'the main trunk' and Mahāmudrā the 'illuminator of wisdom'.

name: The paths of smoke and light (Kapila Gītā)

definitions.definition: Ritualists go by smoke to the moon and return; the desireless go by light to the Person; devotion is best.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:paths-of-smoke-and-light-kapila
checks.note: BhP 3.32.3 (to the lunar world and back) and 3.32.7 ('sūryadvāreṇa ... puruṣam'); devotion to Vāsudeva quickly brings dispassion and knowledge (3.32.23).

notes: Parallels the Upaniṣadic pitṛyāna and devayāna (owned by U03).

definitions.definition: What keeps the balanced tissues balanced and restores the unbalanced is wholesome (Ca Sū 25.33); wholesome food alone makes the person grow (25.31).

name: Pati, paśu, pāśa — the Lord, the bound soul, the bonds

definitions.definition: The three eternal, irreducible categories (padārtha): Śiva, the countless souls, and the bonds (mala, karma, māyā). None is created; souls are not parts or appearances of Śiva; bonds are real.
Mupporuḷ ('the three realities') — pati, pacu, pācam; the Civañāṉa Pōtam's twelve sūtras prove and define each, then give the means and fruit.
All selves in saṃsāra are paśus; Śiva is their lord (Paśupati), who binds them with the noose of māyā and alone frees them; he himself is bondage, binder, noose and bound (Īśvara Gītā).
The Kiraṇa teaches the knowledge of paśu, pāśa and pati; the soul is eternal, pervasive, ignorant and inactive, lodged within māyā and bound through kalā, vidyā, rāga, prakṛti and the instruments.
Śrīkaṇṭha uses the Śaiva triad within a Vedānta frame: Śiva the Lord, souls bound by the impurity, karma and māyā, freed by his grace to equality with him.

relations.note: Kashmir non-dualism derives all categories from Śiva's consciousness; the Siddhānta keeps three
the Siddhānta denies that soul and bonds are superimposed on one reality

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:pati-pasu-pasa
checks.note: KP 2.7.18-19 (paśus, Paśupati, the noose of māyā); the 'he himself is bondage, binder, noose and bound' clause is KP 2.7.32 ('sa eva bandhaḥ sa ca bandhakartā sa eva pāśaḥ paśavaḥ sa eva'), just outside the cited teaching.

notes: Contribution from U08; U18 owns the Siddhānta concept.

name: The dharma of the devoted wife (pativratā)

definitions.definition: The devoted wife's service of her husband as a deity gives her power over an angry ascetic (MBh 3.196–197) and over death (Sāvitrī, 3.281); Anasūyā teaches it to Sītā (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119); Umā expounds women's dharma (MBh 13.126–134).
Everything is won by rightly applied effort; fate is only one's former effort, overcome by present effort; reliance on fate is delusion.

In jyotiṣa, fate is karma made in another birth, and success needs fate and human effort together like farming; neither favourable planets nor rites alone suffice (Yogayātrā 1.3–6); the smṛti likewise calls fate the effort of a former body (YājñSm 1.349–351).

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:paurusa-and-daiva
checks.note: Rests on tea:moksopaya:2.4.8-18, tea:moksopaya:2.6.1-6, tea:moksopaya:2.8.1-5; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

name: The hundred peaceful and wrathful deities

definitions.definition: Forty-two peaceful deities (Samantabhadra and Samantabhadrī, the five buddhas with consorts, eight male and eight female bodhisattvas, six sages, four male and four female gatekeepers) and fifty-eight wrathful (five herukas with consorts, eight gaurīs, eight piśācīs, four gatekeepers, twenty-eight īśvarīs), present in the body and appearing in the bardo of dharmatā.
The inner organ goes out through the sense, takes the object's form, and the consciousness delimited by knower, mode and object become one (Vedāntaparibhāṣā ch.1).
Non-conceptual, non-erroneous cognition of the particular; four kinds — sensory, mental, reflexive and yogic; self-evidently free of construction.
The dharmakāya is beginningless, uncreated, permanent, the cessation of suffering itself; whether or not buddhas appear, the garbha is unchanging.
The Tathāgata's body is the dharmakāya and is not ill (Vimalakīrti 3.44).
Taken literally: the dharmakāya is permanent, stable, peaceful and eternal, not merely 'permanent' as an unbroken continuum.
Beings reborn in the realm of ghosts through miserliness and wrongdoing, relieved by offerings given in their name (Pv; Khp 7); the ghost realm is one of the five destinations (MN 12).

name: The conduct and ethics of the physician

definitions.definition: Friendliness, compassion to the afflicted, delight in the curable, equanimity toward the dying (Ca Sū 9.26); to treat out of compassion not profit (Ci 1.4.57-62); a second birth at completion of study (1.4.52-53); the true, the 'reputed' and the pretending physicians (Sū 11.50-53; 29.5-12); never to give an unknown drug (Sū 1.127-130); the student's oath (Vi 8.13).

relations.note: maitrī, karuṇā, prīti/harṣa and upekṣā as the physician's conduct

name: The qualities of the physician

definitions.definition: Intelligence, altruistic intention (the four immeasurables towards patients), commitment, skill, diligence and knowledge of worldly conduct.

members: skill in body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Pīlupāka: in baking, the pot breaks down to atoms, whose colour changes, and is re-formed.
Piṭharapāka: the colour of the whole pot changes without its dissolution.

name: The after-death body built by the piṇḍas

definitions.definition: Piṇḍa Upaniṣad: the departed passes days in water, fire, space and wind, and the ten rice-balls successively build its new body.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: The body as microcosm (piṇḍa and brahmāṇḍa)

definitions.definition: Everything in the cosmic egg is within the body (SSP 3); the elements, channels and doors of the body are enumerated (AmŚ 11–32); the yogī must know his own body — six centres, sixteen supports, three aims, five voids, a house of one pillar and nine doors (GŚ-Briggs 13–14); 'the swallowing of the body by the body' is the Nāth secret (Jñāneśvarī 6.291).
The fourteen worlds are within the body as principles (KJN 2.4–5); the one who knows the Akulavīra as abiding in the body is freed (Akulavīra B.93).

The Śiva Saṃhitā places Meru, the continents, rivers, oceans, seers, stars, planets, sacred fords and their deities, sun and moon and the elements within the body; 'he who knows this is a yogin' (2.1–5); the body is called brahmāṇḍa (1.91).

name: The fourfold: piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, rūpātīta

definitions.definition: Place is the body (piṇḍa), meditation the state (pada), the letter form (rūpa), the aim beyond form (rūpātīta) (KJN 3.2–5).
The body must be made stable before liberation in life; roots and metals are themselves unstable; only mercury stabilizes (Rasahṛdaya 1.10-13; Rasārṇava 1.11, 1.18-20; SDS 1).

name: The sacred seats shared by Kaula, Nāth and Buddhist tantras

definitions.definition: Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri and Kāmarūpa as the primary seats; Bhairava present with the Goddess at Kāmākhyā where the yoginīs meet.
The twenty-four sites of the Heruka maṇḍala (Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, Oḍḍiyāna, Arbuda, Devīkoṭa, Kāmarūpa …) and the Hevajra's ten classes of sites (pīṭha, upapīṭha …), mapped onto the body.
Kāmarūpa placed between the first two centres in the Gorakṣaśataka; Jālandhara as a siddha's name and a seat.

relations.note: the later Purāṇic network of 51 seats from Satī's body has another origin story

name: The seats and fields of the Yoginīkaula

definitions.definition: Fields: Karavīra, Mahākāla, Devīkoṭa, Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, Caritra, Ekāmraka, Aṭṭahāsa, Jayantī; seats: Kāmākhyā, Pūrṇagiri, Oḍiyāna, Arbuda; meeting places Śrīśaila, Mahendra, Kāmākhyā (KJN 8.16–22; 16.5–8).
By sapiṇḍīkaraṇa the preta is joined to the three generations of ancestors and thereafter receives the pārvaṇa and annual śrāddhas; offerings at Gayā free the ancestors.

definitions.definition: A planet's strength depends on its placement: exaltation at a fixed degree and fall in the seventh sign from it (BJ 1.13), root-trine sign, own sign, friendly and enemy signs, and vargottama.

name: Natural and temporary friendship of planets

definitions.definition: Planets are by nature friends, neutrals or enemies of one another, and become temporary friends when placed in the 2nd–4th and 10th–12th from each other; the combination gives five grades of relationship used in judging strength and in marriage matching (grahamaitra).

notes: From standard horā teaching (BJ 2.15–17; BPHS 3); verse references not checked.

name: The planets and the five elements

definitions.definition: From Brahmā's mind came the moon and from his eyes the sun; then Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn were born from fire, earth, ether, water and air (SS 12.22–24), and Varāhamihira makes them the lords of these elements (BJ 2.6).

name: Pliancy as the measure of calm abiding

definitions.definition: After the ninth state, mental pliancy arises, then physical pliancy with its bliss; when that joy settles, calm abiding is achieved; before it there is only a likeness of calm abiding.

Puruṣas are many, because birth, death and instruments are allotted separately, beings do not act all at once, and the guṇas are differently proportioned (SK 18; SS 1.149, 6.45); some were liberated while others were not (SS 1.157). Scriptures of non-duality refer to sameness of kind, not number (SS 1.154).

There are many puruṣas: the seen ceases for one whose purpose is accomplished but continues for others, being common to them (2.22, YBh 2.22); the end of saṃsāra holds for the skilled, not for others (YBh 4.33).

relations.note: each puruṣa is pure consciousness; plurality is of puruṣas, not of kinds of consciousness

definitions.definition: Selves are many because their states are distinct and on the authority of scripture (VS 3.2.15–17 C).
Individual selves are distinct in each body; the Lord is one (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Advaita's one self; the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika tradition insists on real, eternal plurality.

definitions.definition: The guru's direct introduction to the nature of mind, given when the disciple is ripe — Tilopa's sandal on Nāropa's face; the 9th Karmapa's stages: mind in stillness and movement, appearances as mind, mind as empty, emptiness as spontaneously present and self-liberated.

name: Pointing out the nature of mind

definitions.definition: The guru points out mind's nature directly — though 'a finger pointing at the sky does not show the sky' (Queen Dohā v39); 'look and point out reality by yourself in yourself' (v11–12).

name: The possible and the impossible

definitions.definition: What cannot happen: one accomplished in view taking any formation as permanent or self, killing parents or an arahant; two Buddhas in one world; a woman being a fully awakened Buddha, wheel-turning monarch, Sakka, Māra or Brahmā; bad conduct ripening as pleasant (MN 115; AN 1.268–295).

notes: Recorded faithfully; see dsp:women-caste-liberation.

definitions.definition: Stepping forward from the top of the hundred-foot pole.
Removing habit energies after sudden awakening.
Gogo no shugyō: Hakuin after Shōju's rebuke; Tōrei's stages.
Space enclosed in pots seems many but is one space; so the self appears as many jīvas through bodies.
The wheel keeps turning after the potter's push has ceased; so the knower's body continues until prārabdha is spent.

The three accents (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.29–31) carry meaning and efficacy: Tvaṣṭṛ's mis-accented 'indraśatru' made Indra the slayer (ŚB 1.6.3.10), and a mantra faulty in accent is a thunderbolt against the sacrificer (PŚ 52).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:astadhyayi:1.2.29-31 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:1.6.3.10 (confirmed); tea:paniniya-siksa:52 (confirmed).

name: The power of the divine name

definitions.definition: Uttering the Lord's name, even indirectly, destroys all sin and is the best expiation (BhP 6.2.9-14); it is the fearless way for all (2.1.11), the supreme dharma (6.3.22) and the means of the Kali age (12.3.51-52; VP 6.2.17); offences against it hinder its fruit (Padma, as cited).
The Name (of Rām) remembered inwardly is the only raft; recited on beads while the mind wanders it is nothing; by the Name the Camār Ravidās is honoured by brahmins.
The Name is the Word within, not the spoken name.
The true Name given at initiation frees the soul from Kāl.

name: Powers and freedom of movement from knowledge

definitions.definition: The texts promise results: whoever venerates X as brahman moves at will as far as X reaches (ChU 7); the knower of the self's real desires moves at will in all worlds and by intention alone obtains the fathers' world and the rest (ChU 8.1.6-8.2.10); whatever world the pure-minded desires he wins (MuU 3.1.10); the self-ruled moves at will (ChU 7.25.2).

queries: prepared segments: ChU 7, ChU 8.1.6-8.2.10, MuU 3.1.10, ChU 7.25.2
checks.note: All 4 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 7; ChU 8.1.6-8.2.10; MuU 3.1.10; ChU 7.25.2). It rests on 6 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: 'Cultivation and realisation are not lacking, but it cannot be defiled' (Huairang); polishing a tile does not make a mirror.
Practice and realization are one; the beginner's practice is the whole of original realization (Dōgen).

The Kagyu's self-description as a lineage of practice and realization rather than of scholastic explanation (bshad brgyud); the Tibetan 'eight great chariots of the practice lineages' count the Marpa Kagyu and the Shangpa Kagyu separately.

name: Practice, not garb or learning, is the cause of success

definitions.definition: Success comes from practice alone, not from reading scriptures, wearing an ascetic's garb or talking about yoga (HYP 1.65–66; DYŚ 39–46, which names shaven heads, staffs, ochre robes, matted locks, ash and sectarian mantras as no cause of success and condemns garb-wearers who deceive for 'penis and belly').

name: Prajāpati's falling apart and his restoration

definitions.definition: After emitting the creatures Prajāpati, who is the year, fell apart (vyasraṃsata) — his joints being the junctions of day and night, the moon's phases and the seasons; the gods healed him by the Agnihotra, the new- and full-moon and seasonal rites (ŚB 1.6.3.35–36), and he is rebuilt as the fire-altar whose bricks are his days and nights (ŚB 10.1.1.2–3); he put himself together with the metres, whence 'saṃhitā' (AA 3.2.6).

relations.note: the altar is the means of restoration

notes: Correction to the task wording: the Brāhmaṇas speak of Prajāpati 'coming apart' through the exhaustion of creating, not of a dismemberment by others (contrast the Puruṣa Sūkta, RV 10.90).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:satapatha-brahmana:1.6.3.35-36 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:10.1.1.2-3 (confirmed); tea:aitareya-aranyaka:3.2.6 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: The inauspicious act done by one whose intellect, resolve and memory have lapsed; the provoker of all doṣas (Ca Śā 1.98-109); cause of exogenous and mental disease (Sū 7.51-52), of exogenous insanity (Ni 7.10) and, via adharma, of epidemics (Vi 3.20).

relations.note: it provokes all doṣas
through adharma

definitions.definition: The ultimate is light (prakāśa) whose very nature is reflexive awareness (vimarśa); without vimarśa light would be insentient like a crystal (ĪPK 1.5.11); vimarśa is supreme speech and freedom (1.5.13).
Tripurā is the fusion of prakāśa and vimarśa (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); Maheśa is pure light with self-awareness merged within, and Śakti the mirror of Śiva's form (KKV 1-3).
Kṛṣṇa's play is eternal in the unmanifest abode and becomes manifest on earth once in a day of Brahmā; the parakīyā appearance belongs (for Jīva) to the manifest play.

In the usual list: Catuḥśaraṇa, Āturapratyākhyāna, Mahāpratyākhyāna, Bhaktaparijñā, Taṇḍulavaicārika, Saṃstāraka, Gacchācāra, Gaṇividyā, Devendrastava, Maraṇasamādhi; other lists substitute Candravedhyaka, Vīrastava and others.

Any method that brings one to know the inner self is valid, and none is fixed (Sureśvara); the ancients, intent on the oneness of the self, were indifferent to the explanation of the empirical (Appayya).

The unconscious, productive root (mūlaprakṛti, pradhāna, the unmanifest): uncaused, one, common, of three guṇas in equilibrium (SK 3, 10–11; SS 1.61). Not perceived because subtle, it is inferred from its effects (SK 8): from the limited measure of things, their homogeneity, activity through potency, the distinction of cause and effect and the merging of the manifold (SK 15–16). It acts for puruṣa like milk for the calf (SK 57), withdraws like a dancer once seen (SK 59), and is what is truly bound and released (SK 62). Gauḍapāda lists its synonyms pradhāna, brahman, avyakta, bahudhānaka, māyā; there is only one prakṛti (Gauḍapāda on SK 66).

The seen has the nature of illumination, activity and inertia, consists of elements and senses, and exists for experience and liberation (2.18); the guṇas are called pradhāna (YBh 2.18); it is real and common to all puruṣas (2.22).
Eternal, real, insentient matter with three guṇas (mixed sattva), the Lord's body; called māyā for its wonderful effects, not because it is illusory.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Prakṛti and puruṣa are both beginningless; the modifications and the guṇas arise from prakṛti (13.20); it is the cause in agency concerning effect and cause (13.21); puruṣa abides in it and experiences the guṇas born of it (13.22); all actions are done by prakṛti alone (13.30); the three guṇas are born of it (14.5); the senses and mind abide in it (15.7).

Dvaita: an eternal-and-non-eternal insentient reality, the material cause of the world, dependent on and moved by Viṣṇu, presided over by Lakṣmī; its products are the principles from mahat to the elements. God is not the material cause.

relations.note: Advaita's māyā is not a second reality (the Sāṃkhya–Advaita contrast; interpretive)

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The doṣa predominating at conception — from semen and ovum, season and womb, the mother's diet, the elements — fixes the constitution: vāta-, pitta-, kapha-natured, mixed, or balanced (best) (Ca Sū 7.39-41; Vi 8.95-100; AHS Sū 1.9-10); it does not itself cause disease, as a poison-born worm is not harmed by poison (Su Śā 4.78-79; AHS Sū 1.9).

Dispassion leads to absorption into prakṛti (SK 45) — not liberation: those who take prakṛti or its evolutes for the self dissolve into them (Gauḍapāda on SK 48, 'darkness') and rise again like a diver (SS 3.54); the Kramadīpikā calls it 'bondage to prakṛti'. The one who rises may become an all-knowing lord in the next creation (SS 3.55–57).

Sāṃkhya accepts three: perception (determination concerning each object), inference (threefold; from general correlation for things beyond the senses) and reliable testimony (for what neither establishes) (SK 4–6); other proposed means are included in these (SK 4; Vācaspati). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra defines perception as cognition that, in contact, reflects its object (1.89).

Yoga accepts three means of valid cognition — perception, inference and testimony (YS 1.7) — defined in YBh 1.7; the insight of samādhi has the particular as object, beyond testimony and inference (1.49), and the perception of nirvitarkā samāpatti is the 'highest perception' (YBh 1.42).
Six means, valid for the empirical and following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā; all within the sphere of ignorance; scripture alone reveals Brahman; perception grasps being, not difference.
Three: perception, inference, scripture; all have qualified objects; the Lord is known from scripture alone.

name: The definition of a means of valid cognition

definitions.definition: Non-deceptive cognition (Dharmakīrti), the revealer of a previously unknown object; for Dharmottara, what makes one attain the object; hence memory and re-cognition are not means of knowledge.
The five knowledges are themselves pramāṇa: sensory and scriptural are indirect, clairvoyance, mind-reading and omniscience direct, because only knowledge by the soul alone is direct (TS 1.9–12).
Akalaṅka's system: direct cognition is conventionally direct (sense-perception) or truly direct; indirect cognition is memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and scripture (Laghīyastraya).
Valid cognition illuminates itself and its object and is free of contradiction (Nyāyāvatāra 1); it is the right ascertainment of an object (Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.1.2).

relations.note: Nyāya and Yoga call sense-perception pratyakṣa; the TS calls it parokṣa since it depends on senses.

name: Means and result of cognition are one

definitions.definition: The means of knowledge (cognition's likeness to the object) and its result (understanding the object, or self-awareness) are one cognition, distinguished only figuratively.

The same object may be known by several means (fire by testimony, inference and perception), though some objects are restricted to one (heaven to scripture); knowledge culminates in perception (NBh 1.1.3).

relations.note: Buddhist logicians restrict each means of knowledge to its own kind of object.

definitions.definition: Breath is the eldest and best of the vital powers, on whose departure the body fails (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1); the one god (BAU 3.9.9); born from the self like a shadow, dividing itself fivefold (PrU 3.3-7); brahman (KauU 2.1) and the intelligent self (KauU 3.2); the gatherer into which the senses go in sleep (ChU 4.3.3); breath is father, mother, all (ChU 7.15).

definitions.definition: Life is the union of body and breath (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 5.52); the breath from the navel touches the heart-lotus, goes out to drink the nectar of the sky and returns to nourish the body and the belly-fire (5.51); the prāṇas reside in ten seats (Ca Sū 29.3).

relations.note: the prāṇa of the Vedic and yogic traditions

name: Prāṇa (breath) in the Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas

definitions.definition: The breaths are the primordial seers who made the one Person, Prajāpati (ŚB 6.1.1.1); breath is the consecrated (KB 7.1); the one god is the breath (ŚB 11.6.3); in sleep the breaths enter the self (ŚB 10.5.2.20); the Ṛgvedic seers are forms of the breath (AA 2.2.1); the breaths are counted as five (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna) and sometimes as seven in the head.

name: The five vital airs in Yoga

definitions.definition: Life is the joint activity of the senses, fivefold: prāṇa (mouth and nose to the heart), samāna (to the navel), apāna (down to the soles), udāna (up to the head) and vyāna (pervading); prāṇa is chief (YBh 3.39); mastery of udāna and samāna yields powers (3.39–40).

name: Prāṇa, the life-breath, in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: Wind was born from the Puruṣa's breath (RV 10.90.13); Vāta is the breath of the gods, germ of the world (10.168.4); the Atharvaveda hails Prāṇa as lord of all, clothing creatures as a father his son, death and fever, the swan that never lifts one foot, awake among sleepers, bound to oneself for life (AVŚ 11.4).

name: Prāṇāgnihotra — the fire-offering into the breaths

definitions.definition: The first morsels of every meal are offered with 'svāhā' to prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna and udāna, satisfying in turn the senses, their deities and regions; one who eats knowing this offers in all worlds and all selves and his evils burn up like a reed-tuft in fire (ChU 5.19–24); the mantras 'in faith, entered into the breath, I offer the immortal' frame the meal (TA 10.69–70); the whole body becomes the sacrificial ground (Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
Prescribed in the Dharmasūtra rules for eating as the daily rite of the twice-born at meals.

checks.note: ChU 5.19–24 (five offerings to prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna and udāna; the reed-tuft simile at 5.24.3) was text-located. definitions.definition: The praṇava designates Īśvara by a fixed, not conventional, relation, like a lamp and its light (1.27, YBh 1.27); its repetition with contemplation of its meaning makes the mind one-pointed (1.28, YBh 1.28) and removes obstacles (1.29).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): Om is the udgītha and the essence of essences (ChU 1.1); all speech is held by Om (ChU 2.23.3); Om is brahman, all this (TU 1.8; MāU 1); the word all Vedas proclaim, the best support (KU 1.2.15-17); the bow (MuU 2.2.4); the higher and lower brahman whose measures lead to different worlds (PrU 5); A, U, M and the measureless as the four quarters (MāU 8-12); the upper fire-stick (ŚU 1.14); the word-brahman (MaiU 6.22).

The 'tāra' prefixed to mantras; its three letters are Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra; its subtle phases beyond the three letters (bindu, ardhacandra, nirodhikā, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpinī, samanā, unmanā) are traversed in its meditative utterance.
The one word from which the Veda's knowledge springs (VP 1.9, low confidence).

name: The eightfold praṇava

definitions.definition: Om is the designator of Viṣṇu and has eight components, from 'a' to 'atiśānta', naming eight of his forms (Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turīya, Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman, Jñānātman); the other mantras derive from it.

members: nāda, bindu, ghoṣa, śānta (intermediate names recalled, not verified)

definitions.definition: Action and afflictions come from conceptual construction, which comes from elaboration; elaboration ceases in emptiness (MMK 18.5); the ultimate and nirvāṇa are the pacification of elaboration (18.9; 25.24).
Taking refuge in the Lord with Śrī as the sole refuge, by those with no other means and no other refuge; done once, it brings liberation at the end of the body.
An independent means (svatantra-upāya), performed once with five limbs and self-offering, equal in fruit to bhakti-yoga; the occasion of the Lord's grace.
Not a means but the soul's acceptance of the Lord, who alone is the means; it befits the soul's nature of dependence; regarding it as a means is a fault.

Taking refuge at the Lord's feet with no other refuge, naming Śrī who never leaves his chest (TVM 6.10.10); clinging to the Lord's feet though he cause grief, like a child pushed away that cries for its mother (PT 5.1); giving one's life to the owner of release (TVM 1.2.1); the unbreakable relation pleaded by those with nothing (TP 28).
Having offered self, world and Veda to the Lord, the devotee has no care for worldly loss; self-offering is one of love's eleven forms.
Rāma never abandons one who comes for refuge (Vibhīṣaṇa).
Living as Hari keeps one.

relations.note: the Purāṇic taking of refuge (Gajendra etc.) read as prapatti
the Gītā's 'take refuge in me alone' (18.66)

definitions.definition: A real force that links a dharma to a series; explains ownership of latent defilements and of attainments.
The intact seed in the series; not an entity.

relations.note: The two explanations of the same function.

definitions.definition: For the knower, prārabdha karma continues to move the body but has no hold, like dream-objects after waking; knowledge destroys accumulated and future karma (Nādabindu 21–29).

definitions.definition: Purity of mind is grace; everything to be enjoyed is first offered to the liṅga and received back as prasāda, which purifies the mind; so too the prasāda of guru and jaṅgama.
Refuting by drawing out the unwanted consequences of the opponent's own theses, as Buddhapālita did on MMK 1.1, defended by Candrakīrti (PsP 1).

A question is answered from the chart of its moment and the omens present (Ṣaṭpañcāśikā); in Kerala the aṣṭamaṅgala-praśna uses eight auspicious objects, the querist's touch and a ritual setting, and temple queries (devaprāśna) diagnose the deity's displeasure; afflictions are traced to curses and remedied (Praśna Mārga).
Veda, Gītā, Brahma Sūtra and Bhāgavata, each later one resolving doubts about the earlier.
Upaniṣads, Bhagavad Gītā and Brahma Sūtras, on which every Vedānta ācārya comments.
The seed of poetry, together with skill and practice (KP 1.3); creative in the poet and appreciative in the connoisseur (Rājaśekhara).

name: Pratibhā: the flash of sentence meaning and instinct

definitions.definition: An indescribable intuition, self-evident to each, in which the sentence meaning is grasped; the guide of all action, even animals' instinct; sixfold by origin — nature, conduct, practice, yoga, unseen merit, and gift of the special ones (VP 2.143–152).

relations.note: same word; the grammarian's universal intuition and the poet's genius

definitions.definition: The jīva is Brahman's reflection in avidyā/the inner organ, real and identical with the prototype; Īśvara is the prototype (or, for Sarvajñātman, the reflection in ignorance).

name: The reflection doctrine (pratibimbavāda) of the Trika

definitions.definition: The universe appears in consciousness as a city in a mirror - undivided from the mirror yet appearing distinct - but, unlike a mirror, consciousness is itself the source of the image (TĀ 3; Paramārthasāra 12-13).

Against harmful thoughts (YS 2.33–2.34): contemplate the unwanted ripening that follows them (unending suffering and ignorance) and recall the refuge taken in the dharma of yoga (YBh 2.33, 2.34). Also how the afflictions are attenuated (YBh 2.4).

When harmful thoughts oppress, cultivate their opposites (2.33): reflect that violence and the rest, done, caused or approved, from greed, anger or delusion, have endless suffering and ignorance as fruit (2.34, YBh 2.33–34).

definitions.definition: The series of rites from ploughing the site to installation, performed with a single root āgama; by it the deity is established in liṅga or image.
The fixed and movable images are installed and linked; the fixed stands for the partless, the movable for the partite form.
Installation of the seven deities, reserved to the tantri.
Liberation as recognition: the Lord is already one's self but unnoticed through delusion; revealing his powers brings recognition, as a woman recognizes the lover beside her (ĪPK 1.1.3, 4.17).

name: Perception the only means of knowledge

definitions.definition: (As reported) Only perception is valid; the world is as much as the senses reach.

name: The creation of cognitions (pratyaya-sarga): the fifty

definitions.definition: The intellectual creation of fifty kinds: five errors (darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, blind gloom; 62 subdivisions), twenty-eight incapacities (11 injuries of the organs, 17 of buddhi), nine contentments and eight accomplishments (SK 46–51). Error, incapacity and contentment curb accomplishment (SK 51). With the ten fundamental topics they make the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra.

Four or more strong planets in one sign make a renunciant; the strongest decides the order — for Varāhamihira Śākya, Ājīvika, bhikṣu, vṛddha, caraka, nirgrantha or forest-dweller (BJ 15.1), for Parāśara tapasvin, kāpālika, red-robed, ekadaṇḍin, yati, cakradhara or nirgrantha (BPHS 79.2–3); a planet set in the sun gives devotion without initiation; Saturn's aspect gives initiation; certain royal yogas make a founder of a holy place (BJ 15.2–4).

relations.note: renunciation-yogas and the signs of liberation are distinct: the first shows entering an order, the second the final state

definitions.definition: Engagement (pravṛtti), rooted in delusion, desire, aversion and karma and grown into ego-sense, attachment, doubt and wrong means, is suffering and the root of evil; disengagement (nivṛtti) is release, the supreme brahman (Ca Śā 5.8-11).

Pravṛtta action, done with desire, leads to prosperity and the gods' state; nivṛtta action, desireless and preceded by knowledge, leads beyond the elements (MDh 12.88–90); abstention bears great fruit (MDh 5.56).

name: Preceptor and teacher in the Vinaya (upādhyāya, ācārya)

definitions.definition: A newly ordained monk lives in dependence (niśraya) on a preceptor (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya), serving them as a son serves a father while they instruct him; a preceptor must have at least ten years since ordination and be competent in the Dharma and Vinaya; dependence lasts (normally) five years.
The same structure of preceptor, instructor and dependence governs Tibetan monastic training, the preceptor (mkhan po) conferring ordination.
Upajjhāya and ācariya with the duties of pupil and teacher (Mahāvagga I).

notes: Skeleton summary common to the Vinayas; the ten-year and five-year figures are from memory (moderate confidence); exact locations not given.

definitions.definition: Chinese Pure Land joins recitation with precepts and good conduct: the three meritorious acts; Mao Ziyuan's five precepts confirmed by five recitations; Yinguang's 'fulfil your duties, avoid evil'.

Precepts are not the condition of birth (they are not the selected practice), yet disciples must not claim the nenbutsu has no precepts or encourages evil (Seven-Article Pledge); Jōdo-shū transmits the bodhisattva precepts.
No precepts in the last age; licensed evil is nevertheless rejected.

name: Love of God as the fifth and highest goal

definitions.definition: Prema surpasses the four aims including liberation; devotees reject the five liberations without service.
Puṣṭi devotees seek service and nirodha, not liberation.
Abiding in the limbs of calm taught in the Samādhisambhāraparivarta, without which no concentration is achieved even in thousands of years.
A suitable place, few desires, contentment, few activities, pure ethics, abandoning conceptual thoughts of desire and the like.

The condition of the dead between death and union with the ancestors; it becomes fixed for those who die badly, do great wrong or lack the rites (e.g. no bull released on the eleventh day), who then suffer hunger and thirst and trouble their kin (dreams, signs); it is ended by śrāddha, gifts, nārāyaṇa-bali and hearing sacred texts (the Bhāgavata saptāha frees Dhundhukārī).

name: From the departed (preta) to ancestor (pitṛ)

definitions.definition: The newly dead remains a preta nourished by the rites of the first days and the monthly offerings of the first year, until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa unites him with father, grandfather and great-grandfather, the most distant then passing out of the piṇḍa circle.

definitions.definition: The empty essence of the ground, never stained by delusion; the object of cutting through.

name: Principle and phenomena in Chan (li / shi, huihu)

definitions.definition: Grasping phenomena is delusion, merging with principle is not yet awakening; light and dark interfuse like the steps of walking (Cantongqi).

relations.note: Caodong language of interfusion parallels Huayan's li–shi interpenetration (U54).

name: The prohibition on displaying superhuman powers

definitions.definition: The Vinayas tell how Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja rose into the air to win a sandalwood bowl and the Buddha forbade monks to display powers before laypeople; falsely claiming superhuman states is a pārājika, and a true claim to the unordained a lesser offence (moderate confidence on the parallels in each Vinaya).
Of the three wonders, instruction is the highest, since it never fails and joins beings to the good (AK 7.47).

relations.note: Powers are acknowledged as fruits of dhyāna but their display is restricted.

name: The proof of rebirth (Pramāṇavārttika)

definitions.definition: Breath, senses and cognition do not arise from the body alone without a prior moment of their own kind; so the first moment of mind in a new life comes from a previous mind, and cultivation can continue across lives.

relations.note: consciousness does not arise from the elements of the body alone

notes: Opponent is the Cārvāka/Lokāyata (dsp:mind-body-rebirth).

definitions.definition: Protecting oneself one protects others through mindfulness; protecting others one protects oneself through patience, harmlessness, love and sympathy (SN 47.19).

The Earth is upheld by truth, order, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice; she is mother and the speaker her son; she bears peoples of many speeches and dharmas; one digging her asks not to wound her vitals or heart (AVŚ 12.1).

name: Matter, atoms and aggregates

definitions.definition: Matter (pudgala) consists of partless atoms and their aggregates, formed by union and division and bound by degrees of smoothness and roughness; it has touch, taste, smell and colour and takes the forms of sound, light, shadow and bodies; body, speech, mind, breath, pleasure and pain are its services, and karma is a subtle kind of matter (TS 5.19–28, 5.33–37).

members: vargaṇā (classes of matter: e.g. karmic, linguistic, mental)

definitions.definition: A real person, neither the same as nor different from the aggregates, designated in dependence on them as fire on fuel; inexpressible; the bearer of the burden; that which transmigrates.
No self: only aggregates conditioned by defilement and karma go on like a flame.
The person is a designation of the series; no liberation for those who imagine a self as a separate entity.
The person is not found as a real and ultimate fact.

relations.note: The Pudgalavādins held their person compatible with the Buddha's denial of a self; their opponents did not.

definitions.definition: Reading the radial pulse of both wrists with three fingers, each position linked to organs; constitutional, seasonal, disease and death pulses and the seven 'wondrous' pulses.

relations.note: parallel diagnostic method in later Āyurveda; historical relation not established here

definitions.definition: Those who lack the knowledge or the rite are 'born again and again as Death's food' and die again in the other world; the fire-altar and the Nāciketa fire conquer re-death (ŚB 10.4.3; TB 3.11.8).

relations.note: the Brāhmaṇa fear of repeated death is developed in the later doctrine of rebirth by action

definitions.definition: Auspicious activity binds merit (pleasant feeling, auspicious lifespan, name and status), inauspicious binds demerit (TS 6.3, 8.25–26).

ChU 7.1.2); the Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā before the Vedas (Matsya 53.3); it was composed out of compassion for those without access to the Veda (BhP 1.4.25); the Bhāgavata is the ripe fruit of the Veda-tree (1.1.3).

checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: Creation proceeds from the Lord's Śakti as a pure creation (the vyūhas from pairs of qualities) and an other-than-pure creation from prakṛti; the Jayākhya orders the Vaiṣṇava (pure), primordial-matter and Brahmā's creations.
Śiva creates the pure universe (śuddhādhvan) directly from bindu, and delegates the impure (from māyā) to Ananta, first of the Vidyeśvaras.

name: The patriarchs of the Lotus (Pure Land) school

definitions.definition: Zongxiao (1200) names Huiyuan the first patriarch with five successors (Shandao, Fazhao, Shaokang, Shengchang, Zongze); Zhipan (1269) names seven (Huiyuan, Shandao, Chengyuan, Fazhao, Shaokang, Yanshou, Shengchang); later lists add Zhuhong, Ouyi, Xingce, Shixian, Jixing and Yinguang for thirteen.

notes: The thirteen-patriarch list is the modern standard (recalled); the Song lists are read locally.

name: Pure lands and buddha-fields

definitions.definition: Buddha-fields purified by a buddha's vows, in the ten directions: Amitābha's Sukhāvatī in the west, Akṣobhya's Abhirati and Bhaiṣajyaguru's lapis land in the east; born there beings do not retrogress.

Sukhāvatī lies west beyond ten trillion lands; it surpasses the three realms and is not included in them; it is the reward of Dharmākara's vows; Amitābha became buddha there ten kalpas ago; its 29 adornments are the object of contemplation.

notes: Pure Land doctrine and schools: U43.

relations.note: the Western land with direction and form vs the land that is pure where the mind is pure; later Chinese masters hold both

name: The pure rules (qinggui) of Chan monasteries

definitions.definition: Baizhang's founding of separate Chan monasteries with Dharma hall, Sangha hall and communal labour; later codes (1103, 1338).

name: The aggregates as buddhas, the elements as goddesses

definitions.definition: The five aggregates are the five tathāgatas and the elements their consorts (Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, Tārā); despising one's aggregates is a root downfall.

notes: Correlations follow the Guhyasamāja scheme as commonly given; they differ between systems.

name: Purity of mind, purity of the buddha-field

definitions.definition: As the bodhisattva's mind is purified, so is his buddha-field; the Buddha's field is always pure but appears impure to impure minds.

relations.note: a pure land 'here' vs. pure lands elsewhere; both taught

definitions.definition: The 'I' (aham), union of the letters a and ha, the lump of Śiva and Śakti that has swallowed the worlds (KKV 5).
The perfect 'I' whose essence is light and bliss, the potency of the great mantra (PH 20); the 'aham' spans the letters from A to HA (PTV).

name: The seen exists for the seer (bhoga and apavarga)

definitions.definition: The seen exists for experience and liberation (2.18); its very being is for the seer's sake (2.21); the mind, acting in combination, exists for another (4.24); bondage is the buddhi's not completing the puruṣa's purpose, liberation its completion (YBh 2.18).

Protection of the Veda, adaptation of mantras, obedience to the scriptural command, brevity and removal of doubt; avoiding barbarous speech; the merit of a single well-used word (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā and on 6.1.84).

checks.note: The Mahābhāṣya Paspaśā has 'rakṣohāgamalaghvasandehāḥ prayojanam', matching the five members. It also has the 'na mlecchitavai' passage, and on A 6.1.84 'ekaḥ śabdaḥ samyag jñātaḥ … svarge loke kāmadhug bhavati'. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:mahabhasya:paspasa/2, tea:mahabhasya:paspasa/3, tea:mahabhasya:6.1.84.

definitions.definition: Fame, wealth, knowledge of conduct, removal of evil, immediate supreme bliss, and counsel in the manner of a beloved (KP 1.2); the four aims of life even for the dull, through poetry (SD 1.2); rest for the afflicted and instruction for all (NŚ 1.108–116).

The conscious principle, neither producer nor product (SK 3), the opposite of the guṇa-made (SK 11): witness, isolated, neutral, seer, non-agent (SK 19), unattached and by nature ever free (SS 1.15–19), light itself, without consciousness as a property (SS 1.145–146). Its existence is proved because aggregates are for another, because something must stand opposite the guṇas, because of control, experience and the striving for isolation (SK 17). It is many (SK 18). It is not truly bound or released (SK 62).

The puruṣa is seeing alone, pure, yet conforming to cognitions (2.20); unchanging, it always knows the mind's activities (4.18); consciousness that does not pass over into objects (4.22); utterly unlike sattva (3.35); neither the same as the buddhi nor entirely different (YBh 2.20); pure, alone and liberated when established in itself (YBh 1.51). Knowledge of the puruṣa comes from saṃyama on what exists for itself (3.35).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self in the form of a person at the beginning (BAU 1.4.1); the cosmic person with a thousand heads (ŚU 3.14); the highest principle beyond the unmanifest (KU 1.3.11); the divine formless person (MuU 2.1.2); the person in the eye (ChU 4.15.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Beginningless like prakṛti (13.20), puruṣa is the cause in experiencing pleasure and pain (13.21); abiding in prakṛti it experiences the guṇas, and attachment to them is the cause of its births in good and bad wombs (13.22). The highest person in this body is onlooker, consenter, sustainer, experiencer, great lord, and is called the supreme self (13.23); whoever knows puruṣa and prakṛti with the guṇas thus is not born again (13.24). Chapter 15 speaks of two persons, perishable and imperishable, and the highest person beyond both (15.16-15.18).

relations.note: Both name the self; Sāṃkhya insists on plurality and non-agency, which Advaita's one ātman and Nyāya's qualified ātman do not share (graded partial; interpretive)

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

queries: prepared segments: BĀU 1.4.1, ŚU 3.14, KU 1.3.11, MuU 2.1.2, ChU 4.15.1
checks.note: All 5 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 1.4.1; ŚU 3.14; KU 1.3.11; MuU 2.1.2; ChU 4.15.1). It rests on 5 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: The thousand-headed Person who is all this, past and future, of whom one quarter is all beings and three quarters the immortal in heaven; sacrificed by the gods, he became the world, the Vedas, the varṇas, sun, moon and gods (RV 10.90); 'knowing him alone one goes beyond death' (VS 31.18).

relations.note: One of the Saṃhitās' creation accounts.
The four varṇas are said to come from the Person's mouth, arms, thighs and feet.

definitions.definition: Three accounts: the six dhātus (five elements and consciousness), consciousness alone, or the aggregate of twenty-four (Ca Śā 1.16-17); the conjunction of mind, self and body (Sū 1.46-47); the five elements with the embodied one — the substrate of treatment (Su Sū 1.22).
Śrī intercedes between the soul and the Lord, making the soul turn to him and moving him to receive it; one approaches the Lord through her.

Nammāḻvār surrenders naming Śrī, who cannot part from the Lord even for a moment (TVM 6.10.10); the Tiruppāvai's girls wake Nappiṉṉai to bring them to Kṛṣṇa (TP 16–21); Pēyāḻvār's vision begins 'I have seen Śrī'.

Two Kaula doctrines set out by Lakṣmīdhara before the Samaya view: the pūrva-Kaula on the Goddess as Śiva's body with a shared relation of principal and subsidiary (SL 34), and the uttara-Kaula in which there is no Śiva-principle apart from Śakti and she alone is worshipped (SL 23, 35).

name: The relation of Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā

definitions.definition: The two inquiries (into dharma and into Brahman) are distinguished; Śabara drew his proof of the self from the Śārīraka and Upavarṣa deferred it there (as reported by Śaṅkara); Kumārila says the Upaniṣads make the knowledge of the self firm; later Bhāṭṭas read Upaniṣads on the agent-self as serving rites and those on the non-transmigrating self as serving meditations.

name: The path of grace (puṣṭi) and the path of rule (maryādā)

definitions.definition: In the maryādā path the Lord gives fruits according to scriptural means; in the puṣṭi path his grace alone gives devotion and service, independent of means and merit.

relations.note: partial analogy: Gauḍīya rule-devotion vs spontaneous devotion (both lineages contrast rule and love)

definitions.definition: One Brahman alone exists, but as qualified: souls and matter are its real, inseparable modes and body; hence difference and non-difference are both true, the former of the modes, the latter of the one qualified whole.

relations.note: the positive doctrine against which Advaita's avidyā is rejected

name: The qualified recipient of the tantra

definitions.definition: One who does not revile scripture, has faith and devotion to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and knows ritual, other tantras, yoga, Veda and Vedāṅga, Paśupati's doctrine, logic and all spiritual śāstras.
Those fit for ritual, knowledge or conduct are joined to Śiva accordingly; the incapable receive initiation without the observances.

One impartial, intelligent and eager is a vessel for hearing (CŚ 12.1); one who at the mention of emptiness feels joy, tears and horripilation is a vessel to whom the ultimate should be taught (MA 6.4–5); emptiness wrongly grasped harms the dull, so the Buddha hesitated to teach (MMK 24.11–12).
For the bodhisattva vow, one skilled in its rite, abiding in it, patient and compassionate (Lamp 23–24); for mantra, a master able to give the complete empowerment.
The ten qualities of the Mahāyāna teacher (disciplined, serene, pacified, superior in qualities, energetic, learned, realised in reality, skilled in speech, loving, tireless).

name: The qualities of the devotee

names.name: yo madbhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ ('who is my devotee, he is dear to me')

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The devotee dear to the Lord hates no being, is friendly and compassionate, without 'mine' and without the sense of 'I', the same in pain and pleasure, forbearing, ever content, a yogin, self-restrained, firm in resolve, with mind and understanding offered to the Lord (12.13–14); neither disturbs the world nor is disturbed by it, free of elation, intolerance, fear and agitation (12.15); without expectation, pure, capable, impartial, rid of distress, relinquishing every undertaking (12.16); neither rejoices nor hates, grieves nor craves, having given up good and bad (12.17); the same toward enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, pleasure and pain, free of attachment, the same in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady in judgement (12.18–19). Each group ends with 'he is dear to me'; those who with faith follow this 'nectar of dharma' are exceedingly dear (12.20).

Humility (the Lord dislikes pride), non-violence, truth, purity, compassion and faith; no disputation; no attention to talk of lust, wealth, unbelievers and enemies; all conduct offered to the Lord; among devotees no distinction of caste, learning, beauty, family, wealth or occupation; the one-pointed are chief and purify the world.
Having nothing of one's own and relying on the Lord alone (ākiñcanya); being the servant of the Lord's servants; the observances of the vow — no harsh words, no evil tales, alms and help.

members: mayy arpitamanobuddhi (mind and understanding offered to the Lord)
not disturbing and not disturbed by the world
free of harṣa, amarṣa, bhaya, udvega (elation, intolerance, fear, agitation)
neither rejoicing, hating, grieving nor craving
same toward enemy and friend, honour and dishonour
same in cold and heat, pleasure and pain
notes: Chs. 10–12 contribution, combining extractor A's cpt:priya-bhakta-laksana (members with glosses, parallels) and extractor B's cpt:qualities-of-the-devotee. Several marks recur in the Gītā's other portraits: nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ (2.71), na dveṣṭi (2.57, 5.3), na śocati na kāṅkṣati (18.54), mānāpamāna / mitrāri / sarvārambhaparityāgī / tulyanindā… (14.24–25), śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkheṣu tathā mānāpamānayoḥ (6.7). The commentators divide on whether the marks describe the worshippers of the imperishable (Śaṅkara) or the devotee who relinquishes the fruit of actions (Rāmānuja) (recalled, not checked against the bhāṣyas); the text calls the subject 'my devotee'.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.

relations.note: the Bhāgavata's list of the sādhu's qualities and the Gītā's 'devotee dear to me' cover the same ground

definitions.definition: Some twenty-eight qualities of the holy person (compassionate, harmless, forbearing, truthful ... friendly, merciful, wise).
The same list repeated in the Avadhūta Gītā.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:qualities-of-the-sadhu-bhagavata
checks.note: BhP 11.11.29-31 lists exactly 28 qualities (7 + 11 + 10); the Avadhūta Gītā repeats them at 8.2-4 in rearranged order (8.2 = 11.11.30, 8.3 = 11.11.31, 8.4 = 11.11.29).

name: The qualities of a vajra master

definitions.definition: Steady, disciplined, intelligent, patient, honest, knowing mantra and tantra, compassionate, learned, knowing the ten principles, skilled in maṇḍala and ritual, a teacher of mantra, serene, senses controlled.

name: Rādhā as Kṛṣṇa's pleasure-power and supreme devotee

definitions.definition: Rādhā is the hlādinī-śakti, the embodiment of mahābhāva, one in self with Kṛṣṇa yet in a separate body for the play.
Rādhā, daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, is worshipped on Kṛṣṇa's left as his eternal consort.
Rādhā as Svāminī (mistress), emphasised in Viṭṭhalanātha's writings.

name: The love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in the Gīta Govinda

definitions.definition: Kṛṣṇa's spring dance with all the cowherd women; Rādhā's jealous withdrawal; the longing of both in separation, carried by the friend; Rādhā's vain waiting and her rebuke; the friend's counsel to give up pride; Kṛṣṇa's plea to place her foot on his head; her going to the tryst; union, and Kṛṣṇa adorning her. The poem offers itself to those who delight in remembering Hari and in the arts of love.

relations.note: the spring dance of GG 1 echoes the rāsa of BhP 10.29–33; Rādhā, unnamed in the Bhāgavata, is central here

notes: The traditions' own warning that the Lord's love-play is not to be imitated by those who are not lords (BhP 10.33.30–31) is the standard caution attached to hearing such poetry (tea:bhagavata-purana:10.33.30-31).

definitions.definition: Rādhā is the supreme object of worship; Kṛṣṇa is her beloved and devotee, fulfilled even by the breeze of her garment; her grace is the only gate.

relations.note: Gauḍīya theology makes Rādhā Kṛṣṇa's bliss-power; the Rādhāvallabhīs make her the supreme object of worship with Kṛṣṇa as her devotee

name: The radiant citta as the seat of ignorance

definitions.definition: At the final stage the radiant, seemingly perfect citta is the last hiding place of ignorance and must be seen through (Ajahn Maha Boowa).
The Dhamma is like a raft, for crossing over, not for carrying on one's head; even good states are to be let go of (MN 22); even the pure view of dependent origination is not to be clung to (MN 38).
A particular sound-form adorned with notes and melodic movement that colours the minds of people (Bṛhaddeśī 280–281); later classified by parent scales (mela) and by time, season and rasa.
Practice following the spontaneous love of the Vraja residents, qualified by eager longing (lobha), performed in the practitioner's body and the inner perfected body; kāmānugā or sambandhānugā.

The tirumantra (the soul's nature), the dvaya (the act of surrender and the prayer for service) and the carama-śloka (the Lord's command to surrender), received from the teacher and meditated on daily.

The fruit of direct crossing and sometimes of cutting through: at death the body shrinks and dissolves into light leaving hair and nails, accompanied by rainbows and lights; the great transference body departs without death.
The Zhang Zhung Nyengyü counts twenty-four masters who attained the rainbow body; Shardza Tashi Gyaltsen (1934) in recent memory.

The king protects the people by the science of punishment first composed by Brahmā (MBh 12.59); Rāma's questions to Bharata on counsel, treasury, army and the aims of life (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100); the debate on capital punishment (MBh 12.259).

name: Rājayoga as the goal and its synonyms

definitions.definition: Haṭha is taught solely for rājayoga (HYP 1.2), a stairway to it (1.1); rājayoga is one of sixteen names of samādhi: rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī, manonmanī, amaratva, laya, tattva, śūnyāśūnya, paraṃ padam, amanaska, advaita, nirālamba, nirañjana, jīvanmukti, sahajā, turyā (4.3–4); samādhi is the union of self and mind, the sameness when breath and mind are dissolved, the union of jīvātman and paramātman (4.5–7); the GS equates rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī and the natural state (7.17); the Jyotsnā identifies rājayoga with asamprajñāta yoga.

Haṭha is a stairway to rājayoga (HYP 1.1); rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī, manonmanī, amaratva, laya, tattva, śūnyāśūnya, param pada, amanaska, advaita, nirālamba, nirañjana, jīvanmukti, sahajā and turyā are one (HYP 4.3–4).

relations.note: an identification made by the commentator, not by the root text

definitions.definition: Combinations making the native a king or kingly: by exalted planets in Varāhamihira (the Yavanas say exalted malefics make a cruel king, Jīvaśarman denies they make a king at all: BJ 11.1); by the relation of the lords of angles and trines, the yogakāraka, and the cancelled fall (nīcabhaṅga) in Parāśara (BPHS 34, 39–40).
Rāma with Sītā is the supreme Brahman, formless and embodied; the world is full of Sītā and Rāma and the Lord is the master in the form of all beings.
The Rāmāyaṇa's Rāma, 'dharma in bodily form' (3.37.13), keeps his father's word as dharma (2.21.40), holds truth as the lord of the world (2.109.13), and teaches the duties of kingship (2.100).
Rāma is the maryādā-puruṣottama; his reign is the pattern of dharma; doing good to others is the highest dharma.
Under Rāma no one suffered bodily, divine or elemental affliction; all loved one another and kept their dharma.
Emptiness of own-nature; the Jonang accept it of every conventional phenomenon and deny it of the ultimate.
In Kongtrul's tenet presentation, the Madhyamaka of Nāgārjuna's reasonings, valid for cutting elaborations.

relations.note: not yet reconciled
the self-emptiness of the rangtong Madhyamaka is the Madhyamaka's absence of own-nature applied to all phenomena

definitions.definition: A blind turtle surfacing once a century would put its neck through a yoke drifting on the ocean sooner than a fool gone to the lower realms would regain human birth (MN 129; SN 56.48).
A human life free of the eight unfree states and having the ten endowments, of great value and hard to find by cause, example and number.
Human birth is the stairway to liberation, won only by merit; one who wastes it is a self-slayer (Kulārṇava 1.14-17).
The field of human life left fallow could have yielded gold (Rāmprasād).

name: Mercury and breath: the twofold discipline

definitions.definition: The discipline that stabilizes the body is twofold, mercury and breath; both 'swooned' remove disease, 'dead' revive, 'bound' give sky-going (Rasārṇava 1.18-19; SDS 13-14).

relations.note: HYP 4.26-27 applies the same verse to mercury and mind/breath

name: Aesthetic relish as consciousness at rest (brahmāsvāda-sahodara)

definitions.definition: Rasa is relished in a consciousness freed from personal limits and at rest in itself, a supermundane wonder; it is the 'twin' of tasting Brahman — undivided, self-luminous, bliss and consciousness, untouched by other objects (Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka as reported; Abhinavagupta; SD 3.2–3); for Jagannātha it is consciousness itself with its veil removed.

name: The impurities of mercury and the danger of impure preparations

definitions.definition: Mercury has natural impurities (poison, fire, dirt) and adventitious 'coverings', twelve in all, each causing disease or death; with them it is poison, freed of them nectar (Rasaratnākara Rasa 1.27-30; RRS 11.20-25); impure minerals and metals likewise destroy life (Rasaratnākara Rasa 5-7; RRS 5.47-48, 5.73).

name: Taste, quality, potency, post-digestive effect and specific power

definitions.definition: The five aspects by which a substance acts: taste, the twenty qualities, potency (hot/cold), vipāka (sweet/sour/pungent) and specific power (AHS Sū 1.14-18; Ca Sū 26).

name: Guru, disciple and secrecy in Rasa Śāstra

definitions.definition: Serve the guru with a pure heart; the tantra is secret and gained by his grace; act only with his permission (Rasārṇava 1.54-59); qualities of teacher and disciple; the unfit gain nothing and lose their wealth (RRS 6.2-10); knowledge only from the guru's mouth and experience (Rasaratnākara Rasa 1.20-22).
Kṛṣṇa's dance with the gopīs (BhP 10.29-33), whose hearing gives supreme devotion and removes lust; not to be imitated by those who are not lords (10.33.30-31).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: The HYP compares mind and mercury: both unsteady by nature; bound, they accomplish everything (4.26–27); nāda 'calcines' the mercury of the mind (4.96). An analogy from rasaśāstra; no alchemical procedure is taught.

'Rasa arises from the union of determinants, consequents and transient states' (NŚ 6). Lollaṭa: intensification in the character; Śaṅkuka: inference in the actor; Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka: enjoyment through bhāvakatva and bhojakatva; Abhinavagupta: manifestation and relish in the spectator — the view adopted by Mammaṭa and Viśvanātha.

name: The mercurial liṅga and the worship of mercury

definitions.definition: Seeing, touching, eating, remembering, worshipping and giving mercury bear fruit; worship of the mercurial liṅga surpasses that of all liṅgas (Rasārṇava 1.37-43; RRS 1.23-30; SDS 40-44). RESTRICTED: its making is not recorded.
Work is done in a safe, righteous land, in a spacious hall with windows and a secluded pavilion (RRS 6.11-14). RESTRICTED: no construction or rites recorded.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the means to long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, lustre and strength, the obtaining of excellent tissues (Ca Ci 1.1.7-8; AHS Utt 39.1-2); two modes — entering a hut (better, very hard) and wind-and-sun (Ci 1.1.16; 1.4.27-28); futile in an unpurified body like dye on a dirty cloth (Su Ci 27.4; AHS Utt 39.4) and without purity of mind (Ci 1.4.36-37); lapses are treated apart from it (1.4.29); intellect-promoting rejuvenatives (Ci 1.3.30-31); conduct itself is rasāyana (Ci 1.4.30-35).
Rasa Śāstra: rejuvenation by processed mercury and minerals (Rasaratnākara's Rasāyana-khaṇḍa, 'for the aged'); RESTRICTED — summary only.
Rejuvenation (bcud len) is the seventh branch, taught in the closing chapters of the Oral Instruction Tantra, with virility.

relations.note: the Siddha kāya-kaṟpam

definitions.definition: A Māheśvara system that holds identity with the Supreme Lord yet requires a stable body for the liberation in life accepted by all, and makes mercury the means (SDS Raseśvara 1-5); its end is the vision of the conscious light and brahmanhood here (45-48); mercury is equated with brahman (49-51).

In the Jaimini system signs, not planets, aspect: each sign sees the sign facing it and those at its sides, so movable signs aspect the fixed signs except the adjacent, fixed signs the movable except the adjacent, and dual signs one another (Jaimini 1.1.2–3; BPHS 8).

The aggregate of twenty-four in which action, fruit, knowledge, pleasure and pain rest; born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma; endless while joined with rajas and tamas, ceasing with the increase of sattva (Ca Śā 1.35-38, 1.53).

name: The three gems of the Pāñcarātra and their expansions

definitions.definition: Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya issue directly from the Lord; their expansions Īśvara, Pārameśvara and Pādma govern practice at Melkote, Śrīraṅgam and Kāñcī respectively.

name: The real (sat) and the unreal (asat)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Of what is not (asat — the non-existent or unreal) there is no being, and of what is (sat — the existent or real) no non-being; those who see the truth (tattvadarśin) have seen the conclusion (anta) about both (2.16).

notes: The commentators divide on what sat and asat denote in 2.16 and on whether the verse speaks of existence or of reality; it is later cited in debates on causation. Not the same as data/'s cpt:sat-and-asat (being and non-being at the origin).

definitions.definition: (Jain report) A soul may die and re-enter a body; Gosāla claimed to be Udāyi Kuṇḍiyāyaṇa in his seventh re-entry; (commentators) the liberated soul of the Trairāśikas returns to saṃsāra through fondness for play.

name: Reasoning about the Lord as worship

definitions.definition: Reasoning about the Lord, being reflection (manana) after hearing, is itself a form of worship (NK 1.3); worship of Him is the path to heaven and liberation (NK 1.2).

relations.note: Nyāya places itself at the stage of manana in the Upaniṣadic triad.

name: Rebirth

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: all beings fall into bewilderment at birth through the delusion of the pairs (7.27); the knower takes refuge in the Lord at the end of many births (7.19); one goes to whatever state one remembers on leaving the body (8.6); rebirth is the impermanent abode of sorrow, and all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return, but those who come to the Lord are not reborn (8.15–16); the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly, with Brahmā's day and night (8.19); of the two everlasting courses of the departed, the bright leads to non-return (anāvṛtti) and the dark to return (8.23–26); those without faith in this dharma return to the path of death and saṃsāra (9.3); Vedic sacrificers who reach heaven re-enter the world of mortals when their merit is spent — 'going and coming' (9.21).

The Upaniṣads describe return to this world: like grain a mortal is born again (KU 1.1.6); the path of the fathers returns through rain and food (ChU 5.10.3-6; BAU 6.2.16); the self takes another body as a caterpillar or goldsmith (BAU 4.4.3-4); the third birth (AU 2.1.4); tiny creatures that are born and die (ChU 5.10.8).

Beings pass away and reappear according to their deeds, seen with the divine eye (DN 2); conception requires the gandhabba (MN 38); the other world cannot be seen with the fleshly eye (DN 23); no self transmigrates — consciousness is dependently arisen (MN 38).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The embodied one obtains another body as it passes through childhood, youth and old age (2.13); it casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones as a man changes clothes (2.22); death is certain for the born and birth for the dead (2.27); freedom from the bondage of birth is gained by abandoning the fruit of action (2.51).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna have both passed through many births, which Kṛṣṇa knows and Arjuna does not (4.5); whoever knows the Lord's divine birth and action does not go to rebirth on leaving the body (4.9); the one fallen from yoga dwells in the worlds of the meritorious and is reborn, carrying the understanding and practice of his former body (6.41–44), perfected through many births (6.45).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: attachment to the guṇas causes puruṣa's births in good and bad wombs (13.22); one who knows puruṣa and prakṛti is not born again (13.24); dying in sattva, rajas or tamas leads to the stainless worlds, to birth among those attached to action, or to deluded wombs (14.14–15, 14.18); the living being takes the senses and mind with it from body to body as the wind carries scents (15.8).
Bodies arise for the experience of the fruits of karma; while dharma and adharma remain, a new body arises; when they are exhausted it does not.

relations.note: rebirth without a transmigrating self, against Sāti's view (MN 38)

definitions.definition: Perception is limited (eight causes of non-perception); parental transmission, nature, creation by another and chance fail; rebirth is established by scripture (sages of divine sight), perception (inequalities of birth, untaught infant behaviour, memory of former births), inference (from past karma called daiva) and yukti (no sprout without seed) (Ca Sū 11.6-33); the mind that joins jīva to body carries memory, and with a pure mind one remembers past births (Śā 3.13).

relations.note: Ca Sū 11.8's eight causes of non-perception parallel Sāṃkhyakārikā 7

name: Nyāya arguments for previous and future births

definitions.definition: A newborn's joy, fear and grief presuppose memory of earlier experience; its desire for the breast presupposes the practice of eating in a former life; no one is born free of desire; since the self is eternal, rebirth is established (NS 3.1.18–24, 4.1.10).

The five destinations — hell, animals, ghosts, humans, gods (MN 12) — with the heavens of the sense sphere, the Brahmā worlds and the formless spheres; systematised in the commentaries as thirty-one planes (U37).
The hells, hungry ghosts and animals (lower realms) contemplated by the small scope; gods, demigods and humans (higher realms) whose sufferings are contemplated by the middling scope.
The six realms and their sufferings (Jewel Ornament ch.5); clinging to bliss, clarity and non-thought in meditation leads to the desire, form and formless realms (Moonbeams).

relations.note: the commentarial systematisation owned by U37

name: The receptacle world as shared cognition

definitions.definition: The store-consciousness imperceptibly cognizes the 'place' — the receptacle world — which appears alike to beings of similar karma (as the river of pus to all hungry ghosts); world-systems arise and perish through the shared karmic imprints of beings.

Kṛṣṇa redefines some thirty virtues and states inwardly (calm = intellect fixed on the Lord; strength = breath control; heaven = rise of sattva; the friend = the teacher; the home = the human body) and concludes that seeing merit and fault is the fault, being beyond both the merit.

name: Reflection of the sun in water

definitions.definition: The one sun appears as many trembling reflections; so Brahman appears as many jīvas sharing their adjuncts' changes.

Buddhi, unconscious, takes on the shade of consciousness and appears conscious, while puruṣa, reflected in it, appears to know and enjoy (Vācaspati on SK 5; cf. SK 20); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra speaks of coloring (uparāga) that is misidentification rather than real coloring, like the red flower and the crystal (1.164, 6.28). Vijñānabhikṣu is reported to teach a mutual reflection of puruṣa and buddhi (recalled, low confidence).

name: The refutation of ignorance and of knowledge

definitions.definition: Ignorance cannot exist in the self-luminous; knowledge as its opposite dissolves with it; what remains is neither knower nor known.

name: Refutation of the Lokāyata denial of rebirth

definitions.definition: Consciousness cannot arise from the body alone; each moment of awareness arises from a prior moment of awareness, so the series continues after death (Tattvasaṅgraha, Lokāyata examination).

name: The authority of regional, caste and family custom

definitions.definition: Customs of regions, castes and families are authoritative when not contrary to the Veda (GDh 11.20); marriage follows local custom (ĀśGS 1.7.1); whether southern and northern practices that the cultured reject are valid is debated (BDh 1.1.2.1–8).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:gautama-dharmasutra:11.20 (confirmed); tea:asvalayana-grhyasutra:1.7.1 (confirmed); tea:baudhayana-dharmasutra:1.1.2.1-8 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Caste has no standing before God: do not ask a sādhu's caste; the brahmin and the Turk came by the same way.
Ravidās names his Camār caste and its work without shame; the Lord raises the one whose touch the world calls polluting; in Begampura there is no second or third rank.
Lalon has never seen the form of caste; at birth and death no sign of it remains.
In the Kartā's fellowship there is one caste — while outward custom is kept in the world.
Ghāsīdās's Satnāmīs reject caste hierarchy and untouchability.
Balarām Hāḍi's followers reject brahmanical caste religion.

The conventional awakening mind is the compassionate resolve and its practice; the ultimate awakening mind is the direct understanding of emptiness (Bodhicittavivaraṇa; instructions on cultivating the two awakening minds in the Tengyur).
Sending and taking mounted on the breath, beginning with oneself, applied to the three objects and poisons, and supported by slogans in all activities.

name: Proper reliance on the spiritual teacher

definitions.definition: The root of the path: relying in thought (faith seeing the teacher as a buddha, respect remembering kindness) and in deed (offering, service and practice); the teacher must have the ten qualities.
The spiritual friend through whom faults are exhausted is to be cherished more than one's body.

Because the happiness and sorrow of creatures depend on the planets, their sacrifice is to be performed for peace, prosperity, rain, long life and nourishment (BPHS 84.1–3; YājñSm 1.295–308): images, Vedic mantras, fuel-sticks, food, gifts, recitation and worship for each planet; pacification rites for births at eclipses, junctions, Mūla and Viṣṭi (BPHS 86–96); gifts, cow-milking at a Rudra shrine and the ten-million oblation for portents (BS 45.4–7); gems examined for their fortune (BS 79.1); expiations for curses of past lives (BPHS 83; Praśna Mārga). Varāhamihira warns that rites alone do not bring success (Yogayātrā 1.6).

name: The renouncer's permitted modes of death

definitions.definition: The Jābāla and Kaṭharudra mention modes by which a renouncer may end life; recorded summary-only, with no guidance.

definitions.definition: Staff (one or three), water-pot, sling, strainer, ochre or no cloth, shaven head, topknot and thread kept or abandoned; the texts differ on which marks are kept, and many say the true marks are inner (staff of knowledge, thread of the Self) and that marks do not liberate.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 8 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: The first principal aspect: the wish for liberation arising day and night, from contemplating the leisure and endowment, death, karma and the sufferings of saṃsāra.
Not being attached to saṃsāra.

Pāṇini received the list of phonemes from Maheśvara (PŚ 56–57); Śiva sounded the fourteen sūtras on his drum at the end of his dance (Nandikeśvara-kāśikā); Bṛhaspati taught Indra words for a thousand divine years (Mahābhāṣya).
