name: Reverence for women in Kaula conduct

definitions.definition: Women are never to be blamed, mocked, insulted or struck — 'not even with a flower' — and their virtues, not faults, proclaimed; every woman is a mother born of the Kula (Kulārṇava 11.61-65); women are goddesses and life-breath (Kaulāvalīnirṇaya 10.87-88).
After each path and fruit the noble person may review path, fruit, nibbāna, defilements abandoned and those remaining — nineteen kinds in all.

name: Sukhāvatī as a reward land into which ordinary beings are born

definitions.definition: Amitābha is a reward-body buddha and Sukhāvatī a reward land, not a transformation land (Daochuo); though lofty, ordinary beings enter it by the power of the vow (Shandao).

name: The rightly established state (zhengding ju / shōjōju)

definitions.definition: Those born in the Pure Land dwell in the rightly established group and necessarily reach nirvāṇa (11th vow); recollecting Amitābha one enters the stage of certainty (Nāgārjuna).
Entered in this life, at the one thought-moment of shinjin; the person is 'equal to the Tathāgatas', 'the same as Maitreya'.

relations.note: in China placed after birth, in Shinran before death

definitions.definition: Ordinary mind is dualistic, conceptual, arising from non-recognition; awareness is the non-dual knowing of the ground. Dzogchen practice begins by distinguishing them (ru shan) and then resting in awareness; mistaking sems for rig pa is the principal error.
Bön Dzogchen likewise distinguishes the moving mind from the nature of mind (sems nyid) and awareness.

Every authentic lineage is to be respected, received, practised and preserved in its own terms without mixing; disparaging another tradition is abandoning the Dharma; rare transmissions are to be collected and printed.
The Yogaśikhā's claim that the body must be 'cooked' by the fire of yoga; the unripe body of the mere knower is subject to rebirth.

The Yogabīja teaches that the body must be ripened in the fire of yoga; the unripe body, even of a knower, remains subject to karma and rebirth (compare GS 1.8: the body as an unbaked pot to be fired by yoga).

name: Rlung as the mount of the mind

definitions.definition: Rlung carries the mind as a horse its rider; disturbances of rlung show as mental agitation, and mental disorders are treated largely as rlung disorders.

name: The robe and bowl as tokens of transmission

definitions.definition: Bodhidharma's robe was handed down as a token of faith; Hongren tells Huineng not to pass it on because it causes strife; the Dunhuang version says the robe should not be transmitted.
The Baotang claim that the robe passed via Empress Wu to Zhishen and Wuzhu.
The snake seen in the rope in dim light: superimposition, the substratum, and sublation when the rope is known.

name: The ṛṣi as seer of the mantras

definitions.definition: The seers 'saw' the hymns and had direct perception of dharma, handing them on by instruction (Nirukta 1.20, 2.11); speech was found entered into the seers (RV 10.71.3); Vāc makes whom she loves a seer (10.125.5); Varuṇa made Vasiṣṭha a seer (7.88.4); the hymns also speak of being 'fashioned' by the poets (5.2.11).
A ṛṣi is so called from seeing the hymns; Brahman the self-existent came upon the seers in their austerity; they had direct vision of dharma (Nirukta 2.11; 1.20).
Seers are no longer born because of transgression, yet some become 'seers by learning' through residual merit (ĀpDh 1.2.5.5).

The ĀpDh locator is widened to 1.2.5.4–6 (see tea:apastamba-dharmasutra:1.2.5.5-6); the definition's '1.2.5.5' remains within it.

definitions.definition: Ṛta is the order by which the cosmos moves, the sacrifice succeeds and men act rightly; Agni is its guardian, Varuṇa and Mitra its lords; it was born with satya from tapas (RV 10.190.1); the year is its wheel (1.164.11); by it the Ādityas stand (10.85.1); with truth, consecration and tapas it upholds the earth (AVŚ 12.1.1).

relations.note: The ordinances (dharman, vrata) are the particular forms of the one order.

definitions.definition: In the lucidity of nirvicārā coalescence there is inner clarity (1.47); insight there is truth-bearing (1.48), with the particular as its object unlike testimony and inference (1.49); its impression obstructs other impressions (1.50). Vyāsa quotes: 'having climbed the clarity of insight, the wise one looks on the sorrowing as one on a mountain looks on those below' (YBh 1.47).

Diet and conduct suited to the six seasons and to the 'taking' and 'releasing' halves of the year (Ca Sū 6; AHS Sū 3); doṣas accumulated in one season are to be cleared in the next (Ca Sū 7.46; Śā 2.45).

The Śvetāśvatara names the one God Rudra, Śiva, Hara and Maheśvara: Rudra is one, ruling the worlds, creating and withdrawing them (3.2); his auspicious (śivā) form is prayed to (3.5); he is Śiva present everywhere (3.11), hidden in all beings like the film on ghee (4.16), 'Śiva alone' when there is neither day nor night (4.18); the māyin (4.10).

names.name: Rudra, Tryambaka, Paśupati, Bhava, Śarva, Nīlagrīva, Śiva (epithet)

definitions.definition: Rudra is feared as the archer whose wrath and arrows harm men and cattle and is begged to turn them away, and loved as the best of physicians with a thousand remedies and a healing hand; he is lord of cattle (Paśupati), Bhava and Śarva, blue-necked; the Śatarudrīya pays homage to him as present in all places, beings and callings and names his auspicious, non-terrible body (śivā tanūḥ) and him as 'śiva, śivatara'; the Keśin drank with him from the cup.
Matter occurs in inseparable groups (at least the eight: four elements, colour, odour, flavour, nutritive essence) which arise and cease together.
Seen directly with the light of deep concentration and analysed into their elements before insight.
Their extremely rapid arising and dissolution is felt in meditation as subtle vibration.

name: Form, true form and superimposition (rūpa, svarūpa, āropa)

definitions.definition: Each person has an outer form (rūpa) and a divine true form (svarūpa) — Kṛṣṇa in the man, Rādhā in the woman; by āropa (superimposing svarūpa on rūpa) the partners' love becomes the love of the divine couple.
Vernacular mantras sealed by an oath of Gorakh, effective, according to the tradition, without the Sanskrit rules.
Two brahmans are to be known: the word-brahman and the highest; one skilled in the word-brahman attains the highest; by sound alone the soundless is revealed (MaiU 6.22).
Brahman is the beginningless, endless Word-principle that appears as the world through its powers, time chief among them; all words finally denote it as Being (VP 1.1–4; 3.1–2).
The unmanifest sound arising from the supreme bindu, which is the consciousness of all beings, not the word or the meaning; it dwells as kuṇḍalinī and becomes the letters (ŚT 1.11–14).

relations.note: Brahman approached as the word (grammar, mantra) and as musical sound (saṅgīta)
the Kashmir Śaivas deny that the grammarians' paśyantī is the ultimate

name: Revelation as the decisive means of knowledge, the Bhāgavata as supreme (Jīva)

definitions.definition: Of the means of knowledge, revelation alone reaches the transcendent; the Bhāgavata, natural commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, is supreme.

relations.note: both make the Bhāgavata the decisive scripture

definitions.definition: The guru's word awakens and the inner Word reveals: 'the Bījak shows the hidden wealth, the Word shows the soul'; at the origin were light and sound.
The Word is the audible life stream, the creative power that is also the way back.

relations.note: Both make sound/word the ultimate's own power; the Sant Word is heard within and is not the Veda (which Sant Mat places at Trikuṭī).

definitions.definition: Verbal cognition requires expectancy, compatibility, proximity and knowledge of intention (Tattvacintāmaṇi; Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: Samādhi with seed and seedless (sabīja, nirbīja)

definitions.definition: The four coalescences have an external thing as seed and are samādhi with seed (1.46); when even the impression of truth-bearing insight is stilled there is seedless samādhi (1.51); the three inner limbs are outer relative to it (3.8).
Saying 'this is my faith' without concluding 'only this is true' (MN 95).

Brahmāvarta between the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī, the land of the brahmarṣis, Madhyadeśa and Āryāvarta between the mountains and seas; the land of the black antelope is fit for sacrifice (MDh 2.17–24; VDh 1.8–12; YS 1.2).

name: The sacrifice as the cosmic Person and the world

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas identify the sacrifice with the Person (ŚB 1.3.2.1), with Prajāpati and the year, and with Viṣṇu; the cosmos itself arose from a sacrifice — Brahman offering itself into all beings (ŚB 13.7.1.1), the world-creators' thousand-year session with austerity, truth and breath as priests (TB 3.12.9.3–7) — and the gods live by offering to one another (ŚB 5.1.1.2).

relations.note: the identification is one of the bandhus
the identity of rite, cosmos and person makes an inner rite possible

name: The true teacher and the disciple

definitions.definition: A true teacher belongs to the unbroken lineage, knows the doctrine, lives it, and teaches out of compassion without gain; the disciple approaches with humility, is initiated by the five sacraments, serves, keeps the secret mantras from the unfit and hands them on; Rāmānuja's public disclosure of the mantra is remembered as the compassion that overrides secrecy.

Viṣṇu is known only through the true scriptures — the Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa, consonant Purāṇas and works that follow them — not by reasoning alone or the senses; other texts are false scriptures, some produced to delude.

name: The marks of the true guru

definitions.definition: The true guru gives knowledge of the Self and removes doubt, is established in the Self and pure in conduct; givers of mantras for gain, showers of powers and dealers in magic are false gurus.

name: The marks of the true teacher and how to test a teacher

definitions.definition: The true deity must be faultless, omniscient and the teacher of scripture (Ratnakaraṇḍa 5); outward miracles prove nothing (Āptamīmāṃsā 1); only one whose speech agrees with reason and scripture is trustworthy (Āptamīmāṃsā 6).

Śrīmad Rājacandra's marks of the sadguru: self-knowledge, equal vision, acting only as karma unfolds, unprecedented speech, supreme scriptural knowledge (Ātmasiddhi 10); the sectarian (matārthī) mistakes outward signs for the teacher (Ātmasiddhi 24–33).

Discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues (calm, restraint, withdrawal, forbearance, faith, concentration) and longing for liberation — prerequisites for study of the Upaniṣads (Muktikā prose; Varāha 2).
Discrimination of the eternal and non-eternal, dispassion, the six virtues, and longing for liberation — the prerequisites of the inquiry into Brahman.

definitions.definition: Viveka, vimoka, abhyāsa, kriyā, kalyāṇa, anavasāda and anuddharṣa — purity of food, desirelessness, practice, ritual duties, virtues, freedom from dejection and from elation.

In aesthetic experience the determinants and emotions are freed from belonging to a particular person, time and place — neither 'mine' nor 'another's' — so that the spectator's limited self does not obstruct relish (Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka; Abhinavagupta).

name: The marks of purport (liṅga) in Dvaita exegesis

definitions.definition: Opening and conclusion, their agreement, repetition, novelty, result and praise — with reasoning — are the marks of a text's purport; name, sentence, context and position are further marks.
Devotion deepens through six forms matching the sthalas: śraddhā (faith), niṣṭhā (steadfastness), avadhāna (attentiveness), anubhava (experience), ānanda (bliss) and samarasa (equal flavour).

name: The six liṅgas

definitions.definition: Śiva met as six liṅgas corresponding to the six sthalas: ācāraliṅga (bhakta), guruliṅga (māheśvara), śivaliṅga (prasādi), jaṅgamaliṅga (prāṇaliṅgi), prasādaliṅga (śaraṇa), mahāliṅga (aikya); in the manual tradition each is correlated with a sense (smell, taste, sight, touch, hearing, the heart) and an element.

notes: Not set out in these terms in the SSM (whose liṅga-sthalas differ); sense and element correlations from memory of later manuals — low confidence.

name: The six śaktis on the side of the liṅga

definitions.definition: In the manual scheme the liṅga's power appears as six śaktis facing the six bhaktis of the soul: kriyā, jñāna, icchā, ādi, parā and cit, from the bhakta to the aikya stage.

notes: Reconstructed from memory of ṣaṭsthala manuals; verify.

definitions.definition: Conduct followed with mindfulness that brings health and mastery of the senses; worship, purity, truthful and gentle speech, no taking or coveting what is another's, avoiding bad company; devotion to continence, knowledge, giving, friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity and calm (Ca Sū 8.17-29); in Vāgbhaṭa, dharma as the condition of happiness, the ten sinful acts abandoned, all beings seen as oneself, the middle way, and constant mindfulness (AHS Sū 2.20-47).

name: The innate (sahaja)

definitions.definition: The natural state of the mind free of effort and elaboration; synonym of rājayoga and samādhi (HYP 4.4); the measure of real knowledge — until it arises all talk is hypocrisy (HYP 4.114).

The innate principle in the heart, moving by itself, delighting in others as in oneself (KJN 17.5, 17.18–26); the innate path abiding in samarasa, higher than the 'made' kuṇḍalī (Akulavīra B.43); once the Kaula is known the mind is not to be restrained (KJN 7.26).

The natural state (sahajāvasthā), a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4), which arises spontaneously when śakti has awakened and action is abandoned (4.11) but is hard to reach without a true guru's compassion (4.9); in paricaya 'natural bliss' arises (4.75); GS 7.17 equates it with rājayoga and unmanī.
The natural state in which the Lord is realized without forced yoga: eyes open, every act worship; Kabīr warns that everyone says 'sahaj' and no one knows it.
The innate beyond the two, known only by one who has crossed the darkness; the goal of the couple's discipline.
The sahaj path and the sahaj Man, found in the body under the guru.
The sahaja religion (satya-dharma) revealed by Āulcānd.
lhan cig skyes pa, the co-emergent: the dharmakāya inseparable from mind, appearances and thoughts; 'co-emergent wisdom, clarity-emptiness free of grasping' (Karṇatantravajrapada).

relations.note: the innate as against the made

notes: The Buddhist Sahajiyā 'sahaja' of the siddhas (U44, same concept id expected) is the scholarly-hypothesized ancestor of the Bengali usage (brw:mahasiddha-to-vaisnava-sahajiya); the Sant usage comes via the Nāths (brw:natha-to-sant).

definitions.definition: The divine present as the innate nature of human beings — Kṛṣṇa in the man, Rādhā in the woman; 'the truth of man is above all'.
The Master hidden in the human form, above all in the guru.
The natural Man whose worship in the human makes one golden.

name: Innate absorption (sahaja-samādhi): the mind seeing the mind

definitions.definition: Liberation is where, by the sequence of innate absorption, the mind is seen by the mind (AmŚ 54); cf. seeing the mind by the mind in the midst of Śakti (Candrāvalokana).
Absorption that grows by the guru's grace without closing eyes or stopping ears: going about is circumambulation, work is service, lying down is prostration; the Lord's form is seen everywhere.

relations.note: AmŚ 55–59 calls this path jīvanmukti
Set by Kabīr against yogic absorption obtained by force (closing eyes, stopping ears, torturing the body).

name: The innate (sahaja) in the Buddhist tantras and dohās

definitions.definition: The co-emergent nature of mind, neither thing nor no-thing, found through the true guru; realized as the one taste of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
The innate joy/gnosis of the fourth moment and consecration; known only by oneself (Hevajra I.8).

relations.standpoint: shared vocabulary of the siddha movements
relations.note: The Nāth, Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā and Buddhist siddhas share the word and the goal of 'the innate'; each defines it in its own frame (emptiness-bliss here).

name: The inner lakes of the Sahajiyā body

definitions.definition: Sahajiyā manuals describe lakes (sarovara) in the body — of desire, of pride, of love and of the imperishable — through which the practitioner passes; recorded in outline only.

notes: Names and number of the lakes recalled with low confidence (Dimock's discussion); restricted context.

definitions.definition: Blue and the cognition of blue are necessarily apprehended together; hence they are not different; their difference is an error like the double moon.
The succession of saints forms one building: Jñāneśvar the foundation, Nāmdev the walls, Eknāth the pillar, Tukārām the pinnacle (Bahiṇābāī); the tradition is a single work of the saints' grace.
Brahman has three forms: with parts (sakala), without parts (niṣkala) and both; its most manifest form is Dattātreya (Śāṇḍilya 3; Brahmavidyā 37–40).

checks.note: Śāṇḍilya ch. 3 (e-text) and Brahmavidyā 37-40 (sakala and niṣkala, e.g. flower and scent, tree and shade) are located. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: Late Yogācāra divides over whether cognition's images are real (satyākāra: Jñānaśrīmitra, Ratnakīrti) or false (alīkākāra: Ratnākaraśānti), and whether buddha-cognition has images.
The devotee serves as Rādhā's companion or maidservant, witnessing the pair and delighting in their joy.
The singer is a sakhī in the grove; Svāmī Haridās is Lalitā.
The Rāma-rasik is a companion of Sītā in the inner Ayodhyā.

relations.note: the Gauḍīya maidservant stance is a close parallel

definitions.definition: Dvaita: the soul's own intrinsic faculty of awareness (its essential sense), the seventh kind of perception; it apprehends the self, mind and its states, pleasure and pain, time and space, and the validity of knowledge; its deliverances are infallible and never sublated, and it is the final guarantor of knowledge, including the reality of the world.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'you cannot see the seer of seeing' (BAU 3.4.2); 'by what would one know the knower?' (BAU 2.4.14); the unseen seer (BAU 3.7.23, 3.8.11); the ear of the ear (Kena 1.2); the word sākṣin itself in ŚU 6.11 (the one God, witness, knower, alone, without qualities).

Puruṣa is witness, seer and neutral (SK 19), witness through direct relation (SS 1.161) and of deep sleep and other states (SS 1.148); upon knowledge it sees prakṛti like a spectator, at ease (SK 65).
The unchanging consciousness that illumines the mind's modes, the three states and ignorance itself, never an object (DDV 1; the theatre-lamp of Pañcadaśī 10).

relations.note: the witness establishes the world's reality
the witness of the three states is the fourth

queries: prepared segments: BĀU 3.4.2, BĀU 2.4.14, BĀU 3.7.23, BĀU 3.8.11, Kena 1.2, ŚU 6.11
checks.note: The word 'sākṣī' is located at ŚU 6.11 ('sākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaś ca'). The other refs (BĀU 3.4.2, 2.4.14, 3.7.23, 3.8.11; Kena 1.2) are located. All 6 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 3.4.2; BĀU 2.4.14; BĀU 3.7.23; BĀU 3.8.11; Kena 1.2; ŚU 6.11). It rests on 6 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Countless universes made of the five elements rest like sand-grains on Ananta upon the cosmic tortoise in the ocean of compassion (Nirvāṇa Tantra 1.6-9); the gods arise from Kālī and dissolve into her (10.42-43).
The root Nature divides the Person into jīva and the supreme and herself into māyā and vidyā; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva receive their functions from her (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.98-124).

name: Death and dying in the Kālīkula and Kaula sources

definitions.definition: The Mahānirvāṇa: cremation in the cremation ground; no burning of a wife with her husband, for woman is the Goddess's own form; death beside the Goddess or near Kaulas is praised; whoever dies contemplating the one Truth, forgetting the three worlds, abides in his own nature (10.78-83). Kula worship continues even during death-impurity (10.78).
The Kubjikāmata teaches knowledge of the three times and the yogic departure (ch. 23; restricted).

Kālī dwells in the cremation ground (Kālī Tantra dhyāna); the Śākta poets make her name the refuge at death — Rāmprasād is remembered as dying singing while immersing her image in the Ganges (tradition's account).

name: The Śākta seats (51 / 52 pīṭhas)

definitions.definition: The seats where parts of Satī fell, each with its goddess and guardian Bhairava; the Kālikā Purāṇa knows a small set (18.41-50); the late Pīṭhanirṇaya lists 51 (Bengali lists 51 or 52, with upapīṭhas); other texts count 108.

members: Kāmākhyā, Kāmarūpa — the yoni (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42; high confidence)
Hiṅglāj (Hiṅgulā), Baluchistan — the crown of the head (low confidence)
Kālīghāṭ, Calcutta — toes of the right foot (low confidence)
Aṭṭahāsa, Bengal — the lower lip (low confidence)
Kiriṭeśvarī, Bengal — the crown ornament (low confidence)
Tārāpīṭh, Birbhum — the eye (popular tradition; absent from some lists; low confidence)
notes: The full 51-pīṭha list is not reproduced: it was not checked against the Pīṭhanirṇaya text in Phase B (see REPORT). Members other than Kāmākhyā are recalled from the popular Bengali list and need checking.

name: The Śākta Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads of the Muktikā canon devoted to the Goddess — Sītā, Annapūrṇā, Tripurātāpinī, Devī, Tripurā, Bhāvanā, Saubhāgyalakṣmī, Sarasvatīrahasya, Bahvṛca — read by Śrīvidyā as its śruti; Bhāskararāya commented on the Tripurā, Bhāvanā and Kaula Upaniṣads.

notes: Membership from memory of the Muktikā grouping; U04 owns the texts.

definitions.definition: The Goddess is the power of the absolute without which Śiva cannot stir (SL 1; Subhagodaya); she abides in all beings as consciousness (Devī Māhātmya 5).
She is citśakti and the form of sentience, yet also the power of the insentient (LSN 90); the self-awareness (vimarśa) of Śiva's light (KKV 2; LSN 112).
The Goddess is the supreme power of knowledge, will and action, and the power of sound (Kubjikāmata 2.2).
Kālī is pure consciousness (cinmayī), witness of all (Mahānirvāṇa 13.12); she is the power without which Śiva is inert (Toḍala 1.25).
The root Nature, who as vidyā commands the three gods to create, protect and dissolve (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.98-124).

relations.note: Śakti is the vimarśa side of the one reality

definitions.definition: The beginningless Will-power born of Śiva is Vyomamālinī, Khecarī, Vāmā, Kuṇḍalī, Jyeṣṭhā, Manonmanī, Rudraśakti and Kāmākhyā; unwritten and unread, she is Mātṛkā, the mass of sounds (KJN 20.10–12).
Only the external power transforms into the world; the Lord remains unchanged, like the touchstone that yields gold.

Śrīpati: Śiva (liṅga) qualified by Śakti and the soul (aṅga) qualified by devotion are non-dual; liberation is their union in equal essence (liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya); the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi works this out through the stations (sthala).

Śiva is one, qualified by his inseparable Śakti: the pedestal is the supreme Śakti, the liṅga Paraśiva, and the union of Śiva and Śakti — the universe — is the liṅga; the soul is qualified by devotion (bhakti) as Śiva by power (Śrīpati's formulation; philosophy owned by U16).

relations.note: Śrīkaṇṭha's body–soul model vs Śrīpati's Śakti-qualified union; Vīraśaiva authors claim both as their own

Both lineages use the one term for the Lord's grace and both link it to karmasāmya; they differ on direction (Kiraṇa: equality marks the time of descent; Ahirbudhnya: the Lord's glance brings about equality).
the Kiraṇa's śaktipāta chapter leads directly into its dīkṣā chapter

definitions.definition: Śiva's awakening of the soul by his power, spoken of figuratively as a 'fall'; it occurs at the time of the equality of karma, Śiva remaining its lord as the sun is of the lotus; its sign is a distinctive devotion.
Viṣṇu's compassion, his fifth power of grace, which āgama-knowers call śaktipāta: by his glance the soul's karmas become equal and fall silent, and it is lifted from saṃsāra.
The descent of Śiva's grace-power on a ripe soul, marked by signs such as devotion and the wish for release; it qualifies for dīkṣā.
Catti nipātam in four grades suited to caryā, kriyā, yoga and jñāna.

Omens from the cries, movements and directions of birds and beasts at the start of an undertaking, classified by direction and time (BS 85–95; Vasantarāja Śākuna); the omens present at the moment of a query are part of Kerala praśna.

name: Sallekhanā (the final fast)

definitions.definition: At the approach of inevitable death — from calamity, famine, old age or incurable disease — the practitioner gradually gives up food and passions in equanimity, with the teacher's permission and under the care of attending ascetics (TS 7.22; Ratnakaraṇḍa 122; Bhagavatī Ārādhanā). It is vitiated by wishing to live, wishing to die, affection, recalling pleasures and longing for reward (TS 7.37). The texts hold it is not self-killing because it is free of passion (Sarvārthasiddhi 7.22; Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 177–178).
Known as saṃthārā; three forms of the final renunciation of food are distinguished (bhakta-pratyākhyāna, iṅginī, prāyopagamana).

notes: Restricted topic: summary and the texts' own conditions and warnings only; no procedure.

name: The Sāman notes and the musical scale

definitions.definition: The Sāmaveda sings with seven notes — kruṣṭa, prathama, dvitīya, tṛtīya, caturtha, mandra, atisvārya — which the Nāradīya Śikṣā sets against the flute's madhyama, gāndhāra, ṛṣabha, ṣaḍja, dhaivata, niṣāda and pañcama, places in the body from head to heart and shows on the fingers.

Savikalpa and nirvikalpa samādhi as auxiliaries of contemplation, with eight limbs and four obstacles (Vedāntasāra); six samādhis inner and outer (Dṛg-Dṛśya Viveka); the state of no-mind (GK 3.32). Samādhi is a means; knowledge liberates.
Samādhi is the substance of prajñā and prajñā the function of samādhi, like a lamp and its light.
Calm yet always knowing, knowing yet always calm — the content of cultivation after awakening.

relations.note: Chan's dinghui corresponds to calm and insight but denies their sequence ('do not say samādhi first produces prajñā').

name: Causal efficacy without a separate power (śakti)

definitions.definition: An effect follows from the totality of causes including the absence of counteragents; no distinct causal power need be posited (Udayana; Gaṅgeśa) — an enduring thing produces effects successively as auxiliaries join it (AtV).

Words with different grounds of application referring to one object; the key to reading identity-texts ('tat tvam asi', 'sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma') as naming one Brahman under different modes, since a word denoting a mode ultimately denotes the substance it qualifies.
Samantabhadra was liberated without effort by recognizing the ground-appearances as his own display, without having done a single virtue; he is the model and the nature of every being's awareness.
Kuntu Zangpo is the Bön-body, primordial buddha of Bön.

The vows of good conduct: homage, offering, confession, rejoicing, requesting teaching, requesting the buddhas to stay, dedication — and, in the 40-fascicle Chinese, ten vows adding following the buddhas, according with beings and universal dedication; recited for rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

name: Increase by the similar, decrease by the dissimilar

definitions.definition: At all times the general causes increase and the particular decrease (Ca Sū 1.44); hence the doṣas are allayed by substances of opposite qualities (Sū 1.59-62) and all dhātus increase by the similar (AHS Sū 1.14).

In a mind whose activities have dwindled, like a flawless crystal, coalescence is resting on and taking the form of grasper, grasping or grasped (1.41); it is savitarkā (mixed with word, object and knowledge constructions), nirvitarkā (object alone), savicārā and nirvicārā (subtle objects) (1.42–44), extending to the unmarked (1.45); these four are samādhi with seed (1.46).

relations.note: Shared terms vitarka/vicāra and samāpatti with the Buddhist jhāna system; the structures differ (Yoga's pairs are defined by gross vs subtle objects and presence of constructions) — correspondence contested

definitions.definition: Samādhi is the oneness of equal taste when breath and mind are gone (GŚ 94); the samarasa of body and supreme state by the guru's grace (SSP 5); the yogī becomes non-dual like milk in milk (GŚ 100).
For one abiding in samarasa all is full, the Akulavīra alone; he is every god and every school (Akulavīra A.24–41).
The sameness (samarasatva) when breath is exhausted and mind dissolved — a definition of samādhi (HYP 4.6; GŚ 94).

Tāyumāṉavar's 'harmony' of Vedānta and Śaiva Siddhānta: the Siddhas who have attained it are praised; the Supreme is both the non-dual reality and the Lord of grace. Kaṭuveḷi likewise joins 'pure Vedānta' to Śiva devotion.
Vallalar (Ramalinga Swamigal) takes up camaracam in the name of his 'Camaraca Cutta Caṉmārkkam'.

relations.standpoint: the final union as equal taste
relations.note: Vīraśaiva sāmarasya of liṅga and aṅga uses the same word for the final union; each tradition specifies its own terms of union
Siddhānta's own 'advaita of inseparability' is one pole of the harmony

definitions.definition: Each level of ignorance and body has a collective (cosmic) and individual aspect: Īśvara–prājña (causal), Hiraṇyagarbha–taijasa (subtle), Virāj–viśva (gross).

Calm and insight developed together — insight preceded by calm, calm by insight, or yoked evenly (AN 4.170; MN 149); calm and insight are the path to the unconditioned (SN 43.12); no jhāna without wisdom, no wisdom without jhāna (Dhp 372); the jhānas as a basis for insight into the aggregates (MN 64; AN 9.36).
Śamatha with and then without support settles the mind; vipaśyanā looks directly at the settled and moving mind to recognize its nature; the two are finally united in the four yogas.

relations.note: the Kagyu form of the common Buddhist pair

name: The union of calm abiding and insight

definitions.definition: Calm abiding brings the superknowledges, but only the yoga of the perfection of wisdom joined with method exhausts the obscurations.
Achieved when analysis of emptiness itself induces pliancy and stability; like a bright, unflickering lamp.
Insight joined with calm destroys the afflictions, so calm should be sought first (BCA 8.4).
Calm stabilizes the mind; insight arises from analysis; the two are balanced by removing laxity and excitement (Bhāvanākrama).

name: Equanimity (samatva)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Being the same in pain and pleasure makes one fit for immortality (2.15); pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat are to be made the same (2.38); equanimity is called yoga (2.48); the one of steady wisdom is unagitated in sorrow, without longing in pleasure, and neither rejoices nor hates (2.56–57); the sense-contacts are to be endured (2.14).

notes: Merger: probably the same as the skeleton's cpt:equanimity ('Evenness of mind (samatva)', BhG 2.48); both extractors used this id, so it is kept; flagged for the de-duplication pass.

definitions.definition: The circular assembly hall created by the gods for the omniscient Jina's preaching, with concentric enclosures in which gods, humans and animals sit in twelve assemblies; the Jina appears to face all four directions.

relations.note: follows the attainment of omniscience

definitions.definition: The one eternal relation between inseparables — part and whole, quality and substance, motion and substrate, universal and individual, particularity and eternal substance — known from the notion 'here' (VS 7.2.29 C; Tarkasaṅgraha).
Without the samaya discipline there is no perfection (Kulārṇava 5.96).
Tāmasa disciples who ignore the samayas and slander the guru become dead while living (Kubjikāmata 12.3-9).
Kept by practising the guru's instruction continuously 'like a river'; broken by giving the secret instructions to unfit vessels.

name: Samaya and Kaula modes of worship

definitions.definition: Samaya worship is in the inner space of the heart and crown; Kaula worship uses an external support; the Samayin rejects outer worship, the Kaula rites and the sixty-four tantras (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8, 31, 41).
The Goddess is both Kaulinī and intent on Samaya conduct, worshipped on the right and left paths (LSN 36-37, 169-171); Bhāskararāya defines the two modes without rejecting either.
Outer cakra worship is performed by Śiva himself and by all knowers (YH 3.3 with the Dīpikā).

The commitments of body, speech and mind binding disciple, teacher and deity: kept, they bring accomplishment and great wonder; broken, they ruin the breaker; restored through confession and feast offering.
Pledges taken at consecration — the root and gross downfalls, the pledges of the five families, the vidyādhara vow on top of the prātimokṣa and bodhisattva vows; broken pledges bring the vajra hell.
Tilopa: the vow is the non-conceptual meaning; guarding vows with concepts degenerates from it; Dhūmapa: the supreme vow is not clinging to one's own realization.
The structure of Caitanya's teaching to Sanātana and of the Ṣaṭ Sandarbha: knowledge of Kṛṣṇa and his powers, devotion as the means, love as the goal.
The northern kingdom where the Kālacakra was preserved by King Sucandra and the kalkins; a future kalkin will defeat the barbarian armies and restore the dharma.
Friendly and hostile discussion, rules of conduct, the forty-four terms of debate, vāda as jalpa or vitaṇḍā (Ca Vi 8.15-28).

relations.note: shared vocabulary (vāda, jalpa, vitaṇḍā) with Nyāya Sūtra 1.2

name: The secret teaching of the saṃhitā (continuous recitation)

definitions.definition: Meditations that read the joining of words in recitation as the joining of earth and sky, teacher and pupil, mother and father (AA 3.1.1; TU 1.3), assign phoneme-classes to worlds, gods and senses (AA 3.2.5), and explain 'saṃhitā' as Prajāpati putting himself together with the metres (AA 3.2.6).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:aitareya-aranyaka:3.1.1 (confirmed); tea:taittiriya-upanisad:1.3 (confirmed); tea:aitareya-aranyaka:3.2.5 (confirmed); tea:aitareya-aranyaka:3.2.6 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Reasoning, hearing, study, the three destructions of suffering, gaining friends and giving are the eight accomplishments conducive to knowledge (SK 51) — not supernormal powers (those are aiśvarya). Gauḍapāda explains each as a route to knowledge of the principles (reflection, hearing, study, approaching a teacher, a knowing friend, serving the venerable); Vācaspati is recalled as making the three destructions primary and the other five their means in sequence (low confidence).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's 'siddhi' is not power

name: Sound, word and Veda in Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: Sound is the subtle element from which space arises (SK 22 with Gauḍapāda); speech has sound as its object (SK 34). Testimony is one of three means of knowledge (SK 4–6). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds that the Vedas are neither eternal nor authored by a person, yet valid by their own manifest power (5.45–51); sound is not eternal and there is no sphoṭa (5.57–58).

name: Order of emergence and re-absorption (sañcara, pratisañcara)

definitions.definition: From prakṛti arises mahat; from mahat ahaṃkāra; from ahaṃkāra the group of sixteen — the eleven organs from its sāttvika (vaikṛta) aspect and the five subtle elements from its tāmasa (bhūtādi) aspect, both with its taijasa aspect; from the five subtle elements the five gross elements (SK 22, 24–25; SS 1.61) — sound→space, touch→air, form→fire, taste→water, smell→earth (Gauḍapāda). In re-absorption each dissolves into its cause in reverse order; the unmanifest does not dissolve (Tattvasamāsa commentaries). The Yuktidīpikā records divergent orders taught by Vindhyavāsin and others.

Kapila, the supreme sage and first knower, gave the teaching out of compassion to Āsuri, Āsuri to Pañcaśikha, who expanded it; through a succession of pupils it reached Īśvarakṛṣṇa (SK 69–71). The Māṭhara Vṛtti names Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta and Devala; the Yuktidīpikā names Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya and Mūka, adding that the full lineage cannot be told because it began with the Blessed One. Gauḍapāda places Kapila among Brahmā's seven sons with Āsuri, Voḍhu and Pañcaśikha.
Go together, speak together, let your minds know together (RV 10.191); 'I make you of one heart and mind, free from hatred' (AVŚ 3.30); may we look on all beings with the eye of a friend (VS 36.18).

Samādhi accompanied by reasoning, reflection, bliss and I-am-ness (1.17): the first has all four, the second lacks reasoning, the third lacks reflection, the fourth is I-am-ness alone; all have a support (YBh 1.17); it occurs in the one-pointed mind (YBh 1.1). Commentators differ on the objects of the bliss and I-am-ness levels (Vācaspati, Bhoja RM 1.17, Vijñānabhikṣu YV 1.17).
The round of birth and death without discoverable beginning (SN 15.3); the tears shed exceed the four oceans.

name: The non-difference of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa

definitions.definition: There is not the least difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; their limits are the same (MMK 25.19–20); there is nothing to superimpose on nirvāṇa and nothing to remove from saṃsāra (16.10); those who see reality conceive neither (YṢ 5–6).
(As reported) Every being, fool or wise, is purified simply by completing the fixed round of 8,400,000 great aeons; no vow or austerity can hasten it.
Rejected: purity does not come by transmigration.

relations.note: illustrated by the simile

definitions.definition: Dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion, with effort turning the wheel; ignorance is its leader and root (bhāṣya 4.11).

definitions.definition: Impressions are of one form with memory (4.9); the impressions of emergence and restraint are properties of the mind (3.9-3.10); even in the discrimination-flow other cognitions rise from earlier saṃskāras in its gaps (4.27); their abandoning is like that of the afflictions (4.28).

Activities leave impressions that produce activities again (YBh 1.5); impressions born of samādhi-insight obstruct others (1.50), and those of stilling obstruct even these (YBh 1.51); impressions of emergence and of stilling alternate in the transformation of stilling (3.9); direct perception of impressions gives knowledge of former births (3.18); memory and impressions are of one form (4.9).

name: The sacraments (saṃskāra)

definitions.definition: Rites that purify the body from conception to death and make it 'fit for Brahman' (MDh 2.26–28); Gautama's forty, including the daily great sacrifices and the solemn rites, are of no avail without the eight virtues of the self (GDh 8.14–25); later works fix a list of sixteen from conception to cremation.

notes: The sixteen-fold list is the common later one (it varies between texts); Gautama's forty are given in cpt:forty-samskaras-eight-virtues.

That list has no vidyārambha or antyeṣṭi, and adds the taking of the domestic and the three śrauta fires.

definitions.definition: The blocking of inflow by the three controls, five carefulnesses, ten virtues, twelve reflections, conquest of the twenty-two hardships and the five conducts (TS 9.1–2); inflow is always to be abandoned and stopping adopted (Vītarāgastotra 19).

name: The Jupiter years and the sixty-year cycle

definitions.definition: Jupiter's years are named after the month-asterism of his heliacal rising (BS 8.1–2); the sixty-year cycle, beginning with Prabhava when Jupiter rises in Māgha at the start of Dhaniṣṭhā, consists of twelve five-year yugas whose years repeat the Vedic names saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, anuvatsara and idvatsara (BS 8.23–29).

relations.note: the five year-names of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa's yuga reappear within each yuga of the sixty-year cycle

definitions.definition: The shock at seeing the world struggling like fish in a drying pool, which drove the Buddha to renounce (Snp 4.15); the four sights (DN 14); the four places of pilgrimage are sites of saṃvega (DN 16).

Conviction in the realities (TS 1.2), arising spontaneously or by instruction (1.3); its transgressions are doubt, desire, disgust, praise and acquaintance of wrong-believers (7.23); its eight limbs, three kinds (subsidential, mixed, destructional) and five signs (calm, longing for release, detachment, compassion, affirmation).
Faith in the true deity, scripture and teacher, free of three follies and eight prides, with eight limbs (Ratnakaraṇḍa 4).
To regard the true god as god, the true teacher as teacher and pure dharma as dharma (YŚ 2.2).
The soul that takes refuge in the real (the pure self) is of right view (Samayasāra 11).

Concentration, meditation and samādhi together on one object (3.4). Mastery of it gives the light of insight (3.5); it is applied to the stage next after the one mastered (3.6); the three are inner limbs relative to the earlier five and outer relative to the seedless samādhi (3.7-3.8). Most of the powers of the Vibhūti-pāda are stated as following from saṃyama on some object.

Concentration, meditation and samādhi on one object (3.4); from its mastery the light of insight (3.5); applied by stages, 'yoga itself being the teacher' (3.6, YBh 3.6); applied to various objects it yields the powers.

name: The conjunction of seer and seen (saṃyoga)

definitions.definition: The beginningless conjunction of seer and seen is the cause of what is to be avoided (2.17); it is the cause of apprehending owner and owned (2.23); its cause is ignorance (2.24); its absence is kaivalya (2.25). Vyāsa records eight views on the 'non-seeing' that causes it (YBh 2.23).

The coded language of tantras and songs; the Hevajra supplies a lexicon; the Pradīpoddyotana reads the tantra by six alternatives; the GST's opening 'bhaga' is glossed as gnosis destroying afflictions.
The Caryāgīti's riddles ('among ten million, could it enter one heart?').

Śāṇḍilya's meditation: the person is made of resolve; meditate on the self as made of mind, with breath for body, of the form of light, like a grain of rice within yet greater than sky and earth, and resolve to attain it at death (ŚB 10.6.3).
The Chāndogya version adds 'all this is Brahman' and 'this self within the heart is Brahman' (ChU 3.14).

name: The body's centres in the Saṅgītaratnākara

definitions.definition: Ten centres — ādhāra (4 petals), svādhiṣṭhāna (6), maṇipūra (10), anāhata (12), viśuddhi (16), lalanā (12), ājñā (3), manas (6), soma (16) and the thousand-petalled lotus — each petal giving a state of mind when the jīva rests there, and certain petals giving or destroying success in music (ŚR 1.2.120–144).

relations.note: partial: adds lalanā, manas and soma centres to the six-centre scheme

definitions.definition: Jñāneśvar, alive, entered the chamber at Āḷandī, sat in meditation and was sealed in; he is held to be present there still.

relations.note: the Tamil Siddhars' living samādhi is described in the same terms

definitions.definition: Sixteen forms of the view that the self survives death with perception.

Knowers of the self rise above the desires for sons, wealth and worlds and live as mendicants (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22); wanderers wander forth desiring the self as their world (4.4.22); ascetics purified by the yoga of renunciation are released (MuU 3.2.6); forest-dwellers living on alms go by the door of the sun (MuU 1.2.11); Śvetāśvatara teaches those beyond the stages of life (ŚU 6.21).

Leaving the ritual world and household to wander as a mendicant; in the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads true renunciation is the union of jīva and supreme Self (Maitreya 2.17), undertaken 'the very day one becomes dispassionate' (Jābāla 4); 'by renunciation alone some reached immortality' (Kaivalya 1.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Asked whether renunciation of actions or yoga is better (5.1), Kṛṣṇa says both bring the highest good but the yoga of action is superior (5.2); the constant renouncer is one who neither hates nor craves (5.3); Sāṃkhya and Yoga are one in result (5.4–5); renunciation is hard to attain without yoga (5.6); renouncing all actions by the mind the embodied one dwells at ease (5.13); the renouncer and yogin is one who does required action without depending on its fruit, not one without sacred fires or rites (6.1); what is called renunciation is yoga, for no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (6.2).

definitions.definition: Renunciation of works is enjoined for the knower and for the seeker (vidvat- and vividiṣā-sannyāsa); the paramahaṃsa ideal; institutionalized in the Daśanāmī order.

Penances, śrāddhas including one's own, the virajā homa, placing the fires in oneself, the declaration renouncing the three desires, the gift of fearlessness, abandoning topknot and thread, and receiving praṇava and great saying from the guru — a ritual death to the world (Jābāla 4; Āruṇi 2–3; Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; Kaṭharudra; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).

definitions.definition: Truth above austerity; non-violence and a vegetarian diet (the goat eats leaves and is flayed); honest household labour and contentment (give only as much as my family needs); humility (none worse than I); keep the critic near; the sādhu known by conduct, not garb.
Erase the self, abandon the faults of body and mind, and be without enmity to all beings.
Low deeds, not birth, make a man low.
Four vows: lacto-vegetarian diet, no alcohol or drugs, a moral life, daily meditation.
Speak truth and walk the right path.

name: The inner regions of Sant Mat

definitions.definition: Above the eye centre (tīsrā til) the soul rises through Sahasdal Kanwal (thousand-petalled lotus; bell and conch), Trikuṭī (Brahm; drum/thunder), Daswān Dwār/Sunn and Mahāsunn (sārangī), Bhanwar Guphā (flute) and Sach Khand/Sat Lok (vīṇā), then Alakh, Agam and Anāmī/Radhasoami; the first two belong to Kāl's domain, the rest are purely spiritual.

notes: Beas-line presentation; the Agra texts differ in detail and numbering.

name: The Sants on powers and miracles

definitions.definition: Riddhi and siddhi are māyā's snares; the yogī's feats and garb do not reach the Lord; the Sant seeks only the Name (the hagiographies nevertheless narrate miracles of protection, as signs of the Lord's care).
Inner experiences of light and sound are signposts, not the goal; the disciple is not to display or seek powers.
Sākhī (witness couplet), pad or śabd (song in a rāga), ramainī (doctrinal caupāī stanzas), arranged in aṅgas; sung in satsaṅg and bhajan.
The Bāul gān signed by the guru's and poet's names, sung with ektārā and dotārā; song is teaching, practice and code.

name: The subtle body in Sant usage

definitions.definition: Nāth-derived anatomy: the three channels (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, or Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī) meeting at trikuṭī, the six cakras, the tenth door, the sky-circle where nectar drips and the unstruck sound is heard; the body as a finely woven sheet.
Sundardās's yoga ullāsa sets out the cakras and the serpent power as a subordinate stage.
Six cakras below the eyes belong to the body (piṇḍ); the Sant practice starts at the eye centre and does not work through the lower cakras; above lie the regions.

name: The Sant, Bāul and Sufi exchanges (context only)

definitions.definition: Kabīr addresses Hindu and Turk alike, rejects both their rites, and uses Persian and Sufi words (pīr, the beloved, the lover's pain) beside Nāth and Vaiṣṇava ones. Recorded as context only.
Bāuls and Fakirs share gurus, songs and practice; Lalon sings of the original Mecca in the human body. Context only.
Dārā Shikoh's Persian Upaniṣads (Sirr-i Akbar, 1657) and his comparative Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn (1655), with his recorded questions to Bābā Lāl, are documents of the exchange. Context only.

notes: Sufism is outside the ontology's scope: no Sufi lineage, doctrine or teaching is recorded; only the in-scope side of the exchange and the documents that witness it.

name: Śānta rasa: peace as an aesthetic experience akin to liberation

definitions.definition: The rasa leading to liberation, arising from knowledge of reality, dispassion and purity of mind, acted through yama, niyama and meditation; its stable emotion is calm (NŚ śānta passage; SD 3.245), dispassion (KP 4) or the self itself as knowledge of reality (Abhinavagupta); the natural state from which the other bhāvas arise and into which they dissolve; principal rasa of the Mahābhārata (DhĀ 4.5 vṛtti); denied a place in drama by Dhanañjaya.

relations.note: śānta is the rasa in which the relish of the self is thematized

notes: Advaita (Gauḍapāda, MK 3.45) calls tasting the bliss of samādhi (rasāsvāda) an obstacle — see obs:rasasvada; the poeticians' valuation is the opposite.

name: The inner and outer lineages of teachers

definitions.definition: Akaccantāṉam (inner): Nandi, Sanatkumāra, Satyajñānadarśin, Parañcōti; puṟaccantāṉam (outer): Meykaṇṭār, Aruṇanti, Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar, Umāpati; the ātīṉams descend from Umāpati's disciples.
Incarnations come from Kāl's regions to keep order in creation; Saints come from the highest region to take souls home and are above them.
Kabīr came in all four ages as the Sat Puruṣ's messenger; the three gods are Kāl's sons.
Kabīr is the supreme God above the gods of the three worlds.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī and Aindrī - the gods' śaktis who fight with the Goddess and then dissolve into her.

name: The seven untenables of Advaita's avidyā

definitions.definition: Rāmānuja's sevenfold refutation: no locus, no power to conceal, no coherent nature, no indescribability, no proof, no remover, no possible removal.
Gajendra surrendering to the nameless supreme; the gods taking refuge in the Goddess, 'intent on saving those who come for refuge'.

name: The body–self relation of world and God (śarīra–śarīrin)

definitions.definition: All souls and matter are the Lord's body — wholly controlled, supported and existing for him — and he is their self; this relation, taught by the mediating texts, explains how Brahman is one and yet the world and souls are real and distinct.

members: the Lord as self (śarīrin, ādhāra, niyantṛ, śeṣin)
souls and matter as body (śarīra, ādheya, niyāmya, śeṣa)

definitions.definition: Every word, in its primary sense, names Viṣṇu — 'Brahman', 'Agni', 'Indra' and the rest — and only secondarily other beings; ritual texts too have him as purport.

Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda, Śāṇakavāsin, Upagupta (then Dhītika, Kṛṣṇa, Sudarśana), with Madhyāntika as Ānanda's disciple who brought the Dharma to Kashmir (Aśokāvadāna and related avadānas; the later names with low confidence).
The Vinaya lineage of the elders from Upāli to Moggaliputta Tissa (Dīpavaṃsa, Samantapāsādikā) — a different succession.

relations.note: Succession of masters vs the councils as the two ways the traditions tell their continuity.

definitions.definition: The dispensation disappears in five stages — attainment, practice, learning, signs, relics.
Self and world are eternal, barren, pillar-firm — held on the evidence of meditative recollection of past lives or aeons, or by reasoning.

name: The sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra

definitions.definition: The SK's topics are those of the whole Ṣaṣṭitantra without its tales and polemics (SK 72). The sixty are ten fundamental topics — pradhāna's existence, oneness, purposiveness; puruṣa's distinctness; being for another; plurality of puruṣas; separation; conjunction; the remaining function; non-agency — and the fifty of the creation of cognitions (Yuktidīpikā introductory verses; Māṭhara on SK 72; Kramadīpikā; Vācaspati quoting the Rājavārttika).

name: Being and non-being at the origin

definitions.definition: ChU 6.2.1-2 teaches that in the beginning there was being alone and rejects the view that being came from non-being; TU 2.7.1 and ChU 3.19.1 say that non-being was first and being arose from it; TU 2.6 says one who knows brahman as non-being becomes non-being. See dsp:being-or-non-being-first.

definitions.definition: The nature of Brahman indicated by three words, each excluding its opposite; also the three aspects 'is, shines, dear' present in every object, as distinct from name and form.
Calm, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, faith and concentration (BS 3.4.27; BĀU 4.4.23).
The true guru gives the one word that soaks every limb with love, opens infinite eyes, and is honoured before Govind because he showed Govind; his virtues cannot be written with the earth for paper.
The guru met in the unseen who placed his hand on Dādū's head.
Sahajobāī would give up Rām rather than forget the guru, who cut the round of birth that Hari gave.
The Sant Satguru embodies the highest region.

After Satī's death Śiva carried her corpse; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śani entered it and dropped its parts across the land; where each fell Śiva stayed as a liṅga and the Goddess is worshipped (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.36-50). Later versions have Viṣṇu cut the body with his discus and count 51 or 52 places.

name: The devotee as bride of Śiva

definitions.definition: At the śaraṇa stage the soul is wife and Śiva husband; the śaraṇa, like a faithful wife, is turned from all else; Akka Mahādēvi lives this in her vacanas to Cennamallikārjuna.

The Mahāvidyās accomplish for worshippers the acts of killing, driving away, agitation, bewitching, melting, yawning, paralysing and destroying (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.132-133); the six acts (śānti, vaśya, stambhana, vidveṣaṇa, uccāṭana, māraṇa) are treated in the eastern tantras. Recorded only as a teaching; not described. Kṛṣṇānanda treats such claims as needing the tradition's checks.

name: The doctrine of the cleansing acts

definitions.definition: The HYP prescribes the six acts only for those with excess fat or phlegm, whose humours are unbalanced (2.21), keeps them secret (2.23), and reports that some teachers hold breath-control alone sufficient (2.37); the GS makes the acts the first of its seven means for everyone (1.9–12); the Haṭharatnāvalī and Haṭhatattvakaumudī count eight.

The effect exists in its material cause before production: the non-existent cannot be produced; a definite material is taken up; not everything comes from everything; the capable produces what it can; the effect has the nature of its cause (SK 9; SS 1.114–118). Production is manifestation, destruction is dissolution into the cause (SS 1.121). It grounds the inference of prakṛti from its effects (SK 14–16).
The effect is the cause in another state: the world is Brahman-with-body in gross state, pre-existing as Brahman-with-body in subtle state; transformation is real (pariṇāma), not apparent (vivarta).

relations.note: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika's new-effect view, rejected in SK 9
the pre-existent effect points to an unmanifest cause

name: Apprehension of the real (satkhyāti) — the Viśiṣṭādvaita theory of error

definitions.definition: Every cognition is of something real; error is incomplete apprehension, not the appearance of the unreal or indescribable; explained by the triplication of elements and, in dreams, by the Lord's creation.

relations.note: Nyāya's misplaced apprehension

definitions.definition: What agrees by continuous use; changes to be made gradually so that reduced faults do not return (Ca Sū 7.36-38; Vi 8.118).

Six stations of the soul's progress to union with Śiva — bhakta (devotion has arisen), māheśvara (steadfastness through dispassion), prasādi (serenity of mind through grace), prāṇaliṅgi (the liṅga known within as consciousness whose power is breath), śaraṇa (bridal union with Śiva) and aikya (immersion in Śiva's bliss). The first three are marked by predominance of action, the last three by the yoga of knowledge.
The vacanas, above all Cennabasava's, arrange the whole of devotional life under the six sthalas, each paired with a liṅga, a kind of devotion and a mode of the soul.

relations.note: the SSM's 101 sthalas are subdivisions of the six

name: Pure reasoning and the purification of thought

definitions.definition: In the śākta means thought is purified by pure reasoning, the teacher and scripture until the pure thought 'I am Śiva' becomes thought-free (TĀ 4).
Monasteries under a sattrādhikār with celibate and married devotees and attached lay disciples, grouped after Mādhavadeva into four saṃhatis; each village has its nāmghar.
Superior, middling and inferior mind: the superior bear great pain even with small bodies; the inferior cannot be sustained by self or others (Ca Vi 8.119).

name: The distinction of sattva (intellect) and the knower of the field

definitions.definition: Sattva and the knower of the field are different yet joined, like fish and water, the gnat and the udumbara fruit, the reed and the muñja grass (MBh 12.187.39; 12.240.21–22).

Restraining the mind from unwholesome objects (Ca Sū 11.54); for mental illness: attending to the three aims, serving those who know them, and knowing oneself, place, family, time and strength (Sū 11.46-47); 'knowledge of intellect, steadiness, the self' is the best medicine for the mind (AHS Sū 1.26).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the real behind the real (BAU 2.1.20); dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); 'speak the truth' (TU 1.11); truth alone conquers (MuU 3.1.6); the truthful are not burned by the heated axe (ChU 6.16); Satyakāma accepted for his truthfulness (ChU 4.4); one who speaks untruth withers to the root (PrU 6.1).

name: Truth and untruth — gods and men

definitions.definition: The world is twofold — truth and untruth; gods are truth, men untruth; by the vow one passes from untruth to truth, from men to the gods, and must then speak only truth (ŚB 1.1.1.4–5).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:satapatha-brahmana:1.1.1.4-5 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Truth upholds the earth (RV 10.85.1); taking a vow, one goes 'from untruth to truth' (VS 1.5); Varuṇa's fetters bind the one who speaks untruth and release the truthful (AVŚ 4.16.6); Prāṇa places the truth-speaker in the highest world (11.4.11).

Purifiers include knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, wind, rites, sun and time; purity in wealth is highest; the mind is purified by truth, the self by knowledge and austerity (MDh 5.105–109).

name: The Lord's supremacy and his accessibility (paratva, saulabhya)

definitions.definition: The Lord is beyond all, lord of the eternal ones, the cause of Brahmā and the gods; and he is easy of access to those who love him, taking whatever form and name they love, coming as a cowherd and dwelling in temple images.

relations.note: Śrīvaiṣṇava theology lists both among the Lord's auspicious qualities

name: The Goddess's gentle and fierce forms

definitions.definition: The one Goddess appears as gentle (saumya: Kamalā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī) and fierce (ugra: Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī) forms; the forms are imagined according to her qualities and acts for the benefit of worshippers (Mahānirvāṇa 5.140; 13.13); Satī turns dark and fearsome to show Śiva her Mahāvidyā forms (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.78-80); Dakṣiṇakālī is terrible yet smiling and boon-giving (Tantrasāra).

name: Seeds and the specific transformation of the series

definitions.definition: Latent defilements, 'possession' and karmic potential are seeds — capacities in the psycho-physical series that mature through its specific transformation, as rice from rice or red pulp from a lac-dyed citron flower.

relations.note: Yogācāra reworks the seeds as stored in the ālaya (historical relation; see borrowings).

name: The schools of poetics: what is the 'soul' of poetry?

definitions.definition: Figure (alaṅkāra: Bhāmaha, Daṇḍin), style (rīti: Vāmana), suggestion (dhvani: Ānandavardhana), oblique expression (vakrokti: Kuntaka), propriety (aucitya: Kṣemendra), rasa (Viśvanātha: 'a sentence whose soul is rasa'); inference (Mahimabhaṭṭa) as the critique of dhvani.

name: Schools of Vedic interpretation in the Nirukta

definitions.definition: Yāska reports competing readings of the same deity: the etymologists (natural phenomena), the legend-tellers (persons of old stories), the ritualists, and others (Nirukta 2.16; 12.1; 12.10).

checks.note: All four named groups occur in the Nirukta: nairuktāḥ (2.16, 7.5, 12.10), aitihāsikāḥ (2.16, 12.1, 12.10), yājñikāḥ (e.g. 5.11, 7.4, 7.23, 11.29, 13.8) and vaiyākaraṇāḥ (1.12, 2.3, 9.5). The definition's refs (2.16, 12.1, 12.10) were text-located.

name: The hierarchy of revelations

definitions.definition: Veda < Śaiva (Siddhānta) < Vāma < Dakṣiṇa < Mata < Kula < Kaula < Trika (verse quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 13.301; TĀ 13.300-301 grades grace in the same order); the Trika is the essence of all scripture (TĀ 1.18); all philosophies are stages of the one consciousness (PH 8).

notes: A variant quoted in the Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa places Kula before Mata.

name: Keeping scripture and worldly duty after conviction

definitions.definition: Even after conviction becomes firm, scripture is to be kept, lest one fall; worldly conduct continues so far, and eating and the like as long as the body lasts; until love is attained, worldly activity is not abandoned — only its fruit is given up.
The instructions are sealed: not to be given to unfit vessels ('the white lioness's milk'); breaking the seal breaks the pledge; the method path is 'sealed three times'.
A century later at Vesālī seven hundred elders rejected the ten points of the Vajjian monks, including accepting gold and silver (Cv 12).

relations.note: the councils as remembered by the several schools (U38)

definitions.definition: With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, inner confidence and unification of mind, rapture and bliss born of concentration, like a lake fed from within by a spring (DN 2).

name: Secrecy and the qualified recipient across the tantric families

definitions.definition: The Kaula teaching is not to be given to one without devotion to the Kula and the guru or to a disciple only slightly tested.
The intentional language and the tantric teaching are not to be revealed to the unconsecrated.
Mantras given to one lacking the required qualities bear no fruit.

The teachings are to be given only to a calm, devoted, well-tested disciple or son — never to the unbeliever, ungrateful or unqualified (Muktikā 1.40–49; Subāla 16; Nirvāṇa; Mahāvākya; Yogaśikhā 2.2–3, 'after twelve years of service').
See cpt:srividya-secrecy: the vidyā hidden in all schools (PKS 1.30) and guarded (YH 1.2).

Some rest on teachings whose ref was corrected or only partly confirmed; the content is located, only the numbering changes: tea:mahavakya-upanisad:1-2 (corrected).

definitions.definition: The Great Perfection is kept secret from those without fortune, who are to practise the vehicles of cause and result; the teacher examines the student and gives the essence only to those bearing the signs.
The Guhyagarbha's secret instruction is given only to trained, fit vessels; proclaimed to the deluded it brings ruin to both.

The tantras and their coded language are not to be revealed to the unconsecrated or unripe; revealing the secret is a root downfall; one without consecration who practises is 'deceived by the vidyādhara tantras'.

name: Secrecy and the testing of the disciple

definitions.definition: The teaching is kept from the undevoted, the deceitful and the cruel and given only to a devoted, tested disciple, even one tested for a year; the adept keeps his mark hidden (KJN 4.20; 5.35; 6.13–14; 14.4–11; 17.11; 22.6).
The haṭha knowledge is to be kept secret: kept secret it is potent, revealed it is powerless (HYP 1.11).

Haṭha must be kept secret — potent when hidden, impotent when revealed (HYP 1.11); the mudrās like a jewel box, told to no one (3.9, 3.18; GS 3.5); the yoga śāstra only for a true devotee (SS 1.19); vajrolī only for one as dear as one's life (DYŚ 137); powers never to be displayed (DYŚ 92–93); the Jyotsnā lists who may and may not receive haṭha.

name: The restriction on showing the Senchakushū

definitions.definition: Hōnen asked that the Senchakushū be buried in the wall after reading, lest slanderers see it; copying was permitted only to chosen disciples (Shinran in 1205).

name: Secrecy and restriction of the teaching

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads restrict their teaching: Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga discuss karma apart, not in public (BAU 3.2.13); the honey-doctrine is for the eldest son or a worthy pupil only, not for the whole earth full of wealth (ChU 3.11.5-6); the mantha rite only for son or pupil (BAU 6.3.12); not to be given to one not tranquil, not a son or pupil (ŚU 6.22; MaiU 6.29); only to those who have performed the head-vow (MuU 3.2.10).

definitions.definition: The scriptures were copied in special secret scripts and kept from outsiders for centuries.

name: Seeing the Buddha (jianfo) in samādhi, dream or at death

definitions.definition: The Buddha is seen by the three powers of his vow, the samādhi and one's merit; Huiyuan saw him three times and at death; visions seen should not be told lightly — good ones are known to oneself, bad ones repented (Shandao).
Shinshū does not seek visions: though passions blind us and we cannot see him, the Buddha's compassion always illumines us.

name: The seer and the seen (draṣṭṛ and dṛśya)

definitions.definition: Reality is divided into the seer — pure seeing, the puruṣa (2.20) — and the seen — the guṇas as elements and senses, for experience and liberation (2.18); their conjunction, caused by ignorance, is the cause of suffering (2.17, 2.24), and I-am-ness is their seeming identity (2.6).
Dharmākara selected the nenbutsu alone as the practice of the primal vow, because the name contains all virtues and is easy for all; Śākyamuni and all buddhas likewise selected it.
Shandao: looking to the Buddha's primal vow, its intent is that beings exclusively call Amitābha's name.
A self distinct from body and cognition exists: shown by desire, memory and recognition; known to itself; taught by 'not this, not this' (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
The eternal agent and enjoyer whose existence Śabara proved against unbelief; knowing it enables rites whose fruit lies in another world, and the Upaniṣads make that knowledge firm.
Distinct from cognition, senses and body; all-pervading, permanent, many; not self-luminous, it appears as subject in each cognition and does not appear in dreamless sleep.

relations.note: in release the self remains without body, senses and objects

name: Self and mind in the chart

definitions.definition: In horā the Sun signifies the self (ātman) and the Moon the mind (manas) of Kālapuruṣa, Mercury speech, Jupiter knowledge, Venus desire and Saturn sorrow (BJ 2.1); firmness comes from the Sun and bodily-mental nature from the Moon (BS 68.3); the planet with the highest degrees is the significator of the self (ātmakāraka) (Jaimini 1.1.11; BPHS 32.3); all beings have a jīva-portion and a supreme-Self portion (BPHS 1.21–24).

name: The self as consciousness; the individual as contracted Śiva

definitions.definition: The self is consciousness (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); the individual is consciousness contracted, containing the universe in contracted form (PH 4), and the mind is consciousness descended (PH 5).

name: The self as a dependent designation

definitions.definition: The self is neither the aggregates nor other than them (MMK 18.1), neither the appropriated nor apart from it (27.8), related to them as fire to fuel (10.15); like a plantain tree split apart, the person analysed into elements is nothing (RĀ 2.1).
Like a chariot sought in seven ways, the self is not found yet is designated in dependence on the aggregates (MA 6.151–160).
The 'mere I' designated in dependence on the aggregates is the conventionally existent self that acts and experiences; the inherently existent self apprehended by innate self-grasping does not exist.

relations.note: the Upaniṣadic self is a real, unchanging subject; Madhyamaka finds no such self
the Pudgalavādins' person 'neither same as nor different from' the aggregates is inexpressible but real; Madhyamaka holds it a mere designation

name: The self as its own friend and enemy (BhG 6.5–6)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 6.5–6: one should raise the self by the self and not let it sink; the self alone is the self's friend and the self alone its enemy — friend to the one who has conquered himself, while for the one not self-possessed the self acts with hostility like an enemy.

definitions.definition: The self is its own witness and refuge; the gods and the person within see the evil-doer (MDh 8.84–86).

Bhagavad Gītā 13.23: the highest puruṣa in this body is called the onlooker (upadraṣṭṛ), with consenter, supporter, experiencer, great lord and supreme self. (The Gītā's word here is upadraṣṭṛ, not sākṣin.)

evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)

definitions.definition: The supreme self is changeless, eternal, the seer, cause of consciousness together with mind, elements and senses (Sū 1.56); beginningless, the unmanifest knower of the field, all-pervading yet feeling only through its own senses, witness of all, known by the marks of life, without which the body is an empty house (Śā 1.59-85); the empirical person (rāśi-puruṣa) is born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma (Śā 1.53); the inner self of the embryo is eternal and 'produces itself' (Śā 3.8). Caraka argues against those who teach an ownerless aggregate of momentary things (Śā 1.46-51).

relations.note: Suśruta: selves are eternal but not all-pervading
Caraka rejects the no-self aggregate view

definitions.definition: The self is to be seen by yoga (YS 1.8), is its own witness (MDh 8.84), is distinguished as knower of the field, elemental self and jīva (MDh 12.12–13), is one in all like space in pots or the sun in waters (YS 3.144), and is the one called Agni, Manu, Prajāpati, Indra, breath and Brahman (MDh 12.123); self-knowledge is highest (MDh 12.85); nothing is higher than attaining the self (ĀpDh 1.8.22.2).

name: The knowers of the field in Suśruta

definitions.definition: Many eternal knowers of the field supported by the one unmanifest (Su Śā 1.3); in Āyurveda they are taught as eternal but not all-pervading, born among animals, men and gods (Su Śā 1.16).

name: The self as its own light (svayaṃjyotis)

definitions.definition: The self is the light by which a person acts when sun, moon, fire and speech are gone (BAU 4.3.6); in dream 'the person becomes his own light' (4.3.9, 4.3.14); 'by his light all this is illumined' (KU 2.2.15; MuU 2.2.10; ŚU 6.14).

name: 'A man is born into the world he has made'

definitions.definition: The rites performed (and the knowledge held) here construct the sacrificer's world hereafter (ŚB 6.2.2.27); as one's resolve at death, so one becomes (ŚB 10.6.3.1).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:satapatha-brahmana:6.2.2.27 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:10.6.3.1-2 (confirmed).

name: The self as a substance with qualities

definitions.definition: An eternal, all-pervading substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition; the one who sees and touches the same thing, recognizes, remembers and is born with memories (NS 3.1.1–24, 3.2.40); its qualities (cognition, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain) are adventitious.

One of the nine substances, all-pervading (VS 7.1.29), known by marks such as breath, eye-movements, life and desire (VS 3.2.4 C), and by the distinctive use of 'I' (VS 3.2.9–13 C); perceived in yoga (VS 9.13).
The substrate of cognition, of two kinds: the Lord and the individual selves (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: The Buddhist denial of a self, which Nyāya refutes.
Sāṃkhya's puruṣa is pure consciousness; the Nyāya self has consciousness only as an adventitious quality.

definitions.definition: Reliance on one's own practice for non-retrogression — the difficult path, hard in an age without a buddha.
Reliance on one's own good and calculation, including self-power nenbutsu; leads to the transformed land.

name: Sensation as the root of reaction (Goenka)

definitions.definition: Every contact produces sensation in the body; craving and aversion arise as reactions to it; equanimous awareness of sensations stops new saṅkhāras and lets old ones surface and pass.

name: The senses as made of the elements

definitions.definition: Smell, taste, sight, touch and hearing arise from earth, water, fire, air and ākāśa, and grasp those elements' qualities (NS 1.1.12–14).
Each sense is a product of its element with a bodily seat (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: The hierarchy of senses, mind, understanding and what is beyond them

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The senses are high; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the understanding; what is higher than the understanding is 'he' (3.42); knowing this, steadying the self by the self, one slays desire (3.43). Parallel series in Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.10–11.

The senses are high, the mind higher, the intellect higher still, and beyond the intellect is 'he' (BhG 3.42); the body as chariot with mind as charioteer, senses as horses, understanding as reins (MBh 11.7.13).

notes: Parallels Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.10–11, which has a longer series.

name: The sentence as the indivisible unit of meaning (akhaṇḍa-vākya)

definitions.definition: The sentence is partless; words and letters are abstractions (apoddhāra) from it; its meaning is grasped as pratibhā (VP 1.73; 2.1–2; 2.143).

name: How a sentence conveys its meaning

definitions.definition: Abhihitānvaya: words convey their own meanings, which then connect into the sentence meaning.
Anvitābhidhāna: words convey their meanings as already connected with one another and with what is to be done.

name: The Lord's devotees as one's masters; service to devotees

definitions.definition: The servants of the servants of the Lord, even if caṇḍālas of caṇḍālas, are our masters; brāhmaṇas who revile devotees become outcastes; the Āḻvārs ask to be made servants of the Lord's servants; the Lord made the pāṇar bard be carried into his shrine.

There is no difference between the Lord and his people; among devotees there is no distinction of caste, learning, beauty, family, wealth or occupation, because they are his; the lowest births are eligible for devotion.
A dog-cooker devoted to the Lord is better than a brāhmaṇa with twelve virtues who is averse to him (BhP 7.9.10).

name: Master and servant (śeṣī–śeṣa): the soul's belonging to the Lord

definitions.definition: The soul's essential nature is to exist for the Lord, its master (śeṣin); all its good lies in his pleasure and its fulfilment in service.
Emphasis on belonging to the Lord alone (ananyārha-śeṣatva) and on total dependence (pāratantrya), such that even one's surrender is not one's own act of means.

'Not knowing myself I thought I and mine; I am yours and what is mine is yours' (TVM 2.9.9); the soul's duty is faultless service at all times (TVM 3.3.1); the Lord stamped the Āḻvār and all his possessions with his discus (PAT 5.4.1).

A subsidiary exists for another's sake (MS 3.1.2); Bādari limits subsidiaries to substances, qualities and purificatory acts, Jaimini includes acts (MS 3.1.3–4); subsidiaries help either by acting on a material or remotely toward the final apūrva.

name: The seven books of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma

definitions.definition: The Jñānaprasthāna ('body') and six 'feet' — Prakaraṇapāda, Vijñānakāya, Dharmaskandha, Prajñaptiśāstra, Dhātukāya, Saṅgītiparyāya — with authors as listed by Yaśomitra.

relations.note: The Theravāda also has seven books; only partial correspondences (Dharmaskandha ~ Vibhaṅga; Dhātukāya ~ Dhātukathā).

definitions.definition: Veda, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, Siddhānta, Kaula — each higher than the last, nothing beyond Kaula (Kulārṇava 2.7-8).
Seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking and deep sleep (Mahā 5, following the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha).

name: The seven blisses of the breath

definitions.definition: Nijānanda, nirānanda, parānanda, brahmānanda, mahānanda, cidānanda, jagadānanda (TĀ 5.43-52).

Śubhecchā, vicāraṇā, tanumānasī, sattvāpatti, asaṃsakti, padārthabhāvanā, turyagā (Varāha 4; Akṣi 2; Mahā 5; cf. Yoga Vāsiṣṭha); mapped in the Varāha onto the measures of Oṃ and onto degrees of knowers of Brahman.

definitions.definition: (As reported) Earth, water, fire, air, pleasure, pain and soul — unmade, barren, unmoving, not affecting one another; the sword passes between them.
(As reported) The same seven, eternal and uncuttable, joined to purification after 84 great aeons.

name: The seven bodily constituents (lus zungs bdun)

definitions.definition: Nutritive essence, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and regenerative fluid, each refined from the one before.

relations.note: the seven dhātus of Āyurveda

definitions.definition: MN 118:30-36: aroused in sequence while the four establishments are practised: mindfulness, investigation of dhammas, energy, rapture, tranquillity, concentration, equanimity, each arising in dependence on the one before; developed supported by seclusion, dispassion and cessation and ripening in relinquishment, they fulfil knowledge and liberation (mn118:42-43).
Mindfulness, investigation of dhammas, energy, rapture, tranquillity, concentration, equanimity: the fourth field of dhamma-contemplation (MN 10:42).
