definitions.definition: rlung, mkhris pa, bad kan, the three pairs and the combined type, each with its body and temperament.

name: The seven deities of the Tantrasamuccaya

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa, Durgā, Subrahmaṇya, Gaṇapati and Śāstā, whose installation and worship the Tantrasamuccaya prescribes.

Rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen (AHS Sū 1.13), each nourishing the next (Su Sū 15.5) and cooked by its own fire into essence and waste (Ca Ci 15.15-16); secondary tissues and wastes arise from them (Ci 15.17-19).

name: The seven divine dharmas of the Kadam

definitions.definition: The four deities — Śākyamuni, Avalokiteśvara, Tārā, Acala — and the three baskets.

Seven earths one below another — Ratnaprabhā to Mahātamaḥprabhā — with 8.4 million hells, where beings suffer by their own leśyā, from one another and (in the first three) from the asuras, for up to 1–33 ocean-measures (TS 3.1–6).

name: The seven jewels of the Shangpa

definitions.definition: Vajradhara, Niguma, Khyungpo Naljor, Mokchokpa, Kyergangpa, Nyentön and Sangye Tönpa — the single-line (gcig brgyud) transmission of the first generations, after which the Shangpa spread.
Of what was seen, heard, experienced, longed for, imagined, portending (bhāvika), and born of the doṣas (Ca In 5.43).

name: The seven locations of mind refuted (Śūraṅgama)

definitions.definition: Ānanda places the mind inside the body, outside it, hidden in the eye-organ, in darkness and light, where it meets objects, in between, and in non-attachment; each is refuted.

name: The seven masters of Jōdo Shinshū (shichi kōsō)

definitions.definition: Nāgārjuna, Vasubandhu, Tanluan, Daochuo, Shandao, Genshin and Hōnen, through whom the teaching of the primal vow was transmitted from India through China to Japan.
Freed both ways, freed by wisdom, body-witness, attained to view, freed by faith, Dhamma-follower, faith-follower — distinguished by formless attainment, wisdom and faith (MN 70).

name: The seven noble riches

definitions.definition: Faith, ethics, shame, conscience (consideration), learning, generosity and wisdom — seven inexhaustible treasures to adorn oneself with instead of material things.

notes: In the Tibetan of Jewel Garland v7–8 'khrel yod ngo tsha shes pa' is one 'wealth'; the seven are counted with learning, giving and wisdom.

name: The six (later seven) categories of Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: Substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence (Praśastapāda; Upaskāra VS 1.1.4), to which absence is added as the seventh (Udayana's Lakṣaṇāvalī, Śivāditya, Śrīvallabha); absence was not listed earlier because it is determined through its counterpositive, not because unreal (Kiraṇāvalī). Candramati's treatise counts ten.
Seven categories (Tarkasaṅgraha, Bhāṣāpariccheda); capacity, similarity and number are not additional categories (argued from Udayana's principle of exclusive alternatives).
Accepted as further objects of knowledge besides the twelve (NBh 1.1.9).
BhP 5.24.7: Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Pātāla; VP 2.5.2: Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat, Mahākhya, Sutala, Pātāla - realms of daityas and nāgas, full of delights.

name: The sevenfold cause-and-effect instruction for bodhicitta

definitions.definition: On the basis of equanimity: recognising all beings as mothers, remembering their kindness, wishing to repay it, love, compassion, the extraordinary resolve, and bodhicitta — the first six being causes, the seventh the effect; traced to Atiśa's lineage.

Śiva, mantramaheśvara, mantreśvara, mantra, vijñānākala, pralayākala, sakala - graded by their impurities: the vijñānākala has only āṇava, the pralayākala āṇava and kārma, the sakala all three (ĪPK 3.2.6-10; TĀ 10).

name: The seven purifications (satta visuddhi)

definitions.definition: Purification of virtue and of mind are the roots; purification of view, by overcoming doubt, by knowledge and vision of path and not-path, of the way, and knowledge and vision are the trunk; the list comes from the Rathavinīta Sutta (MN 24).

notes: The path map itself is pth:seven-purifications (owned by U51).

definitions.definition: Hāsya, adbhuta, vīra, karuṇa, raudra, bhayānaka, bībhatsa, occasional within devotion.

name: The seven siddhi texts

definitions.definition: A group of short Indian treatises on the Vajrayāna view (grub pa sde bdun): Padmavajra's Guhyasiddhi, Anaṅgavajra's Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi, Indrabhūti's Jñānasiddhi, Lakṣmīṅkarā's Advayasiddhi and others.

notes: The last three members are uncertain; lists differ.

definitions.definition: Seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking and deep sleep, each branching a hundredfold.

name: The seven stages of knowledge (jñāna-bhūmikā)

definitions.definition: Good desire, inquiry, thinning of mind, attainment of sattva, non-attachment, non-perception of objects and the reaching of the fourth; liberation lies beyond them; the seventh belongs to the jīvanmukta and the state beyond the fourth to the bodiless liberated.

relations.note: the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha pairs the seven stages of ignorance (3.117) with the seven of knowledge (3.118)

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:seven-stages-of-knowledge
checks.note: MU 3.118.5-6 (names) verified, and the vulgate 3.118 (jñānabhūmikopadeśa). The later account (MU 6.140-156) calls the third stage 'asaṃsaṅga'.

notes: The path map itself is pth:yoga-vasistha-seven-bhumikas (owned by U51).

name: The seven states of the jīva (Pañcadaśī 7)

definitions.definition: Ignorance, veiling, projection, mediate knowledge, immediate knowledge, cessation of sorrow, unrestricted contentment.

name: Seven stations of consciousness and two spheres

definitions.definition: Kinds of beings by body and perception (diverse in body and perception such as humans, … the spheres of infinite space, consciousness and nothingness) and the two spheres of non-percipient beings and neither-perception-nor-non-perception; understanding them one is freed by wisdom (DN 15).

name: The seven transmissions (bka' babs bdun) of Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo

definitions.definition: The seven modes by which Khyentse Wangpo held the teachings.

name: The seven types of awareness (blo rig bdun)

definitions.definition: Direct valid cognition, inferential cognition, subsequent cognition, correctly assuming consciousness, awareness to which an object appears without being ascertained, doubt, and wrong consciousness — the classification of the Types of Mind textbooks.

members: snang la ma nges pa (non-ascertaining appearance)
notes: From src:lorig (genre); not tied to a single text here.

definitions.definition: Cāram (chyle/plasma), ceṉnīr (blood), ūṉ (flesh), koḻuppu (fat), eṉpu (bone), mūḷai (marrow), cukkilam / curōṇitam (semen / ovum), nourished in succession and governed by the humours.

relations.note: the Āyurvedic seven dhātus

definitions.definition: Seven degrees of inner exhilaration in the Kula rite: ārambha, taruṇa, yauvana, prauḍha, tadanta, unmanā and anavastha (Kulārṇava 8.4); the first five are waking, unmanā dream, the equal state deep sleep; knowing them one is liberated (8.94-95).
Buddha, dharma, saṅgha, element, awakening, qualities, activity — the body of the Ratnagotravibhāga.

Purification of virtue, of mind, of view, by overcoming doubt, by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, by knowledge and vision of the way, and knowledge and vision — each serving the next like a relay of chariots, the goal being final nibbāna without clinging (MN 24); systematised in the Visuddhimagga (U37).

relations.note: systematised by the Visuddhimagga (U37)

name: The sevenfold analysis of the chariot

definitions.definition: The chariot is not other than its parts, not identical with them, does not possess them, is not in them, does not contain them, is not their collection and not their shape; so the self and the aggregates (MA 6.151–160).

name: The sevenfold final insight (saptadhā prānta-bhūmi prajñā)

definitions.definition: Vyāsa: four belong to the liberation of insight (what is to be abandoned is fully known; its causes are worn away; abandonment is realised by the samādhi of stilling; the means, discernment, is cultivated) and three to the liberation of the mind (the buddhi's office is done; the guṇas dissolve into their cause; there is no further arising) (YS 2.27, YBh 2.27).

The discerning one's insight at the final stage is sevenfold (2.27): four releases regarding what is to be done (known, exhausted, realized, cultivated) and three releases of the mind (buddhi's task done; guṇas dissolving; the puruṣa alone) (YBh 2.27).

name: The seventeen stages of the Yogācārabhūmi

definitions.definition: The basic section's seventeen stages, from the five sense-consciousnesses through the stages of hearing, reflection and cultivation and of the three vehicles to nirvāṇa with and without remainder.

name: The seventy-five dharmas in five groups

definitions.definition: The later Vaibhāṣika count of the real dharmas: 11 of matter, 1 mind, 46 mental factors, 14 dissociated formations, 3 unconditioned — built from the Kośa's classification.
The Prakaraṇapāda's fivefold division (matter, mind, mental factors, dissociated, unconditioned) is the basis of the list.

notes: The number 75 is a later (East Asian / Tibetan scholastic) count from the Kośa; the Kośa itself does not state the total.

name: The five golden dharmas of the Shangpa

definitions.definition: Pictured as a tree: root — Niguma's six dharmas; trunk — the Amulet Mahāmudrā; branches — the three integrations; flowers — the white and red Khecarī; fruit — the deathless body and mind.

name: The shared framework of means of knowledge and debate

definitions.definition: The means of knowledge, the five-membered demonstration, pseudo-reasons and points of defeat; Uddyotakara writes to remove the errors of 'bad reasoners' (the Buddhists).
Two means of knowledge, inference with the three characteristics of the reason; answers to the Jain single-mark theory.
The single mark of a valid reason is 'otherwise-impossibility' (anyathānupapatti); Jain logic adopts and revises the Nyāya and Buddhist frameworks.
Silver seen in mother-of-pearl: error as appearance, like memory, of a previously seen thing elsewhere; the world appears real until Brahman is known.
Suffering is pacified by the realization of the Perfection of Wisdom — the 'mantra that pacifies all suffering' — combined with instructions of sūtra and mantra given according to capacity.
Padampa Sangye's teaching was passed on in early, middle and later transmissions, the later through Dampa Kunga.

The mind of entrusting to the primal vow, free of doubt, given by Amida; the true cause of birth; buddha-nature; arising in one thought-moment, it brings the benefit of being embraced and the rightly established state; it is hard to attain not because the practice is hard but because shinjin is hard.

relations.note: Shinran identifies great shinjin with buddha-nature (quoting the Nirvāṇa Sūtra)

name: The deities of the supports in Pattirakiriyār's map

definitions.definition: Pattirakiriyār's couplets 66–72 place Gaṇapati at the base of the root support, Brahmā in the earth figure, Viṣṇu in the water crescent, Rudra in the triangle with three rings, Maheśvara in the hexagon of air, Sadāśiva in the circle, and the guru's feet at the crown; Kuṭampai 17 speaks of the triangle and the hexagon.

relations.note: the six supports; the element-deity pairing here places earth above the root, unlike the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, which puts earth at the root

definitions.definition: The spiritual identity in which the practitioner mentally serves in Vraja; distinct from the practitioner's physical body, with which external practice continues.
Compare the 'body fit for service' (sevopayogi-deha), a fruit of service.

name: The guru in the Siddha tradition

definitions.definition: The guru comes of his own accord to the one who longs, shows his own form and burns the six supports, letters and principles (Aḻukaṇṇi 33–36); the seeker must find the master and bow at his feet (Pattirakiriyār 26); guru and Lord are one, and seeing the Lord as guru is the unspoken mantra (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6); the gaze on the guru makes one a teacher (5); the silent guru teaches by stillness (Tāyumāṉavar). Alchemy and medicine are to be learned only from a guru; hence the code language.

relations.note: Siddhānta: Śiva comes as the guru

name: Identifications of the same siddha across Nāth and Buddhist lists

definitions.definition: Several siddhas bear the same or cognate names in both traditions and share legends: Mīnapa and Matsyendra (Mīnanātha) both learn Śiva's secret teaching inside a fish; Jālandhara is Hāḍipā of the Bengali Nāth cycle and Jālandharipā of the Buddhist list, teacher of Kāṇha (Kānipā, Kāṇhapā); Cauraṅgī is the maimed prince restored in both; Gorakṣa appears in the Buddhist list as Cauraṅgī's cowherd attendant; Virūpa/Virūpākṣa is named in the Haṭhapradīpikā and credited in Tibet with the Amṛtasiddhi. Each tradition tells the stories within its own teaching.

members: Mīnapa = Matsyendra/Mīnanātha (identification held by some, distinguished by others)
notes: Whether Mīnapa and Matsyendra are one person is itself disputed in the traditions (some Tibetan accounts treat them as two persons, e.g. father and son — recalled, low confidence) — recorded as an identification, not a fact.

name: The three classes of Siddha drugs

definitions.definition: Plants (mūlikai), minerals and metals (tātu) and animal products (jīvam); plant drugs act slowest and gentlest, mineral-metal drugs fastest and most potent, in the tradition's own ranking.

name: Forms of medicine: 32 internal and 32 external

definitions.definition: The tradition counts thirty-two internal forms (e.g. juice, decoction kuṭinīr, powder cūraṇam, electuary lēkiyam, medicated ghee and oil, pill kuḷikai, waxy meḻuku, calcined parpam, centūram, cuṇṇam, kaṭṭu) and thirty-two external forms (e.g. poultice, fomentation, oil application, fumigation, collyrium, nasal drops, massage tokkaṇam, leech and cautery). Treatment involves patient, physician, medicine and attendant (Kuṟaḷ 950) and a regimen of restrictions (pattiyam).

notes: Only examples are listed; the full 32+32 lists are not recalled.

name: How Siddha medicine was transmitted (the tradition's account)

definitions.definition: Śiva taught Pārvatī; the knowledge passed through Nandi to the Siddhars, above all Agastya, who taught it to his disciples (Tēraiyar, Pulastiyar and others) and set it in Tamil verse; the texts were veiled in code language and passed from guru to disciple, later in palm-leaf manuscripts held by families of physicians.

name: Pulse reading (nāṭi)

definitions.definition: The pulse at the wrist is felt with three fingers for vātam, pittam and kapam; in health their beats are said to stand in the ratio one : half : quarter (mātrai). Pulse is the first and chief examination.

notes: Ratio and finger placement recalled at moderate confidence.

definitions.definition: Six seasons of the year and six divisions of the day, taken from Tamil poetics, govern the rise and fall of the humours and the timing of treatment; the physician must weigh the time (Kuṟaḷ 949).

name: The songs of the siddhas: dohā, caryā, vajragīti, sabad and pad

definitions.definition: Couplets (dohā) and rāga-set songs (caryā) in Apabhraṃśa and Old Bengali, signed by the siddha-poet, teach the innate in riddling images.
The Hindi sabadīs and pads ascribed to Gorakh and the Bengali Nāth song-cycles (Gopīcandra, Mayanāmatī) teach the yoga of the body in the same riddling register.
Kabīr's sākhīs (couplets) and pads continue the form, with the upside-down speech (ulaṭbāṃsī).

name: The state of the liberated (siddha)

definitions.definition: Freed of all karma, the soul rises in one instant to the summit of the universe — like a potter's wheel, a gourd freed of clay, a castor seed and a flame — and stops there for want of the medium of motion; it abides bodiless, in its last body's shape, with perfect right view, knowledge, perception and siddhahood, one among infinitely many (TS 10.3–9).
Haribhadra: the one goal, nirvāṇa, is called by others Sadāśiva, the supreme Brahman, the perfected self and suchness (YDS 129–130).

Beyond description: no sound, reasoning or mind reaches it; not long or short, of no colour, not female, male or neuter; it knows and perceives; formless being (Ācārāṅga 1.5.6); the liberated rise to the summit of the world, where the medium of motion ends, and there enjoy unobstructed happiness (Aupapātika, Uttarādhyayana 36).

members: eight qualities (Digambara): samyaktva, jñāna, darśana, vīrya, sūkṣmatva, avagāhana, agurulaghutva, avyābādhatva

definitions.definition: Non-duality means non-separation (ananya), not identity: the Lord is one with souls, other than them, and together with them — as the vowel 'a' in all letters, the soul in the body, the eye's light with the sun's. In release the soul, its malas powerless, abides in Śiva enjoying his bliss, neither lost nor equal as a second agent.

relations.note: rejects identity and the unreality of the world

name: The astronomical schools (pakṣa)

definitions.definition: Siddhānta astronomy runs in schools with their own constants: the Āryapakṣa (Āryabhaṭa, Bhāskara I, Lalla, Kerala), the Brāhmapakṣa (Brahmagupta, Śrīpati, Bhāskara II), the Saurapakṣa (Sūrya Siddhānta), the Ārdharātrika (midnight) school, and later the Gaṇeśapakṣa (Grahalāghava); Varāhamihira already ranked the five early siddhāntas (PS 1.4).

notes: The pakṣa grouping is partly a scholarly (Pingree) organization of the tradition's own school names.

definitions.definition: Within the hollow egg of Brahmā the planetary orbits lie one below another (Saturn outermost, the Moon lowest); in the middle the earth-globe stands in space by Brahman's supporting power, with Meru through its axis, gods above and asuras below (SS 12.29–36); the earth needs no other support and draws heavy things to itself (Siddhānta Śiromaṇi, Gola). For the Jains the luminary gods circle Meru and make the divisions of time in the human region (TS 4.12–15).
Caste has no basis: no difference in flesh, skin and bone between a Paṟaicci and a Brahmin woman (Sivavākkiyar); the castes called unequal are one (Kaṭuveḷi 32); 'one family, one God' (TM 2104).

relations.note: parallel critique in the vacanas

name: The Siddhar critique of images and ritual

definitions.definition: The planted stone does not speak (Sivavākkiyar); chiselled stone, moulded image and polished copper are not the Real (Pattirakiriyār 16); realization comes without ablutions or flowers (Aḻukaṇṇi 37–38); outward worship with books, lamps and cakras is lower than the Siddhars' Meru (Caṭṭaimuṉi 1); the homeless realized need no hymns (Kuṭampai 30).

relations.note: rejects outer worship as a path in its own right; contrast Siddhānta

name: The Siddhar critique of pilgrimage and holy bathing

definitions.definition: Karma does not go by visiting Kāśī or bathing in the Gaṅgā (Kaṭuveḷi 15, 33); temples and tanks are within the mind (Sivavākkiyar).

name: The Siddhar critique of scripture and learning

definitions.definition: The four Vedas cry out but cannot see the secret (Pattirakiriyār 48); abiding alone means leaving Vedānta and Veda (32); recitation without inner knowledge is empty (Sivavākkiyar); learning, śāstra and purāṇa are scorned (Pāmbāṭṭi).

name: Death and impermanence in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: The body is a bubble on water (Kaṭuveḷi 3), a leaking pot of salt (Aḻukaṇṇi 8), a hard-won pot broken in play (Kaṭuveḷi 4); nothing comes at birth or goes at death (Paṭṭiṉattār 7); kin and wealth do not last, only the Lord's feet (13); even an eyeless needle will not come on the last road; Yama comes tomorrow.

Do no sin (Kaṭuveḷi pallavi); no slander, lying, cursing, anger or cruelty, not even stones thrown at birds; no killing or flesh-eating; no ganja, opium or toddy; no false garb; give away the wealth Śiva gave; wish that all beings be happy (Tāyumāṉavar). One Siddhar also enjoins the Veda's rule (Kaṭuveḷi 8).

The tradition holds that the Siddhars did not die: they live on in subtle or perfected bodies in the Potiyil, Caturakiri and Kolli hills, abide in their samādhi shrines, fly and travel far (Bogar to China), enter other bodies (Tirumūlar) and vanish into liṅgas (Paṭṭiṉattār). Recorded as the tradition's account.

name: Karma and rebirth in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: Most Siddhar voices take rebirth under the two deeds for granted — 'how many mothers, how many births' (Paṭṭiṉattār), the Lord drives us by the rope of the two deeds (Tiruttillai 11), one's own deed burns oneself — while a famous Sivavākkiyar verse says the dead are not born again. Burning the old fate ends the two deeds (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 13).

name: Liberation (vīṭu, mutti) in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: Release is knowing the root (Kaṭuveḷi 13), seeing the 'house' once the senses are burnt (14), standing as 'I am He' (Pattirakiriyār 219), the heart left empty in the open space; it is reached in this body — perfected and deathless for some, seen through as a pot of filth for others — by the guru's grace, devotion (Kaṭuveḷi 18) and never forgetting the Lord's feet (Tiruttillai 16).

relations.note: release in this body

name: Mantra and sound in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: The five letters bring birthless release (Paṭṭiṉattār); the three syllables of Vālai are uttered at the root (Rāmatēvar 2); the fifty-one letters are burnt by the guru (Aḻukaṇṇi 35); yet 'for those in the true tantra, why mantra?' (Kuṭampai 7) and the highest mantra is the unspoken one (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6).

Recorded faithfully: the renouncer-poets portray desire for women as a snare and the female body as filth (Paṭṭiṉattār; Pattirakiriyār 8 'thinking of woman as mother'), while the supreme is worshipped as the goddess Vālai/Maṉōṉmaṇi and some Siddhar ritual involved a woman (restricted).
A mantra held already perfected, needing no checks — said of the Mahāvidyās; Kṛṣṇānanda reads it as praise and keeps the checks (Tantrasāra).

name: Powers (siddhi) and the sādhaka in the Mantramārga
notes: The Vidyāpīṭha's observance (vidyāvrata) is recorded in summary only (restricted).

definitions.definition: The sādhaka masters a mantra through observances to gain powers and enjoyments; for the yogin striving in the limbs of yoga, powers shine forth like the sun's rays and no being can overpower him.
Those who reach the Brahma-world by meditation fulfil desires by will alone, but have no power over the world's creation and are equal to the Lord only in enjoyment (BS 4.4.8, 4.4.17, 4.4.21).
Powers belong to the realm of māyā and to saguṇa meditation; they are not liberation; the knower does not relish even the bliss of absorption (GK 3.45).

name: The powers as obstacles in samādhi (3.37)

names.name: The powers as obstacles in samādhi (3.37)

definitions.definition: The powers arising from saṃyama, beginning with prātibha (3.36), are obstacles (upasarga) for a mind in samādhi and powers (siddhi) for the outgoing mind (3.37). At 3.51 the text adds a warning: when invited by those of high stations the yogin is to feel neither attachment nor pride, for heedlessness would find a gap and stir the afflictions, and then the undesirable would follow again.

The powers are obstacles in samādhi and powers only in emergence (3.37); kaivalya comes from dispassion even toward the highest (3.50); invited by the celestials, the yogin should form neither attachment nor pride (3.51, YBh 3.51); kaivalya does not require the powers (YBh 3.55).
The many powers, the nether regions and alchemy, even if obtained, are not to be grasped: they are nets leading down (Akulavīra B.83–84).

The DYŚ lists the powers that arise in the ghaṭa stage (clairaudience, clairvoyance, speed, perfect speech, invisibility, alchemy, flight) and says they are obstacles to the great accomplishment: the yogin should not delight in them, should hide them and live as if dull or deaf, lest disciples crowd round and he forget his practice (84–95). The HYP nonetheless promises the eight powers from the mudrās (3.8, 3.130).

name: Powers (siddhi) in Śrīvidyā and their place

definitions.definition: The eight powers Aṇimā and the rest are deities of the outermost enclosure, the gate where the gods won their powers (SL 93) and rays of the Goddess's own body (SL 96); firm contemplation brings the power of command (PKS 1.13); meditation with the goddesses of speech brings poetry (SL 17) and on the kāmakalā the power to attract (SL 19); the sixty-four tantras aim at particular powers, while the Goddess's tantra accomplishes all aims (SL 31); those who grasp the mantra without lineage are harmed by its rays (YH 2.81).

Powers arise from practice and concentration (far-hearing, far-seeing, invisibility, sky-travel, entering bodies); the Yogatattva calls them obstacles to be hidden; the Yogaśikhā distinguishes contrived from spontaneous powers and treats spontaneous powers as the test of a siddha.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 4 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text. Some rest on teachings whose ref was corrected or only partly confirmed; the content is located, only the numbering changes: tea:sandilya-upanisad:1.60-68 (corrected).

definitions.definition: Cāṅgadev's power over beasts was humbled by the siblings' moving wall; powers breed pride, and the yogī of powers became a disciple.
The enticing powers (ṛddhi-siddhi) come to blow out the lamp of knowledge; devotion's gem is untouched by them.
A guru who displays powers or deals in magic is not a true guru.

relations.note: warnings that powers obstruct the goal

name: Powers and signs in the Kagyu (and the warnings)

definitions.definition: Miracles in dream or waking become path if known as illusion and obstacles if taken as real; when the siddhis are attained obstacles become friends of the path (bka' dpe phyi ma); Milarepa displays powers only to teach; Milarepa tells Gampopa that his visions are neither good nor bad.

relations.note: the Kagyu warning corresponds to the general warning that powers are obstacles when grasped

name: Powers and the warnings about them

definitions.definition: Powers arise from union with power and pure knowledge (Śiva Sūtra 1.19-21; SK 3.1-7), but powers under the veil of delusion are not liberation (Śiva Sūtra 3.6; 2.4; 3.23); light, sound, form and taste arising from the unmeṣa distract (SK 3.10).
The fruits listed for one established in a dhāraṇā (VBT 140-142).

Common siddhis (pacifying, increasing, the eight great siddhis such as the good vase, flight, the sword) and the supreme siddhi (mahāmudrā/buddhahood); Tilopa lists long life, no white hair, radiance and a lion's strength among the signs.
The songs warn against pride in powers and against mistaking experiences for realization.

name: The accomplished means and the means to be done

definitions.definition: The Lord is the already-existent means (siddhopāya); bhakti-yoga or prapatti is the means to be performed (sādhyopāya) which occasions his grace.
The Lord alone is the means; there is no sādhyopāya on the soul's side in the path of surrender.

name: Recognising signs, deviations and obstacles as the path

definitions.definition: Knowing that attainments arise in oneself removes hope for them; knowing māras and deviations as one's own path and dependent arising turns faults into qualities (Vajra Verses).

relations.note: the tantric counterpart of lojong's taking adversity as the path

name: Auspicious signs of birth at death

definitions.definition: The biographies of those born record light, fragrance, heavenly music, purple clouds, visions of the Buddha and foreknowledge of the time of death; Zunshi's vow asks to know the time, be free of pain and die as if in samādhi.
Not relied on: the person of shinjin is settled regardless of the manner of death (letter 1).

Portents by which the yogin knows his death: not seeing Arundhatī, the pole-star, the moon's shadow or the Milky Way (death within a year), a rayless sun, certain dreams, loss of shadow and bodily changes (shorter spans).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: MkP 43.1-3, 43.10 and LiP 1.91.1-2 located. All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

name: Signs of death and their reversal

definitions.definition: Outer, inner and secret signs of approaching death are examined; untimely death can be averted by ransom and longevity rites; when death is certain, one prepares with transference and the bardo instructions.

relations.note: both teach omens of death

name: Signs of death in Sowa Rigpa

definitions.definition: Distant, near and uncertain signs by which the physician judges curability.

relations.note: medical and yogic omens of death overlap

name: Omens of death and cheating death

definitions.definition: Omens read from the flow of winds in the channels; the yogin 'cheats death' by drawing the life-wind into the central channel (restricted).

relations.note: Death omens are catalogued in other systems too.

definitions.definition: Mirage, smoke, fireflies, lamp and a cloudless sky arise when the mind enters 'the vajra of cessation' (GST 18.146–149).

In the Vajra Verses, when elements gather in meditation: earth into water — mirage; water into fire — smoke; fire into wind — fireflies; wind into consciousness — a burning lamp; consciousness into clear light — like a cloudless sky.

The eight stages of dying in the Guhyasamāja-based Gelug presentation: mirage, smoke, fireflies, flickering flame, then the white appearance, red increase, black near-attainment and the clear light of death — also re-enacted in completion-stage practice.

name: The signs of the irreversible bodhisattva

definitions.definition: Aṣṭa ch. 17: he does not look to other teachers, has no doubt, keeps the ten wholesome ways even in dreams, is not deceived when Māra in the Buddha's form denies the teaching; ch. 19-20 add dream-signs.

Sweat, then trembling, then the breath reaching its place (HYP 2.12); sweat, trembling of the spine, rising from the ground (GS 5.57); sweat, trembling, hopping like a frog, levitation, scant sleep and excreta, freedom from disease, great strength (SS 3.40–46; DYŚ 69–76).

name: Signs of the descent of power and of freedom from bonds

definitions.definition: A distinctive devotion (bhakti) marks the descent of power; in one freed from bonds by initiation the sign is steadiness of disposition and absence of wavering in the prescribed action, though signs are not always evident.

name: The signs of the lover of God

definitions.definition: Having love, one desires nothing, grieves over nothing, hates nothing, has no zeal for other ends; becomes intoxicated, still, self-delighting; sees, hears, speaks and thinks only of him; with choked voice, bristling hair and tears the one-pointed purify the world.
Sleeplessness, tears bailed out with the hands, joining palms at the names, melting; the love-sick heroine's wasting; the eyes that, having seen him, will see nothing else.
Rādhā in separation makes a bed of flowers that burns her and calls moonlight fire.

name: Signs of establishment in the restraints and observances

definitions.definition: YS 2.35–2.45: hostility abandoned; actions and fruits rest on the practitioner; jewels present themselves; vigour gained; understanding of the how of births; disgust for one's own body; purity of sattva and the rest; unsurpassed happiness; perfection of body and senses; union with the chosen deity; perfection of samādhi. The text's own descriptions; not promises to the reader.

Established in non-harming, hostility ceases nearby; in truth, actions and fruits rest on one's word; in non-stealing, jewels come; in celibacy, vigour; in non-possessiveness, knowledge of births (2.35–39); purity, contentment, austerity, self-study and devotion yield their fruits (2.40–45). Vyāsa calls these 'powers' (YBh 2.39).

name: First signs of progress in yoga

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): ŚU 2.11 lists the forms that precede brahman's manifestation (fog, smoke, sun, wind, fire, fireflies, lightning, crystal, moon); 2.12 the body made of the fire of yoga free from sickness, old age and death; 2.13 lightness, health, freedom from craving, clear complexion, pleasant voice and smell, scant excreta.

Lightness/freedom from greed, health, gentleness, pleasant smell, scant excreta, radiance, clarity, a pleasant voice; others praise the yogin, creatures do not fear him, he is untroubled by heat and cold (MkP 39.63-65).

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ŚU 2.11). It rests on 3 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: The monk's virtue of abstentions (DN 1; DN 2), the lay precepts, and the Pātimokkha; its purpose is non-remorse leading on to liberation (AN 11.1); ordinary people praise the Buddha only for it (DN 1).
Silence in which words are forgotten and clarity appears; silence and illumination complete each other (Hongzhi).
Criticised by Dahui as 'heretical silent-illumination Chan' that turns practitioners into dead ash.

Offence (āgas) and sin (enas) — one's own, done in the body, through wine, anger, dice or thoughtlessness, even in sleep, and those inherited from the fathers — bind as Varuṇa's fetters; the seer examines himself, asks the wise, confesses and asks to be loosened like a calf from its tether, to be sinless before Aditi (RV 1.24.15, 2.28.5, 5.85.7–8, 7.86–89).
All the Buddha's teachings share one intent, and no vehicle's teaching is to be rejected: the premise of Jigten Sumgön's vajra statements.

The learned, free of envy, pride and greed (BDh 1.1.1.5), free of desire (VDh 1.6), whose practice is authoritative where the Veda is silent; a single Veda-knower's decision outweighs myriads of the ignorant (MDh 12.113).

definitions.definition: The self is a dancer, the inner self the stage, the senses the spectators (Śiva Sūtra 3.9-11).

name: Śiva-, Rudra- and Bhairava-tantras as teaching difference, difference-in-identity and non-difference

relations.note: the Saiddhāntikas read their scriptures as teaching the soul's distinctness and reject this ranking (see dsp:rank-of-siddhanta-and-bhairava-tantras)

definitions.definition: Jayaratha derives the ten Śiva-tantras (difference), eighteen Rudra-tantras (difference-and-non-difference) and sixty-four Bhairava-tantras (non-duality) from the combinations of Sadāśiva's faces: knowledge itself unfolds in these three ways.
The one reality appears as god and goddess, being and manifestation, whose union is the world; they are never two.
Without Śiva no Śakti, without Śakti no Śiva; they go together like fire and smoke, tree and shade (KJN 17.8–9); in dissolution Śakti enters Śiva (2.6).
The one Śakti, the Lord's own power, upholds the body and the cosmos; Śiva and Śakti are not two (SSP 4); if Śiva, mind, Śakti and breath are in different places there is no success (Candrāvalokana).
Nothing is without Bhairava and nothing without the Goddess; by cause and effect each is the other's guru (Kubjikāmata 2.17-18).
Without Śakti Śiva is a corpse (Toḍala 1.25).
Kula is Śakti and Akula Śiva; the Kaula joins them (Kulārṇava 17.27); their union is the bliss that is liberation (5.79).

name: The union of Śiva and Śakti (śiva-śakti-aikya, sāmarasya)

definitions.definition: The Goddess's form is the oneness of Śiva and Śakti (LSN 183); Tripurā is the fusion of light and self-awareness (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); Śiva joined to Śakti can create, without her he cannot stir (SL 1).
Śiva and Śakti are equal in primacy, with fivefold equality (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).
Their union is the great point and the 'I' (KKV 4-5).

relations.note: the Samaya equality is set against the Kaula views

definitions.definition: Liberation as equality with Śiva in bliss and powers except world-governance.
Śiva with inseparable cit-śakti is Brahman; souls and world are his body; he is material and efficient cause.
Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva and Śiva of Viṣṇu (Skanda 8–9); whoever honours Govinda honours Śaṅkara (Rudrahṛdaya); the one Lord is Brahmā, Śiva, Indra and Viṣṇu (Kaivalya 8).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 3 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: The freed soul becomes 'a Śiva': its own omniscience and omnipotence, covered since beginningless time, are manifested; it is equal to Śiva, not identical with him, and does not perform the five cosmic acts.

relations.note: the Tamil school stresses inseparability and enjoyment rather than equal powers

definitions.definition: (As reported) Black, blue, red, yellow, white and supremely white classes of beings — from the cruel to the three Ājīvika leaders (AN 6.57, ascribed to Pūraṇa; DN 2, to Makkhali); in the Tamil report black, dark blue, green, red, golden, white, with release in the supremely white birth.
The Buddha's six: dark or bright birth leading to dark, bright, or neither-dark-nor-bright (nibbāna) results according to conduct.

relations.note: the classes are grades within the fixed round

definitions.definition: Psychic powers, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the divine eye and the destruction of the effluents, attainable from the fourth jhāna (DN 2; AN 3.101; MN 119).

Five mundane direct knowledges developed from the fourth jhāna — supernormal powers, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the divine eye — and the sixth, supramundane, destruction of the taints; the worldling's powers are fragile and an impediment to insight.

Magical power, divine ear, others' minds, former lives, death and rebirth, destruction of outflows; three are 'knowledges'; instruction is the highest wonder; power arises from cultivation, birth, spells, herbs or karma.

relations.note: the powers may be attained, but their display is disparaged (DN 11)
both are powers born of concentration and both texts warn that they obstruct the highest aim; the goals (nibbāna / kaivalya) differ

name: The six paths (ṣaḍadhvan)
notes: No verse-level anchor recorded in this pass.

definitions.definition: The cosmos as six 'paths' — letters (varṇa), words (pada), mantras, kalās, principles (tattva) and worlds (bhuvana) — traversed and purified in nirvāṇa-dīkṣā.

The paths of the denoting - letters, mantras, words - and of the denoted - kalās (nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, śānti, śāntyatītā), tattvas, worlds; purified in initiation and contemplated from gross to supreme (TĀ 6-12; VBT 56-57).
Provisional / definitive, intentional / non-intentional, literal / non-literal: the hermeneutic keys for reading the Guhyasamāja (with the 'seven ornaments').
Recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, one's virtue, one's generosity and the deities, by which the mind is not obsessed and becomes concentrated (AN 6.10).

Equanimity (sāmāyika), praise of the twenty-four Jinas, salutation of the teacher, repentance (pratikramaṇa), abandonment of the body (kāyotsarga) and renunciation (pratyākhyāna) — daily obligations of ascetics and observant laity.
For householders the Digambaras also teach six daily duties: worship, attendance on the teacher, study, restraint, austerity and giving.

name: The six intermediate states (bar do drug)

definitions.definition: The bardos of life (skye gnas), dream (rmi lam), meditation (bsam gtan), dying ('chi kha), dharmatā (chos nyid) and becoming (srid pa); the Heart-essence also counts four (life, dying, dharmatā, becoming).

Ādhāra (anus), svādhiṣṭhāna (genitals), maṇipūra (navel), anāhata (heart), viśuddhi (throat), ājñā (between the brows); knowing their piercing one knows the spotless beyond them (Yogaviṣaya 8–10; GŚ 10–15, 60–62).
Nature, the Lord, time, chance, destiny and transformation are held by far-sighted physicians to be the source (Su Śā 1.11).

relations.note: the list of candidate causes in Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.2

name: Six causes, four conditions, five results

definitions.definition: Six causes (efficient, co-existent, homogeneous, associated, pervasive, ripening), four conditions (causal, immediately preceding, object, dominant), five results (ripening, outflow, dominant, human effort, disjunction); nothing arises from a single cause such as Īśvara.

name: The six characteristics of pure devotion

definitions.definition: Destroys suffering; bestows auspiciousness; makes liberation trivial; rarely attained; intense special bliss; attracts Kṛṣṇa.

name: The six characteristics of seeds

definitions.definition: Seeds are momentary, simultaneous with their fruit, continuous as a series, determinate in moral quality, dependent on conditions and productive only of their own fruit (Mahāyānasaṃgraha).

notes: Sanskrit names reconstructed from the Chinese/Tibetan; list recalled.

name: What destroys and what promotes yoga (HYP 1.15–16)

definitions.definition: Six things destroy yoga — overeating, overexertion, too much talk, clinging to rules, company of people, unsteadiness — and six bring success — enthusiasm, boldness, patience, knowledge of truth, determination, abandoning company.

name: Tilopa's six dharmas (the Indian six yogas)

definitions.definition: Caṇḍālī (Caryāpa), illusory body and clear light (Nāgārjuna), dream (Lavapa), intermediate state and transference (Sukhasiddhi) — the root of the 'six yogas of Nāropa'.
Earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness, of which a person consists (MN 140; AN 3.61).
Feigned snoring, trembling, limping, amorous gestures, senseless acts and senseless speech - 'doors' through which dishonour brings merit and removes demerit.

The universe consists of six eternal, uncreated substances: souls, matter, the medium of motion, the medium of rest, space and time; all but time are 'extended' (astikāya); only matter has form (TS 5.1–5, 5.39).
Some Śvetāmbara authorities treat time only as a mode of the other substances ('time too, according to some', Śv TS 5.38).

relations.note: The substances being eternal and uncreated, there is no creator (TS 5.4).

name: The six cycles of equal taste (Drukpa)

definitions.definition: Thoughts, afflictions, gods and demons, suffering, illness and death carried onto the path as of one taste.

name: The six factors of the embryo

definitions.definition: The embryo arises from the union of mother, father, self, suitability, nourishment and the mind that arises of itself; each contributes specific parts and qualities (Ca Śā 3.3-14).

name: The six fundamentals (ṣaṭpada) of Śrīmad Rājacandra

definitions.definition: The soul exists; it is eternal; it is the doer of its karma; it is the enjoyer; liberation exists; there is a means to liberation (Ātmasiddhi 43), each defended against a doubter.

notes: Recent (1896).

relations.note: the six are 'aprākṛta'; the Lord is nirguṇa with respect to prakṛti's three guṇas

definitions.definition: Knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility and splendour; knowledge is Brahman's very form and the other five its aspects; the six are also Lakṣmī's body; pairs of them manifest as the vyūhas.

name: The six classes of living beings

definitions.definition: Earth-bodied, water-bodied, fire-bodied, wind-bodied and plant-bodied beings (one-sensed) and mobile beings (two- to five-sensed); non-harm extends to all six in thought, word and deed.

name: The six kinds of arhat and falling back

definitions.definition: Liable to fall, able to end life at will, guarding, stable, able to perfect the faculties, unshakeable; five can fall back from what they have obtained.
No falling back from arhatship.
An arahant does not fall away (Kv 1.2).

relations.note: The Pali Abhidhamma person-types do not include arhats who fall back.

definitions.definition: Four (kuṭīcaka, bahūdaka, haṃsa, paramahaṃsa — Bhikṣuka, Āśrama, Śāṭyāyanīya) or six (adding turīyātīta and avadhūta — Nāradaparivrājaka 5; Sannyāsa 2), graded by freedom from marks and rules, food, bathing, worship and the world attained.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 8 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: Accumulation, provocation, spreading, lodging, manifestation and differentiation, each a time for treatment; doṣas removed at accumulation do not advance (Su Sū 21.18-37).

Six colourings of the soul by passion-tinged activity — black, blue, grey (inauspicious), yellow-red, lotus-pink, white (auspicious) — found in hell-beings, gods and humans in differing degrees (TS 2.6, 3.3, 4.2, 4.22); illustrated by six travellers who would uproot, cut, lop, strip, pick or gather from a fruit tree (Gommaṭasāra Jīvakāṇḍa; the jambū-tree parable).

name: The six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅga) in its several forms

definitions.definition: Maitrī Upaniṣad: breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, concentration, reasoning (tarka) and absorption; the Amṛtanāda lists the same six in another order.

The Śaiva Mantramārga teaches a six-limbed yoga with reasoning (tarka) as a limb, called the highest limb (Mālinīvijayottara, as quoted in the Tantrāloka — recalled); the Mṛgendra's yoga section gives breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation and absorption with recitation (japa) and examination (ūha) of what is to be rejected and accepted.
Guhyasamāja and Kālacakra: withdrawal, meditation, breath-control, retention, recollection (anusmṛti) and absorption — the completion-stage yoga of the Kālacakra.
Gorakṣaśataka and Vivekamārtaṇḍa: posture, breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation, absorption (the yamas and niyamas not counted).

relations.note: tarka as the limb distinguishing the Upaniṣadic and Śaiva lists

notes: Same names in different orders with different contents and goals; the Kālacakra tradition defines each limb by its own signs. See brw:sadanga-yoga-shared-limbs (U44) and brw:sadanga-yoga-maitri-to-mantramarga (U49).

name: The six limbs of surrender (ṣaḍaṅga śaraṇāgati)

definitions.definition: Resolve to do what pleases, avoidance of what displeases, faith that he will protect, choosing him as protector, laying down oneself, helplessness.

name: The six marks of purport (ṣaḍ-liṅga)

definitions.definition: Opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise, demonstration — used in hearing to determine that the Upaniṣads' purport is the non-dual Brahman (from Mīmāṃsā).

Mīmāṃsā supplies the criteria that Vedānta manuals list as six marks: the opening and close of a passage (upakrama–upasaṃhāra; their relative strength argued in the Upakramaparākrama), repetition (abhyāsa, which marks a distinct rite, MS 2.2.2), novelty (apūrvatā: an injunction is for what is otherwise unobtained), the stated result (phala, MS 4.3), praise (arthavāda, MS 1.2.7) and reasoned demonstration (upapatti); doubtful sense is settled by the complementary passage (MS 1.4.29).

notes: The versified list 'upakramopasaṃhārāv abhyāso 'pūrvatā phalam / arthavādopapattī ca liṅgaṃ tātparyanirṇaye' is cited by Vedānta authors (e.g. Madhva at BSBh 1.1.4, who ascribes it to a 'Bṛhatsaṃhitā'); I did not find it as a list in the Mīmāṃsā texts consulted.

name: The six meanings of the mantra (Yoginīhṛdaya)

definitions.definition: Literal (bhāvārtha), traditional (sampradāyārtha), hidden (nigarbha: Śiva, guru and self), Kaula (the unity of cakra, deity, vidyā, guru and self), all-secret, and great-principle meaning (the partless supreme) (YH 2.15-16, 2.48, 2.51-52, 2.73-74).

name: The six modifications of being (ṣaḍ bhāvavikārāḥ)

definitions.definition: According to Vārṣyāyaṇi, everything that becomes is born, exists, changes, grows, declines and perishes (Nirukta 1.2).

notes: Later Vedānta uses the list for what the unchanging self is free of.

checks.note: Nirukta 1.2 has 'ṣaḍ bhāvavikārā bhavantīti vārṣyāyaṇiḥ | jāyate 'sti vipariṇamate vardhate 'pakṣīyate vinaśyatīti'; all six members and the attribution match. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:nirukta:1.2.

name: The six mother monasteries of the Nyingma

definitions.definition: Katok, Dorje Drak, Mindroling, Palyul, Dzogchen and Shechen, the principal Nyingma seats and their traditions.

notes: Founding dates from memory; Dorje Drak and Shechen not dated here.

name: The six categories as foundations of medicine

definitions.definition: General, particular, quality, substance, action and inherence, seen by the sages (Ca Sū 1.28-29) and defined (Sū 1.44-52); the nine substances include self, mind, time and directions (Sū 1.48).

relations.note: Vaiśeṣika's six (later seven) categories; Caraka names the same six

definitions.definition: Giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation and wisdom; wisdom leads the other five, which without it are not even called perfections; giving should be unsupported, patience free of the notion of self.

Giving, discipline, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom, each the subject of a chapter of the Bodhicaryāvatāra (5–9) or a ground of the Madhyamakāvatāra (1–6); all are taught for the sake of wisdom (BCA 9.1).
At birth a soul completes, within an antarmuhūrta, the capacities for taking in matter, body, senses, respiration, speech and mind (Gommaṭasāra and Śvetāmbara karma texts).

name: The six powers for calm abiding

definitions.definition: Hearing (1st state), reflection (2nd), mindfulness (3rd–4th), introspective alertness (5th–6th), effort (7th–8th) and complete familiarity (9th).

name: The six rites of the mantra manuals (ṣaṭkarma)

definitions.definition: The manuals classify desire-driven applications of mantras into six rites — pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), immobilization (stambhana), causing enmity (vidveṣaṇa), expulsion (uccāṭana) and killing (māraṇa) — assigning to each its direction, time, seat and fire-pit; they belong to the worldly (kāmya) use of mantras, distinct from their use for liberation.

notes: Summary only; U31 records no procedures. The Śāradātilaka's fire-pit rules mention such rites (paṭala 3, e.g. v. 86); the Mantramahodadhi treats them in a late taraṅga (not fixed).

definitions.definition: Greed, hatred and delusion (unwholesome) and non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion (wholesome or indeterminate) are the roots that give firmness to consciousness.
Through śāmbhavī (meditation), bhrāmarī (nāda), khecarī (bliss of taste) and yonimudrā (laya), through devotion, and through the swoon of the mind — six-fold rājayoga (GS 7.5–16).
Conjunction; inherence in the conjoined; inherence in what inheres in the conjoined; inherence; inherence in what inheres; qualifier–qualified relation (Uddyotakara; Tarkasaṅgraha).

Sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter, astringent (Ca Sū 1.65; 26.9); their source is water; sweet, sour and salt overcome vāta, astringent, sweet and bitter pitta, astringent, pungent and bitter kapha (Sū 1.66).

Sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter and astringent, each formed of two elements, increasing or decreasing the humours; every drug is known by taste, potency (vīriyam), post-digestive effect (pirivu) and action (ceykai).

name: The six tastes in Sowa Rigpa

definitions.definition: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, hot and astringent, each from a pair of elements, each pacifying or aggravating particular nyepa.

relations.note: same six tastes; the element-pair assigned to bitter differs (Tibetan water+wind)

definitions.definition: Six famous leaders of orders contemporary with the Buddha — Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalī, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta — each praised as ford-maker and elder, each reported as answering Ajātasattu off the point; they appear together in DN 2, DN 16, MN 30, MN 36, MN 77, SN 3.1, SN 44.9, Snp 3.6, the Vinaya (bowl episode) and the Milindapañha.
Greedy, hating, deluded, faithful, intelligent and speculative; each has suitable subjects, dwellings and postures; faith parallels greed, intelligence hatred, speculation delusion.
The Vimuttimagga counts fourteen kinds of behaviour including mixed types (as reported).
Phoneme (varṇa), accent (svara), quantity (mātrā), force (bala), evenness (sāma) and connection (santāna) (TU 1.2).

checks.note: TU 1.2 has 'varṇaḥ svaraḥ | mātrā balam | sāma santānaḥ'; all six members match. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:taittiriya-upanisad:1.2.

name: The three and the six transmissions

definitions.definition: All teachings pass by the mind-transmission of the victors, the symbolic transmission of the vidyādharas and the oral transmission of persons; treasures add prophetic authorization, empowerment through aspiration and entrustment to the ḍākinīs.

name: The six limbs of the Veda

definitions.definition: Phonetics, ritual procedure, grammar, etymology, metre and time-reckoning; the Veda's nose, hands, mouth, ear, feet and eye (PŚ 41–42), studied as a duty without motive (Mahābhāṣya); compiled by later seers for ease of learning (Nirukta 1.20); among the fourteen seats of knowledge (YS 1.3); counted as lower knowledge (MuU 1.1.5).

checks.note: The list of six was found in MuU 1.1.5 ('śikṣā kalpo vyākaraṇaṃ niruktaṃ chando jyotiṣam'). The body image was found at PŚ 41–42, and the compilation by later seers at Nirukta 1.20. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:mundaka-upanisad:1.1.4-5, tea:paniniya-siksa:41-42, tea:nirukta:1.20.

name: The Six Yogas (Six Dharmas) of Nāropa

definitions.definition: Inner heat, illusory body, dream, clear light, intermediate state and transference (with 'entering another's body' and, in some lists, the consort practice) — gathered by Tilopa from four Indian transmissions and given by Nāropa to Marpa; the Kagyu 'path of method'. Lists vary between sources: Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa treats transference and grong 'jug together; the Karṇatantravajrapada adds karmamudrā.
Niguma's six dharmas, a parallel set with the same six topics, taught in the Shangpa.

members: las kyi phyag rgya (karmamudrā; some lists)

relations.note: the path of method
parallel sets from two ḍākinī lineages; the Shangpa insists on their distinct transmission

name: The sixteen supports (ṣoḍaśa-ādhāra)

definitions.definition: Sixteen places of the body on which attention is fixed (from the big toe to the brahmarandhra in the usual list), to be known by the yogī (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
Jālandhara 'binds the sixteen supports' (HYP 3.73); the Vivekamārtaṇḍa family lists them among what the yogin must know in his own body; the Haṭhatattvakaumudī devotes a chapter to them.

notes: Membership of the list recalled, not checked; members omitted.

definitions.definition: Purity of view, humility, faultless vows, constant knowledge, fear of saṃsāra, giving and austerity according to capacity, tending ascetics, service, devotion to arhats, teachers, the learned and scripture, the essential duties, promoting the path and love for co-religionists (TS 6.24); Śvetāmbara texts give twenty sthānakas.

Sixteen (ṣoḍaśa-kāraṇa-bhāvanā): purity of faith, humility, faultless vows, constant knowledge, longing for release, giving and austerity according to strength, the monks' composure and service, devotion to Arhats, teachers, the learned and scripture, the obligatory duties, spreading the path and affection for fellow believers.
Twenty 'places' (vīsa-sthānaka), from devotion to the Arhats to the propagation of the teaching (list from the Jñātādharmakathā and niryukti; low confidence on its items).
Āśrama Upaniṣad: four kinds each of student, householder, forest-dweller and wanderer.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: Realization of the truths in sixteen moments

definitions.definition: Acceptance and knowledge of dharma and of subsequent knowledge for each truth; fifteen moments are the path of seeing, the sixteenth begins the fruit.
Realization of the truths in one moment is ascribed to the Mahāsāṃghika side in the doxographies (low confidence).

name: The sixteen categories of Nyāya (ṣoḍaśa padārtha)

definitions.definition: The sixteen topics whose true knowledge yields the highest good (NS 1.1.1): the means and objects of knowledge, and the elements of inquiry and debate. The Bhāṣya explains that the latter are listed separately so that Nyāya is not merely a science of the self like the Upaniṣads.

relations.note: Nyāya's sixteen are topics of inquiry; the Vaiśeṣika categories are kinds of reals; NBh 1.1.9 admits the latter as further prameyas.

name: The sixteen parts of the person

definitions.definition: The person has sixteen parts (kalā), fifteen of which depend on food (ChU 6.7); in PrU 6 the sixteen parts arise from the person and vanish into him like rivers into the ocean, and he becomes partless and immortal; MuU 3.2.7 speaks of the fifteen parts going to their foundations.

checks.note: PrU 6, ChU 6.7 and MuU 3.2.7 ('gatāḥ kalāḥ pañcadaśa pratiṣṭhāḥ') are located. Fidelity note for Phase D: ChU 6.7 says a person has sixteen parts and that after a fifteen-day fast one part remained, revived by food. 'Fifteen of which depend on food' is an interpretive paraphrase, not the text's wording. All 3 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 6.7; PrU 6; MuU 3.2.7). It rests on 4 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Pure mind sevenfold (like Brahmā, the ṛṣis, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Gandharvas); rājasa sixfold (asura, rākṣasa, piśāca, serpent, preta, bird); tāmasa threefold (beast, fish, plant) (Ca Śā 4.37-40; Su Śā 4.81-98).

name: The sixty-four Bhairava tantras
members: Bhairavāṣṭaka: Svacchanda, Bhairava, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Asitāṅga, Mahocchuṣma, Kapālīśa
Yāmalāṣṭaka: Brahma-, Viṣṇu-, Svacchanda-, Ruru-, (5th unnamed), Ātharvaṇa-, Rudra-, Vetāla-yāmala
Matāṣṭaka: Rakta, Lampaṭa, Lakṣmīmata, (Mata?), Cālikā, Piṅgala, Utphullaka, Viśvādya
Maṅgalāṣṭaka: Bhairavī (Picu, twofold), (3rd unnamed), Brāhmī Kalā, Vijayā, Candrā, Maṅgalā, Sarvamaṅgalā
Cakrāṣṭaka: Mantra-, Varṇa-, Śakti-, Kalā-, Bindu-, Nāda-, Guhya-, Kha-cakra
Bahurūpāṣṭaka: Andhaka, Rurubheda, Aja, Mūla, Varṇabhaṇṭha, Viḍaṅga, Jvālin, Mātṛrodana
Vāgīśāṣṭaka: Bhairavī, Citrikā, Haṃsā, Kadambikā, Hṛllekhā, Candralekhā, Vidyullekhā, Vidyumān
Śikhāṣṭaka: Bhairavī Śikhā, Vīṇā, Vīṇāmaṇi, Sammoha, Ḍāmara, Atharvaka, Kabandha, Śiraścheda
notes: Checked against Jayaratha's quotation in the local Tantrāloka e-text; three slots are unnamed or unclear in the quoted text. Surviving texts include the Svacchanda (1), Brahmayāmala (2), Jayadrathayāmala (= Śiraścheda, 8); the Vīṇāśikha and Sammoha belong to the Vāma stream.

definitions.definition: The Śrīkaṇṭhīya's eight groups of eight (Bhairava, Yāmala, Mata, Maṅgala, Cakra, Bahurūpa, Vāgīśa, Śikhā), each group 'spoken' by one of the Bhairavas; together 'the wheel of Sadāśiva'.
The 'eight times eight' of Śiva's teaching, dominated by non-duality.

name: The sixty-four tantras of the Śākta lists

relations.note: different lists of 'sixty-four', overlapping only partly (e.g. Kāmika, Vātula, Candrajñāna and Sarvajñānottara appear here, Siddhānta titles in the Śaiva lists)

definitions.definition: The Vāmakeśvara's sixty-four tantras 'of the Mothers' (Mahāmāyā, Śambara … Viśuddheśvara), by which, the Saundaryalaharī says, Paśupati beguiled the world before revealing the Goddess's own tantra; Lakṣmīdhara judges them Kaula and non-Vedic.

The Saundaryalaharī says Paśupati beguiled the world with sixty-four tantras aimed at particular powers, then at the Goddess's insistence brought down her tantra, which alone accomplishes all aims (SL 31).

name: The sixty-four yoginīs and their temples

definitions.definition: A circle of sixty-four yoginī goddesses worshipped in open-roofed circular temples of c. 9th–11th c. — Hirapur and Ranipur-Jharial (Odisha), Bheraghat near Jabalpur, Mitaoli (Morena), Khajuraho (rectangular) and others; the yoginīs are the Kula's transmitters (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.11-15). Their name-lists differ widely between texts.

notes: Temple locations and dates are historical metadata (moderate confidence); the yoginī name-lists are not reproduced.

name: The sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs and the nine groups of devotees

definitions.definition: The canonical company of Śiva's devotees: 63 individual saints and 9 groups (tokai aṭiyār), first listed in Cuntarar's Tiruttoṇṭattokai (Tēvāram 7.39), expanded by Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi and told at length in Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam; their images stand in Tamil Śiva temples and their days are kept as festivals. Their stories teach that love and service of Śiva and his devotees, not birth, learning or rite, win his grace; they include kings, brahmins, merchants, farmers, a hunter, a potter, a washerman, a fisherman, an outcaste, women and a former Buddhist.

members: (groups) Tillaivāḻ antaṇar — the brahmins of Tillai
Poyyaṭimai illāta pulavar — poets without false servitude
Pattarāyp paṇivār — those who bow as devotees
Paramaṉaiyē pāṭuvār — those who sing only of the Supreme
Cittattaic civaṉpālē vaittār — those who fixed their minds on Śiva
Tiruvārūrp piṟantār — those born in Tiruvārūr
Muppōtum tirumēṉi tīṇṭuvār — those who touch the holy image thrice daily (the priests)
Muḻuniṟu pūciya muṉivar — sages smeared wholly with ash
Appālum aṭicārntār — those beyond, who reached his feet
notes: Order follows the Periya Purāṇam as usually given (moderate confidence); the nine groups' names are given at moderate confidence.

definitions.definition: In each half-cycle: 24 Tīrthaṅkaras, 12 world-emperors (Bharata, Sagara, Maghavā, Sanatkumāra, Śānti, Kunthu, Ara, Subhūma, Mahāpadma, Hariṣeṇa, Jayasena, Brahmadatta), 9 baladevas (the eighth is Rāma, the ninth Balarāma), 9 vāsudevas (Tripṛṣṭha … Lakṣmaṇa, Kṛṣṇa) and 9 prativāsudevas (Aśvagrīva … Rāvaṇa, Jarāsandha).

relations.note: the Jain universal history re-tells figures of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata (Rāma, Kṛṣṇa) inside its own scheme

name: The sixty-two grounds for views (Brahmajāla)

definitions.definition: All speculation about the past (18: eternalism 4, partial eternalism 4, finite/infinite 4, eel-wriggling 4, chance origin 2) and the future (44: percipient 16, non-percipient 8, neither 8, annihilation 7, nibbāna here and now 5) falls within sixty-two grounds; each is conditioned by contact and craving, and the Tathāgata knows them and what is beyond them.

The theories about the past (eternalism, partial eternalism, finitude, eel-wriggling, chance origin) and the future (percipient, non-percipient, neither, annihilation, nibbāna here and now) listed in the Brahmajāla; all arise from contact and craving (DN 1).

relations.note: the Buddhist and Jain canons each catalogue all rival views, in different frames

notes: U36 owns the Brahmajāla Sutta; this unit supplies the view entries.

name: Skambha, the frame of the world

definitions.definition: The pillar or frame in which tapas, ṛta, vows, faith and truth abide and on which the worlds rest; identified with the highest Brahman to which homage is paid (AVŚ 10.7–8); cf. the One that propped apart the six regions (RV 1.164.6).

The buddhas' and bodhisattvas' adaptation of teaching and conduct to beings: three vehicles for one, parinirvāṇa displayed by an eternal Buddha, the householder-sage who visits brothels, the conjured city; paired with wisdom as the bodhisattva's two wings.
Both dissolve the mind, but in sleep it dissolves into tamas and does not liberate; in samādhi the world dissolves into the witness-consciousness (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 2.3).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: Soma is the plant pressed in the sacrifice, the exhilarating drink that makes the drinkers say 'we have become immortal, we have gone to the light' (RV 8.48.3), the god purifying himself through the filter (book 9), bringer of bliss (9.113.6); set in heaven by ṛta (10.85.1).

relations.note: The Ṛgveda itself distinguishes the pressed plant from the soma the brahmins know (10.85.3).

definitions.definition: For stream-entry: association with good persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, practice in accordance (SN 55.5); of the stream-enterer: confirmed confidence in the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha and the virtues dear to the noble ones — the mirror of the Dhamma (DN 16).
The soul is neither Real (like Śiva) nor unreal (like the changing world) but between, taking the nature of what it joins; it knows only when made to know.

name: Sound, light and rays (sgra 'od zer gsum)

definitions.definition: The three forms in which the ground's display first appears; in the bardo of dharmatā they arise again as the thunderous sound of dharmatā, lights and rays, to be recognized as self-display.

name: Sound as a non-eternal quality of ākāśa

definitions.definition: Sound has a beginning and is sense-perceived, hence non-eternal (NS 2.2.13ff.).

Sound is the mark of ākāśa, produced by conjunction, disjunction and sound (VS 2.1.24–27, 2.2.36–37 C); it is inarticulate or phonemic (Tarkasaṅgraha); later authors explain its travel to the ear on the model of waves or of kadamba buds.

notes: The wave / kadamba-bud models are recalled from later manuals.

definitions.definition: The Veda, the smṛti and conduct of those who know it, the practice of the good, and what satisfies oneself (MDh 2.6, 2.12); with desire born of right intention (YS 1.7); where texts are silent, the agreement of the knowers and of a learned assembly (ĀpDh 1.1.1.2; MDh 12.108–113); dharma is what the Āryas praise (ĀpDh 1.7.20.6–7); the rest may be learned from women and all classes (ĀpDh 2.11.29.15).

definitions.definition: The ultimate as dynamic, pulsing awareness - opening and closing (unmeṣa-nimeṣa) - on which all particular movements rest, never lost in any state, and graspable in intense moments and in the gap between thoughts.

relations.note: spanda read as vimarśa

name: The special qualities of the self (ātma-viśeṣaguṇa)

definitions.definition: Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit and demerit — eight special qualities of the self alone (Tarkasaṅgraha); memory-impression also resides only in the self; liberation is their cessation (Praśastapāda, as usually summarized).

The word is a partless, sequence-less entity distinct from the sounds that manifest it; the sounds plant seeds in the intellect and with the last sound the sphoṭa is grasped; the sentence-sphoṭa is finally the only real one (VP 1.44, 1.73; Mahābhāṣya on P 1.1.70; VBhS sphoṭa-nirṇaya).
Rejected: the letters themselves (through their impressions) convey the meaning; a separate sphoṭa is unperceived and superfluous (Upavarṣa in Śabara; ŚV sphoṭavāda).

relations.note: the sphoṭa at its fullest is the sentence

name: The Lord's eternal abode (dhāma: Goloka, Vraja)

definitions.definition: Goloka/Vraja, made of wish-fulfilling gems, is Kṛṣṇa's highest abode above Vaikuṇṭha; the earthly Vraja (Vṛndāvana, Govardhana, Rādhākuṇḍa) is non-different from it.
Vraja and Gokul as the site of the Lord's eternal play into which grace admits the soul.
The luminous nature of the ground in which lights, kāyas and qualities are present without effort; brought out in direct crossing.

name: The cycle of rites for the dead

definitions.definition: Cremation; ten days of piṇḍa and water (building the preta-body); the eleventh-day rites (vṛṣotsarga, the 'middle sixteen'); sapiṇḍīkaraṇa on the twelfth day or later; monthly śrāddhas through the first year (feeding the traveller on Yama's road); the annual śrāddha; periods of impurity for the kin.

definitions.definition: Faith kindles the fire and makes the offering; it is invoked morning, noon and evening (RV 10.151); against doubters, 'have faith in him' (2.12.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 7.21–22; 9.3, 9.23: whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, the Lord makes that faith unwavering, and through it the worshipper obtains desires ordained by the Lord; those without faith in this dharma return to saṃsāra; devotees of other deities worship with faith, and so worship the Lord, but not according to rule.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

name: The five means: faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi, insight

definitions.definition: For yogins samādhi is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi and insight (YS 1.20); Vyāsa: each arises from the previous — faith (serenity of mind, protecting the yogin like a kind mother), energy, mindfulness, concentration of the unagitated mind, and the discernment of insight by which one knows the thing as it is (YBh 1.20).

The means by which samādhi arises for yogins (1.20): faith (serenity of mind, protecting like a mother), from which energy, from which mindfulness, with which the mind is concentrated, to which discerning insight comes; from its practice and dispassion, asamprajñāta (YBh 1.20).
