relations.standpoint: as a list of five qualities leading to samādhi and insight
relations.note: Same five names as the Buddhist indriya/bala (saddhā, viriya, sati, samādhi, paññā); Vyāsa gives them as a causal sequence ending in asamprajñāta samādhi.

name: Śramaṇa and brāhmaṇa

definitions.definition: The two orders of religious men: the śramaṇa, who has gone forth, and the brāhmaṇa by birth and ritual; grammar gives 'śramaṇa-brāhmaṇa' as the type of perpetual enmity, and Aśoka finds both everywhere and urges concord between sects.
A true samaṇa or brāhmaṇa is made by conduct — calm, harmlessness, putting away evil — not by birth, shaving or rites.
One is a śramaṇa by equanimity, a brāhmaṇa by celibacy, and a brāhmaṇa or kṣatriya by deeds.

relations.note: the śramaṇa critique of sacrifice is one side of the contrast

notes: The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka already calls the wind-girdled Vedic seers śramaṇas (tea:taittiriya-aranyaka:2.7.1) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka mentions the śramaṇa (tea:brhadaranyaka-upanisad:4.3.22).

definitions.definition: Wanderers of all sects met in debating halls and parks to compare teachers; the reports of the six teachers come from such debate (SN 44.9, MN 36, MN 77, Snp 3.6).

Dvaita: hearing, reflection, meditation and devotion are the principal means to knowledge; meditation, not a mere subsidiary of hearing, produces the direct realization by which the Lord is pleased; hearing and the rest must never be reduced.
The threefold discipline of the qualified seeker (BĀU 2.4.5): hearing removes doubt about the means (scripture's purport), reflection doubt about the object, contemplation contrary habitual notions.
Hearing is principal, the other two auxiliaries.
Contemplation is principal; the purified mind is the instrument.

relations.note: meditation built on hearing produces direct realization

name: The 'Śreṇika heresy' (eternal mind-nature in a perishing body)

definitions.definition: The view, reported of certain southern teachers, that the knowing nature is permanent and leaves the perishing body at death; Nanyang Huizhong equates it with the heretic Śreṇika.
Dōgen rejects it: body and mind are one, nature and form not two.

relations.note: Chan distinguishes buddha-nature from an eternal self.

definitions.definition: The good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both approach a person; the wise examines and chooses the good, the fool the pleasant for getting and keeping (KU 1.2.1-2); Naciketas is praised for refusing the pleasant (KU 1.1.21-29).

checks.note: All 2 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (KU 1.2.1-2; KU 1.1.21-29). It rests on 2 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: The nature and rank of Śrī

definitions.definition: Śrī is the Lord's inseparable consort, mother of the world and mediator.
All-pervading (vibhu) like Viṣṇu, of the Lord's rank (Īśvara-koṭi), with him the means and the goal; the couple is one object of refuge.
The mediator (puruṣakāra), not the means; commonly reported as atomic and of the rank of souls (jīva-koṭi), though never separate from the Lord.

Four upward Śiva triangles and five downward Śakti triangles interlock around the central point to make forty-three angles, surrounded by eight and sixteen petals, three circles and a square of three lines (SL 11); it arises as the supreme Śakti beholds her own vibrancy (YH 1.9-10) and is ninefold with nine mantras (YH 1.13); it is the Goddess's dwelling (LSN 182) and the body itself (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
For the Samayins it is worshipped within and is the moon-disc in the crown (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10).

name: Śrīkula and Kālīkula

definitions.definition: The two great families of Śākta tantra: the Śrīkula centred on Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā) and the Kālīkula centred on Kālī and related goddesses.

notes: Kālīkula is treated in U24.

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu → Śrī → Viṣvaksena → Nammāḻvār → Nāthamuni → Uyyakkoṇḍār → Maṇakkāl Nambi → Yāmuna → Periya Nambi → Rāmānuja.
Rāmānuja → Embār → Parāśara Bhaṭṭar → Nañjīyar → Nampiḷḷai → Vaṭakku Tiruvīti Piḷḷai → Piḷḷai Lokācārya → Tiruvāymoḻi Piḷḷai → Maṇavāḷa Māmuni.
Rāmānuja → Tirukkurukaippirāṉ Piḷḷāṉ → Engaḷāḻvāṉ → Naḍādūr Ammāḷ → Ātreya Rāmānuja (Appuḷḷār) → Vedānta Deśika.

name: The conduct of the Śrīvidyā initiate

definitions.definition: No censure of other schools or persons, secrecy toward the unqualified, constant immersion in Śiva-hood, avoidance of the six passions, unsanctioned violence and theft, worship of one guru without doubt, non-possessiveness, action without regard to fruit, fearlessness (PKS 1.14-25); inwardly Śākta, outwardly Śaiva, among people Vaiṣṇava (Kaula Upaniṣad).

The cakra — the universe of thirty-six principles — arises when the supreme Śakti beholds her own vibrancy (YH 1.9-10); the Goddess transforms herself into mind and the elements (SL 35); she arose from the fire-altar of consciousness (LSN 1).
Paraśiva's light reflected in the mirror of vimarśa becomes the great point, whence the 'I' and the world of word and meaning (KKV 4-7).
The Goddess alone existed in the beginning and produced the egg and the gods (Bahvṛca Upaniṣad).

name: The fifteen- and sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā (structure only)

definitions.definition: The Pañcadaśī has fifteen syllables in three sections, each closed by the seed called hṛllekhā (SL 32); a further seed added makes the sixteen-syllable Ṣoḍaśī (LSN 118); in the Kādi form the first section begins with 'ka', in the Hādi form with 'ha'; the Triśatī unfolds the fifteen syllables in three hundred names. Syllables are deliberately not recorded here.

The Yoginīhṛdaya is to be guarded with special care (YH 1.2); the Veda is public like a courtesan while this vidyā is hidden in all the schools (PKS 1.30); secrets are told only to a worthy disciple (PKS 1.16; Kaula Upaniṣad); exposure of the Kaula worship leads to hell (PKS 1.12); 'secret' finally means the identity of self and supreme (Bhāskararāya).

The guru is the Śakti that is the cause of all (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad); one guru is worshipped without doubt (PKS 1.20); the teaching is given only to a worthy disciple (PKS 1.16); at initiation the guru makes the disciple his own self (PKS 1.42); those without lineage who are proud of book-knowledge are harmed (YH 2.81).

As many channels as there are embodied kinds of things; thirteen named, with roots and signs of vitiation; for the mind the whole conscious body is the channel (Ca Vi 5.3-7); vitiation is excess flow, obstruction, knotting or wrong course (Vi 5.22).

relations.note: the yogic nāḍīs are channels of breath and energy; Caraka lists nāḍī only as a synonym of srotas

definitions.definition: Before creation Nārāyaṇa alone exists, holding all souls in himself with their awareness quiescent, with Lakṣmī; he creates, as his sport, so that embodied souls may reach happiness, sorrow or the mean according to their natures; creation is the real transformation of prakṛti under his control (not of Brahman itself), unfolding into the uncompounded principles and the cosmic egg.

name: Creation and dissolution as the Lord's play

definitions.definition: Creation, maintenance and dissolution are the Lord's play (līlā) in the realm of prakṛti: he creates to give souls bodies to work out karma and seek him; Brahmā and Śiva are souls whom he empowers; the eternal realm is untouched by these cycles.

name: Creation and dissolution within the body

definitions.definition: Creation and dissolution take place in the body: the fourteen worlds are principles within it; dissolution runs from action into knowledge and will and into the light of Śiva; enjoyment is below, liberation above (KJN 2.4–9); the supreme is that from which all arises and into which all returns like rivers to the sea (14.101).

name: Śruti, svara and grāma

definitions.definition: Twenty-two śrutis arising in channels at the heart; seven notes arising from them; two (or three) grāmas; demonstrated on two vīṇās (ŚR 1.3.7–25; NŚ 28).

members: 7 svaras (sa ri ga ma pa dha ni)

name: The four stages of sensory cognition

definitions.definition: Sensory cognition proceeds by apprehension, speculation, determination and retention (TS 1.15), each over twelve kinds of object (1.16).

name: The stages of love from prema to mahābhāva

definitions.definition: prema → sneha → māna → praṇaya → rāga → anurāga → bhāva/mahābhāva (rūḍha, adhirūḍha: modana, mādana).

name: The states of beings that arise from the Lord (BhG 10.4–5)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Twenty states (bhāva) of beings, in their several kinds, arise from the Lord alone: understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forbearance, truth, restraint, calm, pleasure and pain, coming-to-be and not-being, fear and fearlessness, non-harming, evenness, contentment, austerity, giving, fame and ill-fame (10.4–5).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The text does not say how they arise from him; commentators add 'according to the beings' karma'. Not the Sāṃkhya eight bhāvas.

name: Waking, dream and dreamless sleep (Mīmāṃsā view)

definitions.definition: Dreams present real objects of other times and places, remembered through impressions awakened by the unseen and taken as present by a sleep-affected mind; release resembles dreamless sleep in having no cognition, but without return.
In dreamless sleep the self is not manifest, since there is no cognition.

Puruṣa witnesses deep sleep and other states (SS 1.148); in concentration (samādhi), deep sleep and liberation puruṣa has the form of Brahman — in the first two with seed, in liberation with the seed destroyed (SS 5.116–117). The SK itself does not analyse waking, dream and sleep.

Mental consciousness does not arise among the non-perceiving gods, in the attainments of non-perception and of cessation, in deep dreamless sleep and in fainting; in these the store-consciousness continues.

name: Authority: the Veda, the āptas and the saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The authoritative scripture is the Veda and teachings not contrary to it by examiners approved of the learned (Ca Sū 11.27); the āptas are free of rajas and tamas (11.18); Vāgbhaṭa both calls his text to be applied 'like a mantra, not to be questioned' (Utt 40.81) and asks that what is well said be accepted whoever says it (Utt 40.86-88).

Disparaging women, who are of the nature of wisdom, is the fourteenth root downfall; the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa praises women; women siddhas (Lakṣmīṅkarā, Mekhalā, Kanakhalā, Maṇibhadrā, Niguma, Sukhasiddhi) teach.

name: Sacred places and relics of the incarnations

definitions.definition: Places the incarnations visited and objects they touched carry their presence and are venerated.

name: The fixed and the moving (sthāvara and jaṅgama)

definitions.definition: Temples, images and installed liṅgas are the fixed, which perish; the devotee's body and the wandering devotee are the moving, which endures and is the true temple; worship of stone while despising the living devotee is hypocrisy.

The SSM ranks worship on the palm above worship on a pedestal, the inner liṅga above stone liṅgas and calls those who cling only to the outer liṅga deluded, yet forbids using the nirmālya of fixed liṅgas and bids their protection.

relations.note: the iṣṭaliṅga replaces the temple liṅga

name: The person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Asked for the marks of one of steady wisdom established in samādhi (2.54), Kṛṣṇa describes one who gives up all desires and is content in the self by the self (2.55); is unshaken by sorrow, without craving in pleasure, free from passion, fear and anger (2.56); unattached, neither rejoicing nor hating (2.57); withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.58), the taste itself ceasing on seeing the highest (2.59); sits yoked, intent on Kṛṣṇa, senses mastered (2.61, 2.68); moves among objects with mastered senses and attains serenity (2.64–65); is awake where beings sleep (2.69); is filled by desires like the ocean yet unmoved (2.70); without 'mine' and 'I' attains peace (2.71). This is the brahmic state, reached which even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72).

One who has given up the desires of the mind and is content in the self, unagitated in sorrow and pleasure, senses withdrawn, awake where beings sleep, unmoved as the ocean, in the brāhmī state (BhG 2.54–72); with close parallels in the devotee dear to the Lord (12.13–20) and the one beyond the guṇas (14.22–25).

Bhagavad Gītā 5.20 describes the knower of Brahman in the same terms as the steady-wise of 2.54–72: not elated by the pleasant nor agitated by the unpleasant, steady in intellect (sthira-buddhi), undeluded, established in Brahman.

members: gives up all desires; content in the self by the self (2.55)
unshaken in sorrow, without craving in pleasure; free from passion, fear, anger (2.56)
withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.58)
even the taste ceases on seeing the highest (2.59)
awake in the night of beings (2.69)

relations.note: abiding in this state even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa
the description is of one liberated in this life as the Advaita commentators read it; the Gītā itself does not use 'jīvanmukti'

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

name: Stillness, movement and awareness (gnas 'gyu rig gsum)

definitions.definition: The three aspects examined in Mahāmudrā vipaśyanā: the mind at rest, the mind moving as thought, and the awareness that knows both; seeing that they are not different is the recognition of mind's nature.

Standard images used to teach non-duality: rope-snake, shell-silver, pot-space, the reflection of the sun, dream, clay and pots, the tenth man, the crystal and the red flower, the potter's wheel, the firebrand, the mirror-city, the theatre lamp, the painted canvas.

name: Women's dharma (strīdharma), as the tradition states it

definitions.definition: Women are to be honoured, for where they are not all rites fail (MDh 3.56); a woman is to be under the protection of father, husband and sons (MDh 5.148; 9.3); a widow chooses chastity or (in some later texts) ascending the pyre (Viṣṇusmṛti 25.14); women are qualified for Śrauta rites with their husbands (KŚS 1.1.7); dharma may be learned from women (ĀpDh 2.11.29.15); an older tradition distinguishes women who study the Veda (brahmavādinī) from those who marry directly (sadyovadhū) (Hārīta, quoted).

notes: Recorded as stated in the texts; the Hārīta quotation is known only through later digests.

queries: Harita dharmasutra brahmavadini sadyovadhu two kinds of women quoted Smriticandrika
evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)
checks.note: The six cited passages were confirmed in teaching checks (MDh 3.56, 5.147–148, 9.3, ViSmṛ 25.14, KŚS 1.1.7, ĀpDh 2.11.29.15). The Hārīta quotation, which the entry notes, is also confirmed. Per Wisdomlib's Medhātithi on MDh 2.66 (notes) and Wikipedia's Brahmavādinī article, Hārīta distinguishes two kinds of women, brahmavādinī and sadyovadhū: the former receive upanayana, fire-keeping, Vedic study at home and alms. The verse is quoted in the Smṛticandrikā's saṃskāra section.

definitions.definition: Women can reach omniscience and liberation in a female body: the canon lists women among the fifteen kinds of siddhas, Mallī was a woman Tīrthaṅkara, Marudevī was the first liberated of this era, and nuns hold the great vows.
Affirmed with arguments: nothing in a woman opposes the three jewels; the garment is not possession; incapacity for the lowest hell does not imply incapacity for liberation.

Denied: a woman cannot give up clothing, lacks the strongest bodily constitution needed for pure meditation, and her body is a site of the generation of subtle beings; she can reach the fifth stage (a nun is ranked with advanced laity) and may be reborn as a man; canonical 'female siddhas' refers to psychological sex.

relations.note: the Digambara denial rests largely on the requirement of nudity

name: The five auspicious āgamas and the Samaya way

definitions.definition: Lakṣmīdhara's Vedic Samaya canon — the Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra saṃhitās — opposed to the 'mixed' Candrakalā group and the Kaula sixty-four.
The saṃhitās of Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra, teaching the Vedic Samaya way that Lakṣmīdhara follows (on SL 31); Bhāskararāya also calls them 'Samaya' (on LSN 37).

name: The auspicious support of the mind (śubhāśraya)

definitions.definition: The mind in yoga needs a support: Brahman in its formed and formless aspects; since the beginner cannot hold the formless, he meditates on Viṣṇu's form, the ground of all powers, which alone purifies (VP 6.7.45-78).

queries: rests_on teachings and cited refs located
checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

name: The subtle body across the families: differing counts of channels and centres

definitions.definition: Three principal channels (lalanā, rasanā, avadhūtī) among thirty-two; four (or five, six in the Kālacakra) wheels.
Six (or nine) centres, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids; the bulb below the navel from which 72,000 channels arise.
Eleven centres or kinds of inner knowledge in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya; the worlds located in the body as principles.
The Netra's six wheels, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids.
Word-based meditation places the vowels and consonants on lotuses at the navel, heart and mouth; the Jain texts do not teach the Śaiva centres as such.

notes: The counts differ by text and are not to be harmonized in the text layer; the map is interpretive.

name: The subtle body of the Netratantra

definitions.definition: Six wheels, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids (Netra 7.1), pierced in subtle meditation.

Dharma is hard to know: the hunter Balāka reaches heaven, the truth-telling Kauśika hell (MBh 8.49); the golden rule is its summary (13.114.8; 5.39.57); in distress other rules apply (12.139); the vulgate Yakṣapraśna says its truth is hidden in a cave.

name: Sudden and gradual (dun / jian)

definitions.definition: The Dharma has no sudden or gradual; people are sharp or dull; the deluded cultivate gradually, the awakened accord suddenly (Platform Sūtra); Shenxiu's verse is presented as gradual, Huineng's as sudden.
Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation (Shenhui as read by Zongmi).
Sudden awakening to principle with gradual removal of habit energies (Guishan).
Sudden awakening, gradual cultivation as the path of all sages (Jinul); contested by Seongcheol.

relations.note: The Indian/Pali gradual training is one of the positions the sudden teaching relativises.

notes: Debate owned by U50 as dsp:sudden-or-gradual; this concept records the Chan formulations.

definitions.definition: Brahman, pure of māyā, alone is; the world is its real form produced without change; souls are its parts; only saṃsāra is unreal.

relations.note: rejects māyā as the explanation of the world

name: Sudhana's spiritual friends (Gaṇḍavyūha)

definitions.definition: The good friends Sudhana visits, in the order of Vaidya's sections 3-56; Huayan maps them onto the stages of the path (fifty-three counting Mañjuśrī twice and Samantabhadra).

notes: List read from the section headings of the local Vaidya e-text (sections 3-56).

definitions.definition: Buddha-nature is luminosity-emptiness; it is not established as a self, nor is it a mere non-affirming negation; the qualities are present from the beginning, which is why the ground can be called primordially enlightened.

name: The Sun as the self of time and of beings

definitions.definition: The Sun is the self (ātman) of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 2.1), the self of all embodied beings, maker of time and the opened door of liberation (Yogayātrā 1.1), the path of those not reborn and the self of the self-knowers (BJ 1.1), the Hiraṇyagarbha, the 'self of time and maker of time' whose chariot-wheel is the year (SS 12.15–19).

name: Sun, moon and fire in the body

definitions.definition: The moon at the palate rains nectar, the sun at the navel devours it; the three channels have moon, sun and fire as deities; the reversed practice turns sun above and moon below (GŚ 23, 55–59; AmŚ 71).

The moon in the head (or at the palate) rains nectar; the sun/fire at the navel swallows it, and so the body ages and dies (HYP 3.77; GŚ 55–58; SS 2.6–12; Amṛtasiddhi); iḍā is the moon and left, piṅgalā the sun and right; sun and moon create time, which suṣumnā devours (HYP 4.17); haṭha is the union of ha (sun) and ṭha (moon) (Yogabīja; Jyotsnā). The Śiva Svarodaya reads the alternation of the nostrils as the flow of moon and sun.

name: The void (śūnya) as shared vocabulary of different referents

definitions.definition: The word śūnya/śūnyatā runs through Buddhist, Nāth, haṭha, Vīraśaiva and Sant language but names different things: for the Madhyamaka, the absence of own-nature in all dharmas; in the Buddhist completion stage, four graded 'empties' leading to clear light; in the haṭha texts, the central channel (śūnyapadavī) and the voids pierced in the four stages; for the Nāths and Allama, the fullness beyond the mind; for the Sants, the sky-circle where the Name resounds.

relations.note: Madhyamaka emptiness is a negation of own-nature, not a place or state reached in the body
Buddhist completion-stage series

name: The void (śūnya, bayalu) in Allama Prabhu

definitions.definition: Allama names the ultimate as the void — bayalu, open space without enclosure — in which liṅga, aṅga and every attainment cease to be two; his tests of the other śaraṇas in the Śūnyasampādane bring each attainment to this void.

notes: Needs anchoring in specific vacanas in Phase D.

definitions.definition: In the HYP suṣumnā is 'the path of the void' (3.4); the breath dissolves in the void when śakti wakes (4.10–12); the nāda stages pass through śūnya, atiśūnya and mahāśūnya (4.70–75); 'empty within, empty without, like a pot in space; full within, full without, like a pot in the ocean' (4.56); samādhi is 'void and not void' (śūnyāśūnya, 4.3).

The void is the path of the breath become a royal road (HYP 3.3); the mind 'void of void' (KJN 14.84); the principle known as supportless and without elaboration (GŚ 92); kuṇḍalinī is the pedestal of the liṅga of the void (Jñāneśvarī 6.273).

relations.note: Allama's void is dissolution in the liṅga, which the Vīraśaivas set above Gorakṣa's perfected body

definitions.definition: Every dharma is empty of own-nature because it arises dependently; emptiness is dependent origination, a dependent designation and the middle way (MMK 24.18); it is not a further entity and is itself empty (13.7–8).
The mere absence of own-nature, a non-implicative negation, in persons and phenomena alike (PsP 24.18; MA 6).
The lack of own-nature shown by the absence of true unity and plurality (MAL 1).

relations.note: MMK 24.18 names emptiness and dependent origination as one
the Madhyamaka systematizes the sūtras' emptiness
Madhyamaka refuses to take emptiness as a positive ground; Advaita's Brahman is a positive reality
the Nāth 'void' is a state or ground to be realized; Madhyamaka's emptiness is the absence of own-nature
elaboration ceases in emptiness (MMK 18.5)

name: The superiority of the mantra way

definitions.definition: Same goal as the perfection way, but superior in being unconfused, rich in means, without hardship and for the sharp-witted.

name: Bondage as support, liberation as supportless

definitions.definition: Dharma rests on the mind; what rests on dharma and adharma is bondage; support (āśraya) is bondage, liberation is supportless (Jñānakārikā 1.14–16; 2.24–28).
Everything about the Buddhas is beyond the world: conduct, merit, postures, body, robes, food, even the fleshly eye.
Tathāgatas are supramundane and without outflows; their body, power and lifespan are limitless; they never sleep and are always in concentration (Vasumitra).
Rejects that the Buddha did not live in the human world (Kv 18.1).

The soul is surat, a drop of the ocean of the Supreme, a current of attention now scattered through the body and the senses; gathered at the eye centre it rises on the sound; with nirat (the seeing faculty) it hears and sees within.

name: Union of the soul with the sound current (surat-śabd)

definitions.definition: The soul (surat) joins the sound current (śabd) at the eye centre and is drawn up by it through the regions to its source — the principle of surat-śabd yoga.

relations.note: Both teach absorption through successive inner sounds; the Sant Mat sounds are assigned to regions and the goal is beyond sound.

name: Surrender to the Lord (śaraṇāgati / prapatti)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.14, 7.19, 7.29; 9.32: those who take refuge in the Lord alone cross his guṇa-made māyā; the knower takes refuge after many births knowing 'Vāsudeva is all'; those who take refuge strive for release from old age and death; whoever takes refuge — even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras — reaches the highest goal. Evil-doers of demonic disposition do not take refuge (7.15).
Taking refuge in the Lord alone, who frees from all sins (BhG 18.66); those who take refuge cross his māyā (7.14); Rāma protects anyone who comes once for refuge (Rāmāyaṇa 6.18.33).

Bhagavad Gītā 15.4: after cutting the aśvattha, the place of no return is to be sought with the words 'I take refuge (prapadye) in that very primal person from whom the ancient activity flowed forth'.
Nothing in me is mine; giving back to the Lord what is his costs nothing; saying 'you, you' the 'I' disappears.
Surrender to the Master's will (mauj) and acceptance of pralabdh karma as his gift.
The helpless prayer to be taken across by the merciful one.

Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, combining extractor A's cpt:surrender-to-the-lord and extractor B's cpt:prapatti. The verbs are pra-√pad (7.14, 7.15, 7.19, 7.20), ā-√śri (7.29) and vy-apa-ā-√śri (9.32).

definitions.definition: (Jayanta's report) Refined Cārvākas who hold the number of means of knowledge unfixable and grant a knower lasting as long as the body; distinct from the 'rogue' Cārvāka and the old teachers of bhūta-caitanya.

The middle channel between iḍā and piṅgalā, blocked by kuṇḍalinī and by impurities; when purified and opened the breath enters it, the mind becomes steady (manonmanī) and time is 'devoured' (HYP 2.41–42, 3.3, 4.17); synonyms: śūnyapadavī, brahmarandhra, mahāpatha, śmaśāna, śāmbhavī, madhyamārga (3.4); within it lie vajrā, citriṇī and the brahmanāḍī (SS 2.18; ṢCN 1–2).

name: The perfection vehicle and the mantra vehicle

definitions.definition: Awakening is accomplished relying on both secret mantra and the perfections; Atiśa's conduct texts explain only the perfection side.
The two Mahāyāna vehicles share the same view of emptiness; mantra is superior through deity yoga, the union of method and wisdom in one consciousness, and so is faster.
Only the sūtras are authoritative; the Abhidharma treatises are works of named disciples.
The soul abiding in its own faith, knowledge and conduct is sva-samaya; identified with karmic matter and its states it is para-samaya; the whole path is the return from the second to the first.

Own-nature would be unfabricated and independent (MMK 15.1–2); since everything is produced by causes and conditions, nothing has it, and without own-nature there is no other-nature, existence or non-existence (15.3–6).

relations.note: own-nature of dharmas is the Abhidharma notion under examination

definitions.definition: Pervasion rests on a real relation of causality or identity between reason and property, not on repeated observation.
(As reported) The variety of things is from own-nature, not from an unseen cause or a creator.
One of five co-causes, wrong if held alone.
Souls and world are by their very nature both different and non-different from the Lord: different as dependent, atomic and limited; non-different as his powers without separate existence.
Yādavaprakāśa (as reported by Rāmānuja): Brahman itself naturally transforms into Īśvara, souls and matter, and so is both one and many by nature.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's own dharma as a kṣatriya is to fight a battle in accordance with dharma, the best thing for a kṣatriya and an open door to heaven; abandoning it incurs sin and disgrace (2.31–37). One's own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's well performed; death in it is better; another's brings fear (3.35).

The duty arising from one's own nature and station, to be done even if imperfect in preference to another's (BhG 3.35, 18.47); by it, as worship of the Lord, one reaches perfection (18.46); the meat-seller holds his inherited work as his dharma (MBh 3.198).

The duty of one's class and stage, better imperfect than another's done well (MDh 10.97); each class's work is its austerity (MDh 11.235); following it brings heaven and endlessness (Arthaśāstra 1.3.14) and a good rebirth (ĀpDh 2.1.2.2–3).

relations.note: Kṛṣṇa's argument from svadharma answers Arjuna's argument from family dharma.

definitions.definition: The particular is momentary, causally efficacious, ultimately real, inexpressible and known by perception; the universal is a conceptual exclusion, conventionally real, known by inference and words.
Tukārām received the mantra from Bābājī Caitanya in a dream; Bahiṇābāī and Niḷobā received Tukārām's initiation in dreams; the dream-guru is fully a guru.
Hita Harivaṃśa received his mantra from Rādhā herself, not from a human guru.
Consciousness reveals itself without being an object of another cognition; defined by Citsukha.

The Śiva Svarodaya's teaching that the breath flows by turns through the left (moon), right (sun) or both (suṣumnā) nostrils, that actions should match the flow, that suṣumnā's flow suits only meditation, and that the flow foretells events and death.

The fruit of rites for 'one desiring heaven', understood wherever no fruit is stated; the word denotes happiness (prīti) itself (Śabara); later described as happiness unmixed with sorrow, not followed by loss.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Heaven as the reward of the warrior slain in a dharmic battle (2.32, 2.37), and as the aim of the ritual-minded criticised in 2.43.

Bhagavad Gītā 9.20–21: those versed in the three Vedas, soma-drinkers purified of sin, worship with sacrifices and pray for heaven; they reach the world of the lord of the gods and enjoy the gods' divine pleasures, but when their merit is exhausted they re-enter the world of mortals — 'going and coming'. 8.16: the worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Each soul's innate, beginningless fitness fixes its class, office, the form of worship and vision open to it and its final destiny; it cannot be altered, and to aim beyond it leads to a fall.

Every cognition is aware of itself; this self-awareness is a perception and is the result of the means of knowledge; memory of the cognition proves it had two appearances (of itself and of the object).
The self-witnessing part of cognition (Cheng weishi lun); for Sthiramati the only real part.
Consciousness is self-illuminating because it is not inert; accepted conventionally (MAL 16–17).
Refuted: mind does not see mind, as a blade does not cut itself (BCA 9.17ff); memory does not prove reflexive awareness (MA 6.72–77).
Balanced doṣas, fire, tissues, wastes and functions, with a clear self, senses and mind (Su Sū 15.41).

relations.note: the same state described by its components

definitions.definition: Dvaita: validity is intrinsic and is grasped by the witness; reasoning only removes doubts in a defective intellect; invalidity is extrinsic.
The Mādhyamika must state formal inferences with reason and example, qualified 'ultimately' (Bhāviveka, PP 1).
Not appropriate for one who has no position of his own (PsP 1).
Reality is twofold: the independent, Viṣṇu alone, and the dependent — everything else — which exists, knows and acts only under his control; knowing this frees one from saṃsāra.
The absolute freedom of consciousness, its primary sovereignty, by which it manifests, conceals and reveals (ĪPK 1.5.13; PH 1).
The liberated renouncer's freedom from rule (Nirvāṇa; Avadhūta 33), qualified in the Avadhūta by the option of acting by scripture for the world's good.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 3 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: The island north of the milk ocean where the white, one-pointed devotees dwell and Nārāyaṇa reveals himself (MBh 12.323.23–26; Nārada's visit 12.321–326).

name: The Śvetāmbara canon of forty-five Āgamas

definitions.definition: Eleven Aṅgas, twelve Upāṅgas, ten Prakīrṇakas, six Chedasūtras, four Mūlasūtras and two Cūlikāsūtras (Nandī, Anuyogadvāra), with the Kalpa Sūtra read as part of the Daśāśrutaskandha; the commentarial layers (niryukti, bhāṣya, cūrṇi, ṭīkā) are authoritative with them.

The Sthānakavāsīs accept thirty-two of these: 11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 4 Chedasūtras (Niśītha, Vyavahāra, Bṛhatkalpa, Daśāśrutaskandha), 4 Mūlasūtras (Uttarādhyayana, Daśavaikālika, Nandī, Anuyogadvāra) and the Āvaśyaka; not the Prakīrṇakas, the Mahāniśītha, the Jītakalpa or the Piṇḍa-/Ogha-niryukti.
The Terāpanthīs accept the same thirty-two as the Sthānakavāsīs.
The Digambaras accept none of these as authentic; the original Aṅgas are lost.

relations.note: the two sects' opposed views of what survives

notes: The count of 45 and the grouping are medieval; the Nandī uses the aṅga-praviṣṭa / aṅga-bāhya scheme instead.

definitions.definition: Sudharman, Jambū, Prabhava, Śayyambhava, Yaśobhadra, Sambhūtavijaya and Bhadrabāhu, Sthūlabhadra, Mahāgiri and Suhastin, and their branches down to Devarddhigaṇi, as in the Kalpa Sūtra and Nandī; the gacchas trace their paṭṭāvalīs from it.

Every predication is qualified by 'syāt' (in some respect); with respect to any attribute a thing admits seven predications: is, is not, is and is not, inexpressible, is and inexpressible, is not and inexpressible, is, is not and inexpressible (Āptamīmāṃsā 14, 104–105); statements presenting the whole belong to pramāṇa, partial ones to naya (Rājavārttika).

name: Śyāmā-saṅgīt: devotion to the Mother in song

definitions.definition: The Bengali Śākta songs of Rāmprasād and Kamalākānta address Kālī as Mother with intimacy — pleading, reproaching, claiming the child's right, using her name as protection, and seeing the world as her play; they draw on tantric imagery (the six centres, the cremation ground) but make devotion the path.
A as foremost of letters, unborn, the gate of all dharmas (Nāmasaṃgīti; Mahāvairocana; Hevajra); in Advayavajra's reading the 'a' of amanasikāra.

The unconditioned is taught under thirty-three names — the uninclined, taintless, truth, far shore, subtle, very hard to see, unaging, stable, undisintegrating, unmanifest, unproliferated, peaceful, deathless, sublime, auspicious, secure, destruction of craving, wonderful, amazing, unailing, nibbāna, unafflicted, dispassion, purity, freedom, unadhesive, island, shelter, asylum, refuge, destination (SN 43.12–44).

name: The Tājika system

definitions.definition: Annual horoscopy (varṣaphala) from the solar return, the progressed munthā, sensitive points (sahama) and sixteen aspect-yogas with Perso-Arabic names beginning with itthaśāla; standardized by Nīlakaṇṭha (1587).

notes: The sixteen names are recalled from memory and may be misspelled or misordered.

definitions.definition: (As reported) The soul is the body, bounded by the skin; it ends with the body; no soul can be drawn out of the body and shown.
Both 'soul is body' and 'soul is other than body' are extremes; the middle is dependent origination.
The soul is distinct from the body (Kesi's answer to Paesi).

relations.note: Jain and Brahmanical names for one identification of self with body

definitions.definition: When the world is full of wrongdoing, adverse conditions are transformed into the path by blaming self-cherishing, contemplating others' kindness, seeing appearances as the four bodies, and the four practices.
Taking on others' wrongdoing when harmed without cause (Thirty-Seven Practices 13).

name: Mind and senses in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: The four inner faculties (maṉam, putti, cittam, akaṅkāram) form a 'fourfold fort' to be seized; the five senses are thieves whose forest must be burnt (Kaṭuveḷi 14); the mind is a demon (akappēy) and a fish in a net, to be stilled.

relations.note: karaṇam 4 and pulaṉ 5 are among the 96

name: The self in the Siddhar songs (āṉmā, uyir)

definitions.definition: The soul (āṉmā, uyir) plays the body's play and leaves it to wither (Kaṭuveḷi 21); the house of nine openings is not 'I' (Pattirakiriyār 39); the seeker asks 'who am I, who are you' (225) and longs to stand as 'I am He' (219); to know oneself is to join the Lord (Kuṭampai 31).

Among the ninety-six principles: waking (cākkiram), dream (coppaṉam), deep sleep (cuḻutti), the fourth (turiyam) and beyond the fourth (turiyātītam). The songs add 'sleeping without sleeping' and the blissful awareness that needs no further knowledge (Kuṭampai 15).

relations.note: the same five names as in Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta

name: The ultimate in the Tamil Siddha songs (Civam, Parāparam, the Light, the open space)

definitions.definition: The Siddhars name the ultimate Civam, Parāparam, Paramporuḷ, the Light (cōti, parañcōti) and the open space (veṭṭa veḷi). It is within the body and everywhere, self-luminous, the undivided fullness (akaṇṭa paripūraṇam), identical with love (TM 270), beyond qualities and beyond what devotees can speak; it is found by inner knowledge and the guru's grace, not in stone images, temples or scripture.

relations.note: Tāyumāṉavar describes it as light, fullness of bliss and grace, close to the Vedāntic triad

name: The Tamil Veda (Nammāḻvār's works as the four Vedas)

definitions.definition: Nammāḻvār's four works are the four Vedas in Tamil — Tiruviruttam the Ṛg, Tiruvāciriyam the Yajus, Periya Tiruvantāti the Atharva, Tiruvāymoḻi the Sāman — and Tirumaṅkai's six works the six aṅgas; the Tiruvāymoḻi is the Tamil Upaniṣad.
The Āḻvārs call their Tamil the 'Tamil of wisdom' (ñāṉat tamiḻ) and promise the fruit of the Veda to those who recite their decads.

notes: The four-Veda / six-aṅga correspondence is the tradition's account; the source for it is recalled as the Śrīvaiṣṇava commentators and Deśika's Prabandhasāram, not located to a verse.

name: Subordinating another family's deities or founder

definitions.definition: Vajrapāṇi as Trailokyavijaya subdues Maheśvara and the worldly gods and gives them places in the maṇḍala; Heruka's taking of the twenty-four sites is told as the conversion of Bhairava's retinue.
Viṣṇu sends forth the Great Deluder, who teaches the daityas the doctrines of the naked and the red-robed ascetics so that they abandon the Veda.
The Maitrī tells that Bṛhaspati, in the form of Śukra, created a false knowledge for the asuras' destruction, and warns against the no-self doctrine's tricksters.
The Buddha appears as a Kula-Bhairava perfected by Tārā's mantra, the teacher of Vasiṣṭha.
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are retold as figures within the Jain universal history, subordinate to the Jinas.

name: The tanden (cinnabar field) in Zen practice

definitions.definition: The lower abdomen below the navel, where breath and energy are gathered in naikan; contemplated as one's original face and Pure Land (Hakuin).
Chan generally locates the ultimate in the mind, not in a subtle body; the Platform Sūtra treats the body as a city whose king is the nature.

notes: Chan texts have no system of channels and centres comparable to haṭha or tantra; Hakuin's tanden draws on Chinese medical and Daoist language.

name: How the tantric families place their scriptures relative to the Veda or sūtras

definitions.definition: The Śaiva scriptures are a higher revelation than the Veda, which they do not contradict but surpass; the Veda is the lower, common scripture.
The Pāñcarātra is praised above all śāstras as the brahmin among the classes; its defenders (Yāmuna) argue that it is Vedic in root and authoritative.
The mantra way shares the goal of the perfection vehicle but is superior by its many means, lack of difficulty and suitability for the sharp.
Jain mantra lore is held to derive from the lost Vidyānupravāda Pūrva, part of the Jina's own canon, not from outside.

name: Classifications of the tantras

definitions.definition: Indian classes: kriyā, caryā (ubhaya), yoga, yogottara / mahāyoga, yoganiruttara / yoginī (sources vary); the Tibetan fourfold kriyā–caryā–yoga–anuttarayoga with the later father / mother / non-dual subdivision; Nyingma's nine vehicles (outer three, inner three: mahāyoga, anuyoga, atiyoga).

notes: The Indian nomenclature varies across authors (e.g. five- or six-fold lists); the Tibetan fourfold scheme and the father/mother/non-dual labels are later and are labeled as such.

name: The shared grammar of tantric practice across the families

definitions.definition: Across the Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain tantras the same elements recur: initiation into a lineage and mantra; the mantra as the deity; the maṇḍala or yantra as the deity's seat and body; purification of the elements and installation of mantras on the body before worship; identification with the deity; the subtle body of channels and centres; the guru as the deity; secrecy and eligibility; and the twin aims of power (siddhi, bhukti) and liberation. Each family arranges them within its own view and goal.

The Mantramārga's ritual core: dīkṣā that destroys bonds, daily and occasional worship with nyāsa and bhūtaśuddhi, mantras as Śiva's body, and the sādhaka's pursuit of siddhis beside the liberation-seeker's path.
The Pāñcarātra saṃhitās, spoken by Nārāyaṇa, teach initiation, mantra, maṇḍala, nyāsa and temple worship as the means to reach the Lord; the Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya are called its three gems.
The Mantranaya adds to the Mahāyāna path consecration, the deity's maṇḍala and mantra, and yoga with the channels, winds and drops, holding it swifter than the perfection vehicle.

Jain mantra-kalpas (Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa, Jvālāmālinī-kalpa) teach the worship of the Jinas' attendant goddesses with seed syllables, yantras, body-protection and the six rites, for protection and worldly ends under devotion to the Jina; liberation stays the Jain liberation.

relations.note: the Buddhist fourfold/fivefold classification of tantras is one family's own ordering
the Trika's ranking of revelations orders the same features within Śaivism
initiation, one of the shared features, is the entry point of every tantric family

name: Tantra as the scripture of the Kali age

definitions.definition: In the Kali age only the Āgama's path avails; Vedic mantras are like snakes without poison (Mahānirvāṇa 2.7-15); only householder and mendicant stages remain (8.8); for the Kālīvilāsa only the paśu disposition remains and puraścaraṇa gives way to mental remembrance of the mantra (4.2-6).

Right after creation Śiva divided the one knowledge among ten Śivas and eighteen Rudras, each text then passing through a chain of recipients (a Śiva/Rudra, then gods, sages or gaṇas) to reach humans.
Thirty-six devices in Caraka (Si 12.41-45) and thirty-two in Suśruta (Utt 65.3) by which a treatise is opened as a lotus by the sun; without them the texts are not understood (Si 12.46-49).

name: The tantri and the śānti in Kerala temples

definitions.definition: A hereditary tantri family holds ritual authority over a temple (installation, festivals, purifications), while śānti priests perform the daily pūjās; e.g. the Cēnnās family at Guruvāyūr.

name: The tantric grounds (bhūmi)

definitions.definition: The dohās place realization on 'the fourteenth ground'; the Queen Dohā says grounds, paths and buddhahood are all one innate gnosis.
The Hevajra correlates the ten grounds with ten classes of sacred site; later systems count twelve, thirteen or more grounds.

notes: The numbering systems (13th 'Vajradhara' ground, 14th etc.) belong to later commentaries; not resolved here.

name: The great monasteries of Indian Vajrayāna

definitions.definition: Nālandā, Vikramaśīla (founded by Dharmapāla, c. 800), Odantapurī, Somapura and Jagaddala, where the tantras were studied, commented upon and conferred (Vikramaśīla's 'gatekeepers' included Nāropa, Ratnākaraśānti and Vāgīśvarakīrti); sacked c. 1200.

notes: Dates and gatekeeper lists from memory (Tāranātha's accounts).

name: The fourteen root downfalls of the tantric vow

definitions.definition: The fourteen root downfalls (beginning with disparaging the vajra master) whose avoidance is the core of the tantric vow, as explained in Tsongkhapa's 'Fruit Clusters of Siddhis'.
Sakya Paṇḍita's Three Vows treats the tantric vow's rules as distinct from the lower vows.

notes: Title of Tsongkhapa's commentary recalled with low confidence.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): creation proceeds by tapas (TU 2.6; PrU 1.4; MuU 1.1.8-9, whose tapas is knowledge); Bhṛgu seeks brahman by tapas, 'tapas is brahman' (TU 3.2); tapas as one branch of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); the self is found by truth and austerity (MuU 3.1.5; ŚU 1.15); sickness and cremation are the supreme tapas (BAU 5.11).

queries: prepared segments: TU 2.6, PrU 1.4, MuU 1.1.8-9, TU 3.2, ChU 2.23.1, MuU 3.1.5, ŚU 1.15, BĀU 5.11
checks.note: All 8 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (TU 2.6; PrU 1.4; MuU 1.1.8-9; TU 3.2; ChU 2.23.1; MuU 3.1.5; ŚU 1.15; BĀU 5.11). It rests on 8 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: Tapas is the heat by which That One was born (RV 10.129.3) and from which ṛta and satya came (10.190.1); by tapas the ancients reached heaven (10.154.2); the unheated do not attain soma (9.83.1); the student fills the worlds with tapas (AVŚ 11.5.4); the seers first undertook tapas and dīkṣā (19.41.1); Agastya's long tapas is set beside married life (RV 1.179).

name: Tārā in the Buddhist and Hindu tantras

definitions.definition: Tārā, the saviouress who ferries beings across dangers, a female buddha or bodhisattva of compassion; forms include Green and White Tārā and the fierce Ekajaṭā and Mahācīna-Tārā, the latter crowned with Akṣobhya.
Tārā is the second of the ten Mahāvidyās, fierce and dark blue, with Akṣobhya on her head; her Kula worship is said to have been learned in Mahācīna from the Buddha by Vasiṣṭha.

notes: The Hindu texts themselves narrate the Buddhist connection (brw:tara-mahacina-buddhist).

definitions.definition: Tāraka ('what makes one cross') is the yoga of lights and targets, with and without form; its later part is amanaska, the mind-less state in which the mind becomes 'like an udder after milking' (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 1.3, 3.1–2).

In the haṭha corpus: 'tāraka', which those deluded by Āgamas, Vedas and logic do not know (HYP 4.40), and the mindless (amanaska) state — a synonym of samādhi (4.4) and the goal of the Amanaska, reached effortlessly by the guru's grace (Amanaska 2).

relations.note: Tāraka culminates in the mind-less (amanaska/unmanī) state.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 4 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: Souls are graded, beginninglessly and endlessly, in knowledge, bliss and office — from humans and kings up through gandharvas, ancestors, gods, Indra, Rudra, to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Lakṣmī above and Viṣṇu infinitely above; the gradation is unalterable and continues in liberation, and knowing it is required for liberation.

name: Reasoning (tarka) as a limb of yoga

definitions.definition: In the Maitrī's six limbs reasoning stands between concentration and absorption.

The Śaiva ṣaḍaṅga counts tarka — the discernment of what is to be taken up and left — as the highest limb ('tarko yogāṅgam uttamam', Mālinīvijayottara as quoted by Abhinavagupta — recalled); the Mṛgendra calls the corresponding scrutiny ūha.

relations.note: Patañjali's eight limbs have no tarka

name: Incidental and essential definitions of Brahman

definitions.definition: Brahman is defined incidentally (taṭastha) as the world-cause and essentially (svarūpa) as existence–consciousness–infinitude/bliss.

Whether the Tathāgata exists, does not exist, both or neither after death is undeclared: liberated from reckoning by form and the other aggregates he is deep like the ocean, and 'reborn' or 'not reborn' does not apply (MN 72); since he is not apprehended in truth even here, annihilation cannot be asserted (SN 22.85–86).

name: The Tathāgata sought in five ways

definitions.definition: The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, not other than them, not in them, they are not in him, and he does not possess them; he is a designation, empty as the world is empty (MMK 22.1, 22.8, 22.16).

relations.note: the same fivefold search applied to the Buddha

name: Buddha-nature and the Upaniṣadic self: the question of likeness

definitions.definition: The Mahāparinirvāṇa calls the tathāgatagarbha the 'self' of beings and the Ratnagotravibhāga counts self among the four perfections of the fruit; the Laṅkāvatāra raises the objection that this is like the tīrthakaras' self and answers that it is taught as a skilful name for emptiness, to attract those who cling to a self.
The self (ātman) of the Upaniṣads is permanent, unborn and the inner controller, known as one's own being.

relations.note: the Laṅkāvatāra distinguishes the tathāgatagarbha from any permanent agent-self; the Buddhist tradition insists on the difference (P6-upaya is its own principle)

notes: The tradition of each side rejects identity: recorded as a question of likeness, not as an equivalence. See dsp:buddha-nature-self-or-emptiness and brw:tathagatagarbha-and-atman.

definitions.definition: The Mahāparinirvāṇa: 'self' means the tathāgatagarbha; no-self is saṃsāra, self is the Tathāgata; the Aṅgulimālīya likewise.
The Laṅkāvatāra denies that the garbha-teaching is the tīrthikas' self.

name: The nine similes of the tathāgatagarbha

definitions.definition: Buddha in a withered lotus, honey among bees, kernel in husk, gold in filth, treasure under a poor house, sprout in a fruit, image in rags, king in a poor woman's womb, statue in a clay mould.
The sakhī's joy is only in the pair's joy; she seeks nothing for herself.

name: The many counts of the principles, reconciled

definitions.definition: The seers count the principles as nine, eleven, five, three, twenty-six, twenty-five, seven, six, four, seventeen, sixteen or thirteen; all are right, because the principles enter into one another and each speaker counts as he intends; the dispute itself arises from the Lord's powers and ceases with calm and self-control.
Vallabha follows the Bhāgavata's count of twenty-eight principles (nine, eleven, five and three), treating them as Brahman's own real manifestation rather than as prakṛti's alone.

relations.note: a text-internal instance of reconciling divergent teachings by the intention of the speaker

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:tattva-counts-reconciled-bhagavata
checks.note: Rests on tea:uddhava-gita:11.22.1-9; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

notes: U16 contribution recalled with low confidence; locate in the Tattvārthadīpanibandha.

definitions.definition: Dependent reality divides into negation (prior, posterior, constant) and positive being; positive into sentient (Lakṣmī untouched by sorrow; souls touched by sorrow) and insentient (eternal: Vedas; eternal-and-non-eternal: Purāṇas etc., time, prakṛti; non-eternal: uncompounded — mahat, ahaṃkāra, buddhi, manas, ten senses, five subtle elements, five elements — and compounded — the cosmic egg and its contents).

name: The three realities (tattvatraya: cit, acit, Īśvara)

definitions.definition: Three eternal, real and distinct entities: souls, insentient matter and the Lord, the first two being the body of the third.
No means of knowledge can be defined without circularity; hence no object is established, not even the four elements; everyday practice goes on unexamined.

relations.note: Jayarāśi overturns even perception

name: Teacher and disciple in the Nyingma

definitions.definition: The teacher is examined first (pure vows, learning, compassion, experience, freedom from worldly aims), then followed with faith and service and emulated; devotion is the key to the blessing; the disciple too is tested for signs and faith.

name: Choosing treatise, teacher and student; initiation

definitions.definition: First examine the treatise, then the teacher (learned, experienced, pure, patient, affectionate); serve him like fire, god, king and father; the teacher examines the student; initiation before fire with an oath of celibacy, truth, non-violence and service of the sick; the whole world is teacher to the wise (Ca Vi 8.3-14).

The teacher is unmoved whether disciples listen or not (MN 137); he does not treat disciples as a potter the raw clay but repeatedly admonishes (MN 122); the Tathāgata only points the way (MN 107; Dhp 276); good friendship is the whole of the holy life (SN 45.2).

The Kagyu lives dramatize it as trial and devotion: Tilopa and Nāropa's twelve hardships, Marpa and Milarepa's towers; the disciple needs faith, diligence, wisdom and compassion; instructions given without the root guru's consent bear no fruit.

name: Teacher, student and transmission in Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: The teaching is secret (SK 69), given out of compassion (SK 70), to a qualified student: Kapila tested Āsuri three times over thousand-year intervals before he renounced (Māṭhara). Acquired knowledge arises with the teacher as its occasioning cause (Gauḍapāda on SK 43); among the accomplishments are hearing, study, approaching a teacher and serving the venerable (Gauḍapāda on SK 51). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra: instruction must be repeated (4.3); take the essence from many teachers like a bee (4.13); hearing without reflection does not suffice, as with Virocana, while Indra attained after obeisance, continence and long approach (4.17–19); a defiled mind lets the seed of instruction fail (4.29–30); there must be liberated teachers, else the blind lead the blind (3.80–82); there is no fixed rule since students differ (3.77).
Shinran 'has not a single disciple', for people say the nenbutsu by Amida's working; yet he entrusts himself wholly to Hōnen's teaching; the Tannishō is not to be shown to those without karmic roots.

The teacher is learned in scripture and established in Brahman, calm, compassionate, free of pride; the student approaches with humility, service and questioning, calm, self-controlled and longing for liberation; knowledge of the truth, not birth, makes the guru (Manīṣāpañcaka).
The student brings fuel and begs daily, so Death has no claim on him (ŚB 11.3.3).

The teacher is revered above the father as giver of the Vedic birth (MDh 2.145–146); learning, not age, makes one great (2.154); the serving pupil obtains the teacher's knowledge as a digger reaches water (2.218); knowledge may be received from anyone in faith (2.238); the ācārya is the one from whom the dharmas are gathered, never to be harmed (ĀpDh 1.1.1.14–15).

definitions.definition: (Jain report) A fiery power gained by severe austerity, with which Gosāla burnt two monks; turned against Mahāvīra, it returned upon Gosāla.
Countered by the cool power; its misuse is the downfall of the one who wields it.

name: The temple as the deity's body
notes: Stated in many texts; exact loci not verified in this pass (listed as a gap). U58 owns Vāstu/Śilpa.

definitions.definition: Āgama and śilpa texts treat the temple (prāsāda) as the body of the deity, its parts named as limbs.
Pāñcarātra saṃhitās likewise identify the temple with Bhagavān's body.
Kerala tantra treats the temple and its installed deity as a living body whose power the tantri maintains.

name: The ten wonders (accheraga) of this era

definitions.definition: Events that should not happen but did in this descending half-cycle: an attack on a Jina (Gośāla's); the transfer of Mahāvīra's embryo; a woman Tīrthaṅkara (Mallī); a first sermon in which no one took vows; Kṛṣṇa's journey to Amarakaṅkā; the sun and moon coming down in their own vehicles to Mahāvīra; the origin of the Harivaṃśa from a pair of the happy age; Camara's assault on heaven; 108 liberated at once (in Ṛṣabha's time); the worship of the unrestrained.

notes: List recalled with moderate confidence.

name: The ten aspects of the element (RGV 1.29)

definitions.definition: Essence, cause, fruit, function, endowment, manifestation, states, all-pervasiveness, unchangeability, inseparability.

name: The benefits in the present life (genze riyaku / genshō jūyaku)

definitions.definition: Ten benefits of the person of shinjin, from protection by unseen beings to entry into the rightly established state; the hymns on benefits in this life.
Shandao's augmenting conditions include long life and protection in this life.

name: The ten grounds (bhūmi) of the Daśabhūmika

definitions.definition: Joyful, Stainless, Luminous, Radiant, Hard-to-Conquer, Facing, Far-Going, Immovable, Good Intelligence, Cloud of Dharma — each with its perfection; mind-only realized on the sixth, acceptance of non-arising on the eighth, consecration on the tenth.

relations.note: one perfection predominant per ground

notes: Full path map: pth:ten-bhumis (U51).

definitions.definition: Supreme forbearance, humility, straightforwardness, purity, truth, restraint, austerity, renunciation, non-possession and celibacy (TS 9.6); celebrated in the Digambara Daśalakṣaṇa festival; dharma is also the nature of a thing, the three jewels and the protection of beings (Kārttikeyānuprekṣā 478).

Identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and vows, sensual lust, ill will (the five lower), lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, ignorance (the five higher); abandoned stage by stage (MN 64; MN 2).

name: The ten fires of the body (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad)

definitions.definition: By the adjuncts of the ten breaths the fire is fivefold as led by prāṇa — expelling, filling, drying, burning, flooding (with nectar as their essence) — and fivefold as led by apāna — corroding, splitting, agitating, deluding, yawning; it digests the four kinds of food; these ten digits of fire are the goddesses of the inner ten triangles.

notes: Names from the eBhāratī text; variants exist (e.g. pācaka).

name: Good and bad activity of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Bad: injury, theft, forbidden sex (body); lying, harshness, slander, idle talk (speech); malice, coveting, disbelief (mind) — leading to adharma. Good: giving, protecting, serving (body); truthful, beneficial, pleasant speech and recitation; compassion, freedom from craving, faith (mind) — leading to dharma (NBh 1.1.2).

relations.note: Close parallel to the Buddhist ten courses of wholesome and unwholesome action (list of shared vocabulary; no borrowing asserted).

name: The ten kinds of supernormal power

definitions.definition: By resolve, by transformation, mind-made, by intervention of knowledge, by intervention of concentration, the noble power, born of kamma-result, of the meritorious, accomplished by lore, and success through right application.
Ciṇī, ciñciṇī, bell, conch, lute, cymbal, flute, mṛdaṅga, bherī, thunder — heard in order, each with its effect; the tenth is practised (Haṃsa 4).

The HYP gives its own sequence: first ocean, thunder, kettledrum and cymbals; in the middle drum, conch, bell and horn; at the end tinkling bells, flute, vīṇā and bee (4.84–86), and one sound for each stage (4.70–77).

definitions.definition: Three bodily (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct), four verbal (lying, divisive, harsh, idle speech) and three mental (covetousness, ill will, wrong view), and their opposites (MN 41; AN 10.176).
Tattva-rūpa, tattva-darśana, tattva-śuddhi; ātma-rūpa, ātma-darśana, ātma-śuddhi; śiva-rūpa, śiva-darśana, śiva-yoga, śiva-bhoga.
Conventional knowledge, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation and path, of others' minds, of destruction and of non-arising.

After Jambū, the last omniscient, ten things ceased in Bharata: mind-reading knowledge, the highest clairvoyance, certain supernormal powers, the conveyance body, the two ladders of karmic subsidence and destruction, the Jinakalpa, the three highest forms of conduct, omniscience and liberation (list low confidence).

Ten goddesses who are forms of the one Goddess: Kālī, Tārā, Ṣoḍaśī (Tripurasundarī), Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī and Kamalā (Muṇḍamālā as quoted in the Tantrasāra); each has her Bhairava consort (Toḍala 1.3-19) and they correspond to Viṣṇu's ten avatāras (Toḍala 10.9-11). The lists differ: the Bṛhaddharma names Sundarī and Ṣoḍaśī separately and omits Kamalā.

Satī's ten forms, stationed in the ten directions around Śiva before she goes to Dakṣa's sacrifice; they grant liberation to worshippers and accomplish the magical acts (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.125-134; Mahābhāgavata 8).

relations.note: their origin in the Satī myth

name: The ten Indian masters of the Cheng weishi lun

definitions.definition: The ten commentators on the Thirty Verses whose views Xuanzang compiled: Dharmapāla, Guṇamati, Sthiramati, Bandhuśrī, Nanda, Śuddhacandra, Citrabhānu, Viśeṣamitra, Jinaputra and Jñānacandra; Dharmapāla's view is adopted.

notes: Sanskrit forms are the conventional back-translations of the Chinese names; list recalled.

name: The ten mudrās of the Haṭhapradīpikā

definitions.definition: Mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, uḍḍiyāna, mūlabandha, jālandhara, viparītakaraṇī, vajrolī and śakticālana — taught by Ādinātha, destroying old age and death, to be kept secret (HYP 3.6–9, 3.128); a closely similar set in DYŚ 27–29.

name: The ten mudrās of Śrīvidyā worship

definitions.definition: One seal for each enclosure plus a tenth: sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, sarvavidrāviṇī, sarvākarṣiṇī, sarvavaśaṅkarī, sarvonmādinī, sarvamahāṅkuśā, sarvakhecarī, sarvabījā, sarvayoni and sarvatrikhaṇḍā; the Goddess is 'worshipped with the ten mudrās', 'the yoni-mudrā', 'lady of the trikhaṇḍā' (LSN 179-180).

name: The ten channels and ten breaths

definitions.definition: Seventy-two thousand channels arise from the bulb, of which ten carry the breath (iḍā ... śaṅkhinī); ten breaths (prāṇa ... dhanañjaya) move in them and drive the jīva up and down (GŚ 16–29; AmŚ 21–22).

name: The ten niryuktis ascribed to Bhadrabāhu

definitions.definition: On the Āvaśyaka, Daśavaikālika, Uttarādhyayana, Ācārāṅga, Sūtrakṛtāṅga, Daśāśrutaskandha, Bṛhatkalpa, Vyavahāra, Sūryaprajñapti and Ṛṣibhāṣita (the last two lost).

Giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness and equanimity, discerned by Sumedha as the qualities that make a Buddha (Bv 2.116–165); illustrated (seven of them) in the Cariyāpiṭaka.

relations.note: the Mahāyāna six (and ten) pāramitās overlap but differ in members

name: The ten perfections

definitions.definition: The six plus skillful means, vow, power and knowledge, one predominating on each of the ten grounds.
Generosity, discipline, patience, vigour, meditation, wisdom, skill in means, aspiration, power and knowledge, matched to the ten grounds.
The six with method, aspiration, power and knowledge, each predominant on one of the ten grounds (MA chs. 1–10).

notes: Shared id (U39/U40).

definitions.definition: Ten relaxations of the Vinaya practised by the Vajjiputtakas and judged unallowable at the Second Council.

name: The ten vitalities (prāṇa) of the embodied soul

definitions.definition: An embodied soul lives by up to ten vitalities: five senses, three powers (mind, speech, body), breath and lifespan; one-sensed beings have four; injury is the severing of these (TS 7.13; Dravyasaṃgraha).
Hemacandra also describes the five winds (prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna) with their seats and colours, but does not make their control a means to liberation (YŚ 5–6).

relations.note: The Jain prāṇas are life-capacities rather than a system of winds to be controlled.

name: The ten precepts of the novice

definitions.definition: The eight with entertainments and adornment separated and the refusal of gold and silver (Khp 2).

name: The ten reasons for laying down training rules

definitions.definition: The excellence and comfort of the Saṅgha, restraint of the shameless, ease of the well-behaved, restraint and prevention of effluents, faith of the faithless and increase of the faithful, endurance of the true Dhamma and support of the discipline (Vin Pār 1).

Ten continuous thoughts or voicings of Amitābha at death suffice even for evil-doers because their weight lies in mind, object and decisiveness; they need not be counted (Tanluan, Daochuo); read as ten voicings (Shandao); as ten breaths each morning (Zunshi).

name: The ten points of monastic conduct (sāmācārī)

definitions.definition: Formal courtesies and procedures of the monk toward teacher and fellow monks (announcing going out and returning, asking leave, inviting others to share alms, and the like) and the division of day and night into study, meditation, alms and sleep.

notes: The ten items are not listed here individually (not recalled with confidence).

name: The ten factors of the arahant

definitions.definition: The eight path factors with right knowledge and right liberation (MN 117).
Two lists: temples, the three vital points, throat, blood, semen, ojas and anus (Ca Sū 29.3); head, throat, heart, navel, anus, bladder, ojas, semen, blood and flesh (Ca Śā 7.9).

relations.note: the three great marmas are among the seats

name: The ten signs of the Kālacakra

definitions.definition: Smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, flame, moon, sun, darkness (Rāhu), the digit (kalā, lightning) and the great drop, after which the universal image of empty form appears (Sekoddeśa 26).
The empty forms that appear in the branch of withdrawal of the Jonang six-branch yoga: smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, blaze, moon, sun, darkness, lightning and drop.

relations.note: The first four signs coincide (order differs: mirage and smoke are swapped) with the Guhyasamāja's five signs.

name: The ten sinful acts of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Violence, theft, sexual misconduct; slander, harsh speech, falsehood, idle talk; malice, covetousness, wrong view (AHS Sū 2.21-22).

relations.note: identical list to the Buddhist ten unwholesome courses of action

name: The ten powers of a Tathāgata

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the possible and impossible, of the results of kamma, of the ways leading everywhere, of the world of many elements, of beings' inclinations, of their faculties, of the defilement and purification of meditative attainments, of past lives, of beings' passing and rebirth, and of the destruction of the effluents (MN 12).

Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna and the five minor — nāga (belching), kūrma (blinking), kṛkara (sneezing, hunger), devadatta (yawning, sleep), dhanañjaya (remains after death); each has a seat and function.
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta and dhanañjaya are the goddesses of the outer ten triangles of the Śrīcakra (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).

Five principal breaths (prāṇa in the heart, apāna at the anus, samāna at the navel, udāna in the throat, vyāna throughout) and five minor ones (nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, dhanañjaya) causing belching, blinking, hunger, yawning and hiccup (SS 3.4–8); they move in the channels as the living soul (GŚ 24–25).
Ten winds among the ninety-six: pirāṇaṉ, apāṉaṉ, viyāṉaṉ, utāṉaṉ, camāṉaṉ, nākaṉ, kūrmaṉ, kirukaraṉ, tēvatattaṉ, taṉañcayaṉ; in medicine they are the ten forms of the vātam humour.
Siddha medicine treats the ten vāyus as the subdivisions of vaḷi (vātam).

name: The ten virtuous paths of action

definitions.definition: Refraining from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct, from false, divisive, harsh and idle speech, and from covetousness, malice and wrong views (RĀ 1.8–9); the foundation of higher status.

relations.note: the same list in the Pali suttas

definitions.definition: Keeping the precepts, no pride, no anger, no envy, no stinginess, giving to the needy, using the four means of attraction, rescuing the suffering, restraining offenders, never forgetting the true dharma.

Yamas: non-injury, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, rectitude, forbearance, fortitude, moderate diet, purity; niyamas: austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord, hearing doctrine, modesty, discernment, japa, vows (Śāṇḍilya, Darśana, Triśikhi, Varāha).

The interpolated HYP verses (with 1.17) and the Yoga Yājñavalkya list ten restraints (non-harming, truth, non-stealing, continence, forbearance, fortitude, compassion, straightforwardness, moderate diet, purity) and ten observances; the DYŚ says moderate eating is chief among the yamas and non-harming among the niyamas (30); the SS gives its own lists of things to avoid and to follow (3.33, 3.35).

name: Ten yamas and ten niyamas (Devī Gītā)

definitions.definition: Yamas: non-violence, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, uprightness, forbearance, fortitude, moderate food, purity. Niyamas: austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the deity, hearing the settled doctrine, modesty, discernment, mantra repetition, oblation.

definitions.definition: Steadfastness, patience, self-control, not stealing, purity, sense-restraint, wisdom, learning, truth, absence of anger (MDh 6.92).

name: The tenfold examination of the patient (and the ten things to be examined)

definitions.definition: The patient is examined by constitution, morbid state, tissue-excellence, compactness, measure, suitability, mind, capacity for food, capacity for exercise and age (Ca Vi 8.94); distinct is the list of ten things to be examined before action — cause, instrument, source and effect, its fruit, continuation, place, time, undertaking, means (Vi 8.84).
Ten men each forget to count himself; told 'you are the tenth', each knows it at once: the mahāvākya gives immediate knowledge of what was never lost.

name: The single-ācārya discipline of the Terāpanth

definitions.definition: One ācārya initiates all monks and nuns, who keep no personal disciples; he appoints his successor; the order lives by a written code (maryādā) renewed every year at the Maryādā Mahotsava.

name: How treasures are concealed and revealed

definitions.definition: Padmasambhava teaches a disciple, seals the teaching in the disciple's mind by aspiration and empowerment, has it written in symbolic script and hidden (in the earth or the mind) under a protector; at the prophesied time the disciple's rebirth, the revealer, finds the sign, decodes it and establishes the teaching, often after years of secrecy.
Bön treasures were hidden during the persecutions and recovered by revealers such as Shenchen Luga.

The guru tests the disciple by knowledge or action for a year, six months or three (Kulārṇava 14.19), and the disciple tests the guru by the bliss and signs of his practice (14.25); if they give and receive without testing both become piśācas (14.11); Kula knowledge never stays in the unworthy (2.36).
The guru tests the disciple's devotion and purifies his karma through ordeals (Tilopa–Nāropa, Marpa–Milarepa); the disciple examines the guru for the three trainings and experience.

name: How a teacher is to be tested

definitions.definition: A monk investigates the Tathāgata over time for defiled, mixed or bright states and his conduct under fame (MN 47); a student examines a teacher for states based on greed, hatred and delusion before placing faith (MN 95); faith then grows through approach, listening and practice (MN 70).

name: Testing the teacher's word by valid cognition

definitions.definition: A teacher's word is accepted not out of respect but after examination by perception and inference, as gold is tested; the Buddha himself is shown to be authoritative by proof, and scripture is relied on only for what perception and inference cannot reach and what they do not contradict.
The bodhisattva vow is to be received from a teacher who holds the vow, is learned and capable.

The Saṃhitās speak of a One behind the many: That One which breathed windless by its own power before creation (RV 10.129.2), the One Being the inspired call by many names (1.164.46), the One that has become all this (8.58.2), the one-alone god in whom the gods become one (AVŚ 13.4), the Unborn that propped apart the six regions (RV 1.164.6), of whom there is no likeness (VS 32.3).

relations.note: The One is spoken of both as beyond the gods (10.129.6: the gods are later) and as what the gods' names name (1.164.46).

definitions.definition: The knowing nature of the heart, which observes phenomena; the forest teachers train it but deny that it is a self.

The embodied self (ātman, dehin) is unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain, passing into new bodies as into new clothes, unmanifest and unthinkable (BhG 2.11–30); the knower of the field (13.1–2); an eternal portion of the Lord (15.7); Bhṛgu defends the existence of a living self in the elemental body (MBh 12.175–185).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The self in which, by knowledge, all beings are seen, and then in the Lord (4.35); the yoked yogin sees the self abiding in all beings and all beings in the self (6.29), his self having become the self of all beings (5.7); restrained thought (citta) rests in the self alone (6.18) and, seeing the self by the self, is content in the self (6.20). The same word is used reflexively: one raises oneself by oneself, and the self is one's own friend or enemy (6.5–6). In 4.35 and 6.29 'ātmani' can also be read reflexively ('in oneself').
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord says: 'I am the self (ātman) seated in the resting-place of all beings' (10.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Some see the self in themselves by themselves through meditation (13.25); whoever sees oneself as not the doer sees truly (13.30); the supreme self neither acts nor is stained though in the body (13.32), and the self present in the body is unstained like space (13.33); striving yogins see the one abiding in themselves (15.11).
