names.name: fushō no busshin 不生の仏心

definitions.definition: The buddha-mind is unborn and marvellously illuminating; everything is resolved in it without striving (Bankei).

name: Theistic Sāṃkhya (seśvara)

definitions.definition: Forms of Sāṃkhya that admit a Lord: the epic 'twenty-sixth principle' above the twenty-five (Mahābhārata, Mokṣadharma), Purāṇic accounts where emergence from pradhāna proceeds under the Lord and Kapila is an avatāra (Māṭhara on SK 1; Bhāgavata Purāṇa), a Pāñcarātra Ṣaṣṭitantra (Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā), Yoga as 'Sāṃkhya with Īśvara' in doxographies, and Vijñānabhikṣu, who salutes mahat as the self-born Lord and treats the Sāṃkhya Sūtra's denial of Īśvara as concessive.

relations.note: classical non-theism vs theistic readings

notes: Mahābhārata and Ahirbudhnya chapter details recalled, not checked.

definitions.definition: Viparītakhyāti: only the relation appearing in error is unreal; the related items are real.
Akhyāti: error is non-apprehension of the difference between a perception and a memory.
With the fading of rapture, equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, feeling bliss with the body — 'equanimous and mindful, one dwells in bliss' — like lotuses immersed in cool water (DN 2).
The tantric path of the Lamdre culminates beyond the ten grounds in the eleventh, twelfth and (twelve-and-a-half) thirteenth ground of Vajradhara, where one becomes omniscient.

relations.note: the sūtra system counts ten grounds plus buddhahood

definitions.definition: The instrument is thirteenfold — buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas (internal) and the ten capacities (external); it seizes, holds and illuminates (SK 32–33). The internal works in three times, the external in the present; the internal is the door-keeper, the external the doors (SK 33, 35). The organs act by one another's impulse, for puruṣa's purpose alone (SK 31), and like lamps present that purpose to buddhi (SK 36).
The thirty-eight (traditional count) highest blessings from not associating with fools to a mind unshaken by worldly conditions (Snp 2.4).

name: The thirty-four excellences of a Jina

definitions.definition: Supernatural features of a Tīrthaṅkara — four from birth (e.g. sweet-smelling, sweatless body; white blood), eleven arising with omniscience (e.g. the voice understood by all, the halo, freedom from famine and disease for many leagues), nineteen produced by the gods (e.g. the wheel of dharma, the parasols, the lion-throne).

name: The thirty-nine vibhavas
notes: Forty names result if every epithet is counted separately; the text says thirty-nine (segmentation uncertain).

definitions.definition: The Lord's descents beginning with Padmanābha and ending with Pātālaśayana, whose details the Sātvata teaches.

Four woeful planes (hell, animals, ghosts, asuras), the human realm and six sense-sphere heavens, sixteen fine-material Brahma realms (including the five Pure Abodes and the realm of non-percipient beings) and four immaterial realms; life-spans increase upward.

Four applications of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven limbs of awakening, eightfold path — ten dharmas in substance, prominent in turn at successive stages.

name: The thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā)

definitions.definition: Seven groups taught for the long endurance of the holy life: the four establishments of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of awakening and the noble eightfold path (DN 16; MN 149; SN 43).

relations.note: the same thirty-seven in the Sarvāstivāda sources (U38)

notes: Each of the 37 has its own term entry (trm:kayanupassana … trm:samma-samadhi).

definitions.definition: Huineng's teaching method: answer every question with its opposite so that both extremes are left behind.

name: The thirty-six principles (ṣaṭtriṃśat-tattva)

definitions.definition: Manifestation from Śiva to earth in thirty-six levels: five pure (Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā), the impure boundary of Māyā with its five sheaths (kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati), then the Sāṃkhya series from Puruṣa to earth. All shine in the supreme like images in a mirror (Paramārthasāra 11-13).
The universe is the thirty-six principles (PKS 1.4); the Śrīcakra is the cakra of the thirty-six principles (Dīpikā on YH 1.86).
Lakṣmīdhara holds that the twenty-five principles are accepted by all as Vedic, reads the thirty-six in their light, and places the Śiva-Śakti pair beyond as the twenty-sixth (on SL 11).

Siddhānta form: five pure tattvas (Śiva/nāda, Śakti/bindu, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā) evolved from bindu (pure māyā), not from Śiva; seven vidyā-tattvas (māyā, kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati, puruṣa); twenty-four ātma-tattvas (prakṛti with the guṇas, buddhi, ahaṅkāra, manas, ten organs, five subtle and five gross elements). Placement of details (e.g. a separate guṇa-tattva) varies among texts.
Tattuvam 36 (5 civa, 7 vittai, 24 āṉma), which the soul must see as not-self (tattva-rūpa, -darśana, -śuddhi); expanded to 96 in Tamil lists.

relations.note: tattvas 12-36 correspond to Sāṃkhya's twenty-five; the Śaivas add eleven above them
Sāṃkhya's 25 are the lower range of the 36
in the Siddhānta the tattvas are pāśa (products of bindu and māyā), not Śiva's self-manifestation

notes: The order of the kañcukas varies slightly between sources (e.g. kāla and niyati).

definitions.definition: The gods counted as eleven in heaven, eleven on earth and eleven in the waters (RV 1.139.11), or as 3,339 (3.9.9).
Transient emotions that surge within the permanent love for Kṛṣṇa.

name: The thirty-two postures of the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā

definitions.definition: The list of GS 2.3–6.

name: The thirty-two marks of a great man

definitions.definition: The bodily marks of a buddha (and cakravartin); the Tathāgata is not to be seen by them; they belong to the form-bodies as fruits of maturation.

name: The thirty-two parts of the body

definitions.definition: Head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin … urine — reviewed from the soles up and the crown down as a bag of mixed grains (MN 10; MN 119; Khp 3); the brain appears in the Khp list.

name: The nature of thought is dharmakāya

definitions.definition: Thoughts are not obstacles to be suppressed: their essence is the dharmakāya, 'nothing whatever, yet arising as anything' (Dorje Chang Thungma); like clouds they dissolve in space when mind is seen (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v10).

relations.note: śamatha calms thoughts; this view recognizes them

name: The thousand buddhas of the fortunate aeon

definitions.definition: In this aeon a thousand buddhas appear, Śākyamuni the fourth and Maitreya the fifth.

name: Three kinds of teacher (codaka, bodhaka, mokṣada)

definitions.definition: The one who points out the path, the one who shows the place, the one who grants the supreme (Brahmavidyā 51–53).

name: The three activities of the learned

definitions.definition: Composition, exposition and debate, each governed by its rules (Sakya Paṇḍita's Gateway to Learning).

name: The three appearances (appearance, increase, attainment)

definitions.definition: snang ba, mched pa, thob pa: the three subtle 'appearances' or 'empties' through which consciousness dissolves into clear light at death, sleep and in completion-stage yoga.

notes: The Guhyasamāja (U44) framework; recorded here as used in the Nāropa texts.

definitions.definition: To gain the knowledge of the true dharma, to teach it, and to protect it at the cost of life.

name: The three selves: outer, inner, supreme

definitions.definition: The self in all embodied beings is outer (identified with the body), inner (discerning itself) or supreme (utterly pure); by means of the inner one attains the supreme and abandons the outer (Samādhitantra 4–5; Paramātmaprakāśa; YŚ 12).
Who the supreme self is, that am I (Yogasāra 22) — every soul's own nature is the paramātman.

relations.note: Commentators place the outer self in stages 1–3, the inner self in 4–12, the supreme self in 13–14 and the Siddha.

definitions.definition: Kēvalam: the soul alone with āṇava, without instruments, like darkness; cakalam: embodied with the three malas; cuttam: purified by grace.

The bardo of birth-and-death (this life), the bardo of dream, and the bardo of becoming; in each, clear light, illusory body and union are to be recognized; inner heat and illusory body are trained in the first, dream in the second, and the clear light at death in the third.

relations.note: the Abhidharma intermediate existence is only between death and rebirth

definitions.definition: Beings' contemplation is of Brahman (the Sanandanas), of action (gods down to plants), or of both (Hiraṇyagarbha and others with office).

name: The three dispositions: paśu, vīra, divya

definitions.definition: The worshipper's disposition determines the mode of worship: paśu (pure, without the Kaula substances), vīra (heroic, with them), divya (divine); the Kālīvilāsa assigns divya to Satya–Tretā, vīra to Tretā–Dvāpara and allows only paśu in the Kali age (4.2-3; 6.10-16); the Buddha's instruction to Vasiṣṭha begins in the paśu disposition (Rudrayāmala 17.137); drinking is threefold by divya, vīra and paśu (Kulārṇava 7.94).

name: The three births of a person

definitions.definition: The first birth is as semen in the father and its placing in the mother; the second is the child's birth; the third is rebirth after the self departs at death (AU 2.1.1-4).

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (AU 2.1.1-4). It rests on 1 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

relations.note: gross = food sheath; subtle = vital, mental, intellectual sheaths; causal = bliss sheath

definitions.definition: Gross (quintuplicated elements, waking), subtle (seventeen members, dream) and causal (ignorance, deep sleep) bodies; the self is none of them.
The soul is covered by the physical, astral and causal bodies, which it leaves behind at the eye centre, Sahasdal Kanwal/Trikuṭī and Daswān Dwār respectively.

The Bahvṛca Upaniṣad (4): Mahātripurasundarī pervades the three cities, which are the three bodies, and illumines them outside and within as the inward consciousness; the Sahasranāma names her as the waker, dreamer and sleeper and as the fourth (LSN 62-63).

Dharmakāya (Samantabhadra), sambhogakāya (the five families in Akaniṣṭha), nirmāṇakāya (Garab Dorje, Śākyamuni, Padmasambhava, the six sages); in the Kunjed Gyalpo the retinues of nature, essence and compassion.
Bön-body (Kuntu Zangpo), body of perfection (Shenlha Ökar), emanation body (Tönpa Shenrab).

name: The three bodies in one's own nature

definitions.definition: Dharma, reward and transformation bodies are found in one's own nature (Platform Sūtra).
The three bodies as three lights of one's single thought (Linji).

relations.note: The trikāya read from the standpoint of the self-nature.

name: The bodies of the Buddha (sūtra layer)

definitions.definition: The sūtras distinguish the form-body with its marks, by which the Tathāgata is not truly seen, from the dharma-body; the Lotus's eternal Buddha and his emanations anticipate three bodies.
The RGV: from the dharmakāya arise the enjoyment and emanation bodies for others.

notes: The trikāya doctrine is systematized in Yogācāra (U41).

name: The three bodies of a buddha (Yogācāra)

definitions.definition: The pure dharmadhātu operates as the natural (essential) body, the enjoyment body and the emanation body, the first being the basis of the other two; the Abhisamayālaṃkāra counts four by distinguishing the wisdom dharmakāya.

relations.note: the systematization of the sūtras' buddha-bodies

definitions.definition: Inherent (threads), non-inherent (their conjunction), efficient (loom); the instrument is the special cause (Tarkasaṅgraha).

Unwholesome contact of senses and objects, failure of discernment (prajñāparādha) and transformation/time (pariṇāma), each excessive, deficient or wrong; balanced they cause health (Ca Sū 11.37-43; Sū 1.54; AHS Sū 1.19).

name: The three causes of the world

definitions.definition: Śiva is the efficient cause (nimitta), māyā (and bindu) the material cause (upādāna), Śiva's power the instrumental cause (sahakārin); Śiva does not transform.
Verbal, generalizing and figurative quibbles (NS 1.2.10–17).

name: The three classes of souls (sakala, pralayākala, vijñānākala)

definitions.definition: Souls classed by their bonds: sakala (three bonds), pralayākala (mala and karma), vijñānākala (mala only); subdivided by the ripeness of mala.
Tirumantiram: souls of three kinds, with one, two or three malas.

name: The three continua (rgyud gsum) of the Lamdre

definitions.definition: The causal continuum (the all-base, clarity-emptiness, containing saṃsāra and nirvāṇa), the method continuum (the body and the practices of empowerment and the two stages — the 'explanatory continuum') and the result continuum (Mahāmudrā).

Mahāmudrā result continuum (phyag rgya chen po 'bras bu'i rgyud)

name: The three coverings of the self

definitions.definition: The subtle covering of impurity (mala), the gross covering of the kañcukas from māyā, and the outer body: the self wrapped in three sheaths (Paramārthasāra 24).
Inner absorption (antar-daśā), half-external (ardha-bāhya) and external (bāhya) consciousness, alternating in his last years of divine madness.
A brāhmaṇa is born owing studentship to the seers, sacrifice to the gods and offspring to the ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5); ŚB adds hospitality to men (1.7.2.1–6).
The debts must be paid before seeking liberation (MDh 6.35–37).

definitions.definition: Gross meditation on a form (the chosen deity or the guru), meditation on light (kuṇḍalinī as a flame, the navel sun, the praṇava-light between the brows) and subtle meditation on bindu/kuṇḍalinī by śāmbhavī; each is vastly superior to the one before (GS 6.1–22).

Śāktī by the entry of power, śāmbhavī by the placing of the guru's foot, māntrī by imparting mantra (PKS 1.32); the guru burns the disciple's bonds with a wave of light, gives Bālā and a name ending in '-ānandanātha' and makes the disciple his own self (PKS 1.35-43).

name: The dispositions of disciples in different eras

definitions.definition: The first Jina's disciples were simple and slow (ṛju-jaḍa), the last Jina's crooked and slow (vakra-jaḍa), the intermediate ones simple and wise (ṛju-prājña); therefore the law is stated as five vows for the first and last, four for the middle ones, and discipline is adapted accordingly.

definitions.definition: The signless, desireless and void gateways, entered through the contemplations of impermanence, suffering and not-self.
Emptiness, wishless and signless concentrations; pure, they are the three doors of liberation.

Emptiness, the signless and the wishless, cultivated by the bodhisattva even in dreams, whose fruit he does not realize before his roots are ripe; in the Lotus's Sanskrit they are the herbs that cure the blind.

Vāta, pitta and kapha are the bodily doṣas (Ca Sū 1.57); undisturbed they sustain the body, disturbed destroy it (AHS Sū 1.6-7); they uphold the body as Wind, Sun and Soma the world (Su Sū 21.8), like three pillars (Su Sū 21.3); each five-fold (AHS Sū 12); in their normal state they give strength and long life as the three aims rightly pursued (Ca Sū 12.13).

the bodily doṣas parallel the two mental doṣas

definitions.definition: Attachment, aversion and delusion; delusion is the worst (NS 4.1.3–6); they arise from false knowledge and impel activity (NS 1.1.18; NBh 1.1.2).

name: The three desires (eṣaṇā)

definitions.definition: For life (first, as abandoning life abandons all), for wealth (by blameless occupations) and for the other world (after establishing rebirth, by the doors of dharma) (Ca Sū 11.3-33).

name: The three excellences (dam pa gsum)

definitions.definition: Every practice should begin with bodhicitta, be carried out without conceptual reference and end with dedication of merit.

name: The three forms of the ultimate in Śuddhādvaita

definitions.definition: Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇa (highest, goal of grace-devotion), Akṣara Brahman (his abode, goal of knowers) and Antaryāmin; the world and souls are further forms — as the Gaṅgā is water, holy river and goddess.

In the recitation tradition the presiding deities of the three caritas are Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī, derived from the primordial Mahālakṣmī (Prādhānika Rahasya); the thirteen chapters themselves do not use these three names for the caritas.
In the Prādhānika Rahasya the supreme Mahālakṣmī with the three qualities is the origin; from her arise Mahākālī and Mahāsarasvatī and from them the gods and their consorts.

Grace won by ritual works is lowest and yields heaven; won by hearing and the like is middling and yields higher worlds; won by fullness of knowledge is highest and alone yields liberation.

The knots of Brahmā (after the mūlādhāra), Viṣṇu (after the maṇipūra) and Rudra (at the ājñā) pierced by the Goddess in her ascent (LSN 38-39).

The knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, pierced when kuṇḍalinī awakens (HYP 3.2) and, in the nāda-stages, at ārambha, ghaṭa and niṣpatti respectively (4.70–77); bhastrikā retention is said to break them (2.67).

name: The three great attitudes taught to Bhṛṅgīśa

definitions.definition: The great doer, the great enjoyer and the great renouncer: acting, enjoying and renouncing without ego, preference or notions of merit.

name: The three guṇas

definitions.definition: Sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakṛti, bind the embodied one — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas to action, tamas by negligence, sloth and sleep (BhG 14.5–8); each prevails by overpowering the others; their signs, destinies and the classification of faith, food, austerity, giving, knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness (chs. 14, 17, 18); no being is free of them (18.40).

Sattva, rajas and tamas, the constituents of prakṛti and all its products: of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion; illuminating, activating and restraining; light, mobile and heavy; they dominate, support and produce one another and work together for one purpose like the parts of a lamp (SK 12–13). Prakṛti is their equilibrium (SS 1.61); creation abounds in sattva above, rajas in the middle and tamas below (SK 54).

Sattva (illumination), rajas (activity) and tamas (inertia) (2.18) — mutually dependent, distinct in power, transforming; their conflicting activity makes everything suffering for the discerning (2.15); all things are arrangements of them (4.13); the mind has three guṇas and its states depend on their mix (YBh 1.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make every being act (3.5); actions are done by them (3.27); the knower sees 'guṇas move among guṇas' (3.28); those deluded by them are attached to their actions (3.29); desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain, and Arjuna is to be free of them (2.45). Chapters 1–3 name rajas (3.37) and, on one reading of nityasattvastha, sattva (2.45); tamas is not named.
Cāttuvikam, irācatam, tāmatam — the three qualities (kuṇam) among the ninety-six principles.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): in Caraka rajas and tamas are the doṣas of mind, sattva its pure state (Sū 1.57; Śā 4.34-36); the person bound by rajas and tamas turns on the wheel of births and is freed by the increase of sattva (Śā 1.36, 1.68); sixteen mental types classified by guṇa (Śā 4.37-40; Su Śā 4.81-98); in Suśruta the unmanifest is marked by the three guṇas and the elements are guṇa-dominant (Su Śā 1.3, 1.20).
In jyotiṣa the three qualities are distributed among the planets — Moon, Sun and Jupiter sattva; Mercury and Venus rajas; Mars and Saturn tamas — and read in a person's conduct (BJ 2.7; BS 68.8–9).

Bhagavad Gītā 7.12–14: states of sattva, rajas and tamas come from the Lord, he not in them but they in him; the world, deluded by these three guṇa-made states, does not know him who is beyond them; his divine māyā is made of the guṇas.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Sattva, rajas and tamas arise from prakṛti and bind the imperishable embodied one in the body (14.5): sattva, stainless, illuminating and free of affliction, binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge; rajas, of the nature of passion, by attachment to action; tamas, born of ignorance and deluding, by heedlessness, idleness and sleep (14.6–9). Each prevails by overpowering the other two (14.10). Signs: illumination — knowledge — at all the gates of the body (sattva); greed, activity, undertaking, restlessness, craving (rajas); absence of illumination, inactivity, heedlessness, delusion (tamas) (14.11–13). Dying in each leads to the stainless worlds of the knowers of the highest, to birth among those attached to action, or to deluded wombs (14.14–15); their fruits are the stainless, pain and ignorance (14.16); from them come knowledge, greed, and heedlessness, delusion and ignorance (14.17); those abiding in them go upward, stay in the middle, go downward (14.18). One who sees no agent but the guṇas and knows what is higher than them attains Kṛṣṇa's state (14.19); going beyond them one attains the immortal (14.20; marks 14.22–25; means 14.26). In chapters 13 and 15: the modifications and the guṇas arise from prakṛti (13.20); attachment to the guṇas causes births in good and bad wombs (13.22); the branches of the aśvattha are swollen by the guṇas (15.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: chs. 4–6 name the guṇas only in passing: the fourfold class-order was made according to the division of guṇas and actions (4.13); the yogin to whom supreme happiness comes has rajas stilled (6.27).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): God's power hidden by its own guṇas (ŚU 1.3); the jīva bound to the guṇas and 'three-guṇa'd' (ŚU 5.7); in MaiU 5.2 darkness (tamas), impelled, becomes rajas and then sattva, with Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu as their parts; MaiU 3.5 lists the marks of tamas and rajas.
Māyā/ignorance consists of sattva, rajas and tamas: sattva pure (adjunct of Īśvara) or impure (of jīva); tamas veils, rajas projects.
Sattva, rajas and tamas are qualities (non-substances) of prakṛti, mixed in all bodies and worlds; the Lord and the eternal realm are free of them.

Sattva binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas to action, tamas to delusion; undeviating devotion carries one beyond them (Jñāneśvarī 14); in Eknāth's bhāruḍ tamas is scorpion venom cured by sattva.
The three states and three guṇas are the cotton from which the wick of the fourth state is spun in the lamp of knowledge.

name: The three humours in Āyurveda, Tibetan medicine and Siddha medicine

definitions.definition: Vāta, pitta and kapha, which sustain the body in balance and cause disease when disturbed.
Wind (rlung), bile (mkhris pa) and phlegm (bad kan), which the Four Tantras trace to the three mental poisons — desire, hatred and delusion — rooted in ignorance.
Vaḷi, aḻal and aiyam (the three kuṟṟam).

name: The three humours (mukkuṟṟam: vaḷi, aḻal, aiyam)

definitions.definition: Vaḷi (vātam), aḻal (pittam) and aiyam (kapam), the 'three reckoned by the learned beginning with wind', whose excess or deficiency causes disease (Kuṟaḷ 941). Each has subdivisions (vātam 10 — the ten winds; pittam 5; kapam 5). The Tirumantiram's rejuvenating practice removes aiyam, vātam and pittam at their times of day.

name: Mahāyoga, Anuyoga and Atiyoga as generation, completion and great perfection

definitions.definition: Mahāyoga emphasizes the generation stage and the view of purity and equality; Anuyoga the completion stage and the union of expanse and wisdom; Atiyoga awareness beyond both. The Garland of Views ranks them.
Carrying the guru, the deity and illusion onto the path in all circumstances.

Right view, right knowledge and right conduct together are the path to liberation (TS 1.1); when a later one is present the earlier ones are necessarily present (Tattvārthabhāṣya 1.1); knowledge without conduct and conduct without knowledge are both useless, like the lame and the blind in a burning forest (Rājavārttika 1.1).
In the ultimate sense the three jewels are the self itself — the self knowing, seeing and abiding in the self (Kundakunda; YŚ 4.2).
Yoga is the three jewels (YŚ 1.15; Yogaśataka 2).

relations.note: Both are threefold paths, but the Jain triad begins with right view of the realities and makes conduct the culminating member; not an equivalence.

name: The three processes and the breaking of the knot

definitions.definition: Before right view first arises the soul passes through three processes of purification — the ordinary, the unprecedented and the non-returning — which break the dense knot (granthi) of attachment and aversion; right view then arises (karma literature; Haribhadra places the knot's breaking at the sthirā view).

name: The three karmas in Sant Mat

definitions.definition: Pralabdh (destiny of this body) must be lived out; sinchit (stored) karma is taken over by the Master and burnt through practice; kriyaman (new) karma is avoided by living by the vows; the initiate is not reborn below the human form and returns home within four lives at most.

name: The three kinds of insentient reality

definitions.definition: Pure sattva (śuddha-sattva), mixed sattva (prakṛti with the three guṇas and its twenty-three evolutes — mahat, ahaṃkāra, mind, ten senses, five subtle and five gross elements) and that devoid of sattva (time).
Innate, temporal (season and age) and acquired (diet and activity) (Ca Sū 11.36).
Birth is by agglutination, from the womb, or by spontaneous arising (gods, hell-beings) (TS 2.31–35), in nine kinds of birth-place.

name: The three kinds of bodhisattva discipline

definitions.definition: Discipline of restraint (the prātimokṣa vows), of gathering wholesome dharmas, and of benefiting beings; with the four offences equivalent to defeat.
Compassion for beings who cling to 'I' and 'mine'; compassion seeing beings as impermanent; and compassion seeing them as empty of own-nature, like the moon in rippling water (MA 1.3–4).

Discussion (vāda) for truth; wrangling (jalpa) using quibbles and futile rejoinders; cavilling (vitaṇḍā) without a counter-thesis (NS 1.2.1–3); the last two are allowed to protect truth like a thorn fence (NS 4.2.50); vāda is held with teachers and fellow-seekers (NS 4.2.48).

name: The three kinds of pain (duḥkha) named in YBh 1.31

definitions.definition: Relating to oneself (ādhyātmika), to other beings (ādhibhautika) and to the divine (ādhidaivika): that by which beings are struck and strive to strike it down (YBh 1.31). (Distinct from the three sufferings of transformation, torment and impression at YS 2.15.)

definitions.definition: The absolute (pāramārthika) jīva, in truth Brahman; the empirical (vyāvahārika) jīva, the reflection in the intellect; the illusory (prātibhāsika) jīva of dream.
Accumulated (burnt by knowledge), to come (does not cling) and begun (exhausted by experience, like a potter's wheel's momentum).

Cañcitam (stored), pirārattam (begun, which forms this body) and ākāmiyam (being made): dīkṣā and grace burn the first, the second is exhausted by experience, the third does not bind the freed.

name: Sūtra, mantra and essence Mahāmudrā

definitions.definition: A later Kagyu classification of approaches to Mahāmudrā: sūtra Mahāmudrā (introduced through the pāramitā path, the Ratnagotravibhāga and the guru's blessing, without tantric empowerment), mantra Mahāmudrā (reached through empowerment and the two stages, including the six yogas), and essence Mahāmudrā (direct pointing-out of mind's nature to a ripe disciple, beyond either). The scheme answers the question raised by Gampopa's practice of teaching Mahāmudrā apart from tantra.

name: The three kinds of valid reason

definitions.definition: Souls are created of three kinds, with different natures and destinies: grace-souls for loving service, rule-souls for scriptural liberation, stream-souls for worldly life.

definitions.definition: Scripture speaks of difference (bheda), of non-difference (abheda) and of the body–self relation (ghaṭaka); the last reconciles the first two, so that no text need be set aside as figurative or lower.

Being struck by the three sufferings prompts the inquiry (SK 1); the commentators name them internal (bodily and mental), from other beings, and from the divine (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati). Seen and Vedic remedies do not end them certainly and finally (SK 1–2); their complete cessation is the supreme goal (SS 1.1). Suffering from old age and death belongs to embodied existence until the subtle body ceases (SK 55); the discriminating count even pleasure as suffering (SS 6.6–8).

Resting on the divine (mantra, gems, rites, offerings, vows, pilgrimage), on reasoned application (diet and drugs), and conquest of the mind (Ca Sū 11.54); bodily doṣas by the first two, mental doṣas by knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (Sū 1.58).

Inner (kuṇḍalinī, inner sound, blue light between the eyes), outer (colours and lights in space before the nose and above the head) and intermediate (the sequence of voids) — the objects of tāraka-yoga in the Advayatāraka and Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa.
Inner, outer and middle objects of fixed attention (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).

In the haṭha body-map the three targets (inner, outer, middle) are among the things the yogin must know in his own body (Vivekamārtaṇḍa family); śāmbhavī mudrā is attention on an inner target with the gaze outward (HYP 4.36).

definitions.definition: Devotion is threefold: practice, emotion and love; practice aims at the manifestation of the eternally perfect bhāva.

relations.note: prema is then graded further in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi

name: Gross, subtle and very subtle body and mind

definitions.definition: In Highest Yoga Tantra as Tsongkhapa's tradition explains it: the gross level (sense consciousnesses and the body of flesh), the subtle (conceptual minds and the winds and channels), and the very subtle (the clear-light mind and its wind), which manifests in death, deep sleep and completion-stage practice and continues into buddhahood.

relations.note: the Gelug systematisation

definitions.definition: Ultimate (pāramārthika: Brahman, never sublated), empirical (vyāvahārika: the waking world, sublated only by Brahman-knowledge) and apparent (prātibhāsika: dream, rope-snake, sublated by waking cognition).
Āṇava (innate, one, beginningless), kārma (the stream of deeds) and māyīya (the bond of māyā's products); each a real substance.
Mummalam: āṇavam, kaṉmam, māyai — eternal; in release their power is quelled, not their existence ended.
Āṇava: loss of freedom or awareness; māyīya: the appearance of separate knowables; kārma: agency in an unconscious agent; all through the power of māyā (ĪPK 3.2.4-5).
The root impurity is ignorance, not a substance; knowledge alone liberates (TĀ 1.22-26).
Śiva is free of the three impurities; the soul is atomic through impurity and is freed when the bond of impurity is shaken off.

relations.note: the three plus māyeya and tirodhāna

name: The three circles (maṇṭalam) of fire, sun and moon

definitions.definition: Among the ninety-six: the circles of fire (akkiṉi), sun (ñāyiṟu) and moon (tiṅkaḷ) in the body, from root to head; the moon's nectar flows from the highest.
All formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are not-self (AN 3.136; Dhp 277–279); the conditioned shows arising, passing and alteration (AN 3.47).
Looking (tongue, urine), touching (pulse) and questioning.

name: The three minds of the Contemplation Sūtra

definitions.definition: Sincere mind, deep mind (true entrusting of two kinds) and the mind of dedicating merit and aspiring; with these one is surely born, lacking one, not (Shandao).
The settled mind (anjin) of the nenbutsu practitioner, contained in the conviction of birth.

members: mind of dedicating merit and aspiring (huixiang fayuan xin)

name: The three minds of the eighteenth vow (sincere mind, entrusting, aspiration)

definitions.definition: Shishin (sincere mind), shingyō (entrusting with joy) and yokushō (aspiration for birth) are Amida's true mind given to beings and are one mind, shinjin.

relations.note: Shinran distinguishes the self-power three minds of the Contemplation Sūtra from those of the vow

definitions.definition: Of characteristic, of arising, and ultimate — the intent behind 'all dharmas lack own-being'.

The Prajñāpāramitā's 'all dharmas are without own-nature' was spoken with the three natures in view: the imagined lacks own-characteristic, the dependent lacks self-arising, the perfected is the ultimate naturelessness.

relations.note: one naturelessness for each nature

name: The three natures (sūtra layer)

definitions.definition: Imagined, dependent and perfected (Saṃdhinirmocana 6; Laṅkāvatāra).

Every dharma is understood through the imagined (how it appears: duality, own-being posited by names — non-existent), the dependent (what appears: imagination arising from conditions — existent but not as it appears) and the perfected (the dependent's constant absence of the imagined — suchness); they are neither one nor different; entering them in order, understanding, abandonment and attainment happen at once.
The imputational and the other-powered natures are conventional and self-empty; the thoroughly established nature is the ultimate, self-aware wisdom, empty of the other two (other-empty).

notes: Yogācāra systematization: U41.

relations.note: Madhyamaka reads the Prajñāpāramitā through two truths; Yogācāra through three natures

definitions.definition: Preliminary sign (the object as first taken up), learning sign (the image seen with eyes closed) and counterpart sign (a purified image born of perception, appearing with access).

name: The three nyepa (rlung, mkhris pa, bad kan)

definitions.definition: Three principles that sustain the body in balance and cause disease when disturbed; they arise from desire, hatred and delusion and dwell chiefly in the lower, middle and upper body.

relations.note: the same three doṣas in physiology; the Tibetan system derives them from the three poisons

name: The three streams of gurus (divya, siddha, mānava)

definitions.definition: The guru-lineage worshipped in Śrīvidyā is divided into the divine stream (divyaugha), the perfected stream (siddhaugha) and the human stream (mānavaugha); the Goddess is 'of the form of the circle of gurus' (LSN 138); the mind's flow toward the meaning comes only by the guru's grace (Setubandha).

name: The three transformations of the mind

definitions.definition: Stilling (impressions of stilling overpower those of emergence, 3.9, with a peaceful flow, 3.10), samādhi (all-objectness dwindles, one-pointedness rises, 3.11) and one-pointedness (subsiding and arising cognitions alike, 3.12).
Action, knowledge and devotion lead to liberation; devotion is the easiest, being mental and paining neither body nor mind.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:three-paths-devi-gita
checks.note: DBhP 7.37.2-3: 'mārgās trayo me vikhyātā ... karmayogo jñānayogo bhaktiyogaś ca'; devotion is 'sulabhatvān mānasatvāt kāyacittādyapīḍanāt'.

definitions.definition: The wonders of psychic power, of revealing others' minds, and of instruction; the Buddha is horrified by the first two, which an unbeliever may ascribe to a charm, and praises only the wonder of instruction (DN 11); a monk is rebuked for displaying power to laypeople (Vin Cv 5.8).

name: The three ages of the Dharma (true, semblance, final)

definitions.definition: After the Buddha's passing the Dharma declines through periods (the Candragarbha's five five-hundred-year periods; true, semblance and final ages); teaching must fit the time; in the last age calling the name is the main practice.
The true and semblance ages are over; in the last age there are only nominal monks; the Larger Sūtra alone remains after the scriptures perish.
Following Daochuo, the holy path does not suit the last age; the nenbutsu alone remains after the scriptures perish (Senchakushū 1, 6).

members: extinction of the Dharma (fametsu), after which the Larger Sūtra remains a hundred years

relations.note: partial: Indian accounts of the Dharma's decline (Sarvāstivāda) vs the East Asian three-age scheme; the counting differs

definitions.definition: Practice is first like a torrent in a gorge, then like the Gaṅgā flowing gently, finally like a river meeting the ocean (Gaṅgāmā v21).

name: The three phrases of the Mahāvairocana

definitions.definition: Bodhicitta is the cause, compassion the root, skilful means the culmination; awakening is to know one's own mind as it is.

name: The three principal aspects of the path

definitions.definition: Renunciation, bodhicitta and the correct view: without renunciation one cannot stop pursuing saṃsāra; renunciation without bodhicitta does not lead to buddhahood; neither without the view cuts the root of existence.

relations.note: the Sakya four lines name the same three plus dharma practice

name: The three kinds of worship (parā, parāparā, aparā)

definitions.definition: Parā: abiding in non-duality across all the senses' outflows; parāparā: meditative dissolution of outer into the inner non-dual abode; aparā: worship of the cakra, done even by Śiva and by all knowers because it yields the conviction of non-difference (YH 3.2-3 with the Dīpikā).

name: The three Pure Land sūtras and one treatise

definitions.definition: Hōnen designates the Larger Sūtra, the Contemplation Sūtra and the Amitābha Sūtra with Vasubandhu's treatise as the canon on which the Pure Land school rests (Senchakushū 1).
The Larger Sūtra is the true teaching; the other two have a surface and a hidden meaning.
Mahāviṣṇu (Kāraṇodakaśāyin), from whose pores the universes emerge; Garbhodakaśāyin within each universe; Kṣīrodakaśāyin as the Paramātman in every being.

name: The perishable, the imperishable and the highest person

definitions.definition: The perishable (all beings), the imperishable (the unchanging) and the highest person (Puruṣottama) beyond both, who sustains the three worlds (BhG 15.16–18).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: There are two persons in the world, the perishable — all beings — and the imperishable, called the one standing firm (kūṭastha) (15.16); the highest person is another, called the supreme self, the imperishable lord who enters and sustains the three worlds (15.17); since the Lord is beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable he is celebrated as puruṣottama (15.18); whoever knows him thus worships him with his whole being (15.19). The commentators divide on what the imperishable is.

relations.note: the Gītā's three persons and the Mokṣadharma's 24/25/26 both set a supreme above the knower of prakṛti

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Chs. 13–15 contribution, merged from extractor B's cpt:three-purusas and extractor A's cpt:ksara-aksara-purusottama (the Dvaita unit's concept for the same verses, flagged for S5). What the akṣara denotes is read differently by the commentators (dsp:bhagavad-gita-aksara-purusa).

name: The three realities: cit, acit, Īśvara (Nimbārka)

definitions.definition: Souls (cit), the non-conscious (acit: aprākṛta, prākṛta, time) and the Lord (Īśvara), all established by scripture.

name: The three reasons all beings are tathāgatagarbhas (RGV 1.27-28)

definitions.definition: The buddha's knowledge (dharmakāya) pervades beings; suchness is undivided; the buddha-lineage exists in them.
Going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha (Khp 1); first the form of ordination (Vin Mv 1.12); the 'jewels' of the Ratana Sutta.
Taken three times, kneeling with joined palms, after offerings and the seven-limb worship; the entrance to all practice.
Arises from fear and faith; one knows the qualities of the Three Jewels and keeps the precepts of refuge.

name: The three roots (rtsa ba gsum)

definitions.definition: Guru, yidam and ḍākinī (or protector): the inner refuge and the roots of blessing, accomplishment and activity.
The guru is the root of blessing, the yidam the root of accomplishment, the ḍākinī and protector the root of activity; for the Kagyu, the guru is placed above the deity (Marpa's lesson).

notes: Shared with U45.

name: Mindfulness of death: three roots, nine reasons, three decisions

definitions.definition: Death is certain, its time uncertain, and at death only dharma helps — each with three reasons — leading to the resolves to practise, to practise now, and to practise purely.

name: The three powers: will, knowledge, action

definitions.definition: Icchā, jñāna and kriyā, identified with the goddesses Parā, Parāparā and Aparā (TĀ 1.271-272); knowing and acting are the life of the living (ĪPK 1.1.4).
In the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the power of action is the seat, kuṇḍalinī the power of knowledge is the house, and the power of will is Mahātripurasundarī herself.
Parā (Viṣṇu-śakti), aparā (kṣetrajña) and avidyā-karma, which veils the kṣetrajña and causes saṃsāra; the world as the śakti of Brahman like the light of a fire.
Internal (svarūpa/cit), marginal (the souls) and external (māyā) powers; the basis of acintya-bhedābheda.

definitions.definition: Momentary, access and absorption concentration; development proceeds through preliminary work, access and absorption.

relations.note: absorption with a supporting object in the Buddhist and Pātañjala schemes (band B4); a correspondence of position, not of theory
the calm side of calm and insight

name: The three samādhis of Mahāyoga generation

definitions.definition: Every Mahāyoga sādhana begins from the samādhi of suchness (emptiness), the all-illuminating samādhi (compassion) and the causal samādhi (the seed syllable), from which the maṇḍala is generated.

members: de bzhin nyid kyi ting nge 'dzin
kun tu snang ba'i ting nge 'dzin

definitions.definition: Momentum, memory-impression (in the self), elasticity (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: The three codes (saṅketa): cakra, mantra, worship

definitions.definition: The teaching of Tripurā is a threefold code — of the cakra, the mantra and worship (YH 1.6) — a 'tryst' where Śiva and Śakti meet (Dīpikā); knowing the cakra-code and worship-code makes one liberated while living.

name: The three scopes (persons of small, middling and great capacity)

definitions.definition: Atiśa's division of practitioners by motivation: the lesser seeks saṃsāric happiness (higher rebirth), the middling seeks their own peace (liberation), the supreme seeks the end of all beings' suffering (buddhahood).
The lamrim's structure: the practices of the small and middling scopes are trained as 'common' preliminaries leading to the great scope, so that every teaching becomes a step to buddhahood.
Correlated by Sakya teachers with the first three lines of Parting from the Four Attachments.

relations.note: lines 1–3 of Parting correspond to the three scopes; line 4 to the view
renunciation ~ middling scope, bodhicitta ~ great scope

definitions.definition: That all experience is due to past deeds, to God's creation, or to no cause; each ends in inaction.
That all experience is due to past deeds, to God's creation, or to no cause — each leading to inaction (AN 3.61).
Outer, inner and supreme self (Ātma Upaniṣad); inner self Brahmā, supreme self Maheśvara, eternal self of all Viṣṇu (Rudrahṛdaya); the inner controller whose body is the elements (Subāla 7).

name: The three series of Dzogchen (sde gsum)

definitions.definition: Mañjuśrīmitra divided the Dzogchen teachings into the mind series (sems sde), the space series (klong sde) and the instruction series (man ngag sde).
Consciousness-space, mind-space and elemental space; the latter two arise from consciousness-space.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:three-spaces-yoga-vasistha
checks.note: Rests on tea:moksopaya:3.97.14-19; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

name: Garab Dorje's three statements that hit the vital point

definitions.definition: Introduce directly to one's own nature; decide on one thing; gain confidence in liberation — the whole path of cutting through in three lines.

name: The three states and the fourth (avasthā-traya, turīya)

definitions.definition: Waking (viśva), dream (taijasa) and deep sleep (prājña) come and go; the self as the fourth (turīya) pervades and transcends them, non-dual; analysis of the three states is a means to know the self.
The suffering of suffering (manifest pain), the suffering of change (pleasure that turns to pain) and pervasive conditioned suffering (the appropriated aggregates themselves).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's threefold suffering (internal, external, divine) is a different classification

name: Mind of the three times cannot be got at

definitions.definition: Past, present and future thought cannot be found (Vajracchedikā 18) — a phrase much used in Chan.

Training in higher virtue, higher mind and higher wisdom (AN 3.89); speech, action and livelihood belong to virtue, effort, mindfulness and concentration to concentration, view and intention to wisdom (MN 44); virtue and wisdom purify each other (DN 4).

relations.note: U51's map

definitions.definition: Training well in ethics, concentration and wisdom while abiding in the engaging vow, with purified body, speech and mind.
The path to liberation of the middling scope, with ethics as its foundation.

name: Virtue, concentration, understanding as the frame of the Visuddhimagga

definitions.definition: The Visuddhimagga expounds the whole path through the verse 'established in virtue, developing mind and understanding'.

relations.note: the Visuddhimagga's organization of the path

definitions.definition: Consciousness transforms as (1) maturation — the store; (2) mentation — the afflicted mind; (3) the apprehension of the six kinds of object; all talk of self and dharmas refers to these.

name: The three turnings of the dharma-wheel

definitions.definition: Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 7: the four truths (first), naturelessness taught in a hidden manner (second), and naturelessness well distinguished (third, definitive).
In Tibetan buddha-nature traditions the tathāgatagarbha sūtras and RGV are counted as the third turning.
The Saṃdhinirmocana classifies the teaching as three turnings, the third — distinguishing the three natures — being definitive.
The third turning (with the Kālacakra) is definitive, teaching the other-empty ultimate; the second teaches the self-emptiness of the conventional.

notes: Shared id (U39).

definitions.definition: Each truth known as 'this is …', 'it is to be (understood / abandoned / realised / developed)', and 'it has been …' — three turnings × four truths = twelve aspects; only when this knowledge was purified did the Buddha claim awakening (SN 56.11).
Space, cessation through discernment, cessation not through discernment — real and eternal.
Not entities: mere absences.
Nine unconditioned (Vasumitra; low confidence).
Nine unconditioned (Vasumitra; low confidence).
Food, sleep and continence (brahmacarya) uphold the body as pillars a house (Ca Sū 11.35; AHS Sū 7.52).

name: Pure, good and bad activity of consciousness

definitions.definition: Bad activity (aśubhopayoga: passion, violence) binds demerit; good activity (śubhopayoga: devotion, vows, compassion) binds merit — a golden fetter; pure activity (śuddhopayoga: abiding in the self as equanimity) alone liberates.

Kundakunda's Pravacanasāra distinguishes the pure state (śuddhopayoga) — the soul resting in itself, cause of liberation — from the auspicious (devotion, vows; cause of merit) and the inauspicious (passion; cause of demerit).

notes: Rests on Pravacanasāra (U34's text); no U35 teaching yet.

definitions.definition: Detachment born of suffering, born of delusion, and born of knowledge — only the third is true (Adhyātmasāra, following Haribhadra).
The body, speech and mind of all tathāgatas, with OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ, in which the Guhyasamāja opens; purified in the consecrations.
Śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha and bodhisattva vehicles — skillful means (Lotus) or matched to fixed lineages (Laṅkāvatāra, Saṃdhinirmocana).

Recollection of past lives, the divine eye and the destruction of the effluents, attained by the Buddha in the three watches of the night of awakening (MN 4; MN 36); the Buddhist 'three Vedas' (DN 13).

name: The three visions (snang gsum) of the Lamdre

definitions.definition: Impure vision: appearances of beings under the afflictions; experiential vision: appearances to the yogin in concentration; pure vision: the Sugatas' inexhaustible ornamental wheel of body, speech and mind. The common Lamdre path is taught through them.

members: impure vision (ma dag pa'i snang ba)

relations.note: impure vision covers the small and middling scope topics, experiential vision the bodhicitta of the great scope

definitions.definition: The prātimokṣa vow is the basis of the bodhisattva vow; celibates may not take the secret and wisdom empowerments.
Prātimokṣa, bodhisattva and mantra vows are each to be kept by their own rules and not mixed (Sakya Paṇḍita).
A monk holds all three; the tantric vows and pledges are guarded as one's life.
One in essence, differing in aspect (Gongchig).
To be kept distinct, each with its own ritual and rules (Sakya Paṇḍita).

The Vajrayāna practitioner holds the monastic or lay prātimokṣa, the bodhisattva vow and the tantric (vidyādhara) vow together; Atiśa forbids celibates the secret and wisdom consecrations to protect the first.

name: Turning through the three vows (sangan tennyū)

definitions.definition: From the 19th vow (various goods, welcome at death) through the 20th (self-power nenbutsu) to the 18th (other-power shinjin).

Earth, atmosphere and heaven, formed from the Puruṣa's feet, navel and head (RV 10.90.14), each with its gods — Agni on earth, Vāyu or Indra in the atmosphere, Sūrya in heaven (Nirukta 7.5) — and named by the utterances bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ (VS 36.3).

Knowledge, action and devotion are the only means; knowledge suits those disgusted with action, action those still desirous, devotion those with faith in the Lord's stories who are neither disgusted nor over-attached; action is done until disgust or faith arises.

relations.note: the Devī Gītā also names action, knowledge and devotion as the three paths and calls devotion the easiest

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:three-yogas-by-disposition-bhagavata
checks.note: Rests on tea:uddhava-gita:11.20.6-8, tea:uddhava-gita:11.20.9-11, tea:devi-gita:7.37.1-8; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement. Caveats on tea:uddhava-gita:11.20.6-8, tea:uddhava-gita:11.20.9-11 (see their checks) do not affect this entry.

name: The threefold austerity (tapas) of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Austerity of body (worship of gods, the twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, uprightness, celibacy, non-harm), of speech (non-agitating, truthful, pleasant, beneficial speech and recitation) and of mind (serenity, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purity of being); each again sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (BhG 17.14–19); self-tormenting austerity not enjoined by scripture is demonic (17.5–6).
The world binds a person as body (seat of experience), senses (instruments) and objects (what is experienced); release is its absolute dissolution.

Bondage is threefold: to prakṛti (absorption from taking the eight prakṛtis as highest), to the modifications (domination by the senses and objects), and through gifts (giving with conceit); release is threefold: by increase of knowledge, by calming of the senses' passion, and by total exhaustion (of virtue and non-virtue), whence isolation (Tattvasamāsa 19–20 with the Kramadīpikā). Strictly, prakṛti is bound and released (SK 62).

name: The threefold consciousness (Rāma-hṛdaya)

definitions.definition: As space is threefold — the whole, the space delimited by a pond and the sky reflected in it — consciousness is the whole, the consciousness delimited by the intellect, and its reflection; agency belongs to the intellect with the reflection and is superimposed on the witness.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:threefold-consciousness-rama-hrdaya
checks.note: Rests on tea:adhyatma-ramayana:1.1.44-52, tea:rama-hrdaya:1.1.44-52; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

notes: Combines the Advaita 'limitation' and 'reflection' accounts in one image.

name: The threefold meaning of the Mahābhārata

definitions.definition: The Bhārata has three levels of meaning: the narrative of the Pāṇḍavas with Kṛṣṇa (āstīka), the teaching of dharma, devotion and conduct (manvādi), and the reading of all its words as names of Nārāyaṇa (auparicara).
After the outer breath stops, an accomplished practitioner rests in the clear light of death for days, the body upright or lifelike and warm at the heart, before the consciousness departs.

Three Mūlasarvāstivāda lines: the 'lower Vinaya' from Śāntarakṣita preserved by Lachen Gongpa Rabsal in Amdo; the 'upper Vinaya' from western Tibet; and the lineage of the Kashmiri paṇḍita Śākyaśrībhadra (1204).

name: Tilopa's six words of advice

definitions.definition: Do not recall, do not imagine, do not think, do not examine, do not control, rest — the instruction for resting the mind in its own place.

A six-point instruction attributed to Tilopa in Kagyu sources: do not recall, do not imagine, do not think, do not examine, do not meditate, rest naturally (mi mno, mi bsam, mi sems, mi dpyod, mi sgom, rang sar bzhag).

relations.note: Both express non-engagement of conceptual mind in mahāmudrā.

notes: Known from Tibetan (Kagyu) transmission; not found in the Tengyur texts of Tilopa read locally (Tōh 2281, 2303, 2330). Wording and order recalled; U46 owns the Tibetan context.

name: Teaching fitted to time and capacity

definitions.definition: A teaching that fits the time and the capacity of beings is easy to practise and awaken by; one that does not is like drilling wet wood for fire (Daochuo).

'I am Time, the destroyer of worlds' (BhG 11.32); 'Time takes all and gives all' (MBh 12.217.25); in Vidura's parable time is the serpent, days and nights the rats (11.5–6); all accumulations end in exhaustion (Rāmāyaṇa 2.105.16).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord declares: 'I am Time, grown mighty, the maker of the destruction of worlds, engaged here in drawing in the worlds'; even without Arjuna the opposing warriors will not survive (11.32). They are already slain by him; Arjuna is to be merely the instrument (11.33–34). Earlier he names himself time among reckoners (10.30), imperishable time (10.33) and all-seizing death (10.34); Arjuna sees the warriors enter the form's mouths like rivers into the sea and moths into a flame (11.26–30).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

name: Time as a limb of the rite (Mīmāṃsā and Dharmaśāstra use of timing)

definitions.definition: Vedic rites are enjoined for fixed times — seasons, new and full moon, asterisms — so the knowledge of time serves the rite (VJ y.3); the smṛti and digests fix the times of sacraments, vows, festivals and śrāddha, and have the planets worshipped (YājñSm 1.295–308); jyotiṣa supplies the muhūrta for elective rites, while the digests decide conflicts of times.

For Mīmāṃsā, dharma is known from Vedic injunction (MS 1.1.2); the time an injunction names (e.g. spring for establishing the fires) belongs to the rite as its subsidiary; the Vedāṅgas serve the performance of the enjoined rite.

relations.note: the Vedāṅga's statement that the science of time exists for the sacrifice, extended to the smṛti rites

notes: The Mīmāṃsā definition summarizes the school's general position; specific sūtras on time as a subsidiary not extracted here.

name: Time as the condition of the sacrifice

definitions.definition: The Vedas exist for the sacrifices, which are enjoined for fixed times; hence the science of time is needed and stands at the head of the limbs (VJ Ṛk 3, 35; Yajus 3); fires are set up under the Kṛttikās because they keep to the east (ŚB 2.1.2.3).

Jyotiṣa's later branches keep this purpose: the muhūrta texts fix the times of sacraments, fire-establishment, consecration and other rites (Muhūrtacintāmaṇi, prakaraṇas 5–13), and the planets are worshipped before great undertakings (YājñSm 1.295–308).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:vedanga-jyotisa:r.3 (confirmed); tea:vedanga-jyotisa:y.3 (partially-confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:2.1.2.3 (confirmed). VJ Ṛk 3 and 35 carry the claim. The Yajus-recension number '3' is unverified (see tea:vedanga-jyotisa:y.3), but the verse itself is confirmed as belonging to the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa.

definitions.definition: Present and future are not established without the past, nor with it; time does not exist apart from existents, and no existent exists by own-nature, so time is not found (MMK 19.3, 19.6); saṃsāra has no beginning or end (11.1).
Time and space (direction) are single, all-pervading, eternal substances inferred from the notions 'earlier/later, simultaneous, quick' and 'this from here' (VS 2.2.6, 2.2.12 C; Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: Pilgrimage places and their inner meaning

definitions.definition: Earthly tīrthas are holy by the power of earth and water and the presence of sages; seven cities give liberation; but the virtues are inner tīrthas, purity of mind the highest, and devotees themselves make tīrthas holy.

checks.note: All teachings it rests on were located in the local e-texts (see their checks).

definitions.definition: Nandi's grace made eight masters (nātar) — the four Nandis, Śivayoga, Patañjali, Vyāghrapāda and Tirumūlar (67); by Nandi's grace he received the name nātar and sought Mūlaṉ (68); his mantra-line has seven (listing eight names, 69); four became masters of the four directions and received all he had received (70).

relations.note: the Siddhānta's inner lineage from Nandi

name: The five classes of lunar days

definitions.definition: The fifteen lunar days repeat the classes nandā, bhadrā, jayā, riktā and pūrṇā; each tithi has a presiding deity from Agni (first) to the Moon (fifteenth); their quality changes with the fortnight (MC 1.3–4).

name: The three characteristics of a valid reason (trairūpya)

definitions.definition: Presence of the reason in the subject, presence only in similar cases, absence from all dissimilar cases.

name: Transcendental dependent origination (upanisā)

definitions.definition: Suffering is the proximate cause of faith, faith of gladness, gladness of rapture, rapture of tranquillity, tranquillity of happiness, happiness of concentration, concentration of knowledge and vision of things as they are, that of disenchantment, that of dispassion, that of liberation, liberation of the knowledge of destruction (SN 12.23); a parallel sequence from virtue (AN 11.1–2).

notes: The name 'transcendental dependent origination' is modern-commentarial usage; the text calls the links upanisā.

definitions.definition: Merit is rejoiced in and turned toward awakening for all, without apprehension of the three spheres — otherwise the dedication is 'poisoned'.
The fifth gate: never abandoning suffering beings, making transfer foremost; of two aspects, going and returning.
The transfer is Amida's, not the practitioner's: the nenbutsu is 'non-transferring' practice.

An ancient tree made of karma with two seeds, a hundred roots, three trunks, five branches, five saps, eleven boughs, a nest of two birds, three barks and two fruits, cut down with the axe of knowledge sharpened by devotion to the teacher.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:tree-of-samsara-bhagavata
checks.note: Rests on tea:uddhava-gita:11.12.21-24; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

definitions.definition: The goddesses Parā, Parāparā, Aparā (with Bhairava; Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī above them in Abhinavagupta's Trika); Śiva, Śakti and Nara; will, knowledge and action; non-difference, difference-in-non-difference, difference.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): MaiU 5.2 names Brahmā, Rudra and Viṣṇu as the foremost forms of the one, being its rajas-, tamas- and sattva-parts; MaiU 5.1 hails the one as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and all the gods.

One Lord takes the names Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva for creation, maintenance and destruction (VP 1.2.66); in the Devī Māhātmya and Devī Bhāgavata the three receive their bodies and powers from the Goddess.

definitions.definition: The Lord's transcendent three quarters beyond māyā, as distinct from the one quarter that is the world (Tripādvibhūti-Mahānārāyaṇa, developing Ṛgveda 10.90.3).

checks.note: This was on the least-sure list (low confidence). The Tripādvibhūti is located (e-text no. 54). Its source verse, Ṛgveda 10.90.3 ('pādo'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripād asyāmṛtaṃ divi'), is correctly cited. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: The tripod: mind, self and body

definitions.definition: Mind (sattva), self and body stand together like a tripod; the world rests on their union; that union is the person, the conscious one, the subject-matter of Āyurveda (Ca Sū 1.46-47).

name: The three cities (tripura) and their triads

definitions.definition: Tripurā is prior to every triad — abodes, principles, seats, liṅgas, letters (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); her city is threefold as triangle, circle and square and her mantra three-part (Bhāskararāya); she is 'trayī, abode of the three aims, dwelling in the three, garlanded by the three cities' (LSN 162-163) and 'trimūrti' (LSN 125); the Tripurā Upaniṣad opens with 'three cities, three paths'.
The Bahvṛca Upaniṣad (4) identifies the three cities with the three bodies, pervaded and illumined by Mahātripurasundarī as the inward consciousness.
She existed before the three lights (Cidvallī on KKV 2).

notes: The three cities = three bodies is stated in the Bahvṛca Upaniṣad (4); other triads vary by commentator.

definitions.definition: Every cognition is self-luminous and manifests the knower, the known and itself; the self appears only as subject.

name: The threefold Āyurveda: cause, sign, remedy

definitions.definition: The Āyurveda Indra taught is knowledge of cause, sign and remedy, the refuge of the healthy and the sick (Ca Sū 1.24).
The soul in three modes across the six sthalas: tyāgāṅga (bhakta, māheśvara), bhōgāṅga (prasādi, prāṇaliṅgi), yōgāṅga (śaraṇa, aikya), facing iṣṭa-, prāṇa- and bhāva-liṅga.
The liṅga is threefold: gross (the iṣṭaliṅga worn on the body), subtle (the prāṇaliṅga of inner contemplation) and beyond the highest (the tṛptiliṅga).
The vacanas speak of iṣṭaliṅga, prāṇaliṅga and bhāvaliṅga, and the manuals correlate them with the gross, subtle and causal bodies and with the three aṅgas (tyāga, bhōga, yōga).

relations.note: correlation found in the vacana/manual tradition, not stated in SSM 6.49–50

name: The tripartition (trivṛt) of heat, water and food

definitions.definition: Being made heat, water and food each threefold (ChU 6.3.3); the red, white and black forms of fire, sun, moon and lightning are those of heat, water and food, and the thing itself is only a name (ChU 6.4); eaten food, water and heat divide threefold into body and mind (ChU 6.5).

relations.note: later readers relate the three colours (and the red, white and black ajā of ŚU 4.5) to the three guṇas; the ChU does not name guṇas

queries: prepared segments: ChU 6.3.3, ChU 6.4, ChU 6.5, ŚU 4.5
checks.note: All 4 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 6.3.3; ChU 6.4; ChU 6.5; ŚU 4.5). It rests on 4 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: True and transformed lands; womb-birth and the borderland

definitions.definition: Those who aspire with doubt of the Buddha's wisdom are born in palaces or closed lotuses where for five hundred years they do not see the Buddha — womb-birth or the borderland; those of mixed practice stop in the land of sloth and pride.

The true land (of immeasurable light) is reached by other-power shinjin; self-power practitioners of the 19th and 20th vows are born in the transformed land (womb-palace, borderland, realm of indolence, castle of doubt).

name: The true brāhmaṇa (by conduct, not birth)

definitions.definition: Not shaving, the syllable Oṃ, forest-dwelling or bark garments make the śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, sage or ascetic, but equanimity, chastity, knowledge and austerity; by one's acts one becomes a brāhmaṇa or a śūdra.

name: The true person of no rank

definitions.definition: The one listening to the Dharma here and now, going in and out of the senses, dependent on nothing, yet not to be reified.

relations.note: Linji's 'true person' is not a soul that leaves the body; he calls it a 'dried shit-stick' to prevent reification.

name: Processed mercury (btso thal) and the precious pills

definitions.definition: Mercury, deemed poisonous, is detoxified and processed into an ash that becomes the base of the precious pills; the process is restricted to qualified masters. Restricted: no procedure recorded.

notes: Restricted (metals/mercury).

name: Succession by recognised reincarnation (Dalai and Panchen Lamas)

definitions.definition: Leading lamas are recognised as the rebirths of their predecessors: the Dalai Lamas as emanations of Avalokiteśvara, the Panchen Lamas of Amitābha; the title 'Dalai' dates from Altan Khan's gift to Sönam Gyatso (1578), applied back to his two predecessors.

name: Recognized reincarnation (the tulku system)

definitions.definition: By the tradition's account the Karmapas are the first recognized line of reincarnate teachers: Karma Pakshi as the rebirth of Düsum Khyenpa, Rangjung Dorje recognized by Orgyenpa; Karmapas are said to leave letters predicting their rebirth.

notes: Scholars often date the first formal recognition to Rangjung Dorje; tradition to Karma Pakshi (both recorded).

definitions.definition: The unceasing 'sleep of Śiva-yoga' in which the senses are burnt away and awareness remains (Pattirakiriyār 1–2); 'for those whose sleep is destroyed and who remain in awareness, why seals?' (Kuṭampai 6).

relations.note: a sleep-like absorption with awareness

definitions.definition: Beyond waking, dream and deep sleep: not inward- or outward-knowing, not a mass of cognition, unseen, ungraspable, whose essence is the certainty of the one self, the stilling of the world, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual — 'that is the self, that is to be known' (MāU 7); the measureless (amātra) of Om (MāU 12); 'the fourth is greater than these' (MaiU 7.11).
The haṭha texts use 'turyā/turya' as a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4) and locate it between the brows, 'the place of Śiva', where mind dissolves and time is not (4.48).

checks.note: All 3 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (MāU 7; MāU 12; MaiU 7.11). It rests on 5 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: The fourth and beyond the fourth (turīya, turīyātīta)

definitions.definition: The minor Upaniṣads extend the Māṇḍūkya's four states to five (waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth, beyond the fourth), place them in the body (navel/heart, throat, palate, brows, crown) and in the heart lotus, and in the sixteen-measured praṇava map sixteen states; the turīyātīta is also the name of the highest renouncer.
The state beyond the fourth is reached by firmness in the fourth (Bhāskararāya on LSN 63).

Some rest on teachings whose ref was corrected or only partly confirmed; the content is located, only the numbering changes: tea:hamsa-upanisad:3-heart-lotus (corrected).

definitions.definition: Contemplation of impermanence, no refuge, the round of births, aloneness, otherness of self and body, impurity of the body, inflow, stopping, shedding, the universe, the rarity of enlightenment and the well-taught dharma (TS 9.7); the ladder to meditation (Jñānārṇava); subject of Kundakunda's and Kārttikeya's anuprekṣā poems.

name: The six internal and external sense bases (chaḷ ajjhattikabāhirāyatanāni)

definitions.definition: Eye-forms, ear-sounds, nose-smells, tongue-tastes, body-tangibles, mind-dhammas: the third field of dhamma-contemplation, with the fetter that arises dependent on each pair (MN 10:40).

The six internal bases (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) and six external (forms, sounds, odours, tastes, tangibles, mental objects) — 'the all' (SN 35.23); with the six consciousnesses the eighteen elements (MN 115).
