name: The twelve houses and their significations

definitions.definition: Counted from the ascendant, the houses signify: 1 body and self (tanu); 2 wealth, family and speech; 3 siblings and courage; 4 mother, home, happiness; 5 children, intellect and merit of past lives; 6 enemies, disease, debt; 7 spouse; 8 longevity and death; 9 fortune, dharma, teacher and father; 10 action and position; 11 gains; 12 loss, expense and liberation (BJ 1.15–16; BPHS 11–23).

notes: Significations beyond BJ's house-names follow standard later texts (BPHS 11–23) from memory.

name: The twelve Kālīs of the Krama

definitions.definition: Twelve goddesses as the phases of cognition: Sṛṣṭikālī, Raktakālī, Sthitināśakālī, Yamakālī, Saṃhārakālī, Mṛtyukālī, Rudrakālī, Mārtaṇḍakālī, Paramārkakālī, Kālāgnirudrakālī, Mahākālakālī, Mahābhairavacaṇḍograghorakālī (TĀ 4.148-172; Kramastotra 15-27).

notes: The first six names and the phases are confirmed by TĀ 4.148-154 and the Kramastotra; the forms of names 7-12 (esp. Rudrakālī vs Bhadrakālī, and the full name of the twelfth) are reconstructed - moderate confidence.

name: The twelve topics (lakṣaṇas) of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra

definitions.definition: Means of knowledge, distinction, subsidiarity, prompting, sequence, eligibility, general and specific transfer, modification, cancellation, single performance and incidental benefit — the subjects of the twelve adhyāyas.

name: The twelve vows of the householder

definitions.definition: Five small vows, three supplementary vows and four disciplinary vows (TS 7.20–21 names the seven śīlas: directions, region, purposeless harm, equanimity, holy-day fasting, limiting consumables, sharing with guests); the grouping into guṇa- and śikṣā-vratas differs between authors (Samantabhadra, Kundakunda, Hemacandra).
Guṇavratas: directions, consumables, purposeless harm; śikṣāvratas: sāmāyika, limiting region, pauṣadha, sharing with guests (Śvetāmbara standard, recalled).

Amitābha is called by twelve names of light — immeasurable, boundless, unhindered, incomparable, flame-king, pure, joy, wisdom, uninterrupted, inconceivable, ineffable, surpassing sun and moon (Larger Sūtra, praised by Tanluan).
The true Buddha is the Tathāgata of inconceivable light; Shinran's Jōdo wasan praise the twelve lights.

Ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, ageing-and-death (SN 12.1–2); DN 15 gives a version in which consciousness and name-and-form condition each other.

name: The twelve links in the Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: The twelve links are taught conventionally (MMK 26); they arise from conceiving caused things as real and cease when things are seen as empty (ŚS 64–65); grouped as afflictions, actions and suffering in the Pratītyasamutpādahṛdaya.

name: The twelve panths (bārah panth)

definitions.definition: The Nāth order is divided into twelve panths, traditionally set in order by Gorakhnāth; lists commonly include the Satyanāth, Dharamnāth, Rām(ke), Nāṭeśvarī (Lakṣmaṇnāth), Kanthaḍ, Kapilānī, Vairāg (Bharthari), Mannāth, Āī, Pāgal, Dhajnāth and Gaṅgānāth panths, but the lists vary.

notes: Recalled; list to be checked against sources. Several panths claim founders among the nine Nāths.

definitions.definition: Self, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, faults, rebirth, fruit, pain and liberation (NS 1.1.9) — the objects whose true knowledge liberates and whose false knowledge binds (NBh 1.1.9).

The Lord divided himself twelvefold as the signs (SS 12.25); the signs are the limbs of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4), alternately odd/male/cruel and even/female/gentle, movable, fixed and dual in turn, each with a planetary lord, an alternative Greek-derived name (BJ 1.8) and a figure (BJ 1.5).

name: The similes of illusion

definitions.definition: Illusory-body training uses the similes of illusion — mirror image, rainbow, moon in water, dream, magic show, bubble, conjuring, mirage, city of gandharvas, echo — the 'twelve similes' in Tilopa's and the ḍākinī texts.

notes: The texts say 'twelve similes'; only the ones named in the local texts are listed.

definitions.definition: Six external — fasting, eating less, limiting the alms-round, giving up tasty food, lonely lodging, bodily mortification — and six internal — expiation, humility, service, study, abandonment, meditation (TS 9.19–20); austerity both stops and sheds karma (9.3).
The Śvetāmbara list has saṃlīnatā (withdrawal) for lonely lodging and places meditation before abandonment (Uttarādhyayana 30).

Aupapātika, Rājapraśnīya, Jīvājīvābhigama, Prajñāpanā, Sūryaprajñapti, Jambūdvīpaprajñapti, Candraprajñapti, Nirayāvalikā, Kalpāvataṃsikā, Puṣpikā, Puṣpacūlikā, Vṛṣṇidaśā — each paired with an Aṅga (the order of the 5th–7th varies between lists).

name: The twelve great worshippers of Śrīvidyā

definitions.definition: Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, Manmatha, Agastya, Agni, Sūrya, Indra, Skanda, Śiva and Krodhabhaṭṭāraka (Durvāsas), each with a form of the vidyā, derived in the Jñānārṇava (Bhāskararāya).
Light, complete faculties, healing, provision, right views, freedom from punishment, food and clothing for all who keep his name.

name: Twelve yamas and twelve niyamas (Uddhava Gītā)

definitions.definition: Yamas: non-violence, truth, non-stealing, non-attachment, modesty, non-accumulation, faith in dharma, celibacy, silence, steadiness, forbearance, fearlessness. Niyamas: purity (outer and inner), recitation, austerity, fire-offering, faith, hospitality, worship of the Lord, pilgrimage, acting for others, contentment, service of the teacher.

relations.note: different counts and members

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:twelve-yamas-twelve-niyamas-bhagavata
checks.note: BhP 11.19.33-35 verified. The niyama verse names 11 items; a count of twelve comes from taking śauca as outer and inner, as the BBT (vedabase) rendering of 11.19.33-35 does. Śrīdhara's own gloss was not retrieved.

name: The twenty-eight Indian patriarchs and six Chinese patriarchs

definitions.definition: The line from Mahākāśyapa to Bodhidharma (28) and from Bodhidharma to Huineng (six Chinese patriarchs), as listed in the Platform Sūtra and Jingde chuandeng lu; the Dunhuang Platform Sūtra gives a different list counting Huineng as 40th from the seven buddhas.

members: — Chinese: Bodhidharma, Huike, Sengcan, Daoxin, Hongren, Huineng
notes: Tradition's account. Scholarly: the 28-list was fixed in the Baolin zhuan (801); earlier lists (Fu fazang yinyuan zhuan) end with Siṃha.

name: The twenty-eight root qualities of the Digambara monk

definitions.definition: Five great vows, five carefulnesses, restraint of the five senses, six obligatory duties, and seven special rules — plucking the hair, nakedness, not bathing, sleeping on the ground, not cleaning the teeth, eating standing, eating once a day.

Eighteen concretely produced (four great elements, five sensitivities, four objective fields, two sex faculties, heart-base, life faculty, nutriment) and ten non-concretely produced (space, two intimations, three mutabilities, four characteristics).

relations.note: the Abhidhamma analyses matter into momentary elements, not into guṇas of a single prakṛti
the analysis of the aggregate of matter

name: The twenty-eight Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamas (mūlāgamas)
notes: Member order is the Kāmika's. Variant lists: the Kiraṇa has Nārasiṃha (= Sarvokta slot), Bhadra (= Vimala), Candrabhāsa (= Candrajñāna), Vīraja (= Vīra), Saurabheya (= Vātula); the Śrīkaṇṭhīya puts Maukuṭa among the Śivabhedas and has Madgīta, Nārasiṃha, Candrāṃśu, Vīrabhadra, Visara, Vimala and Saurabheya among the Rudrabhedas. Scholarly note: most titles survive, if at all, as later South Indian ritual redactions; early texts survive for the Niśvāsa, Kiraṇa, Svāyambhuva and Raurava (sūtrasaṅgrahas) and some upāgamas.

definitions.definition: Ten Śivabheda and eighteen Rudrabheda root scriptures of the upper stream, each revealed to a Śiva or Rudra and handed down; they are the limbs of Sadāśiva's mantra-body.
The 'ten' and 'eighteen' of Śiva's teaching, whose essence is the Trika (TĀ 1.18).
In each Dvāpara of the Vaivasvata manvantara Śiva incarnates as a yoga-teacher with four disciples; the twenty-eighth and last is Lakulīśa/Nakulīśa at Kāyāvatāra.

name: The twenty (sixteen, eighteen) emptinesses

definitions.definition: The Large Perfection of Wisdom's list of emptinesses in which the bodhisattva trains: of the internal, external, both, emptiness itself, the great, the ultimate, the conditioned, the unconditioned, the absolute, the beginningless, non-rejection, essential nature, all dharmas, own-marks, the non-apprehended, the own-being of non-being — commonly 'up to' this sixteenth — then of being, non-being, own-being and other-being (twenty); the Chinese tradition often counts eighteen.
Candrakīrti expounds the emptinesses of the Perfection of Wisdom — sixteen in detail and four in brief — as the emptiness of persons and phenomena (MA 6.179–223).

notes: Order and list read in the local Kimura e-text (Pañcaviṃśati I).

definitions.definition: The twenty-fifth is the knower, the self that is 'awakening' (budhyamāna), which on knowing itself becomes alone; the twenty-sixth is the ever-awakened (buddha), stainless and eternal, which the twenty-fifth does not know until it awakens to it and attains its state (MBh 12.294.43, 12.296.7–12; Yājñavalkya 12.306).

name: The twenty-five disciples (rje 'bangs nyer lnga)

definitions.definition: The king and subjects who were Padmasambhava's closest disciples, among them Trisong Detsen, Yeshe Tsogyal, Vairocana, Nupchen Sangye Yeshe, Namkhai Nyingpo and Nyak Jñānakumāra.

notes: Full list varies and is not given (gap).

name: The twenty-five mudrās of the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā

definitions.definition: GS 3.1–3 lists twenty-five: mahāmudrā, nabhomudrā, uḍḍīyāna, jālandhara, mūlabandha, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, viparītakaraṇī, yoni, vajrolī, śakticālanī, tāḍāgī, māṇḍukī, śāmbhavī, the five dhāraṇās, aśvinī, pāśinī, kākī, mātaṅgī and bhujaṅginī.

Six objects, six faculties, six consciousnesses and seven elements (including Mahāsthāmaprāpta's recollection of the Buddha and Avalokiteśvara's hearing) by which sages attained penetration; hearing is chosen for this world.

name: The twenty-five principles (pañcaviṃśati-tattva)

definitions.definition: Reality enumerated as twenty-five principles: puruṣa; mūlaprakṛti, which is not a product; seven principles that are both products and producers — mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra and the five subtle elements; and sixteen that are products only — manas, the five sense capacities, the five action capacities and the five gross elements (SK 3, 22; SS 1.61; Tattvasamāsa 1–3). 'The knower of the twenty-five principles is liberated in any stage of life' (verse quoted by Gauḍapāda and the Jayamaṅgalā).

members: 5–9 the five tanmātras (sound, touch, form, taste, smell) — producers and products
11–15 the five buddhīndriyas (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose) — products only
16–20 the five karmendriyas (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals) — products only
21–25 the five mahābhūtas (space, air, fire, water, earth) — products only

relations.note: Śaiva schemes of thirty-six principles include these twenty-five as their lower principles (the Śaiva account; interpretive link)

name: The twenty-four conditions (paccaya) of the Paṭṭhāna

definitions.definition: Root, object, predominance, proximity, contiguity, conascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, prenascence, postnascence, repetition, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, absence, disappearance, non-disappearance; all reducible to four (object, decisive support, kamma, presence).

Seventeen named in VS 1.1.5 (colour, taste, smell, touch, number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, nearness, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort) and seven more included by 'ca' (heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, impression, merit, demerit, sound) (Praśastapāda).

relations.note: Vaiśeṣika guṇa = quality residing in substance; Sāṃkhya guṇa = constituent of prakṛti. Same word, different concept.

definitions.definition: Objections resting on mere similarity or dissimilarity (NS 1.2.18), listed in NS 5.1.1.
Twenty-four sites of India (Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, Oḍḍiyāna, Arbuda … Kulatā) in three wheels of the Heruka maṇḍala, each with a ḍāka and yoginī; inwardly places of the body.

relations.note: The Buddhist and Śaiva/Śākta pīṭha lists share many names (Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri); see brw:saiva-pithas-to-cakrasamvara.

name: The twenty-four principles (epic Sāṃkhya)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13.6–7: the field is listed as the great elements, ahaṅkāra, buddhi, the unmanifest, the ten senses and the one, the five ranges of the senses, with desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, sentience and steadiness; the text does not number them.

The Sāṃkhyas enumerate twenty-four principles together with prakṛti (the unmanifest), the twenty-fifth being beyond them (MBh 12.294.42); the Gītā's field lists the great elements, ego, intellect, the unmanifest, the ten organs and mind, and the five objects (BhG 13.5).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The epic's lists vary between dialogues (e.g. 'eight prakṛtis and sixteen modifications'); the member list here follows BhG 13.5.

name: Caraka's and Suśruta's scheme of principles

definitions.definition: Caraka: the eightfold prakṛti (unmanifest, buddhi, ego-sense, five elements) and sixteen modifications (ten senses, mind, five objects); the unmanifest is the knower of the field (Śā 1.61-65); creation and dissolution follow (1.66-69). Suśruta: twenty-four principles and the person as the twenty-fifth (Su Śā 1.3-9).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's scheme; Caraka merges puruṣa with the unmanifest (24 not 25)

name: The avadhūta's twenty-four teachers

definitions.definition: The twenty-four teachers from whose ways the avadhūta brāhmaṇa learned freedom, told to King Yadu: earth (forbearance; its mountains and trees: living for others), air (content with bare sustenance; unattached among objects), sky (the self pervasive and untouched), water (purity that purifies), fire (taking all without taint; the Lord in all forms), moon (changes belong to the body), sun (taking and giving without attachment; one appearing many), pigeon (ruin by excessive attachment), python (accepting what comes), ocean (unmoved by gain and loss), moth (lured by forms to ruin), honeybee (begging a little from many; taking the essence of all scriptures; not hoarding), elephant (bound by touch of the female), honey-gatherer (hoarded wealth enjoyed by others), deer (lured by song), fish (the tongue), Piṅgalā (hope is misery, hopelessness bliss), osprey (possession invites attack), child (carefree bliss), maiden with bangles (live alone), arrow-maker (one-pointed absorption), serpent (homeless solitude), spider (the Lord emits and withdraws the world), wasp (one becomes what one dwells on). His own body is a further teacher of dispassion; knowledge from one teacher alone is not firm, for Brahman is sung in many ways.
Bodhya names six teachers — Piṅgalā, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden (Mahābhārata 12.171.61).

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:twenty-four-teachers-of-the-avadhuta
checks.note: List verified at BhP 11.7.33-34 (24 names); Bodhya's six at MBh CE 12.171.61. All six appear among the 24, with sāraṅga as the bee (madhukṛt).

notes: List verified in the local Bhāgavata e-text (11.7.33-34). The six teachers of Bodhya are a subset (Piṅgalā, osprey, serpent, bee, arrow-maker, maiden).

name: The twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras of this era

definitions.definition: Ṛṣabha, Ajita, Sambhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Padmaprabha, Supārśva, Candraprabha, Suvidhi (Puṣpadanta), Śītala, Śreyāṃsa, Vāsupūjya, Vimala, Ananta, Dharma, Śānti, Kunthu, Ara, Malli, Munisuvrata, Nami, Nemi (Ariṣṭanemi), Pārśva and Mahāvīra (Vardhamāna); twenty-four appear in every half-cycle in Bharata and Airāvata, while in Mahāvideha Tīrthaṅkaras are always present.
The nineteenth, Mallī, was a woman.
All were men; they reached nirvāṇa at Aṣṭāpada (Ṛṣabha), Campā (Vāsupūjya), Ūrjayanta (Nemi), Pāvā (Mahāvīra) and Sammeda Śikhara (the other twenty).
Heavy/light, cold/hot, unctuous/dry, slow/sharp, stable/mobile, soft/hard, clear/slimy, smooth/rough, subtle/gross, dense/liquid (Ca Sū 25.36; AHS Sū 1.18).
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa, Vasiṣṭha (YS 1.4–5).

checks.note: YS 1.4–5 lists exactly the twenty named, in the same order. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:yajnavalkyasmrti:1.4-5.

name: The twenty-nine adornments of Sukhāvatī

definitions.definition: Seventeen adornments of the land, eight of the Buddha, four of the bodhisattvas; together they enter the one dharma-phrase.

members: 17 of the land (purity, measure, nature, form, manifold things, colour, touch, water/ground/space, rain, light, sound, lord, retinue, enjoyment, no difficulties, gate of the great meaning, fulfilment of wishes)
8 of the Buddha (seat, body, speech, mind, assembly, leader, lord, unfailing sustaining power)

name: The twenty-one kinds of pain

definitions.definition: The pain whose absolute cessation is the goal is divided into twenty-one kinds (Vācaspati); later manuals list them as the body, the six senses (with mind), their six objects, the six cognitions, pleasure and pain itself; birth itself is pain (NS 4.1.55).

notes: The number is confirmed in the Tātparyaṭīkā e-text; the member list is recalled from later manuals.

name: The twenty-seven (twenty-eight) lunar mansions and their deities

definitions.definition: The moon's path is divided into 27 asterisms of 13°20′ (28 with Abhijit in muhūrta), each with a presiding deity; the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa lists them from Kṛttikā (Agni) to Bharaṇī (Yama), later texts from Aśvinī (the Aśvins) to Revatī (Pūṣan); the Lord divided himself into them (SS 12.25).
The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna expounds the asterisms, their deities and the fortunes of those born under them, in the mouth of the outcaste king Triśaṅku.

Ādima, Candrasena, Laṅkeśa, Viśārada, Kapālin, Matta, Māṇḍavya, Bhāskara, Śūrasena, Ratnakośa, Śambhu, Sāttvika, Naravāhana, Indrada, Gomukha, Kambali, Vyāḍi, Nāgārjuna, Surānanda, Nāgabodhi, Yaśodhana, Khaṇḍa, Kāpālika, Brahmā, Govinda, Lampaka and Hari (RRS 1.2-5).

relations.note: overlaps (Nāgārjuna, Kambali, Govinda) with the HYP list of siddhas

name: The twenty-six qualities of a Vaiṣṇava

definitions.definition: Kindness, truthfulness, equality, mildness, freedom from pride, dependence on Kṛṣṇa alone and the rest.
Faculties by dominance: six sense, female, male, life, five feelings, five spiritual, three pure.
Listed in NS 5.2.1 and defined in 5.2.2–25.

Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, insect bites, nakedness, discontent, women, wandering, sitting, lying, abuse, injury, begging, not obtaining, illness, grass-pricks, dirt, honour, intelligence, ignorance and lack of vision, to be endured for the path and for shedding (TS 9.8–9); eleven are said to occur in the Jina (9.11), a sūtra read differently by the two sects.
Eleven of them (those due to feeling-karma, including hunger and thirst) actually occur in the omniscient; 'nakedness' may be borne as scanty clothing.
In the omniscient the eleven are only figurative; 'nakedness' means complete nudity.

name: The virtues called knowledge (BhG 13.7–11)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13.8–12 (vulgate 13.7–11): twenty dispositions are declared 'knowledge' (jñāna), and what is other than them 'ignorance'. The verse lists them without further grouping.

Absence of pride and pretence, non-harm, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-control, dispassion, absence of ego, seeing the evil of birth, death, age, disease and pain, non-attachment, evenness, unswerving devotion, love of solitude, constancy in self-knowledge and insight into the goal of truth — these are called knowledge (BhG 13.7–11).

members: indriyārtheṣu vairāgya (dispassion toward the objects of the senses)
janma-mṛtyu-jarā-vyādhi-duḥkha-doṣānudarśana (keeping in view the evil of birth, death, old age, sickness and pain)
anabhiṣvaṅga toward son, wife, home and the like (absence of clinging)
nityaṃ sama-cittatvam iṣṭāniṣṭopapattiṣu (constant evenness of thought when the wanted or unwanted befalls)
mayi ananya-yogena bhaktir avyabhicāriṇī (unswerving devotion to the Lord through a yoga with no other)
aratir jana-saṃsadi (no delight in gatherings of people)
adhyātma-jñāna-nityatva (constancy in the knowledge of what pertains to the self)
tattva-jñānārtha-darśana (keeping in view the aim of the knowledge of reality)

notes: The count of twenty depends on counting asakti and anabhiṣvaṅga separately and the two items of 13.12 separately; the text itself gives no number. This edition numbers the verses 13.8–12.
alt_notes: Commentators count the items as twenty; the count is not in the text.

name: Coded and paradoxical speech across the families

definitions.definition: Intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā): substitute words for substances, places and acts, to be kept from the unconsecrated.
Upside-down speech: the upturned well in the sky, dying the sweet death.
Kaula etymologies and code-words give outer terms an inner yogic sense.
Ulaṭbāṃsī: Kabīr's paradox-riddles inherited from the Nāths.
The collection of merit gives rise to the form bodies and the collection of wisdom to the truth body (RĀ 3.12–13).

name: The two ālayas: ālaya-consciousness and ālaya-wisdom

definitions.definition: The basis of all is twofold: the ālaya-consciousness (kun gzhi rnam shes), conventional ground of imprints, and the ālaya-wisdom (kun gzhi ye shes), the ultimate buddha-nature.

relations.note: the Laṅkāvatāra calls the tathāgatagarbha 'ālayavijñāna'; the Jonang reserve buddha-nature for the ālaya-wisdom
the Yogācāra store-consciousness is only the conventional ālaya for the Jonang

definitions.definition: The ordinary person struck by painful bodily feeling adds mental grief like a second dart; the noble disciple feels only the bodily one (SN 36.6).

name: The two aspects of merit transfer: going and returning

definitions.definition: Going: dedicating merit to be born together with all beings; returning: coming back from the Pure Land to teach (Tanluan; Vasubandhu's fifth gate; 22nd vow).
Both are Amida's transfer to beings.

name: The two birds on one tree

definitions.definition: Two birds, companions, on one tree: one eats the sweet fig, the other looks on without eating (RV 1.164.20); the lord, guardian of the world, has entered 'me the simple one' (1.164.21).

Two birds, companions, cling to the same tree; one eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating; the one who grieves, seeing the other, the Lord, and his greatness, is freed from sorrow (MuU 3.1.1-2; ŚU 4.6-7, quoting RV 1.164.20); KU 1.3.1 speaks of two, 'shadow and light', drinking in the cave. Later schools read the two birds as jīva and Lord distinct (Dvaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita) or as the reflected and the witness self (Advaita).

relations.note: the image distinguishes two where the mahāvākyas state identity; see dsp:souls-one-or-distinct

notes: The Upaniṣads (Muṇḍaka 3.1.1, Śvetāśvatara 4.6) read the birds as the individual self and the Lord; the Ṛgveda does not name them.

name: The two dharma-bodies (of dharma-nature and of expedient means)

definitions.definition: From the dharma-body of dharma-nature arises the dharma-body of expedient means, which manifests the former; different but inseparable (Tanluan); the adornments enter the one phrase, the uncreated dharma-body of true wisdom (Vasubandhu).
From the formless dharma-body as suchness appeared Dharmākara, who became Amida; Amida is the means to know jinen.

relations.note: a two-body analysis of the buddha as reality and as saving form, beside the three-body scheme

definitions.definition: Entry by principle through faith in the one true nature and wall-gazing; entry by practice through the four practices.

Brahman has two forms: formed and formless, mortal and immortal (BAU 2.3.1; MaiU 6.3); time and the timeless (MaiU 6.15); sound and non-sound, the word-brahman and the highest (MaiU 6.22); Om is the higher and lower brahman (PrU 5.2).

name: The two gates: the holy path and the Pure Land

definitions.definition: Of two excellent dharmas, the holy path (awakening in this world by one's own practice) is hard to realise in the last age; only the Pure Land gate is passable (Daochuo).
Set aside the holy path and enter the Pure Land gate (Senchakushū 1, 16).
Compassion of the path of sages is limited; that of the Pure Land path is thoroughgoing (Tannishō 4); the 'two pairs and four levels' refine the division.

relations.note: Daochuo's two gates restate Nāgārjuna's two paths in terms of the age

name: The two kinds of deep entrusting (nishu jinshin)

definitions.definition: Deep entrusting that one is an ordinary being without escape, and that Amitābha's vow surely saves.
The structure of shinjin: entrusting concerning the person (ki) and concerning the Dharma (hō).

members: entrusting concerning the person (ki no jinshin)
entrusting concerning the Dharma (hō no jinshin)

definitions.definition: Immovable eternity (kūṭastha-nityatā) belongs to puruṣa; transforming eternity (pariṇāmi-nityatā) to the guṇas; both are eternal because their reality is not struck (bhāṣya 4.33).

name: Deliberate and effortless mindfulness

definitions.definition: Mindfulness in Mahāmudrā begins as deliberate, effortful attention and matures into an effortless mindfulness inseparable from awareness itself.

notes: Recalled from Mahāmudrā manuals in substance; locators not known.

definitions.definition: Time is twofold: the time that ends the worlds, and reckonable time, gross (embodied, from the breath) and subtle (unembodied, from the truṭi) (SS 1.10–11); time is without beginning or end and is inferred from the planets and stars (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11).

relations.note: the jyotiṣa analysis of time

name: The two natures of the Lord (aparā and parā prakṛti)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.4–7: the Lord's lower nature is eightfold — earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of 'I' (ahaṅkāra); his higher nature has become the living being and upholds the world. All beings have these two as their source; he is the origin and dissolution of the whole world; nothing is higher than him, and all is strung on him like gems on a thread.

The Lord's lower nature is eightfold — earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, ego — and his higher nature is the life-element that upholds the world; both are the womb of all beings (BhG 7.4–6); he sends forth beings resting on his prakṛti (9.8).

members: parā prakṛti jīvabhūtā (the higher nature, become the living being)
aparā prakṛti: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, ego

definitions.definition: With residue remaining (the living arahant who still experiences the agreeable and disagreeable) and without residue remaining (when all that is felt becomes cool at death) (Iti 44).

name: Two pairs and four levels (nisō shijū)

definitions.definition: Vertical transcending, vertical going out, crosswise going out, crosswise transcending; the primal vow is crosswise transcendence.

name: The two paths after death (bright and dark)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.23–27: the two perennial courses of departing yogins — the bright (śukla): fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course, by which knowers of brahman go to brahman and do not return; and the dark (kṛṣṇa): smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern course, by which the yogin reaches the lunar light and returns. Knowing the two paths, the yogin is not deluded.

The bright path (fire, light, day, bright fortnight, northern course) leads knowers of Brahman to non-return; the dark path (smoke, night, dark fortnight, southern course) to the lunar light and return (BhG 8.23–26); Bhīṣma waits for the northern course to die (MBh 6.114).

members: śukla gati: agni, jyotis, ahaḥ, śukla pakṣa, uttarāyaṇa → brahman, anāvṛtti (8.24, 8.26)
kṛṣṇa gati: dhūma, rātri, kṛṣṇa pakṣa, dakṣiṇāyana → cāndramasaṃ jyotiḥ, āvṛtti (8.25–26)

names.name: śukla-kṛṣṇe gatī (the bright and dark courses, 8.26); sṛtī (the two paths, 8.27)

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, combining extractor B's entry and extractor A's cpt:devayana-pitryana. The Gītā does not use the Upaniṣadic names devayāna and pitṛyāna; its stations parallel Chāndogya 5.10.1–6 and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2.15–16 (the Upaniṣadic doctrine is cpt:devayana-pitryana; flagged for the S5 dedupe/equivalence review).
alt_notes: U05's contribution; the Upaniṣadic doctrine is covered by U03.

name: The two paths: of the fathers and of the gods

definitions.definition: 'I have heard of two paths for mortals, of the fathers and of the gods' (RV 10.88.15); death is sent off by its own path, other than the path of the gods (10.18.1).

notes: The Upaniṣads (BĀU 6.2; ChU 5.10) develop the two paths; that development is U03's.

definitions.definition: Projection (vikṣepa), which creates the world, and veiling (āvaraṇa), which covers knowledge (Rāma to Lakṣmaṇa).

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:two-powers-of-maya
checks.note: AR 3.4.22-24: 'rūpe dve niścite pūrvaṃ māyāyāḥ ... vikṣepāvaraṇe'; vikṣepa projects the world from the subtle body to Brahmā (3.4.23), āvaraṇa veils knowledge (3.4.24).

name: Only two means of valid cognition

definitions.definition: Perception and inference only, because there are only two kinds of object — the particular and the universal; testimony, comparison, presumption and non-perception are included in inference or are not means of knowledge.

relations.note: Dignāga's and Dharmakīrti's critique

definitions.definition: Perception and inference; verbal knowledge is explained by inference (VS 9.18–19 C); testimony, comparison and presumption are included in inference (Praśastapāda).

name: The two schools: physicians (Ātreya) and surgeons (Dhanvantari)

definitions.definition: Caraka refers surgical and cauterizing procedures to 'the Dhānvantarīyas' (Ca Ci 5.44, 5.63); Suśruta makes surgery the root of the teaching (Su Sū 1.10-18).

name: The two seeds of the mind

definitions.definition: The tree of mind grows from two seeds, the vibration of prāṇa and firm conception (vāsanā); stilling either stills the mind, so yogins restrain the breath and give up vāsanās.

queries: local texts at the refs cited by cpt:two-seeds-of-the-mind
checks.note: Rests on tea:moksopaya:5.92.6-27, tea:moksopaya:5.92.28-36; each was located in the local text and matches this entry's statement.

definitions.definition: No self of persons and no self of dharmas.

Selflessness of persons (removing the afflictive obscuration) and selflessness of dharmas (removing the cognitive obscuration); the first is entered through the teaching of aggregates and fields, the second through cognition-only.
Selflessness of persons and of dharmas: the Buddhas taught self, no-self and neither (MMK 18.6); the aggregates, dharmas and the Tathāgata are all without own-nature.
Both are realized by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as well as bodhisattvas (Candrakīrti, MAbh on 1.8).

The perfection of wisdom realizes the selflessness of persons and of phenomena (Jewel Ornament ch.17); Nāropa counts the tīrthikas' self and primordial nature among the views of those deluded about their own mind.
Generation stage (utpattikrama) and completion stage (utpanna-/niṣpannakrama): the first a staircase to the second; their unity is union.

name: The two truths (satyadvaya)

names.name: bden pa gnyis (rang stong / gzhan stong)

definitions.definition: The Buddhas teach relying on two truths, the worldly conventional and the ultimate; without the conventional the ultimate cannot be taught, and without the ultimate nirvāṇa is not reached (MMK 24.8–10).

Each thing has two natures, found by correct and by false seeing (MA 6.23); saṃvṛti is ignorance that covers reality, mutual dependence, or worldly convention (PsP 24.8); reality is beyond the intellect (BCA 9.2).
The conventional divides into correct and incorrect (Jñānagarbha) and is the ladder to the ultimate (Bhāviveka), which divides into nominal and non-nominal.
Conventionally, things are mind-only and satisfy only when unexamined; ultimately even mind lacks own-nature (MAL 64, 92–93).
All the Buddha's teaching rests on the two truths; conventional truth is false or correct, the ultimate one only; conventional truth is the method, the ultimate what arises from the method.
Two natures of each phenomenon, one found by conventional and the other by ultimate valid cognition; mutually compatible, understood together when the analysis of the view is complete.
For Gorampa the ultimate is beyond mind; the conventional is what appears to mind still affected by ignorance.

The sūtras distinguish conventional designation from the ultimate that is inexpressible, neither the same as nor different from the formations (Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 2-3); the ultimate is beyond even the Buddha's words (Saṃvṛtiparamārthasatyanirdeśa).

Conventional truth is empty of its own nature; ultimate truth is empty of other and not of itself. The two are not one entity, yet not different entities: they are different in the sense that their sameness is negated.

Nāropa's View in Brief: conventionally all phenomena are self-aware mind; ultimately that mind, examined, is beyond existence, non-existence, both and neither; their union is appearance-emptiness like a moon in water.

relations.note: Theravāda's ultimate includes real dhammas; Madhyamaka's ultimate is their emptiness
the Kośa's ultimately existent (paramārthasat) dharmas are what Madhyamaka analyses as empty
under P1-level both distinguish worldly usage from the ultimate; Madhyamaka has no positive substrate and no third 'illusory' level; both traditions reject identity

notes: The Madhyamaka systematization belongs to U40.

name: Conventional and ultimate existence in the Kośa

definitions.definition: What loses its identity when broken or analysed (pot, water) exists conventionally; what does not (matter, feeling) exists ultimately.
Expressions like 'the eye sees' are conventions used at will over a mere flow of dharmas.

name: The two truths in the pramāṇa school

definitions.definition: What is capable of causal efficacy is ultimately real; the rest is conventionally real — while, on the higher (cognition-only) level, even the division into grasped and grasper is conventional.

relations.note: Madhyamaka two truths

name: The two truths in the tantras

definitions.definition: Self-consecration (illusory body) is conventional truth, clear light ultimate; their union is the goal.
The Buddha teaches by the two truths; three consecrations are conventional, the fourth ultimate.

name: Conventional and ultimate truth (sammuti- and paramattha-sacca)

definitions.definition: The Buddha taught both in conventional terms (persons, beings) and in ultimate terms (aggregates, dhammas); both are true on their own level; the Abhidhamma is teaching in ultimate terms. 'Chariot' is a mere term; ultimately only its parts, and only mentality-materiality, are found.
Conventions (sammuti) must be used and respected, but the heart that has seen through them is released (vimutti) from them.

relations.note: the suttas' use of worldly expressions without misapprehension is systematized by the commentaries as the two truths

definitions.definition: The enumerated (rnam grangs pa) ultimate is emptiness as the negation of true existence, an object of reasoning; the non-enumerated (rnam grangs ma yin pa) ultimate is the union beyond the four extremes, realized in meditative equipoise.

name: The two vehicles: calm-first and pure insight

definitions.definition: One whose vehicle is calm develops jhāna and then insight; one whose vehicle is pure insight (the dry-insight worker) begins with the four elements; both reach the paths, whose jhāna-level is determined by the insight leading to emergence.
Both vehicles require at least access concentration strong enough to see ultimate realities.
The pure-insight vehicle through momentary concentration is fully valid.

name: The twofold commitment (dvividhā niṣṭhā): jñāna-yoga and karma-yoga

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Kṛṣṇa taught of old a twofold commitment (niṣṭhā): by jñānayoga for the sāṃkhyas and by karmayoga for the yogins (3.3); freedom from action is not reached by not acting, nor perfection by renunciation alone (3.4). Cf. the understanding 'according to sāṃkhya' and 'according to yoga' (2.39).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the childish, not the learned, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as separate; one properly established in even one of them obtains the fruit of both; the place reached by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached by those of Yoga too, and whoever sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees (5.4–5). In context (5.1–6; cf. 3.3) Sāṃkhya stands with the renunciation of actions and knowledge, Yoga with the yoga of action.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Chs. 4–6 contribution, from extractor A's cpt:unity-of-samkhya-and-yoga-gita (its sentence on 6.2 is left out: 6.2 identifies renunciation with yoga and does not mention Sāṃkhya).

definitions.definition: Saṃnyāsa is laying aside desire-prompted actions, tyāga relinquishing the fruit of all actions (BhG 18.2); obligatory acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be abandoned (18.5); relinquishment is threefold by the guṇas (18.7–9); the true renouncer is the one who acts without depending on the fruit (6.1).

name: Types of person (puggala) in the Abhidhamma

definitions.definition: Persons designated by attainment and disposition: the worldling, the one at change-of-lineage, the trainees, the faith- and Dhamma-followers, the body-witness, the one attained to view, those liberated by faith, by wisdom and both ways, the kinds of stream-enterer and non-returner.

name: Brahman's twofold mark (ubhaya-liṅga): free of all defect, full of auspicious qualities

definitions.definition: Brahman is at once opposed to all that is evil and the sole abode of infinite auspicious qualities; 'nirguṇa' texts deny only prākṛta, defiling qualities, so Brahman is both 'nirguṇa' and 'saguṇa' in these two senses.

relations.note: the Lord is free of prakṛti's guṇas

definitions.definition: The Āḻvārs' Tamil hymns, above all the Tiruvāymoḻi, are a Veda in Tamil equal to the Sanskrit; the teachers comment on both.
The Tamil Veda reveals the heart of the Sanskrit and, by its author's lowly birth, the Lord's accessibility.

name: The two realms of the Lord (nitya-vibhūti and līlā-vibhūti)

definitions.definition: The Lord's domain is twofold: the eternal realm of pure sattva (Vaikuṇṭha), a quarter beyond, and the realm of play made of prakṛti and time, where the world is created and souls transmigrate.
(As reported) Fool and wise alike are annihilated at the breaking of the body; the person is made of four elements that return to their masses.
One of the sixty-two grounds (seven forms) and one of the two extremes avoided by the middle.
(As reported) Death is the end; the body burnt does not return.

relations.note: the Pali 'annihilation' and the Lokāyata 'no other world' state one position from two sides (death of the person / absence of a world beyond)

definitions.definition: The remainder of the sacrifice praised as the ground in which name and form, the world, the gods and the rites rest (AVŚ 11.7).

name: Udayana's proofs of Īśvara (NK 5.1)

definitions.definition: The all-knowing maker is proved from: (1) the world's being an effect (kārya); (2) the combining of atoms at creation (āyojana); (3) the support of the world (dhṛti) and (4) its destruction ('ādi'); (5) traditional skills and usage of words (pada); (6) the validity of the Veda (pratyaya); (7) scripture (śruti); (8) the Veda's consisting of sentences (vākya); (9) special number — the magnitude of dyads, which requires an enumerating cognition at creation (saṃkhyāviśeṣa). The five clusters first answer five objections.

notes: Counted as eight or nine depending on whether 'ādi' is taken separately; glosses follow the usual explanation.

name: Enumeration, definition, examination (the method of the śāstra)

definitions.definition: The śāstra proceeds by naming (uddeśa), defining (lakṣaṇa) and examining (parīkṣā) (NBh 1.1.3); book 1 of the sūtra enumerates and defines, books 2–5 examine.
(Jain report) Five kinds of denier — staff, rope, thief, partial, total.
Riddling paradox used to point to the reversed practice — the woman enjoyed by two (GŚ 56), the inverted well in the sky (Gorakh Bānī).

Riddling songs of impossible images (the lion grazing cows, the son born before the mother, the guru at the disciple's feet) that turn ordinary perception upside down; 'whoever understands this song is liberated'.

name: Reversal (ulṭā sādhanā) and the upward flow

definitions.definition: Turning downward currents upward: the reversed practice with sun above and moon below (GŚ 59), drawing apāna upward (GŚ 37), the upward flow of seed (GŚ 65) — expressed in Hindi as ulṭā sādhanā.
Practice goes upstream against the natural downward flow of desire and seed, as a fish swims against the tide; the one who goes with the current is lost. Doctrine only (restricted).
Kāma is reversed and refined into prema.

relations.note: The haṭha and Nāth idea of the upward-turned seed, in a devotional and couple-based frame; the Bāuls would not accept a purely yogic reading.

definitions.definition: Regarding all phenomena as dreams, examining the unborn nature of awareness, letting even the remedy be released in its own place, resting in the nature of the all-base, and being an illusory being between sessions.

Whether the world is eternal or not, finite or infinite, whether the soul is the same as the body or different, whether the Tathāgata exists after death, does not, both or neither — set aside as not beneficial and not leading to nibbāna (MN 63; MN 72; SN 44.10; DN 9); the blind men and the elephant (Ud 6.4).

name: Understanding, experience and realization (go myong rtogs)

definitions.definition: Intellectual understanding (go ba) is like a patch that falls off, experience (myong ba) like mist that fades, realization (rtogs pa) is unchanging; meditative experiences are not to be mistaken for realization.
At the death of the arahant Vakkali (and Godhika) Māra searches for his consciousness in vain; he attained final nibbāna with consciousness unestablished (SN 22.87).

name: The union of the Kadam and Mahāmudrā streams

definitions.definition: Gampopa joined the Kadam graded path and monastic discipline with Milarepa's Mahāmudrā and six yogas ('the two streams mixed'); the Jewel Ornament is its textual form.

name: The union of method and wisdom

definitions.definition: Wisdom without method and method without wisdom are both bondage; method is all the perfections other than wisdom.
Neither method without wisdom nor wisdom without method liberates the bodhisattva (Bhāvanākrama II); the Buddha's teaching has emptiness and compassion as its essence (RĀ 4.96).

name: The union of wisdom and means (prajñopāya)

definitions.definition: Wisdom (emptiness, feminine) and means (compassion, bliss, masculine) joined — the meaning of 'Hevajra', of the vajra and bell, of deity couples; union is 'knowing the unity of wisdom and compassion' (Pañcakrama 5.7).
Emptiness without compassion is not the supreme path; compassion alone keeps one in saṃsāra; joining the two, one abides in neither (People Dohā v15–17).

name: The unity of guru, mantra, deity and self

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the inner self comes from realizing the oneness of guru, mantra, deity, self, mind and breath (PKS 1.11); the Kaula meaning of the mantra is the unity of cakra, deity, vidyā, guru and self (YH 2.51-52).

name: Unmanī / manonmanī — the state beyond mind

definitions.definition: The state beyond mind: it cannot arise while the channels are impure (HYP 2.4); it is the steadiness of mind when breath moves in the middle (2.42); a synonym of samādhi and rājayoga (4.3–4); through it duality is not perceived (4.61) and the body becomes like a log (4.106); it sprouts from tattva, haṭha and detachment (4.104).
The state in which mind has dissolved (unmanībhāva); reached by nāda and tāraka; beyond merit and sin; the supreme state of Viṣṇu (Amṛtabindu 4; Nādabindu 48; Yogaśikhā 6.61; Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa).
Unmanī is a synonym of samādhi and rājayoga (HYP 4.3); the mind made void of void, motionless, not roused even by drums (KJN 14.83–85).

One whose mind is beyond mind is liberated here (KJN 13.5); placing the mind in the heart until unmanī one turns back death (6.27); the 'great pervasion' in which one neither hears nor sees (17.16); the fourth mind beyond the three guṇas (Jñānakārikā 2.8).

relations.standpoint: the HYP's list of synonyms of samādhi

definitions.definition: Mind and giving not resting on any object; the Tathāgata's mind stands nowhere; Kumārajīva's 'produce a mind that abides nowhere'.
Things, the self, the Tathāgata and emptiness itself exist as designations made in dependence on a basis, as a chariot on its parts (MMK 24.18; 22.8; PsP on 24.18).

relations.note: PsP on 24.18

name: The upāgamas (upabhedas) of the Siddhānta
members: Mṛgendra (classed under the Kāmika by tradition)
Kālajñāna / Uttara (Vātula; cf. the Kālottara corpus)
notes: Only the better-known upāgamas are listed here; the full per-Āgama lists are in the structure.upabhedas_kamika field of each src entry.

definitions.definition: Subsidiary scriptures attached to the 28 root Āgamas; the Kāmika names them one by one (206 by its stated counts; tradition usually says 207); the Kiraṇa calls any division within a division an upabheda and says the divisions differ in knowledge, not in fruit.
Knowledge produced by similarity: seeing the gavaya, one knows the remembered cow as similar to it.
The teacher becomes pregnant with the pupil and brings him forth with the Sāvitrī on the third night (ŚB 11.5.4.12).
The Vedic birth in which the Sāvitrī is mother and the teacher father (MDh 2.170); the best birth, given by knowledge (ĀpDh 1.1.1.16–17); due at eight, eleven or twelve (MDh 2.36; ĀśGS 1.19).

name: Teacher and pupil in the Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The pupil approaches 'with fuel in hand' (MuU 1.2.12; PrU 1.1; ChU 8.7.2; KauU 1.1); the teacher must be learned in the Veda and established in brahman (MuU 1.2.12); pupils are tested — a year of austerity (PrU 1.2), truthfulness (ChU 4.4), 101 years of study (ChU 8.7-12); knowledge from a teacher leads most surely (ChU 4.9.3); 'one who has a teacher knows' (ChU 6.14.2); lineage lists (vaṃśa) trace teachings back to brahman (BAU 2.6, 4.6, 6.5; ChU 3.11.4, 8.15; MuU 1.1.1-2); devotion to the teacher as to God (ŚU 6.23).

definitions.definition: Secondary Purāṇas told by sages or by Vyāsa's disciples (VP 3.6.23; KūP 1.11.280); the Kūrma lists eighteen (Sanatkumāra, Nārasiṃha, Skānda, Śivadharma, Āścarya, Nāradīya, Kāpila, Mānava, Auśanasa, Brahmāṇḍa, Vāruṇa, Kālikā, Māheśvara, Sāmba, Saura, Pārāśara, Mārīca, Bhārgava); the Matsya adds that every Purāṇa apart from the eighteen issued from them (53.64).

definitions.definition: Venerating something as brahman or as the self: name, speech, mind and the rest (ChU 7), the sun (ChU 3.19), mind and space (ChU 3.18), the six teachers' views (BAU 4.1), 'as the self' (BAU 1.4.7); each has a stated fruit. Kena 1.5 denies that brahman is 'this that people venerate here'.

definitions.definition: Meditation on the qualified Brahman or a symbol, seated and one-pointed, until death, purifies and steadies the mind and leads to the Brahma-world; meditation on the attributeless leads to knowledge (Pañcadaśī 9).

name: The four Upavedas

definitions.definition: Sciences attached to the four Vedas: medicine (āyurveda), archery/warfare (dhanurveda), music (gāndharvaveda) and statecraft or architecture (arthaśāstra / sthāpatyaveda), as listed in the Caraṇavyūha.

notes: Assignments vary between sources; not verified here.

checks.note: The four upavedas and their attachment to the four Vedas are confirmed: āyurveda to the Ṛg, dhanurveda to the Yajus, gāndharvaveda to the Sāman, and the fourth to the Atharvan. The fourth is sthāpatya/śilpa in the Caraṇavyūha and arthaśāstra in other lists (Dharmawiki; Hindupedia). This is the variation the entry's hedge 'arthaśāstra / sthāpatyaveda' and its note already record. Nothing to correct; the Caraṇavyūha text itself was not read.

name: Samādhi from means and from birth (upāya-pratyaya, bhava-pratyaya)

definitions.definition: For the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti the state has becoming as its cause (1.19); for yogins it arises from means — faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi, insight (1.20).
Means that transform what binds into what frees — deity, mantra, bliss — always joined with wisdom.
The defining mark of the soul: its activity of knowing (eight kinds: five knowledges and three erroneous) and perceiving (four kinds: visual, non-visual, clairvoyant, omniscient) (TS 2.8–9).

name: Reversing the downward flow: the upward current in the body

definitions.definition: The moon's nectar, consumed by the sun below, is to be kept and turned back; the breath is forced into the central channel.
The fire of caṇḍālī at the navel melts the moon at the head; the drops descend through the four joys and are drawn back upward.
The reversal (ulṭā) of the current to the sky-circle where the nectar dwells.
The upstream journey (ujān) against the current, to the source.

notes: Summary only; sexual and retention practices associated with the theme are restricted and not described.

definitions.definition: Examination of urine in three phases for colour, vapour, odour, bubbles, sediment and film, and the reading of spirit influences.

The perfected yogin may leave the body at will and dissolve in the supreme Brahman, or keep it (DYŚ 115–118); the Haṭhatattvakaumudī has a chapter on a breath practice for utkrānti. RESTRICTED: recorded as teaching only; no method.
At death the tip of the heart lights up and the knower leaves through the crown channel by the power of knowledge and remembrance, helped by the grace of Hari in the heart.

By casting the breath upward the skull splits and the jīva goes to the spotless and becomes the all-pervading Śiva (KJN 20.1–3); at the fall of the body the skull splits for one who has the nyāsa (13.8); once the body is left the jīva is called supreme Śiva (6.7). Restricted: no method recorded.

relations.standpoint: departure through the crown at death
relations.note: yogic departure at death is also taught in Upaniṣadic and Purāṇic yoga

name: Departure of the soul at death

definitions.definition: The knower or surrendered soul leaves through the channel of the head, the Lord in the heart illuminating the way; others leave by other channels to further births.

name: The triple mark of the existent

definitions.definition: Whatever exists is endowed with origination, cessation and persistence (TS 5.30): permanent as substance, changing as modes — the ontological root of many-sidedness and the Jain answer to both eternalism and momentariness.

relations.note: The triple mark grounds many-sided predication (TS 5.32).

definitions.definition: A portent is a change of nature: men's misdeeds displease the gods, who produce heavenly, atmospheric and earthly portents announcing calamity; the king must counter them with pacification; the earthly yield to it, the atmospheric soften, and even the heavenly are calmed by great gifts and oblations (BS 45.1–7); moving, sweating or weeping images foretell ruin (BS 45.8). The great digest of such omens is the Adbhutasāgara.
Favourable cultivation of Kṛṣṇa free of other desires, uncovered by knowledge and works; causeless (ahaitukī).
Speech was Prajāpati's own and his second, which he sent forth to pervade all (PB 20.14.2); speech is the consecration (KB 7.1); correct speech distinguishes gods from Asuras (ŚB 3.2.1.23–24).
The grammarians read the 'four horns' verse as speech, 'the great god who entered mortals', identity with whom grammar aims at (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:pancavimsa-brahmana:20.14.2 (confirmed); tea:kausitaki-brahmana:7.1 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:3.2.1.23-24 (confirmed); tea:mahabhasya:paspasa/4 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Speech is a goddess and cosmic power: she moves with all the gods, is queen and first of the worshipful, the power by which beings eat, see, breathe and hear, who makes whom she loves a seer (RV 10.125); she was found entered into the seers and reveals her body to some like a bride (10.71); gods begot her and animals speak her (8.100.11); the syllable in highest heaven bears the verses (1.164.39); she has four quarters, three hidden (1.164.45).

relations.note: The four quarters are the Saṃhitā's analysis of speech.

name: The vacana as speech of experience

definitions.definition: The vacana is spontaneous speech from experience in the mother tongue, sealed with the aṅkita; speech must be pure as a string of pearls and matched by deeds.
Practice impelled by scriptural command where spontaneous attraction is absent.
Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta and Aniruddha, invoked in worship (Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Aniruddha placed in the directions).

name: Four forms of liberation in the Vaikhānasa tradition
notes: Recalled from Vaikhānasa literature (Vimānārcanakalpa); correlation of these with particular means is not recorded here (unverified).

definitions.definition: Attaining Viṣṇu's world (sālokya), nearness (sāmīpya), likeness of form (sārūpya) and union (sāyujya).
(Jain report) The assembly of those for whom discipline or veneration alone is the way: 32 kinds.

Lower: the consciousness of mastery in one free of thirst for seen and heard-of objects (YS 1.15); higher: freedom from thirst for the guṇas from knowing the puruṣa (YS 1.16); Vyāsa: the higher is only the clearness of knowledge, and kaivalya is inseparable from it (YBh 1.16).

Lower dispassion is the consciousness of mastery of one free of thirst for seen and scriptural objects (1.15); higher dispassion is freedom from thirst for the guṇas, from discernment of the puruṣa — the utmost limit of knowledge, inseparable from kaivalya (1.16, YBh 1.16); dispassion even toward the highest powers yields kaivalya (3.50). Vācaspati divides the lower into four stages (see pth:vacaspati-four-stages-of-vairagya).
Worldly happiness is a barley grain, sorrow a mountain; the avadhūta's teachers teach detachment.
No one in the world is wholly happy; inquire and see.

name: The self common to all men (vaiśvānara)

definitions.definition: The self conceived as the whole cosmos — sky its head, sun its eye, wind its breath, space its trunk, water its bladder, earth its feet — of which each partial meditation grasps only one part (ChU 5.11-18); the waking quarter of the self (MāU 3); the digestive fire (BAU 5.9).
Bhagavad Gītā 15.14: Kṛṣṇa, becoming Vaiśvānara and dwelling in the bodies of breathing beings, joined with prāṇa and apāna, digests the fourfold food.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

All 3 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 5.11-18; MāU 3; BĀU 5.9). It rests on 3 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

definitions.definition: The branch that gives potency, offspring and continuity of lineage (Ca Ci 1.1.9-12; Su Sū 1.8). Summary only.

name: The vajra body (channels, winds and drops) in the Kagyu

definitions.definition: The body abides as channels (rtsa), winds (rlung), drops (thig le/bodhicitta) and the five enlightenments, with the mind as great wisdom dwelling in it (bka' dpe phyi ma); the central channel with left and right channels and four wheels; its formation from confusion is set out in the 3rd Karmapa's Profound Inner Meaning and Yangönpa's Hidden Description.

members: rtsa (channels): dbu ma, rkyang ma, ro ma

relations.note: Buddhist form of the channel system
four wheels in this system

name: Channels, winds and essences in Anuyoga

definitions.definition: The completion-stage body of three channels (central, right, left), the wheels, the winds that move in them and the essences (thig le); worked with in Anuyoga to bring the winds into the central channel and give rise to bliss-emptiness.

name: The vajra body in the Lamdre

definitions.definition: The body as the method continuum: channels (with the three principal channels and the four channel-wheels or 'precious palaces'), winds and drops; the elements 'gather' in successive stages, the channel-knots are loosened, winds cease by measured finger-widths and drops are stabilised at the places marking the grounds.

relations.note: the Sakya/Hevajra presentation

definitions.definition: By vajra-yoga in the innate centre of the bone-circle a man becomes like a thunderbolt; the body stands like vajra and has no dissolution (KJN 15.7–26, 'paramavajrīkaraṇa').

Realization is expressed in spontaneous songs continuing the Indian dohās — Tilopa's and Saraha's songs, Milarepa's Hundred Thousand Songs, the Kagyu Gurtso; the song is itself a teaching and a transmission.

name: The Vajrayoginī cycles

definitions.definition: Sādhana lineages of Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī, notably those of Nāropa (the Nāro Khecarī), Indrabhūti and Maitrīpa, with the 'headless' form linked to Lakṣmīṅkarā and the sisters Mekhalā and Kanakhalā; collected in the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā.

notes: The threefold list (Nāropa, Indrabhūti, Maitrīpa) follows Tibetan presentations; not checked in a text.

definitions.definition: A group of words is one sentence when it serves one purpose and its parts need each other if separated; otherwise the sentence splits (MS 2.1.46–47); arthavādas are one sentence with injunctions (MS 1.2.7).

The goddess as a young girl (Vālai, Bālā), 'mother Maṉōṉmaṇi, the supreme light', worshipped at the root with three syllables and on the Meru of forty-three triangles; she stands in the state beyond qualities.

relations.note: Caṭṭaimuṉi's Meru of 43 triangles is the Śrīcakra; Vālai is Bālā Tripurasundarī of Śrīvidyā

definitions.definition: Validity is intrinsic (svataḥ) both in arising and in being known; invalidity is extrinsic, due to a defect in the cause or a sublating cognition.
Every experience is valid; error is a pair of cognitions not distinguished, not a false cognition.

Lists at the ends of Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka sections naming the teachers from whom a teaching was received, traced back through seers and gods to Prajāpati and Brahman the self-existent (ŚB 10.6.5.9; 14.9.4.33; Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa; JUB).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:satapatha-brahmana:10.6.5.9 (confirmed); tea:satapatha-brahmana:14.9.4.33 (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Each sign is divided into equal parts ruled by planets, each division forming a chart for a domain of life: six in Varāhamihira (BJ 1.9), sixteen 'spoken by Brahmā' in Parāśara — sign, horā, drekkāṇa, fourth, seventh, navāṃśa, tenth, twelfth, sixteenth, twentieth, twenty-fourth, twenty-seventh, thirtieth, fortieth, forty-fifth and sixtieth (BPHS 6.2–4).

name: The vārī and its inner meaning

definitions.definition: The walk to Paṇḍharpūr is outwardly a pilgrimage, inwardly the return of the soul to its mother's home; the saints' company on the road and the name sung together are themselves the tīrtha, and all walk as equals.

relations.note: outer pilgrimage read inwardly: the saints and the name as the true tīrtha

definitions.definition: Points where life-breath concentrates; 108 in the Siddha count (12 paṭu, 96 toṭu varmam); used in healing (varma maruttuvam) and in the martial art; ascribed to Agastya. Summary only; no locations or techniques.

relations.note: Āyurveda's marmas: related idea, different count

name: The varṇas by guṇa and action

definitions.definition: The fourfold order is created by the Lord according to guṇa and action (BhG 4.13), each varṇa's duties arising from its nature (18.41–44); yet the epic also teaches that varṇa arose from actions in a world wholly of Brahman (MBh 12.181.10) and that conduct makes the brāhmaṇa (3.177.16); service is the śūdra's dharma (12.60.27–28).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.13: the fourfold class order (cāturvarṇya) was created by the Lord according to the division of guṇa and karma; though its maker, he is a non-doer. The verse does not say whether the division is fixed by birth or by conduct.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: See dsp:varna-by-birth-or-conduct-epic for the recorded tension.

name: The four varṇas in the Puruṣa Sūkta

definitions.definition: The brāhmaṇa was the Person's mouth, the rājanya his arms, the vaiśya his thighs; from his feet the śūdra was born (RV 10.90.12) — the one Saṃhitā verse naming the four varṇas together.

notes: Its later use and the debates about it are recorded in dsp:varna-origin-purusa-sukta.

definitions.definition: Sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes declared by Svayambhū (PŚ 3), produced at eight places (PŚ 13); vowels are selves of Indra, sibilants of Prajāpati, stops of Death (ChU 2.22.3); stops, sibilants and vowels correspond to earth, atmosphere and sky (AA 3.2.5).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:paniniya-siksa:3 (confirmed); tea:paniniya-siksa:13 (confirmed); tea:chandogya-upanisad:2.22.3-5 (confirmed); tea:aitareya-aranyaka:3.2.5 (confirmed).

name: Varṇa — the four classes, as the tradition states it

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas correlate the classes with Prajāpati's limbs, metres, gods and animals, declaring the śūdra unfit for sacrifice (TS 7.1.1.4–6), with the three Vedas (TB 3.12.9.2), and call learned brāhmaṇas 'human gods' (ŚB 2.2.2.6).

Four classes, three of them twice-born (MDh 10.4), created from the mouth, arms, thighs and feet (MDh 1.31), with duties — teaching and sacrificing; protecting; trade and farming; service (MDh 1.88–91); each earlier class superior by birth (ĀpDh 1.1.1.4–8); a lower class rises and a higher falls in the next birth by conduct (ĀpDh 2.5.11.10–11); a brāhmaṇa who neglects the Veda sinks to a śūdra's state (MDh 2.168); penalties for a śūdra hearing the Veda (GDh 12.4–6).
Bhagavad Gītā 9.32–33: taking refuge in the Lord, even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras reach the highest goal — how much more holy brāhmaṇas and devoted royal seers.

notes: Recorded faithfully as the Brāhmaṇa and Dharmaśāstra traditions state it; the bhakti, Siddha, Buddhist, Jain and Upaniṣadic critiques are recorded by other units and in dsp:women-caste-liberation.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)
checks.note: The four classes and the cited passages were found: TS 7.1.1.4–6, MDh 1.31, 10.4 and 1.88–91, and ĀpDh 1.1.1.4–8 ('catvāro varṇā … teṣāṃ pūrvaḥ pūrvo janmataḥ śreyān'). Recorded as the tradition states it. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:taittiriya-samhita:7.1.1.4-6, tea:manusmrti:1.31, tea:manusmrti:10.4.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, when adharma prevails the family's women are corrupted and varṇa-mixture arises, bringing hell to the family-destroyers and the family and the fall of the ancestors, and uprooting the dharmas of birth-group and family (1.41–43). Kṛṣṇa uses 'saṅkara' of the confusion he would cause if he stopped acting (3.24).

name: Varuṇa and Mitra, guardians of order

definitions.definition: Varuṇa, all-seeing sovereign, knows the paths of birds and ships and the months, is 'the third' when two conspire, counts the blinkings of men, and his spies never close their eyes; with Mitra he guards ṛta; he binds with fetters and releases.

Vāsanās are manifested only in the form fitted to the ripening of karma (4.8), succeed one another without break across birth, place and time because memory and saṃskāra have one form (4.9), are beginningless because the wish to be is universal (4.10), and are held together by cause, fruit, support and object, so that they cease when these are absent (4.11).

Latent tendencies, laid down by the experience of afflictions, karma and fruition, manifest only when suited to the ripening karma (4.8), stay connected across births, places and times (4.9), are beginningless because the will to be is eternal (4.10), and cease when their cause, result, substrate and support cease (4.11); the mind, though variegated by them, exists for another (4.24).
