name: Destruction of vāsanā, dissolution of mind and knowledge of truth

definitions.definition: The Muktikā's triad (shared with the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and Vidyāraṇya's Jīvanmuktiviveka): the three must be practised together for liberation while living; the mind-tree has two seeds, prāṇa-vibration and vāsanā, and stopping one stops the other.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 6 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: Knowledge, destruction of tendencies, dissolution of mind

definitions.definition: Vidyāraṇya's triad, practised together for the stable freedom of the jīvanmukta.
The breath, 'the horse that rose with twelve feet', is to be bound and nourished; mastered in vāci yoga it makes the body endure (TM 722; Caṭṭaimuṉi 4; Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 17). Summary only.

relations.note: vāci is the breath considered as the yogin's mount

definitions.definition: The knowledge of sites came from Brahmā through the sages; a being who blocked heaven and earth was pinned face-down by the gods, who remain where they seized him, and the Creator made him the Vāstu-man, whose god-filled body lies over every building site (BS 52.1–3).

name: The wind-girdled seers (vātaraśana ṛṣayaḥ)

definitions.definition: Ascetic seers called śramaṇas who kept their seed drawn upward and were found by the other seers through faith and austerity (TA 2.7.1).

notes: Related to the long-haired sage of RV 10.136 (U01).

checks.note: TA 2.7.1 has 'vātaraśanā ha vā ṛṣayaḥ śramaṇā ūrdhvamanthino babhūvuḥ'. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:taittiriya-aranyaka:2.7.1.

definitions.definition: Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), of the ṛju class and equal in rank with Brahmā, is the highest of souls; no soul equals him; by Viṣṇu's permission he gives liberation, and grace reaches lower beings through him.

name: Vāyu's three avatāras: Hanumān, Bhīma, Madhva

definitions.definition: The tradition holds, on Madhva's own statements reading Ṛgveda 1.141, that Vāyu descended as Hanumān, as Bhīma and, in Kali 4300, as Madhva, to proclaim the truth about Hari; the hagiographies' feats are told as signs of this.

name: Equal authority of Veda and Śaiva Āgama

definitions.definition: Both proceed from Śiva; Śrīkaṇṭha sees no difference between them.

name: The Veda as authored by a reliable speaker

definitions.definition: The Veda is valid like mantra and medicine because its seers and teachers are reliable (NS 2.1.69; NBh); its validity rests on its being rooted in the Lord's perception (Gaṅgeśa); all Vedic sentences are valid because spoken by the Lord (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by understanding (VS 6.1.1 C); its authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3).

Pleasure and pain arise from the fourfold contact of self, sense, mind and object; craving arises from them and grasps their seats; their seat is mind and the sensate body; all feeling ceases in yoga and completely in liberation (Ca Śā 1.130-139).

Vedic recitation distinguishes the raised (udātta), low (anudātta) and falling (svarita) accents; a mantra wrong in accent or letter does not convey its meaning and harms the sacrificer, as 'Indra-śatru' did (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 52).

name: The Vedic afterlife: Yama and the fathers

definitions.definition: The dead go by the ancient paths, past Yama's two four-eyed dogs, to Yama and the fathers in the highest heaven, where they are rejoined with their iṣṭāpūrta and a radiant body and rejoice in svadhā (RV 10.14); the fathers are lower, middle and higher (10.15.1); those who reached heaven by tapas, battle or great gifts are there (10.154); Kaśyapa asks for the immortal world of light and bliss (9.113).

name: Scripture and its authority in Viśiṣṭādvaita

definitions.definition: The Veda is authorless and eternal, re-promulgated by the Lord in each creation; it alone makes the Lord known; the Itihāsa–Purāṇas (above all the Viṣṇu Purāṇa) and the Pāñcarātra, spoken by the Lord, are authoritative, and the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs are a Veda in Tamil.

name: The named breaths in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The Saṃhitās name in-breath, out-breath and diffused breath (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna) with life (asu) among the goods of the Camaka (TS 4.7) and in long-life charms (AVŚ 8.1); the Vrātya has seven prāṇas, seven apānas and seven vyānas identified with fire, sun, moon, wind, waters, animals and creatures (AVŚ 15.15–17).

members: (udāna and samāna appear in later Vedic lists)

name: Time, the year and the wheel of ṛta

definitions.definition: The year is the twelve-spoked unaging wheel of ṛta with 720 sons (days and nights) (RV 1.164.11, 1.164.48); it was born from the ocean after ṛta and satya (10.190.2); the Disposer fashioned sun and moon 'as before' (10.190.3); generations pass while the dawns return (1.113.11); in the Atharvaveda Time itself is the first god (19.53–54).

name: The plurality of Vedic creation accounts

definitions.definition: The Saṃhitās give several accounts side by side: the Nāsadīya (10.129), the Puruṣa sacrifice (10.90), the Golden Germ (10.121), Viśvakarman the All-maker (10.81–82), Brahmaṇaspati smelting the worlds and being born from non-being (10.72), ṛta and satya from tapas (10.190), Vāc giving birth to the father (10.125.7), Indra's slaying of Vṛtra (1.32); in the Atharvaveda Skambha, Kāla, Kāma, Ucchiṣṭa, Virāj and Prāṇa.

name: The funeral as the hymns present it

definitions.definition: The corpse is burned by Agni asked not to consume it utterly; eye goes to sun, breath to wind, limbs to plants and waters; the unborn part is carried to the world of the well-doers; the flesh-eating fire is sent away; the widow lying beside the dead is bidden to rise to the world of the living; the living set a boundary against death and go back to dancing and laughter; the bones are laid in mother earth (RV 10.16–18); the Atharvaveda includes those buried, cast out, burned and exposed (AVŚ 18.2.34).

Disease is caused by demons, worms, sorcery, the anger of gods, sin or inheritance, and is driven out by plants, waters, amulets, fire and sun, and by the healer's verses and touch; Rudra and the Aśvins are divine physicians; 'the waters are the remedy for all' (RV 10.137.6); the physician is one among whom plants gather (10.97.6).
The metres (gāyatrī, triṣṭubh, jagatī, anuṣṭubh and others) were born from the Puruṣa sacrifice (RV 10.90.9) and are recorded for every verse in the Anukramaṇīs.

Metres defined by syllable count and feet — gāyatrī (24), uṣṇih (28), anuṣṭubh (32), bṛhatī (36), paṅkti (40), triṣṭubh (44), jagatī (48) — described by Piṅgala with light/heavy syllables and three-syllable groups; the gods covered themselves with them against death (ChU 1.4.2); in the Brāhmaṇas each metre corresponds to a god, a class, a season and an animal (TS 7.1.1.4–6).

checks.note: The seven metres and their syllable counts (24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, rising by four) match Piṅgala's chapters 2–3 as checked for tea:pingala-chandahsutra:3. ChU 1.4.2 (the gods covered themselves with the metres) and TS 7.1.1.4–6 were text-located. Rests on teaching checks confirmed in this sweep: tea:pingala-chandahsutra:3, tea:chandogya-upanisad:1.4.2, tea:taittiriya-samhita:7.1.1.4-6.

name: The person and the self in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The person comprises body (tanū, śarīra), life-breath (asu, prāṇa), mind (manas), breath-self (ātman) and, in one reading, an 'unborn part' (RV 10.16.4); at death eye goes to the sun and breath to the wind (10.16.3); the immortal is of one origin with the mortal (1.164.30, 38); the seer does not know what he is (1.164.37) yet can say 'I was Manu and the Sun' (4.26.1); Sūrya is the self of all (1.115.1); the wise, ageless self is known without fear of death (AVŚ 10.8.44).

The Veda is kept by exact oral transmission from teacher to pupil in several parallel recitations (continuous, word-by-word, step and the eight 'modified' ones), with attention to accent and quantity; reading from a written text is a fault (PŚ 32); memorization without understanding is 'dry fuel without fire' (Nirukta 1.18); the Vedas are endless (TB 3.10.11).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:paniniya-siksa:31-33 (confirmed); tea:nirukta:1.18 (confirmed); tea:taittiriya-brahmana:3.10.11.3-5 (confirmed).

name: The recitation modes that guard the text

definitions.definition: The text is learned in the continuous form (saṃhitā), word by word (pada), in overlapping pairs (krama) and in the eight modified recitations (jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha, ghana), with hand gestures marking the accents; understanding the meaning is also enjoined (Nirukta 1.18; Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 32–33, 54–55).

name: The fivefold division of the Veda

definitions.definition: The Veda consists of injunction (vidhi), mantra, name (nāmadheya), prohibition (niṣedha) and explanatory praise (arthavāda); all are meaningful through injunctions directly or indirectly.
The sūtra divides the Veda into mantra and brāhmaṇa (MS 2.1.32–33) and treats injunction, arthavāda, mantra, smṛti and name in adhyāya 1.

name: Waking, sleep and dream in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The mind goes far from the waking and likewise returns to the sleeper (VS 34.1); prāṇa stays awake upright among sleepers (AVŚ 11.4.25); Sleep (svapna) is 'neither living nor dead', child of Yama, and bad dreams are warded off (AVŚ 6.46); even sleep does not keep away wrong (RV 7.86.6).

notes: The Upaniṣadic scheme of three states and the fourth is contributed by U03; any correspondence is interpretive and not asserted here.

name: Transmission of the Veda: teacher, śākhā and oral recitation

definitions.definition: The Veda passes from the seers by instruction (Nirukta 1.20) to pupils who repeat the teacher's words (RV 7.103.5); the teacher initiates the student and bears him as an embryo (AVŚ 11.5.3); Vyāsa divided the one Veda into four and his pupils' lines branched into śākhās (Bhāgavata 1.4.19–23; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4–5); each śākhā preserves its text by exact recitation.

Marathi can carry the highest teaching — Jñāneśvar's words will outdo nectar; if God made Sanskrit, the vernacular was not born of thieves (Eknāth); words are the saints' wealth and weapons (Tukārām).
Tulsī tells Rāma's story in the vernacular (bhāṣā) for his inner joy, in accord with all scripture.
Cakradhar taught in Marathi and bade his disciples keep to it; the scriptures are in Marathi.
Scripture is sung and staged in Assamese and Brajabuli so that all may hear.

name: The verse contest at Huangmei

definitions.definition: Hongren asks for verses to choose his successor; Shenxiu's 'wipe the mirror' verse and Huineng's 'originally not a single thing' (Zongbao) or 'buddha-nature is always pure' (Dunhuang).

notes: Tradition's account; scholars regard the episode as a Southern-school composition.

definitions.definition: The boundless open space above and beyond the body's supports, taken as the truth itself: for those who hold it true no title-deed is needed (Kuṭampai 1); the heart 'standing empty' without ritual (Aḻukaṇṇi 37); 'the open space of pure Vedānta' (Kaṭuveḷi 10).

relations.note: not to be identified with Buddhist emptiness; verbal resemblance only

name: The powers of the Vibhūti-pāda (vibhūti)

definitions.definition: The list of what the text says comes from saṃyama on various objects (3.16-3.49, 3.52-3.54): knowledge of past and future, of former births, of another's mind, disappearance, knowledge of the worlds, the eight powers and perfection of the body, mastery of elements and senses, overlordship and omniscience. They are recorded as the text states them. The text itself calls the perceptions of 3.36 obstacles in samādhi (3.37) and warns against attachment and pride when invited by high stations (3.51).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord's own divine manifestations, by which he stands pervading the worlds (10.16). Asked in which beings and states he is to be contemplated (10.17), he names the principal ones — the self in all beings, then the chief of each class (10.20–39) — says there is no end to them and that the list is only an indication (10.19, 10.40), gives the rule that whatever is glorious or mighty springs from a portion of his splendour (10.41), and ends that he supports the whole world with a single portion (10.42). Whoever knows his vibhūti and yoga in truth is joined with unwavering yoga (10.7).

The Lord as the best in each class — among lights the sun, among words Oṃ, among sacrifices japa, among sages Vyāsa, and so on — every glory springing from a fragment of his splendour; he sustains the world with one fragment (BhG ch. 10; 7.8–11).

Saṃyama on particular objects yields powers: knowledge of past and future, of the cries of beings, of former births, of other minds; invisibility; knowledge of death; strengths; knowledge of the worlds, stars, the body; freedom from hunger; steadiness; sight of siddhas; intuition; knowledge of the mind and of the puruṣa; divine senses; entering another body; levitation and departure at death; radiance; divine hearing; movement through space; mastery of elements and senses; the eight powers; omnipotence and omniscience (3.16–49).

Bhagavad Gītā 7.8–11 and 9.16–19 (the word vibhūti itself is not used in these verses): the Lord is the taste in water, the light of moon and sun, Oṃ in all the Vedas, sound in space, manhood in men, pure fragrance in earth, brilliance in fire, life in all beings, austerity in ascetics, the eternal seed of beings, the intelligence of the intelligent, the splendour of the splendid, strength free of desire and passion, desire not opposed to dharma; and the rite, the sacrifice, the offering, the fire and the oblation, father, mother, sustainer and grandfather of the world, Oṃ and the three Vedas, goal, witness, refuge and friend, immortality and death, sat and asat.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the radiance in the sun, the moon and fire is the Lord's (15.12); entering the earth he sustains beings by his vigour and, becoming soma, nourishes all plants (15.13); becoming vaiśvānara in the bodies of breathing beings, joined with prāṇa and apāna, he digests the fourfold food (15.14). The word vibhūti is not used here; the verses continue the manner of 7.8–11 and 10.19–42.

name: The bodiless and those merged in prakṛti

definitions.definition: Beings who experience a state 'like kaivalya' but return: the bodiless (gods, per Vyāsa) pass through the ripening of their impressions; those merged in prakṛti remain until the mind returns by force of its unfinished task (YBh 1.19); they are placed outside the worlds, 'in the state of liberation' (YBh 3.26). Bhoja identifies the bodiless with those who rest content in the bliss-samādhi and the prakṛtilayas with those content in the I-am-ness samādhi (RM 1.17).

Liberation at the fall of the body when prārabdha is exhausted — like pot-space merging with space or wind becoming still (Muktikā 1 prose, 2.76; Yogakuṇḍalī 3.34); the dissolution of mind 'without form'.

Sāṃkhya's final isolation: 'when separation from the body is attained and pradhāna ceases, its purpose fulfilled, he attains isolation both certain and final' (SK 68). The SK does not use the word videhamukti.
At the fall of the body the knower's prāṇas do not depart; he merges, nothing new being attained.

definitions.definition: The Vedic statement that impels to action; the sole means of knowing dharma, able to make known the future, subtle and remote.
What it conveys is bhāvanā, the prompting force (Kumārila); for Maṇḍana, that the act is a means to the desired (iṣṭasādhanatā).
What it conveys is the command / what is to be done (niyoga, kārya).

relations.note: the injunction presupposes the apūrva

name: Renunciation of the knower and of the seeker

definitions.definition: The knower (vidvat) renounces having realized; the seeker (vividiṣā) renounces in order to realize and keeps the insignia (Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; developed in Vidyāraṇya's Jīvanmuktiviveka).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 1 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: Knowledge and ignorance lead to different ends (KU 1.2.4); fools in ignorance wander like the blind led by the blind (KU 1.2.5; MuU 1.2.8); Īśa 9-11 says both those who worship ignorance and those who delight in knowledge enter darkness, and that one knowing both crosses death by ignorance and gains immortality by knowledge; ŚU 5.1 calls the perishable ignorance and the immortal knowledge; what is done with knowledge is more powerful (ChU 1.1.10).

definitions.definition: Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin: vijñānākala souls raised to office in the pure universe, who act on Śiva's behalf and are liberated at the end of their office.

name: The view as the absence of grasping

definitions.definition: 'If grasping arises, it is not the view': the correct view is not a position held but freedom from grasping at any extreme.
Tilopa's 'kings': view beyond grasped and grasper, meditation without distraction, conduct without effort, fruit without hope and fear; Lakṣmīṅkarā's sequence realization–meditation–conduct.

The fourfold frame of instruction: beyond grasper and grasped is the king of views; without distraction the king of meditations; without effort the king of conduct; without hope and fear the fruit is manifest (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā); a correct view makes meditation and conduct reach the fruit (Nāropa).

At death the soul, with only its fiery and karmic bodies, moves along the rows of space-points to its next birth-place, straight in one instant or with up to three bends; for up to three instants it takes in no matter; the liberated soul rises straight up (TS 2.25–30).

relations.note: The Jain transit lasts at most a few instants; there is no extended intermediate existence.

name: The twenty living Tīrthaṅkaras of Mahāvideha

definitions.definition: In the Mahāvideha regions, where time does not decline, twenty Tīrthaṅkaras are teaching now, beginning with Sīmandhara; liberation is always possible there, and devotees pray to be reborn there.

The three realms are only cognition: objects appearing as external are cognition appearing as objects, as in a dream; this is argued by the Viṃśatikā against objections from proponents of external objects (restriction of place and time, intersubjectivity, efficacy, atoms) and in its final sense is the perfected nature itself, realized when consciousness no longer apprehends an object.
Dharmakīrti argues from the co-apprehension of blue and its cognition that they are not different; cognition, undivided in itself, appears divided into grasped and grasper to deluded vision.

relations.note: the treatise-layer form of the sūtras' 'mind-only'
the atom is refuted as neither one nor many

definitions.definition: The 120-year system counted from the birth-asterism: the lords, repeating thrice from Kṛttikā, are the Sun (6 years), Moon (10), Mars (7), Rāhu (18), Jupiter (16), Saturn (19), Mercury (17), Ketu (7) and Venus (20); since a full life is 120 years it is chief in the Kali age (BPHS 46.12–15).

name: The prātimokṣa rule counts of the Vinayas

definitions.definition: 250 bhikṣu rules, 348 bhikṣuṇī rules.
227 bhikkhu rules (311 bhikkhunī).
218 bhikṣu rules (moderate confidence).
251 bhikṣu rules (low confidence).
263 bhikṣu rules (low confidence).
258 in the Sanskrit prātimokṣa; the Tibetan tradition speaks of 253 vows (low confidence).

notes: Class structure is common to all Vinayas; totals differ mainly in the śaikṣa rules. Only the Dharmaguptaka and Theravāda totals are given with confidence.

name: The six means of determining subsidiarity

definitions.definition: Direct statement, indicative power, syntactic connection, context, position and name — each later one weaker when they conflict, being more remote from the meaning (MS 3.3.14).

name: The fruition of karma: birth, life-span, experience

definitions.definition: Karma ripens as the kind of birth, the length of life and experience (2.13), bearing joy or anguish according to merit or demerit (2.14).
Error apprehends something as other than it is; the relation alone is unreal (Śāstradīpikā, following Kumārila; also Maṇḍana's Vibhramaviveka).

name: Urgency of practice within the dispensation

definitions.definition: Now, while the dispensation lasts, laypeople and monks should develop the requisites of awakening rather than wait for a future Buddha.
The clock of vipassanā has struck: 2,500 years after the Buddha the practice is to spread again (U Ba Khin's account).

name: The marks of the hero and the Śakti

definitions.definition: The Śakti is devoted to Kula and guru, fearless and of good conduct; the hero is truthful, resolute, free of anger, brave, knowing the Śakti born of the body and formed by non-dual conduct (KJN 20.14–22).
Separation (vipralambha) intensifies love; Caitanya's last years and Śikṣāṣṭaka 7–8.
Love in separation is the highest state; renunciation is fitting only when viraha makes home impossible.

The love-sick girl who does not sleep, bails out her tears, joins her palms crying 'conch and discus!' (TVM 7.2.1); Āṇṭāḷ begging for his garment or garland to cool her burning; the grieving father Daśaratha; ended at last in union — Nammāḻvār's longing 'ended' in release.
Supreme anguish at forgetting the Lord is Nārada's own definition of devotion; supreme separation is the last of love's eleven forms.
Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's mutual longing in separation, carried by the friend, fills most of the Gīta Govinda before union.
The gopīs' longing when Kṛṣṇa vanishes or departs, which Kṛṣṇa says he causes so that their minds dwell on him; Uddhava wishes to be the dust of their feet.
The madness and wound of love that only the Lord as physician can heal.
Rādhā's laments in the rains and at the flute's call (Vidyāpati, Caṇḍīdās).
Not real in the eternal union; felt only within it.
Separation is the sultan; the one who has it wakes and weeps while the world eats and sleeps; the arrow of separation is the Beloved's gift.
Longing for the Man of the Heart who comes near and cannot be held.

definitions.definition: Virāj, born from the Puruṣa and giving birth to him (RV 10.90.5), was all this in the beginning and entered the fires, the assembly and the council; gods, men and others milked their foods from her (AVŚ 8.10).

The vacanas refuse caste among devotees: Basava calls himself the son of a cobbler's house and asks to say of every devotee 'he is ours'; the intercaste marriage at Kalyāṇa is remembered as the occasion of the upheaval.

The SSM makes devotion, not birth, the mark of the bhakta (9.4–5), tells the māheśvara to drop jāti-dharmas opposed to the liṅga (10.30–31) and sees brāhmaṇa and outcaste alike at union (14.19–20), but also prescribes eating with twice-born of one's own jāti on the path (9.29) and distinguishes Śiva's and Brahmā's orderings of varṇa and āśrama (10.34–36).

name: Conduct: inner and outer purity, word and deed

definitions.definition: Do not steal, kill, lie, rage, despise others, praise yourself or blame others — inner and outer purity; compassion is the root of dharma; deeds must match words; equanimity under praise and blame.

name: Consciousness, samādhi and the void of mental activity

definitions.definition: The liṅga is consciousness (cit, saṃvit) shining within; śivayoga-samādhi is undivided attention on the supreme self as 'I am He'; in aikya the yogin abides in a heart empty of mental activity, dissolved in Śiva; the realized abides in the self through all dealings of knower, known and knowing.

notes: Waking/dream/deep sleep/fourth are not treated in the passages recorded here — gap.

name: Cosmology: Śiva, Śakti and the world

definitions.definition: The thirty-six tattvas are the waves and bubbles of Śiva's ocean of consciousness; Śiva emits the pramathas; the world arises from Śiva and is not different from him; the five ācāryas appear in every yuga; the descent of Reṇuka at Kollipāki is placed in the Kali age.

name: Inner centres and the liṅga of light

definitions.definition: The liṅga of light shines at the base (mūlādhāra), in the heart and between the brows — gold, coral-red and crystal; the prāṇaliṅga rises from the navel-bulb where prāṇa and apāna meet; six centres from the base to the brows, and above them the thousand-petalled lotus with the moon-disc and the subtle aperture called Kailāsa, from which nectar cools the heart.
The manual tradition places the six liṅgas in the six centres (low confidence).

The one consciousness-brahman is imagined as enjoyer, enjoyed and impeller through the three guṇas; tamas and rajas are removed at the śaraṇa stage; earth and the other elements are Śiva's eight forms, his body and effect; the thirty-six tattvas are waves of Śiva's ocean.

name: The guru: how he is found, tested and honoured

definitions.definition: The disciple, discerning and dispassionate, seeks a guru free of greed, versed in self-inquiry and the Śiva-siddhānta, righteous, of good conduct, wearing ash, rudrākṣa and the liṅga, knowing the yoga of liṅga and aṅga (6.1–6); without a perfected guru there is no end to saṃsāra, and such gurus are rare (13.24–27); the guru is Śiva and is not to be regarded as an ordinary man (11.19–24).
Allama tests every aspirant, including Akka Mahādēvi and Siddharāma, by questioning in the assembly.

Born by karma into castes and burned by threefold suffering, the soul becomes pure-minded when karma ripens and Śiva's grace arises; those who bear the inner liṅga do not return; liberation while living belongs to the one who knows the liṅga as liberation; the knower's karma-seeds are burnt, his acts leave no fruit and every act is worship.
Liberation is liṅgaikya, union with the liṅga, open to all who wear it.
The mind is a mirror soiled by ignorance that the guru cleanses; serenity of mind is grace; outer impressions (vāsanā) project the world, inner ones reveal the self's bliss.
Māyā is not gold, woman or land but the desire standing before the mind.

name: Powers and the warning against them

definitions.definition: Gorakṣa's indestructible body is surpassed by Allama's void body; attainment of powers is not the goal.
The five-syllable mantra is said to give all powers when uttered (8.36–43); the Śivayogin's sight gives accomplishment (11.37–43).
Women receive the liṅga, compose vacanas and sit in the assembly; Akka Mahādēvi is examined and acknowledged by Allama; Dāsimayya teaches that the self is neither man nor woman.

name: Brahman as the locus of contradictory attributes

definitions.definition: Contradictory scriptural statements about Brahman are all literally true; it is not necessary to relegate saguṇa statements to a lower level.

relations.note: Vallabha rejects assigning the qualified statements to a lower level

definitions.definition: The endless particularities residing in eternal substances (atoms, selves, minds) that make each distinct from every other (Tarkasaṅgraha); traditionally linked with the name Vaiśeṣika.

A thing has no real difference from its lasting properties (and God none from his qualities, acts and forms), yet they can be spoken of distinctly by virtue of viśeṣa; with temporary properties there is difference-and-identity. (Distinct from the Vaiśeṣika category viśeṣa.)

relations.note: viśeṣa accounts for distinctions where there is no real difference

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu measured the worlds in three strides; his highest step, where there is a well-spring of honey and where god-seekers rejoice, the wise ever see like an eye stretched in heaven (RV 1.22.20, 1.154).

The sovereign form shown to Arjuna by grace through a divine eye: the whole universe in one body, as bright as a thousand suns, and as Time devouring the warriors (BhG 11.5–34); seen only by undivided devotion (11.52–54); a similar self-manifestation occurs in the Kaurava court (MBh 5.129) and Mārkaṇḍeya sees the worlds within a divine child (3.186).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: At Arjuna's request (11.3–4) the Lord shows his sovereign form, which cannot be seen with ordinary sight and is seen with a divine eye (11.8): countless mouths, eyes, arms and ornaments, a radiance like a thousand suns, the whole world standing as one in his body (11.9–13), without beginning, middle or end (11.16, 11.19); the gods and seers praise it and the worlds tremble (11.20–22); the warriors of both armies rush into its mouths (11.26–30); it declares itself Time (11.32). It was shown by grace and the Lord's own yoga, never seen before by another (11.47), is not to be seen by Vedas, sacrifice, study, gifts, rites or austerity (11.48, 11.53), and is known, seen in truth and entered by undivided devotion (11.54).

definitions.definition: God as Viṭṭhala (Pāṇḍuraṅga), a form of Kṛṣṇa who came for Puṇḍalīka and stands on the brick, hands on hips, waiting for devotees; addressed as mother (māulī, Viṭhāī); for Narahari Sonār one with Śiva; for Jñāneśvar the Self known by itself.

relations.note: Narahari Sonār's vision of Śiva in Viṭṭhala
Sāṃkhya's real transformation of prakṛti; Advaita accepts pariṇāma only for māyā
vivarta speaks of appearance; ajāti denies any origination at the highest level

definitions.definition: The world is an apparent, not a real, transformation of Brahman, as the snake of the rope; effects are non-different from the cause, mere names (BS 2.1.14).
Seeing the distinctness of sattva and puruṣa (3.49, 3.55); when complete in every way it is followed by dharma-megha (4.29); the mind inclined to it slopes towards kaivalya (4.26).

The discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower (SK 2), accomplished by buddhi (SK 37) and culminating, through repeated practice of the principles, in the complete, pure and single knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64); it is the direct realization of the distinctness of sattva and puruṣa (Vācaspati). Liberation comes from it alone (SS 3.23–25); it is reached by renouncing each principle with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

The cognition of the difference between sattva and puruṣa (YBh 2.26); unwavering, it is the means of liberation (2.26); limbs of yoga make knowledge shine up to it (2.28); from it come sovereignty and omniscience (3.49); complete, it yields the cloud of dharma (4.29); the discerning mind bends toward kaivalya (4.26).

definitions.definition: Five vows (abstention from violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity, possessiveness), small or great; five contemplations for each; reflection on harm and suffering; friendliness, delight, compassion and equanimity; reflection on the nature of world and body for dread of saṃsāra and detachment.
Five contemplations for each vow steady it (TS 7.3–8), with the reflections on the harm and suffering of the sins (7.9–10) and on world and body for dread and detachment (7.12).

name: Vrata: the gods' ordinance and the human vow

definitions.definition: Varuṇa is 'of firm ordinances' (RV 1.25); one prays to be sinless under his vrata (1.24.15); the sacrificer undertakes a vow before Agni, lord of vows (VS 1.5).

A self-imposed observance for a day or period (fast, vigil, worship, gifts), bound to a lunar date and deity, with a story and a promised fruit; Ekādaśī, Śivarātri, Navarātra and the Kātyāyanī vow are examples.

name: The observance of the realized yogin (vratacaryā)

definitions.definition: Unconventional conduct in cremation grounds, among outcastes, with ornaments of bone, 'mad' behaviour and equal vision — undertaken after warmth or realization, as a hidden observance.
Only after realizing equality (Mekopa); the unrealized who act so are like a kingdom seized by its subjects (Nāgārjuna's song); the Queen Dohā describes it and also warns against base conduct.

The vow-bound wanderer of Atharvaveda 15 who stirs Prajāpati into creation, becomes the one, the great, brahman, tapas and truth, becomes Mahādeva and Īśāna, stands upright a year, is seated on a throne of seasons and Vedas, has seven prāṇas identified with fire, sun, moon, wind, waters, animals and creatures, and is to be honoured above the king when he comes as guest.

name: The parable of the wolf's footprint

definitions.definition: (As reported) A man faked wolf-tracks to show how the learned mislead people with talk of unseen things.

name: Pervasion by the mode but not by its result

definitions.definition: Ordinary objects are pervaded by both the mental mode and the reflected consciousness (its 'result'); Brahman, being self-luminous, only by the mode, which removes ignorance.

The manifest is caused, impermanent, non-pervasive, active, many, dependent, merging, composite and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite (SK 10); both consist of the three guṇas and are non-discriminating, objects, common, unconscious and productive, unlike puruṣa (SK 11).

Bhagavad Gītā 7.24; 8.18–21; 9.4: manifest things come forth from and dissolve into the unmanifest with Brahmā's day and night; beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest which does not perish when beings perish, called the akṣara, the highest goal and the Lord's supreme abode; the Lord pervades the world in unmanifest form; the unintelligent think of him as unmanifest come into manifestation (7.24; whether 'unmanifest' states what he is or belongs to their mistaken view, the verse does not settle).

definitions.definition: The invariable concomitance of probans with probandum ('wherever smoke, there fire'), known through observation of co-presence and absence of deviation, aided by tarka and extraordinary contact through the universal; defined exactly after rejecting five provisional definitions.

name: The five provisional definitions of pervasion (Vyāptipañcaka)

definitions.definition: Five definitions of pervasion in terms of non-occurrence in loci of the probandum's absence, each rejected chiefly because it fails for a probandum present everywhere (kevalānvayin).

Spaces seen in the intermediate target: ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, sūryākāśa and paramākāśa (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 4.1), or the guṇa-less space, supreme space, great space, space of principles and space of the sun (Advayatāraka) — order and names differ.
The five voids of the Nāth body-map that the yogin must know in his own body (Vivekamārtaṇḍa family); the HYP's khecarī is 'in the space-wheel (vyomacakra) between sun and moon' (4.45).

name: The fourfold form of the Lord (the vyūhas)

definitions.definition: Vāsudeva (the knower of the field), Saṃkarṣaṇa (the jīva), Pradyumna (mind) and Aniruddha (ego, source of Brahmā), each arising from the prior; the liberated pass back through them into Vāsudeva (MBh 12.326.38, 12.326.68–69, 12.327.26, 12.332.13–18).

relations.note: the vyūhas are correlated with jīva, mind and ego in the Nārāyaṇīya

name: The weighing of deeds after death

definitions.definition: In the other world a man is placed on a balance and follows whichever side prevails, good or evil; the knower mounts the balance here and escapes it there (ŚB 11.2.7.33); Bhṛgu sees retribution in kind (ŚB 11.6.1; JB 1.42–44).

name: The 'white self-sufficient remedy' (dkar po chig thub)

definitions.definition: Recognizing mind's nature is by itself sufficient for awakening (Gampopa, Lama Zhang).
A revival of the Chinese Hashang's view, rejected by Sakya Paṇḍita.
Not the jīva, body, birth, learning, action or dharmic deeds, but one who has realized the non-dual Self and is free of faults (Vajrasūci); caste is imagined for convention (Nirālamba).

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 6 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

definitions.definition: Eligibility rules: dispassion, the fourfold means, freedom from certain defects and statuses; the ineligible may renounce when at the point of death; texts differ on whether the unmarried may renounce and on consent of kin.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 5 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

name: The winds as the mount of mind

definitions.definition: Wind is the vehicle of consciousness, five and ten-fold (Pañcakrama 1.3); the natural conceptions run on the winds.
21,600 breaths a day, carried by left and right channels; the middle channel rarely.

The puruṣa is the witness (pratisaṃvedin) of the buddhi (YBh 2.17, 2.20); the mind's activities are always known to it (4.18); Vijñānabhikṣu explains its knowing through the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi (YV 1.7).
The Mahāvairocana's Womb (Garbha) maṇḍala of compassion and the Tattvasaṃgraha's Vajradhātu maṇḍala of wisdom, later paired as the 'two maṇḍalas' in East Asia.

name: Women and awakening

definitions.definition: Women who go forth can realise stream-entry to arahantship (Cv 10.1.3); the nuns Somā and Vajirā answer Māra that womanhood is irrelevant to the concentrated mind (SN 5.2; Thig 3.8); the Therīgāthā records arahant nuns; the canon also states that a woman cannot be a fully awakened Buddha (MN 115; AN 1.279) and the Buddhavaṃsa names maleness among the conditions of the Buddha-aspiration (Bv 2.59).

notes: Recorded faithfully with both kinds of statement; see dsp:women-caste-liberation (U50) and dsp:bhikkhuni-order.

name: Women in the Sant and Bāul traditions

definitions.definition: The Sant verses often name woman with gold as māyā's snare (kanak-kāminī) and warn the renunciant against her; yet women Sants (Sahajobāī, Dayābāī; Mīrā is claimed as Ravidās's disciple) taught with authority, and Kabīr speaks as the bride of Rām.
Every woman is Rādhā in her svarūpa; the female partner is revered and may be the guru of the practice.
Satī Mā led the community and is venerated as the Mother.

notes: Recorded for dsp:women-caste-liberation (owned by U50).

name: Women's bodies and buddhahood in the Mahāyāna sūtras

definitions.definition: The sūtras record both the view that a woman's body cannot attain buddhahood (Śāriputra's objection; the nāga princess transforming into a man; Bhaiṣajyaguru's and Amitābha's vows that women may be freed from the woman's state) and the teaching that all dharmas are neither male nor female (the goddess in Vimalakīrti), together with women teachers (Śrīmālā) and women predicted to buddhahood (the Ganges goddess).

notes: Cross-tradition debate: dsp:women-caste-liberation (U50) and dsp:womens-bodies-and-buddhahood.

definitions.definition: A word means the universal (ākṛti), since action concerns it (MS 1.3.33); meanings follow the śāstra where usages differ (MS 1.3.9) and accept current usage of non-Āryas where uncontradicted (MS 1.3.10); the Buddhist 'exclusion' (apoha) is rejected.

Word, object and cognition are confused through mutual superimposition; saṃyama on their distinction gives knowledge of the cries of all beings (3.17). The word is a single unit grasped by the buddhi from the letters (YBh 3.17); the relation of word and meaning is held eternal (YBh 1.27); savitarkā coalescence is mixed with these constructions (1.42).

name: Word, meaning and their relation as established (siddha)

definitions.definition: Kātyāyana's first vārttika: word, meaning and relation are established (eternal, per Patañjali); grammar only restricts usage for the sake of dharma; the word is that by which the meaning is understood (Mahābhāṣya).

notes: The fuller philosophy of language (sphoṭa, śabda-brahman) belongs to lin:vyakarana (U31).

checks.note: The definition's cited passages were all checked in this sweep and support it: tea:varttika-katyayana:1 (confirmed); tea:mahabhasya:paspasa (confirmed).

definitions.definition: Word-meaning is the individual, form and universal together (NS 2.2.68); the relation of word and meaning is conventional (NS 2.1.56–57; NBh).
Understanding meaning from words is conventional (VS 7.2.24 C).
The denotative power is the Lord's convention (Tarkasaṅgraha); analysed in detail in the Śaktivāda and Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā.

name: All cognition is permeated by the word (śabdānuviddha jñāna)

definitions.definition: No cognition occurs without the word; all knowledge shines as if pierced by it; awareness is word-natured (vāgrūpatā), which makes recognition possible, and speech is the consciousness of beings (VP 1.123–124 and following).

relations.note: the word-nature of awareness is traced back through madhyamā to paśyantī

notes: Denied by Buddhist logicians (non-conceptual perception is word-free) and by Śāntarakṣita's examination of the Word-brahman.

definitions.definition: Chan is 'not established on words and letters', yet the Platform Sūtra warns that saying 'no words' is itself words; reciting sūtras without understanding makes them enemies of meaning.
'Lettered Chan': literary expression is not opposed to awakening (Juefan Huihong).
Words are vehicles of the Way; one must not seek the meaning in the phrase (Yuanwu).

name: The world as the mind's projection

definitions.definition: The seen does not exist apart from consciousness; worlds arise from the mind's conceiving (saṅkalpa, manorājya) like dreams, whole lives occurring in a moment, worlds within a room, a rock or an atom; wiping away the seen is nirvāṇa.
All grasped by mind and senses is māyā, a mental creation; the three states are the mind's play like a whirling firebrand.

definitions.definition: An eon has four incalculable phases; the world is destroyed in turn by fire (up to the Ābhassara), water (up to the Subhakiṇha) and wind (up to the Vehapphala).
The world contracts and expands over aeons; at contraction beings are mostly reborn in the Ābhassara realm (DN 27; DN 1).

The end of the world cannot be reached by travelling, yet there is no end of suffering without reaching it; the world, its origin, cessation and way are declared in this fathom-long body with its perception and mind (SN 2.26).

name: Worship of the Lord and worship of the imperishable unmanifest (BhG 12.1–7)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna asks which are the better knowers of yoga: devotees ever yoked who worship Kṛṣṇa, or those who worship the imperishable, the unmanifest (12.1). The Lord answers that those who fix manas on him and worship him with supreme faith are held the most yoked (12.2); those who worship the imperishable — indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, unchanging, immovable, constant — with senses restrained, even-minded, delighting in the welfare of all beings, also reach him (12.3–4), but their hardship is greater, since the unmanifest goal is reached with difficulty by the embodied (12.5); those who resign all actions to him and meditate on him with undivided yoga he before long lifts from the ocean of death and saṃsāra (12.6–7).

Later schools read the pair in terms of their own doctrines (e.g. Advaita as qualified and unqualified brahman, Viśiṣṭādvaita as the Lord and the individual self); their readings are recorded in dsp:bhagavad-gita-lord-or-unmanifest. The text itself uses only 'you / me' and 'the imperishable, the unmanifest'.

definitions.definition: Learning the Dhamma for criticism and debate is like seizing a snake by the tail (MN 22).

name: The wheel of sacrifice (yajña-cakra)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Prajāpati created beings together with sacrifice, bidding them multiply by it; gods and humans nourish one another through it and so attain the highest good; one who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering is a thief; eaters of the sacrificial remainder are freed from faults (3.10–13); beings come from food, food from rain, rain from sacrifice, sacrifice from action, action from brahman, brahman from the imperishable (3.14–15); one who does not keep this wheel turning lives in vain (3.16). Action other than for sacrifice binds (3.9).

notes: The commentators divide on brahman and akṣara in 3.15 (most: the Veda and the imperishable supreme).

name: Yajña: the sacrifice that sustains the world

definitions.definition: Ritual action is the Vedic paradigm of effective action: the gods first sacrificed the Person and 'sacrificed to the sacrifice with the sacrifice — these were the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16); the sacrifice is woven like a cloth by the fathers (10.130.1); through it the petitions of the Camaka are 'made fit'.

name: Sacrifice reinterpreted (yajña)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24–33 list the sacrifices offered by different practitioners, all born of action and all purifying: every element of the offering seen as Brahman; sacrifice to the gods; offering sacrifice by sacrifice into the fire of Brahman; offering the senses into the fires of restraint; offering sense objects into the fires of the senses; offering the activities of the senses and of breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint; sacrifice with material things, with austerity, with yoga, with study and with knowledge; offering prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa, with breath-regulation; offering the breaths into the breaths with regulated food. The sacrifice of knowledge is the best, since all action culminates in knowledge.

The Gītā keeps the wheel of sacrifice between gods and men (3.10–16) but widens sacrifice to austerity, yoga, study, sense-restraint, breath and knowledge (4.25–30), declares the sacrifice of knowledge highest (4.33) and sees offering, oblation, fire and offerer as Brahman (4.24); sacrifice is to be done without desire for fruit (17.11; 18.5); the Anugītā describes an inner sacrifice of the senses (14.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 9.15–16, 9.24, 9.26–27: some worship the Lord by the sacrifice of knowledge; he is the rite, the sacrifice, the ancestral offering, the herb, the mantra, the butter, the fire and the oblation; he is the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices; a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered in devotion he accepts; every act, eating, oblation, gift and austerity is to be done as an offering to him.

definitions.definition: For evil-doers another body arises after death from the five subtle elements, in which they suffer Yama's torments, then dissolves (MDh 12.16–22).

definitions.definition: Prajāpati is the year (saṃvatsara); the Veda's syllables are arranged to equal its moments (ŚB 10.4.2.22–25); the year is also Death, wearing away mortals' lives by days and nights (ŚB 10.4.3.1).

definitions.definition: Yoga is the stilling of the mind's activities (YS 1.2), after which the seer abides in its own form (1.3); Vyāsa equates yoga with samādhi and admits it only in the one-pointed and stilled mind (YBh 1.1); commentators describe stilling as the inward dissolution of the activities into their cause.

definitions.definition: Seven worlds from the Avīci hell to the world of Brahmā (bhūr, the intermediate world, Mahendra's heaven, Prajāpati's mahar, and Brahmā's jana, tapas and satya), with hells and seven netherworlds below, the earth of seven continents around Meru, and classes of gods whose highest members enjoy the meditations with reasoning, reflection, bliss and I-am-ness; the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti are outside the worlds (YBh 3.26). Known by saṃyama on the sun (3.26–28).

When the mind is steady and established in the self, pleasure and pain cease and mastery arises — this is yoga, which leads to liberation (Ca Śā 1.137-139); its eight powers arise from concentration of the purified mind (1.141); the path of yoga and of the Sāṃkhyas is the recollection of truth (1.150-151).

relations.note: Patañjali's definition of yoga; Caraka defines it by the cessation of feeling

definitions.definition: Breath-control with Oṃ and the utterances, fixation, withdrawal and meditation burn away faults, sin, attachment and ungodly qualities (MDh 6.70–74); the removal of the fifteen faults is rooted in yoga (ĀpDh 1.8.23); seeing the self by yoga is the highest dharma (YS 1.8); the Yājñavalkyasmṛti describes yogic powers (3.202–203) and liberation through music (3.115).

name: The place and hut for yoga

definitions.definition: The haṭha yogin lives alone in a small hut in a righteous, prosperous and peaceful kingdom, free of rock, fire and water around, with a small door, no holes, smeared with cow-dung, walled, with a well (HYP 1.12–14; GS 5.5–7); not in a distant land, forest, capital or crowd (GS 5.3–4); begin in spring or autumn, not in winter, summer or the rains (GS 5.8–9).

name: Yoga declared independent of sect and outward sign

definitions.definition: Brahmin, śramaṇa, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist — whoever practises with faith attains success; garb and sectarian formulas are not the cause of success.
Haribhadra correlates the eight views of the yoga-seeker with the limbs beginning with yama, treating yoga taught under other names as one path of qualities.
Hindu and Turk quarrel over names; neither knows the secret.

name: Karma-yoga, jñāna-yoga and bhakti-yoga in sequence

definitions.definition: As read from the Gītā by Yāmuna and Rāmānuja: karma-yoga (with self-knowledge) purifies and leads to the vision of the self, which jñāna-yoga also yields; this prepares bhakti-yoga, the direct means to the Lord; the three are done as his worship.
When the mind abides in the self (and does not join the senses), the embodied one has no pleasure or pain: that is yoga (VS 5.2.16–17 C).

relations.note: the Nyāya prescription of samādhi as the means to knowledge of truth

name: Death and dying in Yogācāra

definitions.definition: At death the store-consciousness is the last to leave the body and at conception the first to enter it; the body grows cold progressively — for those of good karma from the lower body upward, for those of bad karma from the head downward — until consciousness leaves at the heart; the intermediate existence follows.

notes: Recalled from the Yogācārabhūmi (manobhūmi) and Xuanzang's Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses (Bashi guiju song: 'last to go, first to come'); refs not located in this pass.

name: The two chariots: Yogācāra and Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: Relying on mind-only one understands the non-existence of external objects; relying on Madhyamaka one understands that mind too is selfless; riding both with the reins of reasoning one is a true Mahāyānist (MAL 92–93).

relations.note: Candrakīrti rejects mind-only even conventionally

definitions.definition: Everything is neither empty nor non-empty: unreal imagination exists, duality does not, emptiness exists in it — avoiding both the extreme of superimposition (that duality exists) and of denial (that nothing exists).

relations.note: Madhyamaka's middle way is the emptiness of all own-being, including of consciousness

definitions.definition: Rebirth is the store-consciousness's continuation: when a maturation is exhausted, the imprints of karma and of the twofold grasping produce a new one; the ālaya appropriates the new body at conception.

name: The five yogas of the Yogaviṃśikā

definitions.definition: Posture, sound, meaning, support and the supportless — the first two action-yoga, the last three knowledge-yoga — each in four grades (desire, practice, steadiness, perfection) (Yogaviṃśikā 2), culminating in meditation on the formless Siddha.

At death the yogin fixes the breath between the brows (BhG 8.10) or, closing the gates and holding the mind in the heart and the breath in the head, utters Oṃ remembering the Lord (8.12–13); Bhīṣma chooses his time and his self breaks through the crown (MBh 6.114; 13.154.5); Vidura enters Yudhiṣṭhira (15.33.25); Śuka rises by yoga (12.318–320).

name: Departure through the crown and the path to brahman

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): of the 101 channels one goes to the crown; going up by it one reaches immortality (KU 2.3.16; ChU 8.6.6); the person made of mind goes out through the indrayoni at the parting of the hair (TU 1.6); the self entered through the vidṛti (AU 1.3.12); through the suṣumṇā, joined with breath, Om and mind, one goes upward (MaiU 6.21); the path of the gods leads to the brahma-worlds from which there is no return (BAU 6.2.15).

The yogin may leave the body at will through the crown (BhP 2.2.15-21) and either be liberated at once or rise by the suṣumnā through Agni, Śiśumāra, Mahar- and Satyaloka and be liberated with Brahmā at the dissolution (2.2.22-31); the Vāyavīya also speaks of departure at will (ŚiP 7.2.37.26).

definitions.definition: No perception, however heightened, can know dharma: perception grasps only what is present, and any excellence of a sense stays within its own domain (seeing far or subtle, not hearing colours).

Cognition born of the culmination of meditation on a real object — vivid and non-conceptual; the example of those who, disturbed by desire or fear, 'see' absent things shows that cultivation produces vividness; only cultivation of the real (the four truths) makes it a means of knowledge.

name: Yogic perception and seers' knowledge

definitions.definition: The self is perceived through a special conjunction of self and mind, as are other substances (VS 9.13–17 C); yogins in concentration and out of it perceive the subtle, hidden and distant (Praśastapāda); seers' knowledge and the vision of the perfected arise from merit (VS 9.28).
The perception of one engaged in yoga arises from samādhi (NBh 1.1.3).

notes: The root texts give no warnings about such powers comparable to YS 3.37; none are recorded here.

name: Yogic powers in the epic

definitions.definition: Yogins with yoga-power enter other beings at will (MBh 12.289.24); Sulabhā enters Janaka's mind (12.308); Jaigīṣavya moves unseen between the worlds (9.49); Vidura enters Yudhiṣṭhira's body at death (15.33.25); Śuka rises into the sky (12.318–320).

notes: The epic's warnings: the path of yoga is hard and dangerous (12.289, low confidence on the exact images); the Gītā warns against self-tormenting austerities (17.5–6).

name: The Yoginī period system

definitions.definition: A 36-year cycle of eight yoginīs — Maṅgalā (1 year), Piṅgalā (2), Dhānyā (3), Bhrāmarī (4), Bhadrikā (5), Ulkā (6), Siddhā (7) and Saṅkaṭā (8) — ruled by Moon, Sun, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Saturn, Venus and Rāhu, reckoned from the birth-asterism (named in BPHS 46.10).

notes: Names and planet-assignments from memory.

definitions.definition: The yoginīs move on earth in the forms of birds and animals and seize the 'animal'; women and maidens are to be honoured and never spoken to in anger (KJN 23).

The Kaulajñānanirṇaya teaches rites with meat, fish, wine, a female partner and substances ordinarily held impure, a consecration and vessels; recorded here only in summary, with the text's own limits (no compulsion, secrecy, testing).
Meeting the yoginīs is a fruit of practice and a condition of success; at Kāmākhyā one meets them and becomes their equal (KJN 7.22; 16.8).
The Mahākaula passed from Icchā yoginī to the sky-going yoginīs, the Mothers and the earth-going yoginīs; in Kāmarūpa the scripture is in every yoginī's house (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.11-15; 22.10-12).

name: Vision limited by fitness — the warning against striving for an unfit vision

definitions.definition: One may see God only in the manner one's fitness allows; one who strives for a vision (or office) he is unfit for falls even from what he had; so service is to be rendered according to fitness.

relations.note: the limits of vision follow from intrinsic fitness

definitions.definition: The Goddess's yoni fallen at Kāmagiri is the chief seat (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42); Kāmākhyā is the great vidyā in the form of the yoni (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4); the Yoni Tantra teaches its worship (restricted, summary only).
The supreme is the primal yoni, fourfold (Kubjikāmata 11.6).

name: The youthful vase body (gzhon nu bum sku)

definitions.definition: The ground's luminosity enclosed within like light in a vase, prior to its outward display; its 'breaking open' is the emergence of ground-appearances; the fruit is the return of the ground to itself.

name: The decline of health through the ages

definitions.definition: In the first age men were long-lived and free of disease; from over-eating came heaviness, idleness, hoarding and greed; with each age a quarter of dharma is lost, the qualities of the earth decline and diseases arise; life shortens by a year every hundred years (Ca Vi 3.24-26).

name: The means proper to each age

definitions.definition: Meditation in Kṛta, sacrifice in Tretā, worship in Dvāpara, singing the name in Kali (BhP 12.3.52; VP 6.2.17).

Dharma declines by a quarter in each age and its chief form changes — austerity, knowledge, sacrifice, giving (MDh 1.81–86); each age has its code — Manu, Gautama, Śaṅkha-Likhita, Parāśara (Parāśarasmṛti 1.24); litigation arose with that decline (Nāradasmṛti Mātṛkā 1.1–2); later authorities list practices forbidden in Kali (kalivarjya).

name: The yugas and kalpa in the siddhāntas

definitions.definition: The caturyuga of 4,320,000 solar years is divided 4:3:2:1 by the feet of dharma; 71 caturyugas and a junction make a manvantara; 14 manvantaras and junctions make a kalpa of 1,000 caturyugas, a day of Brahmā, whose life is 100 years, half now passed (SS 1.15–21). definitions.definition: Using things in Kṛṣṇa's service without attachment rather than renouncing them as worldly.

name: Interfusion of one and all in the nenbutsu (yūzū)

definitions.definition: One person is all people and all people one; one practice all practices; the nenbutsu of each interfuses with all — birth by other-power.

name: The Copper-Coloured Mountain (zangs mdog dpal ri)

definitions.definition: Padmasambhava's pure land on the rākṣasa island of Cāmara, where he dwells in his palace of Lotus Light; aspired to as a place of rebirth.
Not attaching to mind or purity, not immobility; 'sitting' is non-arising of thought toward objects, 'meditation' seeing the unmoving nature; there is no time not in samādhi.
Zazen is not learning meditation but the Dharma gate of ease and joy.

name: Other-emptiness (gzhan stong)

definitions.definition: The ultimate — buddha-nature, dharmakāya, dharmatā — is empty of all adventitious conventional phenomena, which are other than it, and not empty of its own nature and qualities; it is permanent and not a dependent arising.
In Kongtrul, the Great Madhyamaka view suited to meditative experience; in Mipham, acceptable in the sense that unconditioned wisdom is empty of the adventitious while not established by own-nature.

relations.note: the two readings of how the ultimate is empty — not yet reconciled
the Jonang take RGV 1.154-155 literally as the doctrine of other-emptiness

notes: Other-emptiness is also held, each in his own form, by Shākya Chokden (Sakya; tch:shakya-chokden), the 8th Situ (tch:situ-panchen) and Jamgön Kongtrul (Rimé); only the Jonang and Rimé definitions are given here.
